TI The impact of teaching games for understanding on game performance,
   motivation, gender equality, and disruptive behaviors in physical
   education
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE disruptive behaviors; football; game performance; gender equality;
   motivation; physical education; TGfU
ID ASSESSMENT INSTRUMENT GPAI; SELF-DETERMINATION; CLIMATE; SPANISH;
   MODELS; SPORT; NEEDS
AB Introduction The aim of the present study was to analyse the effects of the Teaching Games for Understanding (TGfU) model on game performance, motivation, gender equality, and disruptive behaviors in Physical Education.Methods A quasi-experimental design was employed with a sample of 96 secondary school students, divided into an experimental group and a control group. The experimental group received a 10-session intervention program based on TGfU, while the control group continued with their regular Physical Education classes. Data collection instruments included validated questionnaires, and the Game Performance Assessment Instrument. A multivariate analysis was conducted to detect inter- and intra-group differences, considering group, time, and sex as fixed factors.Results The main findings indicated that the TGfU group improved intrinsic motivation, perceived equality, and game performance, while significantly reducing discrimination and disruptive behaviors. In the control group, irresponsibility and game participation decreased. In the findings based on sex within the experimental group, both boys and girls improved perceptions of equality and discrimination; however, only girls significantly increased intrinsic motivation, identified regulation, support, game performance, and participation.Discussion In conclusion, the TGfU program, implemented from a gender equality perspective, has proven effective in Physical Education for both genders, with particularly notable results among girls, despite the social and cultural stereotypes traditionally associated with this subject.

TI Policy analysis of artificial intelligence in social science research at
   higher education institutions: problems and possibilities
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE artificial intelligence; ethics; higher education; regulations; social
   science
AB The rapidly growing landscape of artificial intelligence and its integration in higher educational institutions of India from 2022 compelled us to cautiously analyse the changing dynamics of social science education per se. Most higher education institutions in India now allow students and researchers to use artificial intelligence. India is known as a talent superpower and according to the Stanford AI Presentation Index, it ranks first in skill penetration related to artificial intelligence. In the 2025-26 budget, India committed Indian Rupee500 crore to establish Centres of Excellence in education, marking a strategic investment to elevate academic innovation and infrastructure. Additionally, India's National Education Policy 2020 (Ministry of Human Resource Development, 2020) focuses on promoting AI and technological innovation. Given the intense push to promote technology and artificial intelligence in education, this research paper aims to analyse and evaluate the different policies impacting the usage of artificial intelligence in social science research at higher education institutions in India. The method is based on evaluating the textual content of documents by using human coding. The limitation of this research is that it is based on scanning textual documents and is limited to understanding the usage of AI in teaching and learning for the social science stream. In this process, it aims to deploy critical technology studies with the digital ethics framework. As a result of analysing the policy texts, we find that AI's invisibility is the major issue. Algorithmic bias, trained on historical data reflecting caste, class, religion, region, race and gender disparities, and plagiarism via generative tools erodes authors' dignity. Many of the detection tools are neither precise nor dependable in detecting AI usage and misuse. As educators, it is of urgent necessity to prioritise pedagogy that values human creativity, integrity and judgment. Similarly, too much dependence of Gen-Z learners on AI erodes critical thinking. This violates NEP 2020's vision of balancing innovation with ethical safeguards. Present mechanisms to regulate and monitor AI usage in higher education and in the country are fragmented and indirect. With AI deployment occurring at such a massive scale, establishing a robust India-centric regulatory framework to govern its use is no longer optional but essential.

TI Institutional support and disability awareness: lived experiences of
   secondary school teachers with visual impairments in Uzbekistan
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE interviewing; phenomenological approach; qualitative inquiry; secondary
   schools; teachers with visual impairments; Uzbekistan
ID EMPLOYMENT; WORKING
AB This phenomenological qualitative study examines workplace challenges related to institutional support and awareness among secondary school teachers with visual impairments in Uzbekistan. Participants included 20 visually impaired teachers and six school staff from Bukhara, Navoi, and Samarkand, as well as two experts from Qashqadarya and Tashkent. Analysis identified two principal themes: institutional neglect and limited disability awareness. Participants reported organisational barriers, inequitable treatment, employment insecurity, and insufficient understanding of blindness and disability legislation. The findings indicate that school-level practices significantly constrain the professional participation of teachers with visual impairments and reflect global challenges faced by teachers with disabilities. To advance inclusion, the Ministry of Preschool and School Education should intensify awareness campaigns on disability and blindness, provide staff training, develop accessible career pathways, and implement reasonable accommodations aligned with international standards.

TI Building critical GenAI literacy through mathematical error analysis
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE dual-development framework; error analysis pedagogy; GenAI literacy;
   metacognitive monitoring; quantitative reasoning
ID ERRONEOUS EXAMPLES
AB This study examined gains in undergraduate students' mathematical computation and GenAI error-detection skills following a GenAI-integrated error analysis activity in a quantitative reasoning course. An explanatory sequential mixed-methods design was employed, with pretest and posttest data analyzed quantitatively and open-ended survey responses analyzed qualitatively using thematic analysis. Quantitative results indicated statistically significant improvement in both mathematical computation (M = 2.78 to M = 6.39, d = 1.62) and GenAI error-detection skills (M = 3.61 to M = 7.72, d = 1.81), with large effect sizes for both subscales. Qualitative findings revealed that students developed independent verification habits, recognized recurring error types in the GenAI-generated solutions they analyzed across fractions, decimals, percents, and introductory algebra, and perceived their error-detection skills as transferable beyond the mathematics classroom. These preliminary findings are consistent with a dual-development framework in which mathematical reasoning and GenAI error-detection literacy may be developed simultaneously through error analysis pedagogy and establish a foundation for future larger-scale investigations of GenAI-integrated error analysis in undergraduate mathematics education.

TI Recognition and belonging: high-performing learners' experiences of
   teacher praise in South African secondary school classrooms
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE classroom management; classroom relationships; high-performing learners;
   school belonging; teacher praise
ID MOTIVATION
AB Background Teacher praise is widely regarded as a positive pedagogical strategy for strengthening learner motivation, engagement, and classroom participation. However, emerging research within South African secondary schools complicates this assumption by suggesting that praise is unevenly distributed and may contribute to differentiated learner experiences. Although these studies provide important insight into the absence of recognition, they remain largely centred on low-performing learners, leaving the experiences of high-performing learners comparatively underexplored.Objective This study examined how high-performing learners, who are typically the primary recipients of praise, experience and interpret teachers' praise practices within classroom contexts.Methods Guided by Attribution Theory and Self-Determination Theory, the study adopted an interpretive paradigm and a qualitative multiple-case study design. Data were generated through focus group discussions with 12 purposively selected high-performing learners (Grades 10-11) from two secondary schools and analysed using reflexive thematic analysis.Results The findings suggest that the learners experienced praise as a source of competence affirmation, motivation, and recognition. At the same time, some learners associated public and performance-oriented praise with pressure, peer comparison, peer tension, and perceived conditional recognition. Participants further linked praise to feelings of visibility, inclusion, and belonging within classroom contexts.Conclusion By shifting analytical attention from learners who receive limited praise to those who are frequently recognised through it, the study highlights the complex ways in which high-performing learners experience and interpret praise. The findings suggest that praise may be understood not only as a motivational strategy but also as a relational practice associated with recognition, peer relationships, and learners' sense of belonging within classroom environments.

TI Navigating academic integrity in the age of on-demand artificial
   intelligence: implications for globalizing higher education at the
   University of Ibadan
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE academic integrity; AI ethics and policy; artificial intelligence;
   globalization of education; higher education in Nigeria
AB In the context of globalizing higher education in Nigeria, this study investigates the implications of on-demand Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools on academic integrity. The study focuses on undergraduate students at the University of Ibadan, Nigeria, using a descriptive survey design. The study looks into how AI is used and how this relates to academic integrity. A multistage sampling method was used to choose 205 students from four faculties. Information regarding opinions about academic integrity and the use of AI tools for academic tasks were gathered through a structured questionnaire. At 0.05 level of significance, the Pearson Product-Moment Correlation and descriptive statistics (frequency counts, mean and standard deviation) were used to analyze the data. According to the findings, there is a strong positive correlation (r = .611, p < .05) between the prevalence of academic dishonesty and the use of AI tools. While AI tools improve learning effectiveness and access to knowledge, their unrestrained use poses serious obstacles to upholding academic standards. Especially in a higher education environment that is becoming more digitally and globally connected. Thus, the study comes to the conclusion that Nigerian universities must reconsider their frameworks for academic integrity. Particularly in light of the incorporation of AI into academic practices. The study recommends encouraging students to be AI literate by creating context-sensitive institutional policies that integrate AI ethics into the curriculum. Thereby establishing clear standards for identifying work that has been produced using AI tools. In the age of international knowledge exchange, these steps are crucial to maintaining the competitiveness, legitimacy and moral integrity of African higher education systems.

TI The role of host institutions in advancing sustainable and inclusive
   higher education internationalisation in Africa: lessons from three
   South African universities
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE digital learning; globalisation; higher education; inclusion;
   internationalisation; sustainability
AB Globalisation has increased the internationalisation of higher education across Africa; however, persistent inequalities in access, participation, and knowledge production continue to challenge the sustainability and inclusiveness of these processes. Although considerable attention has been given to internationalisation policies and cross-border collaborations, limited empirical evidence exists on how host institutions operationalise sustainable globalised higher education within African contexts. This study therefore examined the role of selected South African host institutions in advancing sustainable globalised higher education and explored how institutional practices promote inclusion, equity, and sustainability. A qualitative research approach, underpinned by a constructivist paradigm, was employed. Data were generated through one-on-one semi-structured interviews with 20 purposively selected participants representing university executive leadership, directors of international offices, academic staff, ICT specialists, and students across three public universities in South Africa. Thematic analysis was used to analyse the data. Rather than functioning as isolated initiatives, the findings revealed that host institutions advance sustainable globalised higher education through an interconnected system of institutional internationalisation strategies, curriculum innovation, digital learning and cross-border delivery, student and staff mobility support, and inclusive institutional practices. Together, these dimensions demonstrate a shift towards integrated, digitally enabled, and contextually responsive models of internationalisation that simultaneously strengthen global engagement and local relevance. The study contributes to knowledge by providing a holistic and contextually grounded understanding of how selected African universities actively shape sustainable globalisation, while extending Communities of Practice and institutional theory through evidence from African higher education. The study concludes that sustainable globalised higher education is most effectively achieved when internationalisation is embedded as an integrated institutional strategy that balances global competitiveness with inclusion, sustainability, and contextual responsiveness.

TI Can all thrive in inclusion? Teachers' prejudices and opinions regarding
   mainstreaming autistic learners
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE autism; autistic learners; mainstreaming; opinion about inclusion;
   prejudices; teachers
ID SPECTRUM DISORDERS; INCLUDING CHILDREN; ATTITUDES; EDUCATION; PUPILS;
   DISABILITIES; STRATEGIES; IMPLICIT; POLICY; US
AB Introduction Autistic learners are significantly more likely than their peers to experience prejudice, discrimination, and exclusion within mainstream educational settings. Teachers generally report insufficient training to support autistic learners, and often fear that autistic learners and/or peers may not thrive in inclusive classroom settings. Questions regarding how misconceptions and prejudices about autism influence teachers' dispositions toward mainstreaming autistic learners are yet under-explored within the Nigerian context. This study investigated the links between teachers' prejudices about autism and their opinions regarding mainstreaming autistic learners.Methods The study adopted a quantitative, predictive research design. Data were collected using the Modern and Classical Prejudices Scale (MCPS) and the Autism Inclusion Questionnaire for Teachers (AIQT) from 1,167 teachers. Descriptive statistics, Bayesian correlation, regression analysis, and hierarchical multiple regression were employed to analyze data.Results Results revealed considerable levels of modern and classical prejudices, alongside moderately negative opinions regarding autistic learners' mainstreaming. Both classical and modern prejudice significantly predicted dimensions of teachers' opinions, including core opinions, outcome expectations, and perceived impacts of mainstreaming. Among the explored demographics, teaching experience predicted opinion and moderated the relationship between prejudice and opinions.Discussion The findings suggest that prejudice substantially shapes teachers' disposition for inclusion and constitutes a significant barrier to autistic learners' mainstreaming. The study highlights the need for targeted teacher training and inclusive educational interventions for reducing prejudice and promoting more supportive educational environments for autistic learners. Overall, the study contributes to ongoing global discussions on inclusive education.

TI Curriculum innovation through artificial intelligence and its influence
   on pupils' independent learning in Azerbaijan
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE artificial intelligence in education; Azerbaijan; curriculum innovation;
   educational technology; independent learning
AB Background The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a transformative global trend in education, promising to reshape pedagogical methods and learning outcomes. This study investigates the impact of AI-based curriculum innovations on the development of independent learning skills among secondary school students (grades 9-11) within Azerbaijan's evolving educational landscape. The primary objective was to examine the mechanisms through which AI integration influences student autonomy, considering the mediating role of curriculum innovation and the moderating effect of teacher competency. Methods A cross-sectional, quantitative research design was employed. Data were collected from a sample of 1,250 students and 250 teachers across various urban secondary schools in Azerbaijan. Standardized surveys were administered to assess four key constructs: the level of AI integration in the classroom, perceptions of curriculum innovation, students' self-reported autonomous learning abilities, and teachers' AI literacy. The collected data were analyzed using correlation analysis, hierarchical regression, and the PROCESS macro for mediation and moderation analysis. Results The analysis revealed a strong, positive, and statistically significant association between AI integration and perceived curriculum innovation (beta = .55, p < .001). In turn, perceived curriculum innovation was a significant predictor of students' independent learning skills (beta = .51, p < .001). 0.26)], suggesting that AI's influence on student autonomy is substantially channelled through curriculum redesign. Furthermore, moderation analysis indicated that teachers' AI literacy significantly strengthened the positive effect of AI integration on curriculum innovation, highlighting the critical role of educator competence in this process. Conclusion he findings suggest that the strategic adoption of AI can be a powerful catalyst for fostering independent learning among secondary students. However, the effectiveness of this integration is contingent not merely on technological deployment but on a concomitant, thoughtful redesign of the curriculum and substantial investment in teacher training. This study underscores the necessity for a comprehensive policy framework in Azerbaijan that synergizes technological investment with robust professional development for educators to cultivate a new generation of independent, lifelong learners.

TI Predicting entrepreneurial competencies from cognitive and dispositional
   indicators: an elastic net regularization approach in Peruvian
   university students
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE cognitive decision making; elastic net regularization; entrepreneurial
   competencies; entrepreneurial mindset; higher education; Peru;
   predictive modeling; university students
ID SELECTION; VALIDITY; CAREER
AB Introduction Research on university entrepreneurship has concentrated on broad explanatory models of entrepreneurial intention, whereas entrepreneurial competencies have rarely been modeled as a predictable outcome. This study examined whether entrepreneurial competencies can be predicted from specific cognitive, dispositional and contextual indicators in Peruvian university students.Methods A quantitative, cross-sectional predictive design was applied to 98 Peruvian university students who completed a 28-item Likert-scale questionnaire measuring cognitive decision making, entrepreneurial mindset and entrepreneurial competencies, together with selected contextual variables. An Elastic Net regularized regression model was estimated with cross-validation and evaluated through out-of-sample performance, permutation importance and bootstrap confidence intervals.Results The model showed strong predictive accuracy in the test set (R2 = 0.797), retaining 16 relevant predictors while shrinking non-informative variables to zero. The strongest predictors belonged to the entrepreneurial mindset domain, especially anticipatory proactivity, self-efficacy to initiate ventures, opportunity seeking and perceived ability to overcome obstacles; cognitive decision-making indicators showed secondary contributions and demographic variables were negligible. The convergence between model coefficients, permutation importance and bootstrap intervals supported the robustness of the retained predictors. Supplementary psychometric diagnostics indicated inadequate fit for the proposed three-factor measurement structure and insufficient discriminant validity between entrepreneurial mindset and entrepreneurial competencies (HTMT = 0.913).Discussion The findings suggest that entrepreneurial competencies among Peruvian university students are mainly associated with action-oriented dispositions rather than demographic or curricular characteristics, and they support university interventions focused on proactivity, self-efficacy and opportunity orientation. The study introduces item-level predictive, non-causal modeling into entrepreneurship education research; given the measurement diagnostics, the results should be interpreted as exploratory prediction among closely related self-report measures rather than as evidence of fully distinct latent constructs.

TI From learners to contributors: how an AI-infused STEM program shaped
   youth identity and initiated them to an AI-future
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial Intelligence; artificial intelligence education; high school;
   informal STEM learning; machine learning; youth identity
ID WOMEN; EXPERIENCES; CAREER; COLOR; SENSE
AB The expanding role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) across society has created new demands for K-12 education to support young people in developing foundational AI literacies. Although "AI education" remains in its infancy, an emerging field is taking shape that integrates technical learning, authentic applied experiences, and ethical considerations. This study reports findings from SRMPmachine, an out-of-school-time intervention that infused machine learning (ML) literacy into a STEM workforce development program for high school students centered on scientific inquiry. SRMPmachine consisted of a 150-hour summer ML Science Institute followed by mentored scientific research internships, positioning ML as a tool for inquiry within the natural sciences. Using a mixed-methods time-series design, we analyzed survey data from 42 high school participants (hereafter, youth or participants) across three timepoints (pre-Institute, post-Institute, post-Internship) alongside retrospective interviews and research artifact analysis from a representative subset of 17 youth. Quantitative results showed significant gains in ML knowledge and skills following the Institute, with particularly strong learning growth among youth from underrepresented groups. While survey measures of attitudes and perceptions toward AI failed to detect any impact of the intervention, interviews suggested nuanced shifts toward what we describe as "informed ambivalence," characterized by increased ethical awareness, and more differentiated perspectives on AI's societal role. Participants also reported emerging self-efficacy and belonging, describing greater confidence in engaging with AI concepts and communities once they acquired the language and practices of ML. Together, these results suggest that integrating ML learning into authentic science mentorship is associated with gains in AI understanding and youths' emerging sense of themselves as future AI users and contributors.

TI Professional vision in grading student gymnastic routines - a comparison
   of noticing between pre-service teachers, probational and experienced
   physical education teachers using eye-tracking
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE attention allocation; cognitive processing; professional competence;
   teacher professionalization; visual expertise; visual strategies
ID EXPERTISE; JUDGES; PERCEPTION; ATTENTION; MOVEMENTS
AB Introduction Physical education (PE) teachers have to perceive and process information in highly dynamic, complex situations. Research on teachers' professional vision indicates differences between novice and expert teachers' noticing. However, studies in PE, assessing teachers' perception using quantitative eye-tracking, are lacking. The aim of this study is to analyse how PE teachers' perception of gymnastics movements varies by teaching experience.Method To this end, we asked pre-service teachers (n = 36), probational (n = 21) and experienced PE teachers (n = 19) without sport-specific judging experience to observe and assess videos of students' gymnastic floor routines. Gaze was recorded with a stationary eye-tracker. We compared fixation count, duration and stationary Shannon entropy (SSE) as a dispersion measure.Results Descriptive, but not statistically significant group differences were found for fixation count increase, and fixation duration decrease from groups with lowest (pre-service teachers) to the highest (experienced PE teachers) teaching experience. The analysis of SSE revealed a more dispersed fixational pattern in experienced PE teachers than probational teachers and pre-service teachers.Discussion Our study provides initial insight into differently experienced PE teachers' visual perception during noticing of gymnastic movements. The higher SSE indicates a more dynamic and dispersed fixational pattern in experienced teachers. Collectively, our pattern of findings is more in line with studies on experience differences in professional vision outside of PE and tentatively contrasts with results from experience-dependent studies on visual perception within gymnastics or other sports.

TI University support and entrepreneurial intentions: the mediating role of
   task-specific entrepreneurial self-efficacy among Chinese university
   students
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Chinese context; entrepreneurial intention; entrepreneurial
   self-efficacy; mediation effect; perceived university support;
   university students
ID EDUCATION; MODELS; BIAS
AB In the context of global higher education increasingly emphasizing competency development and social contribution, understanding how university entrepreneurship support translates into students' action readiness remains a critical yet under-theorized question. This study explores the associations between three dimensions of Perceived University Support (PUS)-Perceived Entrepreneurship Education Support (PES), Perceived Concept Development Support (PCDS), and Perceived Business Development Support (PBDS)-with university students' Entrepreneurial Intention (EI), while testing the mediating role of task-specific Entrepreneurial Self-Efficacy (ESE). Grounded in Social Cognitive Theory and the Theory of Planned Behavior, a cross-sectional online survey was conducted among 554 Chinese university students (response rate: 96.52%) utilizing a 13-item three-dimensional PUS scale, a 26-item task-specific ESE scale, and a 5-item EI scale. Confirmatory factor analysis confirmed the superiority of the three-factor PUS structure over a single-factor alternative. Mediation analysis using the PROCESS macro (Model 4) with 5,000 bootstrap resamples revealed that PES, PCDS, and PBDS each positively predicted ESE, which in turn positively predicted EI, with all indirect effects being statistically significant. The results indicate a robust partial mediation pattern. Notably, PCDS emerged as a critical developmental bridge. The findings suggest that partial mediation may reflect China-specific institutional mechanisms, such as policy-driven initiatives and honor-based incentive systems. Universities are advised to prioritize concept development support to effectively bridge the gap between classroom knowledge and commercialization.

TI Language and perception in Tagwira's (2020) novel Trapped:
   exploring the psychological, behavioural, and social dimensions of
   language bias and identity
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE cultural gender dissonance; gender equality; psycholinguistic and
   socio-linguistic landscape; quality education; schema theory; social
   identity theory
ID GENDER
AB This paper aims to uncover the psychological, behavioural, and social dimensions of language bias and identity in Tagwira's novel, Trapped. The novel was at one time prescribed as a classroom text. Set against the post-colonial Zimbabwean landscape, the study argues that language functions as a primary mechanism of both oppression and identity formation. The paper is anchored on two complementary psychological theories, social identity theory and schema theory, which illuminate the collective and individual cognitive dimensions of gendered language, respectively. Psychologically, female characters exhibit internalised inferiority and cognitive dissonance produced by structurally enforced linguistic hierarchies. Behaviourally, this manifests as a constant performance of 'gendering', whereby individuals modify their speech to mask fear or negotiate cultural identity. Socially, language serves as a tool for gender stratification, with masculinity functioning as symbolic cultural capital that systematically marginalises femininity. The study makes a dual contribution: it advances psycholinguistic and sociolinguistic analysis of postcolonial Zimbabwean fiction by demonstrating how gendered language simultaneously operates as a tool of oppression and a catalyst for identity negotiation, and it provides educators and gender stakeholders with an evidence-based framework for critically interrogating prescribed literary texts. This framework is directly relevant to advancing gender-equitable curricula in contexts where SDG 5 remains aspirational, as structural linguistic inequalities embedded in classroom texts can either hinder or help the achievement of gender equality targets.

TI "We have a say in the matter": students' voices in school
   self-evaluation
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE school autonomy; school democracy; school democratic governance; school
   self-evaluation; student participation
ID EDUCATIONAL-RESEARCH
AB School self-evaluation processes are recognized as central instruments of democratic school management and self-regulation, with significant potential to promote continuous improvement in educational quality. Within the field of educational administration, research on how student participation can be integrated into and transform these processes-thereby granting them a more democratic and emancipatory character-remains limited. This article analyzes and discusses the role of participation and student voice in the construction of school self-evaluation practices. It draws on a documentary and interpretive analysis and is complemented by qualitative data from a broader study on student participation in school governance, particularly in administrative and management bodies. The analysis of self-evaluation reports from four Portuguese schools, along with interviews with principals and teachers and focus groups with students, enabled exploration of how student participation is recognized, encouraged, and incorporated into internal evaluation processes. The results reveal different levels and types of participation, ranging from occasional consultations to active involvement in decision-making, highlighting persistent tensions between regulation-driven and accountability-oriented self-evaluation practices and more democratic, emancipatory forms of engagement. When students are heard and their perspectives valued within the school's governance and organizational practices, self-evaluation can take on a more formative, collaborative, and transformative meaning while simultaneously reinforcing collective commitment. In this sense, school self-evaluation with student participation emerges as a potentially central space for the democratic development of schools, closely linked to school improvement and student emancipation through a shared process of reflection and action.

TI Safe teaching as compensatory practice: relational potential and
   barriers for vulnerable students in European classrooms
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE attachment theory; focus groups; relational pedagogy; safe teaching;
   teacher-student relationships; vulnerable students
ID ATTACHMENT
AB This study investigates how teachers across six European countries understand and practise Safe Teaching - a set of pedagogical actions rooted in attachment theory designed to foster secure teacher-student relationships. Conducted with 90 teachers from 13 schools in Bulgaria, Italy, Lithuania, Poland, Portugal, and Spain, the research employed focus groups and two-tier content analysis within a Participatory Action Research framework. Findings indicate that teachers understand Safe Teaching as a multidimensional practice encompassing open communication, trust, structure, and individualisation, and suggest its particular compensatory potential for vulnerable students: when teachers function as secure attachment figures, the school may partially offset the absence of relational security in students' home environments. However, the study also identifies a structural obstacle to this compensatory function - a negative feedback loop in which the students who would benefit most from Safe Teaching are precisely those whose histories of insecure attachment make them most difficult to bond with. Additional findings include the centrality of teacher authenticity and socio-emotional competence as internal drivers, and the indispensable role of collegial, family, and institutional support as external conditions. The results underscore the need for targeted professional development and school cultures that deliberately sustain teachers' capacity to provide relational security, particularly where that capacity is most tested.

TI Effectiveness of a multidimensional competency-based training program
   for enhancing clinical competence in novice nurses: A mixed-methods
   study
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Novice nurses; Competency-based medical education; Multidimensional
   competency-based approach; Professional confidence; Passion for nursing
AB Background The transition to competency is challenging for novice nurses, often leading to stress and turnover. Nurse residency programs enhance clinical skills and improve retention. Competency-Based Education (CBE) advances nurses' development through patient-centered care, critical thinking, and accountability. CBE's competency-driven objectives facilitate effective mentorship. Multidimensional training fosters collaboration and inclusivity, strengthening learning and professional relationships. Objectives This study aimed to develop a multidimensional competency-based approach, highlighting how individualized repeated practice, targeted feedback, and dynamic preceptor-learner interactions enhance skill development and competency acquisition. It evaluated the clinical competence, professional confidence, and passion for nursing of novice nursing practitioners. Design Mixed methods approach. Methods A qualitative descriptive approach with monthly facilitated group discussions explored novice nurses' perceptions of patient care needs and barriers. Findings informed the design of a tailored, multidimensional six-month training program. The program featured interactive sessions with faculty guidance and incorporated classroom instruction, simulated teaching, hands-on practice, and reflective exercises. Professional competence, confidence, passion for nursing, and perceived healthcare team support were assessed quantitatively before and after the intervention. Results A total of one hundred and eighty-three participants were recruited. Quantitative results demonstrated significant improvements in professional competence, confidence, passion for nursing, and perceived healthcare team support (p < 0.05). Qualitative findings indicated that simulation-based learning and structured team support enhanced nurses' confidence, clinical care capability, and engagement. Participants reported high satisfaction with clinical skills simulators and perceived healthcare team support as essential. All participants who completed the program-maintained employment at the one-year follow-up assessment, yielding a 100% retention rate. Conclusions The multidimensional competency-based education program significantly improved novice nurses' clinical competency, professional confidence, and passion. Tailored multidimensional training is essential to prepare novice nurses to tackle clinical challenges and build resilience.

TI Construction of an entry-to-practice competency evaluation index system
   for public health nurses in China: A Delphi study
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Public health nurse; Competency; Evaluation index system
AB Background: Public health nurses (PHNs) play a key role in health promotion, infectious disease control, policy development, and emergency response. In China, specialized PHN training has not yet been established, highlighting the need for a competency evaluation system. Objective: To construct a competency evaluation index system for PHNs to guide future training and assessment in China. Design: A two-round Delphi study based on the Iceberg Competency Model. Participants: A panel of 27 experts (associate senior level or above) in community nursing practice, management, education, or public health was recruited from seven cities across China. Methods: A preliminary indicator system was developed through literature review and semi-structured interviews with 17 community nurses and 15 public health physicians. Two Delphi rounds were then conducted with the 27 experts, who rated indicator importance and provided revision suggestions. Indicators were retained if importance mean > 3.5 and coefficient of variation <0.25. Results: Both rounds achieved a 100% effective response rate, with an expert authority coefficient of 0.90. Kendall's W coefficients were 0.518 for the first round and 0.628 for the second (both P < 0.001). The final system comprised 4 first-level, 19 second-level, and 80 third-level indicators. Conclusions: The PHN competency evaluation index system is structured around four overarching domains, namely professional knowledge, professional skills, professional competence, and professional qualities. It demonstrates methodological rigor, thereby offering a standardized and actionable framework for competency assessment, personnel training, and workforce development in China, and ultimately contributing to enhanced public health service quality.

Contribution: The study concludes that reinforcing basic algebraic concepts and using varied teaching strategies can enhance learners' comprehension of trigonometric equations.

AB Background: South Africa's commitment to mother tongue-based bilingual education (MTBBE) depends not on language policy but on teachers' capacity for early reading instruction in indigenous African languages. TI Development and Validation of National Learning Milestones for
   Postgraduate Pharmacist Training: A Consensus Study
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PHARMACEUTICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Competency-based medical education; Pharmacy education; Postgraduate
   year training; Learning milestones; Consensus development
ID GUIDE
AB Objective: Nationally calibrated learning milestone frameworks have not been reported for pharmacists. Therefore, we aimed to develop and validate a national pharmacist learning milestone framework for Taiwan's 2-year postgraduate year training program using a structured, consensus-driven methodology. Methods: This national consensus study comprised 23 certified pharmacist educators from representative teaching hospitals. These educators participated in 8 structured focus group discussions between October and December 2024. Each session involved standardized facilitation procedures, an >= 80% agreement threshold, and anonymous real-time voting. The resulting milestone framework was validated by 115 clinical preceptors through a structured survey that assessed content relevance and clarity using 4-point Likert scales. For each milestone, respondents independently assigned an appropriate performance level (Levels 1-5). Quantitative analyzes included descriptive statistics and Content Validity Index calculations supplemented by qualitative feedback for iterative refinement. Results: The finalized framework comprised 15 subcompetencies and 143 milestones across 5 proficiency levels, with Level 4 (proficient) designated as the expected outcome at completion of postgraduate year training. The consensus process resulted in 55 revisions, 4 performance-level adjustments, 24 deletions, and 11 additions. The findings from the validation revealed strong content relevance (Content Validity Index 0.70-1.00) and high concordance in performance-level assignment (>= 75% agreement). Conclusion: To the best of our knowledge, this study is the first to establish and validate a national pharmacist learning milestone framework in Taiwan. The rigorous consensus and validation processes ensured contextual relevance, strengthened educator engagement, and offered a scalable model for implementing competency-based pharmacy education.

TI Using CoI to Address Emerging Problems in Academic Pharmacy
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PHARMACEUTICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Community of inquiry; Standardized exams; Community of practice; Social
   learning; Crowdsource
ID PROFESSIONAL-DEVELOPMENT; COMMUNITY
AB Pharmacy education is currently facing numerous challenges, such as concerning first-time pass rates on licensure examinations, decreasing applicant pools, new accreditation standards, progression concerns, and changing financial and regulatory landscapes. These complex and shared issues require collaborative and innovative approaches across the Academy. One potential strategy is the development of Communities of Inquiry (CoI), a collaborative model grounded in Garrison and colleagues' theoretical framework of social, cognitive, and teaching presence. CoI emphasize active engagement, shared problem-solving, reflective discourse, and collective responsibility for learning and innovation. This manuscript describes the theoretical foundation of the CoI model and its application within pharmacy academia. Existing applications of CoI principles in the pharmacy education literature, including faculty development initiatives and webinar-based learning experiences, are also reviewed. Additionally, a real-world example of a successful CoI is presented through the development of a North American Pharmacist Licensure Examination (NAPLEX) Preparation CoI. CoI represent an effective framework for addressing new challenges in pharmacy education. Faculty, administrators, and professional organizations are encouraged to establish and participate in CoIs. As pharmacy education continues to evolve, the CoI approach presents a promising strategy for fostering innovation, meeting accreditation standards, and enhancing student outcomes through community-driven solutions.

TI Agency for Sustainability in Pharmacy Education: Perspectives From
   Senior Bachelor Students in Qatar
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PHARMACEUTICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Sustainability; Pharmacy education; Human agency; Health professions
   education
ID QUALITATIVE RESEARCH
AB Objective: Sustainability is increasingly being discussed in pharmacy education. This study explores how senior bachelor's degree pharmacy students conceptualize sustainability within pharmacy practice, how they perceive their agency to enact sustainability in their roles, and what contextual factors exist to enable or constrain their agency for sustainability. Methods: A qualitative research design was employed. Purposive sampling was used to recruit senior bachelor's pharmacy students enrolled in their final year of study (n = 10). Semi-structured interviews were analyzed using thematic analysis, drawing on Bandura's theory of human agency as an interpretive lens. Results: Participants conceptualized sustainability as a multidimensional professional responsibility that encompasses environmental stewardship, patient care, and medicines optimization. Students expressed valuedriven intentionality by emphasizing responsible prescribing, waste reduction, and patient education. However, agency for sustainability was perceived as being constrained by factors such as curricular invisibility, limited experiential exposure, and pressure from the health care system. Sustainability emerged as part of students' professional identity but lacked consistent institutional reinforcement. Conclusion: Senior bachelor pharmacy students view sustainability as aligned with professional responsibility, yet structural and educational gaps may limit the enactment of sustainability. Embedding sustainability longitudinally within pharmacy curricula and practical training opportunities may strengthen agency and identity integration, which prepares graduates for environmentally responsible practices within complex health care systems.

TI Self-Regulated Learning Behavior Clusters Associated With NAPLEX
   Readiness Exam Performance During Advanced Pharmacy Practice Experiences
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PHARMACEUTICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE NAPLEX; Pharmacy education; Licensure readiness exam; Learning
   strategies
ID STRATEGY INVENTORY
AB Objective: Declining North American Pharmacist Licensure Examination (NAPLEX) pass rates have raised concerns, prompting pharmacy programs to administer readiness exams that guide students' self-preparation. The objective of this research is to examine the association between self-regulated learning behavior clusters and performance on a NAPLEX readiness examination during Advanced Pharmacy Practice Experiences (APPEs). Methods: This retrospective observational cohort study surveyed final-year PharmD students enrolled in a required NAPLEX readiness course during APPEs (August 2022-May 2024). Students completed an anonymous survey assessing demographics, external factors, and self-regulated learning behaviors using a modified Self-Regulation Strategy Inventory-Self-Report. NAPLEX readiness and NAPLEX readiness remediation examination performance were collected. Individual study behaviors and conceptually grouped behavioral clusters were evaluated for associations with readiness exam performance using correlation analyses and exploratory regression models. Results: Forty-eight of 105 eligible students completed the survey. A higher pre-APPE grade point average was moderately correlated with readiness exam performance. External factors, including work hours, commuting time, caregiving responsibilities, and total reported study time, were not associated with exam success. Several individual self-regulated learning behaviors were associated with higher readiness exam scores, including environmental control, planning, persistence, help-seeking, and avoidance of last-minute studying. When evaluated as integrated clusters, such as planning, organization, environmental control, persistence, help-seeking, and avoidance of last-minute studying, they demonstrated substantially stronger associations than individual behaviors alone. Conclusion: Clusters of self-regulated learning behaviors show stronger associations with NAPLEX readiness exam performance than isolated study strategies. These findings suggest that academic coaching should emphasize bundled self-regulation strategies rather than isolated techniques to support licensure readiness.

TI "Dialogue with texts" and the fusion of horizons: A hermeneutic approach
   to L2 learner engagement with written corrective feedback
SO ASSESSING WRITING
LA English
DT Article
DE Written feedback; L2 writing; Learner engagement; Hermeneutics;
   Positivism; Chinese as a second language
ID INDIVIDUAL-DIFFERENCES; STUDENT ENGAGEMENT; TEACHER; BELIEFS
AB While written corrective feedback (WCF) intends to support L2 writing, learners do not always respond to feedback as expected. This raises questions about how learner engagement with WCF should be understood. Existing research mainly adopts a positivist approach, assessing engagement in cognitive, behavioural, and affective dimensions to account for learners' responses to WCF. In this study, we adopt a hermeneutic approach, conceptualizing learner engagement with WCF as a "dialogue with texts." We consider WCF as a textual message through which the teacher conveys desired features of L2 writing to the learner, inviting the learner to engage in a dialogue in a written form. Based on a multiple case study of learners of Chinese as a second language, we compare positivist and hermeneutic analyses of the same dataset on the participants' engagement with WCF. We demonstrate how a hermeneutic approach interprets a particular response to WCF as part of the learner's broader horizon of L2 writing, including their background beliefs of writing, learning, and writer identity. By positioning learners as active participants who can justify their purposes through reason, rather than mere passive products of psychological causes, the hermeneutic approach seeks to illuminate L2 writing pedagogy with transformative potential for learner development.

TI Human-AI feedback ecologies in L2 writing: A Q-methodological study of
   evaluation, positioning, and regulation
SO COMPUTERS AND COMPOSITION
LA English
DT Article
DE AI-generated feedback; Feedback engagement; Human-AI feedback ecologies;
   L2 writing; Q methodology; Self-regulated learning
AB The increasing use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in writing instruction has expanded the range of feedback sources available to learners, creating human-AI feedback ecologies in which AI-generated and teacher feedback coexist. In these environments, learners actively evaluate, position, and regulate multiple sources of feedback during writing. Despite growing research on AI-generated feedback, limited attention has been paid to how learners make sense of AI feedback in relation to teacher authority and self-regulated writing practices. This study investigates how learners engage with and position AI-generated feedback in L2 writing contexts. Using Q methodology, data were collected from 40 Chinese learners of Thai as a foreign language who sorted statements reflecting diverse experiences with AI- and teacher-mediated feedback. Analysis identified four learner orientations toward AI feedback: (1) Evaluative Reliance with Teacher Anchoring, (2) Instructionally Aligned Use of AI Feedback, (3) Affective-Relational Engagement with AI Feedback, and (4) Instrumental Use with Epistemic Distance. The findings show that engagement with AI feedback is shaped less by trust than by how learners evaluate, position, and regulate feedback across writing activities. The study advances a human-AI feedback ecology framework and offers implications for AI-supported writing pedagogy and feedback design.

TI Gen-Mentor: A human-in-the-loop instructional framework for dental
   radiography using generative AI
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
LA English
DT Article
DE Dental radiograph analysis; Vision language model; Educational AI
AB Integrating artificial intelligence into medical imaging offers potential for dental education. While existing models automate diagnosis, they often lack the interpretive depth needed for comprehensive student training. To address these limitations, this paper presents Gen-Mentor, a human-in-the-loop instructional framework that integrates the DentDiff-VLM backbone into a dental-radiography workflow. The backbone uses Faster R-CNN to localize four target radiographic findings: Filling, Implant, Impacted Tooth, and Cavity. A conditional diffusion model supports curriculum expansion by generating class-specific synthetic ROI candidates as candidate instructional assets. The framework achieved a mean System Usability Scale score of 72.7, with improvements in case diversity and immediate-feedback support.

TI I hear you: Enhancing middle school mathematics engagement and learning
   outcomes through teachable agent voice design
SO COMPUTERS & EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence; Teachable agent; Voice design; Middle school
   math education
ID SELF-DETERMINATION; KNOWLEDGE
AB Generative AI-powered teachable agents offer new opportunities in mathematics education, yet systematic investigations of how vocal design affects middle school students' engagement and learning outcomes remain limited. We conducted a three-week 2 & times; 2 & times; 3 factorial randomized controlled experiment with 386 middle school students, systematically manipulating three vocal attributes of a generative AI-powered teachable agent: gender congruence (avatar-voice matching vs. mismatching), voice age (youth vs. adult), and emotional tone (sad, calm, cheerful). Engagement was assessed through behavioral coding of ten interaction categories and temporal analysis of dialogue sequences, while learning gains were measured through standardized state mathematics assessments. Analyses employed generalized estimating equations for factorial effects, time-series feature extraction for temporal dynamics, and machine learning models with SHAP-based feature importance for outcome prediction. Results revealed a theoretically significant dissociation between vocal configurations that activate immediate teaching behaviors and those that support long-term achievement. Empathy-evoking, identity-neutral configurations combining gender-mismatched and sad voices significantly enhanced immediate generative processing, including conceptual knowledge demonstration ((3 = 0.776), answer-giving behaviors, and explanatory responses. Conversely, schema-congruent, approachable configurations combining gender-matched and cheerful voices yielded the highest standardized learning gains ((3 = 0.997) and also significantly enhanced conceptual knowledge demonstration ((3 = 0.722), supporting sustained engagement over time. Time-series analysis confirmed that sad emotional tone maintained higher peak and overall levels of instructional behaviors across dialogue sequences. Feature importance analysis identified frustration management as the strongest predictor of standardized learning gains, while explanatory behaviors most strongly predicted conceptual knowledge demonstration. Voice age manipulations showed no significant effects. These findings demonstrate that strategically designed vocal attributes configuring multiple voice dimensions simultaneously activate learning-by-teaching processes more effectively than single-dimensional features. Practically, this means using sad tones with gender-mismatched voices to activate immediate teaching behaviors, and cheerful tones with gender-matched voices to sustain long-term achievement. Future research should explore adaptive designs that transition between these configurations based on learning phases.

TI Comparison of summative assessments between simulated electronic health
   records versus traditional paper-based patient cases: A non-inferiority
   randomized controlled trial
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Electronic health records; Pharmacy; Education; Summative assessment;
   Randomized controlled trial; High fidelity simulation training
AB Introduction: Electronic health records are fundamental to contemporary pharmacy practice, yet evidence supporting their use in pharmacy education is lacking. This single-center, non-inferiority randomized controlled trial with blinded outcome assessment evaluated whether delivering patient cases via a simulated academic EHR (aEHR) was non-inferior to a traditional paper-based format in student exam performance. Methods: 53 third-year PharmD students at the University of British Columbia were randomized 1:1 to complete a mock summative examination using either the aEHR or paper-based case delivery, stratified by self-reported EHR comfort level. The primary outcome was mean written exam score (%). Non-inferiority was pre-specified at a margin of 14%. Adjusted linear regression was used for the primary analysis, with a multiple imputation sensitivity analysis. Student perceptions were explored through post-exam focus groups analyzed using inductive thematic analysis. Results: 42 students (21 per group) completed the exam and were included in the primary analysis. Mean scores were 66% (SD 11) in the aEHR group and 68% (SD 10) in the paper group. The adjusted mean difference (paper minus aEHR) was-2.2% (95% CI-9.2% to +4.8%), satisfying non-inferiority but not superiority. Sensitivity analysis (n = 53) yielded consistent results (-2.3%; 95% CI-7.1% to +4.1%). Focus groups revealed initial student anxiety with the aEHR but recognized its alignment with clinical practice. Discussion: These findings support the feasibility of integrating simulated EHRs into summative pharmacy assessments without compromising performance. Conclusion: Simulated EHRs are a non-inferior assessment medium compared with paper-based formats and represent a viable step toward technology-driven pharmacy practice environments.

TI The effects of structural visualization methods on student performance
   in mathematics word problems: an eye-tracking analysis
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
DE Structural visualization; Tabular representation; Segmentation;
   Mathematics word problem; Problem solving; Eye-movement
ID SEGMENTATION; TEXT; DIFFICULTY; ATTENTION; DIAGRAM
AB Mathematical word problem solving is central to developing students' mathematical reasoning and problem-solving competence. However, students often experience difficulties in extracting relevant information and representing relationships when solving lengthy word problems. Although previous studies have examined various visualization approaches, less is known about how the internal organizational structure of textual information can be optimized to support mathematical problem solving. This study investigated the effects of two structural visualization approaches-text segmentation and tabular representation-on students' cognitive load, attention allocation, and problem-solving performance in mathematics word problems. A 2 (problem presentation: non-segmented vs. segmented text) & times; 2 (problem analysis: text-based vs. tablebased representation) between-subjects experimental design was adopted. Eye-tracking data and learning performance data were collected from 131 eighth-grade students. The results showed that students in the structural visualization conditions reported lower extraneous and intrinsic cognitive load, higher germane cognitive load, greater visual attention to key information, and better problem-solving performance than those in the non-structural conditions. These findings suggest that structural visualization through text segmentation and tabular representation can facilitate students' processing of lengthy mathematics word problems involving systems of linear equations with two variables. The study highlights the value of organizing textual information structurally to support attention guidance, cognitive load management, and mathematical problem solving.

TI An empirical study of ChatGPT use in engineering education: Prompting
   and performance
SO INTERNET AND HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE AI; ChatGPT; Prompt engineering; Engineering education; Academic
   performance; Learning analytics; Human-AI interaction
ID INSTRUCTIONAL-DESIGN; SYNTACTIC COMPLEXITY; ENGAGEMENT; FRAMEWORK
AB This study investigates how specific prompting behaviors influence the academic performance of engineering students using ChatGPT. A total of 128 fourth-year students across four engineering programs participated in weekly sessions involving rotating task types: case analysis, engineering design, multi-step problem-solving, and experimental data analysis. A Python-based interface connected students to ChatGPT-4o via the API, logging all interactions and implementing stratified randomization of AI access across the 16-week semester. Written assignments were used for both grading and analyzing AI content integration. Ten metrics were designed to capture student behaviors-eight focusing on prompting (AI Query Count, Query Depth and Structure, Query Efficiency, Prompt Refinement Depth, Response Utility, Response Complexity, Response Reliance, and AI-Driven ProblemSolving) and two assessing writing quality (Structural Complexity Score and Content Richness and Information Density Score). Inter-metric analysis examined how these behaviors related to one another and to academic performance. Results showed that AI Query Efficiency, which reflects how effectively students crafted clear, wellstructured prompts, and AI-Driven Problem-Solving, which captures how strategically they integrated AI output into their reasoning, were the strongest predictors of academic success. These findings were supported by Mann-Whitney U tests comparing AI and non-AI groups, as well as Spearman correlations, Random Forest regressors, partial dependence plots, principal component analysis, and mixed-effects modeling, and remained significant even after accounting for students' cumulative GPA. The results suggest that prompting strategy plays a meaningful role in shaping how effectively students use AI in engineering education.

TI The double-edged sword effect of AI use on college students' learning
   engagement
SO INTERNET AND HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE AI use; Learning engagement; Information literacy self-efficacy;
   Learning inertia; Teacher's AI symbolization
AB With the growing prevalence of AI-assisted learning, there has been little research that investigated the intricate impacts of AI use on students' learning. In response to this research gap, this paper based on the Self-efficacy Theory, respectively analyzes the double-edged sword effect of AI use on college students' learning engagement by strengthening information literacy self-efficacy and activating learning inertia, as well as the moderating role of teacher's AI symbolization. Through a three-stage questionnaire survey among 452 college students, the results show that: first, AI use promotes college students to increase their learning engagement through its positive impact on information literacy self-efficacy. However, AI use leads to a reduction in learning engagement by inducing learning inertia, and the impact of AI use on learning inertia is more significant. Second, teacher's AI symbolization positively moderates the relationship between AI use and information literacy selfefficacy, and also significantly moderates the indirect effect of AI use on college students' learning engagement through information literacy self-efficacy. The results provide meaningful theoretical insights and practical implications for advancing AI applications in higher education.

TI Artificial intelligence in nursing education: A contemporary issue for
   ethical, safe, and human-centered curriculum reform
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence; Nursing education; Curriculum; Ethics; Clinical
   reasoning; Confidentiality; Generative AI; Patient safety
AB There is a growing acceptance of using artificial intelligence in health care, education, and clinical practice. Artificial intelligence will be used in learning personalization, clinical case design, simulations, academic writing, and feedback to the learner. However, there is a gap in the readiness of students, instructors, curriculum, and standards for safe patient care because of the rapid development of such technology. Artificial intelligence should be viewed as more than simply a threat to digital literacy and academic integrity as highlighted in this Contemporary Issues article. In practice, nurses have to understand how to safely use artificial intelligence, since artificial intelligence should be considered to be an essential component of nursing education, ethics, and practice. Its unique contribution is a three-level accountability system that connects epistemic accountability (verification and clinical reasoning), relational accountability (compassionate, person-centered care), and professional responsibility (ethics, governance, and transparency). This article within this paradigm identifies four nursing curriculum priorities: artificial intelligence literacy, assessment redesign, ethical governance, and faculty development, all of which have consequences for educators, institutional leaders, and legislators.

TI "That's my brother": Perceptions of future involvement among Latino and
   non-Latino youth siblings of autistic individuals
SO RESEARCH IN DEVELOPMENTAL DISABILITIES
LA English
DT Article
DE Siblings; Future planning; Autism; Family; Caregiver; Latino;
   Qualitative research
ID ADULT SIBLINGS; DEVELOPMENTAL-DISABILITIES; MENTAL-RETARDATION;
   GROWING-UP; EXPERIENCES; CHILDREN; FAMILIES; PARENT
AB Purpose: Throughout their youth, non-autistic siblings of autistic individuals may begin considering their involvement in their autistic sibling's life, which may affect their well-being. However, there is little research on how expectations for future involvement differ across cultures. Understanding why and how youth siblings' expectations manifest may inform the design of family interventions that are appropriate for culturally-diverse samples. The present analysis examines how Latino and non-Latino youth siblings perceive their future supportive roles in their autistic sibling's life. Methods: Semi-structured qualitative interviews were conducted in English with 12 Latino and 9 non-Latino youth siblings (N = 21). Eligible families had at least one child diagnosed with autism and a non-autistic sibling between 8 and 17 years old. Audio-recorded interviews were transcribed verbatim and coded using a coding structure. Data were analyzed using applied thematic analysis and were both analyzed in aggregate and stratified by ethnic background. Results: Two themes were identified: 1) expectations of evolving sibling roles and responsibilities into adulthood shape siblings' visions of their future involvement and 2) without family support, anxiety about the future pushes siblings into action or avoidance. Driven by a sense of duty, Latino siblings were more certain of a support role in their autistic sibling's life. Non-Latino siblings expressed more uncertainty and variability in their expectations for a future support role, feeling conflicted between prioritizing their autistic sibling or future family. Conclusion: These themes are consistent with literature emphasizing how cultural values, such as familism and individualism, shape caregiving attitudes and expectations. These findings may inform the design of culturally-responsive family interventions.

TI Assessing computational thinking and creativity skills in games
   developed by autistic youth in online game design and employment
   workshops
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Computational thinking; Creativity; Video game design; Engagement;
   Autistic youth; Online workshops
ID SELF-EFFICACY; EDUCATION; RELIABILITY; DIFFERENCE; VALIDITY; STATE; K-12
AB Computational thinking (CT) and creativity have been identified as key skills for the 21st century workplace. Creativity has also been described as an aspect of CT by some researchers. However, the vast majority of computational thinking measures overlook both creativity and the cognitive diversity that supports it, e.g., neurodiversity. The omission of students with disabilities from most research supporting the validity and reliability of computational thinking measures limits both educators' ability to support neurodivergent students in developing and expressing skills that could help them get jobs and our understanding of computational thinking. This omission may be particularly limiting for Autistic students, who often have skills compatible with careers where computational thinking is particularly needed, yet face pronounced barriers getting jobs. Multi-method approaches to assessing computational thinking that include Autistic students are needed to improve the validity and reliability of computational thinking assessments. We qualitatively coded video games produced by 28 Autistic students enrolled in one of two Game Design and Employment workshops, comparing the quality and quantity of elements in their games (ecologically valid indicators of their computational thinking and creativity skills) to their scores on computational thinking and creativity assessments. Game creativity was operationalised by assessing the flexibility and fluency of elements in students' games. General creative potential was assessed using the alternative uses task (AUT). We used abbreviated versions of two commonly used CT tasks, the Computational Thinking Abilities -Middle Grades Assessment (CTAM) and Exploring Computer Science Unit 4 (ECS), to assess CT. We also examined if creativity and CT were associated with game design self-efficacy, student-reported engagement with workshop activities, and fluid reasoning. CT and AUT scores were associated with the creativity of the students' games. The abbreviated CTA-M was more consistently related with games than the abbreviated ECS and more internally consistent. Student-reported engagement with self-advocacy and feedback activities was associated with game creativity. Cognitive skills were associated with the CTA-M but not games. Findings suggest a need to design and assess computational thinking measures that capture both its cognitive and its potential affective and creative aspects.

TI Commentary: Reframing curricular toolkits as enablers of intentionality,
   prioritization, and academic freedom in pharmacy education
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Curricular assessment; Curricular design; Toolkits
AB Curricular overload remains a persistent and widely recognized challenge in pharmacy education. Faculty often acknowledge the need for a more streamlined curriculum; however, they frequently disagree on which content should be reduced, integrated, or removed, making meaningful consensus difficult. Standardized curricular toolkits offer a structured approach to guide discussions, challenge assumptions, and support deliberate prioritization. When used as flexible, faculty governed decision support tools, they position pharmacy programs to address curricular overload sustainably while strengthening the relevance of pharmacy curricula and improving the educational experience for students and faculty. Rather than constraining pharmacy education, intentionally implemented toolkits can empower it. Pharmacy programs are encouraged to integrate toolkits into their curricular assessment and design processes to support thoughtful, evidence-informed curriculum decisions.

TI Examining theConsistency of Nature of Science inChemistry Curriculum
   Standard and Textbook: An Epistemic Network Analysis
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Chemistry Curriculum Standard; Textbook; Natureof Science; Family
   Resemblance Approach; ChemicalEducational Research
ID STUDENTS VIEWS; CONCEPTIONS
AB Nature of science (NOS) is a core component of scientific literacy and has been integrated into China's junior secondary chemistry curriculum standards. This study analyzes the representations of NOS in the Curriculum Standard and the PEP Textbook and examines the consistency between them. Using the reconceptualized family resemblance approach (RFN) and epistemic network analysis (ENA), the study compares NOS representations across documents. Results showed broad consistency in frequency distribution, with the cognitive-epistemic system appearing more frequently than the social-institutional system in both documents. However, structural differences were observed between the two documents. The Curriculum Standard presented a densely interconnected network, particularly among Scientific Knowledge, Methods, and Scientific Ethos, while the textbook shifted focus toward Aims and Values, with weaker ties to Methods and Ethos. Implications for textbook writers, teachers, and curriculum developers are discussed.

TI Improving Pain Literacy Among Future Educators: Contemporary Pain
   Neuroscience Education in Teacher Preparation
SO JOURNAL OF SCHOOL HEALTH
LA English
DT Article
DE adolescent health; chronic pain; pain literacy; pain neuroscience
   education; school health; teacher education
ID MUSCULOSKELETAL PAIN; PRESCRIPTION OPIOIDS; HEALTH LITERACY;
   ADOLESCENCE; KNOWLEDGE
AB Background: Persistent pain affects approximately one in five children and adolescents globally and is associated with school absenteeism, reduced academic engagement, psychosocial distress, and long-term health consequences. Schools are important settings for developing health beliefs and self-management behaviors, yet educators receive little formal preparation about pain. Contributions to Practice: This Practitioner's Perspective describes integration of a brief contemporary pain neuroscience education (CPNE) module into an undergraduate teacher preparation course. Two interactive sessions delivered by a physical therapist introduced pain as a protective nervous system output influenced by biological, psychological, and social factors. Participants demonstrated improved pain knowledge and beliefs, increased confidence discussing pain-related concepts, and greater appreciation for the relevance of pain literacy to educational practice. Implications for School Health Policy, Practice, and Equity: Pain literacy may improve educator responses to student pain, reduce stigma, support appropriate participation, and promote equitable school environments. Physical therapists may be well positioned to collaborate with teachers, school nurses, counselors, coaches, and other school-based professionals. Conclusions: Teacher preparation programs may represent an upstream opportunity to improve pain literacy, support student health and learning, and contribute to the prevention of persistent pain.

TI Balancing national language policy and classroom realities: teachers'
   negotiations of multilingualism in Turkish schools
SO LANGUAGE POLICY
LA English
DT Article
DE Language policy; Teacher agency; Translanguaging; Multilingual
   education; T & uuml;rkiye
AB This study aims to explore how teachers in Turkish state schools negotiate between national (monolingual) language policy and multilingual classroom practice. T & uuml;rkiye requires that instruction be conducted only in Turkish, and English is the first foreign language to be taught according to a "compulsory-instruction-only" strategy. But many classrooms include students who speak Kurdish, Arabic, or other minority languages as well as Syrian refugee children, making them rich multilingual environments that defy the prescriptions of policy. Informed by three research questions-how teachers' interpretations of policy shape their teaching practice, what multilingual practices teachers enact, and how they rationalize or legitimate these practices-the study assumes a qualitative case study design. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews with 118 teachers, classroom observations of 40 teachers, and document analysis of the Ministry of National Education policies and curricula. Document analysis corroborated that minority and refugee languages are seldom pointed out in official guidelines. The paper foregrounds the role of teachers in shaping multilingual education. It implies flexible policies, teacher training in multilingual pedagogy, and explicit recognition of minority languages. Treating the Turkish case in relation to transnational discussions of language policy and multilingualism, this article participates in recontextualizing national planning for such societies.

TI Spoken language delay in toddlerhood predicts late childhood language
   outcomes in dyslexia: evidence from retrospective parent-report
SO ANNALS OF DYSLEXIA
LA English
DT Article
DE Literacy; Language delay; Language milestones; Reading; Specific
   learning disorder; Late-talking; Dyslexia
ID READING-RELATED SKILLS; LATE-TALKING TODDLERS; SCHOOL-AGE LANGUAGE;
   DEVELOPMENTAL DYSLEXIA; FAMILIAL RISK; CHILDREN; IMPAIRMENT; DEFICITS;
   LITERACY; COMORBIDITY
AB Some children are slower than average to acquire early spoken language milestones. Little is known about how this heterogeneity in expressive language impacts later childhood language and reading outcomes in children with dyslexia. We investigated oral language and reading differences in 63 children with dyslexia aged 8-12 years, comparing those with (35%) and without (65%) a prior history of delayed two-word phrase production (beyond 24 months of age). All children subsequently acquired fluent spoken language. Language outcome measures included standardized tests of current sound awareness, rapid picture naming, memory for words, and sentence repetition. Current single word and paragraph reading abilities were measured using standardized timed and untimed tests. Results indicated that both groups showed comparable single word and paragraph reading performance in middle childhood. Those with early spoken language delay had poorer sentence repetition and memory for words than those who used two-word phrases by 24-months. Our findings point to distinct language contributions to dyslexia in children with and without a history of early spoken language acquisition difficulties, underscoring the importance of considering early language milestones in this population.
