TI The guidance officer as 'middle ground' : charting the positioning and
   positionalities of guidance officers in Queensland schools
SO AUSTRALIAN EDUCATIONAL RESEARCHER
LA English
DT Article
DE Guidance officers; School counsellors; Middle ground; Student support;
   Inclusive schools; School culture
AB Working at the intersection of student counselling, case management, school-wide wellbeing coordination and support programming, guidance officers assume a specialised presence in schools, maintaining responsibility for some of the most complex and challenging of circumstances in student support. Yet, and despite the responsibilities and quantum of work that guidance officers bear, it occurs that guidance officers typically work individually or in small, specialised teams. Occupying this 'middle ground' of specialised practice and close engagement with students generates specific pressures that demonstrate the complexities inherent to guidance work. TI Strategies for Greater Inclusion of Indigenous Students in College
   Science Programs
SO BIOCHEMISTRY AND MOLECULAR BIOLOGY EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Alaska Natives; equity; Indigenous students; Native Americans; Native
   Hawai'ians; underrepresentation
ID LAND-GRAB-UNIVERSITIES; PARTICIPATION; RETENTION; KNOWLEDGE; MODEL
AB The substantial underrepresentation of American Indian, Alaskan Native, and Native Hawai'ian (AI/AN/NH) students in Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM) majors at United States colleges and universities results from systemic barriers in higher education. Efforts to address inequities have thus far not led to increases in AI/AN/NH student participation in STEM at the national level. In fact, while the AI/AN/NH population in the United States is increasing, there was a 17.0% decrease in the number of bachelor's degrees awarded to Indigenous students in STEM during the period 2012-2021. This work reports on steps that can be taken in a variety of types of institutions of higher education to serve our Native students in STEM more effectively. These steps are reported as a series of rationales, followed by practical descriptions of implementations. Ideas for enhancing the Indigenous experience in the academy, together with examples of successful programs, are detailed. These include raising faculty and institutional cultural competency, addressing inequities in college preparation within the K-12 system, making college STEM courses more inclusive, improving one-on-one advising and mentoring, engaging students in research, helping students overcome isolation, and providing physical spaces to build community. Implementation of these strategies will bring vast new talent to the STEM workforce, contributing to increased technical innovation and economic growth.

TI Integrating Virtual Reality and Drone Technology in Geography Education:
   Enhancing Junior High School Students' Spatial Understanding of River
   Process and Landforms
SO COMPUTER APPLICATIONS IN ENGINEERING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE drone technology; geography education; river landforms; spatial ability;
   virtual reality
ID COGNITIVE LOAD; PERFORMANCE; GAME
AB The study developed a virtual drone system that integrates virtual reality with drone technology to create an interactive and immersive 3D learning environment. The effectiveness of this system was evaluated by comparing its impact on junior high school students' learning outcomes, motivation, and cognitive load in the "River Processes and Landforms" unit with that of traditional slide-based instructional methods. A quasi-experimental design employing non-equivalent pretest-posttest groups was adopted. Participants comprised two eighth-grade classes from a junior high school in Hsinchu City, Taiwan. The classes were assigned to an experimental group (n = 39), which received instruction using the virtual drone system, and a control group (n = 37), which was taught via slide presentations and videos. The instruction comprised three subunits: "River Processes," "River Terraces," and "Meanders." Both groups received identical instruction for essential "River Processes" concepts to ensure comparable baseline knowledge, while different instructional tools were used for the following "River Terraces" and "Meanders" units. The results revealed that students in the experimental group achieved significantly higher learning outcomes in the "River Terraces" and "Meanders" subunits compared to those in the control group. Furthermore, these students reported higher levels of learning motivation and experienced reduced cognitive load. Participants in the experimental group also expressed high satisfaction with the virtual drone system, particularly emphasizing its interactive and immersive features. These findings suggest that integrating the virtual drone system into geography education can effectively enhance students' spatial understanding and engagement while alleviating cognitive challenges associated with learning complex terrain concepts.

TI A Developmental Study of Lexico-Phonological Distance in Vocabulary
   Learning: Evidence From Typically Developing and Learning-Disabled
   Arabic-Speaking Children
SO DYSLEXIA
LA English
DT Article
DE Arabic; diglossia; expressive vocabulary; learning disabled (LD);
   lexico-phonological distance; receptive vocabulary; typically developing
   (TD)
ID DIGLOSSIA; ABILITY; QUALITY; IMPACT
AB The present study examines the role of lexico-phonological distance in shaping vocabulary acquisition within Arabic diglossia, drawing on 299 Arabic-speaking children with and without learning disabilities across Grades 1-6. Performance followed a consistent gradient: identical words were easiest; unique words hardest; cognates fell between. This hierarchy held across both receptive and expressive tasks and remained stable over development; the Grade & times; Word Type interaction was non-significant, indicating that distance-related constraints remain stable with schooling. More telling was the Group & times; Word Type interaction: the performance gap between typically developing (TD) and learning-disabled (LD) children widened disproportionately for unique words, where the demands of representational construction meet reduced phonological processing resources. A modality asymmetry further qualified the picture: expressive vocabulary proved more sensitive to diglossic distance than receptive vocabulary, consistent with the heavier retrieval demands production places on underspecified representations. Theoretically, the findings are interpreted within MAWRID, which treats linguistic distance as a constraint on representational quality and the Lexical Quality Hypothesis, which links representational precision to lexical access efficiency. These findings implicate lexico-phonological distance as a structural, developmentally persistent constraint on lexical acquisition in Arabic diglossia, with disproportionate consequences for children with compromised phonological resources.

TI Influence of Audience, Performing Conditions and Mental Health on Music
   Performance Anxiety: A Mediated-Moderated Model
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE audience reaction; mental health; music performance anxiety; novice
   musicians; performing conditions
ID EXPERIENCE
AB Music performance anxiety (MPA) is one of the prevalent issues for musicians' socio-emotional well-being. However, research is scarce on how different psychological aspects influence novice musicians' MPA. Following Folkman's cognitive appraisal theory, this study examines how audience reaction influences MPA, with the mediating role of music performing conditions (MPCs) and the moderating role of their mental health (MH) in live performances in the Chinese context. The research design of the current quantitative study was a cross-sectional survey. Data were collected from 270 final-year music students in Beijing using a questionnaire. These findings suggest that audience-related factors are more critical than contextual conditions. The study highlights the need for training programmes to help novice musicians manage audience pressure and improve psychological readiness.

The learning climate has a vital effect on the educational performance, especially within the English language learning sphere. TI Joining in or opting out? A sociocultural analysis of how students
   navigate classroom talk about personal issues in life skills education
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOLOGY OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Life skills education; Personal experiences; Personal issues; Students'
   meaning-making; Interaction analysis; Sociocultural perspective
ID HEALTH; SCHOOL
AB In a time defined by societal instability, life skills education (LSE) has become an integral part of schooling worldwide. Through its engagement with issues closely related to the lifeworlds and personal experiences of students, LSE has the potential to facilitate meaningful classroom conversations. However, not all students find it comfortable to talk about personal issues and may hesitate to share what they regard as private in class. Since students experience such situations differently, it is important to develop a deeper understanding of how they respond to educational settings in which their own lives and experiences are a central part of the content. Employing a sociocultural and dialogic approach, this study explores how students participate in such learning activities by examining how they navigate talking about personal issues and what opportunities and challenges that emerge from their interactional approaches. The applied analytical procedure involves microanalyses of conversations in two contrasting student groups that navigated the talk in markedly different ways. The analyses show that in one group, the students interacted in a way that rendered their experiences more generalised and less personal, which opened up space for multiple perspectives and exploration of the issue. In another group, the students' way of interacting made them accountable for providing personal answers, which resulted in contributions being withheld and the conversation breaking down. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings and consider how teachers can support meaningful and educational discussions about personal issues in LSE.

TI From OR dialogue to actionable feedback: a scalable method for analyzing
   intraoperative teaching
SO GLOBAL SURGICAL EDUCATION - JOURNAL OF THE ASSOCIATION FOR SURGICAL
   EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Intraoperative teaching; Surgical education; Artificial intelligence;
   Qualitative analysis; Feedback; Competency-based education
ID OPERATING-ROOM; RESIDENT; PERCEPTIONS; MODELS
AB Purpose Intraoperative feedback is essential to surgical training, yet it is transient, inconsistently documented, and difficult to analyze at scale. Traditional qualitative methods for studying operative dialogue are labor-intensive, limiting their use for educational research and surgical trainee feedback. This study describes the development and evaluation of an AI-assisted qualitative coding pipeline for analyzing intraoperative attending-trainee communication. We frame this work as a proof-of-concept feasibility study.Methods Audio-recorded dialogue from 25 general and colorectal surgical operations was transcribed and formatted for line-by-line coding using a 38-category thematic codebook. A custom GPT built on GPT-4o with retrieval-augmented generation was developed to assign codes to each utterance within a human-in-the-loop workflow. AI reliability was assessed through run-to-run agreement on a purposive sample of five transcripts. Coding efficiency and error rates were tracked across AI-assisted and manual workflows.Results The AI-assisted workflow reduced coding time to less than 20% of manual effort, with an overall error rate of 2.0%. Run-to-run AI agreement across 2,245 lines demonstrated 79% agreement with substantial concordance (kappa = 0.75). Agreement was highest for explicit utterance types and lowest for codes requiring contextual interpretation.Conclusions In this proof-of-concept evaluation, an AI-supported, human-verified coding workflow achieved the efficiency and reliability needed to make scalable analysis of intraoperative teaching dialogue feasible. This approach has the potential to convert routine operative communication into structured, actionable feedback for trainees and faculty.

TI Motivations and self-evaluation behind surgical residents'
   self-regulated learning: a qualitative study
SO GLOBAL SURGICAL EDUCATION - JOURNAL OF THE ASSOCIATION FOR SURGICAL
   EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Self-regulated learning; Surgical education; Surgical residents;
   Graduate medical education; Self-evaluation; Motivations
ID STUDENTS; GUIDE
AB Purpose Self-regulated learning (SRL), as defined by Zimmerman, is a cyclical process of forethought, performance, and self-reflection through which individuals take ownership of their learning. While surgical educators have identified behavioral ways to foster SRL, residents' motivations to regulate learning and attitudes toward self-evaluation remain less understood. This study explores these underlying drivers of SRL to better understand how residents sustain their learning and assess their development over time.Methods We recruited senior-level residents across multiple surgical specialties at a single academic medical center for a qualitative study using semi-structured interviews. Directed content analysis was applied to identify themes related to motivation and self-evaluation.Results Fourteen residents participated, representing six surgical specialties. Motivations clustered into two major themes: professional identity formation (responsibility to patients, pursuit of intraoperative autonomy, anticipation of independent practice) and personal values (personal standards of competence and intellectual curiosity). Although these factors sustained engagement in SRL, residents reported difficulty evaluating their progress due to limited peer comparison and varied perception on usefulness of faculty feedback. Hence, many developed personal benchmarks to evaluate growth over time.Discussion Surgical residents' motivation to learn is driven by both personal values and professional identity formation. However, self-evaluation is perceived as challenging due to limited opportunities for peer comparison and varying impact of faculty feedback. Programs may leverage these insights to design learning environments that not only foster autonomy and competence but also provide clearer frameworks for residents to monitor and evaluate their growth over time.

TI Differential engagement with generative artificial intelligence in
   higher education: Gender, motivation, and achievement trajectories
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL TECHNOLOGY IN HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Retrieval-augmented generation; Motivation; Chatbot interaction;
   Achievement; Gender difference
ID ACADEMIC HELP-SEEKING; STUDENTS QUESTIONS; CONTEXTS; CLUSTERS; SUPPORT;
   NUMBER
AB This study moves beyond asking whether generative AI (GenAI) improves learning to examine who engages, how they engage, and what kinds of questions they ask. We investigated how graduate students used a GenAI chatbot designed based on Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) architecture to support statistics learning and how engagement patterns associated with learner characteristics, motivation, and academic growth. Drawing on 2,819 chatbot queries across a semester, motivational measures, and performance data from 97 students, we modeled engagement using a zero-inflated negative binomial (ZINB) framework and identified performance gain profiles through k-means clustering. More than one-quarter of students did not use the chatbot at all, highlighting meaningful non-participation. Engagement frequency was shaped by learner differences: female students, those with stronger autonomous motivation, lower prior knowledge, and higher course performance interacted more frequently, while higher-performing students were less likely to abstain from use. Importantly, engagement was not merely a matter of frequency but of inquiry quality and diversity. Growing Achievers (students who began with weaker achievement but demonstrated substantial performance gains) posed more diverse and conceptually oriented questions. In contrast, Declining Performers engaged minimally and focused on narrower, procedural inquiries despite stronger initial knowledge. These findings suggest that GenAI tools function differently across learner subpopulations and can either amplify growth or remain underutilized depending on motivational and achievement trajectories. The observed variability in student engagement profiles indicates that the efficacy of AI integration depends on moving beyond uniform technological access toward strategies that prioritize autonomous motivation and scaffold concept-focused AI support tailored to individual learner trajectories. Such supports are essential to ensure shared human-AI agency so that AI integration expands learning opportunities and promotes upward academic mobility instead of concentrating benefits among already advantaged learners.

TI Enhancing Science Simulation-Based Learning with Dialogic Feedback from
   Generative AI Agents
SO JOURNAL OF SCIENCE EDUCATION AND TECHNOLOGY
LA English
DT Article
DE Science simulations; Large language model; Generative AI; Pedagogical
   agent; Dialogue feedback
ID INQUIRY
AB Current generative AI educational applications have primarily focused on conceptual interactions, leaving a gap in understanding how generative AI can provide feedback to enhance science learning with science simulations. This study thus proposed a dynamic prompt framework for designing pedagogical agents that addresses the focusing principle to support critical observation and concept development using science simulations. TI Mathematics Policy Across the United States: A Landscape Analysis
SO LEARNING DISABILITIES RESEARCH & PRACTICE
LA English
DT Article
DE mathematics policy; mathematics instruction; mathematics intervention
ID INTENSIVE INTERVENTION; LEARNING-DISABILITIES; INSTRUCTION; STUDENTS;
   DIFFICULTIES; METAANALYSIS; ACHIEVEMENT; PERFORMANCE; IMPLEMENTATION;
   ASSOCIATION
AB In recent years, evidence-based reading instruction has gained in popularity, and states have enacted legislation to require their use. To help move legislation into practice, states have created guidance documents. More recently, legislative attention is being paid to mathematics. This review analyzed mathematics legislation and guidance documents published from 2004 to May 2025. Across the 50 states and the District of Columbia, 93 mathematics legislation and guidance documents were found to exist in 54% of states. Such documents include information for core mathematics instruction, intervention, and implementation. In core instruction, states most frequently require the use of representations and a focus on problem solving. For mathematics intervention specifically, requirements for monitoring student progress are most common. To support the uptake of these practices, states rely on professional development or adoption of new curricular materials. These new requirements demonstrate a shift towards evidence-based mathematics efforts across the country, but policies related to reading still remain more common.

TI More Than a Name: Identity, Culture, and Representation in Children's
   Picturebooks
SO READING TEACHER
LA English
DT Article
AB This article explores how names, name stories, and naming picturebooks affirm children's identities and foster inclusive classroom environments. Drawing on interviews with seven cultural insiders, educators from diverse linguistic and cultural backgrounds, the study examines real-life naming experiences alongside representations in multicultural picturebooks. Through grounded theory methods, employing open coding and thematic analysis, the findings highlight the emotional and cultural significance of names and the consequences of mispronunciation or name alteration in educational settings. Picturebooks such as Becoming Vanessa and Say My Name serve as critical tools for identity affirmation, empathy, and teaching students about names. Pedagogical implications for using naming stories in early childhood and elementary classrooms include emphasizing culturally sustaining practices, read-alouds, and community building to honor every child's name and background.

TI Effects of the gender colon on text comprehensibility, text
   comprehension and mental representation of women: an exploratory
   experimental study
SO SOCIAL PSYCHOLOGY OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Generic masculine; Gender colon; Comprehensibility; Comprehension;
   Mental representation
ID LANGUAGE; BELIEFS; GERMAN
AB In grammatical gender languages such as German, the generic masculine is a linguistic convention argued to foster linguistic imbalances to the disadvantage of women and nonbinary individuals. The gender colon as a form of gender-fair language was introduced to combat this problem. Critics of gender-fair language, however, argue that gender-fair language impedes text comprehensibility and text comprehension without fostering individuals' mental representation of women. The present study aimed to examine these claims for the gender colon. The analytic sample consisted of 260 German-speaking participants (M = 29.67 years, 59.6% female). Applying multiple linear regression models, results showed that the gender colon did not significantly impact text comprehension. Results were less consistent regarding text comprehensibility: The text using the generic masculine was rated as more comprehensible, but this difference was not significant when covariates were included. In turn, participants' mental representation of women was significantly higher in the gender colon condition compared to the generic masculine condition. These findings support the use of the gender colon to promote inclusive communication.

TI Towards a Scenario-Based Framework for Developing Multiple Learning
   Analytics Dashboards
SO TECHNOLOGY KNOWLEDGE AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Learning analytics dashboards; Multiple learning analytics dashboards;
   Scenario-based framework; Visual learning analytics; Educational data;
   VLA development framework
ID DESIGN-BASED RESEARCH; DECISION-MAKING; MANAGEMENT
AB The significant amount of data available about students and their learning activities is spread across many digital educational systems today, making it challenging to use them effectively. This study addresses this issue by proposing a scenario-based framework for the design and development of Multiple Learning Analytics Dashboards (MLADs). The framework guides researchers, developers, and educational stakeholders in designing MLADs that integrate educational data from multiple sources to support the decision-making needs of teachers, school principals, municipal education leaders, and Educational Technology (EdTech) companies across the micro, meso, and macro levels. In this study, the MLADs refer to having different Learning Analytics Dashboards (LADs) tailored for different stakeholders, with each LAD containing multiple pages. The framework operationalizes this process through four stakeholder-specific scenarios, each comprising eight steps that guide the collaborative design and development of stakeholder-specific LADs within an MLAD ecosystem. The proposed scenarios illustrate how data is handled, transferred, analyzed, and visualized to these stakeholders. To explore the application of the framework at the micro and meso levels, we conducted an intervention involving teachers and school principals to illustrate the operationalization of the first two scenarios and provide initial evidence of their feasibility in authentic educational settings. The framework was perceived as beneficial for understanding the various steps involved in creating MLADs and highlighted the significance of user involvement in the design process. These benefits include enhanced clarity and interpretation of educational data, support for understanding students' learning patterns based on available outcomes and activities, and the potential to streamline routine tasks within the teacher scenario. They also encompass the capacity to compare classroom-level indicators across teachers and to interpret school-level patterns in the principal scenario.

TI Localising Inclusion: Pre-Service Teachers' Attitudes and
   Conceptualisations in Germany and Russia
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE attitudes; Germany; glocalisation; inclusive education; pre-service
   teachers; Russia; teacher education
ID STUDENT-TEACHERS; EDUCATION; CHILDREN; INSTRUMENT; POLICY
AB This study examines pre-service teachers' (PSTs) attitudes towards inclusive education in Germany and Russia and investigates how they relate to teacher training curricula and teacher educators' discourse. A mixed-methods design was used, including an online survey of PSTs (n = 460) with an open-ended question, curriculum review and exploratory interviews with university educators in both contexts. The two samples showed non-equivalent attitudinal structures: the three-factor structure supported in Germany did not replicate in Russia. Analysis of open-ended responses demonstrated that German PSTs predominantly expressed a general individualised understanding of inclusion, while Russian PSTs tended to follow placement- and disability-orientated definitions of inclusion. The findings suggest that inclusion is not interpreted uniformly across contexts but relates to national policy legacies, curricular traditions and teacher education discourses. Teacher education institutions should support PSTs in critically analysing both local and global definitions of inclusion and their implications for their future school practice.

TI AI-Driven Instruction and Its Influence on EFL Learners' Self-Efficacy,
   Self-Regulation, and Grit
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE artificial intelligence; EFL learners; grit; self-determination theory;
   self-efficacy; self-regulation
AB Incorporating AI into language education has shaped new opportunities to increase learners' psychological resources; however, evidence on how AI-driven instruction influences key traits such as self-efficacy, self-regulation and grit remains limited. To address this gap, the present research examined the effect of an Artificial Intelligence (AI) teaching intervention on these constructs among English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners. To this end, 123 Chinese EFL learners were selected and assigned to experimental and control groups and received the same syllabus content within 10 weeks. The two groups received the same syllabus material, but the experimental group engaged with an AI Chabot that offered adaptive learning support, customized encouragement and immediate feedback. On the contrary, the control group received conventional teacher-centred teaching through a traditional context. Pre- and post-intervention assessments measured variations in learners' self-efficacy, self-regulation and grit. Results from running one-way Analysis of Covariance (ANCOVA) indicated that the AI Chabot intervention significantly enhanced learners' psychological traits compared to traditional instruction. Indeed, these findings confirm that AI-driven instruction substantially improved EFL learners' self-efficacy, self-regulation and grit, with the most significant gains observed in self-efficacy. These results suggest that AI-driven teaching can serve as an effective tool for strengthening learners' psychological competencies in EFL contexts.

TI The Interaction of Authentic Leadership With Organizational Change
   Readiness
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE authentic leadership; change commitment; change efficacy; organizational
   change readiness; organizational transformation; Sino-foreign
   institutions
ID OF-THE-LITERATURE; ATTITUDES; CONCEPTUALIZATION; COMMITMENT; IMPACT
AB This study investigates how authentic leadership (AL) contributes to organizational change readiness in higher education, with particular attention to the relationships among selected dimensions of authentic leadership, change efficacy, and change commitment within a Sino-foreign university. Drawing on authentic leadership theory and organizational change readiness theory, this study focuses on two established dimensions of authentic leadership, self-awareness (SA) and internalized moral perspective (IMP), and examines how they interact with change efficacy (CE) and change commitment (CC). Using an explanatory mixed-methods approach, the research integrates quantitative partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) with qualitative thematic analysis to examine organizational change within a Sino-foreign higher education institution. The findings indicate that self-awareness positively influences change efficacy, which subsequently strengthens change commitment. Additionally, change commitment was positively associated with internalized moral perspective, suggesting that employees' commitment to organizational change reinforces ethical engagement during organizational transformation. The qualitative findings extend the quantitative results by demonstrating how authentic leadership fosters empathy, belonging, and employee engagement across the initial, transitional, and development stages of organizational change. Rather than treating authentic leadership as a single higher-order construct, the study examines the distinct roles of self-awareness and internalized moral perspective in supporting organizational change readiness. By integrating quantitative and qualitative evidence, the study advances understanding of the mechanisms linking authentic leadership and organizational change readiness and provides transferable insights for leadership practice in culturally diverse higher education settings.

TI "I think people's perception that her reading is good enough. That would
   be a worry to me." Mother and child perspectives of school-related
   reading for children with Down syndrome
SO JOURNAL OF RESEARCH IN SPECIAL EDUCATIONAL NEEDS
LA English
DT Article
DE Down syndrome; literacy; parent; reading; school
ID WILLIAMS-SYNDROME; INTERVENTION; SKILLS
AB There is growing interest in children's reading experiences, both volitional and those initiated by, or connected to, school-related reading. However, the majority of this research focuses on the reading experiences of neurotypical children; limiting understanding and the potential to improve support for other groups of children. This study examined the school-related reading experiences of children with Down syndrome, through semi-structured interviews with 10 mothers and 9 children (aged 5-13, mean age 10) from the UK. Utilising an inductive approach to thematic analysis, school factors (staff and provision) were reported by mothers to be essential to support their child's reading, with specialist training, knowledge of their child, personalised reading instruction/support and high aspirations all important. Parents also discussed: the blending of mainstream (e.g. phonics) and specialist (e.g. specific reading scheme) reading instructional approaches and resources; reading within a broader picture of their child's development; and the importance of home-school connections to support their child's reading. Meanwhile, children's experiences of reading at school varied in terms of whether they reported reading in school or not, who helped them with reading (staff, friends) and the connections between their home and school reading. Implications for supporting school-related reading for children with Down syndrome are discussed.

TI Staff and Students' Reflections on Broadening Student Perspectives
   Through Decolonizing Social Work Pedagogical Approach
SO JOURNAL OF TEACHING IN SOCIAL WORK
LA English
DT Article
DE Decolonizing; social work education; diversity; Western-centric;
   curriculum transformation
ID WHITE
AB The current crises confronting social work - particularly escalating environmental degradation alongside social crises such as entrenched racism, the erosion of Indigenous rights and cultural knowledge systems, and ongoing epistemic injustice - demand a reimagining of the profession. These crises point to the need to move beyond singular knowledge traditions and engage more meaningfully with diverse epistemologies to respond to complex challenges. While social work classrooms and communities are increasingly characterized by cultural and experiential diversity, this has not always translated into epistemological inclusion. Re-imagination therefore lies in recognizing and engaging this diversity as a source of knowledge, rather than treating it as a problem. The continued adoption of deficit views of non-Western cultures and knowledges resulted in their marginalization, while white Western approaches remain privileged, often reinforcing colonial relations. As a result, there are limited examples of how these approaches are meaningfully expanded or disrupted. Drawing on storytelling, this article presents reflective accounts from staff and students adopting a decolonized curriculum and pedagogical approach that broadened perspectives in social work. It is hoped that this example will inspire others to design subjects and curricula that legitimize students' diverse knowledges, languages, and lived experiences, contributing to the transformation of social work education and practice.

TI Developing the Life Quality Scale and Verifying its Psychometric
   Properties Among Inclusive Students in Kingdom of Saudi Arabia
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE World Health Organisation. Students with Special Needs
ID OF-LIFE; DISABILITY; ANXIETY
AB This study aimed to develop the life quality scale and verify its psychometric properties among students enrolled in inclusive schools in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. To achieve the study objectives, the life quality scale was developed after reviewing previous studies and related scales, such as the World Health Organisation Quality of Life Brief Scale, Cummins Scale, and Mansy Scale. It consisted of 40 items, distributed into 5 domains. The study sample consisted of 69 male and female inclusive students. The study results showed that Cronbach's alpha value was 0.94, and the reliability coefficients were 0.89 for the scale as whole, which are considered high values. This indicates that the scale has high validity and reliability coefficients. The study results also indicated that the level of life quality among students was moderate, and there were no differences in the level of life quality according to the gender variable.

TI Philippine University Academics in the Internationalization of Higher
   Education Institutions (HEIs): A Decolonizing Perspective
SO ASIA-PACIFIC EDUCATION RESEARCHER
LA English
DT Article
DE Decolonization; Decolonizing perspectives; Internationalization; Higher
   education institutions; University teachers' voices
ID CURRICULUM
AB This study investigates how Filipino university academics perceive and engage with the internationalization of higher education institutions (HEIs) in the Philippines. Drawing on a qualitative descriptive research design grounded in a decolonial lens, the study explores how global discourses of internationalization, often shaped by Western frameworks, are received, internalized, or contested by local academics. Data were gathered through an online open-ended questionnaire (n = 19) and follow-up semi-structured interviews (n = 5), analyzed using Braun and Clarke's thematic analysis. Rather than treating participants' responses as neutral, the study probed for underlying assumptions, silences, and contradictions that may reveal how colonial legacies continue to influence institutional and individual practices. The findings underscore the individual capital of Philippine Higher Education Institutions academics as a vital factor in internationalization, revealing that internationalization is not merely a response to globalization but also a site of epistemic negotiation. The study emphasizes the importance of a more critical and inclusive understanding of internationalization, one that values local knowledge and challenges the dominance of Western epistemologies. Lastly, this study contributes to the discourse on decolonizing HEI internationalization, emphasizing the need to move beyond Western-centric frameworks and acknowledge the agency of university academics in shaping a more inclusive and equitable internationalization process.

TI ChatGPT-Supported Teacher Feedback on L2 Students' Writing: EFL
   Teachers' Perspectives
SO ASIA-PACIFIC EDUCATION RESEARCHER
LA English
DT Article
DE ChatGPT-supported teacher feedback; Written feedback; EFL writing;
   Teachers' perspectives; GenAI
ID WRITTEN CORRECTIVE FEEDBACK
AB This study explored an innovative approach to providing written feedback, namely, ChatGPT-supported teacher feedback, in the Chinese tertiary EFL context. Two research questions guided this study: (1) What are EFL instructors' perceptions of ChatGPT-supported teacher feedback? (2) How do EFL instructors revise ChatGPT output while providing ChatGPT-supported teacher feedback? Specific training was conducted with four course instructors and two classes of students, and the instructors provided ChatGPT-supported teacher feedback on two writing tasks across seven weeks. Perception data were collected from four instructors via individual semi-structured interviews, supplemented with records of ChatGPT feedback, teachers' responses to ChatGPT output, and students' uptake of ChatGPT-supported teacher feedback. Qualitative content analysis was conducted, and the constant comparative method was utilized. The findings revealed the instructors' perceived benefits of ChatGPT-supported teacher feedback and the perceived constraints of ChatGPT output. In implementing ChatGPT-supported teacher feedback, the instructors added new comments, extended the feedback, modified inappropriate suggestions, condensed repetitive comments, and deleted excessive praise. This study provides novel pedagogical insights into the integration of ChatGPT's capabilities with teachers' agency when providing written feedback.

AB Drawing upon the Interconnected Model of Professional Growth, this study investigates how teacher professional development (TPD) activity characteristics influence classroom teaching quality. TI The Cross-Language Transfer of Chinese Syntactic Awareness to English
   Reading Comprehension: The Mediating Roles of Chinese Reading
   Comprehension and English Syntactic Awareness
SO ASIA-PACIFIC EDUCATION RESEARCHER
LA English
DT Article
DE Syntactic awareness; Reading comprehension; Language transfer
ID MEMORY
AB This study investigates the language transfer effect of Chinese syntactic awareness on English reading comprehension among middle school students. A total of 930 junior and senior high school students participated. The results revealed that: (1) Junior high students' Chinese (L1) syntactic awareness directly predicts their English (L2) reading comprehension, whereas this direct effect is not observed in senior high students. (2) The relationship between L1 syntactic awareness and L2 reading comprehension occurs through three mediating paths: (a) the mediation of L1 reading comprehension, (b) the mediation of L2 syntactic awareness, and (c) a chain mediation effect involving both L1 reading comprehension and L2 syntactic awareness. These results suggest that, native Chinese learners' L1 syntactic awareness directly predicts their L2 reading comprehension and indirectly influences it through the mediating roles of L1 reading comprehension and L2 syntactic awareness. Furthermore, this cross-language transfer is influenced by the learners' L2 proficiency.

TI Pre-Service Teachers' Imagined Identities in Their Teaching Philosophy
   Statements (TPSs)
SO ASIA-PACIFIC EDUCATION RESEARCHER
LA English
DT Article
DE Pre-service teachers; Imagined identities; Teaching philosophy
   statement; EFL; Challenges
AB The teaching philosophy statement (TPS) is a key written genre that allows teachers at all stages to articulate their teaching beliefs, engage in reflective practice, and envision their future professional roles. For pre-service teachers with limited classroom experience, the TPS can serve as a site for the construction of imagined teacher identities. While previous research has explored pre-service teachers' identity construction and transformation, how this group of teachers' imagined identities are constructed through TPSs remains underexplored. To address this gap, this study draws on multiple sources of data, including TPSs and semi-structured interviews, to investigate how nine EFL pre-service teachers construct their imagined identities and the challenges they anticipate encountering in order to attain the imagined identities. Findings reveal that all participants construct positive and nurturing visions of themselves as future teachers, emphasizing roles such as being a teacher that fosters students' social skills, personal growth, and global mindset. However, they also demonstrate an awareness of the challenges that might exist in concretizing the imagined identities. The challenges are multifaceted, including, but not limited to student characteristics, and the constraints imposed by the education system. The study concludes with implications for pre-service teacher training and professional identity development.

TI Functions of EFL Teachers' Code-Switching in Online Courses: Insights
   from the Analysis of a Chinese-English Translation MOOC Through
   Adaptation Theory
SO ASIA-PACIFIC EDUCATION RESEARCHER
LA English
DT Article
DE Code-switching; Massive open online courses; Adaptation theory; The
   matrix language frame model
ID CLASSROOM
AB Over the past decade, research on code-switching has primarily focused on English teaching in traditional classrooms, with little attention to online environments. This study addresses this gap by examining English teachers' code-switching practices in online courses on the Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs) platform in China. Using a Chinese-English Translation MOOC as a case study, this study employed a conceptual framework that combines adaptation theory with the Matrix Language Frame model to analyze the linguistic, interpersonal, and class management functions of code-switching. This analysis includes adaptations to language reality, students' comprehension, teachers' mental motivation, and their roles in class management. Analysis of the data, which involved coding the transcripts of six lecture recordings from the Chinese-English Translation MOOC, revealed diverse uses of code-switching. It was predominantly used for interpersonal functions, such as adapting to teachers' mental motivation. Less frequently, it was used to adapt to the teachers' roles. The least common was adaptation to students' receptive abilities. The findings indicate that code-switching practices in the context of MOOC teaching align with the specific communication needs of virtual teaching environments.

TI Mobile Phone Addiction, Academic Achievement, and Depression in
   Adolescence: Gender-Specific Cross-Lagged Panel Network Models
SO ASIA-PACIFIC EDUCATION RESEARCHER
LA English
DT Article
DE Mobile phone addiction; Academic achievement, and depression;
   Adolescence
ID INTERNET ADDICTION; PERFORMANCE; ASSOCIATIONS; SYMPTOMS; ANXIETY
AB Mobile phone addiction, academic achievement, and depression present intricate challenges among today's adolescents. The prevalence of co-occurring issues, gender differences in these associations, adds complexity to treatment strategies. This study investigates the dynamic relationships within these factors using cross-lagged panel network analysis, a method that enables the identification of symptom-to-symptom pathways across time and provides greater insight than traditional variable-centered approaches. A school-based sample of 665 adolescents (47.4% girls, 52.6% boys; Mage = 13.35) completed measures at two time points, half a year apart. In the symptoms of mobile phone addiction, 'try to hide usage time' and 'influences school work,' academic subjects like 'Moral and Law ' and 'English' are recognized as the most predictive of subsequent issues for girls and boys, respectively, while the depression indicator 'appetite' is significant for both. Additionally, among girls, the primary cross-cluster edges were directed from depression (e.g., appetite) to mobile phone addiction (e.g., always check missed calls or messages). However, for boys, the cross-cluster edges are intricate, involving symptoms of mobile phone addiction (e.g., influences school work), academic achievement (e.g., Math), and depression (e.g., suicide), all of which may influence the emergence of other mental health issues. These findings reveal gender-specific patterns in the interplay among mobile phone addiction, academic achievement, and depression, underscoring that interventions should prioritize central symptoms and account for gender-specific pathways to improve both academic and mental health outcomes in adolescents.

TI Examining University Students' Engagement with ChatGPT in English Essay
   Writing: Interaction Patterns and Perceptions
SO ASIA-PACIFIC EDUCATION RESEARCHER
LA English
DT Article
DE ChatGPT; English essay writing; Interaction analysis; Epistemic network
   analysis; Thematic analysis
ID CHALLENGES
AB This study examines the interaction patterns and perceptions of university students who used ChatGPT during the English essay writing process. Twenty university students in Korea were divided into two groups based on English proficiency: 10 advanced learners and 10 intermediate learners. Participants completed essay writing with the assistance of ChatGPT, and their interaction logs were collected throughout the process. The logs were analyzed using Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA) to identify interaction patterns across proficiency levels. In addition, thematic analysis of interview data was conducted to examine learners' perceptions of ChatGPT-supported writing. ENA results showed that advanced learners used ChatGPT primarily during the prewriting stage for information gathering, word choice exploration, and translation, and later shifted to refining expressions during drafting. In contrast, intermediate learners relied more heavily on ChatGPT during drafting, particularly for lexical and syntactic exploration. Thematic analysis revealed that although learners recognized ChatGPT as an efficient and supportive tool for English essay writing, they also noted its limitations, including unclear information sources and insufficient contextual understanding.

TI Teachers as Agents of Inclusive Education: Developing a Reflexivity
   Cycle and Examining Teachers' Conceptions and Practices in Vietnam
SO ASIA-PACIFIC EDUCATION RESEARCHER
LA English
DT Article
DE Reflexivity cycle; Inclusive education; Binary views; SEN;
   Constructivism; Vietnam
ID PERSPECTIVES
AB This study explores the concept of inclusive education (IE) and the crucial role of teachers in fostering it, proposing a reflexivity cycle model to help educators reflect on their goals and teaching practices. Using this model, the research examines how Vietnamese teachers perceived and implemented IE, particularly for students with special educational needs. Through in-depth interviews with nine teachers from both public and private primary schools in Hanoi, Vietnam, the study gathered qualitative data which were analysed through qualitative content analysis with a constructivist interpretive stance. The findings reveal that teachers tended to view IE through a binary lens, distinguishing between what is considered normal and abnormal rather than embracing student diversity. There is a lack of faith in IE for students with SEN and the progress of such students in mainstream education. Additionally, building a fair and disciplined educational environment, fostering mutual understanding, communication, and trust among various stakeholders inside and outside the classroom emerged as the primary strategies for promoting IE. However, a disconnect existed between national education policies and teachers' actual practices, largely due to the lack of training and involvement from school administrators in advancing IE in Vietnam. This underscores the necessity of integrating practical pedagogical support with reflexivity-oriented professional training that enables teachers to critically examine their beliefs and enact IE more effectively in the Vietnamese context.

TI Differential Effects of Leadership Support and Teacher Collaboration on
   Teacher Innovation: Evidence from Taiwan
SO ASIA-PACIFIC EDUCATION RESEARCHER
LA English
DT Article
DE Administrative support; Competency-oriented teaching; Emotional support;
   Leadership support; Teacher collaboration; Teacher innovativeness
ID ADMINISTRATIVE SUPPORT
AB This study opens new avenues for examining the differential effects of leadership support and teacher collaboration on teacher outcomes in the context of curriculum reform. Using a survey design, the study recruited upper secondary school teachers in Taiwan as participants and employed structural equation modeling to test the proposed relationships. The findings reveal that partially mediated models explain how administrative support is linked to two types of teacher innovation through teacher collaboration. However, emotional support is associated only with teacher innovativeness, highlighting its unique role in mobilizing teachers' psychological resources rather than driving concrete instructional changes. Moreover, both forms of teacher collaboration, professional practice, and exchange and coordination for teaching, positively contribute to teacher innovation, albeit in distinct ways. These results suggest a strategic approach that integrates administrative and emotional support. By providing both structural and psychological resources, school leaders can address teachers' technical needs, strengthen their professional competencies, and foster positive affective states.

TI Distributed Leadership as a Catalyst for Change: Building Emotional
   Capital to Enhance Teachers' Beliefs in AI-Integrated Teaching
SO ASIA-PACIFIC EDUCATION RESEARCHER
LA English
DT Article
DE Distributed leadership; Artificial intelligence; Teaching belief;
   Enjoyment of teaching; Teacher Professional Development; Conservation of
   Resources Theory
AB Teachers' beliefs regarding AI-integrated teaching influence the intelligent application of education, yet there remains a gap in understanding the roles of leadership support and psychological factors. Guided by the Conservation of Resources Theory, this study examines how distributed leadership affects the AI teaching beliefs of junior high school teachers in Vietnam. Using data from TALIS 2024, a chain mediation model was established to investigate the mediating effects of teacher stress and teaching enjoyment. The results show that distributed leadership not only directly and positively predicts teachers' AI teaching beliefs but also exerts an indirect influence through the pathway of stress reduction and enhanced teaching enjoyment. A key finding is that teacher stress itself is not significantly directly associated with AI teaching beliefs, whereas teaching enjoyment plays a central mediating role. This reveals that, in the context of educational intelligence transformation, distributed leadership primarily motivates teachers to embrace AI teaching innovation by cultivating their positive emotional capital, rather than merely reducing their workload. The findings underscore the importance of establishing distributed leadership structures and supportive emotional environments in schools, providing empirical evidence for educational policymakers and school administrators to promote sustainable intelligent education transformation through leadership development and emotional support.

TI Integrating AI into Spherical Video-Based Virtual Reality for Teaching
   Applications in Elementary Chinese Writing Education
SO ASIA-PACIFIC EDUCATION RESEARCHER
LA English
DT Article
DE SVVR; Artificial intelligence; Writing; Elementary school student;
   Epistemic network analysis
ID SELF-EFFICACY
AB Writing is a core competency at the elementary level, influencing both language proficiency and cognitive development. Yet students often produce superficial texts due to limited authentic experiences, resulting in anxiety and low confidence. This study introduces an instructional model integrating artificial intelligence (AI) with spherical video-based virtual reality (SVVR) to promote deep writing. Sixty fifth-grade students participated, with the experimental group using the AI-embedded OOC-SVVR approach and the control group using an experiential SVVR approach. Results show that the experimental group achieved higher writing performance, particularly in expression and creativity, and reported significantly lower anxiety; however, no significant difference was found in self-efficacy. Epistemic network analysis further revealed that AI-supported students developed more interconnected and expansive cognitive networks, whereas the control group maintained fragmented structures. These findings demonstrate that AI-enhanced SVVR not only improves the efficiency of generating and organising writing materials but also fosters deeper and more creative writing, offering practical implications for integrating immersive and intelligent tools in elementary writing instruction.

TI Teachers' Professional Well-Being Across Borders: The Interaction
   Between Job Demands and Resources
SO ASIA-PACIFIC EDUCATION RESEARCHER
LA English
DT Article
DE Demands; Professional well-being; Resources; Teacher
ID SELF-EFFICACY BELIEFS; SCHOOL CLIMATE; SATISFACTION; ENGAGEMENT;
   DETERMINANTS; MOTIVATION; BURNOUT; CONTEXT; STRESS; MODEL
AB This study examined how job demands and resources influence teachers' professional well-being across countries. Using data from 254,170 teachers in 47 OECD countries (TALIS 2018), we applied multigroup path analyses to test the main and interaction effects of workload stress, barriers to professional learning, and two job resources-collegial and participatory climates. Results showed that job resources enhanced well-being, whereas job demands reduced it. The collegial climate had the strongest positive link with job satisfaction and self-efficacy. Both resources buffered the negative effects of demands, supporting the Job Demands-Resources framework. These findings emphasise that supportive and participatory school environments are essential for sustaining teachers' professional well-being globally.

TI Large Language Model Self-Efficacy and Metacognition as Bridges in
   Cross-Linguistic Self-Efficacy Transfer
SO ASIA-PACIFIC EDUCATION RESEARCHER
LA English
DT Article
DE Self-efficacy; Cross-linguistic; Large language model; Metacognition;
   SEM-ANN
ID NEURAL NETWORK APPROACH; ACADEMIC-ACHIEVEMENT; DETERMINANTS; ACCEPTANCE;
   ENGAGEMENT; STUDENTS; ADOPTION; PROFICIENCY; LITERACY; VALIDITY
AB This study investigated the transfer of self-efficacy from the first language environment (L1E) to the second language environment (L2E), with a specific focus on the mediating roles of self-efficacy in large language model (LLM Self-efficacy) utilization and metacognition based on regulated learning strategies. Survey data from 698 Asian students were analyzed using structural equation modeling (SEM) and artificial neural network (ANN). The results of SEM indicate that self-efficacy in L1E learning (L1E self-efficacy) has no direct impact on self-efficacy in L2E learning (L2E self-efficacy) or positive learning behaviour in L2E (L2E PLB). Instead, LLM self-efficacy and metacognition jointly transmit the indirect influence of L1E self-efficacy to L2E self-efficacy and L2E PLB. The ANN findings highlight that metacognition and L2E self-efficacy are the strongest behavioural drivers of L2E PLB, with LLM self-efficacy playing a secondary role. These conclusions confirm that technology-related self-confidence and metacognitive regulation are proximal mechanisms that enable the re-evaluation and application of self-efficacy from L1E to L2E learning tasks. By revealing how self-efficacy can be transferred across language environments and how these factors influence L2E PLB, this study provides valuable insights for designing interventions to support Asian students in higher education contexts.

TI Assessing Teachers' Readiness for AI Integration: Insights from
   AI-Specific TPACK and Attitudes Toward AI
SO ASIA-PACIFIC EDUCATION RESEARCHER
LA English
DT Article
DE AI-Specific TPACK; Attitudes toward AI; Technology integration;
   Educational artificial intelligence; Teacher professional development;
   Technology acceptance model
AB This study aimed to assess teachers' AI-Specific TPACK and attitudes toward AI, and to examine their associations with prior technology experience and demographic characteristics. Guided by the TPACK framework and the Technology Acceptance Model, a cross-sectional survey was conducted with 725 teachers from Surakarta, Indonesia. Data were collected via a validated online questionnaire comprising 29 AI-Specific TPACK items and 12 Attitude Toward AI items, both demonstrating strong construct validity and high internal reliability. These results underscore the importance of targeted professional development that addresses pedagogical integration, ethical considerations, and equitable access, informing educational policy and capacity-building initiatives in AI integration.

TI Teaching Self-Efficacy and English Language Competency: A Study of EMI
   Lecturers in Vietnamese Higher Education
SO ASIA-PACIFIC EDUCATION RESEARCHER
LA English
DT Article
DE Teaching self-efficacy; English language competency; EMI lecturers;
   Vietnamese higher education
ID PROGRAMS; POLICY
AB This cross-sectional study investigated associations between classroom English competency and teaching efficacy among English Medium Instruction (EMI) lecturers in Vietnamese higher education. Data were collected from 187 Vietnamese national lecturers across 12 public universities using the Classroom English Competency Scale and Teaching Efficacy Scale. Results revealed a strong positive association between classroom English competency and teaching efficacy (r =.68, p <.001), with instructional language skills emerging as the strongest predictor (beta =.38, p <.001). Hierarchical regression analysis indicated that classroom English competency components explained 47.2% of variance in teaching efficacy beyond control variables. Pedagogically-oriented competencies (instructional and interactive language skills) demonstrated substantially stronger associations than general language competencies (grammar, vocabulary, pronunciation). The cross-sectional design establishes associations but cannot determine causal direction; findings should be interpreted as relationships rather than causal effects. Vietnam's distinctive EMI context-rapid policy-driven expansion without corresponding infrastructure-shapes interpretation and suggests cautious generalization to settings with different implementation trajectories or institutional support. The study contributes component-level evidence for Freeman's English-for-Teaching construct while informing professional development programs targeting pedagogical language competencies in policy-driven EMI expansion contexts. Longitudinal research is needed to establish temporal precedence and examine causal pathways between language competency development and teaching efficacy.

TI Scopus AI Among Novice Lecturers: Perceptions, Influencing Factors,
   Institutional Support
SO ASIA-PACIFIC EDUCATION RESEARCHER
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence; Enhanced technology acceptance model; Higher
   education; Novice lecturers; Scopus AI
AB Artificial intelligence is reshaping academic work. However, little is known about how Scopus AI supports novice lecturers who must both teach and publish. This study therefore explored how novice lecturers adopted, used and planned to integrate Scopus AI into their research and teaching. Using the Enhanced Technology Acceptance Model as a guide, we conducted a qualitative multiple case study with five lecturers who already used Scopus AI for academic writing. Data from semi-structured online interviews and screen-captured interactions were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Novice lecturers perceived Scopus AI as a time-saving knowledge aggregator and a catalyst for deeper literature engagement, with a low entry barrier and manageable technical friction. They saw it as directly relevant to teaching, supervision and research, and valued one-stop access to Scopus-indexed sources. Trust rested less on understanding the algorithm than on the curated nature of the database, producing "confidence with caution" supported by systematic cross-checking. Collegial recommendations acted as a gentle nudge, but sustained use was shaped more by performance targets, perceived usefulness and professional image. Institutional licenses and brief webinars enabled initial uptake. Nevertheless, uneven training, unclear AI-use policies and access frictions led to varied levels of integration. Overall, this study adds to the Enhanced Technology Acceptance Model by showing that trust can come from the reliability of the underlying database, even when the algorithm itself is not fully transparent. It also suggests that, once basic AI skills are in place, confidence in one's own judgement and the tool's relevance to the job may become more important than peer pressure in supporting long-term adoption.

TI Exploring How Lived Experiences Shape Technology Beliefs and Teacher
   Agency: A Study of Novice EFL Teachers
SO ASIA-PACIFIC EDUCATION RESEARCHER
LA English
DT Article
DE Teacher technology beliefs; Lived experiences; Teacher agency; Novice
   EFL teachers; Narrative inquiry; Higher education
ID EDUCATION
AB This study examines how novice English as a Foreign Language (EFL) teachers' lived experiences shape their technology beliefs and classroom practices, and how those experiences interact with contextual factors to influence the development and achievement of teacher agency. Drawing on narrative interviews and teaching-related artifacts from four Chinese international graduates who completed postgraduate study abroad and returned to China to teach in higher education, the study traces continuity from past experiences to present instructional decision-making. Findings show that teachers' technology beliefs and classroom practices were shaped through experiences across academic learning abroad, formal pedagogical preparation, and personal technology consumption. Findings also indicate that teacher agency emerged as a negotiated process rather than a stable individual attribute: teachers attempted to act on their beliefs while responding to institutional policies, collegial dynamics, student reactions, and material conditions such as professional development opportunities and technological infrastructure. Implications are discussed for language teacher education and school leadership, emphasizing the importance of structured reflection on experience, ongoing mentorship, and institutional environments that support agentive and context-responsive technology integration.

TI Schools' Agency Matters: How Agentic Differentiation Occurs Under
   Institutional Isomorphism?
SO ASIA-PACIFIC EDUCATION RESEARCHER
LA English
DT Article
DE Macro-examination system; School examination arrangement; Autonomy;
   Agency; Differentiation
ID STRATEGIC RESPONSES; PRINCIPALS; ACCOUNTABILITY; AUTONOMY
AB This study reveals the characteristic of "different while being similar" in school examination arrangements and the dual roles of schools in responding to macro-level institutional logic. Based on school samples from 6 East Asian countries/regions in PISA 2022, this study identified four types of school examination arrangements and finds that assessment pressure intensifies schools' adoption of "Screening and Selection" examinations, reinforcing their role as "accomplices" to exam-oriented education. However, under the influence of peer and social pressure, schools can still adhere to the principle of "Teaching for Individual Differences" to act as "buffers", filtering external pressures to meet the developmental needs of students. More importantly, school autonomy and agency not only functions as a buffering mechanism to mitigate the negative reinforcing effect of assessment pressure, but also provides institutional space for the localized sensemaking of "Monitoring and Improvement" examinations. This study uncovers the differentiation mechanism under institutional isomorphism, and offers practical implications for schools to overcome the dilemma of "exam-oriented education".

TI A Multidimensional Classroom Teaching Evaluation Framework Informed by
   Interactional Sociolinguistics: Evidence from East Asian Higher
   Education
SO ASIA-PACIFIC EDUCATION RESEARCHER
LA English
DT Article
DE Classroom interaction; Teaching evaluation; Interactional
   sociolinguistics (IS); Chinese-medium instruction (CMI); English-medium
   instruction (EMI)
ID ENGLISH MEDIUM; INSTRUCTION
AB Classroom teaching evaluation plays a central role in ensuring educational quality. However, classroom interaction is inherently context-sensitive and shaped by regional, linguistic, cultural, and disciplinary conditions. Existing evaluation frameworks tend to prioritize verbal interaction, thereby underrepresenting the multidimensional nature of classroom communication, including non-verbal behavior, instructional modality, and culturally embedded interactional norms. Adopting an Interactional Sociolinguistics (IS) perspective, this study investigates multidimensional classroom interactions within East Asian cultural settings, with particular attention to Chinese higher education contexts encompassing both Chinese-medium instruction (CMI) and English-medium instruction (EMI). Building on the Flanders Interaction Analysis System (FIAS) and the Student-Teacher (S-T) Teaching Analysis method, the study proposes a three-dimensional (3D) visualization model for classroom teaching evaluation that explicitly incorporates verbal interaction, non-verbal behavior, and teaching modality. The findings demonstrate that, compared with conventional evaluation approaches, the proposed 3D model offers a more comprehensive representation of classroom interaction by incorporating cultural, psychological, and linguistic dimensions. The study contributes to the refinement of classroom evaluation frameworks in culturally diverse higher education contexts.

TI Does AI-assisted Learning Improve Students' Learning Outcomes? Evidence
   From A Meta-analysis
SO ASIA-PACIFIC EDUCATION RESEARCHER
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence; Learning attitude; Learning motivation;
   Learning achievement; Meta-analysis
ID ACHIEVEMENT; PERFORMANCE; LEVEL; BIAS
AB Artificial intelligence (AI) technology is increasingly applied in education. This meta-analysis synthesizes findings from 49 controlled experiments (including randomized controlled trials and quasi-experimental designs) to examine the effects of AI-assisted learning on student performance. Using a random-effects model with trim-and-fill correction for publication bias, the pooled effect size was 0.449 (95% CI: [0.194, 0.704]). Future research should explore moderators, cognitive skills, and cross-cultural implementation.

TI Autistic Traits and Academic Procrastination Among University Students:
   Latent Profile Analysis and Mediation Analysis
SO ASIA-PACIFIC EDUCATION RESEARCHER
LA English
DT Article
DE Autistic traits; Executive function; Academic procrastination; Latent
   profile analysis; Mediation analysis
ID EXECUTIVE FUNCTION; INDIVIDUAL-DIFFERENCES; COLLEGE-STUDENTS;
   SAMPLE-SIZE; SPECTRUM; NUMBER; DETECT; ADULTS; POWER
AB While increasingly individuals with autism or high levels of autistic traits enroll in higher education, there is limited research on their academic procrastination. This study examined the relationship between autistic traits and academic procrastination among university students using variable-centered and person-centered analyses. A total of 4,067 university students participated in online self-reporting questionnaires assessing their autistic traits, executive function, and academic procrastination. Compared to the low autistic traits profile, the medium and high autistic traits profiles were associated with higher levels of academic procrastination, with executive function playing a stronger mediating role in this relationship. Practical implications for educators and administrators are outlined, along with suggestions for future research.

TI The Evolution of the Argentine University System and Faculty
   Professionalization: A Pending Challenge for the Twenty-First-Century
   University
SO DEBATE UNIVERSITARIO
LA Spanish
DT Article
DE Argentine university system; university teaching; faculty professional
   development; professional learning; higher education
AB The Argentine university system has undergone profound institutional, political, and academic transformations that have redefined its priorities at different historical moments. University autonomy, access to higher education, the development of scientific research, and, more recently, evaluation and quality assurance have played central roles in this process. This article examines the place of faculty professionalization within the evolution of the university system and considers its relevance in light of contemporary challenges in higher education. Drawing on a historical and conceptual analysis, it approaches university teaching as a specific professional practice that requires specialized knowledge and ongoing professional development. It also argues that faculty professionalization cannot rely exclusively on individual initiative but requires institutional conditions and policies that promote continuous learning, reflection on teaching practice, and the academic recognition of teaching. Faculty professionalization, thus, emerges as a pending challenge for the Argentine university system and a strategic priority for universities in the twenty-first century.

TI The Effects of NTC Methods on Vocabulary Acquisition in Preschool
   Children
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF COGNITIVE RESEARCH IN SCIENCE ENGINEERING AND
   EDUCATION-IJCRSEE
LA English
DT Article
DE early childhood; vocabulary development; lexical-semantic development;
   educational intervention
ID LANGUAGE
AB Introduction/Objective: Lexical development in early childhood is important for later literacy and academic success. This experimental study investigated the effectiveness of the NTC (Nikola Tesla Center) learning system, a pedagogical approach integrating movement, associative thinking, and play, on mother tongue vocabulary acquisition in preschool-age children. Methodology: Apre-test/post-test control group design was employed with 40 children (aged 22-34 months; 20 boys and 20 girls), equally divided into experimental and control groups. Participants completed a 20-item picture vocabulary test at three time points: initial, middle, and final. During four weeks, the experimental group participated in 12 NTC-based workshops involving motor-cognitive polygons, riddles, and associations, while the control group received standard curricular activities covering the same concepts. Due to non-normal data distribution, non-parametric statistics were used. Results: Groups did not differ significantly at initial testing (p > .05). Significant improvement over time was found for 19 of 20 target words in the experimental group (p < .05). The experimental group also demonstrated significantly greater vocabulary gains than the control group (p < .05), particularly for initially less familiar concepts, including iron, garlic, hyacinth, and nail. Progress was independent of age and gender, while dialectal forms were frequently replaced with standard forms by final testing. Conclusion: The findings suggest that integrating movement, associative thinking, and cognitive challenges may support vocabulary acquisition in early childhood. The greatest progress on less familiar words indicates potential benefits for deeper semantic learning. NTC-based activities may therefore represent a useful pedagogical approach for supporting lexical development and standard language competence in preschool children.

TI Perceived Pedagogical Value of Digital Technologies Among Engineering
   Students
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF COGNITIVE RESEARCH IN SCIENCE ENGINEERING AND
   EDUCATION-IJCRSEE
LA English
DT Article
DE Digital Technologies; Pedagogical Value; Engineering Students; Student
   Engagement
ID USER ACCEPTANCE; EDUCATION
AB The increasing integration of digital technologies in higher education raises important questions about their real pedagogical value in teaching practice. The aim of this research was to examine students' attitudes about the use of digital technologies, their representation in teaching, and their influence on the perceived pedagogical value of teaching at the technical faculty, examined through correlational and regression analyses. The research also included an analysis of the relationships among digital technologies, student engagement, and students' assessments of teachers' digital competence, particularly under conditions of limited technical resources. The research was conducted on a sample of 375 students in engineering study programs. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire and analysed using exploratory factor analysis, reliability analysis of the measurement scales (Cronbach's alpha and, for the two-item scale, the Spearman-Brown coefficient), correlation analysis and regression models. Student engagement showed as the most significant predictor of the perceived pedagogical value of digital technologies, along with the institutional support and students' digital competencies, which also made significant contributions. In contrast, teachers' digital competence and level of exposure to digital technologies were not significant predictors when considered alongside other variables. These results demonstrate that the perceived pedagogical value of digital technologies primarily depends on the ability to encourage students' interaction and active participation in the teaching process. The research also provides empirical evidence from the technical faculty context and contributes to understanding the conditions under which digital technologies enhance teaching quality.

DT Article

   Manifestations; Coping and Support
ID LOAD
AB In this qualitative study, I analysed the magnitude of cognitive overload among professors employed in Indian state-run universities and its impairment of their academic performance. The research was conducted in the Indian higher education framework, where the ever-increasing cognitive overload has significantly impacted academic performance and role expectations of professors. This qualitative study examines the causes of cognitive overload among professors at state-run universities, as well as its impact on their academic performance. This study offers a clearer understanding aimed at establishing cognitive overload as an obstacle to work efficiency within the Indian micro-environment. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 40 assistant professors, associate professors and professors working at 20 state-run universities in India. Seven interrelated themes surfaced: (1) Task switching and interruptions-continuous juggling between tasks; (2) Pedagogical impact-effects on teaching quality; (3) cognitive symptoms-difficulty in thinking and understanding; (4) Social symptoms-difficulty in interaction and collaboration; (5) Behavioural manifestations-altering behavioural patterns; (6) Physical and emotional toll-complete physical and mental exhaustion and (7) Coping and support-dealing with the problem and assistance. These themes were persistently mirrored across participants, indicating robust data saturation. The study provides insights on the challenges faced by professors in managing their job-related responsibilities in the context of rising cognitive load arising from the administrative setup of Indian universities. The study reveals the impact of cognitive overload on the effectiveness of academic and research performance of Indian professors.

TI Employee Perceptions of Reward Systems in Public Institutions: Evidence
   from the Republic of North Macedonia
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF COGNITIVE RESEARCH IN SCIENCE ENGINEERING AND
   EDUCATION-IJCRSEE
LA English
DT Article
DE reward system; public institutions; employee; North Macedonia
AB It has always been an issue in the human resource management selecting the right rewards for the employees especially in the public institutions. Many public institutions are unable to identify the types of rewards which are best used to foster employees' work satisfaction. The study aims are to evaluate how reward systems in public institutions influence employee perception and to analyze their impact on job satisfaction, quality of work, and employee retention in the public sector of North Macedonia. Data were collected via self-administered questionnaire of 153 employees in public institutions in North Macedonia. Reliability and validity of the measurement instrument are confirmed through Cronbach's alpha (0.777) and factor analysis. Descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, and regression analysis are applied to test the proposed hypotheses. The results indicate that the re-ward system has a positive but weak effect on job satisfaction (beta = 0.142, p = 0.079), quality of work (beta = 0.146, p = 0.071), and employee retention (beta = 0.144, p = 0.075), with none of the effects reaching statistical significance. Additional hierarchical re-gression analysis suggests that demographic characteristics partially influence these relationships, while the contribution of reward systems remains limited. The findings imply that reward systems in public institutions play a secondary role in shaping employee outcomes, while other factors such as job security, intrinsic motivation, and institutional stability may be more influential. The study contributes to the limited empirical literature on public sector reward systems in North Macedonia and offers practical insights for policymakers and managers seeking to improve human resource management practices.

AB The development of practical competence is an important component of biology teacher education, particularly in laboratory, field, and animal-related studies. The aim of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of adapting selected practice-oriented pedagogical approaches identified during a research internship at Hacettepe University (Turkey) for developing the practical competence of biology students in Kazakhstan.
