TI Microlearning as a Potential Tool to Enhance Learning & Engagement in a
   Biology Laboratory
SO AMERICAN BIOLOGY TEACHER
LA English
DT Article
DE microlearning; engagement; biology; laboratory
ID TRIAL
AB One of the emerging trends in STEM education involves non-traditional learning models, such as microlearning. Microlearning is an educational strategy that delivers focused content in short bursts that is ideal for tackling complex subjects and is available on a flexible timeline. This model is thought to enhance student learning, in part because it's a more flexible and engaging learning environment. Student engagement is crucial for effective learning, persistence, and academic success, and hence has the potential to affect dropout rates and degree completion. Whether microlearning can achieve enhanced student engagement and learning in STEM is largely unknown because most studies address the benefits of microlearning for learning a second language, computer science, or the medical and healthcare fields while ignoring biology, chemistry, and mathematics. This study sought to help fill this knowledge gap by determining whether microlearning when used in a biology-based lab course could enhance student engagement and learning. The study tested whether students who interacted with microlearning modules, when compared with a control group not receiving microlearning content, would show enhanced student learning and engagement, as assessed via student-reported academic grades and student engagement surveys based on previously validated instruments. The results show some positive effects of microlearning that may serve as a launch point for future studies and help to inform strategies for retention and graduation.

TI From Storm Drains to Wetlands
SO AMERICAN BIOLOGY TEACHER
LA English
DT Article
DE water quality; place-based education; environmental stewardship;
   eutrophication; wetlands; stormwater runoff
AB Water quality is a critical yet often abstract topic in middle school science. Students may encounter terms such as dissolved oxygen, pH, and turbidity in textbooks, but they rarely connect these concepts to local systems or to their own daily lives. This article describes the development and implementation of a four-day curriculum module, adapted from Project F.L.O.W. (Future Leaders on Water), that engages students in place-based investigations of stormwater runoff, pond ecosystems, and wetland restoration. Activities combine field exploration, laboratory measurement of water quality parameters, and civic-science extensions that position students as active participants in their community's environmental decision-making. Students examined storm drain systems, collected data on dissolved oxygen and turbidity, built models of eutrophication, and communicated findings through creative assignments such as comic strips and policy letters. The curriculum culminated with students planting native vegetation on the littoral shelf of their school retention pond, reinforcing the principle that biology is both a scientific and stewardship practice. The unit aligns with the Next Generation Science Standards (NGSS) and demonstrates how experiential, inquiry-driven learning can foster both scientific literacy and civic responsibility.

TI Teaching About Human Circulation Using Computational Thinking & Virtual
   Robotics
SO AMERICAN BIOLOGY TEACHER
LA English

TI The Academic Performance and 21st Century Teaching Strategies
   of BPEd Pre-Service Teachers
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE Educational Outcomes; Pedagogical Competence; Professional Preparation;
   Student Engagement; Teaching Effectiveness
AB The study investigated the teaching practices of Bachelor of Physical Education (BPEd) pre-service teachers in relation to 21st century instructional strategies and their academic performance. Employing a descriptivecorrelational research design, the study included 45 BPEd pre-service teachers from the College of Education at Isabela State University, Echague, Isabela, Philippines, who were enrolled during the second semester of the 2022-2023 academic year. Data were gathered using a structured, adapted survey questionnaire and analysed through descriptive statistics and Pearson correlation. The findings indicate that respondents demonstrated fair to satisfactory academic performance and consistently practiced all eight domains of 21(st )century teaching strategies including collaboration, communication, critical thinking, creativity and innovation, media use, information skills, cross-cultural understanding, and learner-centred learning. Notably, only creativity and innovation exhibited a significant positive relationship with academic performance. These results suggest that fostering creativity and innovation may enhance students' capacity to connect theoretical knowledge with practical learning experiences, thereby supporting academic achievement.

TI Numerical investigation of projectile motion with quadratic drag: a
   computational approach for undergraduate physics teaching
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF PHYSICS
LA English
DT Article
DE projectile motion; nondimensionalization; numerical integration;
   Runge-Kutta; computational physics education; inquiry-based learning;
   Python
AB Projectile motion with quadratic air resistance is a classical nonlinear problem and a useful context for introducing numerical methods in undergraduate mechanics. This paper presents a compact computational teaching module that connects physical modeling, nondimensionalization, numerical validation, and inquiry-based exploration. Starting from Newton's second law, the motion is formulated as a coupled first-order system and solved numerically in Python. By using the terminal velocity as the characteristic scale, the model is reduced to a dimensionless form governed mainly by the launch-speed ratio v<^>0=v0/vt and the launch angle theta, allowing different projectile systems to be compared within a common framework. The Euler and fourth-order Runge-Kutta (RK4) methods are compared through trajectory overlays and step-size convergence tests, making numerical error and algorithmic reliability explicit. Students then perform parameter sweeps to examine how quadratic drag modifies classical projectile-motion results and construct a sampled trajectory family and upper envelope as a synthesis task. A three-hour pilot implementation with 16 sophomore students majoring in physics education suggests that the module is feasible in an intermediate mechanics setting and provides preliminary evidence that students with varied Python and numerical-integration experience can engage with connections among modeling, scaling, and numerical validation, while also showing that dimensionless variables require explicit instructional scaffolding.

TI When SunlightMakes Materials Move: A Laboratory ExperimentDemonstrating
   Solar-Driven Hydrogel Actuator
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Upper-Division Undergraduate; Hands-On Learning; Polymer Chemistry;
   Materials Science; PhotothermalConversion; Hydrogel Actuator
ID EVAPORATION
AB Hydrogels, owing to their softness, deformability, and responsiveness to external stimuli, are widely employed in soft robotics as materials for actuation, sensing, and self-healing, enabling biomimetic motion and intelligent control. This laboratory experiment introduces upper-division undergraduate students to the concept of a solar-driven hydrogel actuator by fabricating and demonstrating a temperature-responsive hydrogel. Students prepare a temperature-sensitive poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) (PNIPAm) hydrogel incorporated with polypyrrole, a black photothermal additive that enhances sunlight absorption and photothermal conversion ability. Under solar irradiation, the temperature gradient between the upper and lower hydrogel layers induces asymmetric volume changes, resulting in visible bending or deformation. Conducted over a 4 h session with 32 upper-division undergraduate students, this hands-on laboratory experiment allows students to explore the relationships among polymer chemistry, materials science, photothermal conversion, and soft actuator behaviors. This laboratory experiment not only cultivates students' practical skills in hydrogel preparation and data analysis but also stimulates their interest in polymer chemistry and materials science through the visual observation of solar-driven hydrogel deformation. Furthermore, it encourages students to explore the potential applications of hydrogel actuators in future intelligent materials and soft robotics.

TI Gravitational collapse and shape isotropization in self-gravitating
   systems: a pedagogical simulation
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF PHYSICS
LA English
DT Article
DE self-gravitating systems; gravitational collapse; N-body simulation;
   virial equilibrium; computational physics education
AB Understanding why massive celestial bodies tend to adopt nearly spherical shapes is a central topic in gravitational physics, yet the dynamical pathway from an initially flattened configuration to a more isotropic self-gravitating state is rarely visualized in teaching practice. In this work, we present a Python-based pedagogical N-body simulation designed to illustrate the gravitational evolution of an initially thin rotating disk. The model uses softened Newtonian interactions and time integration of particle trajectories to follow the structural and energetic evolution of the system. Several diagnostic quantities are monitored during the simulation, including the root-mean-square radius, vertical thickness, a sphericity proxy, kinetic and potential energies and the virial ratio. The numerical results show that the initially flattened configuration undergoes gravitational contraction, followed by vertical thickening and progressive virialization, leading to a significantly more isotropic final state. The simulation therefore provides a simple and visually accessible illustration of gravitational instability, relaxation and energy redistribution in self-gravitating systems. Although the model remains highly idealized and does not include dissipation, collisions or realistic material physics, it offers an effective open-source educational framework for introducing key concepts such as free-fall collapse, virial equilibrium, angular momentum effects and numerical integration in computational physics courses. The material is designed for undergraduate students in physics and astronomy, as well as early-stage graduate students and can be readily adopted in classical mechanics, astrophysics and computational physics modules.

TI Experimental visualization of phonon dispersion in one-dimensional
   monoatomic and diatomic chains
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF PHYSICS
LA English
DT Article
DE laboratory experiment; physics education; vibrational modes; phonon
   dispersion; mechanical analogues; discrete lattice dynamics
ID LATTICE
AB We present a low-cost laboratory experiment designed to visualize phonon dispersion relations in one-dimensional monoatomic and diatomic lattices. The system consists of a stretched string under controlled tension with discrete masses attached at regular intervals, providing a mechanical analogue of lattice dynamics. The experimental conditions are selected so that the inertia of the discrete masses dominates that of the string segments, ensuring discrete-lattice behaviour and allowing a meaningful comparison between experimental data and ideal phonon dispersion relations.

TI Determining Accountability in AI-Assisted Scholarship: A Report and
   Recommendations
SO INTERNATIONAL REVIEW OF RESEARCH IN OPEN AND DISTRIBUTED LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE generative AI; GenAI; accountability; authorship; scholarly publishing;
   Goffman; production format; open access
AB The proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) presents a significant challenge to traditional notions of accountability in scholarly publishing. This report addresses the pressing question of who is responsible for the content of academic work when its creation involves AI assistance. It does so by introducing and extending Erving Goffman's (1981a, b) concept of production format, a framework that deconstructs the singular speaker into three distinct roles: animator, author (herein re-labelled designer), and principal. By applying this framework to written, scholarly communication, this report analyzes two key problems: the accountability of publishers and platforms as relaying animators and the apparent displacement of the authorial role by GenAI. The analysis draws on recent empirical evidence of journal policy adoption and theoretical applications of Goffman's work to the AI context. It pays particular attention to the implications for open access publishing, where the democratization of knowledge creation must be balanced with the imperative for rigorous accountability. The report concludes that while GenAI can assume a large proportion of the designer function of shaping textual form, the ultimate accountability for scholarly work must remain with a human principal. Detailed recommendations are provided for scholars, publishers (with specific focus on open access journals), and academic institutions to navigate the new landscape of AI-assisted authorship, ensuring transparency and preserving the integrity of academic discourse.

TI Artificial Intelligence in Online Learning: Using BERTopic to Track
   Research Topics and Their Evolutions
SO INTERNATIONAL REVIEW OF RESEARCH IN OPEN AND DISTRIBUTED LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE artificial intelligence; online learning; BERTopic; research topics;
   topic evolutions
ID EDUCATION
AB Artificial intelligence in online learning (AIOL) has attracted increasing attention in academia. This study applied BERTopic, a transformer-based topic modeling approach that leverages contextual embeddings, to examine the thematic structure and evolution of AIOL research. By analyzing 1,048 AIOL publications, this study sought to answer three research questions. What are the major research topics in AIOL? How have these topics evolved over time? What future research directions are recognized? Several research themes were identified, such as adaptive learning systems, sentiment analysis, and predictive analytics. Temporal analysis revealed a shift from early applications of traditional AI toward machine learning and deep learning approaches. The results also revealed an increasing emphasis on multimodal data integration for emotion recognition and personalized learning support. Based on the findings, a conceptual model has been proposed to guide AIOL research and practice by integrating four components: data, AI processing, adaptive learning, and learner development. Overall, the study offered a data-driven overview of AIOL research and demonstrated how topic modeling can be used to examine thematic development in emerging research fields.

TI Building a Framework to Guide the Design and Development of Open
   Educational Practices for the Digital Training of University Professors
SO INTERNATIONAL REVIEW OF RESEARCH IN OPEN AND DISTRIBUTED LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE teacher digital competence; open educational resources; OER; theoretical
   framework; open educational practices; OEP
ID COMPETENCE; TEACHER
AB In the context of widespread digitalization in higher education, enhancing teacher digital competence (TDC) has become a critical priority. However, institutional efforts to advance TDC, including the development of open educational resources (OER), are often hindered by the prevalence of training models that lack pedagogical depth and rely on transmissive methods. Current literature on open educational practices (OEP) has highlighted the transformative potential of openness in teaching, yet it also suggests a disconnect between the availability of resources and their actual adoption. Building upon this gap, this article describes the creation of a theoretical framework intended to guide the design of OER-based training that effectively integrates OEP for faculty development. The method employed was a qualitative, exploratory approach, constituting the first phase of a design-based research (DBR) project. The framework was constructed in two stages: first, defining its conceptual foundations through a rigorous literature review, and second, validating and refining these elements through input from experts in educational technology. The primary result is a validated theoretical framework for OERbased digital training. The conclusions emphasize that this framework is distinct from others because it serves as a meta-reflective element, focusing directly on the teacher's own professional development and practice, rather than only on student-facing teaching processes. While the framework can guide institutional digital transformation, its initial design was developed within a specific university context, following the DBR approach. Future research will involve implementing, revising, and validating the framework in other contexts.

TI Structure and Content of Interactions: Social Presence in Asynchronous
   Online Whole-Class vs. Small-Group Discussions
SO INTERNATIONAL REVIEW OF RESEARCH IN OPEN AND DISTRIBUTED LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE online learning; class discussion; group size; social network analysis;
   natural language processing
ID GROUP CONFIGURATION
AB This study investigates how the format of asynchronous online class discussions (whole class vs. small group) affects the structure and content of student interactions. Data were collected from 8 weeks of discussion forums in a graduate-level, asynchronous, online course at a comprehensive university in the southeastern United States. Social network analysis (SNA) metrics, such as response rate, reciprocity, transitivity, diameter, density, in-degree, and closeness centrality, were used to evaluate interaction structure. Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC) software was used to analyze the linguistic features of the interaction content. Findings revealed differences between the formats: whole-class discussions exhibited greater diameter and variability in response rate, emphasizing formal and analytical communication. In contrast, small-group discussions displayed higher reciprocity and transitivity, as well as more support and socioemotional engagement. Findings underscore the importance of designing and facilitating collaborative online learning experiences by strategically employing discussion formats to meet specific learning objectives. Implications for practice include incorporating both whole-class and small-group discussions to leverage the strengths of each format, such as creativity and critical thinking in larger groups and mutuality and support in small groups. Future research should examine these effects across different educational levels and subject areas, considering instructional contexts and personal learner characteristics.

AB During the COVID-19 pandemic, various institutions took measures to prevent the spread of the virus. TI From Consumers to Creators: How Student Participation in OER Development
   Transforms Understanding of Open Licensing and Improves Digital Literacy
SO INTERNATIONAL REVIEW OF RESEARCH IN OPEN AND DISTRIBUTED LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE open educational resources; OER; student co-creation; Creative Commons;
   digital literacy
ID EDUCATION
AB Open educational resources (OER) have emerged as key tools in democratizing education, and the levels of student awareness of OER, as well as engagement and use in many Canadian institutions, are increasing. This study explores whether involving undergraduates in the creation of OER improves their understanding of open licensing, their perceptions of OER utility, and their ability to independently access such resources. A pre-/post-activity study was conducted with 57 undergraduate students enrolled in an advanced biochemistry course. As part of the course's activities, students collaboratively contributed to the creation of a new open resource aiming to increase understanding of enzyme mechanisms, to be used by themselves as well as their peers. Data were collected using structured surveys and analyzed via the Wilcoxon signedrank test across three domains: Creative Commons knowledge, OER perception, and OER access. Statistically significant improvements were observed in students' understanding of open licensing, particularly their knowledge of Creative Commons licenses (e.g., understanding license types; p < .001), perceptions of OER credibility (e.g., perceived accuracy and source citation; p = .0049), and behaviors related to accessing diverse types of OER materials (p = .0397). Thematic analysis supported these findings, highlighting learning gains and increased engagement in areas previously unfamiliar to students. Participation in the creation of OER fostered a deeper conceptual understanding and more favorable attitudes toward open education. However, changes in access behavior were modest, indicating the need for institutional scaffolding to fully support learner autonomy in open environments.

   analysis
ID TRENDS; PUBLICATIONS; ACCEPTANCE; LEARNER
AB Although research on distance education has increased substantially in recent years, comprehensive analyses capturing the overall thematic development of the field remain limited. Modeling studies are necessary to address this gap and to uncover long-term research trends. This study aimed to reveal the trends of research conducted in the field of distance education in the last two decades by using machine learning methodology and bibliometric analysis. The unique aspect of the study was its use of the Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) algorithm, a machine learning method for analysing large-scale data. Time series analysis showed an increasing trend for topics such as artificial intelligence and emergency distance education over the years, with less interest shown in topics such as Web-based learning and program design. The study emphasized that distance education is in a technology-driven transformation process and pointed to areas that will offer new opportunities for researchers. Furthermore, recommendations for decision-makers, such as investments in digital infrastructure, integration of artificial intelligence-based systems, and the establishment of quality standards, also emerged.

AB This study investigates how rural teachers in China experience online professional development (OPD), focusing on the affective, motivational, and structural dimensions of their engagement.    learning; distance education; student retention; early warning system

AB Open high schools fulfill a critical function by offering flexible educational pathways for students encountering diverse socioeconomic and personal challenges. Nevertheless, escalating dropout rates represent a significant concern, necessitating robust predictive models to facilitate early interventions. This study employed educational data mining (EDM) techniques to analyze the academic trajectories of 484,158 students enrolled in Turkish open high schools. We evaluated multiple classification algorithms-J48, decision tree, k-nearest neighbors (kNN), na & iuml;ve Bayes, and random forest-across four distinct data preprocessing scenarios to predict student status (dropout/delayed graduation/graduation). This research provides empirically grounded insights for the early identification of at-risk students. It offers data-driven recommendations to enhance student retention policies within open high school systems, contributing a large-scale, multi-class prediction analysis within a unique, under-researched national distance education context.

TI The confidence-competence paradox: Examining leadership capability in
   Indigenous higher education contexts
SO AUSTRALIAN JOURNAL OF INDIGENOUS EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Indigenous; early career researcher; challenges and successes; career
   development; Indigenous futurism; complexity theory
ID CULTURAL COMPETENCE
AB This study examines a critical phenomenon in Australian higher education: the disconnect between university leaders' self-reported confidence and experience in Indigenous contexts. Drawing on data from a national survey and in-depth interviews with 41 university executives, we identifya confidence-competence paradox in which leaders express high confidence in engaging with Indigenous peoples and communities despite limited direct experience. In this study, competence is operationalised through self-reported experience in Indigenous higher education and leadership in Indigenous contexts, rather than through external assessment, enabling examination of the gap between leaders' confidence and their own acknowledged experience levels. We employed a mixed-method approach, utilising the Senior Leadership Capability Model (SLCM) to investigate the level of confidence and competence of executive university leaders in supporting Indigenous success. While only 22% of participants reported being very experienced in Indigenous higher education, 72% expressed confidence in Indigenous engagement. This paradox emerged from a broader study on developing a SLCM designed to foster Indigenous success by enhancing the capacity of non-Indigenous leaders. The model addresses the unrealistic expectations often placed on small numbers of Indigenous leaders who are frequently under-resourced and solely responsible for Indigenous outcomes across institutions. This paper explores the implications of the confidence-competence disconnect for leadership development, cultural competency training and sustainable institutional change. We argue that addressing this paradox is essential for creating authentic partnerships with Indigenouscommunities and distributing responsibility more equitablyamong university leadership.

TI Space, place, and pathways: How a First Nations student centre supports
   diverse transitions into university
SO AUSTRALIAN JOURNAL OF INDIGENOUS EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE First Nations; Indigenous students; higher education equity;
   transitions; student success; belonging; enabling programs; student
   support centres
AB First Nations students' transitions into university are frequently treated as linear and uniform, despite diversity across language groups, communities and life trajectories. This study examines how a dedicated First Nations student centre in a metropolitan Australian university supports students across the "university lifespan": imagining university, application and enrolment, first year and ongoing study. The paper draws on literature, administrative completion data, and interviews with 16 First Nations students and 8 staff. Thematic analysis identified three interlocking mechanisms through which the Centre strengthened success: pathway translation, place-based belonging, and wraparound scaffolding across academic, housing/financial and wellbeing domains, especially during the first weeks of semester. Students described the Centre as their primary access point to university systems, enabling programs, tutoring, accommodation supports and health services. Findings indicate that improving First Nations participation and completion requires not only expanded entry pathways but sustained investment in culturally safe infrastructures that hold students through transition pressure points and support diverse, non-linear journeys.

   schools

DT Article
DE Aboriginal education; Aboriginal community engagement;
   Indigenouseducation; First Nations Australian families and communities;
   Aboriginal students; policy co-design
AB Engagement with Aboriginal communities is often claimed by governments and their institutions as the panacea for improving the lives of Aboriginal peoples, including Aboriginal student outcomes in education. This paper challenges these claims by examining Aboriginal communities' perceptions, experiences and enactments of school engagement that provide critical conditions for these improvements. In the Culturally Nourishing Schooling (CNS) project, five local Aboriginal community case studies prioritised communityvoices through its Aboriginal community-led committee, the Blak Caucus (BC). TI Evaluating Indigenous public health competencies in a Master of Public
   Health
SO AUSTRALIAN JOURNAL OF INDIGENOUS EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Indigenous health; Indigenous knowledges; public health competencies
ID GLOBAL CHARTER
AB A highly ranked global school of public health, the Melbourne School of Population and Global Health (MSPGH) at The Universityof Melbourne offers postgraduate qualificationsthatenable a highlyskilled public health workforce. Through the university's Master of Public Health (MPH) program, students are provided the opportunity to gain comprehensive skills and knowledge, with specialist fields that include biostatistics, gerontology, global health, health economics, health policy, Indigenous health, infectious disease epidemiology and sexual health. While Indigenous health is a specialist area that students can choose to study, this evaluation, led by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander academics, examined the degree to which Indigenous health-related competencies are embedded across the core, capstone and Indigenous Health specialisation units. The review identified strong horizontal integration of teaching Indigenous public health competencies as topics across the core, capstone and Indigenous Health specialisation units. However, inclusion within capstone units was variable and often opportunistic, resulting in inconsistent student exposure to Indigenous public health learning. While it also identified a diversity of learning opportunities to engage with Indigenous knowledges, the evaluation highlighted ongoing gaps in systematic embedding of Indigenous leadership, governance and accountability within curriculum design. Overall, embedding a dedicated Indigenous public health unit as a core subject is recommended to ensure all MPH graduates develop deeper, critically informed competencies. This evaluation hopes to assist educators and MPH course designers in ensuring that Indigenous health knowledges are effectively embedded into all units in the Master of Public Health. It is further recommended that a competency mapping and evaluation of Indigenous knowledges across the whole MPH should be undertaken in the future, including for the long-term benefit of all MPH degrees across Australia and internationally.

TI Towards a Kimberley Aboriginal way of doing research
SO AUSTRALIAN JOURNAL OF INDIGENOUS EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander tertiary students; remote
   education; cultural safety; Indigenous student engagement; Aboriginal
   leadership in research
AB This paper presents an Aboriginal-led study of higher education with Aboriginal students from remote and very remote communities in the West Kimberley, exploring the experiences of Aboriginal students studying in Australian universities. Drawing on an Indigenist methodology grounded in political integrity, resistance to colonial domination and privileging Aboriginal voice, the research identifies two interconnected gaps: limited cultural understanding within universities, and uneven access to knowledge about university systems and practices among students. Findings from yarning conducted with 20 students living and studying in remote and very remote locations show that these gaps can contribute to feelings of isolation, cultural disconnection and structural barriers, despite students' strong aspirations grounded in kinship, culture and community. This paper argues that addressing both gaps requires universities to work relationally; embed Aboriginal knowledge systems, values and care; and co-create pathways that support Aboriginal students to flourish on their own terms. The paper concludes by emphasising the importance of Aboriginal leadership in shaping research, and stresses the value of creating culturally secure, two-way educational practices in learning environments in higher education.

TI Trajectories, epistemic tensions and retention challenges of Indigenous
   university students: A Colombian case mixed-analysis
SO AUSTRALIAN JOURNAL OF INDIGENOUS EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Indigenous peoples; higher education; university; decoloniality;
   decolonial praxis; mixedmethods research
AB In Colombia, only 6% of Indigenous youth access higher education despite legal protections, facing persistent socio-economic exclusion and statistical invisibility within universities. This mixed-methods study investigates the experience of Indigenous students at Universidad Antonio Nari & ntilde;o (UAN), Colombia, combining longitudinal enrolment data with interviews from 37 students, faculty and staff. Despite growing Indigenous youth enrolment amid declining non-Indigenous participation, 40% drop out within the first three years (24% in the first year). Epistemic frictions between Indigenous and Western knowledge systems emerge, with Health/Social Sciences retaining students better than Engineering/others. Women, comprising 59% of UAN's Indigenous youth, demonstrate greater persistence despite intersectional oppressions of sex/gender, class, race/ethnicity and sexuality. Specific strategies include first-year retention programs leveraging communal responsibility and curricular integration of Indigenous epistemologies into culturally resonant fields. Far from special treatment, this constitutes structural redress for historical exclusion, yielding graduates who bridge community needs with professional competencies. Future research should track longitudinal graduation rates across Colombian universities.

TI Reclaiming Eldership in the academy: An examination of the Elders in
   Residence roles in Australian higher education
SO AUSTRALIAN JOURNAL OF INDIGENOUS EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Elders in Residence; higher education; self-determination; Indigenous
   leadership; equity
AB Indigenous Australian Elders are key cultural authorities in higher education, with their presence expanding through Elders in Residence programs over the past two decades. While government reports, sector-wide reviews and institutional strategies recognise the value of Elders in Residence roles, research on the scope, efficacy and integration of such roles into institutional governance remains limited. Reporting on findings from an Australian Research Council-funded study, this paper centres the voices of six Elders in Residence through in-depth qualitative interviews and examines their positioning within complex, nuanced ecosystems of university governance, Indigenous leadership and community engagement. This paper presents the first sector-wide examination of Elders in Residence programs across Australian higher education institutions since the Review of Higher Education Access and Outcomes for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander People, which offered only limited discussion of Elders in Residence roles (Behrendt etal.,2012). Drawing on Moodie's (2018) decolonising race theory, we analyse Elders' contributions across fragmented webs of institutional power and accountability. Conceptually, the paper introduces the Dhurrun model to illuminate the layered, relational and adaptive nature of Elders' roles within higher education ecosystems. Our findings reveal that Elders' roles are often misunderstood, inconsistentlysupported, and at risk of being reduced to symbolic gestures, rather than recognised as vital agents of reform and relational governance. This paper identifies uneven patterns of recognition, participation and authority across institutional governance processes, exposing a fragmented and fragile ecology that undermines Indigenous sovereignty. We argue that (re)claiming Eldership within universities is essential to restoring Indigenous authority and embedding relational accountability at the centre of higher education ecosystems.

TI Indigenising ICT education in Australian higher education: Perspectives
   from educators
SO AUSTRALIAN JOURNAL OF INDIGENOUS EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE ICT curriculum; curriculum Indigenisation; cultural competency in higher
   education; Indigenous knowledge systems; digital inclusion
AB This study investigates the integration of Indigenous perspectives within information and communication technology (ICT) curricula across Australian universities, addressing four research questions relating to the extent of integration, approaches used, influencing factors and characteristics of effective practice. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with eight ICT educators and data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Nine themes were identified. Findings indicate that integration remains limited and inconsistent, often driven by individual initiative rather than systematic institutional approaches. While universities demonstrate policy commitments, these are not consistently enacted in curriculum design. Educators employ strategies such as contextualised assignments, interdisciplinary offerings and emerging Indigenous pedagogical frameworks. Key barriers include limited discipline-specific resources, structural curriculum constraints and lack of targeted support. Enablers include collaboration with Indigenous experts and culturally relevant teaching approaches that enhance student engagement. The study offers insights to inform curriculum development, institutional policy and future research in ICT education.

TI Dirac notation: difficulties of the third-year undergraduate physics
   students
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF PHYSICS
LA English
DT Article
DE quantum mechanics; Dirac notation; higher education
AB Learning quantum mechanics (QM) is widely recognized as a challenging task, as it involves highly abstract concepts and requires a significant shift from classical physics reasoning. Developing expertise in QM requires students to represent physical concepts using multiple formalisms, such as Dirac notation and algebraic representations, and to move flexibly between them. This study investigates two main categories of student difficulties related to Dirac notation. The first concerns difficulties in expressing a generic state vector in the position and momentum representations. The second relates to challenges in writing the eigenvectors of the position and momentum operators in Dirac notation. To explore these issues, we administered questionnaires to third-year undergraduate physics students enrolled in a QM course at the Lyon 1 University. We present a detailed analysis of student responses, identify the principal difficulties encountered, and compare our findings with results reported in prior American studies. Our results show that many students struggle to establish a clear connection between Dirac notation and its functional algebraic representation. In particular, students find it easier to recognize state vectors and eigenvectors than to construct them explicitly. Additionally, common difficulties include confusion between bras (e.g. x| and p|) and the corresponding operators, as well as confusion between the Dirac delta distribution and the Kronecker delta. Finally, we propose some interpretations of our results in light of those reported in previous studies.

TI Experimental determination of g using the DrDAQ sensor
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF PHYSICS
LA English
DT Article
DE physics experiments; methodology of physics laboratory; the
   gravitational acceleration; measurement; DrDAQ sensor
ID PHYSICS
AB In recent years, the integration of digital sensor technologies into physics laboratory instruction has created new opportunities to improve measurement accuracy and experimental efficiency. This paper presents a DrDAQ sensor-based experimental setup for determining gravitational acceleration ( g) using a free-fall object. The system employs a light sensor to record high-resolution temporal and positional data, enabling precise determination of motion parameters. The experimental results show that the DrDAQ sensor provides approximately 1 ms temporal resolution and approximately 1 mm spatial resolution, allowing measurements to be performed with high repeatability. The measured value of gravitational acceleration, g=9.755 +/- 0.009 m s-2, differs from the standard value (9.807 m s-2) by approximately 0.5%, demonstrating the accuracy and reliability of the system. Compared to conventional methods, such as manual timing with a stopwatch or pendulum-based approaches, the sensor-based system reduces human error and enables rapid repeated measurements within a short time frame. The experiment was implemented in a real laboratory setting within a physics teacher education program at the Mongolian National University of Education, where students interacted directly with the sensor system. Qualitative findings from observations and student interviews indicate that the use of the sensor simplifies data collection, supports independent experimental work, and makes data analysis more accessible. These results demonstrate that integrating low-cost digital sensor systems, such as DrDAQ, as didactic tools into physics laboratories is effective in improving measurement accuracy, reliability, and practical feasibility.

TI Not All Received Peer Feedback Is Equal: The Self-Regulation Bridge
   Between Online Peer Feedback and Learning Outcomes
SO JOURNAL OF COMPUTER ASSISTED LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE learning outcomes; online peer feedback; online peer learning;
   self-regulated learning; structural equation modelling
ID FORMATIVE ASSESSMENT; MOTIVATED STRATEGIES; WRITTEN FEEDBACK; EDUCATION;
   REVISION; VALIDITY
AB Background Peer feedback is widely used to enhance learning outcomes in online or blended learning. Previous research has suggested that online peer feedback could promote self-regulation, while the precise role of self-regulated learning in the relationship between specific types of received peer feedback and learning outcomes remains unclear. This knowledge gap limits the effective design of online peer feedback interventions.Objectives This study aimed to examine the effects of three types of peer feedback (affective feedback, cognitive feedback, and metacognitive feedback) on feedback receivers' learning outcomes and to explore the mediating role of self-regulated learning in these relationships.Methods A total of 248 undergraduate students participated in the online peer feedback activity for a blended English writing course. At the end of the course, students completed a questionnaire measuring their perceptions of the received peer feedback and their self-regulated learning. Structural equation modelling was employed to investigate the direct and indirect effects among the variables.Results and Conclusions Results showed that only metacognitive feedback had a significant direct effect on feedback receivers' learning outcomes, but affective feedback and cognitive feedback did not. Importantly, self-regulated learning significantly mediated the effects of all three types of peer feedback on feedback receivers' learning outcomes. These findings highlight that not all received peer feedback is equal, and fostering self-regulated learning is crucial for translating online peer feedback into improved learning outcomes.

TI The Veterinary Education and Training Landscape Beyond Graduation: Where
   Is the Evidence?
SO JOURNAL OF VETERINARY MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE graduate education; post-graduate training; continuing professional
   development; specialty training; assessment; transition to practice
ID CONTINUING PROFESSIONAL-DEVELOPMENT; MEDICAL-EDUCATION; COMPETENCE;
   PERFORMANCE; OUTCOMES; ANESTHESIA; CHALLENGES; FRAMEWORK; QUALITY;
   HEALTH
AB Veterinarians undergo several years of rigorous education in order to qualify in their chosen profession. As they enter clinical practice, or work within other areas of the profession, they embark upon a career-long journey of learning, whether that be formal or informal education and training, in order to develop themselves professionally and remain up to date. However, the vast majority of published educational literature within the veterinary sector relates to undergraduate programs. Research and scholarship relating to veterinary education and training beyond graduation is extremely sparse in comparison. This is somewhat different to what is seen in other health professions, including medical education, where a significant proportion of the literature focuses on education and training beyond graduation, from early career training and residencies through to continuing education. The advantages of publishing high-quality scholarship and research in any field are well known. Sharing more evidence and best practice in post-graduation education and training will inform international advances in this area. Although the specific educational challenges facing the profession at different career stages are distinct, evidence-informed approaches to educational interventions-whether that be supporting graduates' transition into the workplace, specialty training, or continuing education-have the potential to have a positive impact on many levels, from improved patient outcomes and client satisfaction to enhancing veterinarians' job satisfaction and retention in the workplace. This article discusses the gaps in evidence in veterinary education and training beyond graduation, identifying some of the current challenges that could be addressed through a greater focus in this area, and their importance. In relation to graduate transition into the workplace, further work is needed to understand the optimal design and effectiveness of support programs, including coaching and mentoring for graduates. For formal post-graduate education leading to a more advanced level of practice, there is a need to better understand which approaches to teaching and assessment promote high-quality, consistent learning experiences and outcomes. Further evidence regarding how continuing education is identified and undertaken by learners, and the corresponding impact on practice, would be valuable, and a greater understanding into feasible yet robust licensure assessments and mechanisms for revalidation are needed.

TI Fostering Critical Thinking Through Debate in Veterinary Education: A
   Large Classroom Perspective
SO JOURNAL OF VETERINARY MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE debate; active learning; pre-veterinary; engagement; large class
   teaching
ID STUDENTS; SCIENCE
AB As Doctor of Veterinary Medicine (DVM) class sizes continue to increase in the United States, there are concerns about maintaining student engagement and fostering higher-order cognitive skills within large classroom settings. Traditional didactic approaches in these environments may hinder student motivation and critical reasoning, skills essential for Day One-ready veterinarians. Although active learning strategies are recognized for enhancing student engagement and critical thinking, they are often perceived as difficult to implement in large classrooms due to logistical and instructional challenges. This article describes the implementation of a lecture hall-based debate session in a large pre-clinical veterinary classroom as an active learning strategy. Findings showed high student engagement, with nearly all participants actively involved. Students reported that the debate format facilitated recall of presession materials and improved learning, and encouraged them to seek additional resources, reinforcing integration of knowledge. Qualitative feedback highlighted the debate's role in developing individualized decision making and critical appraisal skills relevant to veterinary practice. This article supports the feasibility and effectiveness of debates as an active learning strategy in large classroom settings within the pre-clinical veterinary curriculum.

TI Reflections of Novice Veterinary Clinical Educators on Feedback
   Training: Insights from a UK Training Program
SO JOURNAL OF VETERINARY MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE feedback; reflection; novice veterinary clinical educator; distributed
   model of education; clinical educator training
AB Within veterinary education, there is an increasing shift toward a distributed teaching model, requiring clinicians to assume roles as novice educators. To support their development, the University of Surrey pioneered a training program focused on promoting educational theory and feedback delivery skills. This study investigates the reflections of 79 novice clinical educators on their experiences with structured feedback training, analyzed using inductive thematic analysis.Five key themes emerged: adopting a structured feedback approach, fostering self-assessment and reflection, providing specific and constructive feedback, creating a supportive learning environment, and overcoming challenges in delivering negative feedback. Findings revealed that 99% (n = 79) of educators recognised the importance of structured feedback, advocating for established models to guide delivery. Additionally, 87% (n = 69) highlighted the value of self-reflection, viewing feedback as a two-way dialogue. Specific and constructive feedback was deemed critical by 76% (n = 60), emphasizing the balance between positive reinforcement and areas for improvement.Creating a supportive learning environment was seen as essential by 66% (n = 52) of educators, while 37% (n = 29) acknowledged challenges in delivering negative feedback due to concerns about student demotivation. Training helped reframe negative feedback as a growth opportunity, promoting actionable and constructive guidance.The study suggests redefining "feedback sessions" as "reflective teaching sessions" to better capture the interactive and developmental nature of the process. These findings underscore the necessity of structured training for novice clinical educators, advocating for clear frameworks, reflective dialogue, and a reframed approach to feedback delivery to enhance student learning.

TI Awareness of Veterinary Social Work in Veterinary Professionals
SO JOURNAL OF VETERINARY MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE veterinary medicine; veterinary social work; grief and loss; compassion
   fatigue; well-being; the link; veterinary medicine clinical affiliates
ID SUICIDE
AB Although the specialty field of veterinary social work (VSW) is becoming more prominent within social work education and training programs, there is a lack of awareness of what a VSW professional can do when embedded within the veterinary medicine profession. Social workers often interact with individuals who have companion animals and with veterinary medicine professionals. However, there is a lack of collaborative care, evident in the empirical research and practice experience, between social work and veterinary medicine. Understanding the veterinary profession's awareness of VSW is essential to the development of interdisciplinary collaborations. VSW is a specialized practice of social work that includes four explicit components: (a) grief and loss of pets; (b) compassion fatigue and well-being of veterinarian professionals; (c) animal-assisted interventions; and (d) the link between animal abuse and interpersonal violence. A researcher-created survey was distributed to veterinary practice affiliates connected with a college of veterinary medicine (N = 100). The aims of this anonymous Qualtrics survey were to: (a) explore veterinary professionals' understanding of the concepts of VSW; (b) identify which resources, needs, and support veterinary medicine professionals need for the four components of VSW; and (c) determine if veterinary professionals desire a social worker in their settings to collaborate. The results demonstrated a lack of awareness of concepts by veterinary professionals of VSW. Respondents also expressed a desire for increased social work presence in their veterinary practice. This study highlights the importance of incorporating VSW into veterinary medical training to increase interprofessional collaborations and interventions.

TI Addressing Five Explanations for the Lack of Racial and Ethnic Diversity
   in Veterinary Medicine in the United States: Results from a Survey of
   DVM Students and Early Career Veterinarians
SO JOURNAL OF VETERINARY MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE STEM education; veterinary students; diversity in veterinary medicine;
   race and ethnicity; inclusion
ID IDENTITY; RACE; RECRUITMENT; REASONS; GENDER; CUES
AB According to the United States Bureau of Labor Statistics, veterinary medicine is one of the least racially and ethnically diverse professions in the United States. Drawing from past research in veterinary health, as well as science, technology, engineering, and math (STEM) fields more broadly, we designed and implemented an online survey to address five non-mutually exclusive explanations for the lack of racial/ethnic diversity in veterinary medicine. On the basis of the responses of 2,083 participants to the survey, we found consistent, statistically significant differences in the experiences and perceptions of well-represented compared with underrepresented DVM students and recent graduates. These differences correspond to aspects of each of the five potential explanations for the lack of diversity in veterinary medicine examined in this study, highlighting the complex nature of this issue. Most notably, our results suggest precollege exposure to advanced STEM courses, increased accessibility to paid experiential positions, preprofessional mentorship, and fostering a sense of professional identity are particularly important areas of focus for organizations and institutions interested in targeting barriers to diversity in veterinary medicine.

TI What Is Knowledge Exchange for Educators and Students? A Framework Based
   on Findings from a Literature Search and Veterinary Education Conference
   Workshop
SO JOURNAL OF VETERINARY MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE knowledge exchange; research impact; veterinary; higher education;
   scholarship; co-creation; public engagement
AB There has been growing interest in knowledge exchange (KE) activities as a result of recent calls for higher education establishments in the UK to provide more evidence of how they serve society for the benefit of the economy, the public, and the community. KE has been defined as "a collaborative, creative endeavor that translates knowledge and research into impact in society and the economy," where this exchange takes the form of sharing knowledge, experience, ideas, evidence, or expertise. While well established in the context of research, it is less clear what KE activities are in the context of teaching. The aim of this project was to use a collaborative approach to identify types of KE activity relevant for veterinary educators and undergraduate students (pre-veterinary registration) and ways of measuring these activities. Initially, a literature search identified four main overarching categories of interactions that KE activities for veterinary educators and undergraduate students could be assigned to: people-based activities, problem-solving activities, commercialization activities, and community activities. Second, a workshop with members of the wider veterinary education community evaluated these lists of activities and discussed how the impact of these could be measured. The lists generated provide a starting point for understanding how educators and undergraduate students can maximize their impact in relation to KE activities. It is expected that over time these will be built upon to represent the breadth of current and future activities undertaken in the clinical sciences. While the focus is on veterinary education, this framework can be applied to reviewing KE in a range of health care and client-facing disciplines.

TI Mixed-Mode Learning: Adoption of Cognitive, Social, and Teaching
   Presence Elements on Clinical Rotations
SO JOURNAL OF VETERINARY MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE mixed-mode; veterinary students; community of inquiry; clinical
   rotation; faculty
ID VETERINARY EDUCATION; ONLINE; EXPERIENCES; STUDENTS; HYBRID
AB This study aimed to evaluate the impact of mixed-mode (hybrid and blended) learning on the inquiry process for veterinary students on clinical rotations. An exploratory sequential mixed methods design combining qualitative (focus group) and quantitative (questionnaire) data gathering was used. Deductive qualitative analysis was performed to evaluate ideas confirming the community of inquiry process as indicated by teaching, social, and cognitive presence. Inductive analysis was performed to evaluate ideas that did not fall under the community of inquiry presence. Likert scores and the proportions of different responses from the questionnaire were summarized. Seven students participated in the focus groups, whereas 60 completed the questionnaire. Thirty-one and 49 faculty members participated in the focus groups and completed the questionnaire, respectively. The components of community inquiry were present in the mixed-mode learning approach for students on clinical rotations. Emergent ideas that did not fit under cognitive, teaching, and social presences but directly or indirectly affected the inquiry process in mixed-mode learning included co-participation by students, flexibility for faculty, faculty well-being, and technical, administrative, and peer faculty support. Barriers to effective mixed-mode design of learning activities include a lack of training of clinical faculty, design misalignment between learning activities and rotation learning outcomes, and assessment of students. Implementing a well-designed institutional continuous education training program for clinical faculty on approaches to mixed-mode learning activities in clinical rotations, followed by an assessment of the training program's access, adoption, and quality, is required.

TI Passive 3 × 3-coupler phase demodulation for nanometre displacement
   metrology in an advanced undergraduate fibre Mach-Zehnder laboratory
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF PHYSICS
LA English
DT Article
DE fibre interferometry; 3 & times; 3 fibre coupler; displacement metrology
AB Passive 3 & times; 3-coupler phase demodulation is widely used in fibre-optic sensing but is less common in teaching laboratories because it requires multi-channel acquisition and robust digital processing. Here we present an exploratory implementation of this passive technique for nanometre displacement metrology using a fibre Mach-Zehnder interferometer in which the sensing and reference arms are recombined by a 3 & times; 3 fibre coupler. Three phase-shifted photodiode outputs are digitised and combined through an atan2-based demodulation followed by phase unwrapping in Python to recover a continuous optical phase, which is then converted to displacement. The method enables both millimetre-scale motion tracking of a motor-driven stage and nanometre-scale vibration measurement of a piezoelectric transducer-driven stage (typical amplitudes on the order of 10-100 nm). Rather than aiming for a fully general sensor calibration, the activity is designed to let advanced students examine practical limitations, including digitiser quantisation noise, low-frequency drift, and cyclic non-linearity arising from non-ideal gain and phase relationships in a real 3 & times; 3 coupler. The activity is suitable for an advanced laboratory or project-based module with prior optics and basic programming experience; its transferable elements are phase reconstruction, calibration, uncertainty analysis, and critical interpretation of non-ideal experimental behaviour.

TI Academic staff experiences of a continuously disrupted rural South
   African university campus
SO SOUTH AFRICAN JOURNAL OF HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE multi-campus management; rural campus management; contextual academic
   staff support
ID NUMBER-FEESMUSTFALL
AB Multi-campus universities are not unusual in South Africa, and many researchers have indicated the challenges such university campuses experience. Yet, how university leaders manage these institutions to support academic staff seems to be approached differently by each institution. One such multi-campus institution is the University of the Free State, with two campuses in Bloemfontein and one in rural Qwaqwa (Eastern Free State). When rurality and continuous disruptions are added to the multi-campus model, such as in the case of the Qwaqwa campus, managing an already intricate model becomes even more complex. These disruptions constitute multiple natural and human-created disruptions, including student protests and various events and occurrences which disrupt the academic programme and are possibly linked to the rural nature of the campus. With this context in mind, this research aimed to answer the question, "How do academic staff experience working on a continuously disrupted rural campus of the UFS?" Through this exploratory, mixed-methods study, based on two years' worth of data (collected through surveys), it became apparent that academics experience campus disruptions, workload, personal well-being, and research as primary challenges in such an environment. Various levels of support are thus proposed, including effective campus management communication, creating a flexible work environment across campuses, and ensuring the environment is conducive to meeting required deliverables. Supporting these key university role players based on their concerns while considering their unique environment is crucial to a successful multi-campus institution. This support needs to be embedded into institutional policies and strategic planning documentation.

TI Emotional and user-experience factors influencing student performance: A
   case study of first-year online computer programming assignments
SO SOUTH AFRICAN JOURNAL OF HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Achievement Emotions Theory (AET); Assessment Emotions Questionnaire
   (AEQ); User Experience (UX) Theory; Control-Value Theory (CVT);
   Self-Determination Theory (SDT); Cognitive Load Theory (CLT);
   Expectancy-Value Theory (EVT)
ID SELF-DETERMINATION; SITUATIONAL INTEREST; ACHIEVEMENT; MOTIVATION
AB This study investigates the interplay between achievement emotions, user experience, and academic performance of online university assignments. Drawing on Pekrun's Control-Value Theory (CVT), User Experience Theory (UXT), Self-Determination Theory (SDT), Cognitive Load Theory (CLT), and Expectancy-Value Theory (EVT), the research explores how these factors impact first-year students' engagement and performance in a computer programming module. The sample comprised 350 responses across three assignments, with 30 responses for Assignment 1, 292 for Assignment 2, and 27 for Assignment 3. Achievement emotions were assessed using the Achievement Emotions Questionnaire (AEQ) across eight scales: enjoyment, hope, pride, anger, anxiety, shame, hopelessness, and boredom. The User Experience Questionnaire (UX) evaluated user experience across four scales: ease of use, interest, alignment, and appeal. Additionally, academic performance was measured as a percentage. Descriptive statistics revealed the prevalence of both positive and negative emotions, as well as varied user experiences. Correlation analysis indicated significant relationships between positive emotions (enjoyment, hope, pride) and higher academic performance, while negative emotions (anger, anxiety, hopelessness) were negatively correlated with performance. Positive user experiences (ease of use, interest, alignment, appeal) were also positively correlated with academic success. Reliability analysis examined the extent to which achievement emotions and user experiences significantly predict academic performance. Recommendations for educators are to create assignments that minimise cognitive load, maximise positive user experiences, and support students' intrinsic motivations.

TI Institutional mentorship for graduate empowerment and work-readiness in
   South Africa
SO SOUTH AFRICAN JOURNAL OF HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE graduate unemployment; employability; institutional mentorship; higher
   education; labour
ID EMPLOYABILITY; STUDENTS
AB Despite a growing pool of graduates, South Africa grapples with persistent graduate unemployment. This challenge is frequently attributed to a gap between education and workplace needs, prevalent skill shortages, and concerns that higher education institutions (HEIs) may not fully equip students for the realities of the world of work. Against this backdrop, the main research issue of this study is whether institutional mentorship can effectively empower graduates and improve their work-readiness, therefore providing a workable approach to lower graduate unemployment in South Africa. Under Kram's mentorship theory, which looks at the link between mentorship and employability, the study used electronic survey responses from alumni of a South African HEI to assess the effect of institutional mentorship. The findings reveal that institutional mentorship programmes can positively shape graduates' personal and professional development. Based on these insights, the study puts forward specific strategies and recommendations to enhance graduates' success in the job market and tackle the broader issue of graduate unemployment.

TI Potential impact of scarce skills shortages, identification of
   engineering work regulations and recruitment criteria on the quality and
   sustainability of academic programmes in South Africa
SO SOUTH AFRICAN JOURNAL OF HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Academic recruitment criteria; exit level; identification of engineering
   work; professional registration; scarce skills
AB South Africa is experiencing a shortage of engineering practitioners, with a typical engineer to population ratio of +/- 1: 3 000. Similarly, a shortage of engineering academics is also evident at higher education institutions (HEIs), where the situation is further aggravated by the minimum academic recruitment criteria required. The Identification of Engineering Work (IDoEW) regulations also require engineering academics to be professionally registered in accordance with the Engineering Profession Act (46/2000). This article investigates the potential impact of scarce skills shortages, the IDoEW regulations, and professional registration and academic recruitment criteria on the quality and sustainability of engineering programmes offered at HEIs in South Africa. A qualitative research design was adopted by focussing on the critical review of relevant policies and a benchmark comparison of employment and professional registration statistics at 13 HEIs. It was evident that the non-implementation of scarce skills policy procedures and unrealistic academic recruitment criteria are directly linked to the high level of vacancies and/or long turnaround time to fill vacancies. The high percentage of non-registered engineering academics is regarded as a potential risk, both in terms of academic programme sustainability and quality of offering. Therefore, by implementing the recommended scarce skills allowances and academic recruitment criteria, the professional registration and IDoEW requirements will automatically be included to contribute towards safeguarding the future international accreditation statuses of engineering programmes offered at HEIs in South Africa.

TI The relationship between cognitive load and self-regulated learning
   strategies amongst postgraduate accounting students at a South African
   university
SO SOUTH AFRICAN JOURNAL OF HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Cognitive load; self-regulated learning; accounting; postgraduate
ID CHILDRENS ACHIEVEMENT; ACADEMIC-PERFORMANCE; ARCHITECTURE; METAANALYSIS;
   KNOWLEDGE; DIVERSITY; EDUCATION; EFFICACY; MEMORY; SKILL
AB Studies propose the integration of two prominent learning theories: Cognitive Load Theory (CLT) and Self-Regulated Learning (SRL). The purpose of this study is to provide empirical evidence relating to this field of interest, by investigating the relationship between cognitive load and SRL strategies amongst postgraduate accounting students. Each of 262 participants completed one of three tasks of varying levels of difficulty, followed by a questionnaire that subjectively assessed each participants' cognitive load and self-regulation. The data was statistically analysed. The results indicate a statistically significant positive relationship between cognitive load and perceived task difficulty, in line with existing literature. In addition, a statistically significant negative relationship was observed between cognitive load and one of three self-regulation constructs. A high level of self-regulation in the form of learning strategies was therefore associated with low cognitive load, and vice versa. This study thus provides unique evidence of the benefit of learning strategies for managing cognitive load amongst accounting postgraduate students. It furthermore provides recommendations for instrument design measuring both SRL and cognitive load.

TI Academic staff' perceptions on research integrity at an institute of
   higher education, South Africa
SO SOUTH AFRICAN JOURNAL OF HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE plagiarism; fabrication; dishonesty; research ethics
AB Research integrity encompasses various principles to ensure that research findings are trustworthy. Breaches can occur at any point in the research process and have been flagged as a key area of focus for many institutes of higher education. This study sought to explore the perceptions of academic staff on research integrity and breaches thereof in a higher education institution in South Africa. A qualitative case study design was used. Data was analysed thematically. Fifteen participants were enrolled representing various professional levels. We found a complex array of perspectives on research integrity, shaped by academic disciplines, professional experiences, and personal ethics. None of the staff cited the five principles of research integrity. With regards to breaches in research integrity, the main themes were systemic pressures and incentives, and a lack of awareness. Pressure to publish and academic promotion was cited by many participants as a driver of breaches in research integrity, and some staff reported being aware of breaches that had occurred. Our findings suggest the need for more investments in setting up institutional structures that are dedicated to the management of research integrity; ongoing educational opportunities to build research capacity in research ethics and and institutional to disincentivise breaches in research

TI Enhancing novice mentee postgraduate supervision in open distance
   e-learning: Adaptive systems and transformational processes
SO SOUTH AFRICAN JOURNAL OF HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE adaptive systems; novice mentee postgraduate supervisors; Open Distance
   e-Learning (ODeL); resilience; transformational processes
ID EXPERIENCES; EDUCATION
AB There is a widespread assumption that newly appointed academics at universities have the qualifications and experience to fulfil the requirements of postgraduate supervision. This study explored the adaptive systems and transformational processes critical to helping supervisors and students navigate the complex and evolving landscape of academic research and development in an Open Distance e-Learning (ODeL) institution. Six novice mentee postgraduate supervisors were carefully selected from a pool of freshly hired academics from diverse departments of the College of Education at this ODeL institution in South Africa. Constructivist learning theory served as a theoretical underpinning for the transformational paradigm. The data were collected using an open-ended questionnaire and a follow-up semi-structured interview (conducted face-to-face) with five of the six participants. A thematic analysis was conducted to identify key themes. The findings emphasise the benefits of adaptive systems and transformational processes in postgraduate supervision, raising concerns about experienced mentors' communication abilities as a potential risk. The study proposes establishing a supportive institutional culture that values mentorship, diversity, equity, and inclusion. The study contributes to policy formulation, training, and the successful implementation of modified systems and transformational processes to support novice mentee postgraduate supervisors in their academic and professional development.

TI The dimension of ethics in training student volunteers: A case study of
   a community engagement partnership between a university of technology
   and a child and youth care centre in Durban
SO SOUTH AFRICAN JOURNAL OF HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE community engagement; student volunteerism; volunteer training
   programme; ethics; ethical practices; Social Contract and Ethics of Care
   theory
AB This article examines the importance of training students in ethical practices prior to their interaction with community partners in community engagement. Ethics is commonly understood as the justification of what is right or wrong, or moral principles that guide a person's behaviour. Ethical dimensions that should govern community engagement activities include establishing mutual respect and relationships of trust at community-level and establishing participatory processes both to inform study design and to address concerns related to risks of participation. The aim of this article is to provide a framework on how to prepare student volunteers on ethics and ethical practices, so that they possess the requisite knowledge on community engagement ethics, and also act ethically in their volunteer activities. This study argues that training student volunteers prior to their involvement with community partners can achieve ethical practices. Based on research conducted in 2019 between a Child and Youth Care Centre and a University of Technology in Durban, the study focused on collaboratively developing a training programme for placement of the student volunteers in the Centre. The training programme consisted of four dimensions, one of which focused on ethics. This qualitative study, based on exploratory and developmental designs, was participatory in nature. The study was guided by Social Contract and Ethics of Care theories, which focus on ethical behaviour and ensuring that this behaviour is upheld. The planning and implementation phase of the study highlighted the importance of the principles of ethical behaviour during volunteer training and interaction. The evaluation phase included the extent to which students understood ethics and ethical behaviour in volunteerism. The findings revealed that students gained some knowledge and skills on how to behave ethically. However, the identified challenges indicated that in-depth training in ethics and ethical behaviours for specific organisational needs have to be included in the preparation of student volunteers for community engagement to ensure that ethics are upheld, and that no harm is caused to the participants. The study offers a scalable, participatory model for ethics training in community engagement providing a practical tool for Universities of Technology and higher education institutions aiming to institutionalize socially responsive, ethical engagement practices.

TI Incentivising student learning: Does it work?
SO SOUTH AFRICAN JOURNAL OF HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Incentive; undergraduate; reading comprehension; STEM
ID ACHIEVEMENT GOAL THEORY; ACADEMIC LITERACY; MOTIVATION; PERFORMANCE;
   ECONOMICS; VOUCHERS; PROGRAM
AB Motivation is one of the primary factors that influence students' learning behaviour. This study investigates the impact of extrinsic motivation, through the introduction of an intangible incentive scheme, on undergraduate STEM students' engagement and performance in an online reading comprehension activity. Since 2021, the activity has been conducted on the Read Theory platform and although initial results seemed promising, a gap remained between students' performance and the activity's outcomes. In 2023 an incentive scheme combining two incentives namely, work avoidance and a marks incentive, was implemented to address students' perceived underinvestment in the activity. The study examined participation and performance data from 2021 to 2023 across three STEM modules. In 2023 the intervention was implemented in two of these modules, with the third module continuing with the original programme structure. The data revealed significant improvements in the performance of students who participated in the intervention, while performance of students in the original programme remained unchanged. The results suggest that the combination of work-avoidance and marks-based incentives effectively encouraged students to focus their efforts on reaching higher Lexile levels, thereby improving their overall reading comprehension. Moreover, the incentive scheme enabled effective identification of students in need of targeted support. This study demonstrates that carefully designed incentives, can enhance student engagement and performance in selected academic activities.
