TI Evaluating Students' Learning Experiences in Blended Learning
   Environment Integrated With Interactive GeoGebra Applets: A
   Self-Determination Theory Perspective
SO JOURNAL OF COMPUTER ASSISTED LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE blended learning; GeoGebra applets; learning outcomes;
   self-determination theory; student engagement
ID FLIPPED CLASSROOM; ACHIEVEMENT; MOTIVATION; ENGAGEMENT; IMPACT
AB Background Students' learning outcomes and experiences vary depending on the learning environment, and their reinforcement relies on meeting specific innate needs. In this context, self-determination is considered a key theory that fosters students' learning experiences. The self-determination theory (SDT) has been repeatedly addressed in the literature in online, blended, and face-to-face learning environments in both research and practice contexts. Despite a significant number of existing studies, little is still known about the potential reasons for this impact of learning environments on students, from the perspective of how learning environments integrating various dynamic and interactive technologies affect students' engagement levels and meet their various needs to maintain their motivation.Objectives Therefore, in this study, interactive GeoGebra applets are conceptualized not only as teaching tools but also as need-supportive learning affordances that can transform how students interact with mathematical content. The instructional materials and learning activities were systematically designed in accordance with SDT to support students' autonomy, competence, and relatedness. Accordingly, the present research compares online, blended, and face-to-face learning environments, focusing particularly on how GeoGebra-supported instruction in blended and online settings differently supports psychological needs, student engagement, and learning performance.Methods Using a quasi-experimental design in the study, three carefully defined instructional conditions were compared: a blended learning environment supported by interactive GeoGebra applets, a fully online learning environment with the same applications, and a traditional face-to-face learning environment without such interaction. A total of 400 preliminary undergraduate students participated in the study.Results and Conclusions The results show that the BL setting supported by interactive GeoGebra applets, developed in line with Self-Determination Theory (SDT)-aligned teaching strategies, improves students' learning outcomes and engagement, and fulfils competence and relatedness needs, whereas autonomy satisfaction remained consistent across all instructional conditions. Findings show the promising effects of the BL environment, particularly for low-performing students. The study offers practical implications for educators and instructional designers, providing a robust framework for integrating need-supportive digital tools into mathematics curricula to enhance both cognitive and psychological outcomes.

TI Leveraging Multimodal Large Language Models to Analyse Student
   Exploration Behaviours in Educational Game Environments
SO JOURNAL OF COMPUTER ASSISTED LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE educational games; generative AI; learning analytics; multimodal large
   language model; video analysis
ID VIDEO
AB Background Video data provides rich opportunities to examine student behaviour in game-based learning environments, capturing not only observable actions but also subtle indicators of cognitive engagement. However, traditional video analysis is labor-intensive, and current applications of AI to this task are limited by models trained on general-purpose datasets, which often fail to capture the pedagogical meaning of student actions in authentic educational contexts.Objectives This study explores how multimodal large language models (MLLMs), specifically LLaVA-Video-7B-Qwen2, can support qualitative video analysis of student exploration behaviours in a Minecraft-based STEM learning environment.Methods We conducted an exploratory case study using screen recordings from a Minecraft-based STEM learning environment. TI The equipotential conducting disk: an analytical and computational study
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF PHYSICS
LA English
DT Article
DE conducting disk; elliptic integrals; Bessel functions; integral
   equations; Nystrom discretization
ID FIELD; RING
AB We present a pedagogical analytical and computational study of the classical problem of an isolated conducting disk maintained at a constant electric potential. Although the physical statement of the problem is simple, the determination of the surface charge density is nontrivial and provides a natural introduction to electrostatic integral equations. Starting from the potential of an arbitrary axisymmetric charge distribution on a disk, we discuss both the elliptic-integral and Bessel-function representations of the problem. We then impose the equipotential condition and obtain the corresponding integral equation for the unknown surface charge density. The exact solution is reviewed, emphasizing the inverse-square-root divergence at the rim and the associated edge effect. A direct numerical implementation based on a Chebyshev-weighted Nystr & ouml;m discretization is then developed. The logarithmic singularity of the elliptic kernel is treated by a local diagonal correction, without imposing the known analytical solution. In addition, we introduce a general algebraic edge factor and show numerically that the regularized density remains finite only when the trial exponent is s=1/2. Thus, the characteristic edge singularity is recovered from the numerical solution itself rather than assumed in advance. The numerical density, capacitance, and edge exponent are compared with the analytical results, providing clear tests of convergence and physical consistency. The conducting disk therefore serves as a compact educational example connecting elementary electrostatics, special functions, boundary conditions, singular charge distributions, and the numerical solution of integral equations. The approach is suitable for advanced undergraduate or beginning graduate courses in electromagnetism, computational physics, or mathematical methods in physics.

TI Problem solving in physics classes: Navigating fast and slow thinking
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PHYSICS
LA English
DT Article
ID STUDENTS
AB This paper examines the cognitive foundations of problem solving in introductory physics, drawing on Daniel Kahneman's dual-process theory and research on judgment and decision making. Students often struggle with problem analysis, mathematical reasoning, and cognitive biases. To address these challenges, the paper proposes a six-step problem-solving framework grounded in dual-process principles and integrates it with structured problem-solving journals. The framework and journals were implemented in university physics courses, where students were required to make their reasoning explicit in written homework. In a controlled classroom study, students who consistently applied the six-step structure in written journals scored 24% higher on average on the final exam than peers who completed only online homework. These findings illustrate how slowing down intuitive responses and examining assumptions allows students to engage more fully in analytical problem solving.

TI The inverse velocity force and automotive physics
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PHYSICS
LA English
DT Article
ID DRAG
AB The inverse velocity force F(v)=C/v is central to the analysis of automotive performance, but is often unmentioned in classical mechanics courses. It represents the maximum force that can be delivered from a power-limited engine over a wide range of speeds. We show how such a force arises from a device called a transmission in internal combustion engines, and more simply from circuit controls in electric vehicles. TI A rigorous derivation of the ideal gas law from energy constraints
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PHYSICS
LA English
DT Article
AB Standard introductory courses in thermodynamics typically introduce the ideal gas equation of state as an empirical postulate or a result of kinetic theory. In this work, we show an alternative way of deriving the equation pV proportional to NT from general postulates. By assuming only the functional independence of internal energy from volume and enthalpy from pressure under isothermal conditions, or, equivalently, the opposite conditions, we show how the ideal gas law emerges as a necessary consequence of these energy-based symmetries. TI Revisiting Koehler's experiment of measuring the ratio of the specific
   heats of air by self-sustained oscillations
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PHYSICS
LA English
DT Article
AB We revisit Koehler's experiment, a clever modification of R & uuml;chardt's experiment designed to measure the ratio of specific heats of gas. TI Generalized vibration curves for apodization and super-resolution in
   far-field diffraction
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PHYSICS
LA English
DT Article
AB The Cornu spiral, widely used to analyze Fresnel diffraction, is a familiar example of a vibration curve, also known as an amplitude-phase curve or phasor diagram. A related construction appears in discussions of Fraunhofer diffraction, where the aperture function is uniform, making the curve's shape depend solely on phase. When the aperture function varies with position, however, both amplitude and phase determine the geometry. Here, vibration curves are extended to continuous, monotonic, symmetric, nonuniform aperture functions that produce either apodization (broadening of the central maximum with suppression of side maxima) or super-resolution (narrowing of the central maximum with enhancement of side maxima). These generalized vibration curves provide an intuitive visualization of how aperture structure shapes the far-field diffraction pattern. They clarify the mechanisms behind apodization and super-resolution and reveal how phasor rotation at the first diffraction zero provides a signature that characterizes the two effects. This unified perspective serves as a useful pedagogical tool for connecting Fourier transforms, optical diffraction, and vibration curves in the undergraduate and graduate curriculum.

TI Kapitza's pendulum as a classical prelude to Floquet-Magnus theory
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PHYSICS
LA English
DT Article
ID QUANTUM; STABILIZATION
AB We present a pedagogical introduction to Floquet-Magnus theory through the classical example of Kapitza's pendulum-a simple system exhibiting nontrivial dynamical stabilization under rapid periodic driving. By deriving the equations of motion and analyzing the system using Floquet theory and the Magnus expansion, we obtain analytical stability conditions and effective evolution equations. While grounded in classical mechanics, the techniques are directly applicable to periodically driven quantum systems as well. The approach is fully analytical, using only tools from theoretical mechanics, linear algebra, and ordinary differential equations, and is suitable for instruction at the advanced undergraduate or graduate level.

TI Operator-based derivation of symmetric molecular top wavefunctions
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PHYSICS
LA English
DT Article
AB The symmetric top wavefunctions are important in the study of rotational transitions of rigid body-rotor molecules. Using an explicit construction of the position-space state (determined from the Euler angles) and the definite angular momentum states (determined from the total angular momentum and the projections in the lab and body-fixed frames), we provide an operator-based derivation of these wavefunctions that just uses abstract states and operators without the need to work in position space. TI Bloch's theorem: An operator-based derivation
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PHYSICS
LA English
DT Article
ID QUANTUM-MECHANICS; ELECTRONS
AB We present an operator-based derivation of Bloch's theorem. In this approach, we first construct an explicit operator form of the Hamiltonian by writing the potential part in terms of an infinite sum of the momentum-translation operators. Next, we prove that it commutes with the position-translation operator corresponding to a lattice translation, using the exponential re-ordering identity. We then build on Merzbacher's treatment of simultaneous diagonalization of commuting operators to reproduce Kittel's central equation and also to derive a new formula for the simultaneous eigenket corresponding to a specific energy eigenvalue. Moreover, through the Born rule, we provide a precise account of the position and momentum probability distributions for Bloch states, and we examine the concept of crystal momentum. Finally, we apply our findings to the Kronig-Penney model, where we numerically depict the band structure and illustrate the delocalized nature of the single electron.

TI A time-domain approach to band formation in periodic media
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PHYSICS
LA English
DT Article
AB Band formation in periodic media is a central topic in solid-state physics and is typically introduced using Bloch's theorem as an eigenvalue problem for infinite periodic systems. Although elegant, this approach assumes an idealized infinite lattice, shifts attention away from real-space wave dynamics, and presents band structures as static outcomes rather than emergent features of wave propagation. As a result, students often do not connect band gaps with familiar phenomena such as reflection, transmission, and interference, creating a disconnect between formal band theory and observable wave behavior. We address this problem by discussing how band gaps occur from wave propagation in finite periodic systems. A broadband wavepacket is launched into a layered medium using a staggered-grid finite-difference space-time algorithm, and the transmission spectra are used to identify band gaps. The Bloch dispersion relation and the exponential decay of the wave field within band gap regions are extracted, thus establishing a connection between real-space wave propagation and the Bloch description of periodic media.

TI The asymmetric rotating saddle potential as a mechanical analog to the
   RF Paul trap
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PHYSICS
LA English
DT Article
AB Under specific conditions, a rotating saddle potential can confine the motion of a particle on its surface. This time-varying hyperbolic potential shares key characteristics with the RF-electric-quadrupole ion trap (RF Paul trap), making it a valuable mechanical analog. Previous work has primarily focused on symmetric saddles, characterized by equal curvatures along the trapping and anti-trapping directions. RF Paul traps, however, are asymmetric, because the degeneracy of the transverse motional modes must be lifted for laser cooling and other quantum control. In this paper, we investigate the motion of trapped particles in asymmetric rotating saddles. We demonstrate that even minor asymmetries, including those arising from manufacturing imperfections, can significantly affect particle trajectories and stability. Our analysis includes both theoretical modeling and experimental measurements. We derive the equations of motion for asymmetric saddles and solve them to explore stability and precession effects. Additionally, we present lifetime measurements of particles in saddles with varying degrees of asymmetry to map key features of the a-q stability diagram. This study underscores the importance of incorporating asymmetry into mechanical models of ion traps to better reflect real-world implementations.

TI Demonstrating dynamic stability with rotating saddles and liquid
   nitrogen droplets: A classroom analog to the RF Paul trap
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PHYSICS
LA English
DT Article
AB Rotating saddle potentials provide a compelling visual demonstration of dynamic stability and so are widely used in undergraduate physics education as mechanical analogs to the radio-frequency (RF) Paul trap. Traditional demonstrations typically rely on rolling ball bearings, whose frictional effects and internal rotation obscure fundamental particle dynamics. We introduce a simple yet significant improvement by employing droplets of liquid nitrogen (LN2), which levitate via the Leidenfrost effect, eliminating rolling dynamics and greatly reducing friction. LN2 droplets clearly illustrate the rotating ponderomotive-like force, producing trajectories closely consistent with theoretical predictions. Using experimental data, we compare the stability threshold and particle trajectories of LN2 droplets and traditional ball bearings. LN2 droplets exhibit a sharply defined and visually distinct stability threshold, transitioning abruptly from unstable to stable motion at a critical rotation frequency. In contrast, ball bearings demonstrate a more gradual threshold, accompanied by trajectories complicated by friction-induced deviations. We present detailed measurements of particle lifetimes and trajectories as functions of dimensionless stability parameters for both symmetric and intentionally asymmetric saddles. These improvements significantly enhance visual and conceptual clarity, reduce common misconceptions related to frictional dynamics, and provide natural opportunities for exploring related phenomena such as the Leidenfrost effect. We also offer practical guidance on assembling and implementing this enhanced demonstration for effective classroom and laboratory instruction.

   theories
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF PHYSICS
LA English
DT Article

TI The ramsey block: a robust quantum communication protocol guaranteed by
   combinatorics
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF PHYSICS
LA English
DT Article
DE Quantum communication; quantum protocols; Ramsey theory; quantum
   information
ID KEY DISTRIBUTION
AB Quantum communication protocols are typically introduced in quantum information curricula through two archetypes: quantum key distribution protocols like BB84, which prioritize security, and protocols like Superdense Coding, which optimize channel capacity. This paper introduces the 'Ramsey Block,' a pedagogical protocol designed to bridge the gap between these concepts by focusing on a third, crucial element: infrastructure robustness. Based on a fully connected 6-node quantum network, the protocol leverages Ramsey's Theorem ( R(3,3)=6) to mathematically guarantee the existence of a functional communication channel. We analyze the protocol's resource efficiency and demonstrate that it serves as a 'heavy' infrastructure protocol: it sacrifices the high efficiency of Superdense Coding to purchase guaranteed connectivity and, in a distributed network configuration, provides BB84-like security against eavesdropping. The Ramsey Block serves as an accessible 'toy model' for undergraduate students to explore the multi-variable optimization problems at the heart of quantum network engineering.

TI Low-energy scattering from hard obstacles of arbitrary shape
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF PHYSICS
LA English
DT Article
DE low-energy scattering; scattering length; electrostatic capacitance;
   hard-obstacle scattering
ID LENGTH
AB A familiar classroom heuristic for hard-sphere scattering is that the low-energy cross section 'equals the surface area' because a long-wavelength particle can 'feel' the sphere from all directions. More precisely, this heuristic means that, when the wavelength is large compared with the size of the scatterer, the wave is sensitive to the global boundary condition imposed by the whole hard obstacle; in the zero-energy limit this global response is represented by the monopole term of an exterior Laplace problem. While useful as intuition, the heuristic prompts a natural question for students: is there a general connection between surface area and the threshold cross section of a non-spherical hard target? This pedagogical note, aimed at advanced undergraduates and beginning graduate students, shows how to answer that question systematically. For a perfectly hard obstacle the zero-energy Schr & ouml;dinger equation reduces to an exterior Laplace problem with Dirichlet boundary conditions. Comparing its far-field monopole term with the corresponding electrostatic problem yields a direct mapping between the scattering length and the electrostatic capacitance of the same shape. The mapping provides a simple route to threshold cross sections for bodies of arbitrary shape, without relying on separability. Using published capacitances for several examples, we compare the threshold cross section with surface area and show that the equality for a sphere is not a general surface-area law.

TI Mathematical modeling of thermoacoustic resonance in spherical geometry:
   normal mode analysis of a partially immersed rotating system
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF PHYSICS
LA English
DT Article
DE heat conduction; Helmholtz equation; rotational system; spherical
   geometry; thermoacoustic resonance
ID CONVERSION
AB This study develops a theoretical model of thermoacoustic resonance in a partially immersed rotating spherical system. The model combines the heat conduction equation in spherical coordinates with the Helmholtz acoustic wave equation and incorporates rotational effects through a first-order perturbative correction. The coupling between thermal and acoustic fields is represented through a simplified thermoacoustic formulation that links boundary heat flux, acoustic pressure variation, and spherical normal modes. Using the thermophysical properties of water at 60 degrees C and a spherical radius of 3 cm, the corrected numerical results show that the first three resonance frequencies increase nearly linearly with angular velocity within the range 0 <= Omega <= 10 rad s-1. The fundamental mode increases from 36.708 kHz to 40.378 kHz, corresponding to an average sensitivity of 0.367 kHz (rad s-1)-1. The radial pressure profiles show increasing nodal complexity and phase reversals for higher-order modes, while the rigid-wall boundary condition allows finite pressure values at the boundary. Dimensionless analysis yields a Biot number of 11.2 and a Prandtl number of 2.9, indicating a strong-convection regime with moderate thermal diffusion. The model provides a pedagogically accessible framework for connecting heat transfer, acoustic resonance, spherical mode structures, and rotational perturbation in advanced physics education.

TI The random allocation model as a framework for constrained optimization
   and entropy stability
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF PHYSICS
LA English
DT Article
DE random allocation model; phase transition; most probable configuration
   method; equilibrium occupation distribution
AB Phase transitions and constrained optimization are central to statistical mechanics, yet undergraduate instruction often relies on models that obscure their combinatorial origins or require advanced mathematical machinery. The random allocation model with a power-law weight w(m)=m(-beta) offers a minimal, exactly solvable alternative. We derive the equilibrium occupation distribution using the most probable configuration method, explicitly tracking the emergence of the Lagrange multiplier as a conjugate variable to particle density. Analysis of the entropy density s(rho) reveals a real-space condensation transition at a finite critical density rho(c)(beta) for beta>2. The transition is third-order in the Ehrenfest sense for 2<beta <= 3 and second-order for beta>3, with the exponent beta playing a role mathematically analogous to spatial dimensionality in the ideal Bose gas. The derivation isolates the statistical core of condensation, providing a transparent training ground for the saddle-point method without the overhead of kinetic energy or temperature. Furthermore, the model resolves a persistent pedagogical challenge by explicitly distinguishing the concavity of the extensive entropy S(M) from the convexity of the intensive entropy density s(rho) in the condensed phase. Because the analysis requires only elementary combinatorics and Stirling's approximation, the system serves as a tractable example of higher-order transitions that can be integrated directly into advanced undergraduate or early graduate statistical mechanics courses.

TI From ideal gases to flocking: an emergence-oriented teaching sequence
   for undergraduate physics
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF PHYSICS
LA English
DT Article
DE undergraduate teaching; statistical physics; emergence; collective
   behaviour; flocking models
AB The ideal gas model is one of the first many-particle models encountered in undergraduate physics, yet its standard presentation often suppresses particle-particle interaction in order to foreground tractable statistical ideas. This pedagogical simplification is powerful, but it can also unintentionally suggest that collective behaviour is merely the sum of independent motions. In this teaching article we propose a complementary instructional sequence that introduces flocking models after the ideal gas. The central idea is to help students compare two many-body systems: one in which interactions are neglected and another in which simple local interaction rules generate qualitatively new macroscopic order. Using the flocking model as a bridge, students can discuss emergence, order parameters, phase-like transitions, modelling assumptions and the relation between microscopic rules and macroscopic behaviour. We outline the conceptual motivation, a classroom implementation pathway and a set of discussion tasks suitable for introductory or intermediate undergraduate physics courses.

TI A sterile-neutrino search using data from the MicroBooNE liquid-argon
   time projection chamber performed in an undergraduate teaching
   laboratory
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF PHYSICS
LA English
DT Article
DE particle physics; neutrino; physics education; higher ed; taught labs
ID SOLAR; OSCILLATION; FLUX
AB Fundamental particle physics is a key part of an undergraduate physics curriculum, but can be challenging to incorporate into teaching laboratories. We present an undergraduate laboratory experiment that enables students to work with real data from the MicroBooNE liquid-argon time projection chamber to search for the existence of a sterile neutrino: a new, fourth, neutrino state. This search has galvanised physicists for decades, as the existence of sterile neutrinos could play a critical role in understanding fundamental processes in the early Universe, provide viable dark matter candidates, and offer a natural explanation for the origin of neutrino masses. From an experimental point of view, anomalies observed in several neutrino experiments provide tantalising hints of their existence. The analysis presented here, whilst based on real data, has been adapted as a pedagogical tool for an undergraduate teaching laboratory, in which students are asked to develop an understanding of neutrino oscillation theory, analyse a MicroBooNE data sample, and apply statistical methods to search for a potential sterile neutrino. The analysis incorporates machine learning techniques to improve event classification. Students are encouraged to explore these and other methods to optimise their results.

TI Negotiating academic identity under evaluation: Move-level strategies
   and identity profiles across abstracts and conclusions
SO SYSTEM
LA English
DT Article
DE Academic identity; Evaluative stance; Functional units; Novice and
   expert writing; Corpus-based analysis
ID INTERACTIONAL METADISCOURSE; RHETORICAL STRUCTURE; DISCIPLINARY;
   CITATION
AB Academic writing is a key site for negotiating professional identity under evaluative conditions. Through stance, writers manage epistemic commitment, authorial visibility, and reputational risk while aligning their texts with disciplinary expectations. Although previous studies have documented broad novice-expert differences, less is known about how evaluative resources are distributed across functionally distinct units and whether recurrent distributional patterns reflect different forms of identity positioning. This study adopts a move-sensitive corpus-based approach to examine evaluative stance in abstracts and conclusion sections. The corpus comprises 80 Applied Linguistics texts, including 40 novice-authored theses/dissertations and 40 expert-authored journal articles. Sentence-and sub-sentence-level units were coded by primary rhetorical function, and hedging, boosting, and self-mention were identified and normalized per 100 words. Descriptive and comparative analyses examined the distribution of functional units and stance deployment across writer groups, while k-means clustering of document-level normalized stance rates identified recurring stance profiles. The results show that novice and expert writers differ not only in overall stance density but also in how evaluative resources are distributed across functional units. Expert writing shows denser hedging and slightly greater self-mention, especially in conclusion-oriented discourse, whereas novice writing relies more heavily on boosting, particularly in result-and conclusion-oriented units. Clustering further identifies three recurring profiles (Authorial-balanced, Boosting-oriented, and Hedging-oriented) and their distribution differs significantly across writer groups despite substantial within-group variation. These findings suggest that novice-expert differences are better understood as context-sensitive forms of academic identity positioning than as fixed deficits. The study offers implications for academic writing pedagogy, function-sensitive feedback, and AI-supported writing development.

TI The twin paradox in the vicinity of rotating black holes
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF PHYSICS
LA English
DT Article
DE relativity; twin paradox; black holes; Jacobi field
ID RELATIVITY TWINS
AB The twin paradox is a foundational thought experiment in the special theory of relativity where a returning twin ages less than the one who remains stationary. However, the intricacies of the twin paradox remain relatively underexplored in the curved spacetimes of general relativity. Here we explore the twin paradox in the vicinity of a rotating black hole, where the existence of multiple paths between two events creates significant complexity. We develop a numerical framework based on residual maps and optimisation to identify possible trajectories. We find a strong negative correlation between a traveller's experienced proper time and both the azimuthal distance travelled and the magnitude of acceleration. We apply numerical Jacobi field analysis to examine conjugate points along geodesics within the Kerr geometry, finding that only the geodesic with the minimal azimuthal distance contains no conjugate points. This provides beginner students of general relativity with a visual tool to understand general relativistic concepts, helping to correct flat-spacetime intuitions.

TI A consistency check for energy corrections in finite-dimensional
   Rayleigh-Schrödinger perturbation theory
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF PHYSICS
LA English
DT Article
DE Rayleigh-Schr & ouml;dinger perturbation theory; trace-based sum rule;

   consistency check
AB Rayleigh-Schr & ouml;dinger perturbation theory is a standard method for approximating energy spectra, but higher-order computations are often susceptible to algebraic inconsistencies. In this work, we show that, for finite-dimensional Hamiltonians, the trace identity of the full Hamiltonian yields simple global constraints on the summed perturbative energy corrections. TI Determination of electrical conductivity of metal rods using an
   eddy-current based differential AC Wheatstone bridge
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF PHYSICS
LA English
DT Article
DE conductivity measurement; eddy current; differential ac bridge; metal
   rod
ID THERMAL-CONDUCTIVITY; RESISTANCE
AB The eddy-current methods are widely used in industry to measure electrical conductivity of metals, but they rarely appear in instructional physics experiments. In this article, we report a recently developed experiment for the undergraduate physics laboratory that uses an eddy-current based differential alternating current (AC) Wheatstone bridge to measure the conductivity of metal rods. The experiment enables students to compare the impedance of an empty coil and a coil containing a metal rod, directly linking the measured increase of effective resistance Delta R to eddy-current dissipation. From the frequency( f)-normalized response Delta R/f, the characteristic peak frequency fpeak is identified. To convert fpeak to conductivity sigma, we revisit the Dodd-Deeds framework and derive a geometric prefactor of 6.325 for our specific configuration, a significant refinement over previously reported value of 4. Measurements on copper rods with different radii b and sigma reproduce the expected scaling of fpeak proportional to sigma-1b-2 and also the energy dissipation at peak frequency scaling of b2. The conductivities obtained using the eddy-current method with the corrected prefactor show deviations from reference values ranging from 2.5 % to 16.2 %, which is comparable to the accuracy of the four-probe method ( 1.2 %-16.7 %) within uncertainty. The apparatus therefore offers a clear instructional platform that links electromagnetic induction, skin-effect crossover, AC bridge, and practical conductivity measurement.

TI Paraxial beam propagation from Airy-type initial conditions via the
   operator method
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF PHYSICS
LA English
DT Article
DE Airy beam; Airy-truncated beam; Airy-Gaussian beam; operator techniques
   of quantum mechanics
ID PHASE
AB We employ quantum mechanical operator techniques to solve the equations of (1+1)D and (2+1)D for paraxial waves with initial conditions defined by Airy-type functions. In the first part, we find the expressions of (1+1)D optical beams, considering initial conditions such as Airy, Airy-truncated, and Airy-Gaussian functions. Subsequently, we extended the analysis to (2+1)D optical beams with initial conditions generated by the product of two Airy, two Airy-truncated and two Airy-Gaussian functions, providing a comprehensive study of multidimensional Airy beam propagation. Finally, we remark that this alternative approach offers an elegant and powerful framework for analyzing paraxial wave propagation.

TI A third resonance in the damped and forced harmonic oscillator
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF PHYSICS
LA English
DT Article
DE damped and forced harmonic oscillator; resonance; oscillations
AB In this work, we consider a damped harmonic oscillator (HO) submitted to an applied force which has a harmonic time dependence and show that there is a third resonance that is not discussed in the literature. In fact, the frequency of the applied force that maximizes the average energy of the HO in the stationary regime does not coincide with its natural frequency nor with the frequency that maximizes its amplitude. We compute this third resonance frequency explicitly and verify that it lies between the other two resonance frequencies. Physical interpretations are provided for this (apparent) unexpected result. Finally, we compare the maximum value of the average energy of the HO (evaluated at this new resonance frequency) with its value evaluated at the resonance frequency of the power of the applied force and show that the former can be substantially greater than the latter for high enough values of the damping factor.

TI Performance study of a self-assembled pumping straw
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF PHYSICS
LA English
DT Article
DE pumping straw; fluid mechanics; Bernoulli's principle; Darcy-Weisbach
   equation; critical angular velocity; flow rate
AB This study presents the design and analysis of a self-assembled, triangular straw-based centrifugal pump. A combined theoretical and experimental approach was employed to systematically investigate its pumping mechanism and performance. The effects of key geometric parameters-tube length, inner diameter, and inclination angle-along with the rotational angular velocity on the volumetric flow rate were quantified. The theoretical framework integrates centrifugal force dynamics, Bernoulli's principle, and a comprehensive fluid resistance model accounting for both frictional and local losses. Experimental validation was performed using a custom-built apparatus equipped with a precision rotation control system and a flow measurement setup, testing a series of 3D-printed straw specimens with varying dimensions. The results indicate that the flow rate increases with angular velocity and the square of the tube diameter, shows an approximate linear dependence on tube length, and requires exceeding a critical angular velocity for pump initiation. This work establishes a predictive model and provides empirical data to guide the design and optimization of such low-cost, easily fabricated micro-scale pumping devices.

TI Exploring Professional and Interprofessional Identities in Student
   Pharmacists: A Comparative Analysis
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PHARMACEUTICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Professional identity; Interprofessional identity; Pharmacy education
AB Objective: This study assessed and compared the perceptions of professional identity (PI) and interprofessional identity (IPI) of third-(P3) and fourth-professional year (P4) student pharmacists and explored their inter-correlations. Methods: A cross-sectional survey was administered to P3 and P4 student pharmacists nearing the completion of the academic year. Demographics were collected. Survey instruments included the Macleod-Clark Professional Identity Scale (MCPIS-9) and the Extended Professional Identity Scale (EPIS) to measure the PI and IPI constructs, respectively. Reliability, factor structure, cohort comparisons, correlations, and predictors were analyzed. Results: Seventy-five students (87 surveyed; 86%) were included in the analysis (73% P3, 27% P4; 76% female, 24% male). Survey instruments showed high reliability (Cronbach's alpha: 0.85-0.97). Fourth-professional year (P4) students identified most with the medicines adviser and clinical practitioner PIs. Third-professional year (P3) students identified evenly with different PIs, although they showed greater identification with the business person, entrepreneur, and unremarkable character PIs. Both cohorts positively identified with the profession, with strong interprofessional belonging, commitment, and belief, as reflected in their high MCPIS-9 and EPIS scores, respectively. Fourth-professional year (P4) students exhibited a stronger professional association than P3 students, whereas IPI was similar between cohorts. The overall MCPIS-9 and EPIS scores had weak positive correlations. The EPIS subscales demonstrated strong positive intercorrelations. Conclusion: Third-and fourth-professional year (P3 and P4) student pharmacists had strong PIs and IPI. Students exhibited multiple PIs. Professional identity (PI) and IPI remained consistent across gender, professional years, and academic plans. The positive, weak association between PI and IPI indicates related yet distinct constructs. Advanced pharmacy practice experiences appear to reinforce PI and contribute to IPI.

TI A Survey of Pharmacy Technician Training Programs Within Schools of
   Pharmacy
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PHARMACEUTICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Pharmacy technician education; Academic setting; Pharmacy education;
   Workforce development; Health occupation education
AB Objective: This study examines pharmacy technician training programs offered by schools of pharmacy in the United States. Highlighted are examples of program structures, including hours, funding sources, and faculty involvement. Methods: Two pharmacy technician program databases, the Pharmacy Technician Certification Board and the American Society of Health-Systems Pharmacy/Accreditation Council for Pharmacy Education, were cross-referenced with accredited schools of pharmacy to identify available programs as of Summer 2025. School websites were reviewed to assess faculty teaching involvement and institutional support for the programs. Email invitations requested participation in a survey, either electronically or via phone. Results: Fourteen schools of pharmacy were found to meet the criteria, with 9 schools consenting to the survey. Four schools of pharmacy completed the survey electronically, and 5 consented to participate in the phone survey with the same set of questions. Six programs are offered fully online, with the remaining 3 using a combination of in-person and online instruction. Four programs incorporate pharmacy technicians alongside faculty from the school of pharmacy in teaching. Six programs follow a cohort-style approach. A combination of tuition and/or grants is used to fund programs. Variability exists across programs in terms of structure; funding; faculty involvement; and the number of hours allocated to didactic, simulation, and experiential components. Conclusion: Program structures differ significantly, giving schools of pharmacy the flexibility to design offerings aligned with their resources. Academic pharmacy technician programs may contribute to the development of a sustainable pharmacy technician workforce.

TI Expert Faculty Consensus-Based Development of the Mindful Streamlining
   Self-Assessment Tool to Address Content Overload
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PHARMACEUTICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Curricular hoarding; Streamlining; Content overload; Backward design;
   Mindfulness
AB Objective: To describe the development of the Mindful Streamlining Self-Assessment Tool (MSSAT), designed to address content overload at the instructor level. Methods: The MSSAT was developed collaboratively by 4 pharmacy faculty members and the Director of the Center for Teaching and Learning at the University of the Pacific. Using a modified Delphi process, the tool was iteratively refined through purposive sampling of academic pharmacy experts who provided structured feedback on each version. Participants were recruited via the American Association of Colleges of Pharmacy listserv and required to meet at least 3 of 6 predetermined inclusion criteria and hold a >= 0.5 full-time equivalent faculty appointment. Repeated rounds of inquiry were conducted until feedback saturation was reached. After each round, the development team met to review expert comments and implement consensus-based revisions. Experts' support was assessed using the question, "On a scale from 1 to 10, how likely are you to recommend the MSSAT to another faculty member?" Results: Twenty-one experts were included. Of these, 20 had >= 3 years of teaching experience, 12 had received a teaching award, and 15 had served on a national committee geared toward improving pharmacy education. Three rounds of inquiry were conducted. Expert-guided revisions included clarifying language, improving grammar, adding definitions, incorporating a visual figure, and providing an example of tool application. The mean expert support increased from 7.5 to 9.0, reflecting strong expert endorsement. Conclusion: The modified Delphi process yielded a consensus-driven, user-friendly tool, with relevant examples tailored to pharmacy education.

TI Experimental dynamics of a physical pendulum descending an inclined
   plane
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF PHYSICS
LA English
DT Article
DE physical pendulum; non-inertial frames; effective parameters; smartphone
   video analysis; equivalence principle
ID PRINCIPLE
AB The dynamics of a physical pendulum coupled to a support descending an inclined plane with uniform acceleration are investigated experimentally. Although this configuration is a standard problem in advanced mechanics courses, its direct quantitative experimental validation has received little attention in the physics education literature. A low-cost, reproducible setup based on a cart and smartphone video analysis was employed to study the pendulum dynamics from both inertial and non-inertial reference frames; a key feature of the design is that a second smartphone was mounted directly onto the cart, enabling the observer to operate within the accelerated frame itself. The experimental results are consistent with the theoretical model and reveal a measurable decrease in the effective gravitational field, reaching 8% at the maximum inclination studied, providing a quantitative demonstration of the equivalence principle in a classical mechanical context. A systematic increase in the effective moment of inertia with inclination angle is also observed and attributed to inclination-dependent displacement of the suspension point, offering a natural framework for introducing the concept of effective parameters in real physical systems. The experiment thus constitutes a reproducible pedagogical resource for undergraduate instruction in coupled systems, non-inertial reference frames, and physical modelling strategies using accessible equipment.

TI Transforming introductory physics labs: goals, multilayered experiments
   and modularized courses
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF PHYSICS
LA English
DT Article
DE introductory physics laboratories; multilayered experiment; physics
   experiment; modularized course; lab skills; designing experiments;
   inquiry-based
AB Introductory physics labs engage students in authentic science practices that provide significant benefits for science and engineering undergraduates. With this in mind, we have implemented a comprehensive transformation of the introductory physics lab curriculum. This transformation process involves establishing clear course goals, designing multilayered experiments (MEs) that align with these goals and developing a modularized course. The ME design provides students with varying levels of inquiry and complexity within a single experimental topic. Furthermore, the modularized course design enables customized content that can be tailored to meet the diverse needs of different student populations. This paper discusses the implementation of these course goals in a large-enrollment introductory physics lab course, presents an example of MEs and modularized courses and discusses assessment related to practical implementation. While specific implementations of introductory lab courses may vary significantly across institutions, we demonstrate that two key strategies, MEs and modularized courses, are broadly applicable strategies for improving the quality of lab instruction through well-defined course goals.

ID ALZHEIMERS-DISEASE; DOWN-SYNDROME; OLDER-ADULTS; PEOPLE; PREVALENCE;
   SEVERITY; SYMPTOMS
AB Background Individuals with intellectual disabilities (ID) are at an increased risk of developing dementia. Early detection is essential for providing appropriate support, yet identifying dementia-related changes is challenging due to pre-existing cognitive impairments. Informant-based adapted tools have been developed to support dementia screening in individuals with ID. Among those, the Dementia Screening Questionnaire for Individuals with Intellectual Disabilities (DSQIID) aims to assess behavioural and functional changes related to dementia. This study aimed to examine the associations between the DSQIID total scores, cognitive performance and demographic characteristics of adults with ID.Method This cross-sectional study included 322 individuals with ID (n Down syndrome [DS] = 55; n non-DS ID = 267). Behavioural and functional changes were assessed using the DSQIID, whereas cognitive functioning was measured with the Test for Severe Impairment (TSI), Brief Praxis Test (BPT) and a semantic verbal fluency task. Negative binomial regression analyses were conducted to explore associations between DSQIID total scores and selected demographic and cognitive variables.Results Age was significantly associated with behavioural dementia-related changes, as assessed by the DSQIID, whereas ID severity was not associated. Results further showed that participants with DS had significantly higher scores on the DSQIID compared to participants with ID without DS. Higher DSQIID scores were significantly associated with higher semantic verbal fluency performance.Conclusions Our findings suggest that caregivers may more readily detect behavioural and functional changes in adults with ID who exhibit relatively good verbal capacities. This study underscores the elevated risk of dementia in adults with DS and highlights the importance of supporting caregivers in recognizing early signs of dementia in adults with ID who exhibit lower verbal capacities. The findings underscore the importance of monitoring behavioural, functional and cognitive changes over time. Further research is needed to explore the associations between reported dementia-related changes and the severity of ID.

TI The Multistate Pharmacy Jurisprudence Exam (MPJE): To RIP or Not to RIP
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PHARMACEUTICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE MPJE; Barriers; Patient safety; Assessment
AB Objective: This narrative review aimed to discuss the utility of the Multistate Pharmacy Jurisprudence Examination (MPJE) as a licensure requirement and contrast the advantages and disadvantages of its elimination and to analyze the impact of alternative solutions to MPJE already implemented in different states. Findings: The current utility of MPJE has been questioned by various stakeholders. Currently, several states have either removed the law exam or adopted an alternative assessment to evaluate pharmacy law and regulation competencies. Proponents of removing the MPJE highlight the need to reduce barriers to licensure, challenge the utility of a single exam as a measurement of lifelong competency, and highlight the lack of evidence demonstrating that a single exam preserves patient safety. Advocates for keeping the MPJE exam propose modifying the current exam format and express their concern about eroding public trust with the removal of the exam. Summary: This paper provides a comprehensive, multifaceted analysis of the ongoing national debate surrounding the MPJE as a pharmacist licensure requirement, synthesizing perspectives from major stakeholder organizations and state-level policy changes. It advances the literature by proposing 4 concrete, evidence-based recommendations (reforming the MPJE, exploring alternative ongoing competency models, examining outcomes in states with different assessment methods, and reducing licensure barriers) that offer suggestions for guiding future policy decisions.

TI Rest as Strategy: The Importance of Psychological Detachment From Work
   for Sustained Career Productivity
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PHARMACEUTICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
ID JOB STRESSORS; RECOVERY; PARADOX; WELL
AB Faculty members often face implicit pressure to maintain work engagement during periods intended for rest. These pressures normalize visible busyness and subtly devalue physical and mental restoration as secondary to constant availability. Despite concerted calls to support faculty well-being, working during evenings, weekends, and holidays remains culturally acceptable and, at times, is applauded as a sign of professional commitment. We draw on organizational behavior literature to examine how these norms undermine rest, conceptualized here as psychological detachment, and reframe detachment as essential to sustained performance. Psychological detachment is a multidimensional process crucial for recovery that involves mentally disengaging from work during nonwork time, allowing depleted cognitive and emotional resources to be restored. Stress-recovery research demonstrates that persistent work engagement beyond reasonable work hours is detrimental to well-being, creativity, and long-term productivity, whereas regular psychological detachment improves performance, work engagement, growth, and career vitality. We specify what does and does not constitute psychological detachment and acknowledge the barriers to detachment, which include elevated workloads, administrative responsibilities, preferences for integrated work-life arrangements, and varying work schedules. We recommend that institutions and faculty adopt deliberate practices that protect and promote rest as a core component of academic work. The Academy should recognize rest as a strategic enabler of sustainable faculty careers and personal well-being as an alternative to productivity gained from self-sacrificial overwork.

TI Exploring Student and Faculty Staff Perceptions of a Student-Led
   Cardiovascular Disease Screening Clinic
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PHARMACEUTICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Pharmacy; Student-based clinic; Work-based learning; Qualitative
   research; Public health promotion
ID MODEL; CARE
AB Objective: To explore pharmacy students' and faculty's perspectives on the learning and experience of a student-led cardiovascular disease (CVD) screening clinic as a form of work-based learning, with a focus on identifying opportunities for optimization of the educational experience. Methods: A qualitative study design, using focus groups with second-year pharmacy students (n = 22) and semistructured interviews with faculty staff (n = 5) who supervised the CVD screening clinic. The clinic operated over 88 days at a city center location and offered opportunistic walk-in CVD screening to members of the public. A phenomenographic approach was used to explore the range of ways participants conceptualized their experiences. Transcripts were analyzed thematically, and findings were interpreted using an established work-based learning model to derive broader pedagogical insights. Results: Three key themes were identified: learning in action, consultation barriers, and shaping the future. Students reported enhanced clinical confidence, improved consultation skills, and a greater appreciation of patient-centered care. Challenges included delivering sensitive health messages, navigating lifestyle advice, maintaining motivation after fulfilling assessment requirements, and engaging with complex referral pathways. The work-based learning model highlighted key areas for improvement, including mechanisms to support student-patient interaction, artifacts (tools) to aid participation, and strategies to foster motivation and practical competence. Conclusion: Student-led clinics offer rich learning opportunities but require careful design and support to maximize their educational value. Insights from this study can inform the development of sustainable, pedagogically grounded work-based learning experiences in pharmacy education that promote confidence, patient-facing activities, and consultation skills.

TI Transitional Justice Mechanisms, Collective Memory, and Teacher
   Narratives
SO COMPARATIVE EDUCATION REVIEW
LA English
DT Article
ID HISTORY EDUCATION; RWANDA; CONSTRUCTION; CURRICULUM; IDENTITY; POLITICS;
   GENOCIDE
AB This study examines how Rwandan and Sierra Leonean secondary school teachers negotiate narratives generated by transitional justice mechanisms (TJMs) when teaching histories of violence. TJMs in both countries produced collective memory; yet their integration into national curricula differs. The Rwandan government enforces an official state narrative, whereas Sierra Leone's limited state mediation gives teachers greater discretion. Informed by 60 teacher interviews and over 20 hours of classroom observation, the study reveals that teachers in both contexts adopt TJM narratives, even when such narratives are absent from official educational materials. Drawing upon literature from the sociology of knowledge, comparative and international education, and memory studies, this article underscores the complex relationship between state power, TJMs, and educator narratives. These findings contribute to a growing body of research on postconflict history education, suggesting that TJMs play a crucial role in how educators understand historical trauma and teach it to future generations.

TI Modeling teachers' reflections on school transition practices for
   students with autism and/or intellectual disabilities: Evidence from
   bifactor SEM and associations with mathematics teaching efficacy
SO RESEARCH IN AUTISM
LA English
DT Article
DE Autism spectrum disorder; Teacher reflection; School transition;
   Mathematics; teaching efficacy; Saudi Arabia
ID PROFESSIONAL-DEVELOPMENT; SPECTRUM DISORDER; SELF-EFFICACY; OUTCOMES
AB This study models teachers' reflections on school transition practices for students with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and/or Intellectual Disabilities as a hierarchical cognitive-metacognitive ability and evaluates its latent structure using structural equation modeling (SEM) and bifactor item response theory (IRT). Drawing on hierarchical models of intelligence, we examined whether reflective professional reasoning comprises a general factor alongside domain-specific components. A sample of 237 special education teachers working with students with ASD and/ or Intellectual Disabilities completed measures of reflective transition practices and mathematics teaching efficacy. Results from SEM supported a correlated multidimensional structure, while bifactor modeling indicated the presence of a statistically identifiable general reflective reasoning dimension coexisting with substantial domain-specific variance. The general factor demonstrated high reliability, although explained common variance suggested meaningful differentiation across domains. Reflective reasoning was strongly associated with mathematics teaching efficacy (r = .63), and structural modeling indicated that teachers' reflections on school transition practices positively predicted mathematics teaching efficacy beliefs (beta =.30). These findings position reflections on transition practices for students with ASD and/or Intellectual Disabilities as a hierarchical cognitive construct linked to performance-related beliefs in a reasoning-intensive domain. Implications for modeling professional cognition and teacher development in autismrelated educational contexts are discussed.

TI What Drives Nonstructural School Mobility? An Analysis of School Push
   and Pull Factors in California
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
ID RESIDENTIAL-MOBILITY; POOR; ACHIEVEMENT; DISRUPTION; INEQUALITY
AB Purpose: This study provides a comprehensive portrait of nonstructural student mobility in California, examining its overall incidence, how it varies across racial/ethnic and socioeconomic subgroups, and which school-level characteristics function as "push" and "pull" factors driving school changes. Research Methods/Approach: Using rich longitudinal administrative data from a sample of large, diverse California school districts, we employ a sending-school incidence framework to distinguish summer nonstructural moves from midyear moves and structural transitions. We model the school-level and student-level predictors of each move type and estimate predicted probabilities of mobility as a function of differences in school achievement, racial congruence, and residential mobility across race/ethnicity and free and reduced-price lunch eligibility subgroups. Findings: Low school achievement, high school poverty, elevated absenteeism, and other markers of poor school quality function as significant push factors. High achievement acts as a pull factor for all students, as does moving toward a less racially congruent-typically more diverse-school. Summer nonstructural mobility appears more strategic than midyear mobility, which rarely leads to better schools for any group. Residential mobility enables moves into higher-quality schools for all families, but this effect is substantially stronger for Asian American, Filipino or Pacific Islander and White students than for Black and Latinx students. Implications: Systemic barriers-including residential segregation, restrictive attendance zones, and historical housing discrimination-appear to limit the ability of low-income Black and Latinx families to leverage residential and school mobility into improved academic conditions. Policies aimed at reducing inequitable mobility patterns should attend to these constraints.

SO ECONOMICS OF EDUCATION REVIEW

AB This paper examines earnings differences between first-generation and continuing-generation college graduates across 24 OECD countries using data from the OECD Survey of Adult Skills (PIAAC). In most countries analyzed, first-generation graduates earn significantly less than their peers from college-educated families, with an average gap across all countries of approximately 7.5%. TI Dhyaan: Caring Pedagogy and the Enactment of Inclusive Education
   in India
SO COMPARATIVE EDUCATION REVIEW
LA English
DT Article
ID CARE; DISABILITIES; CHILDREN
AB The lack of clarity within inclusive education is compounded by the ways in which inclusive education reforms circulated from Global North countries to the Global South. Scholars call for contextually and culturally relevant conceptualizations of inclusive education in the Global South. I present a pedagogical approach to inclusive education developed with 22 female teachers in India through 78 interviews and 75 classroom observations, developed through ethnographic case studies of two school-NGO partnerships in Muslim-majority schools. The Hindi term dhyaan, which translates to care or attention, was identified through teacher interviews as a metaphor for teachers' inclusive practices. Conceptualizing dhyaan as a culturally sustaining concept, I demonstrate how teachers practice care and how they reckon with the normative tendencies of inclusive education. Drawing on disability studies and ethics of care, I offer grounded understandings of care and disability in the enactment of inclusive education in India.

   English-language videos: A systemic functional multimodal discourse

LA English
DT Article
DE Systemic functional multimodal discourse analysis; Meta-functions; Civic

   language learning
AB Learners' civic engagement has increasingly been acknowledged as an important component of language curricula, especially in second/foreign language learning contexts. While digital multimodal composing (DMC) has been shown to provide opportunities for learners to engage with issues of public concern, relatively little research has examined how civic engagement is semiotically enacted and made communicable to audiences in multimodal texts. This study further reports learners' orchestration practices of multiple semiotic resources for communicating their civic engagement within the meta-functional construct. SFMDA is argued to be a useful approach for understanding students' civic engagement in multimodal texts. Pedagogical implications are provided for integrating DMC into second- or foreign-language learning classrooms to enhance the civic engagement of multilingual learners.

TI Broker-mediated paraphrasing in ERPP contexts: evidence from Iranian EFL
   teachers as literacy brokers
SO LINGUISTICS AND EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Literacy brokers; Paraphrasing strategies; Plagiarism; Research articles
ID MULTILINGUAL SCHOLARS; GRADUATE-STUDENTS; ENGLISH TEACHERS; STRATEGIES;
   MANUSCRIPTS; PLAGIARISM; ATTITUDES; REVISIONS; ARTICLES; COLLEGE
AB Paraphrasing English manuscripts is a demanding task that requires high academic standards. To achieve this, many non-native English speakers seek assistance from English professionals who act as literacy brokers (LBs). This study investigates LBs' paraphrasing strategies. We analyzed the paraphrasing practices of eleven Iranian EFL teachers functioning as LBs across forty-five manuscripts from various disciplines that required substantial paraphrasing. Drawing on insights from Sun and Yang's (2015) paraphrasing strategy frameworks, we compared the authors' drafts with brokers' paraphrased versions and developed a seven-category taxonomy consisting of substitution, expanding, condensing, reordering, combining, separating, and citing changes. The findings revealed that using synonyms as a lexical substitution and reordering were the most commonly used paraphrasing strategies. Additionally, this study found that the introduction and discussion were the most requested sections for reparaphrasing, containing the highest frequency of paraphrasing strategies. Beyond identifying these patterns, the findings suggest that broker-mediated paraphrasing primarily functions as a form of textual mediation shaped by publication-oriented concerns, particularly textual similarity reduction and linguistic acceptability. By foregrounding literacy brokers as providers of linguistic mediation rather than disciplinary co-authors, the study advances a conceptual distinction between surface-level and deeper forms of paraphrasing in ERPP contexts. In doing so, it reconceptualizes broker-mediated paraphrasing as a role-conditioned and institutionally situated practice shaped by publication-oriented demands.

TI Reading with a purpose: How eye movements and working memory inform
   comprehension across L1 and L2 English readers
SO SYSTEM
LA English
DT Article
DE Adult reading; Eye movements; Reading comprehension; Purposeful reading;
   Working memory
ID INDIVIDUAL-DIFFERENCES; INFERENCE GENERATION; SPAN TASKS; CAPACITY;
   FREQUENCY; KNOWLEDGE; PATTERNS; TESTS
AB This study investigated the influence of reading purpose and working memory capacity (WMC) on eye movement patterns and comprehension outcomes in native (L1) and non-native (L2) English readers. We aimed to determine whether purposeful reading elicits distinct processing strategies across language groups and whether WMC moderates these effects. Seventy-five college students completed an eye-tracking experiment while reading two academic texts under one of two conditions: reading for information or reading for study. Comprehension was assessed through multiple-choice questions and a free recall task. WMC was measured using a standardized Reading Span Task. Linear mixed-effects models on skipping probability, fixation durations, regressions, and comprehension scores revealed that reading purpose significantly affected latestage eye movement measures. Fixation count, regression count, and rereading duration increased in the study condition, indicating more effortful processing. L1 readers skipped more words during study reading, whereas L2 readers skipped less, suggesting more deliberate reading. L2 readers outperformed L1 readers in recall, particularly in the study condition, despite similar fixation durations. WMC did not significantly affect fixation-based measures in either group. However, in the L2 group, WMC influenced recall, with lower WMC readers benefiting more from purposeful reading. Findings highlight the adaptive nature of reading and the role of goal-driven strategies in second language comprehension. Purposeful reading can enhance recall in L2 readers, particularly those with lower WMC, underscoring the need to consider cognitive resources when evaluating reading across languages. Results align with goal-directed models of reading, such as RESOLV and the Construction-Integration Model.

AB This study investigates adolescent students' engagement during a digital language game that has been designed to facilitate learning Swedish as a second language (L2). TI The role of initiation-response-feedback (IRF) sequences in organizing
   learning during a college educational choir's rehearsals
SO LEARNING CULTURE AND SOCIAL INTERACTION
LA English
DT Article
DE Choral education; Interaction analysis; Conversation analysis; Learning
   in the arts
ID DIRECTIVES; DIALOGUE
AB I employ interaction analysis alongside ideas of turn-taking, sequence, and structure from conversation analysis to analyze how a conductor organizes rehearsals for an educational choir. As learning happens, the conductor uses a particular sequence while also modifying the structure of a rehearsal which reflects that learning and promotes further learning. TI Language as mediator of learning opportunities: How teacher discourse
   shapes participation access in Chinese multilingual education
SO LINGUISTICS AND EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Discourse analysis; Discursive positioning; Learning opportunities;
   Multilingual education; Ethnic minority preparatory education; Emotional
   labor
AB This study investigates how teachers' linguistic choices discursively position ethnic minority students and mediate their access to learning opportunities. Drawing on systematic discourse analysis of 730 min of classroom observations and interviews in a Chinese ethnic minority preparatory program, we examine mechanisms through which language constitutes-rather than merely reflects-participation access. Analysis of 310 pronoun instances and 46 teacher questions reveals four discourse mechanisms-pronoun selection, meta-pragmatic framing, temporal deixis, and question design-that systematically constitute students' participation access. Boundary-marking (sic)(sic) appeared 66 times, with 82% co-occurring with deficit-oriented content, demonstrating how automatized linguistic choices constrain learning opportunities beneath teachers' conscious awareness. Longitudinal retrospective data from one student, corroborated by cross-sectional comparison, suggests that identical discourse strategies yield differential positioning effects depending on students' cultural-linguistic distance and proficiency development-for instance, explicit heritage validation may support high-distance students at early stages while being experienced as othering by low-distance students. Students evaluate teacher authenticity not through inferred emotional states but through observable discourse features: longitudinal consistency in cultural knowledge retention, complexity calibration matched to developmental stage, and paralinguistic-semantic alignment. These findings operationalize "cultural responsiveness" as concrete, teachable discourse competencies-pronoun sensitivity, meta-pragmatic awareness, question design, and complexity calibration-amenable to systematic measurement and pedagogical training, providing an empirically grounded framework for teacher preparation in multilingual educational contexts.

TI Feasibility and preliminary outcomes of a parent-mediated telehealth
   intervention for feeding difficulties in children with autism spectrum
   disorder
SO RESEARCH IN AUTISM
LA English
DT Article
DE Autism spectrum disorder; Feeding difficulties; Food selectivity;
   Telehealth; Parent-mediated intervention; Applied behavior analysis
ID MEALTIME BEHAVIOR PROBLEMS; FOOD SELECTIVITY; METAANALYSIS
AB Introduction: Feeding difficulties are highly prevalent in children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and represent a significant source of family stress. Although in-person behavioral interventions have demonstrated effectiveness, access to them is limited. Parent-mediated interventions delivered via telehealth are emerging as a promising alternative, although evidence remains scarce. Objective: To evaluate the feasibility, acceptability, and preliminary efficacy of a parent-mediated behavioral intervention delivered via telehealth for feeding difficulties in children with ASD. Method: A prospective single-arm pilot study with a pre-post design and follow-ups at 3, 6, and 12 months was conducted. Participants were 26 children with ASD, aged 3-8 years, with clinically significant feeding difficulties. The 8-week intervention was based on applied behavior analysis principles and included psychoeducation, training in behavioral strategies, and individualized follow-up via videoconference. Measures included parental adherence, parental satisfaction, feeding behaviors, variety of accepted foods, parental stress, and family quality of life. Results: The intervention showed moderate-to-high levels of parental adherence. Families reported high satisfaction and good acceptability of the telehealth format. Significant reductions in food selectivity were observed, along with a progressive increase in the variety of accepted foods, particularly at 6 months. No significant changes were found in parental stress or family quality of life. Conclusions: This pilot study supports the feasibility and acceptability of a parent-mediated behavioral feeding intervention delivered via telehealth, with preliminary positive effects on food selectivity. Controlled trials are needed to confirm these findings.

TI Linking textbook grammar input to writing accuracy in exam-oriented EFL
   systems: A CEFR-B1, corpus-based study
SO SYSTEM
LA English
DT Article
DE Textbook grammar input; Input frequency; Dispersion and recycling;
   Section distribution; Learner corpus; Writing accuracy; CEFR; EFL
ID INSTRUCTION; FREQUENCY; CURRICULUM
AB In exam-oriented EFL systems, textbooks often function as the practical syllabus for high-stakes writing. This study examined whether corpus-derived properties of textbook grammar input were associated with learner writing outcomes at the CEFR B1 level. Because examinees could not be linked to the specific textbook series or edition they had used, the analysis was interpreted as system-level alignment rather than causal effects of particular materials. A set of 244 B1-level grammar points (GPs) was consolidated from the English Grammar Profile and operationalized through Corpus Query Processor (CQP) patterns validated by dual-tagger checks, manual concordance inspection, and iterative refinement to a precision threshold of at least 90%. Textbook input was quantified in a corpus of 15 Ministry-approved Taiwanese senior-high textbooks representing three series across five volumes using three indices: frequency, cross-volume recycling, and section breadth across six harmonised section types. Learner output was measured in 34,753 timed national entrance-exam essays, from which GP-level attempted use and accurate use were coded from retrieved concordance instances. The main analyses examined conditional accuracy given use for GPs attempted at least once, with supplementary analyses retaining zeroattempt items to capture productive availability. Textbook input showed a strongly frontloaded and highly skewed distribution. All three indices were positively associated with learner outcomes, and section breadth emerged as the most consistent predictor. The associations were substantially stronger when zero-attempt items were retained, suggesting that textbook input aligned more closely with productive availability than with accuracy once use had occurred. These findings highlight the importance of input architecture beyond raw frequency.

TI "African slavery was becoming an essential part": Examining language,
   agency, and power in the representation of enslavement in US history
   textbooks
SO LINGUISTICS AND EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE US history; Textbooks; Systemic functional linguistics; Critical race
   theory; Transitivity analysis; Enslavement
ID CRITICAL RACE THEORY; NARRATIVES
AB Amid a time when bans against curriculum, books, and words have been enacted, we analyze the authors' word choice in the portrayal of enslavement over the past four adopted U.S. history textbooks in Florida from 2005-2024. Drawing upon Systemic Functional Linguistics (SFL) and Critical Race Theory (CRT), this study examines how main participants are positioned, types of verb processes used, and how these linguistic choices create racialized hierarchical representations. Textbook authors position these participants intentionally through the primary use of action and relational verbs that depict events and relationships, while giving minimal attention to emotions and individual voices. The findings reveal that textbook authors overwhelmingly favor white participants by centering their actions, thoughts, feelings, and utterances. In contrast, Black participants have limited space for counterstories, and when included, are minimized or dehumanized. Furthermore, nonhuman entities serve as ways to obscure responsibility for cruelty and the system of enslavement, thereby absolving white actors. Implications call for greater language awareness and correction of textbooks to better reflect the lived experiences and histories of marginalized groups and critically challenge dominant ideologies within historical narratives.

TI Challenging or reinforcing the "native speaker" divide? A
   corpus-informed critical discourse study of linguistic identity in
   language education journal articles
SO LINGUISTICS AND EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Linguistic identity; Native-speakerism; Critical discourse analysis;
   Corpus linguistics; Language ideology; Terminology; Language education
ID ENGLISH SPEAKERS; TEACHER IDENTITY
AB The "(non)native speaker" dichotomy is not merely a linguistic classification but an ideological construct that shapes pedagogical authority, cognitive worth, and professional opportunities in language education. Despite decades of critique, its persistence in academic literature continues to shape and, often, limit the perceived identities and professional participation of learners and educators. This corpus-based critical discourse analysis of 594 journal articles investigates how "(non)native speaker" labels are employed in contemporary research. Integrating quantitative corpus techniques-including collocation analysis, frequency distributions, dispersion patterns, and document-level framework tracking-with qualitative concordance interpretation informed by Fairclough's (2003) dialectical-relational framework, we reveal: (1) a pervasive, uncritical retention of these labels, which are naturalized through genre conventions and often lack operational definitions; (2) the emergent recontextualization of "(non)native speaker" as a contested term, signalling a growing disciplinary unease; and (3) a fundamental contradiction between researchers' critical stances and their actual language practices. We argue that this persistence is rooted in institutional norms that privilege dichotomous categories, creating a trade-off between communicative convenience and terminological precision. The scarcity and limited uptake of robust alternative frameworks means that even critical scholarship often inadvertently reinforces the very paradigm it seeks to dismantle. This study contributes to disrupting monolingual ideologies by demonstrating how scholarly discourse itself becomes a site of ideological reproduction, and it advocates for urgent terminological reform and contextually grounded frameworks to advance equity in language education.

TI Assessing L2 legal writing through a plain English lens: Insights on
   complexity, accuracy, and fluency
SO SYSTEM
LA English
DT Article
DE Complexity; Accuracy; Fluency; L2 legal writing; Writing assessment;
   Plain English pedagogy
ID SYNTACTIC COMPLEXITY; LEXICAL SOPHISTICATION; AUTOMATIC-ANALYSIS;
   QUALITY; PROFICIENCY; FEATURES; PERFORMANCE; JUDGMENTS; INDEXES
AB Legal English writing pedagogy in the United States has been largely shaped by the plain English movement, which prioritizes clarity and concision. At the same time, second language (L2) writing research emphasizes complexity as a hallmark of development, which creates a potential tension for L2 legal writing instruction. Using mixed-effects modeling, we examined how complexity, accuracy, and fluency measures intersect with instructors' evaluations of L2 legal essays within a classroom setting.
