This study offers empirically grounded implications for instruction, suggesting that greater pedagogical emphasis on grammatical accuracy, clarity, and precision aligns more closely with instructor assessment practices within a plain English legal discourse than an early focus on syntactic complexity.

TI Peer assessment of classroom videos as preparation for student teachers'
   future profession
SO LEARNING CULTURE AND SOCIAL INTERACTION
LA English
DT Article
DE Video-based learning; Teacher education; Professional development;
   Epistemic fluency
ID EDUCATION; VISION
AB Researchers and policymakers have emphasized that universities, particularly teacher education programs, could explore new ways to facilitate professional learning, reducing the persistent theory-practice gap, promoting coherence in teacher education, and preparing students better for a rapidly changing professional landscape. TI The intersectionality of gender and location in health education access
   in Chinese vocational high schools
SO HEALTH EDUCATION RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
ID SEXUAL COERCION; ATTITUDES
AB Through intersectionality theory, this study examines how gender and geographical location interact to shape adolescents' access to health education in centralized systems, using sex education in Chinese vocational high schools as an illustrative case. Drawing on data from 3167 adolescents across regions with varying development levels, we demonstrate how educational institutions reproduce gender hierarchies and geographical inequalities through differential access to sex education. Students in economically developed regions and urban areas show significantly higher odds of receiving sex education, with particularly pronounced effects for girls in developed regions. Gender emerges as the primary determinant of exposure to specific content, with girls consistently showing higher chances of being taught topics like pregnancy, contraception, and sexual behavior. These findings suggest two intersecting forms of disadvantage. Resource-wise, boys in less developed regions appear most likely to be excluded from sustained provision. Norm-wise, girls may be more harmed by how sex education is framed through gendered expectations that treat sexual and reproductive health as primarily their responsibility rather than a shared concern. Together, these patterns illustrate how intersecting dimensions of advantage and disadvantage, alongside underlying patriarchal assumptions, create systematic disparities that reinforce both gender and geographical inequalities.

TI Racial Homophily in Context: Tie Types and Organizational Composition in
   Teacher Networks
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article

   WHITE; COLLABORATION; PROPINQUITY
AB Purpose: Racial homophily-the tendency to form ties with same-race colleagues-is common in workplace networks, including schools. But we know less about how it varies across relationship types and organizational racial composition. We examine racial homophily in teachers' instructional advice, disciplinary advice, and friendship networks, comparing Black and White teachers in majority-White and majority-Black schools. There is also a lack of evidence as to whether the pandemic has really boosted digitization in schools. Aims: Our study examines (1) the impact of the pandemic on students' learning gains, (2) the relationship between school context variables related to students' home environment and learning gains, and (3) the extent to which school closures contributed to an increased use of digital learning support systems. TI When to inquire and when to instruct: Prior knowledge and element
   interactivity in medical learning
SO LEARNING AND INSTRUCTION
LA English
DT Article
DE Explicit instruction; Inquiry-based learning; Cognitive load; Element
   interactivity; Instructional sequence
ID EXPERTISE; SKILLS; ACQUISITION; GUIDANCE; DESIGN; WORK; LOAD
AB Background: Teaching in medical education often alternates between explicit instruction and inquiry-based learning, yet their optimal sequencing for high-element-interactivity content as a function of prior knowledge remains unclear. Aims: This study investigated whether sequencing explicit instruction before inquiry, or inquiry before explicit instruction, differentially affects learning of pharmacology concepts with high element interactivity. Sample: Participants were 211 undergraduate prehospital care students. Method: In a randomised design, students were assigned to either explicit instruction before inquiry or inquiry before explicit instruction. Prior knowledge was measured via a pre-test and included as a continuous variable. Post-test performance was analysed using ANCOVA. All participants completed an identical clinical simulation. Results: The main effect of prior knowledge was non-significant, whereas the main effect of instructional sequence was significant, indicating that students in the explicit instruction before inquiry condition outperformed those in the inquiry before explicit instruction condition on the post-test. A significant interaction between instructional sequence and prior knowledge was also found. For students with lower prior knowledge, explicit instruction before inquiry led to higher performance. For students with higher prior knowledge, the reverse sequence was more effective. Conclusions: Findings are consistent with cognitive load theory and the expertise reversal effect. Explicit instruction before inquiry benefited learners with lower prior knowledge, whereas the reverse sequence was more effective for those with higher prior knowledge. Aligning instructional sequence with prior knowledge may optimise conceptual learning in complex domains such as medical education.

TI School Choice and Socioeconomic Stratification: A Comparison of Black
   and Hispanic Student Enrollment in Detroit
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
ID DECISION-MAKING; SEARCH
AB Purpose: A large body of research has studied the dynamics of school choice for racially minoritized students in the United States. An emerging body of research has considered the racial and ethnic differences in school choice opportunities and experiences among racially minoritized groups. In this mixed-methods study, I examine school choice in Detroit and stratified enrollment by socioeconomic status, with specific attention to whether and why the patterns of enrollment stratification differ between Black and Hispanic students in the city. TI How News of Parents' Activism in Schools Frames Educational
   Possibilities
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
ID POLITICS; POWER
AB Purpose: The researchers examine how parents' rights groups gain power and how authoritarianism may spread and be received in educational settings. We analyzed US news reporting on parents' rights activism leading up to the 2024 election and immediately after it, how local place and leaning of news sources inform production of news on parents' rights activism, how news sources framed messages about parents' rights activism in light of the outcomes of the 2024 election, and how teachers, families, and children are positioned within media discourses. Research Methods/Approach: We used ethnographic content analysis of frames and discourses in eight major US newspapers across pre-to-post-2024 presidential election periods. Findings: Parents' rights activists and media tend to use "flood the zone" strategies promoting extremist school politics. Only two parents' rights groups received consistent coverage but monopolized reporting. Countermovement groups worked against the grain but received limited space in news cycles. Subthemes highlighted these key frames for representing parents' rights groups' roles in the authoritarian age of politics: including right-wing mothers' omnipresence in the news, silencing of countermovement groups, and protection and promotion of elite White heteropatriarchy. The roles of silence and representation of children, families, and teachers in promoting parents' rights as well as news influence on communities are discussed, along with strategies for undermining parents' rights. Implications: By studying right-wing women and news representing them, we can gain greater awareness of silences, areas of contestation, and strategies to interrupt threats that parents' rights bring to public education.

TI The Convergence of Institutional Logics in Community Colleges: Adjunct
   Faculty and the Reproduction of Inequities in the Professoriate
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
ID PART-TIME FACULTY
AB Purpose: In this article, we examine the experiences of adjunct faculty in the community college sector and analyze how they use dominant institutional logics to rationalize their decision making and behaviors. We pay particular attention to how adjunct faculty converge dominant institutional logics to explain, and in many instances produce, the disparities they experience. Research Methods/Approach: For this qualitative study, we analyzed interviews from 25 community college adjunct faculty in California, which is the largest community college sector in the United States. Findings: We found that adjuncts in our sample decided to teach in the community college sector because they believed they could make a difference in the educational trajectories of racially diverse students, those attending underresourced schools, or students previously underserved but motivated to learn. However, we also found that adjunct faculty encountered challenges rooted in state and capitalist logics that dehumanized them. Moreover, adjunct faculty experienced tensions between their desire to make a difference and their sense of being exploited by full-time faculty, administrators, and the community college system. Implications: This research contributes to our understanding of the relationship between societal institutional logics and everyday experiences of community college adjunct faculty. It provides empirical evidence for implementing accountability structures to improve adjuncts' working conditions.

TI Generative AI as a psychological Empowerer: The central role of
   self-efficacy in developing pre-service teachers' instructional design
   skills
SO LEARNING AND INSTRUCTION
LA English
DT Article
DE Generative artificial intelligence; Teacher education; Instructional
   design; Self-efficacy; Mediation analysis
ID USER ACCEPTANCE
AB Background: A core theoretical debate persists regarding whether generative artificial intelligence (GAI) serves as a "psychological empowerer" or a "cognitive substitute" in teacher education. Moving beyond prevailing research that focuses on end products or attitudes, this study investigates the internal psychological mechanisms through which GAI influences professional competency. Methods: Grounded in social cognitive theory, a between-subjects experiment (N = 240) was conducted with pre-service teachers, randomly assigned to one of three conditions: a GAI-assisted condition, a search engine-assisted condition, or a no-technology condition. All participants independently designed a 45-min technology-enhanced lesson plan within their major discipline. Results: Key findings show the GAI group had significantly higher instructional design self-efficacy, lower cognitive load, and superior designs in pedagogical soundness, technology integration, and-most notably-innovativeness. Crucially, mediation analyses identified self-efficacy as the core mechanism (full mediator for pedagogical soundness; partial mediator for technology integration/innovativeness), while cognitive load's mediating role was non-significant. Conclusions: These results robustly confirm the "psychological empowerment" pathway, resolving the theoretical debate and providing a foundation for shifting teacher education from a "tool-application" to a "human-AI collaboration" paradigm.

TI Emotion regulation and learning from academic failures
SO LEARNING AND INSTRUCTION
LA English
DT Article
DE EMOTION REGULATION; EMOTIONAL integration; LEARNING; FAILURES
ID ERROR MANAGEMENT; CHILDRENS; INTEGRATION; MOTIVATION
AB Background: Research indicates negative emotions can impede learning, but studies on emotion regulation and learning from failure are limited.<br /> Aims: This study hypothesized emotional integration (i.e., taking interest in negative emotions), anchored in selfdetermination theory, predicts the tendency to learn from academic failure, as opposed to emotion dysregulation and suppression that involve less than optimal responses to failure.<br /> Sample: Two studies were conducted among college students, measured before and after an exam failure. Study 1 involved 907 students, with 385 reporting failure in the second measurement (mean age = 26.89; SD = 4.02). Study 2 included 484 students, with 147 reporting a specific failure in calculus (mean age = 22.19; SD = 2.56).<br /> Method: In the first measurement, participants reported their emotion regulation styles and academic efficacy. In the second measurement, they reported adaptive and maladaptive responses to failure and their tendency to learn from it. Study 2 additionally assessed engagement before and after failure.<br /> Results: Study 1 showed that adaptive responses mediated the positive link between emotional integration and learning from failure, whereas suppressive regulation and dysregulation hindered learning through maladaptive responses. Study 2 found that learning from failure mediated the link between emotional integration and engagement, while rumination linked dysregulation to disengagement; suppressive regulation again predicted maladaptive responses. Analyses controlled for initial engagement and academic efficacy.<br /> Conclusions: Emotional integration, the tendency to be receptive to negative emotions, may foster learning and engagement after failure by treating emotions as informative and engaging non-judgmentally with the experience of failure.

TI Digital readiness in nursing education: eHealth literacy, AI attitudes,
   and associated factors among undergraduate students
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Nursing students; Digital readiness; eHealth literacy; Artificial
   intelligence; Technology use; Nursing education
ID USER ACCEPTANCE
AB Background: Digital readiness has become a critical competency for future nurses in the evolving landscape of healthcare. Two essential components of this readiness-eHealth literacy and attitudes toward artificial intelligence (AI)-have gained prominence in nursing education. However, limited evidence exists regarding their interrelationship and associated demographic and behavioral factors, particularly in middle-income countries. Aim: This study aimed to assess eHealth literacy and attitudes toward AI among undergraduate nursing students, identify associated demographic and behavioral factors, and examine the relationship between these two constructs as key dimensions of digital readiness. Methods: A descriptive and cross-sectional analytic study was conducted with 286 undergraduate nursing students at a public university in T & uuml;rkiye during the 2024-2025 academic year. Participants were recruited using a voluntary, open invitation approach. Data were collected through an online survey, including a sociodemographic questionnaire, the eHealth Literacy Scale (eHEALS), and the General Attitudes Toward Artificial Intelligence Scale. Non-parametric tests and Spearman's rho correlation were used for group comparisons and bivariate associations. Hierarchical multiple regression analysis was performed to evaluate the independent contribution of eHealth literacy to AI attitudes while controlling for potential confounding demographic and behavioral variables. Results: Of the 286 participants, the majority were female (75.9%) with a mean age of 20.7 years (SD = 2.78), predominantly in the 19-22 age range. Participants reported moderate-to-high eHealth literacy (M = 28.3, SD = 4.92) and favorable attitudes toward AI (M = 65.9, SD = 8.37). Significant differences were observed across gender, academic year, grade point average (GPA), and frequency of AI tool use. Students using generative AI tools such as ChatGPT scored significantly higher on both scales. A positive correlation was found between eHealth literacy and AI attitudes (r = 0.214, p < 0.001). In hierarchical regression analysis, demographic variables accounted for a small proportion of variance in AI attitudes, while behavioral factors (e.g., GPA and AI tool use) significantly improved the model. However, eHealth literacy did not make a statistically significant independent contribution to AI attitudes after controlling for these variables. Conclusion: Undergraduate nursing students demonstrated promising levels of digital readiness. However, the relationship between eHealth literacy and AI attitudes appears to be context-dependent rather than independently predictive. Behavioral engagement with digital technologies plays a more prominent role in shaping AI attitudes. These findings underscore the need for nursing curricula to move beyond foundational digital literacy and incorporate experiential, practice-oriented AI learning opportunities to support comprehensive digital readiness.

TI "Perceptions of artificial intelligence in nursing students: A
   qualitative meta-synthesis based on the UTAUT2 model"
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence; Qualitative research; Meta-synthesis; Nursing
   students; Perceptions; UTAUT2 model
AB Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming nursing education and clinical practice. Understanding students' perceptions is essential for designing effective and equitable AI-enhanced learning strategies. The Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology 2 (UTAUT2) offers a robust model for examining factors that shape acceptance and use. Aim: To integrate qualitative evidence on nursing students' perceptions of incorporating AI into academic education, using the UTAUT2 model to interpret constructs influencing acceptance and use. Methods: A qualitative deductive meta-synthesis was conducted following Dixon-Woods' framework. A systematic search (October 2024-July 2025) in PubMed, CINAHL, and Web of Science identified qualitative studies and qualitative findings from mixed-method research published between 2020 and 2025. Methodological quality was appraised using ENTREQ guidelines and the Joanna Briggs Institute's Qualitative Assessment and Review Instrument (QARI). Data were thematically synthesized according to UTAUT2 constructs. Results: Nursing students perceive AI as a tool to enhance learning and efficiency (performance expectancy) yet concerns about the complexity and digital competencies persist (effort expectancy). Faculty support and institutional context emerge as key factors in promoting acceptance (social influence and facilitating conditions). Intention to use relates to interest and prior experience (hedonic motivation). Cost remains a barrier (price value), while accumulated experience strengthens adoption (habit). Conclusion: AI represents a valuable resource in nursing education, offering opportunities for personalized learning, improved access to information, and enhanced competency development. Effective integration requires addressing technical, ethical, equity-related, and training barriers. Importantly, AI should complement, rather than replace, the human dimension of nursing education.

TI Evaluating a pilot nationwide licencing OSCE for
   internationally-qualified registered nurses: Making better decisions
   through mixed-methods triangulation
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Nursing; OSCE; Clinical examination; Performance assessment; Evaluation;
   Simulation; Registration; Licencing
ID COST
AB Background: Nurse migration across global workplaces presents multiple benefits, yet challenges exist in ensuring registration processes in new countries are high-quality, sustainable, and defensible. Performance assessments such as Objective Structured Clinical Examinations (OSCEs) provide one approach to assess whether internationally-qualified health professionals reach a standard of clinical competency for safe registration. This paper presents how integration of a range of data provides improved evaluation of a licencing OSCE for registered nurses (RNs). Objective: To determine the reliability, discriminant validity, cost-effectiveness, and acceptability of a pilot licencing OSCE for RNs. Methods: A 10-station OSCE was developed and piloted with 59 recently qualified RNs. A mixed-methods evaluation was undertaken. Internal consistency was assessed using Cronbach's alpha, and OSCE reliability via Generalizability statistics. R-2 and Inter-grade discrimination was determined to examine the variation in checklist scores due to global grades. Discriminant validity was evaluated by linking OSCE performance to educational attainment, and a logistic regression model was fitted to identify performance predictors beyond knowledge and OSCE complexity. Cost data were collected through expert consultation and observation, and analysed using a consolidated economic framework. Acceptability data were collected through stakeholder focus groups and analysed using the framework method. All data were triangulated to underpin the OSCE evaluation. Results: With 10 stations, acceptable generalisability (G-coefficient = 0.75) and high internal-consistency reliability (alpha = 0.76) were demonstrated. Possessing a postgraduate nursing qualification (p < 0.030) and between-circuit differences (p < 0.035) appeared significant predictors of candidate performance. OSCE stakeholder acceptability was categorised into 12 themes related to either candidate factors or OSCE design. Triangulation of psychometrics and cost data indicated 10 stations were optimal. Triangulation of psychometrics and acceptability data revealed increasing time to complete tasks, improving candidate familiarity with equipment, documentation and/or room layout, and clarity with station objectives could improve station metrics. Conclusions: A holistic approach to determining the quality of an OSCE utilising mixed-methods evaluation sheds additional light on OSCE performance more than any one method in isolation. This paper provides a methodological framework for OSCE assessment in licencing and other high-stakes settings.

TI Artificial intelligence literacy, readiness, and innovativeness:
   Exploring interrelationships in undergraduate nursing students
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence; Literacy; Readiness; Innovativeness; Nursing
   students; Nursing education
AB Aim/objective: This study aimed to examine the relationships between AI literacy, medical AI readiness, and individual innovativeness among nursing students. Background: Integrating artificial intelligence (AI) into healthcare requires future nurses to develop competencies in literacy, readiness, and innovativeness. Evidence on how these domains interrelate in nursing education remains limited. Design: A cross-sectional, relational study design was adopted. Methods: The study was conducted between April and July 2025 with 440 nursing students from two state universities in T & uuml;rkiye. Data were collected online using a Descriptive Information Form, the AI Literacy Scale, the Medical AI Readiness Scale, and the Individual Innovativeness Scale. Descriptive statistics, independent samples t-test, one-way ANOVA, Mann-Whitney U test, Kruskal-Wallis test, Pearson correlation, and multiple regression analysis were used. Results: Students' mean age was 21.13 (SD = 2.80), and 70.5% were female. Most participants (91.4%) had not received prior AI training. University-based comparisons showed significant differences in AI literacy (p = .042), medical AI readiness skills (p = .006), and innovativeness (p = .001). Demographic variables such as gender, grade level, AI training, usage frequency, and openness to new technologies were associated with scale scores. Correlation analyses revealed moderate positive associations between AI literacy and both medical AI readiness (r = 0.532, p < .01) and innovativeness (r = 0.423, p < .01). Regression analyses indicated that AI literacy (beta = 0.475, p < .001) and individual innovativeness (beta = 0.134, p = .003) significantly predicted AI readiness, while university was not a significant predictor, and the model explained 29.8% of the variance. Conclusions: AI literacy, readiness, and innovativeness are interrelated competencies among nursing students. Findings provide evidence for integrating AI-oriented content into curricula and for developing strategies that enhance students' preparedness for technology-driven healthcare.

   Affective empathy; Embodied learning; Reflective practice;
   Person-centred care; Fundamental care
ID VISUAL THINKING STRATEGIES; CARE LEFT UNDONE; OUTCOMES; SKILLS
AB Background: Nurses play a vital role in delivering person-centred fundamental care and ensuring patient safety. Although the nurse-patient relationship is widely acknowledged as essential to fundamental care, nurses often face challenges in meeting patients' relational needs. There is a growing call for educational activities that support nursing students in developing relational competencies. Aim: To explore how undergraduate pre-registration nursing students experience that art-based pedagogy supports their learning and the development of competencies needed to establish relationships with patients. TI Integrating personal continuous glucose monitoring use into a third-year
   therapeutics course: Reflections on combining the experiential with the
   didactic
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Experiential; Didactic; Continuous glucose monitoring; Reflection
AB Purpose: Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) devices represent an important innovation in diabetes management and an opportunity for experiential integration into the didactic curriculum. This reflective work describes pharmacy faculty experiences integrating CGM use into a therapeutics course and examines the insights gained from implementing this activity, using student survey findings on comfort and confidence with CGM counseling as context for reflection. Description: Second-year student pharmacists were invited to wear a CGM, devices were provided through an educational grant from Abbott Laboratories. Students completed surveys assessing comfort with CGM education, interpretation, and likelihood of recommending the technology. Thirty students participated, with 57% wearing the CGM for the full 14 days. After gaining CGM experience, participants' comfort in educating patients improved significantly, shifting from nearly half feeling "not comfortable at all" to over half feeling "extremely comfortable. Key takeaways included an enhanced understanding of how different foods influence glucose levels and an appreciation for the application's ease of use. Students also reported increased confidence in their ability to counsel patients effectively. Analysis: Faculty reflection on implementing this activity highlighted the value of experiential learning in helping students connect foundational science with lived patient experience. Student survey findings, including increased comfort with CGM counseling and data interpretation, provided context for these reflections and reinforced the potential of such activities to deepen engagement with diabetes management concepts. Faculty also recognized the importance of incorporating structured debriefing to help students translate personal experience into professional application in future iterations. Conclusion: Incorporating CGMs into the curriculum reinforced for faculty the importance of experiential learning and helped students engage through diverse learning approaches. Implications: Faculty should actively seek methods to embed experiential learning into coursework and facilitate meaningful reflection on students' personal experiences.

   A qualitative study of postgraduate nursing students' experiences
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY

DT Article

   students; Qualitative study
AB Background: A sustainable future for all is the objective of the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Postgraduate nursing students may incorporate SDGs into their everyday clinical practice; however, there is a paucity of empirical evidence regarding their experiences of the implementation of the SDGs in healthcare settings. Objective: To explore postgraduate students' experiences of engaging with the SDGs in healthcare settings. Design: A descriptive, exploratory qualitative study. Setting: Four postgraduate nursing programmes at a university in Hong Kong. Participants: Twenty postgraduate nursing students, each with at least 2 years of clinical experience, were purposively sampled. Conclusions: Establishing a cohesive culture centred on sustainability within nursing practice is essential. The findings of this study will be beneficial for nurse educators to enhance the planning and redesign of educational programmes aimed at fostering sustainable healthcare by integrating strategies for implementing the SDGs across diverse healthcare settings.

TI Midwifery students' education, use of, and views on complementary
   therapies: A cross-sectional survey
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Complementary therapy; Midwifery; Students; Education
ID ALTERNATIVE MEDICINE CAM; MIDWIVES; EXPERIENCE; WOMEN
AB Problem statement: There is limited understanding of midwifery students' education, their personal use, and their views on complementary therapies. Background: The use of complementary therapies has grown worldwide, with women in the perinatal period among the highest users. Midwifery students, as future practitioners, have a pivotal responsibility to support women with evidence-based information to promote informed choices regarding these therapies. This study explored midwifery students' education, personal use of, and personal views on complementary therapies across four Asia-Pacific countries: Australia, New Zealand, Indonesia, and Japan. Method: A cross-sectional online survey was conducted with midwifery students from the four countries enrolled in an undergraduate or postgraduate program leading to registration as a midwife, who were recruited via purposive sampling. The survey included items on educational exposure, personal use, personal views toward complementary therapies, and demographics. Descriptive and statistical analyses were undertaken. Results: Of 291 respondents, 158 completed at least one section of the survey and were included in the analysis. Indonesian students were more likely to have completed external qualifications (p < .001) and workshops in complementary therapies, in addition to therapies embedded in their curriculum (p = .017). In contrast, Australian/New Zealand and Japanese respondents significantly exceeded Indonesian respondents in their interest in learning more about specific complementary therapies. Most students rated their personal experiences and views of complementary therapies as positive to very positive, with no significant cross-country difference. Conclusion: This is the first study to explore midwifery students' education, personal use, and views on complementary therapies in Australia, New Zealand, Indonesia, and Japan. We found strong support for integrating complementary therapies into midwifery education. Incorporating education on complementary therapies into the undergraduate midwifery program provides students with evidence-based information, enabling them to discuss the safe use of these therapies with women in the perinatal period.

TI AI disclosure uncertainty in nursing education: A pedagogical scaffold
   for professional learning
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Generative artificial intelligence; AI disclosure; Cyberethics;
   Transparency; Accountability; Nursing education; Professional identity
   formation
AB Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly reshaping how nursing students produce and communicate academic work, intensifying questions about authorship, accountability, and trust. Although AI disclosure is widely promoted in nursing education, disclosure practices remain uneven and contested, in part because expectations often outpace pedagogical support. Contemporary scholarship describes a disclosure paradox in which transparency invites skepticism while nondisclosure frequently goes undetected, thus creating incentives for silence. Learners and educators report that disclosure can be emotionally burdensome due to uncertainty about what counts as acceptable AI use. Evidence suggests that when AI is integrated intentionally and transparently, human-AI collaboration can facilitate and ameliorate creative and context-sensitive tasks; therefore, this paper argues that AI disclosure should be reframed as a professional identity formation practice grounded in transparency and accountability rather than treated primarily as a compliance statement. Drawing on established learning theory, we describe the AI Disclosure Coach (AiDiCo) as an illustrative pedagogical scaffold that guides learners to map AI contribution, document verification and revision decisions, and articulate how human judgment shaped the final product. We outline boundary conditions and ethical limits of disclosure scaffolds, identify instructional strategies to sustain meaningful engagement and counter performative disclosure, and consider implications for globally relevant implementation. In particular, we highlight the need for platformagnostic disclosure pedagogy that remains adaptable across varied governance structures, languages, and resource conditions, thereby supporting sustainable approaches to ethical AI engagement. Framed as coevolution, this approach positions nursing education and generative AI as developing in tandem, with disclosure pedagogy strengthening accountability as AI capabilities and professional expectations continue to change.

TI Beyond literacy to clinical competency: A framework for integrating
   generative AI into nursing education
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Generative artificial intelligence; Nursing education; Clinical
   competency; Workforce readiness; Digital health; Competency framework
ID CARE SIMULATION STANDARDS; DELIBERATE PRACTICE; MODEL; PRACTICE(TM)
AB Problem: Health systems are rapidly integrating generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) into clinical workflows, introducing safety risks including hallucinations and automation bias. These risks threaten patient safety when frontline nurses lack preparation to critically verify AI-generated outputs. Nurses are uniquely positioned to serve as safety gatekeepers in AI-augmented care; however, realizing this potential requires strengthened GenAI competencies in nursing education. Current curricula have emphasized academic integrity concerns over clinical preparedness, leaving gaps in verification skills, uncertainty communication, and accountability frameworks essential for safe AI integration. Background: Established nursing education standards, such as the American Association of Colleges of Nursing (AACN) Essentials, Quality and Safety Education for Nurses (QSEN) competencies, and the Nursing and Midwifery Council (NMC) Future Nurse standards, provide foundational scaffolds for integrating digital and AI-related capabilities into nursing curricula. Yet pedagogical approaches often treat GenAI primarily as a threat to academic integrity rather than as a clinical tool requiring systematic verification, critical appraisal, and accountable use. Integrating GenAI-specific competencies into nursing education is therefore essential for prepare practitioners who can use these technologies while maintaining professional accountability and patient safety. Aim: This discussion paper proposes the Generative AI Nursing Competency (GANC) framework, offering educators and health-system leaders a standards-aligned pathway for preparing nurses to use GenAI without relinquishing professional judgment. The framework specifies seven competency domains: patient-centered assessment, safety-critical clinical reasoning, therapeutic communication, evidence verification, documentation integrity, interprofessional collaboration, and ethical accountability. These domains are translated into observable indicators and assessment exemplars, including simulation and objective structured clinical examination (OSCE) stations. By embedding generative-system risks within routine workflows and emphasizing manual-mode readiness when AI reliability is compromised, GANC provides practical guidance for cultivating nurses as accountable clinical validators in AI-augmented practice environments.

TI Pointing-tracing effect in computer-based multimedia learning: A
   potential explanation from the perspective of text-picture integration
SO LEARNING AND INSTRUCTION
LA English
DT Article
DE Cognitive load theory; Pointing-tracing; Text-picture integration;
   Multimedia learning; Attention-guiding strategy
ID FRAMEWORK; GESTURES; TESTS
AB Background: Pointing-tracing is regarded as a supportive strategy for multimedia learning, potentially enhancing text-picture integration. Aim: This study, grounded in cognitive load theory and cognitive theory of multimedia learning, aimed to examine a possible explanatory mechanism for the pointing-tracing effect from the perspective of text-picture integration. Samples: The study comprised two experiments, each with a sample of 160 valid participants, yielding a total sample size of 320. Methods: In Experiment 1, college students learned computer-presented physiology lessons with or without pointing-tracing or cueing. In Experiment 2, students learned the same material using pointing-tracing or cueing within text-picture matched or mismatched tasks. Learning outcomes and cognitive load were assessed after the learning phase in each experiment. Data were analyzed using (generalized) linear mixed-effects models. Results: Experiment 1 revealed that, compared to the non-pointing-tracing groups, the pointing-tracing groups showed superior terminology memory and global comprehension and lower perceived extraneous load. The pointing-tracing-only group outperformed the cueing-only group in terminology memory and global comprehension. Experiment 2 revealed that the pointing-tracing group had better learning outcomes than the cueing group in the matched task. Conversely, for the mismatched task, the pointing-tracing group exhibited poorer learning outcomes compared to the cueing group, indicating that pointing-tracing effect was influenced by mismatched tasks. Conclusions: Text-picture integration may serve as one of the explanatory mechanisms underlying the effectiveness of the pointing-tracing strategy in computer-based multimedia learning, though other possibilities remain.

TI Effects of distinct prebriefing and debriefing on learning outcomes in
   advanced life support training for ward nurses: A randomized controlled
   trial
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Advanced life support; Debriefing; Nurse education; Patient simulation;
   Prebriefing; Self-efficacy; Randomized controlled trial
ID RESUSCITATION
AB Background: Effective training in advanced life support (ALS) is crucial for improving ward nurses' ALS performance and patient outcomes during in-hospital cardiac arrest. However, the comparative effects of prebriefing and debriefing strategies in ALS education remain unclear. Objective: This study aimed to determine whether differences in prebriefing and debriefing strategies in ALS training result in significant variations in metacognition, self-efficacy, ALS performance, and learning satisfaction among novice ward nurses. Methods: In this randomized controlled trial, 205 novice ward nurses were assigned to four ALS training groups. Groups 1 and 2 received prebriefing with a role-modeling video, whereas Groups 3 and 4 received prebriefing with self-directed learning. Instructor-led (Groups 1 and 3) or peer-led (Groups 2 and 4) debriefings followed the prebriefing methods. Participants completed baseline and post-intervention assessments that measured metacognition, self-efficacy. ALS performance and learning satisfaction was measured only at the posttest. Results: All groups demonstrated improved self-efficacy following ALS training. However, Groups 1 and 2, who received prebriefing with a role-modeling video, achieved greater gains in both metacognition and self-efficacy than Groups 3 and 4, regardless of the debriefing method. Among all groups, Group 1 showed the highest ALS performance and learning satisfaction, followed by Group 2. Conclusion: This study highlights the effectiveness of structured prebriefing using a role-modeling video for enhancing critical ALS competencies among novice ward nurses. These findings provide evidence to inform the design of more effective simulation-based resuscitation training programs in clinical settings.

TI Serious games based on scripted mystery role-playing: Exploring tensions
   between legal and social ethical awareness through game-based pedagogy
SO LEARNING AND INSTRUCTION
LA English
DT Article
DE Game-based pedagogy; Legal awareness; Social ethical awareness; Scripted
   mystery role-playing game; Civic education
ID COMPETENCES
AB Background: Legal awareness and social ethical awareness are both unified and contested; how individuals respond to the tension between the two in specific contexts is a key area of concern in civic education. However, evidence derived from the use of game-based pedagogy to examine students concrete responses to this relationship remains scarce. Aims: This study investigates the specific manifestations of and response strategies to tensions between legal awareness and social ethical awareness among non-law major university students, thereby providing practical implications for the further application of game-based pedagogy in civic education. Sample: A total of 48 undergraduate students without a law major participated in the serious game designed for this study. Results: The findings revealed that students exhibited conflicting awareness across three dimensions: social structure and interpersonal equality, social contribution and individual value, and interest-based contracts and fairness and justice. In most cases, social ethical awareness considerations tended to take precedence over legal awareness. Conclusions: The findings can provide useful references for further promoting the concrete application of game-based pedagogy in educational settings and for improving current civic education practices.

TI Evaluating and diversifying philosophy education
SO LEARNING AND INSTRUCTION
LA English
DT Article
DE Transformative education; Philosophy education; Diversifying philosophy;
   Aesthetic evaluation
AB Background: Debates on diversifying the philosophy curriculum often emphasize what is taught rather than how it is taught. Yet, curriculum content and pedagogy are deeply interconnected. Little is known about how philosophy teachers conceptualize and evaluate their teaching approaches, or how these conceptions shape curricular decisions. Aims: This study examines how university philosophy teachers understand and assess their pedagogical approaches, focusing on how they balance intellectual development, transformative education, and engagement with philosophical diversity. Sample: Eighteen philosophy teachers from diverse institutional and cultural contexts participated in the study. Methods: A qualitative research design using semi-structured interviews was used. Thematic analysis identified shared patterns and tensions in teachers' accounts of their pedagogical aims and practices. Results: Participants prioritized fostering students' intellectual growth over transmitting content. Exposing students to diverse perspectives was viewed as key to developing critical reflection. While many regarded their pedagogies as potentially transformative, others expressed ambivalence toward the concept of 'transformative education,' associating it with political or religious indoctrination. Teachers also cautioned that encounters with difference can be disorienting if not carefully facilitated, emphasizing the need for balance. Diversification was seen less as curriculum expansion than as the deliberate design of experiences that help students engage responsibly with difference. Conclusions: The study highlights both the potential and the challenges of intercultural and transformative approaches in philosophy education, suggesting that diversification is best understood as a reflective pedagogical practice rather than simple content inclusion. The study also suggests exploring aesthetic approaches to evaluating transformative education.

TI Training rational thinking: Improvements without transfer to argument
   evaluation
SO LEARNING AND INSTRUCTION
LA English
DT Article
DE Rationality; Thinking style; Cognitive biases; Debiasing training;
   Higher education
ID INDIVIDUAL-DIFFERENCES; COGNITIVE REFLECTION; DECISION; BELIEF;
   INFORMATION; BIAS; COMPREHENSION; HEURISTICS; ABILITIES; TAXONOMY
AB Background: General rational thinking skills are defined as the ability to override heuristic thinking by initiating and carrying out systematic thinking processes. Previous studies have identified rational thinking as a positive predictor of academic performance in higher education. Aims: In two preregistered experiments, we examined the effects of a brief targeted rational thinking training on students' general rational thinking skills and their ability to evaluate scientific arguments. Samples: Experiments 1 and 2 comprised 149 and 155 university students, respectively. Methods: We conducted two pre-post experiments with different active control groups. In Experiment 1, the control group completed a general reading strategy training. In Experiment 2, the control group completed a simple sentence verification task. The treatment group completed a brief computer-based rational thinking training. Results: In both experiments, the rational thinking training group-but not the control group-showed significant improvements in general rational thinking skills. General rational thinking skills were positively correlated with argument evaluation, but no transfer effects of the training on this ability were observed. Unexpectedly, both treatment and control groups improved in argument evaluation, likely due to practice effects. Conclusion: These findings indicate that rational thinking skills can be enhanced through brief targeted interventions in higher education, but additional approaches may be needed to promote transfer to epistemic competencies such as argument evaluation.

TI Student perceptions of teacher messages about the value of science in
   the classroom
SO LEARNING AND INSTRUCTION
LA English
DT Article
DE Situated expectancy value theory; Science; Perceived teacher value
   messages; Achievement; Aspirations
ID EXPECTANCY-VALUE; UTILITY VALUE; ACHIEVEMENT-MOTIVATION; RELEVANCE
   INTERVENTION; GENDER-DIFFERENCES; SCHOOL ENGAGEMENT; VALUE-REAPPRAISAL;
   VALUE BELIEFS; SELF-CONCEPT; TASK VALUES
AB Aim: Teachers are uniquely positioned to shape students' motivational beliefs, yet research examining perceived classroom messages that explicitly convey the value of what students are learning remains scarce. Background: Drawing on the situated expectancy value theory, we examined how student-perceived teacher messages about the value of science longitudinally related to adolescent students' subjective task values, perceived costs, and expectations of success, achievement, and aspirations. Sample: Data were collected from 1591 participants aged 11 to 14 years (57.5% female) nested in 65 science classes in England. Method: Data were collected over four waves. Conclusion: When students perceive that teachers explain the value of science, they report greater expectancy and utility value, and show subsequent higher achievement and aspirations.

TI Exploring educational barriers to pre-registration nursing students
   digital literacy competency in the clinical setting: A descriptive
   qualitative design
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE A B S T R A C T
ID PERCEPTIONS
AB Background: Digitalised clinical settings require pre-registration nursing students to confidently use electronic medical records and other technologies. Due to inconsistent curricula structure and limited exposure to clinical digital systems, nursing students are not adequately prepared for digitally enabled clinical practice. These educational gaps highlight the need to better understand the barriers that impede students' development of digital literacy skills. Aim: To explore the educational barriers that impede pre-registration nursing students' development of digital literacy skills and identify strategies to enhance their preparedness for digitalised clinical practice. Design and methods: A descriptive qualitative approach was employed to capture the participants' subjective perspectives. Data was collected via semi-structured individual interviews with (n = 10) clinical nurse educators and (n = 10) nursing academics and focus group interviews with (n = 13) nursing students. All interviews were conducted online via zoom and analysed using thematic analysis. Results: Three major themes were generated. This paper reports on one main theme: "Educational Needs" describing limited structured teaching, limited opportunities to practice with EMR like systems, and misalignment between curriculum content and expected digital capability. Participants proposed scaffolded learning across year levels, simulated academic EMR activities, and assessment mapped to national capability expectations. Conclusion: While most healthcare institutions are now digitalised, research has shown higher educational providers are not meeting digital literacy needs of nursing students in this area. Future nurses must be digitally competent to overcome technological barriers when providing digitalised patient care. Therefore, contemporary digitally embedded education that includes digital literacy skills will prepare nursing students to provide quality and safe care in a digitalised clinical setting.

   opportunities
SO LEARNING AND INSTRUCTION
LA English
DT Article
DE Process data; Learning processes; Adaptive support; Learning;

AB Advances in learning technologies now enable continuous real-time analysis of learner process data. While these innovations have generated interest in adaptive educational technologies, most research mistakenly assumes that the processes and indicators involved are largely domain-general. This overlooks how domain-specific cognitive structures and practices crucially shape learning and the meaning of process data. TI Usability and feasibility of a Socratic Llm-supported learning tool for
   clinical reasoning in undergraduate nursing education
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Nursing; Clinical reasoning; Artificial intelligence; Large language
   models; Socratic method; ADPIE; Usability; Feasibility study;
   Undergraduate education
AB Aim: To evaluate clinical reasoning outcomes and the usability and feasibility of an AI-supported platform that uses a large language model (LLM) to foster higher-order thinking via the Socratic method. Design: Prospective observational process evaluation guided by the UK Medical Research Council (MRC) and National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) frameworks, conducted alongside outcome evaluation. Methods: Full-time Bachelor of Science nursing students who used the AI-supported platform between February and May 2025 were recruited. The intervention integrated the ADPIE nursing process (Assessment, Diagnosis, Planning, Implementation, Evaluation) and the clinical reasoning cycle via adaptive Socratic questioning. Results: A total of 142 students completed the evaluation. Most used the platform as a supplementary learning tool, particularly to support case management, review clinical procedures, and answer queries during clinical sessions. Students reported improvements in perceived clinical reasoning, especially in analyzing errors, adopting multiple perspectives, and reflecting on plans prior to intervention. Most participants (74.0%) agreed the platform helped them use ADPIE to guide thinking, and many perceived support for applying clinical reasoning frameworks to decision-making. Conclusion: A customized AI-supported platform using an LLM through the Socratic method is a feasible, usable adjunct to traditional nursing education and shows promise for enhancing clinical reasoning. Thoughtful design, grounded in nursing frameworks and dialogic guidance may help encourage deeper learning and discourage a surface-level approach associated with conventional question-answer LLM use.

TI Wearing multiple "hats": Daily identity transitions among nursing and
   allied health clinician-educators: A qualitative study☆
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Professional identities; Roles; Identity transitions; Nursing; Allied
   health; Clinician-educator
ID PROFESSIONAL IDENTITY; MEDICAL-EDUCATION; EXPERIENCES; FACULTY; EXPERT;
   CONSTRUCTION; CHALLENGES; INTERVIEW; TEACHERS; ADJUNCT
AB Background: Nursing and allied health clinician-educators serve a vital function in bridging academic learning with clinical practice. Yet this role can be challenging as it requires shifting between clinician and clinicianeducator identities throughout the day. Aim: To explore how nursing and allied health clinician-educators navigate daily identity transitions from clinician to clinician-educator. Design: A qualitative study employing a secondary analysis of interviews and longitudinal audio diaries (LADs). Settings: We conducted this study in Australia with nursing and allied health professionals working in hospital, residential, rehabilitation, private and community workplace settings. Participants: Twenty-five clinician-educators from ten different healthcare professions, with participants ranging from novice to experienced clinician-educators. Methods: We collected and thematically analyzed data from entrance interviews, weekly LADs, and exit interviews. We used Social Identity Complexity Theory (SICT) to explore clinician-educators daily identity transition processes as intersection, dominance, compartmentalization, and/or merging. Results: Dominance and compartmentalization explained the ways participants navigated their daily workplace identity transitions. Limited role clarity and confidence in educator tasks led to dominance of the clinician identity, particularly when participants perceived conflicting demands between educator and clinician roles. Participants also compartmentalized their identities; contextually activating either the clinician or educator identity. We found little evidence that participants daily identity transitions aligned with intersection and merging of identities. Conclusions: Nursing and allied health clinician-educators face challenges when navigating their clinician and educator identities in clinical workplaces. Understanding these daily identity transitions is essential for designing supports to enhance education. We postulate that tailored induction programs incorporating identity transition theories, alongside organizational cultures valuing educational roles, could support clinician-educators to reconcile competing identities and cope with daily identity transitions.

TI A longitudinal study of school climate influencing nursing students'
   social adaptability: The chain mediating role of teacher-student
   relationships and self-identity
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Social adaptability; School climate; Teacher-student relationships;
   Self-identity; Mediating effect
ID ACHIEVEMENT; CHINESE; POWER
AB Objective To investigate the influence of school climate on nursing students' social adaptability and the chain mediating roles of teacher-student relationships and self-identity, thereby providing a theoretical foundation for improving the social adaptability of nursing students. Methods From March to September 2024, a longitudinal study was conducted at three-time points (T1, T2, and T3) using convenience sampling among 642 nursing students from two comprehensive universities in China. Ultimately, data from 586 valid participants were included in the final analysis. The survey covered general demographic characteristics, perceptions of the school climate, teacher-student relationships, self-identity, and social adaptability. Data were analyzed using SPSS 25.0, and structural equation modeling (SEM) was performed using Amos 24.0 to investigate the impact of the school climate on nursing students' social adaptability, with teacher-student relationships and self-identity examined as mediating variables. Results The mean social adaptability score of the nursing students was 15.76 +/- 8.27. School climate had a significant positive predictive effect on social adaptability (r = 0.426, p < 0.01). Teacher-student relationships and self-identity played a chain-mediating role between school climate and social adaptability, accounting for 6.99% of the total effect (0.029/0.415). The structural equation model exhibited good fit indices (CMIN/DF = 3.362, RMSEA = 0.064, CFI = 0.923, TLI = 0.906). Conclusion School climate significantly influences the social adaptability of nursing students through the mediating effects of teacher-student relationships and self-identity. Therefore, educational authorities and university administrators should prioritize fostering a positive school climate, improving teacher-student relationships, and enhancing students' self-identity to promote their comprehensive social adaptability development.

TI Unconscious behavioral patterns in nursing student professional
   transitioning: A systems psychodynamic perspective
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Professional transition; Personal Philosophy of Nursing; Preceptorship;
   Reflexive thematic analysis; Systems psychodynamics; Unconscious
   behavior
ID CRITICAL THINKING; PRECEPTORSHIP; ENVIRONMENT; EXPERIENCE; NURSES
AB Background: Transitioning from a nursing student to a registered nurse represents a critical stage in professional identity formation, often impacted by unconscious behaviors. Understanding these dynamics is essential for effective integration of the Personal Philosophy of Nursing (PPN) into practice. Aim The study aimed to explore and create an awareness of unconscious behaviors manifesting among fourth-year nursing students transitioning into professional practice, and its impact on their personal philosophy and emotional functioning within the clinical environment. Design: A collective case study design, framed within hermeneutic phenomenology and reflexive thematic analysis, was adopted to socially construct and interpret the lived experiences of nursing students navigating transition into their professional role. Setting: The research was performed in a School of Nursing at a Canadian University. Participants: Purposive sampling was used to extract data from a database containing 53 students who submitted their assignments to complete their Nursing Ethics and Consolidation in Nursing Practice modules, while contemplating their PPN. Consent was obtained. Methods: The assignments were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis (RTA). Seven core themes were developed. Systems psychodynamics (SP) provided an interpretive framework to deepen understanding of the unconscious behavior underlying these themes. Findings: Students struggle to assume critical responsibility during preceptorship, most failing to adopt the PPN idealized as a rational, academic guide containing the benchmark of professional behavior. By combining RTA with SP, the findings highlight unconscious behaviors, such as avoidance, dependency, projection, and resistance, reflecting deeper anxieties, defenses, and relational dynamics that complicate transition into professional practice. Conclusions: Most students do not process the essential properties for professional transitioning. Their lack of selfawareness causes them to react personally to patients' content, taking on and identifying with patients' projections. The study underscores the importance of integrating awareness of unconscious behaviors into nursing education to better prepare students for the complexities of the profession.

TI Improving writing through evidence-based teaching
SO LEARNING AND INSTRUCTION
LA English
DT Article
DE Literacy; Diversity; Motivation; SRSD; Feedback
ID OF-FIT INDEXES; PROFESSIONAL-DEVELOPMENT; INSTRUCTION; METAANALYSIS;
   TEACHERS; STRATEGIES; STUDENTS; IMPACT; INTERVENTION; EDUCATION
AB Background: Writing plays a crucial role in educational achievement in general and the successful transition from primary to secondary school. The aim of the present quasi-experimental study was to investigate the effect of a writing intervention on primary students' writing performance and writing motivation. Method: The sample included 846 children (Grades 3-4) across nine schools. The intervention was delivered through students' regular teachers, with teachers in the experimental group participating in a multi-component professional learning intervention (PLI) focused on evidence-based teaching of writing, emphasizing a Scaffolded Process Approach that highlighted process-oriented instruction with feedback, and supports such as modeling. The practices were implemented by teachers in their regular classrooms. We assessed text length and writing quality through texts produced in response to picture prompts, which were administered at three time points (pre-, post-, and follow-up). In addition, we measured self-efficacy and writing enjoyment (pre-post). The data were analyzed using multilevel modeling with children nested within classes. Results: The findings revealed a significant effect on narrative writing quality from pre-to post-test, and learning gains were largely sustained on the follow-up assessment. Text length and writing self-efficacy increased in both the experimental and the control group, while there was a small decline in writing enjoyment. Conclusion: Overall, the teacher-led intervention positively influenced writing quality. We further discuss the results concerning student motivation and treatment fidelity, underscoring the central role of teachers in supporting writing growth.

TI The learning experiences of basic nursing skills among undergraduate
   nursing students at double first-class universities: A qualitative study
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Undergraduate; Nursing students; Nursing skill; Double First-Class
   universities
ID OUTCOMES
AB Background: Basic nursing skills are vital professional skills for nursing students. However, nursing students demonstrate varying levels of proficiency in skill learning and exams, particularly at Double First-Class universities. Aims: This study aimed to explore the learning experiences of undergraduate nursing students at these universities as they learn nursing skills, thereby providing robust empirical data to inform the development of strategies aimed at enhancing skill proficiency from the students' perspective. Methods: This study employed a descriptive qualitative study design and implemented a purposive sampling approach. Recruitment took place from April to May 2025, targeting full-time undergraduate nursing students at a Double First-Class university in Shanghai. The thematic analysis method was utilized to analyze the collected data. Results: A total of 15 students participated in the interviews. The study's findings delineated four themes: learning motivation, facilitating factors of skills learning, impeding factors of skills learning, and learning management needs. Conclusions: Among Double First-Class universities, some nursing students have a positive attitude towards acquiring nursing skills due to anticipated professional responsibilities, but many still show passive learning tendencies. Faculty guidance and peer support are important for student engagement. Ineffective initial skilllearning, lack of attention to skill learning, the gap between school and clinic, and limited free time negatively affect some students' enthusiasm and commitment. Meeting students' core demands, including sufficient training materials, diverse learning resources, professional guidance, and mandatory measures, can provide empirical evidence for optimizing nursing skills teaching models and refining talent cultivation systems at these universities.

AB Background: Studies based on teachers' self-reports often find that teachers use different disciplinary practices towards students from minoritized ethnic-racial groups and of low socioeconomic status (SES) than towards their peers. However, these studies do not investigate actual student and teacher behaviour or underlying mechanisms. It is also unclear whether the results stemming mostly from US-based studies can be transferred to contexts outside the US. Aims: The present study addresses these issues and investigates teachers' disciplinary behaviour using videographies of real-life classrooms in Germany. The resulting data will be analysed together with demographic and questionnaire data available in the dataset using a series of multilevel logistic regressions. Results: As this study is submitted as a stage I registered report, currently no results can be reported. Conclusions: Results of this study will provide valuable information on classroom processes in which teacher-based discrimination might be observable. It will also elucidate the role of teachers' stereotypes as a potential mechanism.

TI Pull through together or be detached? A qualitative study of
   experiential learning in nurse education during interaction in age suit
   simulation
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Age suit simulation; Blindness; Nurse education; Health problems;
   Nursing students; Older persons
ID STUDENTS
AB Aim: To illuminate nursing students' interactions during age suit simulation from the perspective of being a blind older person and being an attendant guiding the blind person. Background: Nursing students' understanding of age related and long-term, often multiple health problems are crucial for providing person-centred care in the home. In age suit simulation students take the perspectives of an older person which can improve their general attitudes towards older persons. However, focusing on blindness in age suit simulation is a novel concept. Design: The research design of this study is qualitative. During the autumn of 2022 to the spring of 2024 as a part of a larger intervention study project, nursing students (n = 68) were video-recorded during age suit simulation. The data was analysed through reflexive thematic analysis. Results Three main themes were constructed: (1) Pulling through together, (2) Dialogue is key when adapting to health problems and (3) Detached from each other. The third theme signifies the importance of being able to communicate in a meaningful way to adapt to each other's health problems. Students took different approaches to this challenge, which is reflected in the ways the students interacted with each other. Conclusion: The results of this study can be used to formulate a learning strategy to teach nursing students about the perspectives of being an older person with health problems. The simulations can also be utilized to enhance nursing students' knowledge and skills when guiding a blind person in the context of a home environment. Furthermore, the results can be useful in highlighting a holistic perspective regarding care needs as a shared experience by older couples, which is relevant knowledge for any health and social care profession. This embodied understanding of health problems can be used to support and practice person-centred care for older persons.

TI Adding pedagogical agents who point or trace to children's instructional
   videos
SO COMPUTERS & EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Teaching/learning strategies; Pedagogical agents; Instructional
   gestures; Cognitive load; Multimedia learning
ID EXAMPLES; GESTURES; AIDS
AB This study aims to determine how children's learning is affected by an onscreen animated pedagogical agent's use of tracing or pointing gestures for static or dynamic illustrations in a video lesson. Across 3 experiments, children (aged 10-12 years) learned about the water cycle from a narrated multimedia lesson and then completed learning outcome tests and subjective experience ratings. In Experiment 1, children in the PA group outperformed those in the no-PA group on retention and transfer tests, and reported higher germane processing, learning interest and motivation. In Experiment 2, children in the tracing and pointing gesture groups performed better than those in the no gesture group on retention and transfer tests, and also reported lower extraneous and intrinsic load. The tracing gesture group also outperformed the pointing gesture group on retention and transfer tests, and reported higher germane processing. In Experiment 3, when the agent used pointing gestures, children in the dynamic video group outperformed those in the static video group on retention and transfer tests. In contrast, when the agent used tracing gestures, children in the static video group outperformed those in the dynamic video group on transfer test. Additionally, children in tracing gesture groups had higher retention scores, germane processing, social presence, and learning motivation and interest than those in pointing gesture groups. These results support embodiment and signaling principles and suggest that children learn better from multimedia lessons when a tracing gesture agent is added to the screen, especially in static illustration-based videos.

TI Trusting AIto detect AI? A systematic evaluation of the reliability and
   robustness of current AIGC detection tools for student academic work
SO COMPUTERS & EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Academic integrity; AIGC detection; Large language models; Engineering
   education; Assessment reform; Higher education
AB The explosive proliferation of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has posed an unprecedented existential challenge to traditional evaluation systems in higher education. response to this wave, the higher education sector is undergoing a profound transformation, shifting from a focus on technological containment toward an assessment governance paradigm. Understanding the characteristics of detectors is the foundational prerequisite for utilizing such tools to optimize educational assessment; however, their effectiveness within authentic educational contexts remains insufficiently explored. To address this research gap, the study constructs three large-scale ecological datasets-StuTask, StuThesis, and DataCode-comprising over 280,000 authentic samples of student coursework, academic theses, and engineering code. A systematic evaluation was conducted on 13 mainstream detectors, covering both commercial and open-source models, across multiple dimensions including overall performance, task complexity, disciplinary variations, and adversarial robustness. The results indicate that while detectors achieve acceptable performance on long-form theses, they exhibit systematic failures in engineering code and short-form coursework tasks. Due to the formulaic nature technical writing, STEM disciplines are subject to significant algorithmic bias. Furthermore, robustness tests reveal the extreme vulnerability of current detection tools, as a hybrid editing strategy can enable up to 88% of AI-generated content to evade detection successfully. These findings suggest that existing detection technologies are inadequate to support high-stakes educational assessments. In the future educational trajectory of 'embracing AI,' AIGC detectors should function as reference metrics within the assessment system, serving to quantify the depth of human-AI collaboration across distinct disciplinary logical frameworks. Detection technology must evolve toward the optimization of 'logical innovation recognition,' thereby establishing robust academic integrity defense line that is truly resilient within the future ecosystem human-AI symbiosis.

TI Effect of end-of-life care video simulation versus written unfolding
   case study on nursing students' knowledge, communication attitude, and
   clinical judgment: A quasi-experimental study
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
ID PALLIATIVE CARE; FIDELITY SIMULATION; EXERCISE; VERSION; QUIZ; PCQN
AB Background: End-of-life care is a core concept foundational to nursing education. A plethora of evidence shows that undergraduate nursing students are ill prepared to provide care at the end-of-life. Active learning strategies including classroom simulation, unfolding case study, and flipped classroom have shown to positively impact learning, yet these strategies are used sparingly to support end-of-life care instruction. Aim: Our aim was to determine if using flipped classroom video simulation versus written unfolding case study as part of classroom instruction improved sophomore baccalaureate nursing students' end-of-life care knowledge, communication attitude, and clinical judgment. Design: A two-group, pretest posttest quasi-experimental design was used. Settings: The study was conducted at a college in the northeastern USA. Participants: Sophomore nursing students N = 151 consented to participate. Participants N = 130 completed all surveys (comparison group (CG) n = 68 and intervention group (IG) n = 62). Methods: The CG had flipped classroom end-of-life care instruction including a written unfolding case study, while the IG received the same instruction plus a video simulation of the same unfolding case study. End-of-life care knowledge, communication attitude, and clinical judgment were assessed. Data analysis used descriptive statistics, t-tests, and Analysis of Variance. Results: Although there was a significant increase (p = .000) in all three measures for both groups over time, no statistically significant difference was found between groups. The clinical judgment measure had a mean difference in favor of the IG (15.51 vs 11.47), indicating the video simulation had substantial impact on clinical judgment. Scores for the other two measures were also better for the IG. Conclusions: Integration of video simulation unfolding case study within flipped classroom may enhance students' end-of-life care knowledge, communication attitude, and clinical judgment to better care for the dying patient. The combined strategies may better address students diverse learning needs.

TI Innovating diagnostic learning: How generative AI explanation styles
   influence cognitive load and confidence calibration in medical students
SO COMPUTERS & EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Generative AI; Explainable AI; Medical education; Teaching/learning
   strategies; Cognitive load
ID CLINICAL-USEFULNESS
AB Generative AI can augment diagnostic learning, yet the impact of explanation style on novices' reasoning remains unclear. We evaluate two styles-technical (evidence-/probability-based) and analogical (case-based)-in a randomized controlled trial with 60 third- and fourth-year medical students who diagnosed twelve de-identified acute abdominal pain cases. After an initial judgment, participants were randomized to one of three conditions (technical, analogical, or control [no AI advice]) and received ex post AI advice (or none in control) while thinking aloud; outcomes were diagnostic accuracy, confidence calibration, and cognitive load analyzed via mixedeffects models and protocol analysis. Both AI styles improved accuracy over control; analogical yielded the highest accuracy and the lowest cognitive load, whereas technical produced the best confidence calibration but increased load. Think-aloud data showed that technical explanations triggered deeper evidence search, broader differentials, and more active agreement/disagreement with the AI; when the AI was incorrect in 2 of 12 cases, students in the technical condition were less likely to follow it, though estimates were imprecise. Results were robust to alternative measures and specifications and consistent across typical/atypical cases. Positioning explanation style as a design lever for AI-assisted learning, we show how design choices translate into generalizable knowledge for diagnostic training and decision calibration. Technical explanations are suited to cultivating critical reasoning and calibrated confidence; analogical explanations efficiently support Hypotheses generation when cognitive bandwidth is limited.

TI The Interplay of Self-regulation, Cognitive Load and Learner Resources:
   Implications for Learning Outcomes in Virtual Reality
SO COMPUTERS & EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Immersive virtual reality (iVR); medical education; self-regulation;
   cognitive load; learner prerequisites
ID TASK COMPLEXITY; PRIOR KNOWLEDGE; INSTRUCTIONAL-DESIGN; STRATEGIES;
   EFFICACY; PERFORMANCE; INFORMATION; ACCEPTANCE; MOTIVATION; STUDENT
AB This study investigated how cognitive load, self-regulation, and learner resources interact to shape conceptual learning in immersive virtual reality (iVR). Building on Seufert's (2018) model, we examined whether its predictions hold in iVR, how intrinsic (ICL) and extraneous cognitive load (ECL) relate to self-regulation and learning, and how learner resources contribute to these relations. Data from 473 students showed a consistent negative linear effect of ECL on both selfregulation and learning, underscoring the role of ECL as a critical burden in iVR-based learning. ICL did not predict the frequency of self-regulation but negatively moderated its effectiveness for learning. In terms of learner resources, interest and self-efficacy supported the application of selfregulation under load, whereas prior knowledge was more closely related to whether regulatory activity translated into learning. These findings diverge from the U-shaped relations proposed by Seufert (2018) and suggest that in iVR, established relations between cognitive load and selfregulation are overlaid by additional regulatory demands inherent to immersive environments. Consequently, optimizing iVR-based learning requires not only minimizing ECL but also explicitly supporting learning-relevant self-regulation. Overall, the results demonstrate that models of selfregulated learning validated in traditional settings cannot be assumed to transfer unaltered to immersive environments, with implications for both instructional design and theory-driven research on learning in iVR.

TI The experiences of nursing and midwifery students with end-of-life care
   in Neonatal Intensive Care Units: A qualitative descriptive exploratory
   study
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article

   students; Midwifery students; End-of-life care; Palliative care
