AB Background: Research on nursing and midwifery students' experiences with end-of-life care in Neonatal Intensive Care Units (NICUs) is limited, indicating the need for deeper exploration. Understanding their experiences and educational needs may inform curricula, ensuring future healthcare professionals are better equipped for these complex and emotionally challenging situations. Aim: To explore the experiences of nursing and midwifery students with end-of-life care in NICUs. Design: A qualitative descriptive exploratory study using focus group interviews. Settings: This study was conducted at the Erasmus Brussels University of Applied Sciences and Arts, Brussels, Belgium. Conclusions: This study underscores the need for enhanced preparation and support for nursing and midwifery students in NICUs. Integrating end-of-life care competencies, mentorship, and interprofessional simulation-based learning into curricula may help support students to handle the emotional and ethical complexities of end-of-life care. Strengthening emotional support and collaboration may further contribute to students' capacity to provide compassionate care for families and to work effectively within healthcare teams.

TI The impact of the testing environment on gender differences in mental
   rotation performance: Does virtual reality make a difference?
SO COMPUTERS & EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Mental rotation; Gender differences; Immersive virtual reality
ID SEX-DIFFERENCES; SPATIAL ABILITY; OCCLUSION; SKILLS; METAANALYSIS;
   EXPERIENCE
AB Mental rotation ability plays a crucial role in learning outcomes in STEM subjects - the ongoing debate questions whether and, if so, why men outperform women in mental rotation. Existing mental rotation tests (MRTs) have recently been criticized for being male-biased in their design. In our study, we attempted to overcome potential MRT design bias by integrating the renowned MRT into an immersive virtual reality (iVR) environment that reduces those biases. In a sample of N = 731 university students, we examined whether the iVR environment had an impact on MRT performance for males and females compared to (a) the paper-and-pencil condition and (b) a tablet condition. Our findings reveal the consistent superiority of male over female students in MRT performance across the three conditions. However, this discrepancy is attenuated in both technology-supported conditions. Based on the mediation model, cognitive effort partially mediated gender differences in mental rotation performance in the paper-and-pencil and tablet conditions, but not in iVR, suggesting that the role of perceived mental workload in gender disparities may vary depending on the testing environment.

   learning
SO LEARNING AND INSTRUCTION

DT Article
DE Digital technologies; Music pedagogy; Musical perception; Online
   learning; Teaching strategies
AB Aims: In the contemporary world of digital technologies, the use of online platforms for music education is of particular importance. The aim of this study was to compare the effectiveness of vocal training through the cloud platform JitsiMeet in developing musical perception skills with traditional methods. Methods: The statistical analysis included covariance analysis to compare pre-and post-test results within each group, an independent samples t-test to analyze differences between groups after the training, and a two-way analysis of variance to account for initial levels of proficiency. AB Fostering preservice teachers' (PSTs) design thinking (DT) is essential for addressing complex instructional challenges, yet remains difficult to achieve in teacher education. AB Background: Instruction-giving (IG) is central to classroom interaction in Content and Language Integrated Learning (CLIL), yet it is rarely taught explicitly in pre-service CLIL teacher education. TI Deliberate errors vs. induced errors: How best to structure students'
   error generation to promote learning?
SO LEARNING AND INSTRUCTION
LA English
DT Article
DE Deliberate errors; Induced errors; Learning outcomes; Subjective
   experience
ID UNSUCCESSFUL RETRIEVAL; CORRECTIVE FEEDBACK; COGNITIVE-LOAD; IMPROVES
   MEMORY; FAILURE; BENEFIT; HYPERCORRECTION; PERFORMANCE; MOTIVATION;
   EMOTIONS
AB Background: Educators and researchers are increasingly aware of the benefits of making errors in learning. However, different approaches to utilizing errors in learning exist, and their impacts require further exploration. Aims: To explore ways to maximize learning outcomes and promote learners' acceptance of making errors in learning, and to compare the emerging deliberate errors approach with the well-established induced errors approach. Samples: In Experiment 1, 52 undergraduate students participated; in Experiment 2, 60 undergraduate students participated. Methods: Experiment 1 contrasted the two error-based approaches and a copy condition regarding recall test scores and learners' subjective experience ratings. In Experiment 2, we manipulated learners' prior knowledge by providing domain-specific examples, guiding them to generate errors conceptually closer to the correct answers. We then compared test scores across learning approaches to assess the impact of this manipulation. Results: Both error-based approaches surpassed the copy condition in recall test scores in Experiment 1. However, induced errors received higher ratings from learners in positive emotions, task engagement, metacognitive evaluations, and willingness to use the method. In Experiment 2, after increasing the association between errors and correct answers with the induced errors method, the test scores using this method were significantly higher than those of the deliberate errors approach. Conclusions: Both the deliberate errors and induced errors approaches can enhance learning, but learners tend to prefer the induced errors approach. Moreover, when the association between errors and correct answers is strengthened through the induced errors method, this enhanced version leads to better learning outcomes than the deliberate errors approach.

   matrix network analysis

LA English
DT Article
DE Teacher multimodal behavior; Student engagement; Classroom discourse;
   Mathematics teachers; Deep learning technology
AB Background: Mathematics is increasingly important in the AI era, yet student engagement in mathematics classrooms remains low, constraining learning outcomes. Although teacher behavior plays a critical role in shaping engagement, prior research has largely examined isolated behavior types, offering limited insight into the differential and synergistic effects of teachers' multimodal behaviors within classroom discourse, particularly in the Chinese cultural context. In addition, traditional approaches are often limited by subjectivity and small data scales. Aims: This study proposes an ICAPD_Q framework for student engagement and examines the differential effects of primary mathematics teachers' multimodal behaviors and their verbal-postural synergistic patterns on student engagement in China. Conclusions: Different types of teacher verbal behaviors, postural behaviors, and their synergistic patterns exerted significantly different effects on student engagement within Chinese mathematics classrooms.

TI Gaining tolerance of immigrants through simulating migratory
   experiences: Quasi-experimental evidence from secondary school
   classrooms
SO COMPUTERS & EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Simulation; Migration; Intergroup; Intervention; Secondary education
ID INTERGROUP CONTACT; METAANALYTIC TEST; IMAGINED CONTACT; ATTITUDES;
   PREJUDICE; GAMES; NARRATIVES; REDUCTION; OUTCOMES; PEOPLE
AB An increase in migrant inflows across various countries has caused rising levels of anti-immigrant sentiment. Anchored in intergroup contact theory, this study examines whether a classroombased simulation can improve students' attitudes toward immigrants. A digital simulation of a migratory journey from the Middle East and North Africa was implemented in five Swedish secondary and upper-secondary schools (N = 148, ages 14-19). Using a repeated-measures design, we assessed changes in attitudes toward immigrants, encompassing political and social tolerance. Data were analysed using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests and hierarchical regression, including moderation analysis. The findings demonstrate that overall tolerance levels improved significantly after the intervention, suggesting that exposure to a simulated migratory experience can foster tolerance. When analysed as separate outcomes, the effect of simulated migration on social tolerance was significantly greater post-intervention, but political tolerance remained statistically insignificant. Hierarchical regression analysis revealed that attitude changes were associated with variations in students' exposure to the simulation, baseline attitudes, perceived learning, and parental political interest. Additional statistical tests showed that susceptibility to attitude change due to simulated migration may depend on prior knowledge of the reasons for migration. Contributing to a scarce body of research, the study provides insights into the effects and critical considerations when using simulated migratory experiences in educational practice to stimulate positive attitude change. These findings extend the contemporary understanding of the mechanisms at play in the relationship between migration background and attitudes towards immigrants, opening a new line of inquiry into leveraging simulations to improve tolerance.

TI Feedback practices with teacher dashboards in primary education:
   Exploring dashboard-prompted feedback across lesson phases
SO COMPUTERS & EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE (5 to 6): Teacher Dashboards; Dashboard-prompted feedback; Primary
   school; ALT; Data-driven decision making
ID TECHNOLOGY; TAXONOMY
AB In primary education, adaptive learning technologies (ALTs) personalise tasks and provide teacher dashboards that visualise real-time student performance and progress. These dashboards can help teachers to provide targeted, real-time feedback based on the dashboard data, a practice known as dashboard-prompted feedback (DP-feedback). This study examined how teachers give different types of DP-feedback (task, process, metacognitive, social, and personal) across different lesson phases (e.g., instruction, guided practice, independent practice). We observed 25 teachers giving dashboard-supported mathematics lessons in primary education. Using visualised behavioural clustering, we analysed the distribution of teachers' DP-feedback across lesson phases. Our results showed that DP-feedback mainly consisted of task and process feedback and was mostly provided in the later phases of the lessons. Three clusters of DP-feedback were identified: feedback provided in one, two, or three lesson phases. No significant relationship was found between the type of feedback and the number of lesson phases in which DP-feedback was given. In addition, we explored the relationship between the clusters and teacher characteristics. Overall, teachers' dashboard use differed primarily in when DP-feedback was enacted across lesson phases, rather than in which feedback types were used, highlighting the relevance of phasesensitive support and technology-specific experience.

TI A critical examination of blockchain in education: A hybrid bibliometric
   and content analysis of sociotechnical imaginaries and pedagogical
   marginality
SO COMPUTERS & EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Blockchain in education; Bibliometrics analysis; Content analysis;
   Sociotechnical imaginaries; Data science applications in education
ID TECHNOLOGY; CHALLENGES
AB Blockchain has been widely promoted as a transformative technology for education, yet existing reviews largely remain descriptive, emphasizing publication growth and keyword trends while offering limited insight into pedagogical and conceptual implications. To address this gap, this study conducts a hybrid bibliometric and qualitative content analysis of 673 Web of Science--indexed journal articles published between 2018 and mid-2025. The analysis identifies three dominant thematic configurations and eleven co-citation clusters, with bibliometric mapping revealing a strong concentration on credentialing and verification, technical infrastructures, and emerging governance-oriented applications. Research output is geographically concentrated, led primarily by China, India, and the United States. To move beyond structural mapping, qualitative content analysis examines how blockchain is discursively framed in educational research. Drawing on the concept of sociotechnical imaginaries, understood here as collectively shared visions linking technological capabilities with assumptions about educational value, governance, and social order, the analysis reveals a dominant imaginary centered on efficiency, trust, and institutional accountability. In contrast, pedagogical innovation, learner agency, and equity-oriented perspectives remain comparatively marginal across influential publications. By empirically demonstrating how certain imaginaries dominate the field while others remain peripheral, this study bridges bibliometric evidence with critical interpretation. It contributes to the literature by clarifying not only what blockchain research in education focuses on, but also how and why particular educational futures are prioritized. The findings underscore the need for future research and policy to more explicitly integrate pedagogical theory, equity considerations, and learner-centered design into blockchain-enabled educational initiatives.

TI Longitudinal relationships between student ethical considerations,
   behavioral intention, and perceived knowledge in artificial intelligence
   education
SO COMPUTERS & EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE AI for social good; AI in education; AI education; K-12 education;
   Theory of planned behavior
ID OF-FIT INDEXES; BETWEEN-PERSON; WITHIN-PERSON; ACHIEVEMENT; PERCEPTIONS;
   COMPETENCE; BELIEFS; AI
AB Artificial intelligence (AI) has revolutionized various aspects of people's lives, yet its misuse poses risks to society. When introducing AI into K-12 education, the concept of AI for social good (AISG) is crucial, as it orients students toward the ethical application of AI. Based partially on the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB), this study explored how AISG, behavioral intention to learn AI (BIAI), and perceived knowledge of AI (AIPK) associate with one another over three years, utilizing a longitudinal and bidirectional design. Random-intercept cross-lagged panel modeling (RI-CLPM) and three-wave data from 614 middle school students (51% boys) demonstrated the evolution of their AISG, BIAI, and AIPK from 2022 to 2024. The results indicated dynamic transitions of student development in AI education. In the first interval, only AISG positively predicted subsequent AIPK. In the second interval, both BIAI and AIPK were positively associated with later AISG, and a reciprocal relationship emerged between BIAI and AIPK. AISG did not significantly predict BIAI in both intervals. These findings empirically underline the implementation of AI ethics for K-12 students in initial AI education. Furthermore, long-term AI curricula should adapt to students' focus shift from AI ethics to competence- and motivation-focused learning. AI ethics should be front-loaded in AI education, while later instruction should strengthen motivation and perceived competence.

TI From scaffolding to transfer: The impact of AI-powered support on
   children's narrative skills
SO LEARNING AND INSTRUCTION
LA English
DT Article
DE Generative AI feedback; Narrative skills; Storytelling; Children
ID LANGUAGE; STORIES; COMPREHENSION; PRESCHOOLERS; LITERACY; STUDENTS;
   STYLE; SELF
AB Background: Children's oral narrative skills are foundational to their school readiness. While artificial intelligence (AI) offers new opportunities to enhance early narrative abilities, research on AI-powered narrative support for young children remains limited, especially in Majority World countries. Aims: Guided by the Interactive, Constructive, Active, and Passive (ICAP) framework, this training study examined the impact of three AI-powered narrative support conditions on Chinese school-aged children's narrative performance. Sample: 180 children (Mage = 78.91 months, SD = 7.05; 97 boys) from North China. Methods: Children were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: (1) Passive-Active Retelling, (2) Autonomous Storytelling with AI Feedback, and (3) Iterative Storytelling with AI Feedback. Narrative performance (story structure, story complexity, and internal state terms) was assessed at baseline, scaffolding, and transfer phases. Children's perceived enjoyment and interest were also examined. Results: After controlling for baseline performance, age, and interaction duration, children in the Iterative Storytelling condition outperformed those in other conditions on all narrative measures during the scaffolding phase. However, in the transfer phase without continued AI support, no significant condition differences emerged with the same controls. Children in the Iterative condition also reported higher enjoyment and interest. Conclusions: Iterative and Autonomous AI support each enhance children's narrative skills during active engagement, with Iterative AI support proving more effective than the other conditions during the scaffolding phase. However, lasting transfer appears to require sufficient practice and interaction time.

TI Weaving the tapestry of student annotations on perusall: Uncovering
   annotation types, syntactic patterns, and their role in learning
SO LEARNING AND INSTRUCTION
LA English
DT Article
DE Online social annotation; Collaborative reading; Computer-assisted
   collaborative learning; Annotation type; Community of inquiry
ID READING-COMPREHENSION; ONLINE ANNOTATION; CRITICAL THINKING; TOOL;
   CLASSROOM; SYSTEM
AB Background: Online social annotation tools like Perusall enable collaborative reading but the diversity of student annotations is underexplored. Aims: This two-stage study aimed to (1) investigate the different types of students' social annotations and identify the characteristic syntactic patterns associated with each type, and (2) examine the correlation between annotation types and their relationships to learning outcomes. Sample: The participants comprised 54 postgraduate students from a university in Hong Kong, enrolled in an MA (TESOL) course. Methods: Stage One analyzed 6517 annotations on Perusall using content analysis to establish a coding scheme, complemented by N-gram analysis to identify characteristic syntactic patterns. Stage Two used Spearman correlations to analyze relationships among ten annotation types and three learning outcomes (course score, upvotes, engagement), supplemented by an open-ended survey of 11 students to explain key patterns. Results: The analysis yielded a ten-type coding scheme mapping onto Community of Inquiry presences. Correlation analysis revealed a primary trade-off between social annotations and note-taking, which students explained as a strategic choice. Two interaction styles emerged: a supportive style and a debate-oriented style. Notably, discussion initiation was associated with higher course scores and peer upvotes, while schema bridging and reflection were linked to deeper engagement and academic performance, despite the former being one of the least frequent types. Conclusions: The study provides a validated analytical framework for research and specific strategies for teachers to cultivate a balanced ecology of online social annotations that supports both community building and cognitive development.

TI Purpose instructions and task models in multiple-text reading
SO LEARNING AND INSTRUCTION
LA English
DT Article
DE Discourse processes; Purpose instructions; Task models; Think-alouds
ID COMPREHENSION; MEMORY; GOALS; EXPLANATIONS; INFORMATION; STRATEGIES;
   KNOWLEDGE; THINKING; ALOUD
AB Background: Purpose instructions are widely used to guide learning from texts and influence learning outcomes; however, how students interpret these instructions, specifically through the construction of task models (i.e., mental representations that guide why and how to read), and how these interpretations shape reading processes and products remain underexplored. Aims: This exploratory study examines how purpose instructions influence students' task model construction, reading processes, and learning outcomes in a multiple-text reading context. Grounded in the MD-TRACE framework, task models are defined as students' self-generated reading goals and planning strategies. Sample: Participants were 75 undergraduates enrolled in an introductory educational psychology course at public university in the northeastern United States. Methods: Students were randomly assigned to one of four purpose instruction conditions (understanding, quiz, essay, or presentation) and asked to read four complementary texts on natural selection. Task models were captured through open-ended responses; cognitive processing was assessed using think-aloud protocols; and learning was measured via a post-reading transfer test. Results: Results reveal that while purpose instructions shape task model complexity, substantial variability exists even within instructional conditions, highlighting the role of individual interpretation. Regression analyses indicate that task model components (e.g., rereading, writing goals) and reading processes (e.g., paraphrasing, bridging) significantly predict transfer performance. Conclusion: These findings underscore the importance of task model construction in the contexts of learning from texts, highlight the need to explore factors influence students' task model construction, and provide new insights into how purpose instructions affect reading processes and products.

TI Implementing multimodal learning analytics in authentic settings: A
   roadmap for ecological impact
SO LEARNING AND INSTRUCTION
LA English
DT Article
AB Multimodal Learning Analytics (MMLA) refers to the use of heterogeneous data sources (e.g., speech, gesture, gaze, posture, physiological signals, digital traces) to model, interpret, and support learning processes as they unfold over time. Research using MMLA is moving from laboratory settings to real-world applications; however, significant challenges remain in implementing these methods in authentic learning environments. This special issue in Learning and Instruction brings together studies that have successfully applied MMLA in various ecological contexts, including classrooms, makerspaces, and high-fidelity simulations. While these contributions show the potential of ecological MMLA, they also highlight that most work remains in the early, descriptive stages, with a limited number of experimental, interventionist, or longitudinal designs capable of establishing causal relationships or sustained impacts in learning and instruction. To support the field's development, this editorial reviews the state-of-the-art, as exemplified by the papers in this special issue, and outlines a roadmap for the next decade, identifying key stages and challenges, to guide MMLA toward broader ecological impact.

TI Evaluating Emotional Intelligence, Authentic Leadership, Self-Efficacy,
   and Perceived Stress Among Diagnostic Radiography Technology Students in
   Clinical Practice
SO INTERNATIONAL MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE emotional intelligence; authentic leadership; self-efficacy; perceived
   stress; radiography; clinical practice; healthcare students
ID NURSING-STUDENTS; VALIDATION
AB Background: Research on emotional intelligence and its associations with authentic leadership, general self-efficacy, and perceived stress among allied health students, particularly radiography students, remains scarce. This study described the levels of these constructs among radiography students during clinical practice, examined their interrelationships, and identified the emotional intelligence facets predicting perceived stress and authentic leadership. Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted among 135 radiography students enrolled in clinical practice at Jazan University, Saudi Arabia, from March to May 2026 (response rate 61.3%). Data were collected using the Schutte Self-Report Emotional Intelligence Test, Authentic Leadership Questionnaire, General Self-Efficacy Scale, and Perceived Stress Scale. Spearman correlations and hierarchical multiple linear regression were performed. Results: Emotional intelligence was positively correlated with authentic leadership (p < 0.001) and general self-efficacy (p = 0.035) and negatively correlated with perceived stress (p = 0.012). General self-efficacy predicted neither outcome. Female students and those with higher GPAs reported higher emotional intelligence and authentic leadership scores. Conclusions: Specific emotional intelligence facets showed distinct predictive roles, with self-directed emotion regulation predicting lower perceived stress and interpersonal emotion management predicting authentic leadership. These findings support the integration of targeted, facet-specific emotional intelligence training within radiography clinical curricula as a potential approach to support stress management and leadership development.

TI Moderating the Association Between Perceived Academic Stressors and
   Active Coping: The Role of University Students' Good Practices
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE perceived academic stressors; active coping; university students; good
   practices; feedback seeking; cooperative work; time management; active
   learning; moderation
AB University students face academic demands that may be associated with reduced use of active coping when perceived as stressful. This study examined whether feedback seeking, cooperative work, time management, and active learning moderated the association between perceived academic stressors and active coping. A cross-sectional, non-experimental design was used with 1014 undergraduates from the University of Extremadura. Participants completed measures of perceived academic stressors (E-CEA), active coping (A-CEA), and good practices (IBPEU). Four separate moderation models were estimated using PROCESS Model 1 with 5000 bootstrap resamples, adjusting for age, gender, year of study, and field of study. Across all four models, higher reported levels of the corresponding good-practice dimension were associated with a less pronounced negative association between perceived academic stressors and active coping. The findings may inform the development and evaluation of student-support and instructional initiatives focused on feedback literacy, cooperative skills, time planning, and active engagement with learning. They also point to the relevance of educational conditions that may facilitate these practices within university learning environments.

TI Digital Learning Tools in Language Education: An Explanatory Model of
   Their Effects on Language Skills and Quality of Life
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article

   of life; technology integration
AB This study examines the extent to which Arabic language teachers employ digital learning tools and proposes an explanatory model of their effects on language skills development and students' quality of life.    Students with Autism Spectrum Disorder in Hong Kong
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE students with autism spectrum disorder; teacher training; teachers'
   self-efficacy; teachers' willingness; inclusive practices
ID INCLUSION; EDUCATION
AB Background: Today, most students with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) are included in general education settings. Teachers are at the forefront in implementing inclusive practices and supporting these students' learning. Their self-efficacy and willingness can determine the success of including students with ASD. TI Exploring key predictors of teacher well-being, job satisfaction and
   burnout: Building a broader conceptualisation of teacher resilience
SO REVIEW OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE burnout; job satisfaction; self-esteem; teacher resilience; well-being;
   workload
ID SCHOOL GOAL STRUCTURE; SELF-EFFICACY; EMOTIONAL INTELLIGENCE; STUDENT
   MISBEHAVIOR; SOCIAL ECOLOGY; STRESS; WORK; PERSONALITY; COMMITMENT;
   SUPPORT
AB This study responds to the urgent teacher retention and mental health crisis by exploring the factors that enable teachers to thrive (or not) within this challenging profession. Using a social-ecological framework of teacher resilience, we explore the relative importance of multiple individual level and contextual level factors as predictors of three resilience-related outcomes (well-being, job satisfaction and burnout). Relative Weights Analysis was conducted on survey data from 2943 teachers in England, demonstrating that which factors are most important for teacher resilience depends on which outcome of the resilience process is being considered. The explained variance attributed to individual versus contextual factors was approximately two-thirds to one-third for well-being, with the reverse pattern observed for job satisfaction and burnout. In other words, while well-being was primarily associated with individual level factors (e.g. self-care and emotional intelligence), job satisfaction and burnout were mainly linked to contextual level factors (e.g. school culture and leadership practices). These findings highlight the importance of adopting a multidimensional perspective that extends beyond a narrow focus on teacher well-being to encompass broader indicators of thriving. The results underscore the need for a balanced approach to intervention research which targets teachers' environments as well as supporting teachers to develop their repertoire of individual competences and coping strategies, if we are to support teachers to be well satisfied and engaged in their work.

TI An investigation into the place of citizenship education discourse in
   the curriculum of Ethiopia
SO REVIEW OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE citizenship education censorship; lack of professional teachers; regime
   appropriation discourse
ID GLOBAL CITIZENSHIP
AB The study was intended to explore the place of citizenship education discourses and constraints along its trajectory in the curriculum of Ethiopia. The paper examines the dual function of citizenship education, serving both as a tool for empowerment and as a means of enforcing ideological discipline. It employs frameworks derived from critical theory and global citizenship education. Using a qualitative design, data were collected from policy documents, curriculum materials, interviews with secondary school teachers, school directors, and experts from the Ministry of Education, and focus group discussions with students. The study found that citizenship education in Ethiopia reflects authoritarian tendencies, limiting democratic ideals through restrictive discourse censorship. It fosters loyalty and obedience rather than promoting active participation and critical thinking. The investigation revealed structural issues in the implementation of citizenship education, notably the absence of qualified teachers, resulting in instruction by educators from different disciplines. This, in turn, affects how the curriculum is actually implemented. The intended objectives of the programme were also hindered by an unfavourable political climate and inadequate establishment of a suitable learning environment. The exclusion of secondary school students from the citizenship education curriculum is a significant issue that requires immediate attention from policymakers and curriculum developers, aligning it with global citizenship education perspective. The Ministry of Education must provide qualified teachers and promote awareness that citizenship education should not serve as a political tool. Schools are encouraged to create an environment that nurtures active, informed, and responsible citizenship among students.Context and implications Rationale for this study: Citizenship education plays a vital role in preparing responsible, informed, and active citizens, making it essential for nation-building and democratic development. However, the extent to which it is effectively integrated into Ethiopia's school curriculum and classroom practice remains insufficiently understood. This study was conducted to examine its implementation and identify areas for improvement. Why this new findings matter: This study matters because it highlights how curriculum design restricts students' civic engagement and comprehension, demonstrating inconsistencies between policy and classroom practices. In this study, we argue that these findings call for clearer, skillsfocused citizenship learning. Implications for educational researchers and policy makers: For educational researchers, these findings highlight the need for further research on effective teacher training approaches and the integration of citizenship education into the curriculum. Future studies should examine how professional development can strengthen teachers' capacity to foster citizenship values and evaluate the long-term impact of curriculum-based citizenship education on students' knowledge, attitudes, and civic engagement. Further, the study emphasizes the need for policymakers to revise curriculum frameworks to focus on civic competencies, critical thinking, and democratic principles, particularly for secondary students in grades 11 and 12, who should be included in the citizenship education framework.

TI Learning with Reflection: Implementing Weekly Reflection Journals to
   Support Conceptual Learning in Upper-Level Undergraduate Engineering
   Courses
SO TRENDS IN HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE engineering education; ICAP framework; reflection; scholarship of
   teaching and learning
ID BETA REGRESSION; FRAMEWORK
AB Reflection can contribute to learning, helping students actively and constructively recall material and connect it with other aspects of their lives, as described by the interactive-constructive-active-passive (ICAP) framework. For engineering students in particular, reflection may support the lifelong learning required throughout one's professional career. This study focused on weekly reflection journals implemented in two junior-level and senior-level civil and environmental engineering courses, investigating (i) how engagement with this activity impacted student learning and (ii) students' views on reflection. In post-surveys, students stated journals helped them to review, identify areas of confusion, and ask questions. Most survey respondents highly rated the journal's impact on learning, although some found greater value in other, more structured activities. Accordingly, the reflection journal may function effectively as one of multiple options for conceptual engagement.

   experimental teaching of health assessment course: a quasi-experimental
   study

DT Article
DE Modified Mini-CEX; SBAR; Health assessment; Experimental teaching
ID CLINICAL EVALUATION EXERCISE; NURSING-STUDENTS; EDUCATION;
   COMMUNICATION; TEAMWORK; TOOL
AB Objective This study aimed to explore the effects of the modified Mini-Clinical Evaluation Exercise (Mini-CEX) combined with the Situation-Background-Assessment-Recommendation (SBAR) model in the experimental teaching of Health Assessment course. Background The Mini-cex and the SBAR model are widely used in clinical nursing to improve nurses' operational skills and general competence. However, there is a lack of evidence to indicate that their combination can produce a synergistic effect on undergraduates' multiple abilities, such as autonomous learning and critical thinking. Design Quasi-experimental. Methods This study included 311 nursing students in two parallel classes at a nursing college and divided them into an intervention group (155 students) and a control group (156 students). In the intervention group, an modified Mini-CEX combined with the SBAR teaching method was adopted, and the teaching process included classroom scenario simulation and clinical apprenticeship. In the control group, conventional teaching methods were used. At the end of the course, the 2 groups of students were compared in terms of independent learning ability, critical thinking ability, nurse empathy, attitude toward communication skills, and course achievement. Results After intervention, the total independent learning ability score(110.20 +/- 6.37 vs. 98.79 +/- 7.57), the total critical thinking ability score(295.43 +/- 15.34 vs. 272.52 +/- 13.85), the total empathy ability score(93.08 +/- 7.61 vs. 86.22 +/- 6.82), the positive scores of students' attitudes toward communication skills score(50.35 +/- 3.95 vs. 46.58 +/- 4.27), and the clinical skills assessment score(78.83 +/- 8.81 vs. 74.82 +/- 9.41) of the students in the intervention group were significantly higher than those of control group, and with a statistically significant difference (p <0.01). There was no statistically significant difference in the total theoretical examination score (p >0.05). Conclusion The application of the modified Mini-CEX combined with the SBAR model in the experimental teaching of Health Assessment course had a positive effect on students, which can improve students' clinical practice abilities and comprehensive clinical quality. The model can be further promoted in the future to improve the quality of teaching and students' professional abilities.

AB Maintaining a stable STEM learning trajectory over an extended duration is a rare achievement. TI Beyond Teaching and Research: Measuring the Societal Impact of
   Universities
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE higher education institutions; third-mission activities; societal
   impact; impact-assessment framework; evaluation metrics
ID SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT; DEVELOPMENT GOALS; ENGAGEMENT; HELIX
AB Higher education institutions face growing pressure to demonstrate and quantify societal contributions beyond research and teaching; this study addresses measurement challenges for third-mission activity by developing both a conceptual typology and a practical assessment framework. We developed a four-dimension typology-research-based impact, teaching-based impact, campus-management-anchored impact, and administrative infrastructure-that synthesizes the existing literature while drawing attention to under-examined areas such as campus operations and institutional support. Methodologically, we synthesize the literature, analyze national and international best practices, and design an assessment approach that combines individual case studies and evidence-based questionnaires with automated metrics applied in multi-year cycles. We demonstrate that the typology reflects a broad range of impact pathways and argue that the proposed framework balances rigor and feasibility while surfacing key measurement tensions-breadth versus depth; general-purpose versus domain-specific metrics; input versus output indicators; levels of analysis; and assessment burden versus outcome quality. We conclude with actionable recommendations for academic staff, institutional leaders, and national agencies to integrate third-mission activities into evaluation and funding systems, offering a methodological toolkit that may support impact assessment into HEI evaluation without overstating conclusions.

TI Teaching Across Cultures in Music: Rethinking Authenticity and Practice
   in Initial Teacher Education
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE intercultural music education; collaborative autoethnography; culture
   bearers; authenticity; pre-service teachers
ID AGENCY
AB In contexts of growing social polarisation and cultural complexity, tertiary educators are increasingly called upon to move beyond celebratory multiculturalism towards critically informed intercultural praxis in preparing students for 21st-century classrooms. Drawing on a sustained transnational collaboration between Australia and Spain within initial teacher education, this paper adopts a collaborative autoethnographic approach to critically reflect on our pedagogical practices and their implications for culturally responsive music education. We examine how intercultural musical encounters, particularly those involving culture bearers, can foster cultural competence and critical reflection among pre-service teachers, while also generating tensions related to knowledge, cultural ownership, authenticity, and appropriation. We propose a conceptual framework grounded in three interrelated dimensions: collaborative partnerships, relational authenticity, and dialogic mediation through educator facilitation. Together, these principles offer an ethically informed and pedagogically grounded approach to intercultural music education that moves beyond representation towards sustained, meaningful engagement with cultural diversity. By foregrounding the role of the educator as a cultural mediator and drawing on insights generated through sustained intercultural practice and prior research, this paper contributes to ongoing debates on belonging, inclusion, and the development of culturally responsive practices in contemporary music teacher education.

TI Twice-Exceptional University Students: Perceptions of Effective Support
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES

DT Article

ID COLLEGE-STUDENTS; HIGHER-EDUCATION; LEARNING-DISABILITIES;
   ACCOMMODATIONS; CHALLENGES; LEARNERS
AB Twice-exceptional (2e) students are both gifted and neurodivergent, and are underrepresented in higher education research, particularly outside the United States. This exploratory qualitative study examined Australian 2e university students' perceptions of effective supports for navigating tertiary education. Guided by Gagn & eacute;'s Talent Development Mega Model, the study explored how institutional and personal supports shape academic engagement, identity, and achievement. Participants (N = 12) self-identified as 2e and were recruited from a large research-intensive Australian university. Participants emphasised the value of flexible, strengths-based learning environments and institutional recognition of twice-exceptionality. However, existing supports were perceived as generic and deficit-focused, highlighting the need for tailored practices, staff training in neurodiversity, and collaboration to support 2e students.

TI Assessing Linguistic and Content Characteristics of First-Grade

SO EDUCATION SCIENCES

DT Article
DE elementary school; writing; assessment; AI; large language models

AB The present study examines how accurately a common large language model (ChatGPT 5.0) assesses linguistic and content characteristics of texts written by first-grade students. TI Effects of van Hiele-Based Instruction on Pre-Service Teachers'
   Geometric Thinking Across the School-University Transition
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE Euclidean geometry; mathematical discourses; primary teacher education;
   van Hiele model of thinking; van Hiele phases of learning
AB This study investigates how pre-service primary education teachers (PSTs) develop geometric thinking when exposed to an instructional approach based on van Hiele's theory. Ninety undergraduate students were divided into experimental and control groups and were assessed before and after a semester of Euclidean geometry instruction. Using mixed-methods analysis, the study examined participants' initial levels of geometric thinking, their progression over time, and the comparative impact of traditional and van Hiele-based instruction. TI An exploratory feasibility study of adaptive assessment: a multivariate,
   data-driven approach to formative evaluation
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE adaptive assessment; AI in education; multi-layer perceptron (MLP);
   online learning; performance prediction; personalised learning; student
   engagement
AB Introduction Adaptive assessment has emerged as a promising approach for addressing learner heterogeneity in digital and online education, yet many existing systems rely on predefined psychometric assumptions that inadequately capture the complex, non-linear relationships among learner characteristics, engagement patterns, and academic performance. This study reports an exploratory feasibility study of a data-driven framework for personalised adaptive question recommendation, designed to estimate anticipated item difficulty using a multivariate set of learner indicators comprising prior academic achievement, engagement levels, study behaviours, and prior course experience. Because the anticipated-difficulty label is derived from four of these same learner indicators, the framework is best understood as a proof-of-concept for recovering a theoretically motivated scoring rule rather than as an independently validated measure of difficulty.Methods To explore this proof-of-concept, an exploratory research design was adopted using an authentic dataset of 71 undergraduate students enrolled across two courses at a higher education institution in Saudi Arabia. A multilayer perceptron (MLP) model was employed to capture non-linear interactions among learner variables, with preprocessing safeguards including ordinal-preserving feature encoding, LOWESS-based outlier suppression, and stratification-controlled oversampling applied exclusively to the training partition. Model performance was evaluated using Repeated Stratified K-Fold cross-validation across nine classifiers, with holdout test evaluation and post hoc feature influence analysis conducted to support pedagogical interpretability.Results The proposed MLP (RMSprop) achieved 93.33% test accuracy (Wilson 95% CI: 70.2%-98.8%, n = 15), demonstrating stable predictive performance and generalisation beyond training data despite sample size constraints. However, the small holdout sample, and the single observation underlying the Hard-class result in particular, mean these figures should be read as indicative rather than precise. Feature analysis indicated that learner engagement and prior academic performance were the most influential contributors to anticipated difficulty estimation, while misclassification patterns were primarily confined to adjacent difficulty levels, reflecting the inherent continuity of learner challenge.Discussion The findings suggest that data-driven adaptive mechanisms can complement traditional assessment approaches by providing context-sensitive, learner-relative difficulty estimation aligned with formative assessment principles. Fairness was not empirically evaluated in this study and is identified as a direction for future work rather than a current contribution. While exploratory in nature, this work contributes to bridging the gap between machine learning-based modelling and principled educational assessment design, offering a foundation for future large-scale and multi-context investigations.

TI Development and validation of the Digital Detox Need Assessment Scale
   among young adults
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE digital detox; digital well-being; factor analysis; psychometrics; scale
   development; self-regulation; young adults
ID SELF-REGULATION; ADDICTION; MODEL
AB The increasing use of digital devices in everyday life has raised concerns about unhealthy patterns of digital engagement and the growing need for measures that assess digital well-being beyond addiction-focused approaches. The present study developed and validated the Digital Detox Need Assessment Scale (DDNAS), a 30-item self-report instrument intended to assess perceived digital detox needs among young adults. The scale was developed based on self-regulation theory, the I-PACE model, compensatory internet use theory, and digital well-being literature. Six dimensions were identified: Behavioural Patterns of Overuse, Psychological Distress, Social Influence and Pressure, Perceived Impact on Well-Being, Self-Regulation Difficulties, and Awareness of the Need for Digital Detox. An initial pool of 90 items was created and pilot tested with 50 young adults to examine item clarity and suitability. The final version of the scale was administered to 1,009 participants aged between 18 and 30 years. Exploratory factor analysis supported a six-factor structure explaining 47.90% of the total variance (KMO = 0.956; Bartlett's test, p < .001). The overall scale showed high internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha = .935), while subscale reliability coefficients ranged from.751 to.837. Confirmatory factor analysis indicated an acceptable model fit (chi & sup2;/df = 3.027, CFI = .935, TLI = .927, RMSEA = .045, PCLOSE = .998). Composite reliability values ranged from.79 to.85. Convergent validity was supported for most dimensions; however, Behavioural Patterns of Overuse and Social Influence and Pressure demonstrated AVE values slightly below the recommended threshold of.50. Discriminant validity was examined using the Fornell-Larcker criterion and was generally supported across constructs. Normative data were also established to facilitate interpretation and practical application of the scale. Overall, the findings suggest that the DDNAS is a reliable and valid measure for assessing digital detox needs among young adults and may be useful in research, psychoeducational programmes, and digital well-being intervention settings.

TI A multidimensional, morphology-sensitive analysis of L2 writing in
   Turkish: an analytic rubric-based approach
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE agglutinative languages; analytic writing assessment; L2 writing;
   morphological processing; writing fluency
ID COMPLEXITY; FLUENCY; ACCURACY
AB Writing in a second language is a multidimensional process shaped by the interaction of linguistic, cognitive, and textual components; however, existing frameworks often underrepresent the role of morphology in structurally complex languages. Addressing this gap, the present study examines writing performance in Turkish as a foreign language through a multidimensional analytic framework. Data were collected from 38 A2-level learners and analyzed using an analytic rubric encompassing content, organization, grammatical accuracy, lexical quality, syntactic complexity, morphological accuracy, mechanics, and writing fluency, complemented by systematic error analysis. Results revealed a clear differentiation across dimensions, with higher performance in discourse-level components (content and organization) and lower performance in morphosyntactic and fluency-related dimensions. In this relatively small exploratory sample, morphological accuracy did not account for additional variance in overall writing performance beyond grammatical accuracy. This finding should therefore be interpreted cautiously and is better understood as preliminary evidence of the embedded role of morphology within the broader morphosyntactic system rather than as evidence that morphology lacks independent importance. Error analyses further indicated that morphological difficulty is not primarily reflected in overt error frequency, but in processing-related constraints affecting fluency and structural complexity. These findings challenge assumptions of dimensional independence in writing and demonstrate that, in agglutinative languages, morphology operates as a cross-cutting system linking accuracy, complexity, and fluency. The study contributes to a reconceptualization of writing as an integrated morphosyntactic system and highlights the need for linguistically sensitive models of writing assessment and instruction.

TI A living archive of JEDI curriculum reform in graduate STEMM education
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE course development; education justice; equity diversity and inclusion
   (EDI); graduate STEMM; transformative education
AB Educational reform has become an important response to intersecting sociopolitical pressures, not only in the broader field of education but also in graduate education in science, technology, engineering, math, and medicine (STEMM), where systemic equity, inclusive training environments, and community belonging have become central goals. Within this broader reform landscape, this perspective article traces the evolution of GRAD 210: Justice, Equity, Diversity, and Inclusion (JEDI) Academic Leadership, a graduate-level elective course for learners across basic and social science disciplines at an Academic Health Center. Developed in relation to student advocacy and broader movements for racial and social justice since the summer of 2020, GRAD 210 has become a living archive documenting how students engage questions of JEDI within shifting political and institutional contexts. We characterize three phases of the curriculum's evolution: (1) 2021-2023: naming harm, building solidarity; (2) 2024: Shifting from DEI to JEDI as a framework; (3) 2025: building infrastructure for justice through sustained, systems-level interventions. Across these phases, we show that student knowledge is historically situated, politically responsive, and strategically generative. We argue that the current moment is not only a period of political contestation but also an opportunity to reflect on how curriculum reform efforts emerge, adapt, and persist. Looking forward, this perspective suggests that future STEMM graduate education reform should prioritize historically grounded curricula that center community care, transformative action, and relational practices for holding difficult conversations while recognizing the different risks people carry.

TI Re-imagining emotionally healthy schools: current challenges and future
   directions
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE children and young people; educator responsibilities; health promotion
   and prevention; mental health and wellbeing; school policies and
   practice; schools
ID ADOLESCENT MENTAL-HEALTH; STUDENT VOICE; CLIMATE
AB Against the backdrop of a complex and unpredictable world, the mental health and wellbeing (MHWB) of children and young people (CYP) is a global concern with high rates of anxiety and depression endemic. The World Health Organisation (WHO) estimate that over five million children in the European Region alone are at risk of not reaching their full developmental potential. Responsibility for MHWB is increasingly incumbent on the education sector in many countries including the UK. Health promoting schools can offer a pivotal gateway to improved MHWB whilst mitigating the risk of poor educational outcomes. Research suggests that school culture is one of the strongest predictors of CYPs' psychological wellbeing. More relational, participatory and inclusive settings can help to minimise anxiety and encourage engagement. Conversely, performative and punitive environments undermine both MHWB and learning. Current evidence from the UK suggests that the impact of school-based MHWB support is limited and provision fragmented. Moreover, with successive governments placing MHWB firmly on the agenda for schools, growing concerns exist around the role of educators and the burden of additional work pressures. The current article considers barriers preventing schools from realising their potential as ideal sites for health promotion and prevention. Predictors of health and wellbeing are discussed in the context of the school environment and wider systemic influences. The author calls for more collaborative, compassionate and relational approaches - re-imagining emotionally healthy school settings - so that all pupils can access their right to an optimal education, good health, and opportunities to flourish.

TI What predicts second-language vocabulary retention? A common-metric
   comparison of behavioural learning traces and self-reported strategy use
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE learning analytics; measurement; second-language acquisition;
   self-report; spaced repetition; vocabulary learning strategies;
   vocabulary retention
AB Introduction Research on second-language vocabulary retention has typically drawn on two largely distinct measurement traditions: learner self-reports of strategy use collected using questionnaires, and behavioural records of practice collected by digital learning platforms. Findings from the two traditions are often cited interchangeably, yet no study has compared their predictive value for retention using a common effect size metric at the level of the individual learner.Methods We report three linked analyses framed as estimation rather than significance contrast. Study 1 modelled 1,930,889 practice traces from 17,230 learners of six languages in a public Duolingo dataset under leakage-strict, user-level cross-validation. Study 1b aggregated the same data to the person level in a prospective design, predicting week-2 recall from week-1 behaviour for 3,957 learners. Study 2 measured 109 English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners with a 45-item strategy questionnaire and a two-wave vocabulary test, analysed under four pre-defined specifications with permutation-based inference.Results Recorded practice history and lag predicted recall (gradient-boosting area under the ROC curve = 0.607 +/- 0.009; Spearman rho = 0.138 +/- 0.013), with near-perfect calibration (expected calibration error = 0.002) and robustness to the exclusion of immediate-retest traces. At the person level, week-1 behaviour predicted week-2 recall [practice-only features, r = 0.195, 95% CI (0.165, 0.225); with week-1 accuracy added, r = 0.469 (0.445, 0.493)]. Self-reported strategy use did not predict measured retention [primary r = -0.108 (-0.290, 0.082)]: none of the 36 subscale-level and none of the 45 item-level associations survived false-discovery-rate correction, and cross-validated classification did not exceed chance (permutation p >= 0.43).Discussion The upper confidence bound of the self-report estimate lies below the lower bounds of both person-level behavioural estimates, and this ordering survives correction for measurement unreliability. We discuss implications for measurement choices in instructed second-language acquisition research.

TI Interpretable and explainable analysis of informal learning behaviors in
   digital education using interaction logs
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE artificial intelligence; explainable artificial intelligence; informal
   learning; interaction log analysis; learning analytics
ID CLUSTERS
AB The digitization of education has increased the availability of student interaction logs on educational platforms, a significant portion of which are non-evaluative interactions associated with informal learning. However, learning analytics and educational artificial intelligence have primarily focused on formal processes and on predicting academic performance, limiting the use of explainability to justifying algorithmic decisions. This paper proposes an empirical-computational framework grounded in interpretable and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) to analyze informal learning processes arising from non-evaluative digital interactions. The findings support the use of explainable learning analytics to understand informal learning behaviors in digital educational environments.

AB Despite widespread recognition of the importance of youth leadership, approaches to assessing leadership abilities remain inconsistent and underexamined.    Survey of Program Directors
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PHARMACEUTICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Academic training; Fellowship; Pharmacy education; Faculty; Postgraduate
AB Objective: This study characterized academic pharmacy fellowship programs, with particular attention to teaching, research and scholarship, practice, and service, as well as institutional and program director demographics and barriers to program offering. By providing contemporary data on program structure, this study sought to inform the broader discourse on workforce development in academic pharmacy. Methods: A 35-item online survey was distributed to academic pharmacy fellowship program directors and pharmacy practice department chairs at 138 US colleges and schools of pharmacy in July 2025. Data were presented using descriptive statistics and analyzed by the unpaired t test and chi 2 test. Results: Fifty-two usable responses were received (38% response rate). The most common barrier to program offering was lack of funding (44%). Conclusion: Academic fellowship programs provide structured exposure to teaching, research, practice, and service, potentially addressing gaps that may exist in traditional postgraduate training pathways. Continued expansion of these programs, improved program visibility and funding, and greater collaboration among institutions and professional organizations may help strengthen the pipeline and cultivate the next generation of academic pharmacists.

   Achievement Among Pharmacy Students
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PHARMACEUTICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Learning styles; Pharmacy education; Academic achievement; Career
   preferences; Social learning
ID PERFORMANCE
AB Objective: To examine the associations between social learning styles, career preferences, and academic achievement among pharmacy students. Methods: This cross-sectional study included 458 Turkish pharmacy students. Social learning styles were assessed using the Grasha-Riechmann Student Learning Styles Scale, which measures independent, dependent, participant, avoidant, collaborative, and competitive dimensions. Academic achievement and career preferences were analyzed using nonparametric tests with bootstrap confidence intervals for effect sizes. Students aspiring to academic careers exhibited higher independent and participant scores alongside markedly lower avoidant tendencies compared with their peers pursuing community, hospital and public sector, or industry roles. Gender differences in learning styles were present, but small in magnitude. Conclusion: Social-interaction learning styles are meaningfully related to academic performance and career orientation in pharmacy education. Avoidant tendencies may serve as academic risk markers, while participant and independent orientations are aligned with academic-career aspirations. These findings suggest value in incorporating learning-style-informed approaches into student support and career guidance.

TI Artificial intelligence ethical awareness of university students in
   Ghana: A network and latent profile analyses
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence; Ethical awareness; Ghana; Higher education
   students; Latent profile analysis; Network analysis
ID FIT
AB Artificial intelligence is becoming increasingly integrated into students' academic lives in Ghana, making it crucial to examine their perspectives on ethical dimensions.    outcomes in Early Head Start programs
SO EARLY CHILDHOOD RESEARCH QUARTERLY
LA English
DT Article
DE Family instability; Child care instability; Early head start; Baby
   FACES; Child developmental outcomes; Teacher change; Toddlers
ID RESIDENTIAL-MOBILITY; DIFFERENTIAL SUSCEPTIBILITY; BEHAVIOR PROBLEMS;

AB Despite growing evidence on the effects of early instability in family and child care, two of the most immediate caregiving environments, few studies have simultaneously examined how disruptions across both settings are associated with infants' and toddlers' social-emotional outcomes, particularly within low-income populations. To address this gap, the present study investigates the developmental risks associated with instability in early childhood using data from the Early Head Start Family and Children Experiences Survey (Baby FACES), a longitudinal, nationally representative dataset including an one-year-old cohort of 463 children fromEarly Head Start programs. These results underscore the importance of considering gender differences in children's responses to early instability and offer important insights into how boys and girls may be differentially affected by disruptions in their caregiving environments.

TI Decoding the pattern-academic nexus: Math reciprocity versus word
   reading directionality
SO EARLY CHILDHOOD RESEARCH QUARTERLY
LA English
DT Article
DE Repeating pattern; Growing pattern; Mathematical ability; Word reading
   ability; Kindergartner
ID FIT INDEXES; CHINESE; MATHEMATICS; PREDICTORS; KNOWLEDGE; AWARENESS;
   NUMERACY
AB Pattern understanding represents a foundational cognitive ability that shapes children's early development in mathematics and reading domains. Despite growing research interest, critical questions remain about the domain-specific characteristics, the unique contributions of different pattern types to academic skills, and the directionality of these relations. To address these gaps, the current study tracked 115 Chinese kindergartners (Mean age = 5.04 years, SD = 0.59) across three measurement waves spanning 12 months, examining the longitudinal relations between repeating pattern, growing pattern, mathematical abilities, and word reading abilities. Cross-lagged analyzes revealed that pattern understanding exhibited bidirectional relations with mathematical abilities, with mathematical ability exerted a stronger facilitating effect on subsequent pattern understanding. By contrast, word reading showed a unidirectional relation, with repeating pattern facilitating later word reading development. Repeating pattern consistently related to growing pattern development in both the mathematics and reading models. These relations remained significant even after controlling for child's age, spatial perception, working memory, and nonverbal intelligence. These findings suggest that pattern-based instructional interventions may effectively support both mathematics and word reading development, while mathematical instruction may offer opportunities for strengthening pattern understanding.

TI Appropriating formative assessment in Mathematics: reported practices
   and professional narratives of secondary school teachers
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
DE Formative assessment; Mathematics education; Teacher professional
   development; Self-regulated learning; Teacher role; Pedagogical change
ID SENSEMAKING; IMPACT
AB Formative Assessment (FA) has demonstrated positive effects on learning, yet a gap remains in understanding how it takes shape in specific disciplines such as mathematics. Grasping this situated dimension is essential for advancing theoretical and practical frameworks on how teachers appropriate and re-interpret formative assessment principles under real classroom conditions. This study examines how secondary mathematics teachers construct professional narratives about FA after participating in a professional development program. We conducted a qualitative analysis of 213 meaning units derived from open-ended responses to a final survey completed by 88 teachers and triangulated these data with 135 excerpts from four focus groups involving 24 of the participating teachers. Through inductive and comparative coding, we identified 14 FA practices organized into four dimensions: (1) a culture of dialogue and peer learning, (2) supporting selfregulation, (3) feedback loops, and (4) tasks and dialogues that make mathematical thinking visible. Focus group analysis also revealed two emergent dimensions: reconfiguration of the teacher's role and emotional tensions associated with pedagogical change. The findings show that, in mathematics, FA is appropriated not as a set of discrete techniques but as an interdependent system of practices that reshapes classroom interaction, learning regulation, and the roles of teachers and students. The study contributes evidence on the situated appropriation of FA in mathematics and suggests that its implementation transforms not only classroom practices, but also teachers' understandings of teaching, learning, and their professional role.

AB The rise of generative AI (GenAI) has made AI literacy and academic literacy critical competencies for students in higher education (HE). TI Rethinking resilience in nursing education: Workplace bullying,
   resilience, and work stress among undergraduate nursing students during
   clinical placements
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Workplace bullying; Resilience; Work stress; Nursing students; Clinical
   placement
AB Background: Clinical placements expose undergraduate nursing students to complex interpersonal and organizational challenges that may contribute to work-related stress. Workplace bullying has emerged as a significant psychosocial stressor, while resilience is often conceptualized as a protective resource. However, its role in this relationship remains unclear. Aim: To examine the relationships among workplace bullying, resilience, and work stress among undergraduate nursing students during clinical placements and to clarify the role of resilience in shaping work stress within the context of workplace bullying. Design: Cross-sectional correlational study. Methods: A total of 325 undergraduate nursing students in Taiwan completed a structured questionnaire measuring workplace bullying (NAQ-R), resilience (Brief Resilience Scale), and work stress (Chinese version of the HSE Indicator Tool). Data was analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). Results: Workplace bullying was positively associated with work stress, whereas resilience was negatively associated with work stress. No significant association was found between workplace bullying and resilience. Neither mediation nor moderation analyses supported resilience as an intermediary mechanism between workplace bullying and work stress. Conclusions: Workplace bullying and resilience appear to function as independent risk and protective factors in relation to work stress. Neither mediation nor moderation effects were observed, supporting a parallel-effects model in which environmental and personal factors contribute independently to nursing students' stress experiences. Implications for nursing education: Interventions should adopt a dual-focused approach that simultaneously addresses the clinical learning environment and actively fosters resilience through structured educational strategies.

TI Understanding maltreatment among autistic children: Insights for
   practitioners and future research directions
SO RESEARCH IN AUTISM
LA English
DT Article
DE Autism; Autism spectrum disorder; Youth; Child welfare; Scoping review;
   Risk factors; Consequences
ID DEVELOPMENTAL-DISABILITIES; SPECTRUM DISORDER; UNITED-STATES;
   PREVALENCE; ABUSE; VIOLENCE; SAMPLE; YOUTH; RISK
AB Purpose: This study identified factors associated with the maltreatment of children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Methods: A scoping review identified 15 studies documenting correlates of maltreatment in children with autism and their parents, families, and/or social context. Results: The findings indicate that autistic girls experience maltreatment more often than autistic boys. Children on the autism spectrum are often reported for physical abuse, but these reports are not necessarily substantiated more often than reports concerning children with different disabilities or who have no disability. Although the associations are modest, several studies reveal that maltreated children with ASD experience more mental health problems, such as self-harm, anxiety, and aggression, than non-maltreated children with ASD. Parents of children diagnosed with ASD also have more mental health issues, including symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder. A few significant findings concern social correlates, including services, discrimination, or socioeconomic status. Conclusion: These results can provide recommendations on questions, designs, and priority variables for future research projects. Specific recommendations are also made regarding assessment practices for maltreatment reports concerning children with ASD.

TI From teacher perceptions to institutional diagnosis: A hybrid
   algorithmic-interpretive framework about innovation processes in school
   networks

LA English
DT Article
DE Institutional diagnosis; Teacher perceptions; Pedagogical transition;
   School networks; Multilevel analysis; Sensitivity analysis; Educational
   change
ID TECHNOLOGY
AB Teacher perceptions provide valuable evidence about how educational change is experienced, but they are more commonly analyzed as individual or contextual outcomes than transformed into reproducible evidence for multilevel institutional diagnosis. This study develops and evaluates a hybrid algorithmic-interpretive framework designed to address this gap in a school network undergoing a shared pedagogical transition. The analysis used a clean sample of 2150 teachers from 87 schools and combined reliability analysis, exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis, factor-specific composite scoring, internally normed classification, multilevel aggregation, school typology detection, and sensitivity analysis. Sensitivity analysis identified Mediating Style, Mastery, Need Coverage, and Pedagogical Leadership as robust critical dimensions across alternative percentile specifications. The framework offers a transparent and auditable procedure for converting validated teacherperception data into differentiated institutional profiles that can support professional interpretation, strategic decision-making, and repeated monitoring of pedagogical change.

TI Development and validation of the Digital Trans-Literacies Scale (DTLS)
   for multilingual youth
SO SYSTEM
LA English
DT Article
DE Digital trans-literacies; Multilingual youth; Social media; Scale
   validation
ID PERCEPTIONS; VALIDITY
AB Due to the widespread use of social media and its affordances, multilingual youth typically draw on diverse linguistic and semiotic resources when engaging in online social networking activities. Such practices require them to possess digital trans-literacies (DTL) - the ability to flexibly and appropriately use multilingual, multimodal, and multi-semiotic resources on social media to meet social, learning, and informational purposes. Nonetheless, there has been limited research on DTL, and no valid instruments exist to measure it. To address this research gap, this study developed and validated the 24-item Digital Trans-Literacies Scale (DTLS), which measures technical, cognitive, and social-emotional dimensions. The questionnaire was administered to 825 university students in Hong Kong. The survey cases were randomly split into two halves: one for exploratory factor analysis (EFA) and the other for confirmatory factor analysis (CFA). After validation, the final scale consists of 12 items. The findings supported the three-factor model, demonstrating good model fit as well as construct validity and reliability. This study deepens insights into the conceptualization of DTL and enriches our knowledge about how multilingual youth develop their digital trans-literacies on social media. It also provides a valid survey instrument for examining digital trans-literacies and will prepare the way for future research on DTL, its antecedents, and its effects.

TI Teacher educators' involvement in the internationalisation of teacher
   education in Vietnam
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Internationalisation involvement; Teacher educator; Teacher education;
   Vietnam
AB Teacher educators are central actors in the internationalisation of teacher education, yet their lived experiences in non-Western, politically governed contexts remain undertheorised. This qualitative study conceptualises the self-internationalisation of 13 Vietnamese teacher educators across five institutions, drawing on semi-structured interviews and an exploratory online questionnaire analysed through reflexive thematic analysis. Three overarching themes were identified: firstly, internationalisation is perceived as inevitable yet structurally unsupported, unfolding as a fragmented, individually driven endeavour in the absence of formal institutional policy; secondly, career phase, international education experience, and gender function as systematic differentiating forces shaping the nature and intensity of involvement; and, finally, four interlocking socialist-neoliberal ideologies, including patriotism, Confucianism, state-centralised control, and competition and productivity, simultaneously enable and constrain self-internationalisation. The findings hold relevance beyond Vietnam for other Asian and socialist-oriented higher education systems navigating the intersecting pressures of global academic integration, state-centralised governance, and market-driven competition.

TI Culturally diverse teachers navigating AI integration: Identity,
   pedagogy, and ethics in multicultural contexts
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article

   Teacher identity; Ethical AI use; Linguistic diversity
ID TECHNOLOGY ACCEPTANCE MODEL
AB This study examines how diverse teachers experience and interpret the integration of generative artificial intelligence within multilingual educational contexts. Drawing on qualitative data from twenty Palestinian-Israeli and Jewish-Israeli teachers, the study explores how linguistic, cultural, and professional conditions shape teachers' engagement with AI. Findings indicate that while participants identified opportunities such as differentiated instruction, instructional flexibility, and content development, they also reported challenges related to accuracy, student overreliance, language accessibility, and ethical responsibility. TI Improving Faculty Performance in Providing Written Feedback to Learners
SO AEM EDUCATION AND TRAINING
LA English
DT Article
AB Background Faculty acknowledged the importance of completing resident and student assessments yet demonstrated difficulty in consistently performing this task. The investigators aimed to increase the completion of written assessments by faculty in an academic medical center between the years of 2019 and 2024, with success defined as assessments of 100% of medical student shifts and 50% of resident shifts in the emergency department.Methods To meet the objective, the investigators established faculty assessment targets in 2020 and implemented annual interventions over 4 years, including incorporation into annual faculty evaluations, use of a tracking dashboard, and integration into the compensation plan. Performance was retrospectively analyzed for the year prior to and the 4 years of interventions.Results Faculty completed assessments for 70% of student shifts and 28% of resident shifts in the 2019-20 academic year. Completion rates improved incrementally over the 4 years of successive interventions and reached 99% of student shifts assessed and 76% of resident shifts assessed. Secondarily, the proportion of faculty meeting assessment targets increased over the study period, with 100% completion rising from 16% to 56% and >= 50% completion rising from 34% to 81%.Conclusions Faculty assessment completion improved substantially after implementation of targets, dashboards, and compensation incentives. These interventions increased both the proportion of learner shifts assessed and the percentage of faculty meeting assessment targets, demonstrating a sustainable strategy to enhance feedback practices in academic medicine.
