TI Development, Implementation, and Evaluation of a Faculty Scholarship
   Program for Emergency Medicine Clinician Educators
SO AEM EDUCATION AND TRAINING
LA English
DT Article
DE curriculum improvement; faculty development; implementation science;
   PRISM framework; protected time
AB Background Scholarship is essential for career progression within academic settings. Unfortunately, time pressures, uncertain processes, and unclear or absent resources remain barriers. We describe the development, implementation, and effectiveness of an internally funded scholarship program for EM faculty clinician educators led by the effort from 2 faculty physician scientists and a full-time Health Science Research Analyst.Methods The program was developed through a needs assessment survey, discussions with faculty development leadership, and components of the PRISM implementation framework. Effectiveness was assessed using an interrupted time series (1 year pre- and 1 year post-implementation). Scholarship was defined a priori as manuscripts, abstract acceptances, regional/national presentations, book chapters, and online publications. The target audience was faculty, residents, fellows, attendings, and advanced practice providers.Results Our needs assessment survey suggested deficiencies in mentorship, formal curriculum, academic writing, and navigating journal submissions. A conceptual framework for scholarship was developed with 4 domains: education, clinical trials and studies, administrative, and training. The program was implemented July 1, 2024, and adopted by 17% (n = 17) of the audience. Acceptability ratings were high, with over 88% of respondents selecting 4/5 or 5/5 (1-5 ordinal scale). Overall scholarship increased from pre-implementation (146 manuscripts, 69 abstracts, 54 presentations, 27 book chapters, 34 online publications; total 330) to post (195 manuscripts, 90 abstracts, 78 presentations, 28 book chapters, 57 online publications; total 448), representing a 35.8% growth. The most notable increases occurred in manuscripts, followed by abstracts and presentations. For adoptees, output increased from a mean of 0.4 to 0.58 per participant per year.Conclusion A faculty scholarship program for EM clinician educators was successfully executed within an implementation science framework. Our program was well received by end users and displayed an increase in scholarly output. Future evaluations will focus on program sustainability, growth, and impact on promotion.

TI Supporting Early Career Teachers: What's the problem represented to be
   in England and South Australia?
SO AUSTRALIAN EDUCATIONAL RESEARCHER
LA English

AB The widespread acceptance of the importance of supporting Early Career Teachers (ECTs) through mentoring, induction, and coaching is reflected in the proliferation of support programs for ECTs across many educational contexts. By understanding the representations, it was possible to identify alternative strengths-based representations of the problem along with solutions that could be implemented.

TI Improving Spatial and Assembly Learning in Modular Building Education:
   An Augmented Reality-Based Instructional Approach
SO COMPUTER APPLICATIONS IN ENGINEERING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE augmented reality (AR); building information modeling (BIM); engineering
   education; modular construction education; procedural learning; spatial
   visualization
ID BIM
AB Modular construction is increasingly adopted in industry; however, undergraduate civil engineering students often struggle to comprehend assembly sequencing and structural connection logic when instruction relies primarily on two-dimensional (2D) drawings and text-based materials. These limitations hinder the development of spatial visualization and procedural cognition, skills essential for modular construction planning and coordination. To address this instructional gap, this study designed and evaluated an augmented reality (AR)-supported Building Information Modeling (BIM) learning environment named AR-ModuConnect aimed at enhancing students' conceptual and procedural understanding of modular steel building connections. The instructional approach enables interactive three-dimensional visualization of intra-module, inter-module, and module-to-foundation connections, supported by animated assembly sequencing. A quasi-experimental implementation was conducted with civil engineering undergraduates to compare learning outcomes between the AR-supported instruction and conventional methods. Learning effectiveness was assessed through measures of conceptual understanding, spatial visualization, and procedural clarity, while usability was evaluated using the System Usability Scale (SUS). Results indicate that students exposed to the AR-BIM instructional approach demonstrated significantly improved comprehension of connection systems and assembly processes. The SUS score of 69.46 suggests acceptable usability for integration into engineering curricula. These findings contribute empirical evidence to immersive technology-enhanced learning in construction education and highlight the potential of AR-supported BIM environments for strengthening procedural learning in modular construction courses.

TI Indlela Ibuzwa Kwabaphambili: integrating indigenous knowledge systems
   into African environmental education
SO CURRICULUM PERSPECTIVES
LA English
DT Article
DE Integration; Indigenous Knowledge Systems; Environmental Education;
   Sustainable Development
ID SCIENCE-EDUCATION; CHALLENGES
AB This conceptual study explores the integration of Indigenous Knowledge Systems (IKS) into African environmental education, using the Zulu proverb Indlela Ibuzwa kwabaphambili (The path forward is to enquire from those who have preceded us). IKS are rich in environmental knowledge and education, yet formal education and training sideline them. Additionally, the study calls for a shift in environmental education that acknowledges the interconnectedness of indigenous wisdom and scientific knowledge, fostering a holistic, culturally relevant and sustainable learning experience.

TI Promoting Engagement in Elementary School: A Systematic Review and
   Meta-Analysis of Intervention Effects
SO EDUCATIONAL PSYCHOLOGY REVIEW
LA English
DT Article
DE Student engagement; Elementary school students; Interventions;
   Systematic review; Meta-analysis
ID TEACHER-STUDENT RELATIONSHIPS; CHILDRENS ENGAGEMENT; LEARNING SCIENCE;
   RANDOMIZED-TRIAL; PEER REJECTION; ACHIEVEMENT; BEHAVIOR; IMPACT; TOOL;
   MOTIVATION
AB Vital to long-term academic success, student engagement is a key intervention target, especially during the early years of schooling when initial signs of disengagement may appear. The primary goal of this systematic review was to identify interventions promoting elementary student engagement and determine the best intervention approaches. We systematically searched Education Resources Information Center, PsycINFO, and Web of Science (July 2024) to identify intervention studies examining behavioral, cognitive, or affective engagement among elementary students, as compared to standard instruction, through experimental or quasi-experimental designs. Methodological bias was assessed using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (Hong et al., ). Data were synthesized through meta-analyses and subgroup analyses using a three-level model with robust variance estimation. Forty-six interventions (38,225 students) met inclusion criteria, reporting data for behavioral (k = 41; n = 36,122), affective (k = 14; n = 5,065), and cognitive engagement (k = 5; n = 1,907). Three main types of intervention were identified and compared for behavioral engagement: teacher support (i.e., professional development; g = .503, 95%CI [.105, .901], k = 9), student-directed (g = .370, 95%CI [.198, .542], k = 27), and multimodal interventions (g = .385, 95%CI [.202, .569], k = 4). Among student-directed interventions, three strategies were compared: social-emotional skills development (g = .171, 95%CI [.027, .314], k = 12), learning strategy development (g = .801, 95%CI [.318, 1.285], k = 6), and classroom physical activity (g = .478, 95%CI [-.100, 1.056], k = 7). Methodological biases were also used as moderators. Evidence is strongest for behavioral engagement, for which teacher-focused and learning-strategy interventions appear particularly promising. Conclusions for affective and cognitive engagement remain more tentative.

TI Four Decades After the Big-Fish-Little-Pond Effect: Critical Boundary
   Tests and Integrative Models of Mean-Context, Ordinal-Standing, and
   Distributional-Scaling in 46 Countries
SO EDUCATIONAL PSYCHOLOGY REVIEW
LA English
DT Article
DE Big-Fish-Little-Pond Effect; Academic self-concept; Social comparison;
   Ordinal standing; Adaptation-level processes; Distributional scaling;
   Statistical-Mechanism Gap Fallacy
ID ACADEMIC SELF-CONCEPT; GERMAN SCHOOL SYSTEMS; DIMENSIONAL COMPARISONS;
   ACHIEVEMENT; PERFORMANCE; MULTILEVEL; REUNIFICATION; METHODOLOGY;
   CLASSROOM; FAILURE
AB The Big-Fish-Little-Pond Effect (BFLPE) is the negative association between class-average achievement and students' academic self-concept after controlling individual achievement. Over four decades, the BFLPE has become one of educational psychology's most robust cross-national findings. However, psychological, economic, and contextual-judgment traditions propose different representations of social comparison: adaptation-level models emphasize contextual means, ordinal-standing models emphasize relative rank, and distributional-scaling models emphasize broader properties of local achievement distributions. Using TIMSS 2019 Grade 8 mathematics data from 46 countries (11,684 classes; 262,988 students), this study provides the first large-scale cross-national test of these formulations within a unified modeling framework. Consistent with prior BFLPE research, higher individual achievement positively predicted mathematics self-concept, whereas higher classroom mean achievement negatively predicted it. Ordinal standing also positively predicted self-concept in simpler models. However, strong ordinal-standing formulations predict that the negative contextual-mean effect should substantially attenuate or disappear when ordinal position is fixed at the top of the classroom distribution. Inconsistent with this prediction, the BFLPE remained evident even for the highest-ranked student in each class. Models integrating all three approaches further indicated that much of the apparent ordinal-rank effect reflected broader forms of distributionally scaled relative achievement embedded within classroom distributions. The findings support an integrative interpretation in which ordinal standing is relevant, not sufficient: contextual means, ordinal standing, and distributional structure jointly shape comparative self-evaluation, while contextual means remained the most robust comparative indicator. More broadly, the study highlights the Statistical-Mechanism Gap Fallacy: interpreting statistical contextual indicators as psychologically transparent representations of comparison mechanisms.

DT Article

AB Gamification has gained increasing traction as an innovative approach to science communication. In this work, we present and evaluate Finding Gaia, a virtual treasure hunt designed during the COVID-19 pandemic to engage secondary school students in climate change education.The activity transforms a conventional lesson on climate risks and mitigation into a series of cooperative online challenges. TI 3-Dimensional versus 2-dimensional visualization on laparoscopic skills
   training in a low-cost simulation model: a randomized cross-over trial
SO GLOBAL SURGICAL EDUCATION - JOURNAL OF THE ASSOCIATION FOR SURGICAL
   EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Laparoscopy; Simulation training; Spatial navigation; Training
   technique; Financing; Healthcare
ID PROSTATECTOMY; PERFORMANCE; SURGERY; COMPARE; VISION; IMPACT
AB Introduction Three-dimensional (3D) visualization may improve spatial orientation and depth perception during laparoscopic surgery and simulation-based training. However, the cost of commercially 3D available systems remains a major barrier to widespread implementation, particularly in resource-limited educational settings. This study aimed to compare the effects of 3D and 2D visualization on a low-cost laparoscopic simulation-basic model.Methods A randomized, comparative, crossover simulation study was conducted with 48 medical students who had completed an operative technique and experimental surgery course. Participants were randomized to perform four standardized laparoscopic tasks in one of two visualization sequences: two-dimensional high-definition followed by 3D high-definition visualization, or 3D high-definition followed by two-dimensional high-definition visualization. Task completion time and number of errors were recorded for each task and each visualization modality. A study-specific post-task questionnaire assessed perceived depth perception, performance, speed, visual adaptation, and adverse symptoms.Results Among participants who performed tasks first with two-dimensional visualization and then with three-dimensional visualization, three-dimensional visualization was associated with shorter completion times and fewer errors in all four tasks. Initial testing also favored 3D visualization in three of the four tasks. Most participants reported better depth perception (97.9%), better performance and more accurate gestures (79.2%), and faster task execution (85.4%) with three-dimensional high-definition visualization. Reported adverse symptoms included discomfort related to instrument handling, blurred vision, and dizziness.Conclusion In this low-cost simulation model, three-dimensional high-definition visualization was associated with faster task completion, fewer errors, and greater participant preference than two-dimensional high-definition visualization. These findings support low-cost stereoscopic platforms as feasible adjuncts for early laparoscopic skills acquisition and justify future comparisons with contemporary virtual-reality, haptic, and autostereoscopic training systems.

TI STEM Participation in Global Higher Education: Core-Periphery Structures
   and Scientific Capital in Fulbright Foreign Student Program
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF SCIENCE AND MATHEMATICS EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Core-periphery theory; Global STEM participation; International higher
   education; Scientific capital; Structural concentration
AB Science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) participation is a central concern in mathematics and science education because it reflects how global higher education systems distribute access to advanced knowledge, research infrastructure, and scientific recognition. Yet participation in international STEM mobility remains unevenly structured across national, regional, and economic contexts. This study examines global patterns of STEM participation within the Fulbright Foreign Student Program as a window into how scientific opportunity is organized internationally. Drawing on administrative data for 16,627 Fulbright STEM scholars from 161 countries awarded between 2015 and 2024, the study employs a structural descriptive quantitative design using inequality and concentration measures. Guided by a dual theoretical framework integrating core-periphery theory and scientific capital, the analysis examines how STEM participation is distributed across world regions and income classifications, the extent to which participation is concentrated among a small number of countries, and how these patterns evolve over time. The findings reveal pronounced concentration, with a limited set of countries accounting for a disproportionate share of STEM scholars, alongside modest evidence of diffusion across a broader range of national contexts. These patterns are interpreted as structural associations, reflecting distributional tendencies within this program during the study period. Differences across income groups further indicate distinct configurations of scientific capital, with high-income systems exhibiting more diversified participation and lower-middle-income systems relying on concentrated national hubs. The findings suggest that STEM participation in Fulbright reflects persistent global structures alongside expansion across national contexts. These findings contribute to STEM education research by advancing a macro-structural perspective on participation and by extending scientific capital beyond individual trajectories to the level of global higher education systems.

TI Enriching a critical emancipatory approach to global citizenship
   education: Conceptual reflections on using Oskar Negt's "creation of
   context" as leitmotif
SO INTERNATIONAL REVIEW OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Global citizenship education; Creation of context; Imperial mode of
   living; Contradiction of education and domination; Emancipation
AB This conceptual article aims to enrich critical emancipatory perspectives on global citizenship education by drawing upon the meta-competence "creation of context" introduced by German social philosopher and adult educator Oskar Negt (1934-2024). Negt is well-known in Germany (though not so much elsewhere) for his landmark work on critical theory (in the context of the so-called "Frankfurt School"), social sciences and (adult) education. The authors of this article discuss his seminal perspective with reference to two other theoretical approaches that are also widely discussed in Germany but have yet to enter the debate in education and social sciences elsewhere. First, they address the critical theory on education and liberation proposed by Heinz-Joachim Heydorn in his paper on the contradiction between education (Bildung) and domination. Second, they elaborate on the social diagnosis of the imperial mode of living proposed by Ulrich Brand and Markus Wissen, which features in contemporary discourse on the emancipatory power and potential of education in Germany. Both help to underline why "creation of context" might serve as a leitmotif for a critical emancipatory approach to global citizenship education.

TI Exploring Team Creativity Through Wallas's Framework
SO JOURNAL OF CREATIVE BEHAVIOR
LA English
DT Article
DE creativity; critical incidents; team creativity; Wallas's four-stage
   model
ID CRITICAL INCIDENT; TRANSFORMATIONAL LEADERSHIP; EMPLOYEE CREATIVITY;
   LEARNING-BEHAVIOR; GOAL ORIENTATION; INNOVATION; WORK; DIVERSITY;
   PERSPECTIVE; CLIMATE
AB In this study, we examine how Wallas's (1926) four-stage creative process, including Preparation, Incubation, Illumination, and Verification, can be adapted to describe the dynamics of team creativity. While this model is widely applied at the individual level, Wallas's model has been rarely tested in collaborative settings. Using the Critical Incident Technique (CIT), we conducted semi-structured interviews with 33 experienced team leaders from diverse industries in Thailand. Our analysis revealed 17 types of critical incidents that emphasize team creativity is recursive, socially situated, and shaped by mechanisms such as co-illumination, collective reflection, iterative feedback loops, and leadership facilitation across stages. Our findings show that Wallas's stages remain a useful heuristic but require extension to accommodate social interaction, emergent sub-stages, and context dependencies. This study contributes to creativity theories by extending Wallas's model for collaborative settings by demonstrating the value of CIT in uncovering team-level processes. For practical implications, this study provides guidance for managers and leaders who seek to foster conditions that enable collaboration, iteration, and breakthrough innovation.

TI The Creative Greenhouse: A Systems-Ecological Framework for Designing
   Environments That Cultivate Creative Resilience
SO JOURNAL OF CREATIVE BEHAVIOR
LA English
DT Article
DE adaptive learning; creativity; educational ecology; ethical design;
   pedagogy; resilience; systems thinking
ID CLIMATE
AB Although creativity is frequently conceptualized as an individual trait or a collection of skills, increasing evidence highlights the decisive role of environmental conditions in shaping creative development. This paper proposes the Creative Greenhouse as a systems-ecological framework for understanding how creative resilience could be cultivated through the calibrated interaction of care, challenge, constraint, and temporal rhythm within designed learning environments. Drawing on ecological theory, creativity research, and pedagogical design, the framework reframes creativity as an emergent property of adaptive systems rather than a fixed learner attribute, positioning the school as an intentionally designed Creative Greenhouse within the learner's wider developmental field. The framework specifies how psychological safety, productive tension, ethical boundaries, and cyclic structures of exploration and reflection can collectively support learners in navigating uncertainty and sustaining creative engagement over time. The Creative Greenhouse provides conceptual guidance for designing educational ecosystems that balance support with purposeful disturbance. Implications for curriculum design, classroom practice, and future empirical inquiry are discussed, including avenues for operationalizing the framework through design-based and longitudinal research.

TI How Construal Level Affects Innovative Intention at Work
SO JOURNAL OF CREATIVE BEHAVIOR
LA English
DT Article
DE construal level; innovative intention; perceived difficulty; perceived
   importance
ID BEHAVIORAL INTENTIONS; PERCEIVED IMPORTANCE; FEASIBILITY; PEOPLE;
   DESIRABILITY; ABSTRACTNESS; DEFINITION; CREATIVITY; ATTITUDES; DISTANCE
AB Recently researchers have paid increasing attention to how perception and cognition at the individual level affect innovation at work. The present research investigated whether and how construal level affects individuals' innovative intention at work. Four studies were conducted to examine the relationship between construal level and innovative intention, as well as the underlying mechanism. Study 1 (N = 157) and Study 2 (N = 167) examined the causal relationship between construal level and innovative intention by manipulating construal level by "why" versus "how" mindset and temporal distance, respectively. Study 3 (N = 175) further tested the applicability of this causality in one specific innovative context in the workplace (i.e., teaching innovation) and replicated the findings of the previous two studies. Study 4 (N = 171) explored the potential mediators in the relationship between construal level and innovative intention, and found that perceived importance of innovation rather than perceived difficulty of innovation mediated this relationship. The current research adds evidence to how construal level affects attitudes and behaviors in organizations and has significant practical implications for motivating individuals' innovation at work.

TI Modeling Item Responses to Understand Change over Time and Diagnostic
   Needs in Tandem
SO JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL MEASUREMENT
LA English
DT Article
ID CLASSIFICATION MODELS; IRT; AGREEMENT; FIT
AB Achievement tests are often designed to measure student growth over time using vertical scales while also providing diagnostic information on mastery of specific skill areas. However, traditional assessments rarely integrate psychometric models appropriate for both purposes. This study examines an approach combining vertical scaling with Diagnostic Classification Models (DCMs) to provide both overall achievement scores and subtest-level diagnostic classifications to provide growth and diagnostic information simultaneously. We compared four model specifications against traditional unidimensional vertical scaling using empirical data from the Virginia Language and Literacy Screening System with 17,302 kindergarten and 18,339 first-grade students. We evaluated model fit, score comparability, and classification reliability, and added Monte Carlo simulations to assess parameter recovery. Results revealed important tradeoffs between approaches. While no single approach provided an ideal solution, second-order DCMs with appropriate constraints offer practical viability for operational assessment contexts that wish to measure student growth while also providing diagnostic information.

TI A rubric to assess generative AI-based feedback on student writing
   assignments
SO JOURNAL OF MICROBIOLOGY & BIOLOGY EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE undergraduate; science writing; writing feedback; generative artificial
   intelligence; STEM
AB Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools are an increasingly common resource used in the classroom and writing process. The landscape of available GenAI tools is rapidly evolving, so having a systematic and straightforward way to evaluate new tools for incorporation into the classroom is key. For example, in science writing education, GenAI tools can be used as a supplement to instructor feedback on student writing, allowing an additional opportunity for critique and revision by the student. Here, we describe a rubric we developed to enable instructors to assess differences between feedback provided by GenAI models based on five key areas: (i) accuracy, (ii) constructiveness, (iii) clarity and readability, (iv) recognition of strengths, and (v) original text. We show data comparing the feedback provided by multiple GenAI models on student work based on course guidelines. This rubric can serve as a resource for other instructors interested in evaluating various GenAI models for use as scientific writing feedback supplements in their own classrooms.

TI The Separate Worlds of Science and Science Teaching, According to
   Potential Science Teachers
SO JOURNAL OF RESEARCH IN SCIENCE TEACHING
LA English
DT Article
DE apprenticeship of observation; figured worlds; science identities;
   science teaching; teacher shortages; teaching
ID IDENTITY WORK; SCHOOL; GIRLS; PERCEPTIONS; MATHEMATICS; EDUCATION;
   PEDAGOGY; FUTURE; COULD; THINK
AB In the context of severe and worsening science teacher shortages in many countries and a body of literature reliant on retrospective accounts from those already teaching science, this paper explores the views and assumptions held about school science teaching by potential future science teachers. Using a theoretical lens informed by the concept of 'figured worlds', this paper presents analyses of qualitative data collected in the UK and Canada via longitudinal and life history methods to examine what science majors assume to be true about science teaching, and what influences shape these assumptions. Analyses demonstrate that the world of science teaching is distinct, and even isolated, from the world of science according to potential future science teachers. These data evidence contrasting epistemologies between the worlds of science teaching and science, and indicate that those who have worked to conduct their identities in line with science may struggle to develop identities within, or towards, the figured world of science teaching. We end this paper with a discussion of the implications of these findings in relation to ongoing science teacher shortages.

TI Inclusive education in Portugal: 50 years following the 25th April
   revolution
SO JOURNAL OF RESEARCH IN SPECIAL EDUCATIONAL NEEDS
LA English
DT Article
DE democracy; educational policy; inclusion; people with disabilities;
   Portugal; special educational needs
AB After the 25th of April 1974, Portugal was marked by legislative developments in major areas defining a democratic society, including education. The aim of this paper is to describe a comprehensive analysis of the legislation on education for children with disabilities in Portugal, exploring commonalities with international developments regarding children's rights and access to education. A document analysis was conducted on the chronology of laws on education for children with disabilities over the last 50 years coupled with assessment of quantitative indicators of their access to mainstream schools. Findings confirm the accomplishment of significant legislative developments following the 25th April 1974 affirming and reaffirming the right of children with disabilities to education in mainstream settings and establishing support for them to succeed in school. Legislative developments were analysed within G & ouml;ransson & Nilholm's framework (2014), describing evolving categories to education from physical placement in mainstream schools towards the building of an inclusive and supportive school community based on principles of equity, care and justice. Legislative developments were consistent with the focus of international conventions as well as the emphasis on access to education in mainstream schools, highlighting that inclusive education for children with disabilities has been mainly a policy-driven process.

   and sexuality diverse autistic students' perspectives of Internet
   threats
SO JOURNAL OF RESEARCH IN SPECIAL EDUCATIONAL NEEDS
LA English
DT Article
DE autism; D/discourse; gender diversity; inclusive learning environment;
   intersectionality; online safety; sexuality diversity
ID SPECTRUM DISORDER; ADOLESCENTS; INTERSECTIONALITY; NEURODIVERSITY;
   COMMUNICATION; IDENTITY; PEOPLE
AB Autistic students often face unique challenges related to Internet threats. When intersected with gender and sexuality diversity, challenges can compound and lead to increased risk of bullying, discrimination, marginalisation and exclusion. Although there is an intersection between autism and gender and sexuality diversity, the voices of gender and sexuality diverse autistic students about Internet threats remain an underexplored research area. Most studies have focused on neurotypical, heterosexual and cis-gender students or addressed autism, sexuality and gender separately. This paper builds on findings from a recent exploratory pilot study offering new empirical insight into autistic perceived Internet threats-an area currently underrepresented in inclusive education and digital safety. This paper presents considerations from the exploratory pilot study to inform future research on gender and sexuality diverse autistic students' perspectives on Internet threats. The pilot study engaged with autistic voices and employed a D/discourse theoretical framework, the Inclusive New Literacies and 4 CO:RE Classification of Online Risk to Children frameworks when interpreting the data. Recommendations may inform educators, parents/carers, policy-makers and practitioners regarding appropriate Internet safety education to promote positive and safe online learning experiences of gender and sexuality diverse autistic students who are a population with unique neurodiversity, identities and experiences.

TI Unrecognized Sleep Difficulties and Caregiver Awareness at School Entry:
   A Population-Based Study of First-Grade Children
SO JOURNAL OF SCHOOL HEALTH
LA English
DT Article
DE caregivers' awareness; child sleep; early identification; school entry;
   school readiness; sleep health
ID FUNCTIONAL CONSEQUENCES; INADEQUATE SLEEP; UNITED-STATES; PATTERNS;
   ASSOCIATIONS; DURATION
AB Background Sleep difficulties are common in childhood and affect behavior, emotional regulation, and school functioning, yet are often unrecognized by caregivers. Methods This population-based, repeated cross-sectional study included 1168 first-grade children (6-7 years) in & Eacute;vora, Portugal. Sleep was assessed using the Portuguese Children's Sleep Habits Questionnaire (CSHQ-PT) and a structured family questionnaire. Associations with sociodemographic and family factors were examined using multivariable logistic regression; short sleep duration was analyzed using penalized logistic regression. Results Across cohorts, 46%-49% of children met the criterion for clinically significant sleep disturbance (SDI >= 48). Bedtime resistance, daytime sleepiness, and sleep-related anxiety were the most prevalent difficulties. Fewer than 10% of caregivers reported sleep problems, even among affected children. Clinically significant sleep disturbance was associated with caregiver education and later dinner timing, while longer commuting distance was associated with short sleep duration. Implications for School Health Policy, Practice, and Equity Findings support brief sleep screening and family-oriented sleep health guidance at school entry. Conclusion Many children begin primary school with unrecognized sleep difficulties, highlighting the value of integrating sleep health into early school health frameworks.

TI Feeling the Best Fit: The Role of Emotions in College Decisions
SO SOCIOLOGY OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE transition to college; emotions; college access and choice; students
   from systematically marginalized groups; college
   aspirations/expectations
ID STUDENTS; EXPECTATIONS; PERCEPTIONS; ASPIRATIONS; TRANSITION;
   ENROLLMENT; SELECTION; FAMILISM
AB Using ethnographic observations and interviews with students and staff in a college access nonprofit (CAN), I show that college-going inequalities may also reflect structurally based emotional barriers and that these barriers can be overcome through opportunities to imagine futures with positive emotional valences where the student "fits" in college, and where college is a "fit" for the student. Before joining the CAN, students aspired to attend college, but their sense of fit was low and grounded in negative emotions (e.g., worries about challenges, ambivalence about college choices). Through CAN-sponsored college visits and precollege career-opportunity programs, students were able to imagine futures where they fit in college and where college fit their goals-imagining futures with positive emotional associations. This sense of fit allowed students to confidently make emotionally informed decisions about colleges and majors. I argue emotional barriers play an underdiscussed role in college transitions and clarify how emotions, by undergirding college decisions, shape youths' paths to college.

AB Empathy is an implicit goal of sociology curricula, central to linking structure and agency and fostering a sociological imagination. It is also a valued "soft skill" in fields like social work, health care, and counseling. This study extends Rockwell et al.'s finding that introductory sociology can foster empathy by examining whether such outcomes differ across in-person and online-asynchronous courses. Our sample consisted of 190 students enrolled in introductory sociology courses, including 158 in in-person and 32 inonline-asynchronous courses. In contrast to Rockwell et al., we found no statistically significant overall change in empathy scores for our sample from pretest to posttest regardless of modality. These findings highlight both the limits and the promise of teaching empathy across modalities in sociological education.

TI Artificial Intelligence and the Sociological Imagination: Cultivating
   Reflexive Algorithmic Capital through Sociology Pedagogy

LA English
DT Article

   experiential learning
ID BOURDIEU; ETHICS
AB Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly reshaping social life, yet AI literacy remains underdeveloped in undergraduate sociology. This article offers a sociology-forward framework for integrating AI into the curriculum. Drawing on Bourdieu's theory of practice, it emphasizes experiential learning, justice-oriented instruction, and critical sociotechnical reflexivity. TI Understanding oral corrective feedback in Chinese university EFL
   classrooms: a qualitative study of cognitive, affective, and relational
   processes
SO ASIAN-PACIFIC JOURNAL OF SECOND AND FOREIGN LANGUAGE EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Oral corrective feedback; Affective mediation; Sociocultural theory;
   Feedback ecology; Teacher-student interaction; EFL pedagogy; Chinese
   higher education
AB Oral corrective feedback (OCF) is widely recognised as a key pedagogical mechanism in the development of second language speaking proficiency; however, existing research has largely examined OCF in controlled settings or focused on isolated feedback types, offering limited insight into how feedback is interpreted, negotiated, and enacted within authentic classroom interaction. Addressing this gap, this qualitative study examines how cognitive, social, and affective processes shape teachers' and students' experiences of feedback in Chinese university English as a foreign language (EFL) classroom. Rather than treating OCF as a purely technical corrective move, the study conceptualises it as a relational and context-sensitive pedagogical process. Drawing on interactionist and sociocultural perspectives, the study investigates the perspectives of 12 university English teachers and 24 undergraduate students across fluency- and accuracy-oriented speaking tasks. Data were generated through semi-structured interviews, non-participant classroom observations, and stimulated-recall sessions, and analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. The findings indicate that OCF is understood not merely as a technical response to linguistic error but as a relational pedagogical practice embedded in task demands, classroom norms, and interpersonal considerations. Teachers emphasised the strategic calibration of timing, explicitness, and scaffolding to support noticing and self-repair, while students foregrounded relational sensitivity, emotional safety, and face protection as conditions for meaningful engagement with feedback. Three interrelated tensions were identified: negotiating explicit correction alongside affective comfort, managing face and hierarchical relations during public feedback, and orchestrating teacher, peer, self-, and technology-supported feedback within everyday classroom activity. Overall, the study demonstrates that the effectiveness of OCF emerges from the dynamic coordination of cognitive, affective, and interactional factors rather than from isolated feedback techniques. The study contributes to EFL pedagogy in Asian higher education by offering a reconceptualised understanding of OCF as a relational, affect-sensitive, and contextually mediated process, with implications for designing task-sensitive and learner-responsive feedback practices.

   AI-generated revision podcasts on learning outcomes and retention among
   medical students
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence; Medical education; Podcasting; Mobile learning;
   Mixed methods; Retention; Community medicine; India; Self-directed
   learning; Distributed practice
ID QUALITY
AB Background Medical curricula overload necessitates efficient, self-directed learning strategies that can utilize 'dead time' for study. AI-generated audio offers a scalable resource for this purpose, yet evidence regarding its efficacy in low-resource settings is limited. This study evaluated the effectiveness and learner perceptions of AI-generated podcasts on learning outcomes and retention among Indian medical students. Methods A multicentre, quasi-experimental, mixed-methods explanatory sequential study was conducted at two geographically distinct medical colleges in India. Third-professional undergraduate MBBS students received six AI-generated, faculty-validated revision podcasts covering high-yield Community Medicine topics. Knowledge was assessed via a validated 60-item MCQ test at baseline (pre-test), immediately post-intervention, and at 30 days (delayed post-test). The intervention and assessments targeted both lower-order (remember, understand) and higher-order (apply, analyse) cognitive domains per Bloom's Taxonomy. The primary analysis employed a Linear Mixed-Effects Model (LMM) to estimate learning trajectories. Qualitative data from Focus Group Discussions (FGDs) were analyzed using Framework Analysis to explore mechanisms of impact and integrate findings with quantitative outcomes. Results The analytic cohort comprised 239 participants. Retention trajectories diverged: Centre 1 showed stable retention at 30 days, while Centre 2 experienced significant knowledge decay. In multivariable analysis, higher episode completion (> 50%) was independently associated with greater learning gain (adjusted beta = 5.15, p = 0.005) after controlling for baseline scores and centre. Qualitative integration revealed that while learners valued the tool for portability, high-intensity 'binge-listening' at Centre 2 aligned with the observed decay, whereas distributed usage at Centre 1 supported stability. Students identified lack of pauses and AI voice monotony as key design barriers. Conclusions The robust post-test rise validates AI-generated podcasts as an effective tool for rapid revision and pre-exam preparation. While the intervention successfully augmented study time, long-term retention favored distributed over massed practice. Future AI tools should incorporate engineered pauses and improved prosody to optimize cognitive load and sustained engagement.

TI Challenges andResponses to the Misuse of ArtificialIntelligence in
   Chemistry Education in China
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Second-Year Undergraduate; Physical Chemistry; Ethics; Online
   Assessment; Cheating Detection
AB The rapid integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) into higher education presents a dual reality: it functions as a powerful pedagogical tool while simultaneously creating unprecedented challenges to academic integrity. This study examines the impact of AI on academic integrity in chemistry education. Focusing on second-year environmental engineering undergraduates at Jinggangshan University, online physical chemistry examinations (N = 104) were compared with a historical control group assessed through paper-based exams (N = 54). AB Teaching in higher education has evolved towards incentivizing approaches that involve active student participation. The use of educational games is a proven approach to enhancing motivation, making students engage with the material. A contemporary illustration of this genre is digital educational escape games (DEEGs). Due to their problem-solving approach, they are particularly suitable for STEM disciplines. The differences detected lead to the conclusion that vocational education and training students have different study habits than higher education students, leading to different effects of the predictors on the target construct. Nevertheless, the differences detected in the two samples are to be examined further to verify the results of this exploratory study.

TI Exploratory NLP Analysis of Ideathon Presentation Content: Cambodia
   (2023-2025) and Thailand (2025)
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE entrepreneurship education; ideathon; entrepreneurial pitch;
   computational text analysis; TF-IDF; generative AI; sector designation;
   lexical diversity
ID ENTREPRENEURSHIP EDUCATION; PREPAREDNESS; TEXT; NEED
AB Ideathons and pitch competitions have expanded rapidly as experiential learning devices, but the textual artefacts they produce-presentation slides-remain under-examined. This study applies interpretable computational text analysis to 104 ideathon decks (1289 content slides) from four cohorts: Cambodia 2023, 2024, 2025 and Thailand 2025. Measures include lexical frequency, TF-IDF, lexicon-based sentiment, a ten-component pitch-completeness proxy, numerical density, and Jaccard similarity. Because sector designation was absent in Cambodia 2023 and present from 2024 onward, the longitudinal Cambodian data support an observational cohort comparison with an institutional change between cohorts; year effects, programme evolution, and sector designation cannot be separated. The Cambodia 2025 vs. Thailand 2025 contrast is a single-year cross-country comparison, not a longitudinal one. Between Cambodia 2023 and 2024, presentations show large Cohen's d differences with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals (CIs) in total words, unique words, slide count, pitch completeness, and market-related vocabulary, alongside a small decline in type-token ratio. At fixed sector composition, Cambodia 2025 and Thailand 2025 differ sharply in surface vocabulary (top-50 Jaccard = 0.176): Cambodia leans toward agriculture, rural markets, and community development, while Thailand leans toward AI, learning, and cassava-centric agronomy. AI use was not directly measured, so all claims about generative AI are hypothesis-generating; the drop in within-cohort pairwise Jaccard from 2024 to 2025 (0.061 -> 0.041) is consistent with-but does not establish-an augmentative rather than homogenising effect of AI assistance. Findings are reported as descriptive associations and interpreted through the lens of constraint-based creativity and institutional theory. We discuss implications for curriculum designers who wish to balance structural templates with exercises that promote diverse problem framings.

TI A Pedagogically Enriched Technology Acceptance Model: The Role of
   Inquiry-Oriented Instructional Design
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE inquiry-based learning; instructional design; teachers' acceptance;
   Technology Acceptance Model; Virtual-SEM
ID TEACHERS INTENTION; USER ACCEPTANCE; PERCEIVED EASE; TAM
AB This study examines teachers' acceptance of an inquiry-oriented, Crime Scene Investigation (CSI)-based teaching sequence supported by a Virtual Scanning Electron Microscope (Virtual-SEM) using an extended Technology Acceptance Model (TAM). While TAM has been widely used to explain technology adoption, its traditional focus on cognitive perceptions may not fully capture the pedagogical complexity of educational settings. To address this, the study integrates pedagogical and affective variables, namely Inquiry Engagement (INQ), Trust (TR), and Self-Efficacy (SE), into the TAM framework. Data were collected from 30 teachers who evaluated a teaching sequence designed according to constructivist principles and the 5E Instructional Model. Descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, correlation analysis, and multiple regression analyses were employed to examine the relationships among constructs. The findings indicate high perceived usefulness, positive attitudes, and strong behavioral intention to adopt the sequence. Inquiry Engagement was significantly associated with both Perceived Usefulness and Attitude Toward Use, while Trust was significantly associated with Perceived Ease of Use and attitudes. In contrast, Perceived Usefulness showed a weak and non-significant association with attitudes, suggesting that pedagogical factors may play a particularly important role in technology acceptance. Attitude Toward Use showed the strongest association with Behavioral Intention. The findings provide preliminary support for an extended, pedagogically enriched TAM and highlight the potential importance of instructional design in technology acceptance.

AB Higher education is undergoing a profound transformation driven by online and generative learning environment expansion, rapidly evolving labour market demands, and the emergence of new educational providers offering flexible, industry-aligned learning activities. TI The Motivations of Graduate Students in Choosing the Postgraduate

DT Article
DE collage; motivation; pre-service teachers; teaching; PGCE
ID PERSPECTIVE; COLLAGE
AB The aim of this study was to identify the motivations held by graduate teachers at the onset of their initial teacher education. Students were asked to create a collage based on the theme "I come from", providing a visual and reflective account of their backgrounds and their reasons for enrolling in the PGCE programme. A key finding of the study is that students' motivations have antecedents deeply rooted in their socio-cultural and economic backgrounds, indicating that personal history, community context, and prior experiences collectively shape their decision to pursue a career in teaching.

TI Structured play-based motor activities and joint-attention behaviors in
   autistic individuals: an exploratory repeated-measures mixed-methods
   pilot study
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION

DT Article
DE autism spectrum disorder; inclusive education; joint attention;
   play-based intervention; psychomotor intervention; social skills
AB Background Structured play-based motor activities may provide meaningful opportunities for shared attention, social engagement, and task participation in autistic individuals. However, evidence from real-world institutional contexts remains limited, particularly when exploratory observational measures are used.Objective This study aimed to describe within-participant changes in observed social-behavioral scores during a structured play-based motor program with psychomotor and developmental features, and to contextualize these findings through qualitative observations.Methods This exploratory uncontrolled repeated-measures mixed-methods pilot study included ten autistic individuals who met predefined adherence and assessment-completion criteria. Qualitative findings suggested contextual changes in task engagement, responsiveness to cues, adaptation to structured routines, and participation quality.Conclusion The program appeared feasible in a real-world institutional context and may inform future hypothesis-driven studies. Findings should be interpreted as exploratory and feasibility-oriented, not as confirmatory evidence of intervention efficacy. Future controlled studies with larger samples, validated outcomes, blinded assessment, and psychometric validation of the observational instrument are warranted.

TI The relationship between kindergarten type (public vs. private) and
   academic achievement and behaviour of third-grade girls
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE academic achievement; classroom behaviours; early childhood education;
   input-process-output theory; kindergarten; private tutoring
ID SCHOOL
AB This research examined the relationship between kindergarten type (public or private) and academic performance and classroom behaviours of Kuwaiti third-grade girls, and the role of parents' educational level in their choice of kindergarten and private tutoring. This study used a comparative quantitative, cross-sectional design, with a purposive, complete sample of 46 third-grade girls from two classes taught by the researcher. The study involved tests, observations and surveys. The findings showed that girls who attended private kindergartens achieved higher scores in Arabic, with a statistically significant and moderate effect size (Cohen's d = 0.60); however, given the borderline significance (p = .049), this finding should be interpreted with caution. Although higher mean scores were also observed in English, and slight differences in Mathematics and classroom behaviours were noted, these differences were not statistically significant. There was also a statistically significant relationship between fathers' educational level and kindergarten type, with more educated fathers sending their daughters to private kindergartens. But no significant associations were observed between kindergarten type or fathers' education level and private tutoring. These results indicate that the association between kindergarten type and outcomes may be complex and confined to certain areas. Socio-cultural factors, including the use of private tutoring, play an important role in learning. This study calls for more longitudinal and qualitative studies to explore these issues further and provides implications for policy and practice. Findings are interpreted through the Input-Process-Output (IPO) framework to contextualize interactions between early educational environments and later outcomes. A key limitation is the reliance on a small, purposive sample, which may affect generalizability.

AB Digital transformation has intensified the need for educational approaches capable of fostering meaningful civic participation within digitally networked societies. While digital citizenship has become an important focus of contemporary education, empirical evidence examining how digitally mediated participatory learning contributes to measurable civic competence development remains limited, particularly within Global South contexts. This study investigates whether participation in Project Citizen Digital, a digitally mediated participatory civic learning model, is associated with changes in students' civic competence in online higher education. TI Enacting culturally responsive STEAM-based mathematics learning through
   Bugis cultural wisdom: integrating AR and GeoGebra
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE augmented reality (AR); Bugis; creative thinking ability; culture;
   GeoGebra; metacognitive; STEAM
ID IDENTITIES
AB The integration of cultural values into mathematics education has increasingly been recognized as a way to support contextual and meaningful learning. This study aimed to develop and implement a culturally responsive Science, Technology, Engineering, Arts, and Mathematics (STEAM)-based mathematics learning framework that integrates Bugis cultural wisdom within a metacognitive learning model and to examine its impact on the creative thinking ability of students. This study employed a design-based research approach involving iterative stages of prototype development, expert validation, implementation, and refinement. The framework incorporated Bugis cultural values-including siri', reso, alempureng, and asitinajang-supported by augmented reality and GeoGebra. The study was conducted in two private junior high schools in Makassar, Indonesia, involving Grade VIII students in an experimental group (n = 19) and a control group (n = 20). Data were collected through classroom observations, interviews, pretest-posttest assessments, and analysis of learning activities. The developed framework was categorized as valid to highly valid based on expert evaluation. Students in the experimental group demonstrated higher posttest scores (M = 78.947, SD = 9.513) than those in the control group (M = 74.650, SD = 8.898). The experimental group also achieved a higher normalized gain score (0.770) compared with the control group (0.714), both within the high category. In addition, 89% of students in the experimental group achieved mastery learning criteria. Classroom observations and interviews indicated that the integration of cultural contexts, augmented reality, and GeoGebra supported students' engagement, visualization, collaboration, and mathematical modeling activities. The findings suggest that culturally responsive STEAM-based mathematics learning integrated with Bugis cultural wisdom can support students' creative thinking and promote more contextual mathematics learning experiences. The framework also contributed to the development of metacognitive awareness, collaborative learning, and problem-solving skills in mathematics classrooms.

TI Academic dissatisfaction in teacher evaluation: a natural language
   processing approach and multimodal semantic analysis for the generation
   of pedagogical evidence
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE artificial intelligence; data mining; education computing; education
   management; educational data mining; educational management; machine
   learning; students
AB This study converts student voices into actionable pedagogical evidence through a Spanish-language NLP pipeline that integrates Likert-type evaluation items and open-ended comments from 411 master's students in business sciences. The dataset contained ten positively oriented item indicators and 411 records; all item responses were valid, no respondent was excluded, and 410 substantive comments were available for textual analysis. The pipeline normalized item responses, cleaned Spanish text, estimated polarity, subjectivity, and basic affective categories, extracted bigrams, modeled six topics using Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA; K = 6), and computed two indicators: the textual climate score (S_text) and the Multimodal Course Climate Aggregate (MCCA). Item reliability was acceptable for an exploratory institutional instrument (Cronbach's alpha = 0.636). The mean item score was 3.63/5, while the normalized item score was 65.77/100. The textual score averaged 56.68, and the fused MCCA averaged 59.79. Positive comments emphasized professional usefulness, clarity, examples, and applicability; negative comments concentrated on lack of focus, ambiguous tasks, feedback timing, and class management. The fused indicator showed that textual evidence adds decision value beyond Likert scores by identifying pedagogical frictions that are not fully captured by item averages. This study contributes to educational data science by offering a replicable Spanish-language NLP pipeline that transforms qualitative student feedback into interpretable, actionable evidence for institutional improvement and teacher professional development.

AB Background Scientific research is the basis for the ongoing evolution of the healthcare field. TI Development of creative abilities of future teachers of fine arts in
   Kazakhstan: individual lessons, creative self-expression and
   institutional training conditions
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE art teacher education; creative abilities; creative self-expression;
   higher education; individualized learning; institutional support;
   Kazakhstan; teacher training
AB The development of creative abilities is an essential component of preparing future teachers of fine arts. However, limited empirical evidence exists on how individual lessons, creative self-expression, and institutional training conditions jointly contribute to this development in Kazakhstan. This study examined students' perceptions of these factors and the relationships among them. A quantitative descriptive and correlational design was employed. Data were collected from 90 undergraduate and graduate students enrolled in art teacher education programs at two universities in Kazakhstan using volunteer-based convenience sampling. The 25-item questionnaire measured three constructs: individual lessons, creative self-expression, and institutional conditions. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, Cronbach's alpha, exploratory factor analysis with Varimax rotation, and Pearson correlation analysis. The questionnaire demonstrated satisfactory internal consistency (alpha = .89 for individual lessons, alpha = .88 for creative self-expression, alpha = .78 for institutional conditions, and alpha = .89 overall), while the three-factor solution explained 58.3% of the total variance. Students strongly agreed that individual lessons developed creative thinking (M = 4.85, SD = 0.45) and artistic potential (M = 4.75, SD = 0.55). However, they also reported barriers involving insufficient institutional support (M = 4.32, SD = 0.50), limited alignment with professional development goals (M = 4.55, SD = 0.71), and dependence on external instructional models (M = 4.52, SD = 0.60). Significant positive correlations were found between individual lessons and creative self-expression (r = .68, p < .001), institutional conditions and creative self-expression (r = .71, p < .001), and individual lessons and institutional conditions (r = .59, p < .001). The findings indicate that individual lessons are perceived as valuable for developing creativity and artistic individuality; nevertheless, their effectiveness depends on appropriate pedagogical guidance, sufficient resources, methodological clarity, and a supportive institutional environment.

TI Private and vocational schools from oversight to insight: external
   evaluation of schools and self-evaluation in dialogue
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE data-based decision making; external evaluation of schools; private
   schools; reinforcement data use; school evaluation; school improvement;
   school self-evaluation; vocational schools
ID INSPECTIONS; LEADERSHIP; IMPACT
AB Introduction External School Evaluation and School Self-Evaluation are increasingly understood as complementary mechanisms within national regulatory architectures, yet the way this relationship unfolds in types of schools only recently incorporated into state inspection frameworks remains under-researched. This study examines that relationship within Portuguese private and vocational schools, both of which entered the third cycle of External School Evaluation in 2018.Methods The corpus comprised 47 inspection reports published between 2018 and 2025 (24 from private schools and 23 from vocational schools), analysed using quantitative document content analysis. Qualitative inspectorate judgements for the self-evaluation domain were converted into a discrete five-point numerical scale to perform non-parametric comparative tests, while specific institutional strengths and areas for improvement were coded inductively to trace longitudinal trends.Results The statistical findings reveal a steady upward trend and progressive convergence between global inspection averages and self-evaluation scores across the cycle, suggesting that external judgements operate as a comparative baseline that stabilises internal routines. Vocational schools achieved significantly higher scores on both indicators and relied predominantly on the European Quality Assurance Reference Framework for Vocational Education and Training, which correlated positively with evaluative outcomes. Conversely, private schools relied on self-designed models, displaying lower procedural systematicity but a more pronounced textual focus on curricular and pedagogical dimensions.Discussion Rather than establishing a direct causal link, the findings suggest that external evaluation operates as a discursive mechanism that consolidates internal administrative regularities, while the translation of evaluative evidence into concrete classroom practice persists as a complex institutional challenge. Reconciling managerial compliance with shared pedagogical reflection remains a critical condition for sustainable school development.

AB In this article, we converse about a program called InterGen, a series of artist-led interventions that critically reflect on modes of intergenerational knowledge making and sharing. AB This study aimed to identify distinct mathematics anxiety profiles among gifted middle school students and to investigate whether gender significantly predicted latent profile membership. TI Shifting gaze, shifting performance: The role of individual gaze
   behavior and joint attention in collaborative learning in tech-enhanced
   classrooms
SO INTERNET AND HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Collaborative learning; Artificial Intelligence (AI); Deep learning;
   Visual attention; Higher education
ID SYSTEMS
AB The increasing integration of digital tools in classrooms necessitates a deeper understanding of how students interact with peers, instructors, and the surrounding technologies. From am embodied cognition perspective, students' gaze behavior is important indicator of their attention and engagement in collaborative learning while this modality remains underexplored. This study aims to examine students' gaze behavior in tech-rich classrooms, revealing how gaze behaviors to various components and joint attention influences collaborative learning outcomes. A total of 68 university students from Singapore participated in this study and finished one-hour collaborative learning task. Their gaze objects were analyzed in a moment-by-moment way with deep learning models including their own screen, partner's screen, partner's face, worksheet, mobile phone and offtask space. Epistemic network analysis was conducted to reveal the gaze object networks and quantitative analysis was employed to examine the difference in joint attention levels between higher and lower performing groups. The results show that higher performing students primarily focused on their own screens, with occasional shifts to their partner's screen, while lower performing students exhibited more scattered gaze patterns, frequently switching between multiple objects. Higher performing groups presented significant higher level of common attention than lower performing groups, simultaneously focusing on the shared task on their own screens. These findings provide evidence that effective collaboration in technology-rich classrooms may be associated with task-aligned and strategically distributed visual attention rather than extensive peer-oriented gaze. This study contributes to the growing joint attention literature by extending gaze analysis beyond screen-based environments, demonstrating the utility of noninvasive AI-driven methods for classroom research, and linking visual attention patterns to collaborative learning performance.

   Role of Parents

DT Article

ID PITFALLS; BRAIN
AB Objective: Explore how adolescents' TikTok use influences their dietary intake and the role of parents in that influence. Methods: Four semistructured focus groups were conducted with 25 students (aged 15-16 years) from a Midwestern high school. Participants completed demographic and TikTok use surveys. TI Time across the term: Weekly dynamics and anticipated time use as
   predictors of motivation in introductory chemistry
SO LEARNING AND INDIVIDUAL DIFFERENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE Time management; Motivation; Expectancy-value theory; Self-regulated
   learning; STEM
ID ACADEMIC-PERFORMANCE; BETWEEN-PERSON; SELF-EFFICACY; WITHIN-PERSON;
   MANAGEMENT; EXPECTANCY; SCIENCE; CHOICES; COST; MATH
AB College students regularly shift time among coursework, employment, and leisure as demands change across a semester. Drawing on situated expectancy-value theory and a multiple-goals framework, we used intensive longitudinal data from an introductory chemistry course (N = 440) to examine how weekly deviations in time use, semester averages, and baseline expectations predicted motivation (competence, interest, importance value, and four costs). TI University students' academic self-concept and components of academic
   procrastination: A longitudinal analysis of reciprocal relations
SO LEARNING AND INDIVIDUAL DIFFERENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE Academic self-concept; Academic procrastination; University students;
   Cross-lagged panel model; Multi-group analysis
ID GENDER-DIFFERENCES; MEASUREMENT INVARIANCE; HIGHER-EDUCATION; FIT
   INDEXES; ACHIEVEMENT; PERFORMANCE; VALIDATION; DIFFERENCE; EFFICACY;
   STRESS
AB This study examined reciprocal relations between university students' academic self-concept (ASC) and behavioral and emotional components of academic procrastination (delay and subjective discomfort). We analyzed data from NT1 = 1406 students from the beginning of one semester to the beginning of the next with a latent cross-lagged panel model (CLPM). We found no reciprocal relations but, nevertheless, interesting medium to large cross-lagged relations. From the beginning to the middle of the semester, delay was positively, and ASC negatively, related to subsequent discomfort. Surprisingly, from the end to the beginning of the next semester, delay related negatively to discomfort. Exploratory multi-group analyses revealed gender differences. For female students, delay at the end of the semester was negatively related to subsequent discomfort. Among male students, ASC and discomfort were negatively related over time. These findings offer valuable insights into potential negative dynamics between ASC and academic procrastination that may affect students' achievement. Educational relevance and implications statement: Students' academic self-concept is meaningfully interrelated with their achievement, but before achievement comes into play, students may find themselves in adverse dynamics between their academic self-concept and dysfunctional learning behavior and experiences, which warrant closer examination. In light of this, we took a closer look at the longitudinal relations between academic self-concept and academic procrastination, whereby students delay tasks and experience subjective discomfort (e.g., worry, guilt). Our study shows that a negative academic self-concept and frequent delay are related to more subsequent subjective discomfort. Notably, the longitudinal relations between academic self-concept, delay, and subjective discomfort differed between female and male students, highlighting the importance of considering these gender differences in educational practice. Overall, our findings suggest that promoting students' academic self-concept and functional learning behavior can help prevent subjective discomfort associated with delay.

TI Social contact and xenophobia as predictors of nursing students'
   attitudes toward refugees: Evidence from a multicultural university
   context
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Attitudes toward refugees; Nursing students; Social contact; Xenophobia
ID DISCRIMINATION; IMMIGRANTS; RACISM
AB Aim: This study aimed to investigate the predictive roles of xenophobia and social contact in shaping nursing students' attitudes toward refugees. Background: Refugees are a highly vulnerable population who often face barriers to equitable healthcare access. Nursing students' attitudes toward refugees are important because they may influence future care quality, communication, and culturally safe practice. However, evidence on how xenophobia and social contact jointly shape these attitudes remains limited, particularly in university settings where a high proportion of international students creates frequent multicultural interaction. Design: This study employed a descriptive, cross-sectional, correlational design. Methods: The study was conducted with 421 nursing students at a public university in T & uuml;rkiye where the number of international students, particularly Syrian students, is relatively high. Data were collected using a Descriptive Information Form, the Attitudes Toward Refugees Scale, the Xenophobia Scale, and the Social Contact Scale. Descriptive statistics and multiple linear regression analyses were performed. Results: The mean scores were 92.36 +/- 16.48 for attitudes toward refugees, 47.20 +/- 9.96 for xenophobia, and 25.97 +/- 6.74 for social contact. Xenophobia was the strongest predictor of more negative attitudes toward refugees (beta = 0.526, p < .001). Both contact frequency (beta = -0.149, p < .001) and contact quality (beta = -0.161, p < .001) were significant negative predictors of attitude scores, indicating that more frequent and more positive contact was associated with less negative attitudes. Female sex predicted more negative attitudes (beta = 0.125, p = .001), whereas being a fourth-year student predicted more positive attitudes (beta = -0.091, p = .019). Social contact frequency (beta = -0.122, p = .013) and contact quality (beta = -0.291, p < .001) were also significant negative predictors of xenophobia. Conclusions: Xenophobia appears to be a key barrier to positive attitudes toward refugees, whereas both the frequency and quality of social contact may play a protective role. Nursing curricula should therefore strengthen intercultural education and create opportunities for meaningful, positive contact with culturally diverse groups to support inclusive and equitable care.

TI What are professionals' attitudes to stimming? A brief report
SO RESEARCH IN AUTISM
LA English
DT Article
DE Autism; Stimming; Professionals; Qualitative
ID BEHAVIORS; CHILDREN; AUTISM
AB Self-stimulatory behavior (stimming) is a common, often functional aspect of autistic experience, yet it has historically been targeted for reduction within clinical and educational settings. Although recent scholarship and autistic self-advocacy have increasingly framed stimming as a meaningful form of self-regulation, little is known about how professionals currently conceptualize stimming or how those views shape practices. This study reports findings from an online survey examining professional perspectives on stimming among individuals who work with autistic children and adults. Fifty-nine professionals from a range of disciplines completed a Qualtrics-based survey assessing self-rated knowledge of autism and stimming, training experiences, workplace norms, and beliefs about the purpose of stimming. Quantitative results indicated that while most participants reported high knowledge of autism, fewer reported extensive knowledge of stimming, and over half had been encouraged to reduce stimming as part of their professional role. Qualitative analyses of open-ended responses revealed that participants most frequently conceptualized stimming as serving sensory and emotional regulation functions, with additional themes including communication, focus, information processing, and expression of positive affect. Many respondents endorsed allowing stimming, prioritizing safety, and seeking to understand its underlying purpose, and expressed interest in learning directly from autistic individuals. Overall, findings suggest that professionals in this sample largely endorsed neurodiversity-affirming views of stimming, while also identifying a need for additional training and accessible educational resources. These results underscore the importance of professional education that centers autistic perspectives and supports consistent, affirming practices across service settings.

TI A perioperative management elective as a transition-to-practice
   intervention: effects on preparedness, professional identity, and career
   decision-making
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Perioperative care; Medical education; Elective course; Career
   orientation; Transition to practice; Surgical education
ID INFORMED-CONSENT; MEDICAL-EDUCATION; MOTIVATION; KNOWLEDGE; STUDENTS;
   NEED
AB Background Perioperative management requires a broad range of knowledge and practical skills essential for early clinical practice, yet perioperative care is often taught in fragmented rather than integrated fashion across undergraduate medical curricula. Beyond technical skills, perioperative care involves anticipatory planning, prioritization, escalation decisions and interdisciplinary coordination. Electives may help bridge this gap but are often assessed primarily by satisfaction or specialty recruitment. We evaluated a perioperative management elective with respect to self-perceived preparedness, educational value across baseline career interests, and its potential role in informed career decision-making. Methods We conducted a prospective evaluation of a two-week perioperative elective at a German medical school. Students completed pseudonymized questionnaires before and after the course and at residency entry. Outcomes included self-assessed preparedness across six perioperative domains, perceived readiness for practice, educational value, and career intentions (5-point Likert scales). Paired pre-post comparisons were analyzed using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Subgroup analyses explored outcomes by baseline interest in orthopedics and trauma surgery (OTS). Results Forty-three students participated; 40 provided paired pre-post data and 22 completed follow-up. Self-perceived preparedness improved significantly across all perioperative domains (all p < 0.001). Post-course educational value was high (median 5; 97.6% top-box = Likert 4-5). Gains were independent of baseline OTS interest. Although group-level career interest remained stable, significant within-person changes were observed (p = 0.002), indicating bidirectional shifts rather than unidirectional recruitment. At residency start, participants reported high perceived readiness (median 5; 95.5% top-box). Conclusions A structured perioperative elective improved perceived preparedness and was valued irrespective of baseline specialty interest. Beyond improvements in self-perceived preparedness, it supported professional identity formation and informed career decision-making. Perioperative teaching may therefore function as a transition-to-practice intervention rather than a specialty recruitment tool, with relevance across specialties.

TI Self-sponsored writing and rhetorical awareness: An empirical study of
   students' Instagram posting practices
SO COMPUTERS AND COMPOSITION
LA English
DT Article
DE Instagram; Self-sponsored writing; Multimodal composition; Writing
   process; Rhetorical awareness; Feminist teacher research; Composition
   pedagogy
AB Despite the grounding influence of shared process-centered traditions in the first-year composition (FYC) classroom, teacher researchers have struggled to study and theorize the composing processes happening in the web-based world of 21st century writing, particularly in the social media spaces that many students frequent. This study applied a feminist teacher research methodology and mixed-methods design to explore FYC students' self-sponsored writing practices on a popular, albeit under-examined, social media application: Instagram. Through survey, interview, and process journal data, we report and categorize students' complex, social, rhetorical, multimodal composing processes, including planning, drafting, collaborating, evaluating, selecting, and styling images and captions for Instagram publication. Study data also revealed rhetorical awareness, though audience awareness was often implicit and inconsistently or inaccurately articulated. Findings from this study extend and nuance prior research on students' self-sponsored social media composing practices and offer new findings that address the lack of empirical data about writing process, especially on Instagram. The article concludes with a description of a self-study assignment that invites students to name and claim the rhetorical awareness and writing processes implicit in their social media posting practices.
