TI The agency gap in AI-supported writing: How reactive and proactive agent
   designs shape multimodal reasoning
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
LA English
DT Article
DE Generative AI literacy; Human-AI interaction; Academic writing; Agency
ID GENERATIVE AI; FRAMEWORK; LITERACY
AB Generative AI is becoming part of academic writing, but its educational value depends on how control is shared between learner and system. This study examined an agency gap: performance differences that may arise when AI agent initiative is misaligned with learners' generative AI literacy. Seventy-nine medical and nursing students completed two multimodal analytical writing tasks using healthcare simulation data visualisations. They were randomly assigned to a reactive agent that responded only when prompted or a proactive agent that provided sequenced questions and feedback. Generative AI literacy was measured using the validated 20-item Generative AI Literacy Assessment Test. Epistemic network analysis showed that proactive interaction created stronger links among conceptual reasoning, evidence use, and constructive engagement, whereas reactive interaction was more factual and procedural. Ordinal regression showed that generative AI literacy predicted immediate independent writing performance after support was removed, particularly for visual data integration, critical thinking, and overall quality. Condition-specific mediation estimates showed a literacy-performance association in the reactive condition but not in the proactive condition; however, the indirect effects and literacy-by-design interactions were not significant. This pattern is consistent with smaller literacy-related performance differences under proactive scaffolding, but it does not establish a compensatory causal effect. Learner reflections indicated that effective AI writing support requires contextual feedback, dialogic scaffolding, and calibration of initiative to learner needs and task complexity. These findings position interaction design as a potential mechanism for supporting equitable and agency-supportive educational AI agents.

TI Standardized assessment of LLM English proficiency
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
LA English
DT Article
DE Proficiency assessment; CSE; Item response theory; Cognitive diagnosis;
   Benchmark evaluation; Large language models
AB Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in language learning and assessment, yet their English proficiency is seldom reported against interpretable proficiency standards. We introduce the China's Standards of English Language Ability (CSE) framework to assess the proficiency levels and subskills of LLMs. The test is referred to as the CSEBench and comprises 624 expert-annotated multiple-choice items across CSE Levels 2-7. Each item is accompanied by metadata, including difficulty level and subskill labels covering vocabulary, syntax, phonology, and cohesion/discourse. Critically, the dataset includes test responses from 2050 middle school and and sophomore college students who are learning English as a second language. We evaluate closed-source models, open-source baselines, and enhanced open-source variants incorporating additional supervision and external knowledge. Results show a clear proficiency divide: after mapping model scores to CSE levels, closedsource models consistently reach CSE Level 6, whereas most open-source baselines cluster around CSE Levels 3-4. A follow-up cognitive diagnostic analysis reveals that while closed-source LLMs exhibit broad competence across subskills, open-source models display persistent deficits-most pronounced in phonology. Crucially, these weaknesses are shown to be substantially reducible through targeted enhancements. CSEBench thus offers a proficiency-interpretable testbed for reporting LLM English ability and diagnosing subskill gaps.

TI Incorporating pedagogical agents into desktop virtual reality: Does
   visual-tone emotional congruency matter?
SO COMPUTERS & EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Desktop virtual reality; Pedagogical agent; Emotional design
ID PERFORMANCE; MOTIVATION; LEARNERS; IMPACT
AB In real classrooms, teachers often display mismatched emotional tones and visual expressions, yet the effects of such incongruency on learning remain underexplored. In this study, we investigated how (in)congruency between a human-like pedagogical agent's (PA's) vocal tone and visual expressions affects students' learning performance and experience in a desktop virtual reality (DVR) environment. Learners were randomly assigned to one of four PA conditions: (1) positive congruency (positive tone and visuals), (2) neutral congruency (neutral tone and visuals), (3) tonedominant incongruency (positive tone with neutral visuals), and (4) visual-dominant incongruency (positive visuals with neutral tone), where they learned the inner workings of the human eyeball through hands-on DVR activities. Results showed that the positive congruency PA yielded significantly higher retention, positive emotions, and intrinsic motivation than the visualdominant incongruency condition and outperformed the neutral congruency condition on most measures. Notably, the tone-dominant incongruency produced effects comparable to positive congruency across all outcomes and surpassed visual-dominant incongruency in retention and positive emotion. Mediation analysis further confirmed that the tone-induced positive emotions contributed to improved retention, motivation, and perception of the PA. These findings suggest that in emotionally expressive instructional design, tone of voice may override visual cues in influencing affective and cognitive outcomes, offering implications for the design of emotionally intelligent agents in immersive learning environments.

TI Pharmacy education in Vietnam during the 2015-2025
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Pharmacy education; Quality assurance; Accreditation; Competency
   standards; Curriculum; Vietnam
AB Background: Pharmacy education plays a pivotal role in strengthening the healthcare workforce in Vietnam amid rapidly increasing healthcare demand. However, the expansion of training capacity over the past decade has raised significant challenges related to quality assurance and alignment with professional practice requirements. Objective: This study aims to provide a comprehensive system-level analysis of the pharmacy education system in Vietnam during the 2015-2025 period, focusing on quality governance mechanisms and the implementation gap between policy design and practice. Methods: A structured narrative review was conducted, synthesizing data from regulatory documents, accreditation databases of the Ministry of Education and Training, and relevant academic literature. Results: The findings indicate that the system has undergone significant reforms, including the establishment of minimum admission thresholds, the introduction of the Basic Competency Standards for Pharmacists (2019), and the expansion of program accreditation. However, an implementation gap persists, reflected in the proportion of unaccredited programs (48%) and uneven implementation across institutions, suggesting disparities in institutional capacity. Conclusion: Pharmacy education in Vietnam is transitioning from a model focused on expansion to one oriented toward quality enhancement. However, current challenges are systemic rather than isolated, requiring coordinated and integrated reforms. For sustainable development, strategic priorities should include institutionalizing mandatory accreditation through a phased roadmap linked to enrollment regulation, and strengthening the alignment between the 2019 Pharmacist Competency Standards, curriculum design, and accreditation mechanisms. Such integration is essential to enhance the consistency, transparency, and comparability of training quality in the context of regional integration.

   Doubao AI assistant
SO EDUCATION FOR CHEMICAL ENGINEERS
LA English
DT Article
DE Combustion heat; Fully-connected neural networks; Molecular structure;
   Generative AI
ID ARTIFICIAL-INTELLIGENCE; EDUCATION; FUELS
AB With the rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI), particularly the emergence of generative large language models (LLMs), AI technologies have been widely adopted across diverse sectors, significantly enhancing operational efficiency and transforming traditional workflows. However, integration of AI technologies into chemical engineering education remains constrained by students' limited programming proficiency and the scarcity of labeled datasets, thereby limiting the effective implementation of data-driven methodologies in experimental teaching. To promote the digitalization and intelligent transformation of experimental education, a digitally enhanced reform of the heat of combustion measurement experiment was proposed to bridge the gap between traditional laboratory instruction and emerging AI technologies. TI The Impact of Non-Fellowship Trained General Surgeon Faculty on Resident
   Career Plans at Graduation
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE General surgery; workforce development; surgical education; residency;
   mentorship
ID MEDICAL-STUDENTS; SURGICAL CAREER; SHORTAGE; DECISION
AB BACKGROUND: Despite the shortage of general surgeons in the United States, >80% of general surgery residents pursue fellowship training at graduation. Surgeon mentors can influence a resident's career choice. The number of non-fellowship trained general surgeons on faculty at each general surgery residency program within the United States is unknown. We hypothesize that as the proportion of non-fellowship trained general surgeons on faculty increases within a program, so too does the proportion of residents who enter full-time practice at graduation. STUDY DESIGN: We conducted an observational study by reviewing websites of general surgery residency programs (n = 348) in the United States from July 2024 to February 2025 to determine the total number of faculty within each department and each faculty's training history. We obtained program characteristics, including percentage of residents who entered full-time practice upon graduation, from the Association of American Medical Colleges' Residency ExplorerTM tool. Analysis of variance was used to analyze relationships between various program characteristics and resident career plans at graduation. RESULTS: An average of 20% of faculty within a department of surgery were non-fellowship trained general surgeons. As the proportion of non-fellowship trained general surgeons on faculty increased, there was an increase in the proportion of residents who entered fulltime practice upon graduation (p < 0.0001). When adjusting for institutional setting, this relationship was observed at university (p = 0.00348) and affiliated hospital (p < 0.001) programs, but not independent academic medical center programs (p = 0.371). The presence of a community hospital rotation, or its rural track, within a program did not significantly correlate with resident career plans to enter full-time practice at graduation. CONCLUSION: Exposure to non-fellowship trained general surgeons during residency can increase the number of residents who enter full-time practice at graduation. This finding highlights the importance of general surgeons as faculty mentors and their impact on resident career plans. This finding also points to the role general surgeons play in workforce development and the importance of recruiting general surgeons as faculty at university and affiliated hospital residency programs. ( J Surg Ed 83:104095. Published by Elsevier Inc. on behalf of Association of Program Directors in Surgery.)

TI Institutional Research Collaborations and Match Outcomes in Orthopedic
   Surgery Residency: A Cross-sectional Analysis of 954 Residents
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE graduate medical education; institutional affiliation; medical
   education; orthopedic surgery; residency match; research productivity
AB OBJECTIVE: To determine whether publishing at a given institution is associated with matching there for orthopedic surgery residency, and whether this association reflects publication presence or sustained concentration of work at an institution, with exploratory analyses of publication network characteristics. DESIGN: Cross-sectional bibliometric analysis of the 2024 to 2025 NRMP and military match cycles using manually verified publication data with institutional affiliations. Primary analysis used chi-square tests and logistic regression with Bonferroni correction (a = 0.025) to examine associations between institutional publication affiliations and match outcomes. SETTING: Multi-institutional analysis of 221 ACGME-accredited orthopedic surgery residency programs across the United States. PARTICIPANTS: Of 954 matched first-year orthopedic surgery residents, with verified publication data obtained for 661 residents (69.3%) comprising 4077 PubMed-indexed publications classified by institutional affiliation as home or external with network characteristics. RESULTS: Among residents with verified publications (mean 5.92 publications per resident, median 3.0), 165 (25.0%) matched at an institution where they had previously published, compared with 3.8% expected by chance (x(2) = 178.3, p < 0.001). To distinguish whether this association reflected publication presence or sustained engagement, we used the home institution-identifiable for every applicant-as a test case. Of 153 (23.1%) matched at home, but having a single home institution publication was not associated with home matching (19.6% vs 18.8%, p = 0.865); however, the proportion of publications at the home institution was the strongest predictor of home matching (odds ratio = 2.17, 95% confidence interval: 1.27-3.73, p = 0.005). CONCLUSIONS: Publishing at a residency program was strongly associated with matching there, at a rate approximately 7 times higher than chance. The mere presence of a home institution publication did not predict home matching, but the proportion of publications concentrated at the home institution did. TI Competence by Design Strains Surgical Residency Training Programs
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE design; Surgical education; Resident wellness; Burnout; Competency-based
   medical education; Entrustable professional activities
ID PERSPECTIVES; EDUCATION; FAILURE
AB OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the impact of Competence by Design (CBD) on surgical training at the University of Calgary, with a focus on burnout and well-being among residents and surgeons. DESIGN: Cross-sectional survey-based study. SETTING: Surgical residency training programs at a Canadian academic university. PARTICIPANTS: Surgical residents and surgeons at the University of Calgary across multiple specialties. METHODS: A single-phase survey was distributed via email (July-September 2024) to Surgery and Obstetrics/ Gynecology departments. The Maslach Burnout Inventory (MBI) measured burnout, additional Likert-scale items assessed emotional/physical, occupational, and intellectual/educational wellness. Responses were dichotomized ("agree" vs. "disagree"). Quantitative data were analyzed using Chi Square and Fisher's exact tests (GraphPad Prism v10.0.0, p < 0.05). Open-text responses assessed perceived impact on the same domains of wellness and resultant qualitative data was analyzed using Braun and Clarke's thematic approach with NVivo 15 software. RESULTS: Subjective self-reported burnout was higher among residents than surgeons (67% vs. 38%; p < 0.001). The MBI confirmed burnout in 29.6% of residents vs. 9.3% of surgeons (p < 0.05). Most residents (75%) self-attributed their burnout to CBD. Emotional wellness was more negatively affected in residents (p < 0.05), who reported greater stress (p < 0.0001), sleep disruption (p = 0.0021), and interference with physical wellness from EPA tasks. Surgeons were more likely to believe CBD motivates residents (68% vs. 26%; p < 0.001) and strengthens relationships (33% vs. 6%, p = 0.0026). Few participants felt that CBD improved surgical skills (38% of staff, 23% residents), autonomy (38% staff, 17% residents), or readiness for practice (23% of staff, 18% of residents). The most common themes identified in the open-text responses included: operational burden, psychological impact, perceived ineffectiveness and structural issues. These themes were present in all domains of wellness. Overall, residents reported more burnout and a greater perceived negative impact of CBD/EPAs across wellness domains compared to staff surgeons. CONCLUSIONS: CBD aims to enhance autonomy and preparedness for practice; however, its implementation at the University of Calgary introduced challenges that have impacted resident and staff surgeon wellness. Our findings highlight the need for programmatic adjustments that better support surgical trainees. ( J Surg Ed 83:104071. (c) 2026 The Author(s).    study

DT Article

ID FRAMEWORK; EDUCATION; STUDENTS
AB Background: Critically ill children in pediatric intensive care units (PICUs) are highly vulnerable during fires. Metaverse-based education platforms such as Roblox offer immersive, accessible training in clinical disaster preparedness for nursing students. Aim: To develop a PICU disaster evacuation simulation program using Roblox and evaluate its effectiveness vs. lecture-only education in improving nursing students' disaster evacuation competency, learning presence, learning flow, and learning satisfaction. Design: A nonrandomized, quasi-experimental, pretest-posttest design was used to develop, implement, and verify a metaverse-based disaster evacuation enhancement program at nursing schools in South Korea. TI Autism and hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (hEDS): A challenging
   combination
SO RESEARCH IN AUTISM
LA English
DT Article
DE Hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome (hEDS); Autism; Health services;
   Quality of life; Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis
ID PHYSICAL HEALTH; CHRONIC ILLNESS; ADULTS; EXPERIENCES; DISORDERS;
   PEOPLE; LIFE
AB Hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (hEDS), a multi-systemic connective tissue disorder with extensive biopsychosocial impacts, occurs with greater than expected frequency in autistic people, yet the specific impacts on their daily lives and healthcare experiences are largely undocumented. In particular, there is limited information regarding ways in which each condition (autism, hEDS) might complicate or ameliorate the needs associated with the other one. We conducted semi-structured interviews with five women diagnosed with both autism and hEDS, which were analysed using Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis (IPA). While journeys to diagnosis were lengthy and distressing, obtaining diagnoses yielded the benefits of self-knowledge and self-compassion, improved self-management of their health, and better negotiation of practical and emotional support. Participants also noted that while autism facilitated some aspects of hEDS self-management, hEDS could exacerbate the medical challenges already disproportionately faced by autistic individuals. Overall, our preliminary findings suggest that the unique healthcare needs of this poorly understood and vulnerable subgroup may be unmet by current healthcare provision; moreover, potentially adaptive autistic strengths for illness management may not be commonly facilitated. To better accommodate these needs, communication training for healthcare professionals, adaptation of patient care environments and adoption of a holistic management approach are recommended.

TI Whether and how family socioeconomic status shapes students' educational
   expectations: Evidence from large-scale survey data in China
SO STUDIES IN EDUCATIONAL EVALUATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Family socioeconomic status; Educational expectations; Meta-analytic
   mediation approach; Academic performance; Parental academic support;
   School educational quality
ID METAANALYSIS; MEDIATION; MODELS
AB A central question in educational equity is how family socioeconomic status (SES) shapes students' expectations for higher education and through which mechanisms this association emerges. Using data from 27,341 eighthgrade students across 120 districts in China, this study examined the SES-expectation link through a twostage meta-analytic mediation approach. Results showed that family SES had a significant positive but weak association with students' educational expectations. Among three SES components, parental education showed the strongest association, followed by parental occupation and family wealth. Student's academic performance, parental academic support, and school educational quality significantly mediated this association, with academic performance showing the strongest mediating effect and the greatest district-level heterogeneity. These findings suggest that family SES shapes educational expectations through both socioeconomic advantage and academic and contextual pathways. Promoting educational equity requires attention to low-SES students' academic development, and the family and school conditions that make higher educational expectations attainable.

   post-pandemic)

DT Article
DE Online learning; Academic achievement; Meta-analysis; Educational
   evaluation; COVID-19
ID ROBUST VARIANCE-ESTIMATION; DEPENDENT EFFECT SIZES; META-REGRESSION;
   BIAS; PERFORMANCE; PLATFORMS; EDUCATION; TUTORIAL
AB This meta-analysis examines the effect of online learning on academic achievement compared to face-to-face instruction, incorporating a temporal perspective spanning pre-COVID-19, during-COVID-19, and post-COVID19 periods.    Addressing Misconceptions with Experimental Learning

   chromatography; gas properties
ID SCIENCE
AB Early science education plays an important role in shaping children's engagement with natural phenomena and in making their intuitive explanations visible before they become more resistant to revision. Beyond the educational findings, the study provides a set of classroom-tested chemistry activities that may support primary teachers in addressing common misconceptions through experimental learning. Four experimental modules were developed around everyday phenomena: color mixing, gas mass, air pressure, and water properties. These topics were selected for their relevance to early chemistry education and for their potential to reveal children's alternative conceptions. Pupils' written responses, collected through pre- and postactivity reflective worksheets, were analyzed through qualitative content and thematic analysis. The findings suggest that the laboratory activities offered opportunities to mobilize pupils' prior knowledge, foster engagement with chemical phenomena, and support the emergence of preliminary forms of scientific reasoning, such as making predictions, describing observations, and comparing initial ideas with observable events. However, the results also show that conceptual development was uneven across the four laboratories. In particular, the activity on water properties proved difficult for pupils, whose responses often remained generic or linked to prior intuitive explanations. Therefore, the study does not provide evidence of stable conceptual change but rather highlights the educational potential of guided laboratory experiences for eliciting and discussing children's naive ideas in early chemistry education. The results also point to the importance of developmentally appropriate design, reflective scaffolding, and interdisciplinary collaboration among chemistry experts, pedagogical researchers, and primary school teachers.

   Investigation of Oppenauer Oxidation (OPP) andMeerwein-Ponndorf-Verley

AB Connecting the textbook definition and mechanisms of oxidation and reduction with practical applications is a lasting challenge for early undergraduate students. This Laboratory Experiment presents the design and implementation of a cost-effective pedagogical experiment of complementary redox reactions (MPV reduction and OPP oxidation) to strengthen first-year undergraduate students' understanding of the principle of oxidation and reduction with an emphasis on the identification of oxidizing agents, reducing agents and equilibrium through a hands-on lab experiment. This module, which can be replicated in any educational setup with the use of the provided supporting material, has successfully strengthened the core redox terminologies, equilibrium concepts, and practical skills in students.

TI A Scoping Review on the Evidence for Virtual Reality Simulation in
   Surgical Training
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE KEY WORDS; simulation; surgery; systematic review; virtual reality
ID COMPUTER-SIMULATION; SURGERY; SKILLS; TOOL; IMPROVES
AB OBJECTIVE: Simulation has become a mainstay in surgical education as it is proven to improve trainees' surgical skills. Virtual reality is a relatively new technology that allows for high-fidelity surgical simulation for many surgical procedures across many specialties. However, there is currently a lack of evidence regarding the effectiveness and value of virtual reality simulation across all surgical specialties. Therefore, we performed a systematic review on the impact of virtual reality surgical simulation on the acquisition of surgical skills. DESIGN: The review was performed across MEDLINE, Embase, and Web of Science from date inception until April 28, 2025. Articles were included if they explore virtual reality simulation for surgical skills in medical students, surgical residents/interns/fellows, or surgical staff. Outcomes of interest were performance, time, errors, and confidence. RESULTS AND CONCLUSIONS: The review yielded a total of 22,198 studies, of which 7282 were duplicates. After abstract and full text review, 235 studies were included in the systematic review. The studies came from over 30 countries, and about half studies were randomized controlled trials (51.49%). Residents were the most studied population, and most of the studies were either in general or orthopedic surgery. Most studies reported improvements in performance (75.8%), time (69.9%), errors (66.2%), and confidence (76.2%). Over 60% of studies demonstrated consistent efficacy for all but one outcome subcategory. Ultimately, this review demonstrates that virtual reality surgical simulation has clear benefits for surgical trainee skills. ( J Surg Ed 83:104097. (c) 2026 The Author(s). TI Bridging GAPS in Perioperative Education: Implementation of the Goals,
   Autonomy, Preparation, and Strategy Framework
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Educational Briefing; Perioperative Education; Training; Cognitive Load;
   Surgical Culture
ID GENERAL-SURGERY; TIME; US
AB OBJECTIVE: To collate perspectives on preoperative educational briefing practices, and assess the impact of the Goals, Autonomy, Preparation and Strategy (GAPS) framework on perioperative education and intraoperative cognitive load. DESIGN: Phase 1 of this mixed-methods study was a survey to ascertain perceptions of perioperative education from surgical trainers and trainees. Phase 2 was the introduction of the GAPS framework into routine surgical practice, with quantitative and qualitative data collected pre-and postimplementation. Intraoperative subjective cognitive load was self-reported (SURG-TLX) and assessed with a linear mixed-effects model. SETTING: The Phase 1 survey was disseminated to attendees at surgical education workshops and operating surgeons at the Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh (RIE). Phase 2 took place within the Department of Vascular Surgery, RIE. PARTICIPANTS: Phase 1 included 46 faculty surgeons and 46 surgical trainees from an international cohort. Phase 2 included 7 faculty vascular surgeons and 8 residents/fellows. RESULTS: Ninety-two surgeons completed the Phase 1 survey, demonstrating trainee vs. faculty surgeon disparity in the perceived frequency (p = 0.05) of educational briefings, and discussion surrounding trainee educational goals (p = 0.05) and operative strategy (p = 0.04). Fifteen surgeons participated in 95 (51 pre-, 44 postimplementation) procedures in Phase 2. Following GAPS implementation, significant improvements were reported in briefing frequency (p = 0.008), discussion around resident learning objectives (p = 0.004) and autonomy (p = 0.02), and intraoperative teaching quality (p = 0.01). Higher rates of satisfaction were reported with briefing structure (p = 0.02), quality (p = 0.04) and frequency (p = 0.02). Similar improvements were observed in debriefing satisfaction and content. GAPS implementation did not significantly impact SURG-TLX score (+2.66 points; 95% CI-0.62 to 5.94; p = 0.10). CONCLUSIONS: There is a persistent lack of alignment between trainers and residents as to the quality and frequency of educational briefing. Implementation of the GAPS framework into daily surgical practice was feasible, and resulted in measurable improvement in perioperative education, with no significant impact on cognitive load. TI Reimagining digital literacy and virtual identity in the Age of AI" -
   Special Collection Editorial
SO PEDAGOGY CULTURE AND SOCIETY
LA English
DT Article
DE Circular Pedagogy; digital literacy; education; innovation; pedagogy;

AB This special collection reflects on the need to reimagine teaching and learning spaces in the age of artificial intelligence (AI). Understanding digital literacy and virtual identity is essential to engaging with our contemporary society, which is defined by the fast pace of socio-economic digitalisation. Experts in the development of educational models, systems, and curricula need to consider how to integrate the development of advanced digital literacy skills, ensuring that learners can interact with technology and have the competencies to find, evaluate, and communicate information online, protect themselves from online threats, and secure personal information. Spaces that should be accessible and foster collaboration, discussion, and critical inquiry through community-driven activities that go beyond content delivery. Learners are shifting towards being co-creators in AI-mediated working and learning environments. As such, there is a need to combine elements of innovative and transformative pedagogy, cultural studies, and critical literacy to engage in and lead educational transformations.

SO EARLY CHILD DEVELOPMENT AND CARE

   methods; photovoice
ID MIGRATION; PLACE
AB Despite growing migration worldwide, relatively little is known about how very young migrant children experience and construct a sense of home during the preschool years through qualitative research. TI Learning to Read in Chinese: A Meta-analytic Structural Equation
   Modeling Analysis of Cognitive-Linguistic Skills in Chinese Word Reading
SO EDUCATIONAL PSYCHOLOGY REVIEW
LA English
DT Article
DE Rapid Automatized Naming; Orthographic Awareness; Phonological
   Awareness; Morphological Awareness; Word Reading; Meta-Analysis
ID CROSS-LANGUAGE CONTRIBUTIONS; MORPHOLOGICAL AWARENESS; PHONOLOGICAL
   AWARENESS; ORTHOGRAPHIC KNOWLEDGE; LITERACY ACQUISITION; NAMING SPEED;
   HONG-KONG; VOCABULARY; ENGLISH; RECOGNITION
AB This paper reports the first meta-analytic structural equation modeling on the associations of lower-level cognitive-linguistic skills (rapid automatized naming/RAN, orthographic awareness/OA, phonological awareness/PA, morphological awareness/MA, and vocabulary) with word reading among native Chinese-speaking children, based on pooled correlational matrices (k = 446; N = 70,734). Moderator analyses explored how the (relative) associations of these skills varied across readers of different Chinese scripts, literacy-instruction contexts, grade levels, and word reading tasks. We found that (1) all skills were significantly and independently associated with word reading with the meaning-based pathways (MA and vocabulary) playing a more salient role than code-based pathways (OA and PA); (2) children reading the traditional script showed stronger associations of OA and MA with word reading than those reading the simplified script; (3) contexts involving phonological instruction were associated with a stronger role of PA but a reduced role of MA in word reading; (4) developmentally, there was a decreasing association of code-based strategies but an increasing association of meaning-based strategies (i.e., increased effects of MA and vocabulary) with word reading; and (5) the association of RAN was stronger with word reading fluency than with accuracy, whereas a converse pattern was found for that of PA. These findings pointed to interrelated patterns of cognitive-linguistic skills in Chinese word reading. They suggested universal and language/script-specific processes in reading acquisition, while also underscoring the differential functioning of component processes in reading acquisition across contexts, developmental stages, and reading tasks.

TI Synergy and complexity: How teacher support modifies motivational
   pathways from cognitive activation to mathematics achievement
SO INSTRUCTIONAL SCIENCE
LA English
DT Article
DE Teacher academic support; Teacher emotional support; Reading
   achievement; Mastery goal orientation; School belonging
ID CLASSROOM SOCIAL-ENVIRONMENT; INTRINSIC MOTIVATION; EMOTIONAL SUPPORT;
   ADOLESCENTS; DIFFERENCE; IMPUTATION; ENGAGEMENT; STUDENTS
AB Teacher academic and emotional support play a crucial role in students' reading achievement, yet the underlying mechanisms remain underexplored. Utilizing data from PISA 2018, this study investigates how school belonging moderates the indirect effects of teacher academic and emotional support on reading achievement via mastery goal orientation. Based on a sample of mainland Chinese students (N = 12,058), the findings indicate that: (a) both academic and emotional teacher support positively predict reading achievement; (b) mastery goal orientation mediates these relationships; and (c) contrary to expectations, school belonging negatively moderates the indirect effects - the indirect effects are stronger when school belonging is low. The findings highlight the importance of providing targeted support to students with low belonging and call for culturally sensitive models of motivation and achievement.

DT Article
DE First-Year Undergraduate; Biochemistry; PhysicalChemistry; Hands-on
   Learning; Kinetics; Spectroscopy; Thermodynamics; Protein-binding;
   Crystal Violet; Nonlinear regression
AB This integrated laboratory project bridges the gap between fundamental physical chemistry and biochemical application through a cohesive '' one-molecule '' pedagogical strategy. Students utilize crystal violet (CV) as a central probe to explore three core pillars of physical chemistry: spectroscopy, kinetics, and thermodynamics. Initially, students characterize the photophysical properties of CV alongside rhodamine B and Congo red, determining absorption maxima and molar absorptivity while evaluating solvent-induced moves. The focus then shifts to a colorimetric kinetic study of the alkaline hydrolysis of CV, where students derive reaction orders, rate constants, and activation parameters via temperature-dependent studies. The project culminates in a biological context by investigating the noncovalent binding of CV to casein. Students analyze binding stoichiometry and dissociation constants to elucidate the nature of the protein-ligand interaction across varying pH environments. By maintaining a single molecular focus throughout these distinct modules, the curriculum provides horizontal integration across subdisciplines, fostering active learning and data interpretation skills. This approach reinforces the relevance of physical and chemical principles in understanding complex biological systems, making it an ideal candidate for upper-level biochemistry or physical chemistry laboratory courses.

   Students: Youth Risk Behavior Survey, 2023
SO JOURNAL OF SCHOOL HEALTH
LA English
DT Article
DE adolescents; chronic disease; health behaviors; life stressors; soda;
   sugar-sweetened beverages
ID SUGAR-SWEETENED BEVERAGES; EATING BEHAVIORS; CHILDREN; HEALTHY
AB Background Life stressors might influence health behaviors, including frequent sugar-sweetened beverage (SSB) consumption. We described associations between life stressors and soda/sports drink (SD) consumption among US high school students.Methods We tested associations between life stressors and daily (>= 1 time/day) and heavy daily (>= 3 time/day) consumption of soda/SD using the 2023 national Youth Risk Behavior Survey (daily n = 12,308; heavy daily n = 11,980). We calculated prevalence ratios (aPRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) adjusted for grade, sex, weight perception, and race and ethnicity. Not experiencing the stressor was the reference group.Results Daily consumption was significantly higher among those who experienced unstable housing (aPR = 1.6, 95% CI = 1.2, 2.2), lacking a household adult trying to meet basic needs (aPR = 1.3, 95% CI = 1.1, 1.5), bullying at school (aPR = 1.3, 95% CI = 1.2, 1.4), missing school due to safety concerns (aPR = 1.3, 95% CI = 1.1, 1.5), or feeling unfairly disciplined at school (aPR = 1.2, 95% CI = 1.1, 1.3). Results for heavy daily consumption were similar.Implications for School Health Policy, Practice and Equity Initiatives to reduce soda/SD consumption could benefit students with relatively high consumption prevalence, including those experiencing life stressors.Conclusions The prevalence of consuming soda/SD was higher among US high school students who experienced life stressors than those who did not.

TI How generative AI guided-professional development supports teachers'
   engagement with mathematical creativity, content knowledge, and
   pedagogical content knowledge
SO ZDM-MATHEMATICS EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE AI-guided professional development; Mathematical creativity; Content
   knowledge; Pedagogical content knowledge
AB This embedded case study examined how eight in-service teachers from rural and under-resourced districts engaged with mathematical creativity (MC), content knowledge (CK), and pedagogical content knowledge (PCK) during an AI-guided professional development program, and how specific AI-mediated mechanisms shaped that engagement. Teachers completed ten interactive modules in which a generative AI system served as a cognitive and instructional partner by prompting problem solving, problem posing, representational reasoning, simulated student interpretation, and reflective instructional decision-making. Data sources included teacher-AI dialogue logs, teacher-generated mathematical artifacts, and interviews, which were analyzed through iterative thematic analysis. Findings showed that teachers engaged with MC, CK, and PCK as interconnected forms of reasoning rather than as isolated domains. Three cross-case themes characterized this engagement: creative mathematical exploration, conceptual deepening of proportional reasoning, and expansion of pedagogical reasoning. These trajectories were shaped by six core AI-mediated mechanisms: adaptive and personalized prompting, real-time feedback, progressive scaffold fading, simulated student reasoning, conversational nonjudgmental tone, and flexible pacing. Two cross-cutting mechanisms, representational nudges and cycles of creative challenge and reflection, further supported teachers' movement between mathematical exploration, conceptual reasoning, and pedagogical decision-making. Teachers emphasized that these mechanisms enabled productive struggle within a psychologically safe environment and positioned AI as a thinking partner rather than a content-delivery tool. The study contributes to research on AI-supported teacher learning by showing how mathematical creativity-aligned AI scaffolding can support teachers' integrated engagement with mathematics and pedagogy in rural professional learning contexts where access to sustained professional development is limited.

TI Modal verb variations in L1 and L2 written discourse: a corpus-based
   analysis of can and would
SO ASIAN-PACIFIC JOURNAL OF SECOND AND FOREIGN LANGUAGE EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Modal verb; English as a foreign/second language (EFL/ESL); L2 writing;
   Learner corpus; Collocation; Modal auxiliaries; Epistemic modality
ID COULD
AB Modal verbs (can, could, may, might, will, would) pose a persistent challenge for both learners and educators despite substantial scholarly exploration of the topic. Using an extensive dataset comprising 2,800 essays, this study investigates the variability in the use of modals among English first language (L1) speakers and second language (L2) learners from Asian backgrounds, focusing on the modals can and would. A comparative analysis of collocational patterns identifies these modals as a major source of divergence between the L1 and L2 groups, notably the prevalent use of the negated form of can and the skewed and restricted use of would among L2 learners. Further, while L1 speakers typically employ would to assert the validity of statements with evidence believed to be indisputable, L2 learners tend to use it when presenting opinions with little or no support. The findings identify specific areas requiring pedagogical interventions for L2 learners, and from a methodological perspective, underscore the importance of complementing corpus-driven results with qualitative analyses when seeking to understand the contextual uses of modals. The integration of qualitative and quantitative approaches is a vital step in formulating effective pedagogical strategies to enhance L2 learners' pragmatic proficiencies.

ID STUDENTS; EXPERIENCES; ADHD; AD/HD
AB Many adolescent attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) boys find schooling unenjoyable and challenging. This small-scale, qualitative Australian study using individual semi-structured interviews reports on how teachers and school leaders in one alternative secondary school academically support the learning for adolescent ADHD boys in their classrooms. The analysis of data revealed one major theme of teaching and teacher strategies for optimum learning, along with four minor themes related to adjustments, technologies, ways to reduce distractions, and the optimum classroom environment. Findings showed that teachers and school leaders used a variety of innovative teaching practices and strategies to support the learning and academic needs of adolescent ADHD boys. The results provide starting points for more in-depth investigations into the kinds of alternative secondary schools that are a good fit for adolescent ADHD boys. The study also highlights the importance of developing policies and practice approaches for alternative schooling to ensure that ADHD young people remain engaged in education so they too can thrive in a schooling environment that is best suited to their individual needs.

TI Antecedents, Process, and Consequences of AI-Based Education in Design
   Thinking Among Engineering Students: A Theory-Generating Meta-Synthesis
   Approach
SO COMPUTER APPLICATIONS IN ENGINEERING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE artificial intelligence; design thinking; engineering; higher education
ID TEACH
AB This study seeks to investigate the antecedents, processes, and outcomes of AI-based education in fostering design thinking among engineering students. Through a meta-synthesis of 151 peer-reviewed articles published between 2015 and 2025, sourced from databases including Web of Science, Scopus, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, and ScienceDirect, we generated a grounded theory. Findings revealed two major antecedent domains: Students' prerequisites (including positive attitudes, basic skills, and foundational knowledge of design thinking) and Instructors' triple competencies (technological, pedagogical, and content knowledge). These factors collectively shape students' intention to learn design thinking (DT), represented by the core themes of usefulness and success, and moderated by variables such as demographics and ethical awareness. The instructional process was structured around the five core stages of the design thinking framework-Empathy, Definition, Ideation, Prototyping, and Testing-with relevant AI tools integrated into each stage to facilitate activities, yielding 46 open codes. The outcomes were categorized into two themes: the development of design thinking competencies and social-psychological growth. The findings highlight AI's significant contribution to fostering both technical skills and ethical reasoning, offering an instructional model that can serve as a practical guide for enhancing design thinking skills among engineering students.

TI The Experiences of International School Teachers in Practicing Respect
   for Cultural Differences Through Intercultural Interaction
SO JOURNAL OF RESEARCH IN INTERNATIONAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE International School Teachers; ISTs; Respect for Cultural Differences;
   RFCD; Intercultural Interaction; International Schools
ID IDENTITY
AB Globalization and increasing international mobility have led to a proliferation of international schools worldwide, including international school teachers. This trend has presented numerous multicultural challenges and issues, particularly for those who experience difficulties adapting to multicultural environments. Implementing respect for cultural differences can be crucial and may serve as a key indicator in successful intercultural interactions. The purpose of this phenomenological study is to investigate the experiences of eight international school teachers in practicing respect for cultural differences at international schools. Data collection was conducted through semi-structured interviews and the study employed thematic analysis to address research questions systematically. The study highlighted that each international school teacher has unique experiences in practicing respect for cultural differences according to their perspectives, personal experiences, and individual backgrounds. However, the findings of the study showed that there were several values that can be summarized as an interconnected circle in practicing respect for cultural differences, including self-awareness, open-mindedness, empathy, being non-judgmental, and always learning. The study suggested that school support, ongoing professional development, and a collaborative school culture are essential to equip international school teachers with the necessary tools to practice respect for cultural differences effectively.

TI How a positive classroom environment relates to EFL achievement: a
   mediation study of engagement among Chinese secondary school students
SO LEARNING ENVIRONMENTS RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article

   school students; Student engagement
ID ACADEMIC ENGAGEMENT; PEER FEEDBACK; PERCEPTIONS; MOTIVATION; TEACHER;

AB Although a positive classroom environment has been recognized as an important factor in learning of English as a Foreign Language (EFL), it remains unclear how it is associated with EFL achievement, particularly across different stages of secondary education. To address this issue, the present study examined how student engagement mediated the relationship between perceived classroom environment and EFL achievement among junior and senior secondary school students in China. A total of 1781 secondary school EFL learners completed measures of classroom environment, student engagement, and their EFL achievement was assessed through standardized tests. These findings suggest that fostering a supportive classroom environment can enhance EFL achievement by promoting student engagement, particularly in the earlier stages of secondary education.

TI Design and exploratory evaluation of an AI-supported blended learning
   environment for big data education
SO LEARNING ENVIRONMENTS RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
DE AI-supported blended learning; Big data education; Learning environment;
   Outcome-Based Education; Practical competence; Competency-oriented
   instructional design
ID TECHNOLOGY
AB The rapid development of artificial intelligence and the digital economy has intensified demand for big data talent, while higher education continues to face challenges in aligning curriculum provision with changing industry requirements. Drawing on Outcome-Based Education and a learning environment perspective, this study examines an AI-supported blended learning environment for big data education. The environment combines face to face instruction with a set of digital learning supports. Rain Classroom and Chaoxing are used to facilitate interaction and classroom participation, while Edu Coder supports practical training in a cloud-based setting. In this way, the learning environment is intended to support both students' conceptual understanding and the development of observable practical competence. The study draws on multisource data from a Big Data Technology course, including 1358 records of in class learning activities, 168 records of experimental tasks, and 92 valid student questionnaires. The questionnaire demonstrated excellent internal consistency and strong sampling adequacy, with a Cronbach's alpha of 0.977 and a KMO value of 0.936. The blended learning environment is examined in terms of four dimensions, including instructional support and feedback, student involvement and interaction, task organisation and practice support, as well as learner autonomy and temporal flexibility. Multiple regression was used to examine how students' perceptions of these dimensions were associated with their endorsement of the blended learning environment. The results show that students' endorsement was most strongly associated with the perceived capacity of the environment to compensate for limitations of traditional classroom teaching and with their positive acceptance of the digital learning arrangements. The findings further suggest that the environment was associated with higher engagement, stronger practical skills and problem-solving, and improvement in self-directed learning. Overall, the study shows how an AI-supported blended course in big data education can be examined as a coordinated learning environment through behavioural, task based, and perceptual evidence.

AB Centrally developed English lesson plans provide structure and ensure curriculum coverage, yet they can constrain preservice teachers' creativity, responsiveness, and capacity to engage students meaningfully. TI Required Contact Hours and Academic Performance in an Evolving Medical
   School Curriculum: A Single-Institution Cohort Study
SO INTERNATIONAL MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE education; curriculum; students; academic; self-directed learning;
   medicine
ID ATTENDANCE; CLERKSHIP; CLASSROOM; TIME
AB Medical schools are increasingly reducing required contact hours and incorporating self-directed learning strategies, yet the impact of these curricular changes on academic performance remains uncertain. This retrospective cohort study compared performance on NBME-based organ system examinations across three consecutive pre-clerkship cohorts at a U.S. allopathic medical school that experienced different levels of required instructional time. Cohorts included 178 students and differed in total required contact hours from 306 to 412 h. Mean MCAT scores did not differ significantly among cohorts (510.4 +/- 5.4, 509.6 +/- 6.3, and 510.0 +/- 4.9; p = 0.74). Across cohorts experiencing different contact-hour requirements and concurrent curricular changes, examination performance did not demonstrate a consistent pattern corresponding to the amount of required instructional time. These findings demonstrate that lower contact-hour requirements were not accompanied by consistently poorer short-term standardized outcomes in these cohorts; however, the independent contribution of contact hours cannot be separated from concurrent curricular changes.

AB Background We introduced a BOPPPS-based peer instruction approach supported by the Chaoxing Xuexitong platform and examined its association with examination performance and students' learning experiences.<br /> Methods This study employed a total of 180 s-year undergraduate clinical medicine students from six pre-existing administrative classes at Northwest Minzu University. TI Seeing MolecularRecognition in Action: A Visual,Amplification-Free
   Sandwich Assay for DNA Detection Using Noble MetalNanoparticles
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Upper-Division Undergraduate; Interdisciplinary; Hands-On Learning;
   Nanotechnology; Visual Detection; DNA; Materials Science
ID SILVER NANOPARTICLES; GOLD NANOPARTICLES; NUCLEIC-ACIDS; SIZE
AB This laboratory experiment introduces upper-division undergraduate and early stage graduate students to the design and implementation of a nanoparticle-based DNA sandwich assay for colorimetric DNA detection. The assay leverages sequence-specific hybridization between DNA-functionalized magnetic microparticles (MMPs) and noble metal nanoparticles (Au and Ag NPs), forming a "sandwich" complex in the presence of a complementary target DNA. Students synthesized Au and Ag NPs (20-80 nm) and functionalized them with thiolated DNA. In parallel, streptavidin-coated MMPs were conjugated with biotinylated DNA probes. Upon hybridization, the MMP-DNA-NP complexes were magnetically separated and subsequently dissociated to release signal Au and Ag NPs into solution. The color and absorbance intensity of the released particles, quantified via UV-vis spectroscopy, correlated with target DNA concentration, enabling both qualitative and quantitative analysis. Varying NP size, material, and mixing conditions (vortex vs rotation) revealed that larger NPs and vigorous agitation enhanced assay sensitivity via higher extinction coefficients and increased hybrid formation. The experiment reinforces concepts including plasmonic signal transduction, hybridization thermodynamics, and colloidal stability, while providing hands-on experience with synthesis, conjugation, and spectroscopy. Students demonstrated strong engagement and the ability to relate NP properties to analytical performance, interpreting assay results in the context of molecular recognition and surface chemistry. Overall, this modular, inquiry-driven experiment effectively bridges nanotechnology and bioanalysis in the undergraduate and graduate curriculum, offering a versatile platform for teaching interdisciplinary chemical principles in a visually intuitive and experimentally accessible format.

TI Formation of Children's Interests in Physical Versus Life Sciences:

AB Women and Hispanic people in the United States (U.S.) are underrepresented in many physical science and engineering fields, despite higher representation in life science fields. This study examines how science topic (physical vs. life science) influences the role that parents play in the development of their elementary school-age (fourth grade) children's science-related interests, attitudes, and problem-solving strategies, including differences related to parent and child ethnicity (Hispanic and non-Hispanic) and gender. Interactions that occurred between topic and ethnicity or gender, and implications for representation of women and Hispanic students in physical versus life science majors in later years, are also presented.

TI Content and Cohorts in Engineering Education: Leveraging
   Self-Determination Theory in Authentic Learning Experiences for
   Undergraduates
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE undergraduate engineering students; authentic learning experience;
   Self-Determination Theory; semiconductor advanced manufacturing
ID INTRINSIC MOTIVATION; STUDENTS; ENVIRONMENTS; DESIGN
AB Motivation and retention in engineering education are critical elements of a national strategy for many reasons, and thus merit exploration in traditional venues as well as extracurricular settings. We use Self-Determination Theory (SDT) to understand students' motivation in an authentic undergraduate learning experience geared toward retention in the semiconductor industry, an example of an industry of national importance around the world. Twelve students participated in two cohorts of training in cleanroom techniques and equipment. We conducted semi-structured interviews with participants to probe their perceptions of authenticity, motivation, and engagement in the program. We used thematic analysis to identify emergent themes from interview transcripts and deductively coded for concepts of interest. In the connections between students' perceptions of authentic learning experiences and motivational drivers, relatedness, an often-overlooked factor in engineering curricula, emerged as particularly relevant to enhance student motivation.

TI Virtual International Work-Integrated Learning as a Pathway to Education
   for Sustainable Development and Global Citizenship
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE work-integrated learning (WIL); global mobility; sustainability
   education; sustainable development goals (SDGs); international
   education; higher education; global citizenship; online education;
   social impact
ID STUDENT
AB This article examines virtual international work-integrated learning (VIWIL) through the lens of Education for Sustainable Development (ESD). ESD, as defined by UNESCO, seeks to equip learners with the knowledge, skills and dispositions required to make informed decisions and take responsible actions to contribute to environmentally sustainable, socially just, economically viable, and peaceful futures. Drawing on UNESCO's four interdependent sustainability dimensions, we highlight its environmental benefits in reducing carbon-intensive travel, its social contribution to broadening equitable access to international learning opportunities, its political role in fostering global citizenship and intercultural competence, and its economic potential in providing a scalable and financially viable model for work-integrated learning. We present a series of ten design principles for enhancing the contribution of VIWIL to ESD outcomes. Through an anonymised case study, we argue that VIWIL has the potential to offer a practical and inclusive mechanism for developing socio-emotional, cognitive and behavioural global citizenship competencies through digitally mediated workplace learning. In doing so, VIWIL is positioned as an important approach for advancing ESD and contributing to the UN Sustainable Development Goals.

TI The Paradox of Enjoyment: Unpacking the Relationships Among Enjoyment,
   Engagement, Burnout, and L2 Achievement Among Left-Behind Students
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE academic achievement; foreign language enjoyment; learning engagement;
   learning burnout; left-behind children
ID PSYCHOLOGICAL NEEDS SATISFACTION; FOREIGN-LANGUAGE ENJOYMENT; SCHOOL
   BURNOUT; EMOTIONS; CHINESE; RESOURCES; CHILDREN; ANXIETY; CONTEXT;
   TRAJECTORIES
AB This study investigates the dual pathways of foreign language enjoyment (FLE) among left-behind children (LBC), a population constituting more than 20% of China's child population and largely under investigated in the second-language learning context; the focus of this study is on the unique and joint contributions of FLE to learning engagement (LE) and learning burnout (LB) in determining academic achievement (AA). Our results confirm that FLE and LE are positively correlated with EFL achievement, while LB shows a significant negative correlation with EFL achievement. However, they also reveal counterintuitive positive correlations between FLE and LB and between LE and LB among LBC-contradicting prior findings from the general population. More importantly, our path analysis reveals a blocked positive association and an opened negative association: while FLE is significantly associated with LE, LE is not significantly linked to achievement; conversely, FLE is positively connected to LB, which is negatively associated with achievement. This "paradox of enjoyment" reveals that FLE acts as a double-edged sword for Chinese LBC, challenging the unidirectional positive view of FLE in second-language learning and demonstrating that positive emotions alone cannot drive sustainable EFL learning success within this vulnerable group. Our findings highlight the unique socioemotional complexities of LBC, underscoring that fostering enjoyment alone might be insufficient without targeted interventions to alleviate burnout and translate engagement into actual success, and offer valuable insights for educators and policy-makers aiming to improve foreign language education among LBC.

TI Rethinking Inclusion in Drama Pedagogy: Developing Indicators Within a
   4R Holistic Framework
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE drama-based pedagogical approaches; inclusion; redistribution;
   recognition; representation
ID JUSTICE; EDUCATION
AB Contemporary research increasingly distinguishes between narrower and broader understandings of inclusion. Another perspective adopted in the recent literature is the 4R justice framework, which examines inclusion through four interrelated dimensions of justice-redistribution, recognition, representation, and relationality. Building on this framework, the study argues that, among pedagogical approaches associated with inclusive education, drama-based pedagogical approaches can be meaningfully interpreted across all four dimensions of justice and within both narrower and broader understandings of inclusion. However, the analysis reveals a key limitation in the existing research on drama-based pedagogical approaches: inclusion-related processes are predominantly examined in a fragmented manner, with individual dimensions addressed in isolation rather than as part of a coherent multidimensional construct. In response, the article proposes an integrative analytical framework for examining inclusion-related changes associated with drama-based pedagogical approaches. This framework is explored empirically through a preliminary set of teacher-informed indicators derived from the descriptions of inclusive practices associated with the use of drama-based approaches, based on written submissions collected through a structured form and follow-up semi-structured interviews with teachers. The proposed analytical framework thus adapts the existing 4R conceptualisation for the analysis of inclusion-related changes associated with drama-based pedagogical approaches and provides a preliminary operationalisation through practice-based, teacher-informed qualitative indicators that may inform future instrument-development aimed at systematically investigating inclusion in drama-based pedagogical approaches. The findings further suggest that the most critical challenge may concern representation, which emerged as the most difficult dimension to operationalise through teacher-informed indicators.

TI Examining Industrial Engineering Students' Perceptions of Course Skills
   and Knowledge and Alignment with Their Interests
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE engineering curriculum; industrial engineering; sociotechnical
   engineering; comprehensive skills; figured worlds
ID EXPERIENCES; PATHWAYS
AB Representations of engineering work in the curriculum influence students' perceptions of valued skills and knowledge in the field. Industrial engineering attracts a diverse group of students and is well positioned to incorporate longstanding calls for comprehensive skills because of its systems-level approach to problem-solving. Examining students' perceptions of the curriculum of industrial engineering can elucidate how the curriculum shapes diverse students' understandings of engineering practice and their decisions to persist or leave. Using Holland's framework of figured worlds, we examined the role of the core industrial engineering curriculum at a Midwestern university (MU) in the United States (U.S.) in shaping undergraduate students' perceptions of valued skills and knowledge and sense of fit in engineering. Findings from a series of two interviews with 15 upper and lower division industrial engineering students indicate that students perceived the core curriculum at MU to minimally emphasize comprehensive skills, reinforcing a purely technical view of engineering. Further, students expressed a desire for course content that emphasized application of theoretical concepts and social and cultural context and impact. Findings indicate a continuing need for curricular reform incorporating comprehensive skills to engage students, align coursework with real-world engineering practice, and shape the perception of engineering work as inherently sociotechnical.

TI Underexplored Pathways to Perceived Academic Reputation in Arab Teacher
   Education: The Roles of Institutional Support, Faculty Competence,
   Employability Skills, and Financial Well-Being
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE supportive university environment; faculty competence; employability
   skills development; financial confidence; financial well-being; academic
   reputation; pre-service teachers; PLS-SEM
ID SELF-EFFICACY; DISCRIMINANT VALIDITY; SERVICE QUALITY; UNIVERSITY;
   MANAGEMENT; STUDENTS; MODEL; PERCEPTIONS; EXPERIENCES; EMPLOYMENT
AB This study examines how supportive university environment (SUE), faculty competence (COMP), employability skills development (ESD), and financial confidence (FC) shape pre-service teachers' (PSTs) financial well-being (FWB) and perceived university academic reputation (REP). Drawing on social cognitive theory, human capital logic, and signaling perspectives, this study develops and tests a PLS-SEM model using survey data from 1225 pre-service teachers in Egypt and Kuwait, with ESD and FC operating as key mechanisms linking institutional and instructional factors to student and reputation-related outcomes. Cross-country analysis suggests that the model is broadly stable across Egypt and Kuwait. The findings suggest that teacher education institutions should integrate employability-oriented learning, financial confidence-building activities, and faculty-supported career preparation to enhance PSTs' financial well-being and strengthen perceived academic reputation.

TI Acquired characteristics of physical education teachers and students'
   motor development: a multilevel analysis
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE acquired character; basic motor competencies; motor development;

   KNOWLEDGE; QUALITY; FITNESS
AB Introduction Despite extensive research on teachers' acquired characteristics, their effects on student outcomes remain inconsistent, and evidence in physical education (PE) is particularly limited. Existing studies have focused predominantly on mathematics, science, or language subjects, have often relied on cross-sectional designs, and have rarely accounted for the hierarchical structure of educational data. Consequently, the role of teachers' acquired characteristics in students' motor development remains insufficiently understood.Methods This longitudinal multilevel study examines whether teachers' general acquired characteristics, including teaching qualification, PE professional development, general teaching experience, and PE teaching experience, as well as teachers' level of physical activity as an additional PE-specific movement-related characteristic, are associated with students' development of basic motor competencies (BMCs). The significant association with teachers' physical activity may indicate the relevance of PE-specific movement-related teacher characteristics, but this interpretation remains tentative because instructional processes, motivational orientations, and embodied competence were not directly assessed.

TI From borrowed spaces to a National Engineering University: a
   narrative-historical analysis of institutional identity construction at
   a Philippine State University Campus, 2000-2025
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE gender-inclusive historiography; higher education; institutional
   identity; narrative inquiry; organizational memory; Philippines
ID ORGANIZATIONAL IDENTITY; WOMEN
AB Institutional histories of regional state universities in the Global South remain underrepresented, limiting understanding of how identity forms under resource scarcity. This study examines how Batangas State University-The National Engineering University Lipa Campus, which began in June 2000 in borrowed classrooms, evolved into a constituent campus of the country's first National Engineering University. It traces the campus's development from inception to its constituent-campus designation following the 2022 enactment of Republic Act No. 11694, identifies mechanisms through which institutional identity was constructed across five historical phases, and characterizes its contemporary niche in education, research, and extension. A qualitative descriptive design integrated with narrative-historical inquiry was employed. Data came from key-informant interviews with purposively selected pioneering faculty and administrators (n = 18, gender-balanced), two focus group discussions, and analysis of institutional archives, photographs, and policy issuances. Transcripts were examined using Braun and Clarke's reflexive thematic analysis, triangulated with documentary evidence, and assessed through Lincoln and Guba's trustworthiness criteria. Eight identity-construction mechanisms operated across five phases: borrowed spaces, transition and territorial identity, academic and cultural flourishing, institutional maturity, and constituent-campus status. Faculty improvisation and leadership sense-giving shaped early development, while governance formalization and strategic branding became prominent later. Resilience emerged not only as a coping capacity but as a constitutive identity claim embodied in the #LeapHighLipa mantra. The study contributes to organizational-identity scholarship by showing how material precarity, narrative work, and gendered institutional labor produce durable identity claims in emerging-economy higher education and inform ethical, inclusive institutional communication practice.

TI Partner models of explainers: a qualitative interview study
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE content analysis; explainee; explainer; explanation; learning; partner
   model; social cognition; understanding
ID COMMUNION; AGENCY
AB Explanations are frequent interactional phenomena in educational and further professional settings. Constructivist instructional approaches emphasize that effective explanations must be adapted to learners' individual characteristics. This requires that explainers form an adequate mental "partner model" of their audience. This study investigates which dimensions of such models are considered particularly important when explaining. We conducted 26 semi-structured interviews with professionals who regularly explain complex content: schoolteachers, university lecturers, and physicians. A qualitative content analysis was based on five literature-based (deductive) categories identified as key partner model dimensions: explainees' Understanding, Prior Knowledge, Interest, Emotions, and Engagement. These were complemented by the inductively derived categories of Skills & Abilities and Agency. To address how the central dimension Understanding was associated with the other dimensions relational analyses were conducted. Strong associations emerged particularly with Skills & Abilities and Engagement. The findings highlight how experienced explainers actively consider multiple dimensions of their audience when explaining and suggest that considerations of Understanding are tightly linked to other dimensions as prerequisites and outcomes. Implications for teacher education and digital learning tools designed to foster adaptive explanation skills are discussed.

TI Pandemic-related disruptions to childcare and English-Spanish bilingual
   language acquisition
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE bilingualism; COVID-19; English; Spanish; vocabulary
ID CROSS-LANGUAGE; COMPREHENSION; MAINTENANCE; VALIDITY; NORMS
AB The COVID-19 pandemic altered the landscape of children's language experiences. Across the nation, many childcare centers closed with the result that bilingual children spent more time with their caregivers, potentially increasing heritage language exposure and reducing majority language exposure. This brief report evaluates age during the pandemic as a predictor of relative language exposure, source of exposure, and Spanish and English language proficiency in a sample of Spanish-English bilingual children. The vocabulary of 28 Spanish-English bilingual children was tested in each of their languages. Children were classified on a continuous variable representing their age in months at the end of the first wave of the pandemic. This allowed us to evaluate children's language exposure and vocabulary scores as a function of their age during the widespread disruption that occurred in the initial wave of the pandemic. Spanish exposure increased and English exposure decreased during the pandemic and this was reflected in children's vocabulary scores. Although vocabulary scores improved with age in each language, English vocabulary scores were negatively associated with age during the pandemic, whereas Spanish vocabulary showed no evidence of disruption. In summary, Spanish language vocabulary was preserved, relative to English, for bilingual Spanish-English children who were infants or toddlers during the COVID-19 pandemic. Implications for heritage language maintenance and majority language acquisition are discussed.

TI Digital anchors: the homeroom teacher's role in active conflict zones
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Bronfenbrenner's bioecological model; conflict zones; digital care;
   emotional resource depletion; homeroom teacher-student relationship
   quality; pedagogy of emergency
ID SELF
AB Introduction: The homeroom teacher's role integrates pedagogy and social-emotional support, assuming heightened significance during emergencies. Unlike general health crises, active conflict situations compel homeroom teachers to contend with both pedagogical disruption and acute security threats. This study examines Digital Care-advanced here as a preliminary conceptual framework describing the use of technology not only for instruction but also as a primary care mechanism under conditions of life-threatening instability. Methods: The current study employed a convergent mixed-methods design, surveying 696 homeroom teachers (from the Jewish, Arab, and Druze sectors), integrating quantitative rapid assessment scales and qualitative responses to maximize ecological validity under active threat. Results: Findings indicated that 55% of respondents reported a role change during the emergency (preliminarily characterized as "Adaptive Teachers"), while the remainder maintained pre-crisis routines ("Traditional Routine-Keepers"). Role adaptation involved expanded after-school support and continuous digital caregiving. A central finding suggests a potentially paradoxical pattern: Teachers who expanded their roles to provide continuous Digital Care maintained high emotional availability for their students, while simultaneously reporting lower levels of personal social-emotional resources, suggesting a potential risk of emotional resource depletion. Discussion: Analyzed through Bronfenbrenner's Bioecological Model, this pattern points to a possible systemic tension between institutional expectations and direct student needs, which may theoretically increase vulnerability to professional burnout. This study underscores the need to re-examine the teaching profession and consider safeguarding educators' emotional boundaries. It further points to the potential value of the integration of Digital Care, socio-emotional competencies, and crisis-boundary management into teacher education programs.
