TI Translation, cultural adaptation, and psychometric validation of the
   WHO-5 well-being index for Arabic-speaking university students
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE construct validity; cultural adaptation; psychometric validation;
   university students; WHO-5
ID OF-FIT INDEXES; PSYCHOLOGICAL DISTRESS; UNDERGRADUATE STUDENTS; JAZAN
   UNIVERSITY; MENTAL-HEALTH; VERSION; DEPRESSION; VALIDITY; ANXIETY;
   RELIABILITY
AB Introduction University life is a formative period characterized by increased autonomy, evolving social roles, and sustained academic demands, placing students at heightened risk of psychological distress. Reliable assessment of subjective well-being is essential for early identification, prevention, and the promotion of adaptive functioning. This study aimed to translate, culturally adapt, and evaluate the psychometric properties of the Arabic version of the World Health Organization-Five Well-Being Index (WHO-5) among university students in the United Arab Emirates (UAE).Methods A cross-sectional psychometric validation study was conducted between February 2024 and March 2025 using an online survey of 568 university students in the UAE. The translation and cultural adaptation followed a standardized seven-step process, including forward translation, reconciliation, backward translation, comparison with the original instrument, pilot testing, and psychometric evaluation. Construct validity was assessed using confirmatory factor analysis with robust maximum likelihood estimation. Model fit was evaluated using McDonald's fit index (MFI), comparative fit index (CFI), incremental fit index (IFI), normed fit index (NFI), non-normed fit index (NNFI), and root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA). Convergent validity, internal consistency reliability, and measurement invariance across gender were also examined.Results The original one-factor model demonstrated suboptimal fit. After specifying two theoretically justifiable residual correlations between WHO_1 and WHO_4 and between WHO_2 and WHO_5, the modified one-factor model showed good fit under the robust solution (CFI = 0.993, NFI = 0.990, NNFI = 0.976, RMSEA = 0.068; 90% CI: 0.027 -0.113). Standardized factor loadings ranged from 0.508 to 0.805. Convergent validity was supported by an average variance extracted of 0.533, while internal consistency was demonstrated by a Cronbach's alpha of 0.833 and composite reliability of 0.848. Multi-group confirmatory factor analysis provided preliminary evidence of configural, metric, and scalar invariance across gender. However, the elevated absolute RMSEA values observed in the gender-specific and multi-group models indicate that these invariance findings should be interpreted with caution.Discussion The Arabic WHO-5 demonstrated satisfactory preliminary evidence of construct validity, convergent validity, internal consistency, and measurement invariance among university students in the UAE. These findings support its use as a brief measure of subjective well-being in this population. Nevertheless, the results represent an initial validation rather than definitive evidence for widespread research or clinical application. Future multicenter and longitudinal studies should evaluate test -retest reliability, relationships with established mental health measures, diagnostic performance, clinical utility, and measurement invariance across broader Arabic-speaking populations.

TI A context-sensitive scale for assessing GenAI-contextualized acceptance
   in conservation-related architectural education: development and initial
   validation
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE conservation-related architectural education; context-specific scale;
   GenAI-contextualized acceptance; generative artificial intelligence;
   higher education; psychometric validation; scale development
ID INFORMATION-TECHNOLOGY; USER ACCEPTANCE; MODEL
AB Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly shaping higher education in professional fields where AI-supported outputs must be evaluated against disciplinary, ethical, and evidentiary criteria. Conservation-related architectural education is one such context because technically convincing outputs still require assessment against authenticity, material knowledge, intervention ethics, and heritage standards. This study developed and initially validated the Scale for Generative AI Technology Acceptance in Conservation Education (SGATE-CE) to assess GenAI-contextualized acceptance among undergraduate architecture students receiving conservation- and restoration-related coursework.Methods After expert review, a 35-item pool was reduced to 27 items and examined using principal axis factoring with direct oblimin rotation in an exploratory sample (n = 157). Following pre-confirmatory measurement-model finalization, a 17-item structure comprising Perceived Usefulness, Behavioral Intention, Applied Educational Engagement, and Perceived Conservation-Specific Utility was tested through confirmatory factor analysis in a separate validation sample (n = 201). Reliability, convergent validity, discriminant validity, and theoretically specified structural associations were also examined.Results The unmodified four-factor model showed acceptable fit: CMIN/df = 2.044, GFI = .880, CFI = .942, TLI = .930, RMSEA = .072, SRMR = .058, and RMR = .037. Alpha ranged from .797 to .896, omega from .804 to .897, composite reliability from .843 to .897, and AVE from .574 to .636. Structural modeling showed positive associations overall, although the PU-to-BI association was weaker and less stable under bootstrap sensitivity analysis.Discussion The findings provide initial psychometric support for the four perceived-acceptance dimensions in conservation-related architectural education. Because some retained items may evoke broader AI or digital technologies, SGATE-CE measures GenAI-contextualized acceptance rather than exclusive GenAI acceptance. It does not measure subject knowledge, ethical judgment, critical evaluation, responsible AI use, or disciplinary competence. The Turkish version was tested, whereas the English wording is an informational translation. Further validation in dedicated conservation and heritage programs is required.

AB This study investigates the psychological and pedagogical conditions required to prevent cyberbullying among students in Kazakhstan's educational context, where rapid digitalization has expanded both learning opportunities and online risks. The findings highlight that effective prevention requires a holistic, culturally grounded approach combining emotional intelligence, ethical digital pedagogy, and institutional psychological support.

TI Predicting at-risk undergraduate students and high-impact modules:
   evidence from a South African University of Technology
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE at-risk students; early warning; learning analytics; Module Impact
   Index; predictive modelling; student attrition; university of technology
AB Scientific problem High failure and dropout rates remain a persistent challenge at South African Universities of Technology, where routinely collected institutional data are seldom used systematically to identify at-risk students or structurally high-impact modules at the faculty level.Aim This study identifies the key predictors of academic risk and determines which modules most negatively influence student progression within the Faculty of Management Sciences at Durban University of Technology.Method Quantitative, non-experimental research design grounded in the post-positivist paradigm and informed by Tinto's model of student departure and Bourdieu's theory of cultural capital. Anonymised institutional records spanning 2017-2025 were analysed using binary logistic regression and random forest classification. A retrospective full-programme model was developed for explanatory purposes, while a deployable Year 1 early-warning model was constructed to support prospective student risk identification.Results The full-programme Student Risk Classification Model achieved an ROC-AUC of 0.888, with sensitivity of 59.0% and specificity of 92.7% at the 0.50 classification threshold. The Year 1 early-warning model achieved an ROC-AUC of 0.835 and identified 78.9% of future non-graduates before Year 2, with a specificity of 74.0% at the Youden-optimal threshold. Academic performance variables were substantially stronger predictors than demographic characteristics, while first-time entering status, race, and gender were not statistically significant within the Diploma-restricted sample. Twenty-two high-impact modules were identified, of which eighteen remained statistically significant after false-discovery-rate correction. These modules were concentrated within three departments, with student-level and module-level risk indicators converging on the same departments, providing multi-level evidence that academic risk is structural rather than compositional.Conclusion Learning analytics can be effectively implemented using routinely collected institutional data without requiring specialist infrastructure. The study contributes two practical decision-support instruments-a Student Risk Classification Model and a Module Impact Index-that provide a replicable faculty-level framework for early intervention, targeted academic support, and evidence-based curriculum reform.Future research Future studies should externally validate the Student Risk Classification Model and Module Impact Index across other faculties and higher education institutions. Incorporating psychosocial, socio-economic, behavioural, and learning management system data may further improve predictive accuracy and strengthen institutional early-warning systems.

TI The influence of integrating national dance elements into children dance
   curriculum on cultural identity and aesthetic literacy: a randomized
   controlled trial
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE aesthetic accomplishment; art education; children; cultural heritage
   education; cultural identity; learning with body; national dance;
   randomized controlled trial (RCT)
ID ETHNIC-IDENTITY; ADOLESCENTS
AB Background Then, cultivating children's cultural identity and aesthetic ability is of great significance to children's growth process, and it also constitutes the basic pursuit of modern art education. As an artistic activity originated from culture, national dance has become an educational way to enhance cultural cognition and aesthetic appreciation. Therefore, this artistic approach not only has the basis of understanding, but also cultivates the aesthetic vision. At present, the empirical evidence generated by randomized controlled trials is still lacking. Purpose The research focuses on the introduction of folk dance elements into children's dance teaching, investigates the effect of this practice on children aged eight to twelve in the two dimensions of cultural belonging consciousness and aesthetic ability, and discusses the potential relationship between the promotion of the two. Method In a 12-week randomized controlled trial, RCT recruited 100 children from primary schools and community art education centers in China. Both the national dance integration course group and the traditional dance course group included 50 subjects, and the grouping process was realized by the principle of randomness. The measurement will be carried out at the beginning, that is, T0, the sixth week, that is, T1, and the twelfth week, that is, T2. Cultural identity uses the multi-group national identity scale, that is, MEIM, as a measuring tool to measure, and aesthetic literacy uses the children's suitable version of the aesthetic literacy scale to evaluate. Repeated measurement analysis of variance (RM-anova) and Pearson correlation analysis were used in the study. Results Against the background of the control group, the children who participated in the folk dance, their sense of cultural belonging and artistic appreciation will show a more obvious progress trend with the progress of time. Through the strengthening of aesthetic literacy, cultural identity has been significantly promoted. The intensity coefficient of this correlation has reached 0.73, and its statistical significance is less than one thousandth. The differences will not be adjusted by age and gender. Conclusion The integration of national dance elements into children's curriculum system greatly improves the sense of cultural belonging and aesthetic taste. Cultural and artistic intervention promotes children's multi-dimensional development with its profound connotation. The experimental results verify the rationality of cultural identity theory, aesthetic education theory and body feeling learning theory. The promotion of national dance courses in schools can effectively deepen students' understanding of their own traditions, improve their artistic appreciation, and encourage the younger generation to actively participate in the preservation of traditional skills.

TI Constructive thinking as a key competency in initial teacher education:
   differences in emotional and cognitive profiles among pre-service
   teachers
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE constructive thinking; educational quality; emotional competence;
   emotional intelligence; initial teacher education; pre-service teachers;
   teacher competencies; teacher training
AB Introduction Constructive thinking and emotional competence are increasingly relevant in initial teacher education, particularly for pre-service teachers who must develop emotional intelligence and adaptive strategies before entering the teaching profession. Teacher preparation therefore requires not only continuous professional development, but also the acquisition of socioemotional competencies from the earliest stages of training.Methods A quantitative, non-experimental, cross-sectional, ex post facto descriptive-comparative study was conducted with 307 students enrolled in Early Childhood Education and Primary Education teacher-education degrees at the Faculty of Education of Albacete, University of Castilla-La Mancha, Spain. Participants were recruited through non-probability convenience sampling and completed the Constructive Thinking Inventory. Group differences were examined by gender, academic year, and degree programme.Results Participants showed low Global Constructive Thinking scores and comparatively elevated Magical Thinking and Esoteric Thinking scores. Gender comparisons indicated that men scored higher in Global Constructive Thinking, Emotional Coping, Acceptance, Absence of Negative Overgeneralization, and Absence of Hypersensitivity, whereas women scored higher in Magical Thinking, Esoteric Thinking, Superstitious Thinking, and Exaggerated Optimism; the corresponding effects were small to moderate. Academic-year groups differed in several adaptive and non-adaptive dimensions, but the cross-sectional design precludes interpreting these differences as developmental change or as effects of teacher education. Degree-programme comparisons showed higher Emotional Coping, Acceptance, and Absence of Negative Overgeneralization scores among Primary Education students, whereas Early Childhood Education students scored higher in Magical Thinking and Exaggerated Optimism. No statistically significant programme difference was observed in Global Constructive Thinking.Discussion and conclusion The findings identify specific constructive-thinking dimensions that may warrant attention in initial teacher education. Training focused on adaptive coping, cognitive flexibility, critical appraisal of beliefs, and emotional regulation may support pre-service teachers' professional well-being. However, the observed group differences should be interpreted as cross-sectional associations and not as evidence that teacher education caused the profiles identified.

TI Procedural feedback lock-in in laboratory education: a micro-meso-macro
   analysis of feedback practices
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE chemistry laboratory education; feedback culture; feedback literacy;
   micro-meso-macro framework; procedural feedback lock-in
ID SCIENCE
AB Feedback is increasingly conceptualised as a dialogic and socio-culturally embedded process; however, little is known about how feedback practices operate across structural levels in laboratory-based higher education contexts. This study investigates how feedback is enacted across micro-, meso-, and macro-level dimensions of feedback culture in undergraduate chemistry laboratory courses within a Kazakhstani university. A qualitative case study design was employed, combining naturalistic classroom observations and semi-structured interviews. Data were collected from three laboratory instructors and 40 undergraduate students across twelve observed laboratory sessions (approximately 24 contact hours), supplemented by interviews with 3 instructors and 3 students. Observation and interview data were analysed using a hybrid deductive-inductive thematic approach guided by feedback literacy frameworks. Findings indicate that feedback was frequent but predominantly enacted at the micro level as immediate procedural correction supporting task completion and laboratory safety. Meso-level feedback processes such as reflection, feedforward, and continuity across sessions were weakly structured, while macro-level structural support for feedback was limited. These cross-level conditions produced a stable configuration conceptualised as procedural feedback lock-in, whereby corrective feedback becomes normalised despite pedagogical intentions toward developmental learning. The study contributes to feedback culture scholarship by extending feedback literacy research into laboratory-based STEM education and offering analytically transferable insights for strengthening feedback design in practice-intensive higher education environments.

TI Strategies for enhancing sustainable research funding in Tanzanian
   public universities
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE research funding; public universities; resource dependence; stakeholder
   engagement; Tanzania
ID INTERVIEW
AB Introduction Sustainable research funding remains a major challenge for public universities in Tanzania, limiting research productivity, institutional autonomy, and long-term research sustainability. Although diversified funding models are increasingly advocated, limited qualitative evidence exists on the integrated institutional strategies that can strengthen sustainable research funding in resource-constrained higher education systems.Methods Guided by Resource Dependence Theory and Stakeholder Theory, this study employed a qualitative, exploratory design to examine strategies to strengthen sustainable research funding at three research-intensive public universities (UDSM, MUHAS, SUA) in Tanzania. Thirty-seven purposively selected participants, including university administrators, research leaders, heads of department, principal investigators, early-career researchers, and finance and grants officers, were interviewed, and institutional strategic plans, research policies, annual reports, and research guidelines were reviewed. Data were analysed thematically in NVivo 14.Results Four interrelated strategies emerged: strengthening internal institutional funding mechanisms; expanding local partnerships and stakeholder engagement; enhancing international collaborative funding strategies; and establishing supportive national and institutional policy frameworks. The findings indicate that sustainable research funding depends on an integrated institutional ecosystem that combines resource diversification, institutional capacity building, stakeholder collaboration, international partnerships, and effective research governance. Reducing excessive dependence on external donor funding requires coordinated institutional and policy interventions that strengthen research resilience and institutional autonomy.Conclusion This study contributes context-specific evidence on sustainable research funding in Tanzanian public universities by demonstrating how Resource Dependence Theory and Stakeholder Theory complement one another in explaining research funding sustainability. The findings highlight the need for integrated institutional strategies that combine diversified funding sources, stakeholder collaboration, and supportive governance frameworks to strengthen the long-term sustainability of research. Because the study focused on research-intensive public universities, future research should examine other categories of higher education institutions and broader stakeholder perspectives.

TI Development of a conceptual model of an intelligent system for
   forecasting career trajectories of students in technical specialties
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE academic performance; alignment of educational programs; artificial
   intelligence in education; career trajectory forecasting; IT students;
   labor market analysis; learning preferences; machine learning
AB The article presents a conceptual architecture of an intelligent system for predicting the career trajectories of students in technical disciplines, based on the integration of educational analytics and labor market requirements analysis. A comprehensive analysis was conducted to substantiate the proposed architecture: (1) employer requirements based on data from the HeadHunter.kz platform using web scraping methods in Python; (2) students academic performance and learning preferences using logistic regression, decision trees, and principal component analysis (PCA). It was found that most vacancies in the IT sector require 1-3 years of work experience, while the key in-demand competencies include communication skills, teamwork, and analytical thinking. It is shown that practice-oriented activities of students (internships, projects, additional courses) are among the most significant factors of successful career development. A conceptual dual-loop architecture of an intelligent forecasting system is proposed, comprising an institutional loop (analyzing the alignment of educational programs with labor market requirements) and an individual loop (providing personalized recommendations to students). The architecture consists of three database layers and three specialized analyzers: an educational program alignment analyzer, an academic performance and student preferences analyzer, and a curriculum-to-student profile matching analyzer that correlates program courses with individual student data. The proposed architecture is designed to automate the identification of gaps between educational programs and labor market demands, as well as to generate evidence-based recommendations for curriculum revision and course selection by students. It is expected that the implementation of the proposed architecture will improve the quality of specialist training, increase graduate employability, and enhance the adaptability of higher technical education to the requirements of the digital economy.

TI Challenges of global citizenship education: an analysis of innovative
   teaching practices in primary education
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE educational innovation; educational leadership; global citizenship
   education; primary education; teaching practice
ID SCHOOLS
AB Introduction This research analyzes the challenges of implementing Global Citizenship Education (GCE) through innovative teaching practices in primary education centers.Methods A multiple case study design was adopted, utilizing a descriptive and interpretive approach. Purposive and convenience sampling were employed to select n=71 in-service teachers from twelve primary schools in southern Spain. Data were collected digitally via an ad hoc 34-item questionnaire and analyzed using descriptive and correlational statistics, alongside hypothesis testing.Results The results reveal that the teaching staff exhibits a high ethical commitment and a very favorable attitude towards innovation, but they perceive barriers in institutional culture and leadership and in actual practice, especially in resource provision and school climate. TI How does nomophobia affect academic engagement? The mediating role of
   socio-emotional skills in secondary school students in the Peruvian
   Amazon
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE academic engagement; emotional; nomophobia; social; students
AB This study evaluated the mediating role of socioemotional competencies in the relationship between nomophobia and academic engagement in Peruvian secondary school students, hypothesizing that these competencies would mediate this relationship. A cross-sectional explanatory design was used with a convenience sample of 408 participants. The instruments employed were the Nomophobia Questionnaire (NMP-Q), the Socioemotional Competencies Test for Secondary School Adolescents (CSE-AS-Per & uacute;), and the Utrecht Work Engagement Scale-6S (UWES-6S), whose reliability was assessed using McDonald's omega coefficient. Descriptive, correlational, and mediation analyses were conducted with observed variables and SEM. The structural model demonstrated adequate fit indices [chi & sup2; (33) = 117, p < .001, CFI = 0.975, TLI = 0.966, RMSEA = 0.079, 90% CI (0.064, 0.095), SRMR = 0.039]. The indirect effect of nomophobia on academic engagement through socioemotional competencies was significant in both analyses [beta = -0.20, p < .001, 95% CI (-0.268, -0.125)], accompanied by a non-significant direct effect, configuring a pattern of indirect-only mediation. These findings suggest implementing programs under the CASEL framework, with evidence-based practices, to comprehensively strengthen students' socioemotional competencies in response to the effects of nomophobia on their academic engagement.

TI Perceived negative acts and emotional well-being in healthcare education
   at a Hispanic-serving institution: a cross-sectional study
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE bullying; education; professional; educational environment; emigrants
   and immigrants; students; health occupations
ID STUDENT MISTREATMENT; MEDICAL-STUDENTS; EXPERIENCES; MICROAGGRESSIONS;
   DISCRIMINATION; HARASSMENT; UNIVERSITY; RESIDENTS; COLOR; ABUSE
AB Purpose Negative acts (NA), including work-related bullying, person-related bullying, and physical intimidation, are inappropriate behaviors that should not occur in workplaces or schools. Healthcare students may be exposed to these experiences during their training, although exposure may vary across demographics. This study aimed to assess self-reported NA and the emotional well-being among healthcare students from different family immigration backgrounds at a Hispanic-serving institution on the U.S.-Mexico border and to explore potential associations between NA exposure and demographic characteristics.Methods The NA Questionnaire-Revised (NAQ-R) assessed work-related bullying (WB), person-related bullying (PB), physical intimidation (PI), and total NAQ-R score (TNAQ-R). Participants also completed the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (PANAS) to evaluate emotional engagement. Groups were compared using the Kruskal-Wallis Test, while the Fisher Exact Test analyzed the association between demographic data and NA scores. Spearman Correlation assessed the relationship between NAQ-R and PANAS. All analyses considered alpha=5%.Results 72 students (mean age 26.26 +/- 8.34 years) participated: 63.9% Hispanic, 18.1% White, 9.7% Asian, and 8.3% Black. The average TNAQ-R score was 29.25 +/- 9.95, indicating low bullying risk. Additionally, the average scores for PI, PB, and WB were 3.56 +/- 1.02, 15.42 +/- 5.1, and 10.28 +/- 4.6, respectively. According to the Mikkelsen and Einarsen criteria, 15.3% (n = 11) of participants were at risk of exposure to NA. There were no significant differences or associations between NAQ-R scores and demographic information. TNAQ-R scores were positively correlated with PANAS- scores (Spearman's rho = 0.251, p = 0.033).Conclusions Healthcare students at this Hispanic-serving institution reported similarly low NA levels across diverse family immigration backgrounds. No significant demographic differences were observed, and greater exposure to NA was associated with higher negative affect. These findings provide insight into the relationship between NA and emotional well-being in diverse healthcare education environments.

TI Convenience without convergence: perceived influence of e-wallet use on
   five dimensions of expense management among Filipino university students
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE digital payments; e-wallet; expense management; financial literacy;
   GCash; Philippines; technology acceptance; university students
ID ACCEPTANCE
AB E-wallet adoption among university students in emerging economies is often framed as a uniformly positive influence on financial management, yet little is known about which expense-management competencies students perceive as benefiting them, and for whom. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model, the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology, consumer behavior theory, and goal-setting theory, this Brief Research Report examined students' perceived influence of e-wallet use on five expense-management dimensions-financial awareness, budgeting and goal setting, debt reduction, emergency preparedness, and investment opportunities-and whether those perceptions were associated with demographic characteristics. A total of 358 undergraduate e-wallet users at a Philippine regional state university completed a content-validated, pilot-tested 25-item instrument with acceptable-to-good internal consistency. Non-parametric between-group tests with false-discovery-rate correction, Dunn-Bonferroni post-hoc comparisons, and effect sizes were used to evaluate group differences. Students rated all five dimensions in the "high" interpretive band, perceiving e-wallets as most helpful for transactional tasks-fee awareness, simplified payments, and quick access to emergency funds-and least helpful for curbing impulsive purchases, which was also the most frequently self-reported expense-management problem. Perceptions did not differ by sex; after correction for multiple testing, robust differences were associated with year level, degree program, and e-wallet platform, particularly on financial awareness and investment opportunities, while no differences emerged on the aggregate composite. Findings suggest that e-wallets are perceived not as uniform financial enablers but as context-sensitive tools whose perceived benefits are associated with academic exposure and platform features.

AB Introduction Digital learning in early childhood has expanded rapidly, yet many educational applications remain weak in cultural grounding, teacher mediation, and age-appropriate social interaction. TI From arrival to integration: ecological approach for learning Latvian in
   schools of Latvia
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE language immersion; language proficiency; monolingual education;
   motivation; multilingual learners; PPCT model
ID 2ND-LANGUAGE
AB In the context of a monolingual educational model, there is a growing need to understand effective mechanisms that support state language acquisition among students with diverse linguistic backgrounds. The aim of this study is to examine internal motivational orientations and language proficiency development. This study examines language competence through the ecological Process-Person-Context-Time (PPCT) model. The model analyses the interrelationship between individual characteristics, motivational factors, language practices, and institutional context. The empirical base comprises data from 647 students attending general education schools in Latvia. The sample was con-structed with regard to differences in linguistic background and duration of language immersion. The analytical strategy combines network analysis of motivational structures with regression modelling to identify key predictors of linguistic development within an ecological PPCT framework. The findings indicate that proficiency in the state language largely depends on the intensity and regularity of language use both within and beyond the school environment. Autonomy-oriented motivation enhances engagement in language practice, whereas social orientations do not lead to sustained outcomes without active language use. Across all groups, everyday language interaction exerts a more consistent influence than formal educational conditions. The results have practical im-plications for educational strategies supporting sustainable language development in multilingual societies within a monolingual system.

TI Teaching quality as a proximal mechanism for social-emotional
   development in kindergarten STEM classrooms: a lagged multilevel
   analysis
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE context-dependent effects; early childhood education; early STEM
   education; social-emotional competence; teaching quality
ID CHILD RELATIONSHIPS
AB Introduction Early STEM education has been identified as a promising model for nurturing children's social-emotional competence (SEC), especially among preschoolers exposed to structured STEM activities. What remains unknown is how these benefits might be propagated in the classroom and whether teaching quality functions as a context-independent or context-dependent factor (especially in kindergarten STEM settings). In this study, we investigate how teaching quality predicts SEC development in kindergarten classrooms (lagged and context-dependent effects), taking into account the fact that these classroom settings may differ from regular educational settings with respect to STEM.Methods We used a quasi-experimental longitudinal design. Our sample comprised 224 children (5-6 years) from 12 classrooms and three kindergartens. Children's SEC was assessed at four time points. Classroom teaching quality (cognitive activation, supportive climate, and classroom management) was assessed at three time points. Lagged multilevel models estimated the predictive role of teaching quality in subsequent SEC (without baseline competence).Results Rather than showing a uniform effect, teaching quality demonstrated a dimension-specific and context-dependent pattern of associations with children's later SEC. When compared with overall teaching quality, no significant lagged effect on SEC was observed. Unpacking the dimensions revealed more interesting results. Supportive climate predicted children's later SEC in every instructional context. For cognitive activation and classroom management, we found that these dimensions were context-bound: In STEM classrooms, these dimensions were positively associated with SEC, while in regular settings, they were null or trended negative (at least in the present data). Interaction and simple slope analyses showed that these effects were hidden when compared as global averages.Discussion This study advances the understanding of development science by moving beyond domain-general models to context-dependent models of teaching quality. We demonstrate that high cognitive demands can be used to construct a social resource for SEC development if connected to collaborative STEM task architectures. Finally, we show that proximal processes are transactional processes, and that teaching quality is not a static structure input but a situated relational process.

DT Article

ID VALIDITY
AB Based on a model of chemistry disciplinary competence, this study compares the competence structures of five selected 2023 Gaokao chemistry examination forms: the National Paper B form, the New Curriculum Standards form, and the Beijing, Shanghai, and Jiangsu forms. Using directed content analysis, cognitive task units were coded within a framework of three first-level indicators-learning understanding, applied practice, and transfer and innovation-and nine second-level indicators. Results: Eighty-five percent of students (372) completed the survey. Most respondents agreed or strongly agreed that an intern with visible tattoos, non-ear piercings, unkempt hair, and/or unnatural hair color would experience pharmacist hiring issues (n = 258, 72.7%) and pharmacist career advancement difficulties (n = 219, 61.7%). Six themes were identified from open-ended responses: (1) personal beliefs vs professional expectations; (2) appearance does not define professionalism; (3) generational differences in PA standards; (4) acceptable limits for tattoos, piercings, and hair color; (5) hygiene concerns are distinct from personal or cultural expression; and (6) appearance standards help maintain professionalism. Conclusion: In society, there is a trend toward less conservative appearances. The PA of health care professionals has traditionally remained conservative, but this convention has recently been tested by the desire for personal expression. Student perceptions regarding what is considered professional vary, and it is important for pharmacy schools to understand these perceptions as they guide students in professional development.

   AGREEMENT; QUALITY; SCALE; KAPPA; MODEL
AB Academic and scientific writing in the first language (L1) is cognitively demanding, yet few Spanish-language computational tools support it through well-grounded pedagogical frameworks. TI Developing argumentation skills for democratic citizenship: addressing
   controversial societal issues with personal stakes
SO CONTEMPORARY EDUCATIONAL PSYCHOLOGY
LA English
DT Article
DE Argumentation; Dialogue; Controversial issue; Democratic citizenship
ID MYSIDE BIAS; PERCEPTIONS; HISTORY
AB Amid rising polarization, misinformation and disinformation, exclusionary discourse, and global conflict, developing individuals' reasoning skills for contemporary controversial issues constitutes a pressing educational priority, yet evidence on effective approaches remains limited. TI For a few dollars more: Compensatory spending in schooling☆
SO ECONOMICS OF EDUCATION REVIEW
LA English
DT Article
DE Compensatory education programs; Disadvantaged students
ID REGRESSION DISCONTINUITY DESIGN; ACHIEVEMENT; STUDENTS; IMPACT
AB Compensatory education programs seek to reduce educational inequality, yet evidence on their effectiveness remains mixed. I estimate the impact of a program in Chile that targets additional resources to schools with a share of disadvantaged students above four different thresholds (15, 30, 45 and 60%). Effect estimates are consistently statistically indistinguishable from zero at each cutoff, for both academic and non-academic outcomes. I link the absence of detectable effects to the fact that schools at the cutoffs do not meaningfully increase their spending. These results suggest that policies that provide modest, formula-based marginal revenue increases may prove ineffective if they are not accompanied by strong implementation guidance on how to spend.

TI Beyond "Good Hands": Simulation Training and Objective Assessment of
   Medical Students' Suturing and Knot Tying Skills in the Obstetrics and
   Gynecology Clerkship
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE clerkship; medical student; surgical skills; suturing; knot-tying;
   assessment
ID STRUCTURED ASSESSMENT; TECHNICAL SKILLS; CURRICULUM
AB OBJECTIVE: The primary objective was to evaluate whether implementation of a structured suturing and knot-tying curriculum during the OB/GYN clerkship was associated with improvements in proficiency, as measured by a checklist-based video assessment. Secondary outcomes included changes in students' self-reported confidence in surgical knowledge and technique. DESIGN: Validity evidence for a checklist-based assessment of suturing and knot-tying skills was collected using Messick's framework. This was a prospective pre-post study with randomized baseline sampling of OB/GYN clerkship students. A subset completed baseline preintervention assessments, and all students underwent postintervention assessments. Both assessments utilized video-recorded checklist evaluation during a formative examination. Pre-and postclerkship surveys assessed self-reported confidence and prior surgical experience. SETTING: The OB/GYN clerkship at Columbia University College of Physicians and Surgeons from December 2024 to December 2025. PARTICIPANTS: Participants consisted of 126 OB/GYN clerkship students. All students completed the postintervention skills assessment at the end of the clerkship. RESULTS: Of 126 students enrolled, 123 were included in the analyses. Median checklist scores were significantly higher after the intervention across all skills (all p <0.001). Self-reported confidence scores also improved significantly across all assessed domains (p < 0.001). CONCLUSIONS: A structured suturing and knot-tying curriculum implemented during the OB/GYN clerkship was associated with significant improvements in objectively assessed technical performance across multiple foundational surgical skills.

TI Implementation of an Intern Night Float Rotation in a Neurosurgery
   Residency Program: Perspectives on Patient Safety and Educational Value
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Medical education; surgical training; night float; residency;
   competency-based education; graduate medical education; neurosurgery
ID GENERAL-SURGERY RESIDENTS; SYSTEM
AB Objective Traditional 24-hour call systems in surgical training often result in educational fragmentation, with post-call days causing interruptions in operative experience, particularly for senior residents. By contrast, night float systems may help reduce interruptions. This study evaluates the implementation of an intern night float rotation in a neurosurgery residency program and assesses perspectives on educational value and patient safety. Design, Setting, and Participants An intern night float system was implemented at Massachusetts General Hospital (a tertiary care center) from April to June 2024. Interns provided in-house overnight coverage, managing >50% of admitted neurosurgery patients. Senior residents on home call provided supervision, performed procedures overnight as needed, and subsequently returned for a regular operative experience the following day. Participants' perspectives were evaluated through Likert-scale surveys administered to attending faculty (n = 5), senior residents (n = 3), junior residents (n = 3), and neuroscience nursing staff (n = 23). Interns (n = 6) completed retrospective open-ended surveys. Outcomes included perceived patient safety, educational value, and nursing satisfaction with communication. Results Improvement in perceived patient safety was rated highly by faculty/residents (median 5/5) and nursing staff (median 4/5). Faculty/residents also rated educational value highly (median 5/5), with 100% agreeing or strongly agreeing that the rotation provides valuable learning for residents. Qualitative responses highlighted accelerated intern readiness for PGY-2 responsibilities and protected operative time for senior residents. Nursing staff reported improved ability to escalate concerns (78% agreement) and better response times (78% agreement) after the implementation of the night float rotation. More variability was observed in nursing responses regarding appropriate triage of pages (61% agreement, 39% neutral). Conclusions An intern night float rotation received positive feedback from faculty, residents, interns, and nursing staff regarding patient safety. The rotation provided educational opportunities for interns and improved operative experience for senior residents. This study suggests that intern night float models can align educational needs across training levels without affecting perceived patient safety.

   tangible programming and unplugged activity interventions
SO LEARNING AND INSTRUCTION

DT Article

   activity

AB Background: Computational thinking (CT) is a cornerstone for children's participation in a digitally mediated society. However, early childhood CT interventions are limited in several ways: (a) mixed evidence on the developmental appropriateness and effectiveness of different approaches; (b) limited attention to families' role in CT development; (c) weak methodological rigor; and (d) scarce evidence from non-Western contexts. TI Comparing traditional and continuous norming models for neurobehavioral
   assessments: A simulation study
SO RESEARCH IN AUTISM
LA English
DT Article
DE Continuous norming; Generalized additive models; Simulation; Sample
   size; Test development
AB Developing accurate test norms is crucial to developmental disability practice but requires substantial resources. Continuous norms show promise relative to traditional norms, yet there is limited guidance on optimal methods and minimum sample sizes. This simulation study compared traditional norming with continuous norming models across 96 data conditions varying in sample size (500-1500), age trajectories (ages 2-22), variance patterns, and skewness. Generalized Additive Models for Location, Scale, and Shape (GAMLSS) that approximated the data generating conditions tended to be the best fitting models. Best fitting GAMLSS models showed closer fit to the data at N = 500 than traditional windowing norms at N =1500 with the largest GAMLSS performance gains occurring by N = 750. Real-world neurobehavioral data supported the need for an iterative model selection process when developing continuous norms. Test developers can achieve high norming accuracy with smaller samples using a GAMLSS model selection process, potentially reducing costs while improving precision.

TI Exploring the Generative Gateway to Computational Thinking (EGG Model):
   Reversing the Perspective from Outside-In to Inside-Out
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE computational thinking; STEM education; professional development;
   grounded theory; learning design; TPACK
ID TEACHERS ATTITUDES; SCHOOL; STEM; INTEGRATION; ROBOTICS; DESIGN
AB The integration of computational thinking (CT) into science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) education is often approached through external interventions, including curricula, technological tools, and policy initiatives. This study examined how teachers interpret these contextual conditions and translate their understanding of CT into instructional practice. Using a Straussian grounded theory approach, one-to-one semi-structured interviews were conducted with 13 middle-school science, mathematics, and computer science (CS) teachers in T & uuml;rkiye. Data were analyzed iteratively through open, axial, and selective coding, as well as constant comparison. The analysis generated the Exploring the Generative Gateway to CT (EGG) Model, a context-specific substantive framework comprising three interconnected domains: external factors, internal factors, and learning-design factors. External factors included instructional, managerial, organizational, social, and technological contexts. Internal factors concerned teachers' awareness, pedagogical interpretations, emotions, commitment to self-development, and risk of professional stagnation. Learning-design factors comprised the competencies and professional development processes through which teachers designed, adapted, implemented, and assessed CT-integrated STEM activities. The findings indicate that external conditions enable, constrain, or redirect teachers' practice, while teachers' interpretations and learning-design competence shape how they respond to those conditions. Teachers sometimes adapted activities, sought resources, collaborated with colleagues, or pursued professional learning; however, these actions mitigated particular difficulties rather than eliminating structural barriers. Sustainable CT integration, therefore, requires complementary support for teachers' conceptual understanding and learning-design competence together with adequate curricular, institutional, collaborative, and technological conditions.

TI Remodeling Resident Research: A Qualitative Study of Emergency Medicine
   Residents Who Struggled to Complete Their Scholarly Project
SO AEM EDUCATION AND TRAINING
LA English
DT Article
ID REQUIREMENT
AB Objectives The scholarly activity requirement by the Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education (ACGME) is broadly defined and variably applied by residency programs. The scholarly productivity of trainees is variable and it is unknown why some may struggle to meet this requirement. This study aims to explore the perspectives of residents who struggled in completing scholarship during residency.Methods We performed a qualitative study using a constructivist paradigm and conducted semi-structured interviews at four ACGME-accredited emergency medicine residency programs. The programs reflect diverse locations and training formats. We invited residents who self-identified as struggling with scholarship. Two researchers independently performed a content analysis of interview transcripts. We resolved discrepancies through in-depth discussion and negotiated consensus.Results We interviewed 13 residents (6 Male and 7 Female; median age 31; 7 PGY-3, 3 PGY-4, 3 post-graduation). Many participated in scholarship before residency. We identified three major themes: barriers/challenges to scholarly activity, recommendations to programs to support residents in scholarly work, and strategies for residents to mitigate challenges. Challenges to scholarly activity included lack of understanding of the scholarly project requirement, lack of time, lack of perceived value, and mentorship challenges. Participants recommended programs set clear expectations, provide infrastructure, and facilitate high-quality mentorship, including a faculty champion. Participants advised residents to start the project early, seek out good mentorship, and find a meaningful, but simple, project.Conclusions Our study reveals that even residents with prior experience can struggle with scholarship and we identified multiple barriers trainees face. Strategically investing in infrastructure, clarifying expectations, and prioritizing mentorship represents an actionable roadmap that may transform the scholarly project from a burdensome requirement into a meaningful educational opportunity.

TI Do or Die: A Rapid-Fire Tabletop Review of "Must Know" Emergency
   Medicine Pathologies
SO AEM EDUCATION AND TRAINING
LA English
DT Article
DE clinical competency; clinical skills; emergency medicine; graduate;
   medical education
ID SIMULATION
AB Background Emergency medicine (EM) physicians must rapidly recognize and manage time-critical conditions; however, standardized methods to teach and assess competency in these scenarios remain limited and resource-intensive.Objective To develop and implement a low-resource, standardized tabletop simulation to evaluate EM residents' ability to manage high-risk, time-sensitive pathologies.Methods Twenty-five critical EM pathologies were identified through expert consensus. We designed "Do or Die" (DoD), a rapid-fire, case-based program grounded in progress testing principles that required a faculty facilitator, laptop and 25 index cards. Residents independently prepared using a provided pathology list. During timed sessions, residents completed five randomly assigned cases, each scored using dichotomous critical action checklists. Performance thresholds varied by postgraduate year (PGY).Results The program was piloted with 54 residents during the 2025-2026 academic year. Fifty-six percent of residents passed on the first attempt with variation noted across training levels. Iterative attempts led to progressive improvement, and all residents ultimately achieved passing performance thresholds. The exercise identified both individual learner gaps and curricular opportunities.Conclusions The DoD program is a feasible, low-resource innovation that provides standardized, formative evaluation of EM residents' management of time-critical conditions. It offers a reproducible and adaptable approach to educational assessment and curricular refinement.

AB Despite increasing interest in academic motivation among university students, limited research has explored how distinct motivational profiles relate simultaneously to mental health, wellbeing, and perceived social support. TI Achievement emotions in primary and middle school: the role of sex, age,
   personality, and emotion regulation
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOLOGY OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Achievement emotions; School; Demographic variables; Big Five traits;
   Emotion regulation strategies
ID TEST ANXIETY; GENDER-DIFFERENCES; REGULATION QUESTIONNAIRE; NEUROTICISM;
   ELEMENTARY; PREVALENCE; CLASSROOM; FEEL
AB Achievement emotions are influenced by a series of antecedents, but the role of some of them - such as personality traits and emotion regulation (ER) strategies -, particularly in primary and middle school students, remains underexplored. Guided by the Control-Value Theory, this study examined the additive contribution of demographic variables (sex and age), personality traits, and ER strategies to 10 school-related achievement emotions. A sample of 330 fourth, sixth, and seventh-grade students completed measures of Big Five personality traits, two behavioral (Actively Approaching and Withdrawal) and two cognitive (Positive Refocusing and Catastrophizing) ER strategies, and five positive (enjoyment, pride, hope, relief, and relaxation) and five negative (anxiety, anger, shame, hopelessness, and boredom) school-related emotions. Results showed that females reported higher anxiety and lower boredom, while older students reported lower positive and higher negative emotions. Personality traits and ER strategies displayed consistent patterns of associations across emotions: Extraversion, Conscientiousness, Openness, Actively Approaching, and Positive Refocusing were associated with higher positive emotions and lower negative emotions, and vice versa for Neuroticism, Withdrawal, and Catastrophizing. Despite the cross-sectional design, which limits causal interpretations, these findings highlight the role of both stable individual characteristics (sex, age, and personality) and more malleable factors (ER strategies) in students' emotional experiences at school. The results may inform future research and interventions aimed at promoting adaptive ER in educational settings.

TI A Methodology to Analyze Students' Comics Created in the Context of
   Science Inquiry in Secondary Education Reveals Their Modes of Reasoning
SO JOURNAL OF RESEARCH IN SCIENCE TEACHING
LA English
DT Article
DE comics; methodology; modes of reasoning; physics education; semiotics
AB This article introduces a methodology for analyzing comics drawn by students in the context of a science inquiry. Within a pragmatist situated semiotic approach, comics created by the students in the context of a science inquiry are semiotic representations reflecting learning viewed as a sense-making inferential process via the building of a network of signs. Moreover, comics are viewed as following the linguistic system of the Visual Narrative Grammar of sequential images which is used to access meaning in the comics. We include an example of the methodology application on one student's comics on the topic of the difference between weight and mass. Results show that the methodology in use provides a nuanced analysis of the students' modes of reasoning in science inquiry, including abductive reasoning whose importance in school science is increasingly recognized.

AB Quality assurance in education essentially focuses on all relevant aspects of school life since various procedures of objectively monitoring, evaluating, and reporting are conducted by all stakeholders in an educational institution. These procedures are highly dynamic and often adopted to provide the much-needed guidance for continuous improvement of educational quality. Accepting this notion of quality assurance, this study investigated the influential factors in the quality of an Intensive English Program (IEP) according to perceptions of all stakeholders by analysing the strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats through international accreditation criteria applied to SWOT framework. The opportunities entail international partnership projects, job market connections through alumni while the threats contain accommodation and transportation issues in addition to natural disasters and financial issues in the national socioeconomic status quo. The study is unique in applying accreditation criteria to SWOT analysis and using this ecological SWOT ToC framework in an IEP to collect data from all stakeholders through a mixed-methods research design.

TI Enhancing Practical Skills Through Task-Based Learning in Asynchronous
   Online Engineering Education: A Case Study in Practice-Oriented
   Instruction
SO COMPUTER APPLICATIONS IN ENGINEERING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE asynchronous online learning; computer-aided design; engineering
   education; experiential learning theory; task-based learning
ID STUDENTS
AB Asynchronous online education has expanded rapidly, yet its effectiveness in practice-oriented engineering courses remains underexplored. This study examines the application of task-based learning (TBL) within an asynchronous online course on computer-aided drawing, focusing on academic achievement and learner satisfaction. The course was designed based on Kolb's Experiential Learning Theory, integrating its four cyclical learning stages with TBL strategies. A total of 266 students participated in the 15-week course, with academic performance assessed through sequential assignments and learner satisfaction evaluated via a post-course survey. Repeated measures ANOVA showed that assignment scores increased over time, while multiple regression analysis indicated that intermediate assignments were associated with final performance. Survey results indicated high levels of satisfaction (average score 4.42 out of 5), with strong internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha = 0.89). The findings suggest that the integration of TBL with asynchronous online learning may support the development of learners' practical competencies and satisfaction. This instructional model suggests potential for delivering skill-based education in online environments and may serve as a reference for future course designs in engineering and related fields.

AB Compared to linear time-invariant (LTI) systems, linear time-variant (LTV) systems represent a crucial conceptual extension in the foundational "signals and systems" course for electronic information majors. Furthermore, the proposed methodology has been integrated into the "signals and systems" course taught by the author for undergraduate students majoring in electronic information at the University of ***. Feedback and suggestions for practical teaching reference are also presented. The proposed methodology holds the potential to benefit electronic and electrical engineering education and related studies.

TI When do tests help learning? The role of working memory capacity and
   test frequency in secondary school students
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOLOGY OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Retrieval practice; Learning; Working memory; Long-term memory; Real
   classroom situations
ID RETRIEVAL PRACTICE; INDIVIDUAL-DIFFERENCES; DISTRIBUTED PRACTICE;
   PERFORMANCE; BENEFITS; METAANALYSIS; SCIENCE; YOUNGER; RECALL; MIDDLE
AB Retrieval practice requires learners to retrieve previously learned information from memory. It has proven to be a powerful strategy for long-term learning. The aim of the present paper is to investigate the effectiveness of this strategy, as a function of the students' working memory capacity and the number of tests performed in real class settings conditions and over the course of a school year. Study 1 aimed to determine whether the effectiveness of retrieval practice was affected by the students' working memory skills. Students were tested on half of the content taught throughout the school year. Study 2 aimed to test the effect of the number of tests on the retrieval practice. Throughout the school year, the learning content was either tested frequently, moderately frequently, or not at all. Results showed that the more frequent the tests, the better the long-term learning. These results offer promising prospects for more systematic retrieval practice in the classroom.

TI Examining the nature of biology teacher explanations and resulting
   student heightened interaction: A topic-specific PCK analysis approach
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF SCIENCE AND MATHEMATICS EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Classroom interactions; Dialogic discourse; Teacher explanations;
   Topic-Specific Pedagogical Content Knowledge
ID SCIENCE; FRAMEWORK
AB Teacher explanations are often viewed as monologic instructional methods associated with authoritative classroom discourse. This study challenges this assumption by examining how Life Sciences teachers' mobilisation of Topic-Specific Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TSPCK) components within explanations shapes subsequent classroom interaction. Drawing on a qualitative single embedded case study of three experienced Grade 11 Life Sciences teachers in South Africa teaching population ecology, I analysed nine video-recorded lessons to explore how explanations function as pedagogical and interactional resources. Teacher explanations were analysed through four TSPCK components, which include learner prior knowledge, representations, what is difficult to teach, and curricular saliency. The fifth component, conceptual teaching strategies, was treated as emergent from their integration and was not coded as a separate category. Classroom interaction following the prompt embedded in explanations was examined for dialogic interaction patterns and categorised as knowledge-sharing or argumentative. The findings reveal that dialogic interaction emerged irrespective of the nature of the prompt (open-ended questions, closed-ended questions, or instructions) when explanations foregrounded and integrated multiple TSPCK components. In such cases, learners appropriated, re-voiced, and transformed the pedagogical and conceptual resources embedded in explanations, particularly representations and key conceptual distinctions, to justify claims, challenge peers, and extend lines of reasoning. I argue that teacher explanations function as framing devices that establish shared semiotic resources and discursive affordances, enabling heightened dialogic interaction beyond the effects of prompt type alone. These findings extend TSPCK research by empirically demonstrating how explanations mediate classroom discourse. I highlight implications for science teacher professional development that integrate explanatory practices with dialogic teaching.

TI Changes in Medical Students' Perceptions of Family Medicine Following a
   Clinical Rotation: A Rural-Urban Comparison in Romania
SO INTERNATIONAL MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE family medicine; undergraduate medical education; clinical rotation;
   career intention; rural medicine; student perceptions; Romania; primary
   care workforce
ID PRIMARY-CARE; SPECIALTY CHOICE
AB Background/Objectives: Romania faces a shortage of family physicians, particularly in rural areas. Undergraduate Family Medicine rotations may influence students' perceptions before residency selection, but the contribution of rural versus urban training settings remains insufficiently documented. This study examined differences between post-rotation perceptions and students' recalled pre-rotation perceptions, and explored whether these differences varied according to placement setting. Methods: This single-centre study used a single-administration retrospective pretest-posttest observational design. After completing the mandatory one-month Family Medicine rotation, 141 sixth-year medical students completed a questionnaire containing recalled pre-rotation and post-rotation ratings on 12 five-point Likert items. Paired comparisons used Wilcoxon signed-rank tests; multiple-testing corrections were applied within the defined item families. A baseline-adjusted model with robust standard errors examined rural placement. Results: The composite score increased from 3.62 +/- 0.84 to 4.10 +/- 0.74 (mean change 0.483; W = 602.5; Z = -7.990; p < 0.001; r = 0.673). All 12 paired item comparisons remained significant after Bonferroni correction. No rural-urban item comparison remained significant after correction. In the adjusted model, rural placement was not associated with a statistically significant difference in the post-rotation score (beta = 0.197, 95% CI -0.002 to 0.397; p = 0.053). Among the 86 rurally exposed students, the mean willingness to practice rurally was 2.87/5. The apparent association with career intention was not retained when excluding the overlapping career-likelihood item (11-item composite: H = 6.695, p = 0.153). Conclusions: Students reported more favourable perceptions after the rotation than they recalled having before it, but their willingness to practice rurally remained limited. The uncontrolled, retrospective design does not permit causal attribution, and the data do not establish a rural-placement advantage or subsequent specialty choice.

TI Positionality Statements in Health Professions Education: A Practical
   Guide for Novice Researchers
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE positionality statement; health professions education; reflexivity;
   guide
AB Positionality refers to a researcher's stance within the social context of their research study. It can include information such as gender, race and class, and other characteristics like location. In addition, positionality statements can also include researchers' personal traits, such as their thoughts, feelings and behaviors. They convey a researcher's position and are incorporated within research articles to make readers aware of the beliefs and assumptions that a scholar may be bringing into the study. Describing one's positionality can be particularly beneficial within health professions education (HPE) research, where complex power dynamics often exist between the researcher and participants. However, there is currently limited literature on how positionality statements should be written for HPE research. This paper aims to present an introductory guide on how a novice researcher can write a positionality statement within HPE research, including elements such as reflexivity, location and context, power dynamics, and insider-outsider positioning, as well as the potential risks tied to positionality statements. Additionally, this paper provides readers with a practical step-by-step guide and a real-life example to follow when developing their own positionality statement. By practicing reflexivity and considering how their location and presence impact the research process and participants, a scholar can articulate how their identity and context shape their research approach. Consequently, adding a positionality statement can increase trustworthiness and enhance transparency of a study when they are reflexive, context-specific, ethically constructed and integrated into the research process.

TI Measuring AI Usage in Geometry Learning Among Pre-Service Mathematics

SO EDUCATION SCIENCES

DT Article

   education; AI literacy; van Hiele theory
ID INTELLIGENT TUTORING SYSTEMS; KNOWLEDGE; FRAMEWORK
AB Pre-service mathematics teachers engage with AI as both geometry learners and future teachers, yet domain-specific instruments for measuring this usage remain scarce. This study developed and validated the AI Usage in Geometry Learning Scale (AIGLS) and compared usage between two Indonesian teacher-education institutions. A comparative survey covered 178 pre-service mathematics teachers at Universitas Negeri Makassar (UNM, n = 89) and Universitas Negeri Jakarta (UNJ, n = 89). ChatGPT was the dominant tool (96.6%), and UNM reported significantly higher usage intensity than UNJ (chi(2)(4) = 27.917, p < 0.001). Mann-Whitney U tests with Bonferroni correction confirmed UNM scored higher overall (U = 4749.5, p = 0.022, r_rb = -0.20), with Geometric Visualisation showing the largest institutional gap (r_rb = -0.38, medium effect). The validated AIGLS supports measuring AI usage in geometry teacher preparation and informs AI-literacy policy.

AB This study explores the potential role of higher education (HE) achievement on the development of Recovery Capital (RC) in individuals recovering from addiction. The purpose of the study is to examine an ongoing collaborative project which embeds provision of HE programmes into the residential addiction recovery setting, providing opportunities for HE achievement to marginalised individuals. The collaborative project between South East Technological University (SETU), a higher education institution (HEI) in Ireland and an addiction recovery provider is examined through the theoretical lens of RC. This study compares Irish and international research and the existing literature on RC as it pertains to addiction recovery, including HE achievement. The theoretical lens through which the collaboration is analysed identifies consistencies, gaps or deviations between the case study which includes Pierre Bourdieu's capital theory and Cloud and Granfield's RC hypotheses to explore potential alignment with the principles of both concepts. This paper has identified opportunities for further research on several elements of RC, such as the contribution of peer support in HE achievement, particularly within a residential recovery setting, the stage of recovery in conjunction with the timing of the educational intervention, and the weighting or value of certain RC ingredients. These elements could form the basis of future national and international research into the impact of HE achievement on RC and long-term addiction recovery outcomes.

TI Teacher Wellbeing in Bilingual Primary Education: An Exploratory
   Tensional Ecological Interpretation of Teachers' Accounts from France

DT Article
DE teacher wellbeing; CLIL; primary education; bilingual education;
   reflexive thematic analysis; France-Andalusia comparative study
ID LANGUAGE TEACHERS; SAMPLE-SIZE; CLIL; CATALONIA; READY
AB Primary CLIL teacher wellbeing remains underexplored in France and Spain. This exploratory, context-specific qualitative study examined the factors that ten primary teachers, five in France (Montpellier and Lille) and five in Andalusia, associated with their wellbeing. Bronfenbrenner's ecological framework, enriched with the ontosystem and the flourishing/floundering distinction, was used as an interpretive device. The interviews were analysed through reflexive thematic analysis. Participants' accounts converged around perceived gaps in CLIL-specific training, time, coordination, and human and material resources, while differing in how they interpreted programme stability and recent policy change. It also identified native-speaker-oriented linguistic self-demand and an emerging pattern of AI-assisted material adaptation across six accounts. We offer a provisional, context-specific tensional ecological framework to organise the relationships participants described between conditions perceived as structural pressures and personal, relational, formative, and material resources. The framework is intended as a heuristic and hypothesis-generating contribution rather than a validated causal or longitudinal model. The findings identify areas for institutional review and further research.

   organizational change; Chilean higher education
ID HIGHER-EDUCATION; FORMAL-STRUCTURE; RESPONSES
AB Quality assurance has become a major force reordering the contemporary university, and in Chile, its most visible expression is the ascent of quality units, which have moved from peripheral offices to, in many cases, vice-rectorate rank. This article examines that trajectory through a descriptive-comparative documentary analysis reconstructing the hierarchical position of these units in the 51 universities recognized by the Ministry of Education and comparing it with the 2008-2009 and 2019 time points, distinguishing the state, traditional private, and private non-Council of Rectors subsectors. AB In Australia, Family Day Care (FDC), the caring and educating of young children in the educator's own home, plays a role in the diversity of offerings across the early childhood sector.    and Competencies, and Psychometric Characteristics of the Survey
   Instrument
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE artificial intelligence; preservice teachers; i-TPACK; teacher
   education; AI literacy; educational technology; AI integration
AB Preparing future educators for technology-enhanced learning environments has become increasingly important as artificial intelligence (AI) continues to influence teaching and learning. Guided by the Intelligent Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (i-TPACK) framework, this mixed-methods study examined preservice teachers' perceptions of AI and the competencies they considered necessary for effective AI integration. Participants included 108 preservice teachers enrolled in a teacher preparation program at a public university in the southeastern United States. Data were collected using a survey containing Likert-scale and open-ended questions. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, exploratory factor analysis, and independent-samples t-tests, while qualitative responses were analyzed using thematic coding. The exploratory factor analysis identified a four-factor empirical structure that partially corresponded with the original theoretical domains, with varying levels of internal consistency. Preservice teachers generally viewed AI favorably and recognized its potential to support teaching and learning. Qualitative findings identified five competencies considered important for responsible AI integration: AI literacy, prompt engineering, critical evaluation, ethical AI use, and pedagogical balance. Participants also expressed concerns about academic dishonesty, misinformation, overreliance on AI, reduced critical thinking, and loss of human interaction. The findings highlight the importance of preparing preservice teachers to integrate AI in pedagogically meaningful and ethically responsible ways.

TI Teaching through trauma: Israeli teacher education in crisis
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE preservice teachers; professional identity formation; psychological
   distress; PTSD; social and emotional learning (SEL); teacher education;
   trauma-informed education (TIE); war-related distress
ID STRESS; ADJUSTMENT; RESILIENCE
AB Teacher education in Israel currently unfolds within a landscape of collective trauma following the ongoing War. Although emerging surveys document elevated distress among Israeli students and school-based educators, the prevalence and severity of psychological distress within teacher education institutions remain largely undocumented. This study provides an institution-level portrait of war-related distress in a teacher education institution, encompassing preservice teachers, in-service educators, and academic and administrative staff. TI Navigating professional dilemmas in inclusive classrooms: pre-service
   teachers' reflective narratives, wellbeing, and emerging professional
   agency
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE accessibility of learning; inclusive education; initial teacher
   education; pre-service teachers; professional agency; professional
   dilemmas; reflective narratives; teacher wellbeing
AB Inclusive education has become a central policy orientation in contemporary school systems. Yet pre-service teachers often encounter inclusive classrooms as complex pedagogical environments in which no standardised response is sufficient. While extensive research has examined teachers' attitudes towards inclusive education and the pedagogical strategies that support inclusive practices, less is known about how pre-service teachers interpret situated professional dilemmas and how these experiences contribute to their professional judgement, wellbeing, and emerging agency. This article addresses this issue by examining reflective narratives produced in initial teacher education. This qualitative study analyses 107 reflective narratives produced by pre-service teachers enrolled in a French master's programme for initial teacher education. The narratives were written as part of a module devoted to inclusive education and the accessibility of learning, and focused on professional situations encountered or observed during placements in primary and secondary classrooms. The data were examined through reflexive thematic analysis, combining an inductive approach with a theoretically informed reading centred on inclusive classrooms, professional dilemmas, emotional work, teacher wellbeing, and professional agency. Four interconnected themes were identified: encountering classroom heterogeneity; navigating pedagogical and ethical dilemmas; engaging in emotional work and constructing fragile forms of teacher wellbeing; and developing professional agency in no-size-fits-all pedagogical environments. The findings show that pre-service teachers progressively move beyond the identification of pupils' educational needs towards an analysis of the situated conditions that make learning activities more or less accessible. The narratives also reveal recurrent dilemmas involving individual adaptation, collective progression, support, autonomy, assessment, participation, and the risk of stigmatisation. The study argues that inclusive classrooms can become formative professional spaces when such dilemmas are analysed within structured reflective settings. Preparing teachers for inclusive classrooms therefore requires more than transmitting knowledge about educational needs or pedagogical adjustments; it also requires supporting their capacity to interpret situated complexity, work through emotional and ethical tensions, mobilise collective resources, and construct sustainable forms of professional agency.
