AB Introduction: Student well-being is increasingly recognised as a critical determinant of academic engagement, persistence, and success in higher education. However, STEM programmes are characterised by high cognitive demands, intensive assessment, and practical requirements that may increase stress and reduce students' sense of belonging. In South Africa, these challenges are compounded by historical inequalities and uneven access to academic and psychosocial support. Guided by Self-Determination Theory, this study explored how well-being strategies can be embedded within STEM education to support students' psychological needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness.Methods: A qualitative, interpretivist research design was employed. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 20 undergraduate STEM students at a South African public university. Data were analysed using Braun and Clarke's six-phase thematic analysis, combining inductive coding with deductive interpretation informed by Self-Determination Theory.Results: Four interrelated themes emerged. First, students conceptualised academic success beyond grades, emphasising mastery, understanding, and the application of knowledge. Second, motivation and persistence were enhanced through recognition, constructive feedback, and acknowledgement of effort. Third, participants highlighted the importance of psychological well-being, work-life balance, and boundary-setting to prevent burnout. Finally, students described employing personal and relational coping strategies, including planning, leisure activities, and social support networks, to sustain engagement and resilience.Discussion: The findings demonstrate that student well-being is embedded within everyday learning experiences rather than existing as a separate support function. Pedagogical practices that foster autonomy, competence, and relatedness can strengthen both well-being and academic engagement. The study highlights the value of mastery-oriented assessment, formative feedback, reflective learning opportunities, and peer learning communities in promoting sustainable student success. Embedding well-being within STEM pedagogy offers a practical pathway for enhancing equity, resilience, and educational outcomes in South African higher education.

AB This brief research report examined teacher-reported perseverance, self-discipline, motivation, and critical thinking among primary learners, their academic-achievement categories, and classroom challenges as an empirical basis for a proposed Strategic Intervention Management Program (SIMP). TI Reading comprehension across paper and screen: performance, processes,
   and cognitive predictors in different tasks
SO DISCOURSE PROCESSES
LA English
DT Article
ID WORKING-MEMORY; TEXT; METAANALYSIS; INFERIORITY; JUDGMENTS; KNOWLEDGE;
   INFERENCE; ACCURACY; MEDIA; MODEL
AB Going beyond the study of differences between media, the present study investigated the extent to which individual (i.e. reading comprehension, updating, and verbal/nonverbal reasoning) and contextual (medium) factors contribute to explaining variability across performance (accuracy), process measures (time-on-task and lookbacks), and metacognitive calibration (calibration bias) obtained through different comprehension tasks (inferential, cloze, and error detection tasks). The sample of 197 students (grades 4-7) completed the paper-based and computer-based comprehension tasks on small narrative texts, differentiated by grade. Nonetheless, results varied across tasks, with the cloze task showing no effect of medium. These findings suggest that the impact of reading medium is more evident on process and metacognitive measures, while individual differences should be taken into account when evaluating comprehension. This underscores the need to contextualize the use of different media according to the specific demands of the individual and the assessment setting.

TI Rising Costs Without Rising Match Rates: Orthopedic Surgery Application
   Spending Before and After the USMLE Step 1 Pass/Fail Transition
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Orthopedic surgery; Match; Residency; Medical student; Application costs
AB OBJECTIVE: Orthopedic Surgery remains one of the most competitive specialties to match into, yet limited research has examined the financial element of the match process. This study aimed to analyze trends between applicant spending and match rates from 2017 to 2025, including before and after the USMLE Step 1 Pass/Fail transition. DESIGN: Retrospective analysis of self-reported financial data from the Texas STAR database across nine application cycles (2017-2025). Financial variables included total application-related costs, encompassing ERAS fees, travel, housing, food, and second-look expenses. Independent t-tests compared average total costs between matched and unmatched applicants and between Step 1 scored and Pass/Fail cohorts, with significance set at p < 0.05. To account for inflation, figures were converted to 2024 dollars using federally reported inflation estimates, given the lack of finalized 2025 data. SETTING: The Texas STAR database, a national, multi-institutional survey collecting self-reported application and financial data from residency applicants. PARTICIPANTS: 1939 prospective Orthopedic Surgery residency applicants. Applicants who did not align with their expected Step 1 scoring system were excluded from primary analyses; a secondary analysis was performed to capture this data. RESULTS: Cost figures are presented in 2024 pricing using aggregate inflationary adjustment. Of 1939 applicants, 1644 (84.8%) matched and 292 (15.1%) did not. Average total spending was $6983.55 (SD = $4692.42) for unmatched applicants and $7063.00 (SD = $4533.27) for matched applicants, with no statistically significant difference between groups (p = 0.80). When comparing applicants from the Step 1 scored era (2017-2022, n = 1168) to those from the Pass/Fail era (2023-2025, n = 484), average spending increased significantly from $6684 (SD = $4893.92) to $7625 (SD = $4225.33) (p < 0.001). Match status was not significantly associated with application cost in either the Step 1 scored or Pass/Fail cohorts (p = 0.20). An additional 284 applicants from 2023 to 2025 with a Step 1 score were analyzed separately, with mean spending of $7340.93 (SD = $3695.42), not statistically different from applicants who applied after Step 1 became Pass/Fail. CONCLUSIONS: There is not a statistically significant relationship between successful Orthopedic Surgery match status and capital spent on applications, travel, food, and housing; spending more money does not appear to directly influence an applicant's likelihood of matching. Since the implementation of a Pass/Fail Step 1 exam, average applicant spending has increased by approximately $941.00 in 2024 dollars after adjusting for inflation (p < 0.001). Based on these findings, the transition to a Pass/Fail for Step 1 appears to have increased the application costs for Orthopedic Surgery applicants, without improving match success. Applicants, on average, may anticipate spending around $8000 between application submission fees and costs associated with acting internships and interviews.

TI Pragmatic users and skeptical nonusers: A qualitative typology of
   ChatGPT adoption in physics education
SO PHYSICAL REVIEW PHYSICS EDUCATION RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
ID INFORMATION-TECHNOLOGY; CONSUMER ACCEPTANCE; INTENTION; POWER
AB Physics students' use of ChatGPT or other generative AI tools is a topic broadly discussed in physics faculties around the globe, with discussion often outpacing evidence. What remains unclear is how physics students truly engage with these tools and by what perspectives their choices are shaped. This study develops a data-driven typology of how students perceive the tool's usefulness and its risks. Through a qualitative content analysis of 1189 survey responses, followed by latent class analysis (LCA), we identified two distinct user profiles. The majority (70%) are "Pragmatic Users" who, while aware of the tool's inaccuracies, use it for scaffolding tasks like conceptual clarification and finding starting points for problem-set questions. The minority (30%) are "Skeptical Non-Users," who avoid the tool over concerns about overreliance and its potential to hinder independent problem-solving. These profiles show students making a calculated trade-off between usefulness and risk, suggesting one-size-fits-all policies on AI are inadequate. Thus, rather than promoting uniform adoption, a differentiated pedagogy could create space for students to make informed, self-determined choices-supporting reflective AI use for those who opt in, while equally validating and enabling the learning practices of those who choose not to use generative AI.

TI Investigating transitional processes in learning progressions: A case
   study of force and motion
SO PHYSICAL REVIEW PHYSICS EDUCATION RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
ID KNOWLEDGE; MODELS; PIECES; MATTER; WORK
AB Learning progressions (LPs) are widely used to describe the long-term development of students' understanding of core scientific ideas. However, as increasing attention has been paid to the contextdependent nature of student learning, the limitations of traditional LP models in capturing the complexity and dynamics of cognitive development have become more apparent. This study integrates the partial credit model (PCM) and model analysis to systematically investigate students' cognitive developmental characteristics within the Force and Motion Learning Progression (FM-LP). Using Force Concept Inventory data from 1619 Chinese students, we repeated the study by Fulmer et al. on U.S. students to examine the applicability of the established FM-LP across Chinese student populations. The findings show that most students do not stably occupy a single LP level; instead, they display thinking patterns spanning multiple levels, with clear differences observed between middle school and high school students. Further analyses based on PCM reveal that, as students' ability increases, their model states shift from strongly mixed states to less mixed states and eventually toward the relatively consistent use of the scientific conception. The model-state-based approach offers a new perspective on capturing cognitive complexity in learning progressions and provides important implications for progression-oriented assessment.

TI Trust-utility gap in introductory physics education: Students' adoption,
   domain-specific skepticism, and preferences for AI integration
SO PHYSICAL REVIEW PHYSICS EDUCATION RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
ID INTELLIGENT TUTORING SYSTEMS; INSTRUCTION; FRAMEWORK; SCIENCE
AB We report results from a mixed-methods survey study (N = 81) examining how undergraduate students in introductory physics courses use, trust, and prefer to integrate artificial intelligence (AI) tools into their learning. Among respondents, 91% (95% confidence interval (CI): [83%, 96%]) reported using AI for physics coursework, yet only 41% (95% CI: [30%, 52%]) trusted AI-generated physics explanations-a 50-percentage-point trust-utility gap consistent with domain-calibrated skepticism rather than uncritical adoption. Thematic analysis of open-ended responses (n = 67; Cohen's kappa = 0.78) identified eight themes; the most distinctly physics-specific finding was that 40% of qualitative respondents spontaneously articulated whereAI fails in physics-visual-spatial reasoning, circuit analysis, and abstract physical reasoning-aligning with physics education research on student difficulties with multirepresentational tasks. This skepticism is also consistent with Kortemeyer's benchmarking results, which show that AI performance is weakest on precisely the multirepresentational task types that students identified as failure-prone, suggesting that student trust calibration may track underlying AI competence boundaries in physics. A majority (65%) preferred optional over mandatory AI integration. Because high-performing students were overrepresented by 13.9 percentage points, the estimated preference for optional integration (and/or resistance to mandatory) may be inflated in this sample. These findings highlight a critical unresolved priority-the verification gap between self-reported and actual verification behavior-and inform recommendations for AI-integrated physics pedagogy.

TI Performance of ChatGPT in solving wave problems
SO PHYSICAL REVIEW PHYSICS EDUCATION RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
ID ARTIFICIAL-INTELLIGENCE; EDUCATION; PHYSICS
AB The ability of ChatGPT, especially its latest versions, attracts significant attention from educators and researchers in fields such as physics. Several studies on this topic explore the performance of ChatGPT in answering physics questions across different versions of ChatGPT. In this study, we evaluate the development of ChatGPT in answering physics questions using the Mechanical Waves Conceptual Survey (MWCS) to examine whether its capabilities improve across different versions. A total of 75 responses per item are generated using ChatGPT versions 4, 4.o, and 5.2, resulting in 4950 responses for comprehensive analysis. Based on the comparison between the three versions of ChatGPT, we find that some difficult types of questions that are answered incorrectly by previous versions, as reported in earlier studies, can now be answered correctly, although there are still minor mistakes, especially when examining the reasoning. A generalized linear mixed model (GLMM) analysis, together with post hoc comparisons, indicates that ChatGPT 5.2 significantly outperforms both ChatGPT 4 and 4.o, suggesting that the capabilities of the latest version included in this study significantly improve. These findings highlight a future direction for this type of research, as our study shows that the latest version of ChatGPT can correctly answer more types of questions in MWCS.

TI Primary and secondary school students' academic achievement trajectories
   before and during COVID-19
SO CONTEMPORARY EDUCATIONAL PSYCHOLOGY
LA English
DT Article
DE Pandemic; School grades; Primary school; Secondary school; Latent growth
   class analysis
ID MANAGEMENT-PRACTICES; CHILDREN; PARENTS; CLOSURE
AB The COVID-19 pandemic had dramatic impacts on educational systems worldwide. The current study aimed to investigate whether some students experienced different patterns of mathematics and language arts achievement before and during the pandemic. Therefore, we used latent class growth analyses to investigate the distinct trajectories of 50,100 primary and 14,600 secondary school students' academic achievement between fall of 2018 and spring of 2021. We identified four classes of primary school achievement trajectories and five classes of secondary school student achievement. Overall, with the exception of a minority of students in at-risk trajectories, we found that most students' achievement remained relatively stable over time. Furthermore, all trajectories reflected trends that already appeared to be present prior to the pandemic. We also examined sociodemographic characteristics associated with students' membership in different classes. The results revealed that boys and students with special needs were overrepresented in at-risk achievement trajectories. Although our results highlight that the consequences of COVID-19 for students' achievement were less dramatic than expected, they also point out the need to develop interventions for at-risk students.

TI Integrating in silico modeling into undergraduate
   education to enhance students competency in biopharmaceutics and
   pharmacokinetics
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Undergraduate education; Biopharmaceutics; Pharmacokinetics; In silico
   modeling; Active learning
ID DRUG DISCOVERY; GASTROPLUS; ONLINE; TOOLS
AB Objectives: Pharmacokinetics and biopharmaceutics are core components of pharmacy education, providing the scientific foundation for drug development and therapeutic application. This case report describes the design, implementation, and feasibility evaluation of an integrated in silico educational module within an undergraduate Biopharmaceutics and Pharmacokinetics course. Methods: The module was implemented across four course offerings in a third-year Bachelor of Pharmacy Technology program. Students completed a semester-long project using GastroPlus (R), ADMET Predictor (R), and DDDPlus (R) (Simulation Plus, Inc.) through sequential activities involving molecule selection, physiologically-based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) and physiologically-based biopharmaceutics modeling (PBBM) simulations, physicochemical property prediction, dissolution modeling, and scientific communication through poster preparation and presentation. Implementation was evaluated using student performance data and alignment with the Seven Principles for Good Practice in Undergraduate Education. Results: The module was implemented across four cohorts involving 79 undergraduate students. Mean project grades ranged from 94.95 f 2.56% to 98.66 f 1.21%, while mean overall course grades ranged from 89.18 f 5.08% to 91.60 f 4.32%. The instructional design demonstrated alignment with established educational principles through active learning, student-faculty interaction, timely feedback, sustained engagement, clear expectations, and authentic scientific communication activities. Conclusion: This case report demonstrates the feasibility of integrating computational modeling into an undergraduate biopharmaceutics and pharmacokinetics course through a structured, project-based educational framework. The module provides a practical approach for incorporating PBPK, PBBM, and related computational methodologies into pharmacy curricula. Future studies using controlled educational designs and direct assessment of learning outcomes are needed to evaluate the educational impact of this approach.

TI Adaptation and psychometric evaluation of the Perceptions of Structural
   Equity (POSE) tool for PharmD students
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Cultural humility; Structural humility; Assessment; Measure; Validity;
   Measurement
ID COMPETENCE
AB Objective: The purpose of this study was to examine the psychometric properties of a modified measurement tool, termed the Perception of Structural Equity (POSE) tool by the current authors, for assessing student perceptions of social determinants of health (SDOH) and health equity, with a focus on structures (eg, policies, economic system) that interact with SDOH. The revised POSE tool included subscales measuring comprehension, readiness, awareness, and perceptions. Methods: An existing measurement tool was adapted to include 19 items using a 5-point Likert agreement scale. The POSE tool was administered to first-year PharmD students from four schools. Internal structure validity evidence for the POSE tool was examined using item descriptives, Cronbach's alpha, and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA). Results: There were 237 valid responses. Most items correlated with the measures, however, two did not and were removed, resulting in a final 17-item POSE tool. Cronbach's alpha values for each subscale and the overall POSE tool were generally above 0.70, suggesting acceptable reliability. CFA results for the 17-item model suggested good model fit. Conclusion: Overall, the revised POSE tool demonstrated strong psychometric properties, acceptable reliability, and detected change in perceptions over time. The final 17-item tool demonstrated good internal structure validity evidence, suggesting that the POSE tool may be useful as part of a comprehensive assessment plan. The tool can be used in its entirety or through use of one or more subscales. Future studies should examine the POSE tool in additional samples and continue evaluating its ability to assess change over time.

TI Doubling down: Leveraging residents and faculty as mentors in a
   residency preparation program
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Residency; Mentors; Post-graduate training
AB Introduction: Colleges or schools of pharmacy have tried various ways to prepare students for the residency recruitment process, including didactic courses, curricular tracks, and mentorship programs. The fellowship and residency advising program (FRAP) expanded mentorship to include both faculty and a resident, along with resources and recordings to support students through the residency application process, mock interviews, and phase II match Perspective: This commentary describes the use of dual mentorship for residency-bound student pharmacists, utilizing residents from a Teaching and Learning Certificate program and faculty members. TI Natural disasters and early child development: Evidence from an
   earthquake
SO ECONOMICS OF EDUCATION REVIEW
LA English
DT Article
DE Natural disasters; Earthquake; Early childhood; Cognitive development;
   Non-cognitive development; Smoking
ID CIGARETTE TAXES; INTERGENERATIONAL TRANSMISSION; OUTCOMES EVIDENCE;
   MATERNAL STRESS; FAMILY INCOME; JOB LOSS; EXPOSURE; IMPACT; ALCOHOL;
   SMOKING
AB This paper evaluates the persistent impact of the 2010 Chilean earthquake on children's cognitive and non-cognitive development. Using a difference-in-differences strategy that exploits quasi-random spatial and birth-cohort variation, I track children exposed between the prenatal period and age four over a sevenyear period, comparing them with children born after the earthquake. I find that early-life exposure leads to significant and enduring declines in both cognitive and non-cognitive test scores seven years later, with suggestive evidence of short-term cognitive disruption. The adverse cognitive effects are particularly pronounced among boys in both the short-and medium-term. To explain these deficits, I investigate a multidimensional disruption of the early caregiving environment. First, the disaster triggered a sharp increase in maternal smoking participation and stress. Second, I provide suggestive evidence of a structural asset shock: I observe a short-term reduction in household income per capita and maternal labor force participation. While these indicators recovered within two years, exposure to higher seismic intensity is associated with significant private expenditures on home repairs. Taken together, these results are consistent with a stress-budget trap: while households preserve the quantity of formal human capital investments, the evidence points to a combination of compounding stressors and a reallocation of resources away from the unobserved quality of the domestic environment to finance physical recovery. These findings suggest that early-life developmental penalties can be triggered by acute behavioral responses to trauma and the temporary dismantling of the domestic buffer, persisting even after household income and institutional access return to baseline.

TI From stories to skills: The impact of narrative-based financial
   education on students' knowledge and behavior
SO ECONOMICS OF EDUCATION REVIEW
LA English
DT Article
DE Financial literacy; Fiscal education; Civic education; Narrative media;
   Primary education; Randomized controlled trial
ID LITERACY; MEDIA; TELEVISION; CURRICULUM
AB We study a low-cost, teacher-led program for 4th-5th graders in Brazilian public schools that embeds financial, fiscal, and civic concepts in short, comics-based stories paired with structured class activities. We evaluate a school-level randomized trial in Brazil's capital Brasilia covering 106 schools (approximate to 13,600 students). Outcomes-knowledge and self-reported habits/beliefs-were measured with an age-appropriate instrument administered in person by an independent survey firm under exam-like conditions. Intent-to-treat estimates on a complete-case analysis sample show gains of 0.10 SD in financial knowledge, 0.06 SD in fiscal knowledge, and 0.06 SD in civic knowledge, all statistically significant and robust to alternative treatments of missing responses. We also find significant improvements in declared financial habits and beliefs and in civic beliefs. Beyond knowledge and beliefs, students also report greater school interest, more family interaction around money and public services, and higher future-self expectations. Placebo outcomes not targeted by the program, such as mathematics and monitoring of common goods at school, show no robust impacts. Monitoring data indicate that higher teacher engagement with the materials is associated with better student outcomes. Overall, the results indicate that culturally salient narrative media, delivered during regular class time, can measurably improve targeted economic and civic competencies at scale.

TI Finding their way: Students' fraction misconceptions and errors over two
   years of fraction learning
SO LEARNING AND INSTRUCTION
LA English
DT Article
DE Fractions; Misconceptions; Errors; Mathematical development
ID RATIONAL NUMBERS; WHOLE-NUMBER; INDIVIDUAL-DIFFERENCES; STRATEGIES;
   REPRESENTATION; TRAJECTORIES; ACQUISITION; MAGNITUDE; KNOWLEDGE; GROWTH
AB Purpose: This study examined the longitudinal stability and consistency of student misconceptions across five fraction subconstructs during two years of mathematics instruction. Method: In this study, 1055 students (546 boys; Mage = 9.8 years) were assessed at four time points in Grades 4 and 5 across five subconstructs: part-whole, measurement, quotient, operator, and density. Using a methodical pre-registered error-classification framework, supplemented by exploratory mixed-effects modelling, we examined the frequency and stability of student errors. Results: Results revealed a clear distinction in conceptual stability across domains. Part-whole meanings were mastered early in instruction and remained stable over time, whereas tasks involving magnitude and density were characterized by high response entropy and frequent strategy shifts. Students simultaneously held multiple misconceptions, which were highly dependent on the specific subconstruct being assessed. For example, in fraction arithmetic, errors varied across representations and operations. While accuracy generally improved, the progression of errors was often variable, with students frequently reverting from correct responses to whole number bias or unique, unclassified strategies when new topics, such as decimals, were introduced. Conclusion: These patterns indicate that a correct response at a single time point is not always a sign of stable understanding. Instead, the high degree of variation suggests that early fraction knowledge is context-dependent and that unique error patterns often signal active conceptual reorganization. These findings suggest that because misconceptions are a moving target, interventions must be adaptive and responsive to the specific errors that emerge as students transition between new fraction concepts.

TI How to communicate evidence to teachers: Comparing the effects of verbal
   and visual effect size representation [Registered Report - stage II]
SO LEARNING AND INSTRUCTION
LA English
DT Article
DE Evidence-informed practice; Effect sizes; Visualization; Science
   communication
ID SCIENCE; UNDERSTAND
AB Background: Teachers are encouraged to consider relevant evidence from educational research to improve the quality of their instruction. This approach requires them to have a reasonably accurate understanding of the effectiveness of educational interventions. However, currently prevalent ways of communicating effect sizes often lead to imprecise effect magnitude estimates. Aims: We investigated how teachers estimate and perceive verbally and visually communicated effect sizes. Sample: We recruited N = 120 English-speaking teachers (Mage = 43.5 years, 69% female) from the UK and USA via Prolific. Methods: We employed a randomized 4 & times; 6 & times; 2 between-within-within-person experiment, with the outcomes of interest being teachers' effect magnitude estimates, relevance, perceived informativeness, and perceived difficulty. Results: Across conditions, teachers' estimated effect magnitudes correlated strongly (tau = 0.70) with presented effect sizes, indicating that they can differentiate effectively between small and large effect sizes. Split by condition, teachers were less accurate in the verbal than in the visual condition (Cohen's d = -0.31, 95% CI [-0.43, -0.19]). Additionally, teachers' person-standardized relevance perceptions correlated moderately (tau = 0.35) with presented effect sizes. Moreover, they perceived verbally communicated Cohen's U3 expressions as more informative (rrb = -0.34, 95% CI [-0.39, -0.29]) and less difficult (rrb = 0.39, 95% CI [0.33, 0.44]) to understand than visually communicated effect sizes. Conclusion: Communicating effect sizes to teachers works verbally and visually. However, there appears to be a trade-off between the two presentation modes: higher accuracy in the visual versus greater user-friendliness in the verbal mode.

TI Exploring the impact of a GenAI-supported writing program on primary
   students' writing motivation, engagement, and performance: A mixed
   methods study
SO LEARNING AND INSTRUCTION
LA English
DT Article
DE GenAI; Writing motivation; Writing engagement; Writing performance
ID INSTRUCTION
AB Background: The integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into second language (L2) writing has attracted increasing interest, particularly in higher education. Yet little is known about its pedagogical value in primary education, especially regarding how younger learners' writing motivation, engagement, and performance may change in GenAI-supported contexts. Aims: This study investigates the impact of a GenAI-supported writing program on primary students' motivation (i.e., growth mindset, ideal L2 writing self, academic buoyancy), engagement (i.e., cognitive, behavioral, emotional, metacognitive), and performance (i.e., opinion and content, organization, language use). Sample: Participants were 301 Grade 5 and Grade 6 students from a primary school in Eastern China. Methods: A mixed-methods approach was adopted. Eight classes were randomly assigned to either a GenAIsupported writing experimental group or a conventional writing control group. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with selected students in the experimental group (N = 12) to explore their learning experiences. Results: Quantitative analyses (MANCOVA and paired sample t-tests) revealed significant group effects on ideal L2 writing self, academic buoyancy, behavioral and emotional engagement, and two performance domains: language use, and opinion and content. Within-group analyses showed varying degrees of improvement across constructs. Qualitative findings highlighted GenAI's multifaceted roles in shaping these outcomes. Conclusions: This study extends GenAI-integrated writing research to the primary level, demonstrating its potential to enhance L2 writing by supporting key motivational, engagement, and performance dimensions. Practical implications are offered for integrating GenAI meaningfully into primary-level L2 writing instruction.

   education: A photovoice qualitative study
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence; Nursing education; Photovoice; Qualitative

AB Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming an integral part of nursing education; however, the perspectives of graduate nursing students on its use remain underexplored. Aim: This study aimed to examine graduate nursing students' views on AI in nursing education. Methods: A qualitative phenomenological design incorporating the photovoice method was adopted. TI Preliminary evaluation of an adapted snack delay task for measuring
   inhibition in young children with Down syndrome
SO RESEARCH IN DEVELOPMENTAL DISABILITIES
LA English
DT Article
DE Down syndrome; Executive function; Inhibitory control; Assessment; Snack
   Delay
ID SYNDROME BEHAVIORAL-PHENOTYPE; EXECUTIVE FUNCTION; CHILDHOOD; EMOTION
AB Background: Individuals with Down syndrome (DS) often experience challenges in executive functioning (EF), including inhibitory control. Despite interest in EF research and intervention in DS, there is a lack of feasible and developmentally sensitive measures of EF for young children in this population. This study evaluated the feasibility, developmental sensitivity, and test-retest reliability of a modified Snack Delay task for children with DS aged 2-7 years. Methods: The Snack Delay task was administered to 118 participants with DS (mean age = 5.21, SD = 1.53; 51.7% male). Three outcome metrics were evaluated for feasibility, developmental sensitivity, and preliminary psychometric properties. Feasibility was assessed by task completion rates. Distributional characteristics, including range and floor and ceiling effects, were examined. Intraclass correlation coefficients assessed test-retest reliability, and t-tests evaluated practice effects across a two-week period. Developmental sensitivity was evaluated as a function of chronological and mental age. Results: The Snack Delay task was feasible for 89% of participants and captured meaningful variability in inhibitory control among children with DS aged 3-7 years. Floor effects ranged from 0% to 17.1% and ceiling effects from 20% to 56.2%. Test-retest reliability was moderate for one metric and strong for two. A small, non-significant practice effect was observed for one metric, with lower average waiting times at retest. Performance scaled with age and developmental level, though ceiling effects were observed in older children. Lack of motivation was more common among participants with younger chronological and mental ages. Conclusion: The Snack Delay task is a reliable, developmentally sensitive measure of inhibition in young children with DS and may be a valuable tool for assessing EF in this population.

TI Translingual practices and academic identity in multilingual higher
   education contexts
SO REVIEW OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE academic identity; English as a lingua franca (ELF); English as a medium
   of instruction (EMI); higher education; translanguaging
AB This paper investigates translingual practices and their influence on academic identity within higher education settings. It emphasizes a shift from traditional monolingual perspectives towards a more inclusive, plurilingual approach, driven by globalization and the rise of English as a medium of instruction (EMI) and lingua franca (ELF). Focusing on faculty members navigating across multiple languages, the study explores the complexities of translating ideas and concepts between languages and how language choices shape cognitive viewpoints and personal identities. It highlights the importance of mobility and internationalization, which foster viewing languages as flexible repertoires or thresholds rather than fixed national identities. The research specifically examines faculty members who teach in a second language (L2), analysing how their translingual practices influence their professional identities. Employing a qualitative, phenomenological methodology, the study involves interviews with faculty members at a German university to capture their experiences, strategies and perceptions. Findings reveal diverse uses of translingual practices, such as enhancing clarity, expressing emotions, navigating informal interactions and explaining culturally specific concepts. Strategies include simplifying language, reframing ideas, switching to L1 when needed, utilizing online tools and applying translanguaging as a pedagogical method. The interaction between translingual practices and academic identity emerges as a fluid, dynamic process involving identity shaping, social interaction, meaning-making, power relations and reflexivity. These practices reflect a translingual mindset aligned with the goals of internationalization and the global scientific community. Overall, the study underscores the importance of understanding how translingual practices contribute to identity formation in a rapidly evolving, multilingual higher education landscape.

TI Beyond class size: Understanding student academic achievement through
   student, school, and national contexts
SO STUDIES IN EDUCATIONAL EVALUATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Student academic achievement; Student-teacher ratio; Class size;
   Globalization; PISA; GDP per capita
ID INTERNATIONAL DIFFERENCES; SOCIOECONOMIC-STATUS; ECONOMIC-DEVELOPMENT;
   PISA; QUALITY; PERFORMANCE; RESILIENCE; CHILDHOOD; POLICIES; ECOLOGY
AB Educational systems now operate in a globalized and highly competitive environment, making international assessments like PISA central to policy discussions. This study investigates how variables at the student level (i.e., student socioeconomic status (SES) and educational track), the school level (i.e., classroom structural conditions of class size and student-teacher ratio, and school selectivity), and country level (i.e., GDP per capita) contribute to variation in student academic achievement in PISA. Overall, the results indicated that the variance in student academic achievement in the PISA assessment is similarly distributed across all three levels, suggesting a multi-level structure of influences. The study offers meaningful insights for improving educational outcomes globally.

TI A multilayered analysis of university students' experiences with human
   and AI-based feedback: A comparative examination of BERTopic, LLM
   models, and mixture of agents approaches
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Student experience; AI-based feedback; Human feedback; Topic modeling;
   BERTopic; Large Language Models; Mixture of Agents
ID AUTOMATIC FEEDBACK
AB This study presents a multilayered text analysis framework for examining university students' experiences with human-and artificial intelligence (AI)-based feedback. The empirical corpus consisted of 322 feedback-related reflection statements obtained from 110 undergraduate students. The analysis combined data preprocessing, corpus-driven thematic modeling with BER-Topic, zero-shot thematic extraction using large language models (LLMs), ensemble-based semantic alignment, psycholinguistic emotion-theme integration, and high-resolution thematic refinement through a Mixture of Agents (MoA) framework. BERTopic identified six core themes: trust and transparency, cognitive load and clarity, learning contribution and perceived benefit, emotional discomfort and uncertainty, human-AI comparison, and complementary feedback expectations. The results showed that students' feedback experiences were multidimensional, involving cognitive, affective, explanatory, and comparative dimensions rather than a simple preference for either feedback source. BERTopic provided a stable corpus-grounded thematic baseline, whereas Large Language Model (LLM)-based zero-shot extraction produced pedagogically interpretable and conceptually expressive theme labels. The ensemble approach reduced variation across individual LLM outputs by consolidating semantically similar labels. MoA further refined thematic distinctions and improved emotion-topic alignment, particularly in statements involving cognitive ambiguity or emotionally charged feedback experiences. Comparative analyses indicated that AI-based feedback was more strongly associated with speed, accessibility, consistency, and immediate learning support, whereas human feedback was more strongly associated with contextual richness, empathy, pedagogical explanation, and perceived authority. The findings suggest that effective feedback design should combine the scalability and immediacy of AI-based feedback with human oversight, contextual interpretation, emotional calibration, and transparent justification. Overall, the study contributes to learning analytics and feedback research by demonstrating how corpus-driven topic modeling, LLM-based interpretation, ensemble alignment, and MoA-based refinement can be integrated to model the cognitive and affective dimensions of students' feedback experiences.

TI Barriers and multilevel strategies for accessibility and belonging in
   surgical clerkships: a narrative review
SO GLOBAL SURGICAL EDUCATION - JOURNAL OF THE ASSOCIATION FOR SURGICAL
   EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Surgical clerkship; Medical students; Medical education; Accessibility;
   Inclusion; Belonging; Equity
ID MEDICAL-STUDENTS; IDENTITY; RESIDENTS; PROGRAM; BIAS
AB Purpose Surgical clerkships are pivotal in shaping professional identity and career trajectories but may exacerbate inequities for students from historically excluded groups. Evidence addressing accessibility and belonging in surgical training remains fragmented across identity domains and intervention types. This study synthesizes existing literature to characterize barriers and identify strategies to promote equity in surgical clerkships.Methods We conducted a structured search of PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science (2014-2025) for studies addressing accessibility, inclusion, or belonging in surgical clerkships. Two reviewers independently screened studies and selected eligible articles. Data were extracted using a standardized form and synthesized narratively. Barriers and strategies were categorized across structural, institutional, and cultural domains.Results Of 1,828 records identified, 25 studies met inclusion criteria. The most frequently examined domains of inclusivity were gender (n = 13), race (n = 10), ethnicity (n = 8), and disability (n = 7). Barriers clustered into structural, institutional, and cultural domains. Structural barriers included inaccessible clinical environments and limited adaptive resources. Institutional barriers reflected inconsistent accommodation processes and inequitable evaluation practices. Cultural barriers included bias, microaggressions, and diminished sense of belonging. Strategies to promote inclusion emphasized multilevel interventions, including structured mentorship, standardized accommodations, and inclusive curricular and learning environments.Conclusions Barriers to accessibility and belonging in surgical clerkships are multifactorial and persistent across identity domains. Addressing these challenges requires coordinated structural, institutional, and cultural interventions. These findings provide a framework that may help guide surgical educators to identify areas for future intervention, evaluation, and institutional improvement.

TI Emotional intelligence influences surgical resident's self-perception of
   competency: an exploratory, multi-institutional study
SO GLOBAL SURGICAL EDUCATION - JOURNAL OF THE ASSOCIATION FOR SURGICAL
   EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Clinical Competency Committee; Milestones 2.0; Surgical Residents
ID SURGERY
AB Purpose To determine, via an exploratory cohort analysis, whether a resident's emotional intelligence (EI) is associated with greater alignment between their self-assessment and faculty evaluations of clinical competency.Methods A multi-institutional, prospective observational cohort study assessed EI using the validated 33-item Schutte Self-Report Emotional Intelligence Test. Residents' self-evaluations and Clinical Competency Committee (CCC) evaluations were based on ACGME Milestones 2.0, with concordance measured at mid-year and end-of-year evaluations during the 2022-2023 academic year. EI scores were compared between residents with low and high evaluation concordance.Results Performance evaluation data from 88 residents were collected and analyzed for concordance; of these, 36 also completed the EI survey. By year's end, low concordance decreased to 38%, and high concordance increased to 62%, suggesting improved self-assessment accuracy over time. Program size was strongly associated with concordance: residents in medium-sized programs showed higher concordance (86%) compared to those in small (58%) and large programs (52%) at year's end (p = 0.029). No significant associations were found with PGY level or program type.Conclusions This exploratory study highlights an association between EI and the accuracy of surgical residents' self-assessments, possibly reflecting greater self-awareness. The increase in concordance over time suggests that ongoing feedback may enhance residents' insight into their clinical performance.

TI Enhancing EFL learners' speaking performance through ChatGPT-assisted
   practice: evidence from complexity, accuracy, and fluency measures
SO ASIAN-PACIFIC JOURNAL OF SECOND AND FOREIGN LANGUAGE EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE ChatGPT; Large language models; EFL speaking pedagogy; Complexity,
   Accuracy, and Fluency (CAF); Technology-assisted language learning
ID ANXIETY
AB This study examined whether ChatGPT-assisted speaking practice could strengthen English as a Foreign Language speaking development in an IELTS preparation context. Sixty-five intermediate Iranian learners participated in a ten-week quasi-experimental intervention, with one group receiving structured ChatGPT-supported speaking practice and a comparison group receiving teacher-led instruction. Learner performance was assessed through IELTS-aligned speaking tasks and analyzed using complexity, accuracy, and fluency indicators. The findings showed a clear pedagogical advantage of ChatGPT-assisted practice for syntactic complexity and fluency, while accuracy improved over time in both groups without a distinct between-group advantage. At the same time, the pattern for accuracy indicated that generative AI should be integrated as a complement to, rather than a replacement for, teacher guidance, especially for form-focused feedback. The study contributed evidence from an underrepresented EFL context and supported a blended instructional model in which ChatGPT expanded speaking opportunities, promoted learner autonomy, and enhanced key dimensions of oral performance within communicative language teaching.

AB Reasearch findings: Young children's verbal interactions with teachers and peers in preschool settings are a key mechanism for development. Evidence suggests individual differences in children's access to verbal interactions with teachers and peers in the classroom, yet such evidence comes primarily from brief, infrequent observations, and reveals little about how children's social network experience shapes access to talk in the classroom. This study examined the extent to which preschool children's interactions with teachers and peers vary within and across classrooms, and whether aspects of the classroom social network help explain that variation. Practice or Policy: Results highlight the importance of identifying children at the periphery of the classroom social network, as these children are most at risk of being isolated from verbal interactions in the classroom.

TI Existential Constructions and Syntactic Complexity in Chinese EFL
   Writing: A Corpus-Based Comparative Study With ChatGPT-Enhanced Analysis
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE ChatGPT; Chinese EFL writing; corpus-based analysis; existential
   constructions; mean dependency distance; syntactic complexity
ID DEPENDENCY DISTANCE; LANGUAGE
AB Existential constructions (ECs) play an important role in academic writing by introducing new information, expressing epistemic stance and facilitating information flow. Examining how EFL learners use different EC types can offer valuable insights into their syntactic development and writing proficiency. Previous research, however, has focused mainly on EC acquisition independently, with limited attention to the relationship between constructional usage and sentence-level syntactic complexity. The present study investigates Chinese EFL learners' use of ECs across three categories: presentational, epistemic/evidential and interrogative forms. A corpus-based comparative analysis was conducted using four corpora, with ECs extracted via ChatGPT-assisted annotation and subsequent manual classification. The results show that learners exhibit a restricted EC repertoire. Presentational ECs were significantly overused, whereas contracted forms were categorically absent. Within the epistemic/evidential category, all evidential ECs were completely unattested and most epistemic ECs were significantly underused. Interrogative ECs were pervasively underused, with six forms categorically absent from learner corpora. Regression analysis further indicated that presentational and interrogative EC frequencies are negatively associated with Mean Dependency Distance (MDD), whereas epistemic/evidential EC frequency is positively associated with MDD. These findings underscore the pedagogical implications of promoting constructional diversity, particularly epistemic and evidential forms that are essential to academic discourse.

TI Teaching With AI, Engaging With Purpose: University Teachers' Work
   Engagement in AI-Supported Higher Education
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE AI literacy; AI-supported teaching; higher education; teacher
   professional development; teacher work engagement
ID JOB DEMANDS; RESOURCES
AB Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly reshaping higher education, requiring university teachers to adapt their pedagogical roles, technological competence, and professional engagement. Drawing on the Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) model, this study examined how organizational support and AI literacy were associated with university teachers' work engagement in AI-supported teaching, with professional identity, resilience, and self-efficacy as mediating personal resources. TI Tools facilitate cheating, or partner supports learning? GenAI and
   academic integrity issues from students' perspectives
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL FOR EDUCATIONAL INTEGRITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence; Academic integrity; Plagiarism; Originality;
   Assessment
AB The rapid expansion of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has increased concerns about academic integrity in higher education, reshaping the way it was previously conceptualized. As GenAI becomes more prevalent, an in-depth understanding of students' perspectives appears to be crucial to navigate the ethical use of the innovation. The objective of this study is, therefore, to explore students' perspectives of academic integrity issues regarding the use of GenAI, focusing on plagiarism, originality, and the fairness of academic assessment results. This study utilized a qualitative research approach, based on a reflexive thematic method. The participants of this study are undergraduate students from Ambo University. The result of the study is unexpectedly paradoxical. GenAI tools have emerged as an essential revolution to improve student academic engagement. They offer students several perceived benefits, such as overcoming language barriers, access to up-to-date resources, and improved academic support. However, a serious concern arises as a substantial number of students are positive about using GenAI and relying on it for coursework as a minor violation. It is also noted that GenAI creates uneven playing fields between students who genuinely work on their own efforts and those who submit work generated by GenAI. Finally, it can be concluded that the students' view of GenAI can shape their ethical use of these tools, which requires prioritizing awareness raising, developing policy frameworks, and monitoring policy reinforcement. TI Greening a Great Experiment: Optimizing the
   Nickel-CatalyzedSuzuki-Miyaura Cross-Coupling of Phenylboronic Acid and
   1-Bromo-4-(trifluoromethyl)benzene
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Second-Year Undergraduate; Upper-Division Undergraduate; Inorganic
   Chemistry; Green Chemistry; LaboratoryInstruction; Hands-On
   Learning/Manipulatives; Catalysis; NMR Spectroscopy; Organometallics
ID CHEMISTRY; HYDRODEHALOGENATION; PALLADIUM; CATALYSIS; NI(I); NI
AB Optimized procedures are provided for the Suzuki-Miyaura cross-coupling of 1-bromo-4-(trifluoromethyl)benzene with phenylboronic acid using molecular nickel(II) precatalysts in the green solvent 2-methylbutan-2-ol in the presence of base. Emphasis is placed on evaluating the procedures in the context of the principles of green chemistry. When compared with the existing undergraduate experiment, significant gains are made in reducing the reaction scale, minimizing catalyst loading, reducing or eliminating cooling water use, and improving energy efficiency. The cross-coupling reaction is flexible and can be tailored to a variety of laboratory schedules, equipment availability, and student skill levels. While the greatest efficiency is realized when a commercial microwave synthesizer is employed, viable options are presented for simple reflux and sealed vial reactions. The experiment is suitable for typical 3-4-h lab periods and can easily be incorporated into a variety of laboratory curricula, including mini-projects with or without teamwork.

AB Recent policies in education have prompted the implementation of scripted core literacy programs, resulting in increased teacher-directed, systematic phonics instruction. TI Identification of pre-service biology teachers' opinions about benefits
   and challenges in developing mobile augmented reality teaching
   materials: a nominal group technique study
SO EDUCATIONAL MEDIA INTERNATIONAL
LA English
DT Article
DE Mobile augmented reality; pre-serve biology teachers; nominal group;
   SAMR model
ID VIRTUAL-REALITY; EDUCATION
AB This study examines pre-service biology teachers' (PSBTs) opinions on the benefits and challenges of self-developed mobile augmented reality (mAR) biology teaching materials. In this research, 27 PSBTs participated and were divided into three nominal groups. The study is grounded in the Substitution, Augmentation, Modification and Redefinition (SAMR) framework, which was used to examine how PSBTs perceive different levels of technology integration through self-developed mAR materials. Following our objective, we employed a mixed methodological approach. Data were collected through the Nominal Group Technique (NGT), including written reflections, group discussions, and ranking of identified themes. PSBTs singled out 15 themes that indicate the benefits of mAR materials, as well as three themes that highlight challenges in their implementation. The key findings highlight enhanced visualization, increased motivation and personalization as main benefits, and limited time and resources as major challenges. Using the four levels of the SAMR model, found themes were organized into Substitution, Augmentation, Modification and Redefinition. Most themes were located in the first two SAMR levels. Nevertheless, the participants pointed out that mAR teaching materials enable greater personalization and inclusiveness and a stronger emotional connection between students and nature.

TI Comparing instructor and role-play AI chatbots for EFL writing: effects
   on anxiety, engagement, and feedback perception
SO EDUCATIONAL MEDIA INTERNATIONAL
LA English
DT Article
DE EFL writing; AI chatbots; foreign language writing anxiety; learner
   engagement; feedback preferences
ID LANGUAGE; TECHNOLOGIES
AB Grounded in foreign language anxiety (FLA) research and second-language acquisition theories, this mixed methods study investigates how two pedagogically distinct artificial intelligence (AI) GPT-4o-powered chatbots influence adult English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners' writing anxiety, engagement, feedback perception, and future-use preferences. In a counterbalanced within-subjects design, 21 learners each completed two 15-minute writing sessions: one with an Instructor Bot providing explicit corrective feedback, and another with a Role-Player Bot delivering implicit, scenario-based conversational guidance. Quantitative analyses showed that the Role-Player Bot significantly reduced learners' mistake-related anxiety. At the same time, the Instructor Bot's explicit feedback was rated as significantly more useful and confidence-boosting. Engagement and enjoyment were high and comparable across conditions; however, participants' preferences for future chatbot use varied based on their learning goals, which were either accuracy-oriented or fluency-oriented. Qualitative thematic analysis revealed a clear preference for hybrid chatbot designs combining conversational immersion with structured, explicit corrections. These results underscore key trade-offs between accuracy-focused and narrative-driven AI tutors, highlighting the importance of adaptive chatbot architectures that dynamically balance explicit feedback and engaging, low-pressure interaction. The study provides novel insights into chatbot-assisted writing support and offers actionable guidelines for designing personalized, anxiety-sensitive AI tools in EFL contexts.

TI Emotional Labour in Shaping Pre-Service Teachers' Well-Being: A Case
   Study of Rural Practicum Journeys
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE emotional labour; pre-service teachers; rural education; teacher
   well-being; teaching practicum
ID BURNOUT; EFFICACY
AB This study explores the emotional journeys of three pre-service teachers during their rural teaching practicum in China, focusing on how emotional labour develops and shapes teacher well-being. Using reflexive thematic analysis of three narrative cases, the study traces participants' emotional labour trajectories over time. The findings show that all three teachers initially engaged in genuine expression before shifting to surface acting in response to practicum tensions, with two subsequently developing deep acting, whereas one remained reliant on surface acting. These divergent trajectories emerged through guided reflection that fostered critical emotional reflexivity, which was enabled or constrained by structural and contextual conditions. By providing a process-oriented account of emotional labour trajectories during practicum, the study contributed to a deeper understanding of how pre-service teacher well-being evolved and fluctuated over time and offered practical implications for teacher education and rural practicum support.

TI Learning-Style Preferences Across Clinical and Surgical Specialties in a
   Brazilian Medical Residency Program
SO INTERNATIONAL MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE medical residency; learning styles; medical education; Felder-Soloman
   index of learning styles; clinical and surgical specialties
ID AMERICAN BOARD; HABITS
AB Medical residency is a demanding stage of specialty training characterized by extensive clinical exposure, heavy workloads, and ongoing knowledge acquisition. Characterizing residents' learning-style preferences may help residency programs refine their educational strategies and better address residents' needs. This study assessed learning-style preferences using the Felder-Soloman Index of Learning Styles in 152 residents from clinical and surgical specialties in a Brazilian medical residency program. In the overall sample, the predominant preferences were sensing (90.79%), visual (73.68%), active (62.50%), and sequential (70.39%). Clinical and surgical residents differed significantly only in the understanding domain: sequential preference was more frequent among clinical than surgical residents (80.0% [95% CI: 68.7-87.9] vs. 63.2% [95% CI: 52.7-72.6]). The limited variation between groups suggests that most residents shared a broadly similar learning profile, although some cognitive-processing preferences may differ according to specialty-related demands. These findings may inform diversified educational strategies that combine visual resources, practical activities, and structured progression across clinical and surgical training contexts.

TI Faculty development programme grounded in an interprofessional
   collaboration: shaping teaching practices
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Faculty Development; Peer Learning; Health Professions Education;
   Interprofessional Education; Teaching Practice
AB Background Effective teaching in health professions education is essential for preparing competent graduates and promoting safe, high-quality clinical care. Faculty development is a key strategy for enhancing teaching competencies and fostering change in educational practices. It is increasingly recognized that peer learning can contribute to the intended outcomes in faculty development. However, it remains unexplored how and in what ways interprofessional collaboration can further strengthen these programs. This study aims to examine how participation in interprofessional faculty development influences educators' reactions and self-reported learning, and how this experience shapes their subsequent learning and teaching practices.Methods We conducted a qualitative descriptive study, grounded in a constructivist paradigm, at a higher education institution in Brazil. A purposive sample included 16 health professions educators who participated in a mandatory faculty development program between the second semester of 2024 and the first semester of 2025. The group was diverse in terms of professional background, consisting of nurses, physiotherapists, nutritionists, dentists, and physicians. Data were collected through three face-to-face, semi-structured focus group interviews and analyzed inductively using thematic analysis.Results Three themes emerged: (1) Faculty development as a starting point for becoming a teacher and developing a teaching identity; (2) Learning with educators from other professions broadened perspectives on teaching; (3) Collaboration across different health professionals shaped and transformed teaching practice.Conclusion By promoting active interprofessional collaboration and exchanges, the program enhanced educators' confidence and professional identity as teachers. Interprofessional collaboration was a key driver for refining and transforming teaching practices.

AB While most research on biographical narratives has concentrated on the analysis of the final textual product as a means of understanding the narrative, the present study explores the underlying processes of narrative construction and presentation within peer groups in a teacher education college, drawing on the narrators' own reflections and accounts. Employing on a qualitative grounded theory design, semi-structured interviews were conducted with 15 current and former special education college students. Participants reflected on the deliberative and interpretive processes, shaping both disclosure decisions and modes of self-presentation. Findings indicate that peer groups constitute a significant force in narrative co-construction. Boundaries of disclosure and degrees of vulnerability were continuously negotiated, through engagement with others' narratives. Participants employed various narrative strategies, including redemption and normalization frameworks, in order to sustain a coherent and resilient professional self-concept. A key theoretical contribution of the study is the conceptualization of emotional regulation, as an integral component of narrative construction. Participants actively modulated the emotional intensity of their storytelling. Overall, the study suggests that Biographical Narrative practices function as a collaborative and meaning-making process that supports reflective capacity, peer-based scaffolding and resilience, thereby contributing to teacher well-being and professional identity development, in preservice education contexts.

TI Mapping the Typologies of Pedagogical Practice: A Latent Profile
   Analysis of UAE Teachers' Classroom Strategies
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE teacher typologies; latent profile analysis; instructional practices;
   UAE public schools; TALIS 2024; professional development
AB This study investigates instructional practices among 4228 UAE public school teachers using data from the 2024 Teaching and Learning International Survey (TALIS). Latent Profile Analysis (LPA) of 15 self-reported teaching-practice items identified four distinguishable pedagogical profiles: (1) Comprehensive Practitioners (77.2%), reporting mildly above-average use of practices across all domains with no pronounced emphasis in any area; (2) Limited-Repertoire Teachers (10.1%), reporting the lowest use of nearly all practices; (3) Emerging-Repertoire Teachers (4.5%), showing a similar but less extreme pattern; and (4) Traditional Teachers (8.2%), reporting above-average classroom management alongside below-average cognitive activation and content-linking. The LPA was conducted using mclust (v. 6.1.3) in R. Classification quality was high (entropy = 0.987), although AIC, BIC, and ABIC continued to favour solutions with more than four profiles through the eight-profile models tested; the four-profile solution was retained for its comparatively high entropy, interpretability, and parsimony. The profile structure should therefore be treated as a description of self-reported practice patterns within this analysed, unweighted sample. By mapping diverse teaching behaviours, this study contributes to global discourse on evidence-based pedagogy and supports data-driven reform efforts aligned with the UAE's national educational vision for world-class schooling.

TI Project-Based Science Learning: Adaptations That Promote Productive
   Disciplinary Engagement and Disrupt Exclusionary Practices
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE ambitious science teaching; STEM learning; disciplinary engagement;
   epistemic inclusions; curriculum redesign; virtual learning; e-learning;
   COVID-19 impacts
ID EDUCATION; KNOWLEDGE; CULTURE; JUSTICE; TALKING; EQUITY
AB This paper examines how exclusionary epistemic practices embedded in science as a discipline are reproduced in classroom settings and how these practices can be disrupted when teachers adapt existing materials toward goals of epistemic inclusion. The inequities in access, participation, and representation in science that are reproduced at a societal level are developed in the classroom. Students learn how to do science-they develop the epistemic and social practices of the scientific discipline-in science education classes. When exclusion of some students from classroom knowledge building is normalized, marginalization becomes part of how students learn to engage in science and engineering practices. Drawing on a curricular redesign project conducted during the COVID-19 transition to virtual learning, the study highlights how the repositioning of teachers as active agents and experts in curriculum adaptation was central to the work. Five themes associated with disruption of entrenched exclusionary practices emerged that can be codified as adaptation principles: 1. adapt features of project-based learning to: (1) bring in and leverage students' identities and intellectual resources from home; (2) provide student-centered choice; (3) elicit diverse knowledge, expertise and ideas; (4) support students to make use of many different modalities; (5) dismantle the usual (traditional) structures between the teacher and students.

AB The rapid expansion of ChatGPT in higher education and the increasing adoption of generative AI in the financial industry raise important pedagogical questions for finance education.    Educational Experiences
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES

AB Research on twice-exceptional Autistic (2eA) individuals has predominantly focused on children and adolescents, leaving a limited understanding of adult reflections on schooling. This qualitative retrospective study explored perceived barriers and facilitators to talent development among 17 intellectually gifted Autistic adults from Australia, the United States, and Canada. Using semi-structured interviews and inductive thematic analysis, the findings revealed two overarching themes: barriers to talent development and facilitators of talent development. The findings highlight a need for improved professional learning, systematic identification practices, and strengths-based, context-responsive approaches to support equitable talent development for 2eA students.

TI Psychological Distress Mediates Between Autonomous Learning and Academic
   Engagement Among University Students
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES

DT Article

ID SELF-DETERMINATION THEORY; DEPRESSION; ANXIETY; MOTIVATION; EFFICACY;

AB Grounded in self-determination theory, the present study examined the role of psychological distress as a mediator between autonomous learning and academic engagement among university students in China. In this cross-sectional study, survey data from 234 Chinese university students were collected to evaluate autonomous learning, psychological distress including symptoms of depression, anxiety, and stress, and academic engagement. TI Impact of using an educational robotics model on students' innovation:
   the case of a final year class at a technical high school in Morocco
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE composite innovation index (CII); educational robotics; innovation;
   Moroccan curriculum; students' competencies
AB The current Moroccan high school curriculum, especially in the final year class of the mechanical science and technology discipline, looks like it insufficiently promotes the development of interdisciplinary and practical skills. Students' overall development, both technically and personally, reflects this shortcoming. In fact, the selected approaches to teaching often concentrate on theory, ignoring practical application and real-life situations where the knowledge gained is used. In order to remedy this problem, it is essential to include more creative approaches focused on practical projects, such as robotics. This article presents an exploratory quasi-experimental study in which we try to evaluate how integrating AlphaBot2 educational robotics (STM32WB55RG-based) impacts innovation level among Moroccan technical high school students. Eight students were selected based on their academic status, previous experience, and availability. Three methodological frameworks are introduced and applied to the extent permitted by the sample size: (1) a quasi-experimental within-subjects design comparing two experimental conditions; (2) construct validity assessment of the Composite Innovation Index (CII) (which comprising eight indicators of innovation) through Cronbach's alpha, which proved statistically unstable at N = 8, confirming that full psychometric validation (CFA, SEM) requires a substantially larger sample; and (3) a Wilcoxon signed-rank test as a feasible non-parametric analogue to MANOVA for within-subjects comparisons. The mean CII score in Condition A (without time constraint) was 4.195 out of 5 (SD = 0.114), with the highest scores in critical thinking (M = 4.250) and autonomy (M = 4.333). A Wilcoxon signed-rank test comparing CII composite scores between Condition A (M = 4.195) and Condition B (with time constraint, M = 4.291) did not reach statistical significance (W = 8, Z = -1.40, p = 0.195), although the effect size was medium-to-large (r = 0.495). Six of eight students showed improvement under time pressure, while two (S6, S8) showed slight decreases. These findings confirm the exploratory potential of educational robotics for fostering innovation in Moroccan STEM education, while underscoring the methodological requirements for confirmatory research.

TI Turning tension into educational momentum: a ten-year action research
   study of music-integrated ideological and political education in higher
   education
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE action research; aesthetic education for moral development; higher
   education; ideological and political education; mixed methods; music
   education; tension transformation
AB Ideological and political education (IPE) in higher education has long faced the problem of transforming knowledge transmission into value identification. Music can open new educational routes through aesthetic experience, collective participation, and meaning co-creation, but the tension between aesthetic autonomy and educational intention still lacks a mechanism-based explanation grounded in long-term practice. This article draws on a ten-year action research study conducted from 2015 to 2025 in a Chinese higher vocational institution and frames the inquiry as model-building and theory-generating action research. The study integrates anonymous paired questionnaires from 428 students at T1, T2, and T3, voluntary non-clinical SCL-90 self-reported psychological-state data from 96 volunteers, practice archives, dissemination records, and three illustrative cases. Qualitative materials indicated that full-progression, partial-progression, and differentiated trajectories coexisted. On this basis, the study proposes a one-core, two-wing, three-driver, six-domain project architecture, a three-stage interpretive pathway, and a tension-transformation spiral model. The contribution of the study is to move music-integrated IPE from activity integration toward model generation within action research and to conceptualize tension as a dynamic condition for student meaning inquiry and the return of educational intention.

TI Empowering higher education in China ethnic folk dance with the
   metaverse: a study on the impact on student satisfaction
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE China ethnic folk dance education; educational policy and innovation;
   educational technology innovation; metaverse; student satisfaction
ID PERCEIVED SERVICE QUALITY; EMOTIONAL INTELLIGENCE; USER SATISFACTION;
   USEFULNESS PU; USE PEOU; EASE; LOYALTY; MODEL; INFORMATION; ACHIEVEMENT
AB This study aims to explore how metaverse technology empowers higher education in China ethnic folk dance and enhances student satisfaction. A questionnaire survey was conducted among 485 Chinese students after they completed a metaverse-supported China ethnic folk dance course, focusing on their learning experiences, outcomes, and satisfaction. Structural equation modeling was used for empirical analysis. TI Self-assessment as a heutagogical mechanism for double-loop learning in
   teacher induction
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE double-loop learning; heutagogy; novice teachers; self-assessment;
   teacher induction
ID EDUCATION
AB Introduction The first year of teaching is often organized around external standards, leaving novice teachers limited authority over what counts as professional growth. This study examines what becomes possible when teachers construct and apply criteria for evaluating their development. It conceptualizes criteria-making as a form of heutagogical evaluative agency and asks whether this process opens opportunities for assumption-questioning and double-loop reflection.Methods The study used a qualitative, interpretive document-analysis design in two induction workshops. Thirty-one first-year teachers collaboratively generated and operationalized assessment criteria and selected four to six criteria for self-assessment reports. The corpus comprised two collaborative presentations and 31 reports. Analysis combined inductive constant comparison to identify dimensions of professional practice with theory-informed coding for learner agency, capability, reflection and metacognition, learning how to learn, and three levels of reflective depth: descriptive or confirmatory, single-loop, and double-loop reflection.Results Participants' criteria clustered around four interdependent dimensions: relational-moral practice, instructional design and classroom orchestration, responsive noticing and adaptation, and professional participation and self-development. The task enacted evaluative agency by requiring participants to select, justify, operationalize, weight, and apply criteria to their experience. Reflective depth varied. Some passages confirmed existing understandings, many proposed changes to strategies and routines, and some contained textual evidence consistent with double-loop reflection. Assumption-questioning was most evident in accounts of unexpected pupil responses, unsuccessful strategies, difficult encounters with parents, and tensions between care and authority.Discussion The study contributes to heutagogical theory by conceptualizing criteria-making as evaluative agency: participation in constructing the standards, evidence, and values through which professional learning is interpreted. It also shows that this agency was scaffolded and relational, emerging through collaborative deliberation, facilitator-provided structure, and individual judgment rather than unsupported independence. The findings suggest that learner-generated criteria may provide a language for retrospectively examining professional surprise and reframing the assumptions it exposes. Criteria-making may therefore create an opportunity for double-loop reflection but does not guarantee it. Because the data are participant-generated documents, the findings concern reflective meaning-making, evaluative agency, and reported adaptive judgment; they do not establish causal effects, sustained changes in classroom practice, or pupil outcomes.

TI When leadership becomes epistemic: paradoxes of educational leadership
   in AI-mediated systems
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE AI-mediated education; digital resilience; educational leadership;
   epistemic leadership; paradoxical leadership; reflective sensemaking
ID SENSEMAKING; MODEL
AB The growing presence of artificial intelligence in education does not merely introduce new tools; it fundamentally shifts the context that educational leadership must confront: the logic of information scarcity and coordination is replaced by interpretive overload and uncertainty regarding knowledge legitimation. The study argues that this shift makes the leadership of AI-mediated educational systems fundamentally epistemic and, as a result, structurally prone to paradox. Established (instructional, transformational, distributed) and technocratic models are insufficient to capture this condition on their own, as each assumes the stability of knowledge legitimation. By integrating paradox theory and epistemic leadership, the study identifies six structural leadership paradoxes, which are organized into three clusters (pedagogical, epistemic, and temporal-organizational). The common structural consequences of these paradoxes-interpretive overload, the compression of time for reflection, and increasing psychological strain-call for two focal, mutually dependent leadership capacities: reflective sensemaking as an epistemic operation, and digital resilience as its enabling condition. The study concludes that the focus of educational leadership in the AI era is shifting from technological control toward epistemic orientation, and it advances a set of testable propositions through which this claim-and the proposed framework as a whole-can be empirically examined.
