TI How to get students motivated in the classroom. A comparative study
   between the 2nd year of Basic Vocational Training and the 4th year of
   Compulsory Secondary Education in Spain
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE FPB; motivation; secondary school; self-regulated learning; teachers
AB Introduction Motivation is a key factor influencing academic performance and learning. This study aimed to identify differences in motivation levels between students in the fourth year of Compulsory Secondary Education (ESO) and the second year of Basic Vocational Education and Training (FPB), to propose guidelines to help teachers foster student motivation.Methods A cross-sectional design was employed with a final sample of 63 students (ages 15-17). Motivation was assessed using the MAPE-II questionnaire (Motivation towards Learning and Performance). Multivariate analyses of variance (MANOVA) were conducted to examine differences by school year and gender.Results Significant differences were found in the fear of failure dimension: girls scored higher than boys, and fourth-year ESO students scored higher than second-year FPB students. Additionally, ESO students showed higher scores on the high work capacity and performance scale, while FPB male students exhibited higher ambition levels.Discussion Differences may be explained by the distinct student profiles associated with each educational track and the academic demands placed on them. ESO students, oriented toward academic pathways, may experience greater pressure and fear of failure, whereas FPB students, closer to entering the labour market, display higher ambition. Based on these findings and previous literature, a set of guidelines is proposed to help teachers promote intrinsic motivation among students. Limitations include a small sample size and low reliability of some scales, suggesting caution in generalising results.

TI Emerging lessons about equity in funding, design, and goals for
   education research-practice partnerships in California
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE collaboration; community-engaged research; equity; funding; funders;
   research-practice partnership
ID UNIVERSITY
AB As research-practice partnerships (RPPs) in education expand to more geographic areas across the U.S. and internationally, the field has much to learn about how varied sociopolitical contexts influence RPP development and their pursuit of equity-centered goals and processes. We draw from a landscape study of RPPs in California, to highlight patterns and variation across a sample of RPPs in one state. Among a sample of RPPs receiving funding from national funders, we explore variation in RPP design and composition elements and their pursuit of equity-centered goals. TI Mind the gap: The role of workers' automation perceptions for the
   automation training gap
SO ECONOMICS OF EDUCATION REVIEW
LA English
DT Article
DE Human capital investments; Training; Automation risk
ID TECHNOLOGY; FUTURE; IMPACT; TASKS; JOBS
AB Technological advancements in automation are transforming job tasks and skill demands, raising concerns about the adaptability of the workforce. While reskilling and upskilling are widely recommended for workers in highrisk occupations, empirical research consistently finds an "automation training gap": workers in occupations classified by experts as highly susceptible to automation participate in less training than workers in lower-risk occupations. Existing studies have primarily focused on employer-side explanations, but the role of workers' own perceptions has received less attention. Using representative survey data for the Dutch workforce matched to occupational OECD automation risk indicators, we examine whether self-assessed job automation risk is associated with training participation and helps explaining the automation training gap. Our findings show that workers who perceive high automation risk have a 7 percentage-point higher probability of participating in training. Moreover, the negative association between expert-assessed automation risk and training is significantly attenuated when workers perceive their own job to be at risk. We also find that lower rates of self-initiated training among workers who do not perceive automation risk contribute to the overall gap. These results suggest that worker perceptions play a critical role in human capital investment decisions under automation risk. Policies aimed at increasing awareness of task-based technological vulnerability may enhance training participation and help mitigate skill mismatches in the evolving labor market.

TI Selective school admissions and student achievement: Evidence from a
   policy reform in Chile
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL DEVELOPMENT
LA English
DT Article
DE Selective schools; Student selection; School effectiveness; Student
   achievement; Education policy reform; Chile
AB Whether selective school admissions generate genuine academic value added or whether observed achievement differences primarily reflect student selection remains contested. This paper examines this question using a nationwide reform in Chile that substantially restricted selective admissions to Bicentennial secondary schools after 2016. The reform provides an opportunity to compare cohorts admitted before and after selection was curtailed. I draw on linked administrative enrolment records and national achievement data (SIMCE) covering six student cohorts, three admitted before the reform and three after it, and estimate a pooled difference-indifferences model interacting Bicentennial status with a post-reform indicator, conditioning on prior Year 4 achievement and socioeconomic background. The main results are robust to school fixed effects, to corrections for non-random attrition, and to multilevel specifications. Before the reform, Bicentennial Schools enrolled more socioeconomically advantaged and higher-achieving students and displayed sizeable achievement gaps relative to other schools. Following the reform, the socioeconomic and academic composition of their student intake moved markedly closer to the system average. Consistent with this convergence, the estimated achievement advantage associated with attending a selective school declines sharply in the post-reform cohorts. Prior to the reform, the Bicentennial advantage was about 0.28 SD in reading and 0.39 SD in mathematics; as selection was restricted, it attenuated by roughly 0.15 SD in reading and 0.18 SD in mathematics. The residual post-reform advantage is concentrated in the one channel through which these schools can still select on academic grounds. Overall, the findings suggest that much of the previously observed performance advantage of selective schools reflected student sorting rather than superior instructional effectiveness.

TI Choosing vocational bachelor's programmes in China: Decision logics,
   information ecology, and criteria stabilisation
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL DEVELOPMENT
LA English
DT Article
DE Bounded rationality; Digital information environments; Educational
   inequality; Postsecondary choice; Vocational higher education
ID PROSPECTIVE STUDENTS; SOCIAL MEDIA; CHOICE
AB The expansion of vocational bachelor's education has opened new routes into higher education while also creating uncertainty about skill formation, credential legitimacy, and mobility. Focusing on China, this study examines how students enrolled in vocational bachelor's programmes retrospectively reconstruct how they chose these programmes within contested status hierarchies, high-stakes admissions, and platform-mediated information environments. Drawing on semi-structured interviews with 20 students from three public vocational universities and using two-cycle coding, the study identifies four decision logics: Calculated Pragmatists, SignalFollowing Safeguarders, Identity-Seeking Explorers, and Constrained Acceptors. These logics differ in how students assess credibility, stabilise criteria, manage risk, and justify their decisions. The article treats the mechanism as an analytic reconstruction of enrolled students' retrospective narratives rather than as direct observation of real-time decision-making. It argues that vocational higher education choice is a developmentally consequential process shaped by bounded rationality, unequal access to interpretable information, and stratified agency. By linking information ecology to criteria stabilisation and decision closure, it offers a framework for understanding student choice in newly institutionalised and socially contested higher education pathways.

TI Impact of climate change on eco-distress and academic performance of
   high school students in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Pakistan
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
DE Eco-distress; Eco-anxiety; Eco-grief; Eco-guilt; Self-reported academic
   performance; Climate change; Climate vulnerability
ID YOUNG-PEOPLE
AB Climate change has emerged as a significant psychosocial stressor for adolescents, particularly in climate-vulnerable regions of Pakistan. This study assessed the prevalence of eco-distress and examined its association with academic outcomes among climate change exposed (CCE) and non-exposed (NE) high school students in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. A cross-sectional study was conducted among 1260 students in grades 8-10 from public and private schools in Abbottabad, Haripur, Swat, and Chitral using multistage cluster sampling. Standardized self-report scales measured eco-anxiety (22 items), eco-grief (6 items), eco-guilt (11 items), and Self-reported academic performance (8 items). Overall, 76.7% resided in climate-vulnerable areas and 60.3% reported disaster exposure. Moderate-to-high eco-distress was highly prevalent (eco-anxiety 98.5%, eco-grief 97.3%, eco-guilt 95.5%). Mediation analyses indicated partial indirect effects via eco-distress, and eco-anxiety significantly moderated the climate media Self-reported academic performance relationship. CCE is associated with elevated eco-distress and reduced Self-reported academic performance among adolescents. Integrating school-based climate resilience and mental health support strategies is essential to mitigate psychological burden and protect educational outcomes.

TI Short-term knowledge gains and learner satisfaction after a basic
   radiology course for family medicine residents in a 3-dimensional
   virtual environment: a multi-cohort pretest-posttest study in Spain
SO JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL EVALUATION FOR HEALTH PROFESSIONS
LA English
DT Article
DE Family practice; Internship and residency; Radiology education; Computer
   simulation; Educational measurement; Spain
AB Purpose: This study aimed to evaluate a structured basic radiology course for Family Medicine residents delivered in a 3-dimensional (3D) virtual environment (Second Life). We hypothesized that participation would be associated with higher post-course knowledge test scores and high learner satisfaction. Methods: A quasi-experimental multi-cohort pretest-posttest study was conducted across 3 consecutive cohorts of Family Medicine residents in Spain in 2019. Ninety-six participants engaged in a 15-day course combining synchronous and asynchronous activities. Sixty-five participants provided paired pre-and post-intervention knowledge assessments, which were analyzed using paired t-tests. Learner satisfaction was evaluated using a structured questionnaire with Likert-scale items, numerical ratings (0-10), and open-ended responses. Content relevance, usefulness for clinical practice, and instructor performance received the highest ratings. Lower scores were observed for peer interaction and platform usability. Conclusion: A structured radiology course delivered in a 3D virtual environment was associated with higher immediate post-course knowledge test scores and high learner satisfaction among Family Medicine residents. The findings support the feasibility of repeated course delivery, although controlled studies are warranted.

TI Social, emotional, and behavioral skills as resources for student
   engagement: A one-year longitudinal study in high school students
SO LEARNING AND INDIVIDUAL DIFFERENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE Soft skills; Life skills; 21st century skills; Student engagement; High
   school
ID FIT INDEXES
AB Social, emotional, and behavioral (SEB) skills refer to capacities that support social relationships, emotion regulation, and engagement with new experiences. These skills are considered crucial for high school students' academic success and well-being. The present study examined the longitudinal associations between five SEB skill domains (self-management, social engagement, cooperation, innovation, and emotional resilience) and four dimensions of student engagement (affective, behavioral, cognitive, and agentic). A sample of 1555 Italian high school students completed self-report measures of SEB skills and engagement at the beginning (T1), middle (T2), and end (T3) of the academic year. Latent change score modelling showed that student engagement generally declined across the school year, particularly between T1 and T2. However, students with higher levels of selfmanagement, innovation, and social engagement at T1 showed smaller declines in engagement. Overall, these findings suggest that SEB skills help students sustain engagement, especially during the first part of the school year. Educational relevance statement: Social, emotional, and behavioral (SEB) skills are increasingly recognized as key competencies that foster student engagement in learning and academic activities. Using a comprehensive SEB framework and a three-wave longitudinal design, our study examined whether SEB skills contribute to the maintenance of engagement across the school year. Results indicated that students who reported higher levels of self-management, innovation, and social engagement also experienced smaller decreases in engagement, although the effects varied across engagement dimensions. Overall, these findings highlight the educational value of integrating SEB skills instruction into school curricula. Strengthening these skills may help students sustain engagement throughout the academic year, with potential benefits for academic achievement and wellbeing.

TI Achievement goals shape emotion regulation during goal pursuit
SO LEARNING AND INSTRUCTION
LA English
DT Article
DE Achievement goals; Emotion regulation; Goal pursuit; Mastery-approach
   goals; Performance-approach goals
ID STUDENT MOTIVATION; HIERARCHICAL MODEL; PERSONAL GOALS; MASTERY GOALS;
   SELF-REPORT; PERFORMANCE; CLASSROOM; ADOLESCENCE; MINDFULNESS;
   EXPERIENCE
AB Background: Achievement goals are relatively high-order goals that shape how students pursue daily academic goals. When facing setbacks, students use emotion regulation strategies to cope. We extended achievement goal theory to examine whether distinct emotion regulation strategies underlie the links between mastery-approach and performance-approach goals and daily goal pursuit outcomes. Aims: We hypothesized mastery-approach goals would predict volitional emotional exploration (emotional integration), whereas performance-approach goals would predict rumination. Emotional integration and rumination, in turn, were expected to differentially predict daily goal outcomes. Sample: Sample 1 comprised 366 U.S. undergraduates. Sample 2 comprised 187 Israeli undergraduates. Sample 3 comprised 102 Israeli high school students. Methods: We conducted three correlational intensive longitudinal studies: a 10-day diary study (Sample 1), an experience sampling study (Sample 2), and a 7-day diary study (Sample 3). These designs and samples allowed examination of both day-level and real-time momentary reports of emotion regulation processes within different educational and developmental contexts. Students reported achievement goals, emotion regulation strategies, and goal outcomes (progress, effort, depressed mood). Mediation hypotheses were tested using multilevel structural equation modeling (MSEM). Results: Across studies, mastery-approach goals predicted emotional integration, whereas performance-approach goals were associated with rumination (with one study also showing links to integration). In turn, emotion regulation strategies differentially predicted goal outcomes. Conclusions: Motivational and emotion regulation processes are tightly interconnected. These findings suggest that interventions aimed at promoting mastery-approach goals should also incorporate emotional integration as a strategy for coping with academic setbacks.

AB Background: Sign language is vital for the deaf or hard-of-hearing (D/HH) community, but traditional learning methods (books, videos, face-to-face classes) often lack interactivity, feedback, and cultural immersion. The metaverse provides a cost-effective, interactive alternative for sign language education, where learners interact via digital avatars. Aims: This study compares metaverse-based learning with traditional face-to-face instruction for sign language education, focusing on learning outcomes and motivation among secondary and university students. Sample(s): The study involved 66 hearing students with no prior sign language experience, individually and randomly assigned to either a traditional face-to-face (n = 35) or metaverse-based learning group (n = 31). Methods: Sign language classes followed a four-stage curriculum, using identical materials in both groups. Non-parametric Mann-Whitney U tests analyzed differences due to small sample size. Results: Traditional methods yielded significantly higher scores in word memory, expressive, receptive, grammar, and sign accuracy tests, while no significant difference was found for interactive signing fluency. Conclusions: While the metaverse boosts motivation through immersive engagement, traditional methods remain superior for learning outcomes. Future research should refine metaverse-based instruction to bridge this gap.

TI Parental argumentative strategies during parent-child homework
   interactions in China: A pragma-dialectical perspective
SO LEARNING CULTURE AND SOCIAL INTERACTION
LA English
DT Article
DE Argumentative strategies; Parent-child interactions; Parental
   involvement; Pragma-dialectics; Strategic maneuvering
ID SELF-EFFICACY; SUPPORT
AB This study explores the argumentative strategies employed by Chinese parents to resolve differences of opinion with their children during homework, focusing on how these parents navigate the process of negotiation through strategic maneuvering, an essential notion in pragmadialectics. Within a corpus comprising 12 h of recordings of parent-child conversations during homework from 12 middle-class families in China, 117 argumentative sequences were identified for qualitative analysis. The findings indicate that the parents employed various types of arguments to negotiate divergent opinions with their children, including argument from authority, argument from analogy, conditional granting, appeal to learning habits and appeal to examples. Situated in the communicative activity type of parent-child homework interactions, the identified argumentative strategies can be understood as contextually shaped tendencies that align with parental autonomy support in contemporary educational psychology and Chinese educational values emphasizing discipline alongside individual engagement. By examining how argumentative strategies are employed by parents in a specific cultural context, this study provides both theoretical and practical insights into the dynamics of parent-child interactions.

TI Beyond class: Transnational mobility, raciolinguistic ideologies, and
   linguistic discrimination in US higher education
SO LINGUISTICS AND EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Linguistic discrimination; Linguistic racism; Transnational mobility;
   Raciolinguistic ideologies; Neo-racism; Higher education
ID LANGUAGE; PERCEPTIONS; RACISM; SPEAKING; RACE
AB In U.S. higher education, who is most exposed to linguistic discrimination, students from lower-class backgrounds, or students positioned as transnationally mobile? Drawing on raciolinguistic ideologies as the primary analytic lens and Bourdieusian linguistic capital theory as a competing prediction, we use a mixed-methods design combining logistic regression models with thematic analysis of open-text discrimination descriptions from 1434 students at a large U.S. public research university. Contrary to the Bourdieusian prediction, first-generation status, low income, and Pell Grant eligibility are imprecise predictors of both experienced and witnessed linguistic bias. International student status is instead the dominant predictor of experienced bias, while multilingual status is the strongest linguistic predictor of witnessed bias. The institutional settings where bias occurs differ by outcome. Social events are the primary site of experienced bias, while classrooms dominate for witnessed bias. Thematic analysis of 220 open-text responses reveals that accent mockery, differential treatment by authority figures, language-based social exclusion, and overt linguistic policing are the primary mechanisms through which linguistic discrimination operates, with Chinese/Mandarin-speaking and East Asian students most frequently identified as targets. These findings indicate that linguistic discrimination in U.S. higher education is structured by raciolinguistic ideologies targeting transnational mobility rather than by domestic class hierarchies; the operative axis of targeting differs across racial groups, with neo-racism best fitting the Asian-identified pattern and domestic raciolinguistic ideologies better fitting the Hispanic-identified pattern, where racial-categorical effects persist even with international student status controlled. TI AIlessphobia, AI-supported self-regulated learning, and academic
   self-efficacy in nursing students: A structural equation modeling
   approach
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence; AIlessphobia; Self-regulated learning; Academic
   self-efficacy; Nursing students
ID POWER ANALYSIS; SAMPLE-SIZE
AB Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) technologies are increasingly integrated into higher education and influence students' learning behaviors. Although AI tools can support learning processes, excessive reliance on them may lead to AIlessphobia, defined as anxiety about completing academic tasks without AI support. Understanding how this emerging psychological factor relates to students' self-regulated learning and academic selfefficacy is particularly important in nursing education. Aim: This study aimed to examine the relationships between AIlessphobia, AI-enhanced self-regulated learning, and academic self-efficacy among undergraduate nursing students. Design: A quantitative, descriptive, cross-sectional correlational design was employed. Setting: The study was conducted in two universities in T & uuml;rkiye. Participants: A total of 503 undergraduate nursing students participated in the study. Methods: Data were collected using a Demographic Information Form, the AIlessphobia in Education Scale (AILPES), the AI-Enhanced Self-Regulated Learning Scale (AI-SRL), and the Academic Nurses' Self-Efficacy Scale (ANSEs). Descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation analysis, confirmatory factor analysis, and structural equation modeling were conducted using SPSS and AMOS to test the hypothesized relationships among the variables. Results: Participants had a mean age of 20.88 +/- 2.61 years, and 66.20% were female. Structural equation modeling indicated that AIlessphobia had a statistically significant but practically negligible negative effect on academic self-efficacy ((3 = -0.049, f2 = 0.002), accounting for less than 1% of its variance. AIlessphobia did not significantly predict AI-enhanced self-regulated learning ((3 = 0.046, p = .089), and AI-enhanced self-regulated learning did not significantly influence academic self-efficacy ((3 = -0.008, p = .729). Model fit indices indicated an acceptable, although not ideal, model fit (chi 2/df = 3.899, RMSEA = 0.076, CFI = 0.936, TLI = 0.916). Conclusion: The findings suggest that AIlessphobia may be modestly associated with lower academic self-efficacy among nursing students; however, this relationship appears to have limited practical impact. AI-enhanced selfregulated learning did not mediate this relationship. These findings highlight the importance of promoting balanced AI use and supporting students' independent learning skills in nursing education.

TI Quiet quitting before entry into professional practice: An explanatory
   sequential mixed-methods study of senior nursing students
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Quiet quitting; Nursing students; Mixed-methods research; Professional
   commitment
ID INTERVIEWS; SATURATION; RESILIENCE; ENGAGEMENT; SUPPORT; NURSES
AB Background: Quiet quitting has increasingly been examined among healthcare professionals, yet little is known about how it manifests before entry into professional practice. Although nursing students experience substantial academic and clinical pressures, the extent of quiet quitting among them and the meanings underlying pronounced quiet quitting scores remain insufficiently understood. Objective: This study aimed to determine the level and distribution of quiet quitting among senior nursing students and to explore how students with high or very high quiet quitting scores experienced this phenomenon within academic, clinical, and professional contexts. Methods: An explanatory sequential mixed-methods design was used. Quantitatively, data were collected from 93 senior nursing students using the Quiet Quitting Scale. Quantitative data were analysed using descriptive statistics. Students scoring in the high and very high categories were purposively invited to the qualitative phase. Qualitatively, 16 students with "high" or "very high" quiet quitting levels participated in semi-structured indepth interviews. Interview data were analysed using thematic analysis. Findings: The mean quiet quitting score was 48.92 +/- 8.89, and 19.4% of students were in the high or very high score categories. Qualitatively, five main themes emerged: (1) meanings attributed to quiet quitting, (2) behavioral manifestations of quiet quitting, (3) quiet quitting: an internal conflict area, (4) triggers of quiet quitting, and (5) conditional and reversible nature of quiet quitting. Students in the high or very high score categories described emotional withdrawal, minimum-necessary participation, internal ethical conflict, and self-protective responses to academic and clinical pressures. Conclusions: Quiet quitting among nursing students emerged as a multidimensional phenomenon shaped by academic and clinical contexts, with a moderate level. Students with more pronounced scores described emotional withdrawal and minimum-necessary participation in response to hierarchical pressure, perceived injustice, excessive demands, and fear of violence. Supportive mentorship, fair educational practices, clear clinical roles, and psychologically safe learning environments may help address disengagement and support renewed participation.

TI Examining textbook effects in primary mathematics: The moderating role
   of teachers' professional knowledge
SO STUDIES IN EDUCATIONAL EVALUATION

DT Article

ID INSTRUCTIONAL QUALITY; SCHOOL STUDENTS; CLASSROOM; CURRICULUM; MODEL;

AB Mathematics textbooks are central resources in the classroom, yet research on their impact on student learning outcomes remains limited. This study analyzes textbook effects on grade 2 mathematics achievement and tests whether teachers' professional knowledge moderates these effects. Data from 1134 students nested within 63 classes using four widely used textbook series in Germany were analyzed using multilevel random intercept models, controlling for prior achievement and teaching quality. Results indicated significant differences in student achievement across textbooks, with some series yielding higher achievement than the reference textbook. Teachers' professional knowledge can moderate these effects: textbook effects were higher at lower levels of teachers' professional knowledge and diminished at higher knowledge levels for some textbooks. TI How does AI match students' proficiency levels to provide support?
   Student-driven AI-mediated scaffolding in EFL writing instruction
SO SYSTEM
LA English
DT Article
DE AI-Mediated scaffolding; Instruction model; English writing; EFL
   students; Improving classroom teaching
ID ENGAGEMENT
AB The emergence of artificial intelligence (AI) has brought innovative changes to language instruction by offering personalized and flexible educational opportunities. Although AI is widely recognized for delivering personalized feedback, its potential as a systematic, student-driven, mediated scaffolding tool that calibrates support to students' evolving writing needs remains underexplored. We therefore designed a student-driven AI-mediated scaffolding model (AI-MSM) for writing instruction and examined whether it was associated with gains in English as a foreign language (EFL) students' writing performance, engagement, and motivation. Forty Chinese EFL students were assigned to the experimental group and participated in a 10-session AI-MSM intervention, wherein they received implicit and explicit AI-mediated scaffolding to support their writing processes. Empirical data were collected through pre- and post-writing tests, engagement scales, motivation scales, and semi-structured interviews. The results of MANCOVA demonstrated that students in the AI-MSM condition showed greater gains in writing performance and engagement than those in the control group and exhibited preliminary trends in certain motivational dimensions under the present instructional arrangement. These findings suggest that AIMSM may hold potential for addressing persistent challenges, such as insufficient personalized feedback in EFL writing instruction, although its implications for motivation warrant further investigation. To further explore students' perspectives on AI-mediated scaffolding, we conducted semi-structured interviews, which revealed students' positive perceptions of AI's potential as a mediated scaffolding tool in EFL writing instruction. The study provides a theoretical framework and practical guidelines for optimizing AI-assisted writing instruction.

DT Article
DE Positive psychological resources; Latent transition analysis;
   Occupational satisfaction; Class teacher; Conservation of resources
   (COR) theory
ID JOB-SATISFACTION; WORK ENGAGEMENT; EMOTIONAL INTELLIGENCE;
   SELF-EFFICACY; CONSERVATION; EMPOWERMENT; LEADERSHIP; DEMANDS; IMPACT;
   PERFORMANCE
AB This longitudinal, person-centered study examined teachers' psychological capital, psychological empowerment, and work engagement using two-wave data from 650 primary and secondary school teachers collected one year apart.    Report of the 2025-2026 AACP Research and Graduate Affairs Committee
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PHARMACEUTICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
AB US colleges and schools of pharmacy face mounting challenges in sustaining robust research programs, supporting early-stage investigators, modernizing graduate education, and integrating emerging technologies into academic practice. TI Enhancing higher-order thinking in a pharmacy physiology course through
   game-based, collaborative instructional workshop
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Active learning; Game-based learning; Autonomic nervous system; Pharmacy
   education; Higher-order thinking
AB Active learning strategies are increasingly recognized for their role in improving long-term retention and higher-order thinking in health professions education. In this study, we evaluated the impact of replacing a traditional labeling lab with a team-based, game-oriented instructional workshop (IW) session on student learning in a first-year pharmacy physiology course, specifically focused on the autonomic nervous system (ANS). The intervention was grounded in three core physiological concepts: structure-function relationships, cell-cell communication, and interdependence. The 2-h IW session included pre-class assignments, individual and team readiness assessments (iRAT/tRAT), microlectures, a collaborative application exercise using a life-sized ANS diagram, and a debrief with a formative review game. Students worked in teams to match terms and functions to anatomical structures, reinforcing integrative learning. We compared summative assessment results and student feedback from three intervention cohorts (academic year [AY] 2019/20 to 2021/22) to control cohorts (AY 2015/16 to 2017/18) who received only traditional lecture and lab instruction. While overall exam scores were not significantly different, intervention cohorts performed significantly better on ANS-related questions requiring higher-order thinking. Student evaluations indicated strong support for the team-based format, citing improved understanding, engagement, and collaboration. This low-cost, scalable intervention demonstrates the value of integrating game-based, collaborative strategies into foundational science courses. It supports the development of both cognitive and professional competencies, offering a replicable model for enhancing active learning in pharmacy education and other health professions.

TI Examining Chinese University Students' Engagement Through Academic
   Self-Efficacy, Teacher-Student Rapport, and Flourishing: A PLS-SEM and
   fsQCA
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE academic self-efficacy; flourishing; fsQCA; higher education; PLS-SEM;
   student engagement; teacher-student rapport
AB Student engagement is an important indicator of learning quality in higher education, yet its personal, relational, and psychological mechanisms require further examination. Based on data from 469 Chinese undergraduate students, this study investigated the relationships among academic self-efficacy, teacher-student rapport, flourishing, and student engagement. Partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) was used to examine direct and indirect relationships, while fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) was used to identify configurations leading to high and low student engagement. The PLS-SEM results showed that academic self-efficacy, teacher-student rapport, and flourishing all positively predicted student engagement. Teacher-student rapport and flourishing also mediated the relationship between academic self-efficacy and student engagement, and the serial mediation pathway was significant. The fsQCA results showed that no single condition was necessary for high or low engagement. High engagement was produced by three configurations: academic self-efficacy with teacher-student rapport, academic self-efficacy with flourishing, and teacher-student rapport with flourishing. Low engagement was linked to the absence of flourishing or the combined absence of academic self-efficacy and teacher-student rapport. These findings suggest that improving student engagement requires more than strengthening individual motivation. Universities also need to build supportive learning environments that connect teacher-student relationships, academic support, and student well-being. This study shows how personal, relational, and well-being resources jointly support learning quality and student development in higher education.

TI Investigating student-tutor interpersonal interactions for enhanced
   teaching quality in a first-year undergraduate anatomy and physiology
   unit
SO LEARNING ENVIRONMENTS RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
DE Higher education; Interpersonal relationships; Psychological safety;
   Questionnaire on teacher interaction; Relational pedagogy and teaching
   practices; Student learning
ID ACHIEVEMENT; ENGAGEMENT
AB Teaching in higher education relies on effective communication and interpersonal skills to foster student engagement and learning, however, formal training in these areas is often limited. This descriptive mixed-methods study explored how students provide structured feedback on tutor interpersonal behaviour using the validated Questionnaire on Teacher Interaction (QTI), with the aim of informing professional development opportunities. Tutors and students from a first-year anatomy and physiology unit completed the QTI to examine descriptive patterns of aggregate profile overlap between tutor self-perceptions and student perceptions of teaching quality. Tutors rated themselves highly on leadership (M = 3.17), friendliness (M = 3.43), and understanding (M = 3.33). Student responses were generally positive across both cohorts. Both cohorts returned low mean scores on negative QTI dimensions; however, university students reported descriptively lower mean scores on uncertainty (M = 0.72), dissatisfaction (M = 0.68), admonishing (M = 0.68), and strictness (M = 1.96) relative to pre-university students (uncertainty M = 0.98, dissatisfaction M = 0.96, admonishing M = 1.05, strict M = 2.30) while university students reported slightly higher mean scores on helpfulness and friendliness (M = 3.28) and leadership (M = 3.30). Qualitative analysis of open-ended responses reinforced the importance of approachability, clarity of communication, engagement, and academic support in effective teaching. Greater aggregate profile overlap between tutor and student ratings was observed as a descriptive strength in pre-university teaching. Relational qualities were especially prominent in university student responses, which also returned lower mean scores on negative dimensions. Although tutor and student aggregate profiles did not overlap across all QTI dimensions, areas of agreement were observed between tutors and the pre-university cohort, pointing to potential opportunities for targeted professional development. Overall, findings demonstrate the value of the QTI as a reflective tool for professional development and highlight the importance of relational teaching practices in higher education.

TI Background music in chemistry laboratories: motivation and classroom
   learning environment among 12th-grade students
SO LEARNING ENVIRONMENTS RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
DE Background music; Chemistry education; Classroom learning environment;
   Laboratory learning; Motivation; Science education
AB This study examined whether low-volume instrumental background music can support 12th-grade students' motivation, perceived classroom learning environment, and laboratory engagement during chemistry experiments. The study used a school-based, pretest-posttest control group design with 60 chemistry students from two public high schools in northern Israel. One intact class completed a 6-week redox laboratory sequence with soft non-lyrical music, while a comparison class completed the same sequence without music. Students completed an adapted Science Motivation Questionnaire, an adapted What Is Happening In this Class? Learning environment questionnaire, and, in the music condition, a brief music impact survey. Adaptations aligned the instruments with Grade 12 laboratory chemistry and retained the constructs of motivation, student cohesiveness, teacher support, involvement, cooperation, equity, personal relevance, and material environment. Baseline analyses indicated no significant group differences in motivation or overall learning environment. Post-intervention analyses showed higher motivation in the music condition, M = 4.38, SD = 0.11, than in the control condition, M = 3.66, SD = 0.11, t(58) = 24.59, p < .001, d = 6.35. Students in the music condition also perceived a more positive learning environment, M = 4.76, SD = 0.13, than students in the control condition, M = 3.75, SD = 0.12, t(58) = 30.95, p < .001, d = 7.99. Descriptive survey findings indicated improved concentration, lower stress, and more comfortable peer collaboration. The findings suggest that carefully selected background music can function as a modest, low-cost support for laboratory climate when used with clear procedures, teacher guidance, and safe practical routines.

TI Allies or adversaries? A reflection on the relationship between case
   officers and parent/carers
SO SUPPORT FOR LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE EHCP; inclusion; parents; SEND reforms; special educational needs and
   disabilities
AB The relationship between Special Educational Needs and Disabilities (SEND) case officers and parents/carers is central to the effective implementation of inclusive education policy, yet it is often characterised by tension, mistrust and conflicting expectations. By critically reflecting on whether SEND case officers and parents/carers function as allies working towards shared outcomes for children and young people, or as adversaries positioned within structurally oppositional roles, we can begin to address the areas of tension. Drawing on practitioner reflection, policy analysis and existing literature on collaborative practice, power dynamics and advocacy within statutory assessment processes, we can explore how systemic pressures, such as resource constraints, legislative frameworks and accountability measures, shape interactions and perceptions on both sides. This critical discussion highlights the tensions illustrated in the literature and uses theoretical frameworks as a useful lens to understand the SEND case officer role. Reframing the relationship from compliance-driven negotiation to co-produced partnership is essential for improving outcomes for children and young people with SEND, particularly considering the Schools White Paper (2026) and the associated SEND reforms. This decade-long implementation process requires careful consideration of the role that SEND case officers play, and how they interact with parents/carers during the process.

TI The co-design of an educational launchpad for improving linguistic
   proficiency for students in French as a foreign language
SO ASIAN-PACIFIC JOURNAL OF SECOND AND FOREIGN LANGUAGE EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Co-design; Service design; Educational launchpad; Action research;
   French as a foreign language; Communicative competence; Learner agency
AB This mixed-methods, design-based study examined the co-design of an educational launchpad for supporting transferable linguistic proficiency among adult university-affiliated learners of French as a Foreign Language (FLE). Grounded in Service Design and operationalised through Action Research cycles, the intervention treated language learning as a service journey in which learners functioned as co-design partners rather than passive recipients of instruction. Fifty-eight Egyptian adult FLE learners (N = 58; CEFR A2-B1) participated in an eight-week implementation organised around Discovery, Define/Ideate, Develop/Prototype, and Deliver/Evaluate phases. Pretest-posttest outcomes were assessed using a 25-point French proficiency performance test (FLE-PP) and an 8-item Self-Perceived Communication Competence scale (SPCC). Participants showed higher posttest scores on both outcomes, with FLE-PP means increasing from 10.22 to 18.36 and SPCC means increasing from 2.20 to 4.13. Because the study used a one-group pretest-posttest design, these gains are interpreted as changes associated with the launchpad implementation rather than as definitive causal effects. The qualitative sub-corpus of 18 paired participant accounts, user stories, and workshop artifacts showed a movement from a perceived linguistic wall toward artifact-based agency, with participants using scripts, visual maps, simulators, and peer support to navigate institutional encounters. The integrated interpretation suggests that co-designed artifacts and socially validated rehearsal may help learners convert classroom knowledge into usable communicative resources, although replication with a comparison condition and stronger measurement evidence is required.

TI Digital Tool-Supported Problem-Based Assessment for Teaching Process
   Integration
SO COMPUTER APPLICATIONS IN ENGINEERING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE chemical engineering education; outcome-based assessment; PBL; process
   integration; reflective learning
ID STUDENTS; PERCEPTIONS; EDUCATION; DESIGN
AB Increasingly, problem-based learning (PBL) has been applied within chemical engineering courses to develop higher-order thinking and industry-level problem-solving skills; nevertheless, the quantitative evidence from PBL-based assessments incorporating digital reflective tools remains limited. The current study examines an outcomes-based PBL assessment strategy applied to a Final Year chemical process integration and intensification (CPII) module delivered to 44 third-level chemical engineering students. The assessment comprised three components of increasing cognitive complexity that evaluated Bloom's Levels 3 and 4 for assessing course outcomes (hereafter, CO) of CO1-Open-ended industrial case study, CO2-Numerical pinch analysis, and CO3-Flowsheet design and synthesis. It was found that students showed better performance on structured tasks (CO2: 56.1%) compared to design synthesis tasks (CO3: 39.1%) through quantitative analysis, which was supported by repeated measures ANOVA. Students had an overall pass rate of 84.09%. The evaluation conducted through a validated questionnaire (alpha = 0.849; KMO = 0.730) showed that the design of the assessment was consistent. One of the main contributions of this study is that it has included a phase of post-assessment self- and peer-reflection by using the open-source software called HINT (Heat Integration). The diagnostic capability of visual pinch analysis allowed 68% of the students to identify errors in their analysis or diagrams, while 56% reported improved confidence in interpreting HEN results.

TI A design blueprint for supporting voluntary retrieval practice during
   gaps in instruction
SO ETR&D-EDUCATIONAL TECHNOLOGY RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT
LA English
DT Article
DE Low-stakes learning; Voluntary engagement; Retrieval practice; Learning
   continuity; Mathematics education
ID FORMATIVE ASSESSMENT; CLASSROOM; KINDERGARTEN; ACHIEVEMENT; BENEFITS;
   ENHANCE; SCHOOLS; NUDGES; FORMS
AB School vacations disrupt learning continuity and often erode the momentum students need to stay engaged across time; more recently school closures due to the pandemic have produced similar outcomes. When students are not in school for an extended period, breaks in continuity and waning momentum often translate into irregular engagement with learning activities, allowing previously learned skills to grow rusty. The Keep in School Shape (KiSS) Program repurposes online survey software to provide students with convenient and engaging daily reminders and opportunities to maintain the math skills they need for their future studies via text message or email during times when school is not in session. This paper articulates the architectural logic of a low-stakes, voluntary review environment through a bounded design case and advances a set of transferable design commitments that can inform the design of similar interventions.

TI Contested Recognition: Schools' Binary-Gendered Institutional
   Architecture and the Erasure of Trans, Intersex and Nonbinary Students
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE educational justice; gender diversity; heteronormativity; intersex;
   nonbinary students; recognition; school; trans
AB Although legal recognition and visibility of gender diversity have increased in Germany since 2019, schools still enforce binary gender norms, which excludes or marginalises trans, intersex and non-binary (TIN) students. This article examines based on Grounded Theory analysis of interview data how gender diversity is simultaneously recognised and negated in everyday school practice in Germany: by (a) linguistic-discursive practices and norms, (b) epistemic-discursive content taught or omitted, (c) physical-symbolic organisation of facilities and PE, alongside (d) teachers' role. These dimensions mutually reinforce non-recognition, producing invisibility/hypervisibility, safety risks as well as reduced participation in education of TIN students. Finally, the article discusses necessary transformations required in schools to foster the inclusion of TIN students.

TI Predictors of Self-Regulated Learning in AI-Supported Language
   Education: A Social Cognitive Theory Perspective
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE AI-supported language learning; Chinese students; psychological network
   analysis; self-regulated learning; social cognitive theory
ID FLOW
AB Guided by Social Cognitive Theory, this study explored how language learning curiosity, perceived teacher support, and AI literacy predict learners' self-regulated learning (SRL) in AI-supported language education, with grit and flow as mediators. Data collected from 1022 Chinese undergraduate students were analysed using descriptive statistics, confirmatory factor analysis, structural equation modelling with bootstrapped mediation analysis, and psychological network analysis via SPSS, AMOS, and R. The results showed that all three antecedent variables were positively associated with grit and flow, which in turn significantly mediated their influences on self-regulated learning. Network analysis further revealed that self-regulated learning was the most pivotal node among the six constructs. These findings suggest that effective AI-supported language learning requires not only technological access, but also motivational, contextual, technological, and psychological resources to foster learners into agentic and self-regulated language learners.

TI Relations between parents' failure mindset, numeracy expectations, home
   numeracy activities, and young children's numeracy competence
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOLOGY OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Failure mindset; Numeracy expectations; Home numeracy activities;
   Numeracy competence; Parents
ID LITERACY; SKILLS; PERFORMANCE; ENVIRONMENT
AB Parents' mindsets play a critical role in children's academic achievement. Nonetheless, little is known about whether and how parents' failure mindset contributes to early numeracy development. This study therefore explored whether parents' failure mindset was associated with young children's numeracy competence through parents' numeracy expectations and home numeracy activities (including operational, mapping, and informal activities). Participants were 222 third-year kindergarteners in Hong Kong and their parents. The children individually completed various numeracy and cognitive tests, and their parents completed a questionnaire. Results of structural equation modeling showed that when children's gender, their verbal and visuospatial working memory, and parents' educational level were controlled, parents' failure mindset was directly positively associated with young children's numeracy competence. An indirect association, first through parents' numeracy expectations and then operational activities, was also found. Parents' numeracy expectations were positively associated with mapping and informal activities, but these two types of activities were not significantly correlated with young children's numeracy competence. These findings indicate that helping parents appreciate the educational value of failure and coaching them to initiate home numeracy activities conducive to children's numeracy learning is beneficial.

TI Systematic Review on Automatic Math Word Problem Generation and a
   Comprehensive Framework for Quality Evaluation
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF SCIENCE AND MATHEMATICS EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Automatic question generation; Evaluation framework; Mathematics word
   problem; Systematic literature review; Mathematics; Technology
ID VALIDATION; EDUCATION; DESIGN
AB Several methods in Natural Language Processing (NLP) have been developed to automate Mathematics Word Problem (MWP) generation. However, there are concerns regarding the practicality of the MWP for collaborative application and the suitability of the evaluation method for specific MWP generation tasks. Addressing this issue, we carried out a systematic literature review (SLR) of 315 peer-reviewed articles published in the past 10 years to identify the current state of research on MWP generation and the current evaluation method, then propose a comprehensive framework for evaluation with the inclusion of the socialization aspect. The findings revealed the current state of MWP generation research including the generation purpose, generation method with input and output information, publication trends, etc. This study also summarized current evaluation methods for MWP research and introduced a framework applicable to both individual and collaborative settings. As Artificial Intelligence (AI) in education research is continuously progressing, the findings of this SLR can provide a valuable reference for researchers, allowing them to generate more advanced and good quality MWP with different input information and conduct quality evaluation using our proposed framework. Furthermore, recommendations for future studies also provided valuable insights to uncover potential research opportunities enabled by AI and the Large Language Model (LLM).

TI Pre-Service Science Teachers' Judgment Accuracy Across Science
   Competencies: Evidence From a Digital Classroom Simulation
SO JOURNAL OF RESEARCH IN SCIENCE TEACHING
LA English
DT Article
DE biology teachers; digital classroom simulation; judgment accuracy;
   pre-service teachers; science competencies; teacher education
ID KNOWLEDGE; FOUNDATIONS; LITERACY
AB Science teachers' ability to accurately judge students' knowledge and skills is essential for successful teaching and, thus, highly relevant to science teacher education. Findings from studies focusing on language and mathematics have shown that (pre-service) teachers' judgment accuracy is not only subject-specific but may also vary across particular competencies within a subject. Science is a highly multifaceted domain. Therefore, the question arises as to whether (pre-service) science teachers' judgment accuracy is specific to particular science competencies. In the present study, we investigated the judgment accuracy of pre-service science teachers across two science competencies of the PISA 2025 Science Framework: "Explain phenomena scientifically" and "Research, evaluate and use scientific information for decision making and action." We assessed participants' judgment accuracy in these two competencies using two distinct modules of the digital classroom environment Simulated Classroom Biology (SCR Bio ). Further, we examined factors influencing their judgment accuracy using blockwise hierarchical regression analyses. For each science competency, 53 participants conducted a simulated lesson in the SCRBio and judged a total of 2831 virtual student answers. Participants' judgment accuracy was not significantly correlated across the two competencies examined, providing an initial indication that pre-service science teachers' judgment accuracy might be specific to particular science competencies. Based on our results, we suggest that judgment accuracy should be promoted separately for each competency; however, future research should further investigate the specificity of science teachers' judgment accuracy with larger sample sizes. In both SCRBio modules, participants' content knowledge related to the respective competency was a predictor of their judgment accuracy. Our simulation-based approach proved to be beneficial for controlling potential biases and examining the judgment accuracy of pre-service teachers. Moreover, the SCRBio enabled us to analyze both participants' evaluations of student answers during a simulated lesson and their judgments of virtual students' overall performance.

TI Modernizing How Students Compute Interval Estimates in Mathematical
   Statistics Courses
SO JOURNAL OF STATISTICS AND DATA SCIENCE EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Confidence intervals; Interval estimation; Mathematical statistics;
   Statistical inference; Undergraduate statistics curriculum
AB The calculation of confidence intervals is a fundamental aspect of statistical inference that undergraduate students are expected to master when taking calculus-based mathematical statistics courses. In this work, we describe an interval estimation framework that we present to statistics majors at Carnegie Mellon University, one that supersedes the traditionally taught pivotal method. When using this framework, which we dub "cdf inversion," students determine the cumulative distribution functions of interval-estimating statistics through any of a number of approaches, including analytic derivations, numerical simulations, and the bootstrap; importantly, these statistics need not be pivotal quantities. Given the cdf, students then derive interval bounds analytically (when possible) or by coding a numerical root-finding algorithm. We find that using cdf inversion offers numerous advantages: for instance, by removing the need for pivotal quantities, we greatly expand the space of interval-estimation problems that mathematical statistics students can solve, while at the same time making solutions easier to formulate. In addition, because it is possible for students to fully implement cdf inversion via code, we feel that elements of the cdf-inversion framework can, with proper scaffolding, be incorporated into introductory statistics and data science class settings.

   Development; SAS; R

AB This paper describes the implementation of oral exams, a more authentic and potentially more informative form of assessment than written exams, at a large scale (over 600 students), in the context of undergraduate introductory programming classes. TI Decision Milestones and Decision-Based Learning in a Canine Lab
   Exercise: How Students Decide
SO JOURNAL OF STATISTICS AND DATA SCIENCE EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Business analytics teaching; Decision-based learning; JMP; Laboratory
   exercise; Real data application
AB This paper introduces decision milestones, which are intermediate judgments students make during a lab paired with a written final justified decision, as a mechanism for making student reasoning visible in Decision-Based Learning. The lab was about evaluating evidence of cheating in voluntary submissions of dog agility run times and their video documentation. Comparing decision milestone selections with final decisions about cheating was used to partition students into concordance groups. Qualitative coding of written justifications revealed substantial variation within concordance groups in how students reached their conclusions. Cluster analysis identified six relatively clean reasoning patterns, four within the correct conclusion groups and two within the incorrect conclusion groups. The study (N = 78, three semesters, one undergraduate business analytics course taken after an initial statistics course) is descriptive; it does not measure learning outcomes or test whether the approach improves student performance. The patterns offer instructors a vocabulary for recognizing how students reason. It should be possible to add decision milestones to other DBL-based labs where a culminating judgment is reached through stages of analysis; the results suggest that the concordance patterns identified here can guide how instructors structure subsequent feedback and pedagogy.

TI Beyond the gaze violence, disappearance & the art of the feminine touch
SO REVIEW OF EDUCATION PEDAGOGY AND CULTURAL STUDIES
LA English
DT Article
DE Art; disappearance; beauty; the gaze; feminine touch
AB This essay addresses gendered violence and enforced disappearances in Mexico. Setting out the history of disappearance and the aesthetic challenges it presents, especially in terms of the relationship between tragedy and beauty, I look at the way color is integral to memories of absence, and the way art can allow us to see the shape of disappearance. TI How does a growth mindset predict K-12 student learning? A systematic
   literature review

DT Article

ID SELF-EFFICACY; ACADEMIC-ACHIEVEMENT; OUTCOMES; MOTIVATION; MEDIATION;

AB A growth mindset plays an important role in explaining student learning. In addition to learning outcomes, there are numerous variables (e.g. learning motivation, emotions and strategies) that can be predicted by a growth mindset. To better understand how the growth mindset works in the context of K-12 student learning, the authors synthesised all variables predicted by the growth mindset based on an analysis of 91 journal articles. TI Two Cheers for Physical Literacy: Reconsidering the Whiteheadian Account
   Through Radical Embodied Cognitive Science
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE physical education; embodiment; monism; radical enactivism; pedagogy;
   Margaret Whitehead
ID EDUCATION
AB Physical literacy has become influential across education, sport, health, and recreation. Yet the field contains multiple definitions and distinct traditions rather than a single agreed position. One especially influential strand is the Whiteheadian account, the philosophically oriented tradition associated with the British philosopher and physical educationalist Margaret Whitehead and extended through allied writers and institutional work. Whitehead did not invent the term physical literacy, which has a longer history, but she provided its most influential contemporary philosophical reconstruction and helped shape its current international meaning. The Whiteheadian account has been important because it rejects narrow mind-body separation and offers a holistic, lifespan-oriented account of movement, meaning, and human flourishing. The argument advanced here is that the Whiteheadian account is non-dualist in declaration but not always in operation. Its explicit commitment to monism and lived embodiment is not always matched by its practical grammar, in which bodily competence, bodily participation, and visible movement often carry more pedagogical and evaluative weight than minded engagement as a process of learning. Radical embodied cognitive science, especially radical enactivism, offers additional conceptual resources for developing a more explicitly relational account of learning and physical literacy because it begins with situated organism-environment engagement rather than with the later integration of bodily and mental domains. The article concludes by proposing a more relational, process-oriented, and pedagogically robust understanding of physical literacy.

TI Exploring Student-, Teacher-, and Classroom-Level Factors That Influence
   Attendance and Performance Gains in Adult Education Programs
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE student characteristics; teacher characteristics; attendance;
   educational gains; adult education
ID BASIC EDUCATION; LITERACY; PERSISTENCE
AB This study used archival data from 30,453 students enrolled in 289 adult education programs in the state of Georgia, United States during the 2018-2019 school year. We explored how student-, teacher-, and classroom-level factors predict student attendance and academic performance (reading, language, and math) over time. Results indicated several student-level factors predict attendance and educational performance, including age, gender, race/ethnicity, previous educational attainment, low-income status, special needs status, reported barriers to education, and dual enrollment. Teacher-level factors such as teacher experience predicted educational performance; classroom factors such as whether the course was an Integrated Education and Training (IET) class predicted attendance, and distance classes predicted attendance and performance. Certification predicted growth over time for language, and employment status and designation as a distance class predicted growth over time for math. These findings will help state officials improve the delivery of services to further enhance and improve student outcomes.

This study examined adult-child interactions in a dedicated digital play space located within a children's museum on a university campus. Thirty-six families with a child aged 2.5-5 years old attended 2-h digital playgroup sessions, during which continuous video and audio recordings captured dyadic exchanges. Using inductive analysis of 71 digital interaction episodes, we identified three interrelated themes that shaped how digital play unfolded: expertise, control, and pace. These themes influenced whether adults supported or constrained children's agency as they navigated digital and non-digital play materials. The findings show how adults' moment-to-moment decisions-including their own curiosity about the technology-can redirect, extend, or limit children's discoveries. Digital tools created distinctive opportunities for joint exploration but also introduced challenges to interactional richness when adult attention shifted toward the technology rather than the child. This paper offers an account of how digital play is co-constructed and highlights the importance of attuned adult participation in technology-inspired play.

TI Navigating Autonomy, Competence, and Relatedness in Blended Higher
   Education: A Qualitative Study of Digital Study Practices
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE autonomy; blended learning; competence; digital practices; digital
   strain; reflexive thematic analysis; relatedness; student well-being;
   technology mediated learning
ID ONLINE
AB Blended learning has become a structural feature of contemporary higher education, yet little is known about how students experience the digital study practices that shape their everyday learning rhythms. This qualitative study explores how students navigate autonomy, competence, and relatedness within digitally mediated blended environments. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 20 students enrolled in blended programs at a Belgian university. Using reflexive thematic analysis, four themes were identified: fostering flexibility without losing orientation, cultivating belonging in blended spaces, providing scaffolds to build competence and motivation, and navigating digital strain. Students valued the autonomy afforded by flexible study rhythms, yet this autonomy was fragile when digital structures were unclear or inconsistent. Belonging depended on visible instructor presence and intentional opportunities for interaction, while competence was shaped by clarity, coherence, and timely feedback across platforms. Digital strain accumulated through extended screen time, technical frictions, and blurred boundaries between study and personal life. These findings offer a situated understanding of how students experience technology-mediated learning as both enabling and demanding. The study highlights the importance of predictable digital routines, relational presence, and coherent design in supporting sustainable engagement in blended higher education.

TI From Illusion of Competence to Productive Uncertainty: A Longitudinal
   Mixed-Methods Study of Team-Based Learning in Anatomy Education
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE active learning; anatomy education; cognitive levels; flipped learning;
   learning outcomes; metacognition; perceived learning; veterinary
   education; team-based learning
ID STUDENT EVALUATION; TBL
AB Team-based learning (TBL) is increasingly being implemented in health sciences education to promote active learning and higher-order cognitive skills. However, the long-term effects of TBL on student performance and perceptions remain unclear. This study evaluated the impact of TBL on veterinary anatomy practical sessions over four academic years (2022/2023-2025/2026) using a longitudinal, mixed-methods design. Quantitative measures included performance across TBL components such as individual and team readiness tests, application exercises, formative assessments, and final scores. Cognitive level analysis was based on Bloom's taxonomy. Student perceptions were collected through Likert-scale surveys, and qualitative responses were analyzed thematically. The results showed consistently low individual readiness scores, indicating persistent challenges in pre-class preparation. However, team performance improved over time, highlighting the benefits of collaborative learning. Application exercise scores and overall performance increased over time, with notable improvements in higher-order cognitive skills compared to a traditional cohort. Students' perceptions evolved from initial resistance and perceived difficulty to more positive evaluations, with significant reductions in negative comparisons and metacognitive miscalibration, as well as increased positive perceptions. Overall, TBL supported progressive improvements in academic performance and cognitive development. Collaboration mitigated limitations in individual preparation, and student adaptation enhanced the effectiveness of this pedagogical approach in veterinary education.

TI The Relational Foundations of Teacher Resilience: Recognition and
   Professional Authority
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE teacher resilience; teacher recognition; teacher authority;
   self-determination theory; teacher well-being
ID SELF-DETERMINATION; EDUCATION; TRUST
AB Teacher resilience (TR) is essential for teacher well-being, professional commitment, and educational quality. Although recognition, authority, and resilience have received considerable scholarly attention, limited research has examined how recognition and professional authority interact to support TR. Guided by Self-Determination Theory (SDT), this exploratory qualitative study investigated these dynamics through semi-structured interviews with 12 purposively selected teachers (>= 3 years' teaching experience), 12 purposively selected Primary 4-6 students (aged 10-13), and 12 purposively selected parents from selected urban public primary schools in Kigali, Rwanda. Data were analyzed using thematic analysis. Findings suggest that TR is a relational process shaped by interactions among recognition, authority, and supportive professional relationships. Recognition was perceived to foster teachers' sense of relatedness through student success, parental trust, collaborative engagement, and collegial affirmation, while authority was associated with competence and autonomy through pedagogical expertise, fairness, and care. Based on these findings, the study proposes a preliminary SDT-informed interpretive framework in which recognition and authority function as interconnected relational resources that may support TR. By integrating recognition and authority into a single explanatory framework, this study contributes to TR scholarship and offers insights for strengthening teacher well-being and professional sustainability in resource-constrained and evolving educational contexts.

TI Knowing Is Not Enough: Perceived Familiarity with Generative AI, Support
   Needs, and Critical-Responsible Orientation Among Higher Education
   Students
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE perceived familiarity with GenAI; higher education; self-reported GenAI
   use; student support needs; critical-responsible orientation
AB Generative AI tools are spreading rapidly through higher education, yet relationships among students' perceived familiarity with GenAI, self-reported use, support needs, and critical-responsible orientation remain insufficiently understood. We surveyed 449 students from four Slovenian faculties of education and arts. Perceived familiarity with GenAI was measured using a single self-assessment item rather than a test of knowledge or competence. Critical-responsible orientation was operationalized as the importance students assigned to nine ethical and societal issues; it did not measure observed responsible behavior. Perceived familiarity with GenAI was positively but modestly associated with the frequency, breadth, and diversity of self-reported learning-related GenAI use. Descriptively, students with lower perceived familiarity reported greater support needs across all five areas, while responsible-use guidance was widely requested in both groups. These findings distinguish perceived familiarity with GenAI, self-reported use, support needs, and critical-responsible orientation as related but non-equivalent dimensions of GenAI readiness. Higher education institutions should provide curriculum-based support that combines practical GenAI skills with critical evaluation and attention to responsible use.

TI Beyond Admissions and Financial Aid: Demystifying the College-Going
   Process for Latine Students Through Relational Engagement
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE college access; Latine college students; college access program;
   relational engagement; hidden curriculum
ID HIDDEN CURRICULUM; ACCESS; SCHOOL; IMPACT
AB College access programs are well documented to build procedural knowledge of admissions and financial aid, yet less is known about how they demystify the hidden curriculum of college-going for Latine students. To address this gap, we examine a four-day college access immersion program for Latine high school students in North Carolina. Guided by a relational engagement framework, we analyzed 205 open-ended survey responses from 96 Latine high school juniors and seniors, collected through the program's anonymous daily evaluations, using a two-cycle iterative coding approach. The study extends relational engagement theory by demonstrating how culturally sustaining programmatic networks render implicit institutional knowledge visible and accessible. Implications for research and culturally responsive practice are discussed.

TI Student-level affective learning analytics to support programme outcome
   evaluation in chemical engineering education
SO EDUCATION FOR CHEMICAL ENGINEERS
LA English
DT Article
DE Affective learning analytics; Student-level assessment; Programme
   outcomes; Outcome-based education; Accreditation-aligned assessment;
   Chemical engineering education
ID RUBRICS
AB Accreditation frameworks governing engineering programmes require credible evidence that graduates attain affective programme outcomes such as ethical responsibility, societal awareness, teamwork, leadership, and lifelong learning. In practice, these outcomes are frequently assessed using episodic surveys or indirect indicators, producing coarse, cohort-level evidence that limits early identification of affective disengagement and weakens programme-level improvement. This study evaluates a learning-analytics-based approach for the continuous, student-level assessment of affective programme outcomes in undergraduate engineering programmes aligned with chemical engineering accreditation standards. An Affective Learning Analytics (ALA) approach was implemented that integrates daily micro-assessments, event-based e-rubrics, structured e-portfolios, and multi-stakeholder feedback to capture longitudinal affective evidence mapped to societal responsibility (PO6), ethics (PO7), and lifelong learning (PO11). Unlike conventional methods, the approach enables cohortwide data capture while preserving individual affective trajectories across academic semesters. Application of the ALA approach across multiple semesters consistently produced lower affective attainment values than those generated by traditional programme-level assessment methods, indicating reduced attainment inflation and improved measurement sensitivity. Longitudinal analytics further enabled identification of sustained affective risk patterns at the student level, supporting timely mentoring and engagement interventions, as reflected in participation and behavioural indicators. Rather than signalling diminished student capability, the observed reduction in attainment highlights limitations of episodic affective assessment and demonstrates the value of continuous, student-level analytics for accreditation-aligned evaluation in engineering education.

TI Quantity and quality of test-taking motivation: A person-centered study
   of test-taking motivation in a low-stakes mathematics assessment
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
DE Test-taking motivation; Cluster analysis; Self-determination theory;
   Test anxiety; Low-stakes mathematics assessment
ID SELF-DETERMINATION THEORY; TEST ANXIETY; EXTRINSIC MOTIVATIONS; EMERGING
   TRENDS; R PACKAGE; PROFILES; STUDENTS; SCHOOL; ACHIEVEMENT; PERFORMANCE
AB Test-taking motivation attracts attention in educational research, as large-scale assessment results reflect students' skill and will. While previous research has mainly focused on the amount of testtaking motivation, motivational quality has been less explored. This study examined motivational profiles among 5881 eight-grade students participating in a low-stakes central mathematics assessment in Flanders (Belgium) using hierarchical and k-means clustering. Four motivational profiles differing in amount (high vs. low) and type (autonomous vs. controlled) were identified. Compared to boys, girls were underrepresented in the low-motivated profile and overrepresented in the controlled profile. Moreover, students reporting higher autonomous motivation for mathematics as a subject were more likely to approach the mathematics assessment out of interest and perceived personal value. Test-taking motivation was significantly associated with test anxiety and, to a lesser extent, with test results, whilst controlling for gender, socio-economic status, educational track and domain-specific mathematics motivation. Autonomously and lowmotivated test-takers reported the lowest levels of test anxiety. Controlled and highly motivated test takers reported the highest, which is not conductive given the negative association between test anxiety and mathematics test results. Overall, this study highlights the importance of considering the quality of test takers' motivation, above and beyond its quantity. Moreover, the findings suggest that students who report greater interest in and valuing of mathematics also tend to report lower levels of test anxiety and more autonomous forms of test-taking motivation highlighting its potential relevance for educational practice and policy.
