DT Article
DE Undergraduate nursing students; Academic success; Polytechnic
   institutions; Nursing education; Grounded theory; Qualitative research
ID STUDENTS; KNOWLEDGE
AB Background: Academic success for nursing students has traditionally focused on metrics like grade point averages and exam performance but fails to reflect key abilities such as clinical reasoning, ethical decision-making, and the effective transfer of knowledge to practice. Additionally, there is a paucity of literature investigating academic success in undergraduate nursing education within polytechnic institutions, despite their growing role in nursing education. Aim: The objective of this study was to explore the processes and strategies undergraduate nursing students in Canadian polytechnic institutions use to achieve academic success. Conclusions: The findings revealed key phases of navigation, offering a dynamic, student-centered framework that illuminates students' evolving challenges and adaptive strategies throughout their educational journey. The framework can be used to guide research, practice, and educational reform to strengthen the nursing workforce through responsive, inclusive approaches.

TI Enhancing students' mathematics achievement through teacher professional
   development on peer- and self-assessment: A randomized controlled trial
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Formative peer; and self-assessment; Professional development program;
   Mathematics education; Primary school; Randomized controlled trial
ID FORMATIVE ASSESSMENT; STRATEGY FLEXIBILITY; KNOWLEDGE; EXPERTISE; IMPACT
AB This cluster-randomized trial examined whether a content-specific professional development program on formative peer- and self-assessment supports primary students' calculation strategy repertoire. Therefore, N = 96 Grade 4-5 teachers with their classes (N = 1525 students) were assigned to peer-assessment, self-assessment, or waitlist control conditions. The researcher-developed professional development program targeted teacher orchestration of peer- and self-assessment on multiplication and division strategies, grounded in formative assessment theory and mathematics-specific frameworks (e.g., Developing Mathematical Thinking). Results suggest that a concise, content-focused professional development can help teachers implement formative peer- and self-assessment in ways associated with a broader strategy repertoire in multiplication and division.

TI Cultivating Enduring Changes in Assessment Through a Life Sciences
   Community of Practice
SO BIOCHEMISTRY AND MOLECULAR BIOLOGY EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE assessment; community; peer learning; professional development;
   workshops
ID REFORM
AB To provide instructors with personally relevant, discipline-based training in assessment, the Community for the Assessment of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology Learning (CABL) conducted a series of six participant-centered workshops between July 2020 and January 2024. Key features of the workshops included emphasizing backward design, peer editing, and the use of participant-generated questions and rubrics as teaching tools. Five of the workshops focused on summative assessment and one on alternative assessment, with half offered virtually and the latter half delivered in person. In total, 110 unique scientist-educators participated. To investigate how effective these CABL workshops were in fostering changes in assessment attitudes and practices, attendees completed an Exit Survey at the end of each workshop and responded to a single Follow-Up Survey administered in the spring of 2024. Exit Survey responses indicated a high degree of satisfaction with the structure and content of the workshops and their immediate positive impact on knowledge about assessment. The Follow-Up Survey revealed lasting impacts: Sixty percent of respondents reported revising their overall approach to assessment, while nearly a third described specific actions they had taken to implement inclusive teaching practices. Focus Group participants noted that transformative change could occur through both adopting best practices and disseminating knowledge to their professional networks. Together, these findings suggest that the participant-centered CABL workshops catalyzed changes in assessment perspectives and self-reported practices among a substantive portion of attendees.

TI Muduligadia as an Eco-Village Experiment: Opportunities and Limits of
   Contextual Replication
SO CASE STUDIES IN THE ENVIRONMENT
LA English
DT Article
DE eco-village; community development; rural development; livelihood;
   shared resources
AB This case study examines the transformation of Muduligadia, a small forest-fringe village located near the Satkosia Tiger Reserve in Odisha, India, into the state's first officially recognized eco-village. In 2011, Muduligadia consisted of 27 households facing severe livelihood insecurity, seasonal flooding, low literacy levels, and high dependence on forest resources. By 2019, the village had grown to 35 households and developed a diversified local economy centered on eco-tourism, organic agriculture, waste management, and community-led environmental stewardship. Central to this transformation was the formation of the Eco-Development Committee, which functioned as a local governance institution facilitating collective action, conflict resolution, and coordination with government programs. Through initiatives such as LPG adoption, sanitation improvements, community-managed eco-tourism at the Satkosia Sand Resorts, and organic farming practices, Muduligadia reported reduced dependence on forest extraction while generating new income streams. Village committee records and media reports suggested that household incomes increased following the expansion of eco-tourism and related livelihood activities, while villagers and local reports associated improved sanitation and cleaner cooking fuel adoption with better household health conditions. Local accounts and village records also suggested modest reverse migration as some households returned following the emergence of new livelihood opportunities. Drawing on concepts from commons governance, institutional theory, and the sustainable livelihoods framework, this case analyzes the institutional mechanisms that enabled Muduligadia's transformation. It also critically examines the conditions under which elements of eco-village models may or may not be adapted across rural contexts. While Muduligadia demonstrates how community institutions can enable environmental stewardship and livelihood diversification, its success is shaped by context-specific factors including strong local leadership, small population size, and tourism potential. The case invites students and policymakers to examine how grassroots governance, state support, and local ecological conditions interact in shaping sustainable rural development.

TI Rethinking (curriculum) history: a conceptual framework
SO CURRICULUM PERSPECTIVES
LA English
DT Article
DE Curriculum history; Curriculum inquiry; Discourse; Temporality;

AB The role and significance of history in curriculum scholarship is a matter of increasing interest and debate. From a position where curriculum history seemed sometimes to be set in opposition to curriculum theory, it now seems to be increasingly accommodated within, in dialogue with, and even welcomed by, the contemporary field. TI The Impact of Writing Instruction for English Language Learners in the
   United States: A Meta-Analysis
SO EDUCATIONAL PSYCHOLOGY REVIEW
LA English
DT Article
DE English language learners; Writing; Meta-analysis
ID IMPLEMENTATION; INTERVENTION; BILINGUALISM; ATTITUDES; FIDELITY;
   STUDENTS; MODEL
AB Writing is a cornerstone of academic success, yet English language learners (ELL) in the United States must learn to write while also developing English proficiency. Although descriptive reviews suggest that writing instruction can benefit these learners, no prior meta-analysis has synthesized its effects quantitatively. This study addressed that gap by synthesizing 39 comparisons in 20 experimental and quasi-experimental investigations of writing interventions in K-12 classrooms with ELL students in the United States. From 122 effect sizes, the overall impact of writing instruction was statistically significant and positive (g = 0.33). Writing quality was the most frequently assessed outcome (in 33 comparisons across 16 studies) and showed an effect of 0.33. With regard to the most often implemented interventions, strategy instruction (g = 0.36) was statistically significant, while process writing (g = 0.51) yielded a meaningful but not statistically significant result. Moderator analyses found no significant variation by study quality indicators, participant characteristics, or intervention characteristics. Findings underscore the promise of writing interventions for English language learners in the United States and suggest directions for future research, including the importance of examining linguistic supports.

TI Dimensionality, Reliability, and Validity of Academic Resilience Scales:
   A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
SO EDUCATIONAL PSYCHOLOGY REVIEW
LA English
DT Article
DE Academic resilience; Reliability; Validity; Dimensionality
ID HETEROGENEITY; CONSTRUCT; BUOYANCY; EVERYDAY; STUDENTS
AB Academic resilience refers to students' capacity to maintain or regain adaptive academic functioning when confronted with academic stressors, setbacks, failure, or threat. Although the construct is often considered central to educational psychology, its psychometric foundations remain fragmented. This systematic review and meta-analysis synthesized evidence from 46 studies evaluating academic resilience and closely related academic buoyancy measures. Evidence on dimensionality was mixed. Unidimensional models showed higher pass rates for CFI, TLI, and SRMR, whereas multidimensional models showed a higher RMSEA pass rate; however, exploratory Welch comparisons showed significant differences for CFI and TLI, but not for RMSEA or SRMR, indicating that the available global-fit evidence does not clearly favor either model family. Pooled internal consistency was high, alpha/ = 0.89, 95% CI [0.86, 0.90], 95% PI [0.62, 0.97], although heterogeneity was substantial. Construct validity evidence showed a moderate pooled association with theoretically relevant external criteria, r = .55, 95% CI [0.46, 0.63], 95% PI [-0.19, 0.89], with substantial variability across outcome domains. After direction alignment, associations were strongest for distress and vulnerability, learning strategy/self-regulation, and resilience-aligned constructs, and weakest for academic achievement. Overall, the findings suggest that current academic resilience measures are reliable and show theoretically coherent validity patterns. Dimensionality evidence indicates that many measures may be dominated by a broad general resilience factor, but the available global-fit comparisons do not establish whether proposed subdimensions provide differentiated explanatory, diagnostic, or predictive value beyond composite scores. Future research should further clarify construct boundaries, strengthen content-validity evidence, and directly compare competing measurement models.

TI How do university students feel about statistics?": Relationships among
   achievement goals, achievement emotions and learning outcomes
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOLOGY OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Achievement emotions; Achievement goals; Learning strategies; Statistics
   education; University
ID MATHEMATICS ANXIETY; MOTIVATION; PERFORMANCE; APPRAISALS; STRATEGIES;
   EXPERIENCE; MODEL
AB This study examined how university students' motivations and emotions shape their engagement and success in a social-science statistics course (N = 376). Drawing on Achievement Goal Theory and Control-Value Theory, we explored three types of goal orientations-mastery, performance-approach, and performance-avoidance-and their connections to achievement emotions, use of learning strategies (help-seeking, cognitive processing), and end-of-semester performance. Data were collected using the Patterns of Adaptive Learning Scales (PALS), the Achievement Emotion Scale (AES), and the Learning Strategies Questionnaire. Additionally, students' performance was measured using final semester exams. Findings revealed that students with mastery goals reported greater enjoyment before learning and more frequent use of strategic help-seeking and deep cognitive processing. In contrast, those with performance-avoidance goals experienced more negative emotions after studying and tended to avoid seeking help. Negative emotions emerging after learning were linked to lower performance, whereas positive anticipatory emotions supported engagement. Emotional responses also served as a pathway through which motivations influenced learning behaviors and outcomes. These results highlight the importance of fostering mastery-oriented goals and positive emotional experiences to support effective learning in statistics.

TI Working memory predicts the collaborative performance of young children
   during pair programming
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOLOGY OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Working memory; Collaborative performance; Pair programming; Young
   children
ID COGNITIVE LOAD THEORY; N-BACK TASK; COMPUTATIONAL THINKING;
   INDIVIDUAL-DIFFERENCES; EARLY-CHILDHOOD; ATTENTION; CAPACITY; VALIDITY;
   RELIABILITY; EXPLORATION
AB Recently, the widespread use of computers to support collaborative learning has introduced a new challenge for children, as they coordinate their cognitive resources to interact simultaneously with both the computer and their peers. However, there are lack of studies to investigate whether individual cognitive ability, such as working memory, can predict computer-supported collaborative performance in a group. This study examined whether children's working memory predicts collaborative performance during pair programming and whether children's working memory and collaborative performance predict learning outcomes. Participants were 115 children aged 6-10 years. Children's working memory capacity and coding ability were assessed, and they engaged in pair programming lessons. All lessons were recorded, and the videos were analyzed using the collaborative performance assessment framework, focusing on attentional states, emotional states, and interactive behaviors. The results indicated that children's working memory significantly predicted collaborative performance in a pair programming environment through its interaction with their mate's working memory, including task-related attention and joint attention. Specifically, for children with higher working memory capacity, being paired with a mate who also had a high working memory capacity was associated with higher levels of task-related attention and joint attention. In addition, children's individual working memory capacity significantly and positively predicted neutral emotions. Furthermore, task-related attention and peer observation behaviors during pair programming were linked to fewer debugging behaviors. These findings suggest that collaborative performance is influenced by the interaction between children's working memory capacity and their mate's working memory capacity. Additionally, collaborative performance observed during pair programming appears to have an impact on learning outcomes. Accordingly, the current study suggests that grouping children based on their working memory capacity is important for enhancing collaborative performance in computer-based collaborative learning contexts such as pair programming.

TI From Head Start to kindergarten: the role of formal cross-system
   agreements to support school transitions
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF CHILD CARE AND EDUCATION POLICY
LA English
DT Article
DE Transition to kindergarten; Head Start; Early childhood education;
   Memoranda of understanding; Policy documents; Formal agreements
ID MEMORANDA
AB In the United States, many children ages 3-5 are enrolled in preschool. Preschool occurs prior to kindergarten, which is the first year of free universal public school education, but is optional in all locales and often operates separately from the free public school education system. The federal government funds one comprehensive early education program that includes preschool programming-Head Start. Successful transitions from preschool into kindergarten can lay an important foundation for students' success in school. Indeed, legal federal requirements direct Head Start programs to coordinate and collaborate with local education agencies (LEAs) into which children will transition for school, including requirements to establish formal agreements-often called memoranda of understanding (MOUs)-to guide coordinated efforts to support children and their families. Despite these requirements, little research exists around their existence, use, and influences on young children's transitions. We examined the structure and content of a sample of 23 Head Start-LEA MOUs using content analysis. We found that kindergarten transitions were not the primary focus of the MOUs. However, when they were, some documents included detailed descriptions of partnerships across Head Start and LEAs to align expectations, resource allocations, and key activities. When MOUs explicitly mentioned kindergarten transitions, there were three federal priorities often noted: (1) creating cross-system communication channels; (2) developing family collaboration and involvement practices; and (3) transferring, sharing, and obtaining student records and data. Findings suggest that while few MOUs contain explicit references to kindergarten transitions, MOUs remain an important potential vehicle by which to establish greater collaboration between Head Start and LEAs and ensure young children experience effective transition practices through intentional planning and documentation.

ID SELF-EFFICACY; ENVIRONMENT
AB The integration of OBE principles into the Physical Chemistry curriculum signifies a shift from merely covering subject knowledge points to achieving multidimensional learning outcomes. TI Synergistic Effects of Collaboration and Problem Construction in
   Creative Problem-Solving: An Experimental Study Comparing Collaborative
   Work in Three-Person Groups With Individual Work
SO JOURNAL OF CREATIVE BEHAVIOR
LA English
DT Article
ID COGNITIVE STIMULATION; IDEA GENERATION; BEHAVIOR
AB This study examined whether the effects of problem construction on creative problem-solving differed between individuals and groups. A 2 (collaboration: individual vs. three-person group) & times; 2 (problem construction: present vs. absent) between-participants experiment was conducted on 175 university students who solved an ill-defined problem. We assessed creative outcomes (solution originality and usefulness) and process measures (fluency and flexibility of problem restatements and ideas). The results revealed that problem construction did not enhance the originality or usefulness of final solutions. However, this increased the number and diversity of generated ideas, particularly in groups. Groups engaging in problem construction produced more problem restatements than individuals. Furthermore, mediation analysis indicated that part of the group advantage in idea fluency was explained by their greater production of problem restatements. These findings suggest that problem construction in groups activates more diverse problem representations, which stimulate idea generation. Overall, collaboration and problem construction synergistically boosted idea productivity but did not improve the creativity of final solutions.

TI Optimizing Operational Cut Scores under Misclassification Costs and
   Retake Policies Using IRT-Based Conditional Uncertainty
SO JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL MEASUREMENT
LA English
DT Article
ID CLASSIFICATION ACCURACY; STANDARD ERRORS; CONSISTENCY; ABILITY
AB Cut scores are typically applied to observed or estimated scores that contain measurement error. Even if the criterion cut score itself were error free, error in examinee scores leads to false-negative and false-positive classifications. The relative costs of these classification errors may be asymmetric and may be further affected by retake policies that increase the probability of passing across repeated administrations. We propose a decision-theoretic procedure for selecting an operational cut score that minimizes a weighted expected misclassification loss while respecting the committee-designated criterion cut score. The method is formulated for item response theory (IRT) scales and accommodates one-, two-, or three-parameter models. Rather than relying on a single reliability-based standard error, we represent measurement error through the conditional sampling distribution of the proficiency estimator given true proficiency, approximated via parametric bootstrap. Expected false-negative and false-positive rates are obtained by Monte Carlo integration over a specified target proficiency distribution, and the optimal operational cut is found by numerical minimization over a feasible cut-score set. The key feature is that misclassification probabilities are computed from an approximation to the conditional sampling distribution of the proficiency estimator, rather than from a reliability-based approximation. An empirical illustration using a three-parameter logistic item response theory model fit to response data from a 36-item examination shows that the optimal operational cut increases as false positives are weighted more heavily and as the number of permitted administrations increases. The proposed approach provides a practical, model-based tool for aligning cut-score policy with explicit misclassification costs and retake rules.

TI Care Praxis-Driven STEM Design for Sustainable and Just Communities in
   Middle School
SO JOURNAL OF RESEARCH IN SCIENCE TEACHING
LA English
DT Article
DE care praxis; families/community-engaged STEM; justice; participatory
   critical design-based research; sense-making; STEM education
AB Despite the growing interest in incorporating care ethics into STEM education, these topics are rarely integrated into K-12 standards and pedagogical practice. We explore how care praxis, a political and ethical approach to STEM education, supports students' sense-making in addressing real-world problems throughout STEM design, merging social, environmental, and technical aspects. Care praxis highlights the iterative, reflective method of initiating action, acting as an ethical, political, humanistic, and justice-oriented mode of engagement with the world, thereby fostering sustainable communities. Drawing upon participatory critical design-based research and ethnographic methods, we collaborated with two teachers, students, and families from an urban middle school classroom to adapt and implement a STEM curriculum that focuses on engineering for sustainable communities. Our findings show how a care praxis in the context of a STEM unit focused on engineering for sustainable communities can support students in more expansive sense-making by enacting care-oriented, community-engaged engineering practices. The process was facilitated through four stages of caring within the design cycle: (1) caring-about social needs (identifying a problem), (2) taking-care by solidifying and prioritizing these needs (refining a problem in collaboration with community and determining criteria for solving a problem), (3) care-giving by designing solutions that connect social, environmental, and technical aspects (designing and iterating solutions), and (4) nested-care by expanding the design functionality to foster well-being and active participation in community building (integrating designs into everyday practice). We discuss how to enact the transformative potential of integrating a care praxis into middle school STEM education, thereby fostering a more contextual and ethical approach to design solutions. A care praxis approach bridges epistemologies and ontologies, creating a productive space for students to engage in sense-making around humanization and justice-oriented aspects of science and engineering.

AB Background We examined patient and visit trends in pediatric emergency department (ED) usage during the school year and summer breaks before, during, and after the COVID-19 pandemic.Methods We extracted data on mental health-related visits to the ED of an academic medical center from 2018 to 2023 among youth aged 5-18. TI Effects of the "highly adaptive testing design for PISA" on plausible
   value-based population estimates
SO LARGE-SCALE ASSESSMENTS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Computerized adaptive testing; PISA; Plausible values; International
   large-scale assessments; Item response theory
ID STUDENT; MODEL
AB Background The recently introduced highly adaptive testing (HAT) design allows for a transparent and straightforward construction of the testing design of the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA). It outperformed the multistage testing (MST) design used in PISA 2018 regarding test information and RMSE of individual ability estimates, but it is yet unknown whether it can also promote the estimation of population statistics which are used for reporting PISA results. The present paper thus examines the impact of HAT on plausible value-based estimates of population statistics (country means, standard deviations, proportions of students on proficiency levels) and the error variance components associated with these estimates.Methods The study involved simulating the PISA 2018 Reading assessment under both the MST design used in PISA 2018 and the HAT design across 18 OECD countries (N = 110,958 students), utilizing the publicly available assessment and background data, and the official PISA item pools for Reading, Mathematics, and Science. Data generation, item administration, and population modeling, including the drawing of the PVs, followed the official PISA 2018 procedures.Results The HAT design significantly reduced the mean imputation variance of the country-specific mean reading proficiency by 19%, compared to the MST design. With regard to the proportions on the proficiency levels, the HAT design led to significant reductions in the imputation variance (- 8 to - 13%) and the total error variance (up to - 9%) compared to the MST design. In most countries and on average, the proportions on the proficiency Levels V and VI were significantly smaller for the HAT design; this indicates an overestimation of these proportions with the MST design.Conclusions The HAT significantly increases the measurement precision of population statistics. Moreover, it seems to make a more nuanced categorizations of individuals into proficiency levels possible. These results on population level illustrate the importance of using the best possible design. This will become even more important if future PISA assessments utilize improved stratification schemes that reduce the sampling variance, as the influence of the design on the precision of the reported population statistics will increase.

TI Digital reading, analog foundations: reading literacy in the digital age
SO LARGE-SCALE ASSESSMENTS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE ePIRLS; PIRLS; Digital reading literacy; Digital self-efficacy; Process
   data
ID ONLINE; PERFORMANCE; TIME; ACHIEVEMENT; MOTIVATION; ENGAGEMENT; BEHAVIOR
AB Background Digital reading has become an essential component of contemporary literacy, yet questions remain about whether digital reading assessments measure a construct distinct from traditional paper-based reading. This study examined whether variance unique to ePIRLS reflects a distinct digital-reading construct or is better explained by student background, engagement, and familiarity with digital task demands.Methods Data were drawn from the linked PIRLS 2016 and ePIRLS 2016 assessments, administered to the same students on consecutive days in 16 participating countries and benchmarking entities. Survey-weighted hierarchical linear regression models were estimated using five plausible values for PIRLS informational reading and ePIRLS achievement. Models were specified sequentially to examine the additional contributions of student background characteristics, digital self-efficacy, and behavioral engagement indicators derived from ePIRLS process data, including pages visited, ad clicks, and task enjoyment. This stepwise approach was used to evaluate whether digital reading performance reflected primarily general reading ability or additional variance associated with digital engagement and familiarity.Results Paper-based reading ability accounted for the majority of variance in ePIRLS digital reading performance, explaining 60.4% of score variance in the pooled analysis. Student background factors contributed a small but significant increment in explained variance, while digital self-efficacy and behavioral engagement indicators added further modest improvements in model fit. Performance was positively associated with pages visited and task enjoyment and negatively associated with off-task ad clicks. While country-level variation existed, paper-based reading remained the dominant predictor across all systems, accounting for 46% to 72% of the variance.Conclusions The findings indicate that ePIRLS primarily reflects traditional reading literacy assessed in a digital environment rather than a substantively distinct digital-reading construct. Process data provided useful supplementary evidence by clarifying how engagement-related behaviors shaped performance. These results have implications for construct validation and for the interpretation of scores from large-scale digital reading assessments.

TI Pedagogical and contextual barriers to inquiry-based science education
   in Ghana: a multilevel analysis
SO LEARNING ENVIRONMENTS RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
DE Curriculum implementation; Ghana education; Inquiry-based science
   education; Multilevel analysis; Pedagogical reform; Self-efficacy;
   Teacher beliefs
ID BELIEFS
AB This study examines the persistent gap between inquiry-based science education policy and classroom practice in Ghana. It investigates how teacher-level and school-level factors are jointly associated with inquiry-oriented instruction. Specifically, it examines teachers' epistemic beliefs, self-efficacy for inquiry, and perceived instructional constraints alongside school-level resource availability and assessment pressure. Using cross-sectional survey data from 397 science teachers, drawn from an initial respondent pool of 412 and nested within 62 basic schools, the study applies multilevel structural equation modelling to test a mediated and moderated framework. Inquiry self-efficacy showed the largest direct teacher-level association with inquiry-based instructional practice. Epistemic beliefs were positively associated with both self-efficacy and instructional practice. The indirect association between epistemic beliefs and practice through self-efficacy was significant, while a residual direct association remained, indicating partial mediation. At the school level, resource availability strengthened the self-efficacy and practice association, whereas assessment pressure weakened the association between epistemic beliefs and practice. These findings show that inquiry enactment is related to the alignment between teachers' dispositions and the environments in which they work. The study contributes an integrated multilevel account of teacher cognition, motivation, and institutional conditions in a resource-constrained setting. It also extends learning environments research by showing how school contexts are associated with teacher-level processes. Given the cross-sectional design, all findings are interpreted as associations rather than causal effects. The results point to the need for reforms that develop teacher capacity while aligning resources, assessment expectations, and school support with inquiry-based pedagogy.

TI Enhancing science-related social cognitions: effects of an active
   learning science intervention with high school students
SO SOCIAL PSYCHOLOGY OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE STEM interventions; Minoritized groups; Educational climate; STEM
   education; STEM diversity; High school
ID SELF-EFFICACY; STEREOTYPE THREAT; AM I; STEM; IDENTITY; GENDER;
   PERFORMANCE; TECHNOLOGY; MATHEMATICS; EXPERIENCES
AB Educational environments play a critical role in shaping students' science-related social cognitions, such as identity, social belonging, and intentions to pursue science, which in turn influence future science pursuits and participation. However, traditional educational environments provide students from ethnic-racial underrepresented groups (URGs) in STEM with limited support in science, potentially undermining their science-related social cognitions. Active learning, which encourages student-driven learning activities and promote an inclusive learning culture, can be particularly beneficial to URG students' science-related social cognitions. The current research adopted a non-randomized quasi-experimental design to examine whether URG high school students' science-related social cognitions and ethnic-racial stereotypes changed after they participated in a four-week active learning-based geoscience education program. Overall, students who participated in the program showed higher levels of science-based social belonging and intentions to pursue science at the end of the program than at the start of the program. To further validate the program, we compared participants with two distinct comparison groups, one at the beginning and one at the end of the program. By the end of the program, intervention participants reported higher science identity, social belonging, self-efficacy, and intentions to pursue science than comparison participants. No differences emerged between intervention participants and comparison participants at the beginning of the program. The present research underscores the benefits of positive, inclusive educational climates in promoting science success among students from URGs in STEM, with implications for educational policies and programs aimed at improving STEM participation among URG adolescent students.

TI Student perspectives on workplace english: a qualitative study of
   language skills, psychological barriers, and employability training in
   Malaysia
SO ASIAN-PACIFIC JOURNAL OF SECOND AND FOREIGN LANGUAGE EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE English proficiency; Graduate employability; Communication anxiety;
   Higher education; Student perspectives
ID GAP; EXPECTATIONS; SPEAK
AB English proficiency is an important factor in graduate employability in Malaysia, yet perceived gaps between university training and workplace communication demands continue to affect professional readiness. While employer perspectives on these gaps are well documented, less is known about how students themselves conceptualise workplace English, interpret feedback, and navigate psychological barriers. This study addresses that gap through a qualitative exploration of 137 Malaysian graduates from diverse disciplines, using an open-ended survey to capture their experiences and recommendations. Thematic analysis suggested three interrelated perceived barriers. First, the Language Readiness Gap reflects a perceived misalignment between academic English instruction and authentic workplace communication needs, particularly in speaking and professional writing. Second, the Confidence Ceiling highlights students' reported anxiety, low self-efficacy, and hesitation in using English despite perceived language knowledge, pointing to psychological dimensions of employability. Third, the Feedback Disconnect illustrates how vague or non-actionable guidance from employers may undermine learning and reinforce uncertainty. Students consistently identified spoken English as the primary employability skill, supported by professional writing and listening, and recommended workplace simulations, interactive learning, and stronger academia-industry partnerships. Framed by Communicative Competence Theory, the study proposes an exploratory student-centred model of employability barriers with implications for curriculum reform, feedback practices, and policy development.

   Areas and Reflexive Governance
SO TRENDS IN HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE transdisciplinarity; institutionalization; reflexive governance;
   strategic areas; higher education
AB This article proposes a practice-informed institutional design framework for embedding transdisciplinarity (TD) as an operational orientation in higher education. TI Relationship Between High School Students' Perseverance and Depression:
   Serial Mediating Role of Study Stress and Problematic Social Media Use
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE perseverance; depression; study stress; problematic mobile social media
   use; serial mediation
ID ADOLESCENTS; SYMPTOMS
AB The current study employed a convenience sampling method and conducted a questionnaire survey among 1066 high school students from a regular high school in the Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, China. The study explored the relationship between perseverance and depression, as well as the serial mediating roles of study stress and problematic mobile social media use. The following questionnaires were administered: The Perseverance Scale, Study Stress Questionnaire for Middle School Students, Assessment Questionnaire of Problematic Mobile Social Media Usage, and Patient Health Questionnaire. Descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, and the bootstrap method were used to test the serial mediation effect. Results showed that 220 students might exhibit moderate or more severe depressive symptoms (potential prevalence = 20.64%). Significant correlations were observed among the variables and their dimensions. The results indicated perseverance was directly associated with depression. Study stress and problematic mobile social media use played serial mediating roles in the relationship between perseverance and depression. The current findings suggest that perseverance, study stress, and problematic social media use are important factors closely associated with depression risk among high school students. These findings provide potential intervention directions for future mental health promotion efforts in this population.

TI Mental Fluid Transformation: Thinking Beyond Mental Rigid and Non-Rigid
   Transformation
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE rotating tanks; oceanography; atmospheric science; mental models; event
   processing
ID ROTATION; ABILITIES
AB Building on previous work to understand mental transformation of solid objects, our work aims to contribute to theory on how individuals visualize fluid transformation. Working at the intersection of discipline-based research in fluid-Earth sciences (oceanography and atmospheric science) and cognitive science, we began by characterizing students' mental models of fluids in solid body rotation. Using a common pedagogical tool of oceanography and atmospheric science instructors-large water filled rotating tanks-we conducted semi-structured, interactive interviews in conjunction with demonstrations of solid body fluid rotation to elicit participants' sketched predictions and explanations of their reasoning. We used emergent coding to analyze the data and found that participants confidently predicted fluid behavior; however, their predictions were highly inaccurate, much to the participants' surprise. These results suggest that the behavior of rotating fluids is unintuitive, and that the mind adopts prior experiences with fluids to fill the gap. We suggest that a better understanding of how humans reason about fluids can inform the cognitive science of event processing and suggest that framing mental transformation using an event perspective may be a productive approach.

TI Preparing Future Social Educators for Artificial Intelligence: Perceived
   Use, Self-Reported Learning Competencies, and Professional Knowledge
   Requirements
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE artificial intelligence; AI readiness; Social Education; perceived AI
   use; self-reported learning competencies; professional knowledge
   requirements; higher education; mixed-methods research
AB Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming higher education, requiring universities to prepare graduates who can use these technologies critically, ethically, and responsibly. However, socially oriented professions remain comparatively underexplored. This study examined preparedness for AI-mediated professional practice among Social Education students through a convergent mixed-methods design integrating perceived AI use, self-reported learning competencies, and professional knowledge requirements. Participants were 49 undergraduate students enrolled in a Social Education degree programme. Quantitative data were collected using a single self-report item assessing perceived AI use and the abbreviated Basic Learning Competencies Scale (COMPES), while qualitative data were obtained through an open-ended question analysed using the Reinert method with IRAMUTEQ. The findings suggest that preparedness for AI-mediated practice may involve perceived AI use, self-reported learning competencies, ethical-professional judgement, and professional knowledge requirements. The study provides a preliminary integrative interpretation with implications for curriculum development in Social Education.

TI Faculty Perceptions of Power Distance, Value Cohesion, and Lived
   Experience in a Sino-British Joint Venture University
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE transnational higher education; Sino-British joint venture universities;
   power distance; faculty experiences; institutional hierarchy; China
ID TRANSNATIONAL HIGHER-EDUCATION; CULTURAL-DIFFERENCES; HOFSTEDES MODEL;
   ACADEMIC STAFF; CHINA; MANAGEMENT; POLICY; FORMS
AB Transnational Education (TNE) at the university level is commonly evaluated through visible pedagogical and institutional mechanisms, including quality assurance, curriculum alignment, and degree legitimacy. Less attention has been given to the socio-cultural conditions through which faculty experience power in Joint Venture Universities (JVUs). This article examines power distance as a lived institutional practice at an anonymised Sino-British JVU in mainland China, drawing on 32 semi-structured faculty interviews, as part of a wider paired-site qualitative study. The interview schedule was informed by Geert Hofstede's Cultural Compass. Interviews were analysed inductively, with Hofstede used experimentally as a sensitising analytical framework rather than as a measure of national culture. This article presents findings on the power distance dimension and identifies four organisational themes-authority, hierarchy, inequality, and networks-which are presented as finding-led groupings rather than formal sub-dimensions of Hofstede's power distance. Faculty described and perceived power as an everyday professional experience shaped by control over teaching, regulation, and institutional direction; chains of command and indirect disagreement; inequalities in voice, promotion, favouritism, funding, language, and gender; and informal networks affecting access, visibility, and professional boundaries. These accounts indicate that power is produced through the intersection of Chinese regulatory conditions, institutional centralisation, professional status, and informal relational norms. The article argues that greater attention to these relations is essential for understanding faculty voice, autonomy, and value cohesion in Sino-British TNE partnerships, and thus offers leadership recommendations towards strengthening cross-cultural value cohesion.

TI Invisible struggles: the reality of food insecurity among students at
   the University of the Western Cape
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE basic needs; food insecurity; food insecurity experience scale; higher
   education; South Africa; student success; student well-being
AB Food insecurity is a student-success, equity and well-being concern in South African higher education. At historically disadvantaged institutions, the issue is shaped by national patterns of inequality, the transition from school-based nutrition support to more fragmented post-school support, and the limits of using income or funding status alone as a proxy for basic needs. This study examines the prevalence and severity of food insecurity among students at the University of the Western Cape (UWC) and explores demographic and socio-economic patterns associated with vulnerability. An anonymous online census survey was administered to registered UWC students between March and September 2023. The survey combined demographic questions with the eight-item Food Insecurity Experience Scale (FIES). Responses were analysed descriptively and through Rasch-based FIES procedures to examine prevalence, item severity, residual correlations and comparability with the global reference scale. Among 655 valid FIES cases, 66% of respondents were classified as experiencing moderate or severe food insecurity; 49% were classified as severely food insecure. The item hierarchy indicated a progression from anxiety about food access and limited dietary variety to skipped meals, hunger and going a whole day without eating. Descriptive subgroup patterns showed higher mean food insecurity scores among students with no formal income and those relying on government grants, and higher mean scores among African and Coloured students than among Indian and White students. Here, 'Coloured' is capitalised and used in its specific South African context to denote a recognised population group and social identity, not in the derogatory sense the word may carry elsewhere. Food insecurity at UWC is not a marginal welfare issue but a basic-needs constraint on learning and participation. Institutional responses should therefore connect food relief, financial aid advising, psychosocial support, data-informed referral systems, and sustainable campus food initiatives, while recognising the structural limits of what a single university can resolve on its own.

TI ESCAPE: a mixed-methods pilot study of a movement-based learning circuit
   for earthquake safety education in kindergarten
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE earthquake safety education; educational feasibility; kindergarten;
   mixed methods; movement-based learning circuit; observed task completion
ID PHYSICAL-ACTIVITY; CHILDREN; PERSPECTIVE; DISASTERS
AB Introduction Indonesia's seismic exposure makes developmentally appropriate earthquake-safety education important in early childhood settings. This study examined the classroom implementation of ESCAPE, a movement-based learning circuit. Methods A mixed-methods pilot study was conducted with 45 children aged 5-6 years across three kindergartens in Pekanbaru, Indonesia. Completion of eight binary classroom tasks was recorded at the initial and final observation occasions. Because one final participant row could not be verified, the primary complete-case analysis included 44 children. Teacher and parent perspectives were also examined qualitatively. Results The median task-completion score increased from 4 [IQR 3-6] to 8 [IQR 7-8] on the 0-8 scale. The mean within-child increase was 2.98 tasks, t(43) = 10.27, p < 0.001, and the Wilcoxon signed-rank result was consistent with this pattern (W = 5.0, p < 0.001). Teachers described greater familiarity with the activity sequence and sustained engagement, while several parents reported discussion or re-enactment of selected activities at home. Discussion The findings support preliminary classroom feasibility and increased completion of practised tasks. They do not establish comprehensive earthquake preparedness, causal effectiveness, or technical safety certification.

TI Developing social values among future teachers: a practice-oriented
   approach in Kazakhstan
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE education; higher education; pedagogical formation; practical
   orientation; social values of future teachers
AB Introduction: Knowledge of the social values held by future teachers, and the capacity of higher education to shape these values constructively, is highly relevant in contemporary teacher education. Social values are understood here as a constellation of moral, civic, and professional qualities-including dignity, conscience, charity, kindness, honesty, civic responsibility, social engagement, love for children, and the capacity to work collaboratively-that teachers first internalize personally and subsequently transmit to their students. Methods: This quasi-experimental study evaluated a practice-oriented intervention, "Formation of Social Values of Future Teachers," implemented with second-year pre-service teachers in Kazakhstan. Pre- and post-intervention data were collected using an adaptation of B. S. Kruglov's "Value Orientations of the Personality" methodology (derived from M. Rokeach's Value Survey) in an experimental group (n = 27) and a control group (n = 28). Results: Aggregate-level non-parametric analysis (Mann-Whitney U) showed a statistically significant increase in rated values within the experimental group following the intervention (terminal values: p = .0004; instrumental values: p < .001), while the control group showed no significant change over the same period (p = .59 and p = .75, respectively). The two groups were not fully equivalent at baseline, and the post-intervention between-group comparison did not reach statistical significance at the aggregate level. Discussion: These findings are interpreted cautiously as suggestive, rather than conclusive, evidence that structured, practice-oriented coursework can support the development of social values among future teachers. Implications, limitations, and directions for further research are discussed.

TI Student engagement and performance in online assessments: evidence of
   ceiling effects and implications for adaptive assessment design
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE adaptive learning; behavioural engagement index; ceiling effect;
   computer science education; K-means clustering; online assessment; Saudi
   higher education; student engagement
ID MODEL
AB Introduction Online assessments often fail to differentiate student performance because scores compress near the maximum, a ceiling effect that can make a genuine engagement-performance relationship statistically invisible, whether or not one exists. This study demonstrates that risk.Methods Among undergraduate female computer science students at King Khalid University (KKU), Saudi Arabia (N = 242), just over half achieved perfect assessment scores, and no significant relationship between behavioural engagement and performance emerged across correlation, regression, or classification analysis.Results Cluster analysis, which does not depend on score variance in the same way, tells a different story: it reveals four distinct engagement-performance profiles, including a high-effort, low-performance group invisible to the correlational approach. TI Assessing the trustworthiness of experimental research in education-A
   reliability study with an adapted version of the EEF padlock tool
SO REVIEW OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE inter-rater reliability; risk of bias; systematic reviews;
   trustworthiness
ID GUIDELINE; RISK
AB Systematic reviews have become a widely used methodology in education. Understanding the extent to which rigorous, trustworthy research is included in the reviews is crucial to the dependability of conclusions drawn from this method. Here, the reliability of judgements of research trustworthiness was investigated using an adapted version of the Education Endowment Foundation's padlock security rating tool as a rubric; this being a tool designed specifically for appraising trustworthiness in educational research. Fifty research manuscripts using experimental or quasi-experimental designs were selected for review. Ten raters attended a training course on the application of the tool and independently rated the manuscripts. Moderate inter-rater reliability was found (ICC = 0.54) for the final ratings, meaning that a single rater would not produce dependable ratings. Generalisability Theory analyses showed that approximately half of the variance in ratings was due to the manuscripts and over a third was associated with the manuscript by rater interaction. A low proportion of the variance was due to systematic rater effects (0.08). Estimated dependability coefficients indicated that including four raters in a study would likely reach generalisability coefficient of 0.82. Score resolution methods would improve the reliability but were not part of this research since the aim was to investigate independent ratings. Many manuscripts received low trustworthiness ratings due to incomplete reporting. This study establishes the need for further methodological work to improve judgements of trustworthiness of research to underpin systematic review methodology.Context and implications Rationale for this study Systematic reviews rely on trustworthiness appraisal tools, yet it is unclear whether these tools produce consistent judgements across raters in education research. Why the new findings matter: Reliability was only moderate, indicating that single-rater judgements may not be dependable and may undermine conclusions in systematic reviews. Implications for systematic reviewers, authors of primary research, and journal editors: Systematic reviews should use multiple independent raters to improve reliability of trustworthiness appraisal. The authors of primary studies should adopt clearer, more complete reporting to reduce judgemental uncertainty. Journal editors should require duplicate trustworthiness appraisal in any systematic review they consider for publication and promote the use of reporting standards in reports of primary research, as both directly affect the credibility of evidence syntheses.

TI Effect of traditional versus video-assisted problem-based learning on
   pediatric nursing students' academic self-efficacy and self-directed
   learning: implications for pediatric patients care
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Pediatric Nursing; Problem-Based Learning (PBL); Academic Self-Efficacy;
   Self-Directed Learning Readiness
AB Background High-quality pediatric care depends on well-prepared nursing students. Innovative educational strategies, such as problem-based learning (PBL), have gained recognition for their potential to enhance students' self-efficacy and self-directed learning, which are essential for providing safe and effective care to children. Objective This study aims to compare the effects of traditional PBL versus video-assisted PBL on pediatric nursing students' academic self-efficacy and self-directed learning in order to explore their implications for pediatric patient care. Methods An experimental research study was conducted at the Faculty of Nursing, Benha University. A systematic random sample of 150 pediatric nursing students was utilized. Participants were evaluated using a structured interviewing questionnaire for knowledge, the Academic Self-Efficacy Scale, and the Self-Directed Learning Readiness Scale. The study compared experimental groups (Traditional PBL and Video-assisted PBL) against a control group. Results Following the intervention, significant improvements were observed in total knowledge, academic self-efficacy, and self-directed learning readiness among both experimental groups compared with the control group (P < 0.001). The video-assisted PBL group achieved the highest post-intervention mean scores in total knowledge (77.30 +/- 4.42), academic self-efficacy (72.16 +/- 6.18), and self-directed learning readiness (118.38 +/- 3.76), followed by the traditional PBL group (72.22 +/- 6.96, 67.70 +/- 7.78, and 113.84 +/- 11.72, respectively), whereas the control group demonstrated the lowest scores (59.98 +/- 12.89, 45.74 +/- 5.88, and 84.86 +/- 10.28, respectively). Post hoc analyses further confirmed that video-assisted PBL significantly outperformed traditional PBL and conventional teaching across all measured outcomes (P <= 0.001). Conclusion This study provides evidence that both traditional and video-assisted PBL are effective in improving students' learning outcomes. However, Video-assisted PBL is superior in enhancing knowledge, academic self-efficacy, and self-directed learning readiness, offering a more effective strategy for nursing education.Trial registration Not applicable.

TI Federated learning for privacy-preserving at-risk student prediction in
   health professional education: A multi-scenario evaluation of FedAvg and
   FedProx
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
LA English
DT Article
DE Federated learning; At-risk student prediction; Health professional
   education; Privacy-preserving machine learning; FedProx; SHAP
ID ANALYTICS; DROPOUT
AB Student attrition in health professional education (HPE) carries serious implications for institutional performance and healthcare workforce supply, yet cross-institutional prediction is impeded by privacy regulations that prevent raw data sharing. This study presents, to the best of the authors' knowledge, the first simulation-based evaluation of federated learning (FL) for privacy-preserving at-risk prediction in an HPE programme-discipline context, using the Open University Learning Analytics Dataset partitioned to simulate five programme-discipline clients as HPE analogues. A systematic search of Google Scholar, Scopus, and the ACM Digital Library (terms: "federated learning," "at-risk student prediction," "health professional education," "privacy-preserving learning analytics"; May 2026) identified no prior study combining these elements. Grounded in Tinto's Student Integration Model, LMS behavioural features were operationalised as integration proxies. FedAvg and FedProx were evaluated under logistic regression (LR) and MLP architectures across four scenarios: IID baseline, pedagogical heterogeneity, data quality variation, and temporal drift. Federated LR retained 99.3-99.9% of centralised performance across all scenarios (maximum gap: 0.64 pp AUC-PR), confirming a negligible privacy-utility trade-off. FedProx delivered no statistically significant advantage over FedAvg for LR in any scenario (AUC-PR differences of-0.03 to +0.19 pp, overlapping confidence intervals, Wilcoxon p > 0.05), but gained up to 6.40 pp AUC-PR for MLP under data quality heterogeneity, reducing training variance 40-fold - establishing proximal regularisation as a stability mechanism for non-linear architectures rather than a universal performance enhancement. Cross-semester evaluation showed no statistically significant temporal drift (Wilcoxon p = 0.32). SHAP attribution identified Active Days, Assessments Submitted, and Mean Assessment Score as globally dominant predictors; per-programme analysis revealed discipline-level differences in feature salience, informing targeted early intervention. Forum Interactions ranked last across all disciplines - diverging from Tinto's social integration predictions and attributed to HPE's reliance on clinical placements and in-person peer learning rather than asynchronous online forums.

TI Addressing Gender Disparity in Surgery: Rethinking A One-Size-Fits-All
   Approach to Immersive Endoscopy
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Female; Trainee; Immersive endoscopy; Ergonomics
ID CERTIFICATION; WOMEN
AB OBJECTIVE: Using the lenses of Maslow's hierarchy of needs, this study examined the experience of female surgical trainees in endoscopy training. It investigated the influence of ergonomics on learning in this setting and in particular, looked to assess whether immersive training is a viable method by which female surgical trainees can learn colonoscopy. DESIGN, SETTING AND PARTICIPANTS: Training Programme Directors (TPDs) across the UK were approached to seek gatekeeper access to female higher general surgical trainees. A total of 10 trainees were recruited and semi-structured interviews were carried out over video conferencing software to gain insight into their views on the topic. Interviews were recorded, transcribed and analyzed using the Braun and Clarke method of thematic analysis. RESULTS: The majority of female surgical trainees find the endoscope difficult to handle, straining to reach all the component parts and experiencing issues maneuvering the scope. This led some to feel frustrated and even "mentally defeated" over time. Several trainees reported a lack of awareness of ergonomics as an issue for women in endoscopy, with many themselves identifying that they thought their issues were a "me problem," rather than being a wider issue with the scope. There were a number of positives regarding immersive training, including the volume of scopes achieved, building confidence and nurturing a training environment. The majority still felt, however, that condensed training in the immersive setting could be physically and mentally demanding. CONCLUSION: There is a lack of acknowledgement and awareness of ergonomic issues in endoscopy for female surgical trainees. Immersive training may be of benefit to tackle some of the issues with access to endoscopy, but incorporating ergonomics and spaced learning need to be considered when planning its provision. TI Pedagogical infrastructure to support students' self-regulation in
   flipped learning: A learning diary with individualized learning goals
SO LEARNING CULTURE AND SOCIAL INTERACTION
LA English
DT Article
DE Flipped learning; Diversification; Individualized learning; Learning
   goal; Learning diary; Pedagogical infrastructure; Self-regulated
   learning; Teacher education
ID UNIVERSITY-STUDENTS; CLASSROOM; EDUCATION; PERFORMANCE; MOTIVATION
AB Large variations in the knowledge, skills, and interests of entry-level students are increasingly challenging higher education learning designs to support the individualization of learning experiences. To provide pedagogical infrastructure with space for individualization and capable of activating students to take accountability for their own learning, a flipped-learning environment to support students' self-regulative learning was designed. This study focuses on learning goals and students' use of a semi-structured learning diary-an important part of the pedagogical infrastructure. TI Structural alignment in conversation at different proficiency levels:
   evidence from native and second language speakers of Italian in
   task-based dialogues
SO SYSTEM
LA English
DT Article
DE Structural alignment; Interactive alignment; L2 dialogue; Proficiency;
   Task-based dialogue; Syntactic priming
ID EFL LEARNERS PRODUCTION; INTERACTIVE ALIGNMENT; LINGUISTIC ALIGNMENT;
   SYNTACTIC INFORMATION; LANGUAGE PRODUCTION; REPRESENTATION; FREQUENCY
AB This paper investigated structural alignment, defined as the tendency for speakers to reuse syntactic structures recently encountered in discourse, in dialogues between second language speakers of Italian at different proficiency levels. Dialogues between native speakers of Italian collected using the same Map Task are taken as a baseline for comparison. Results showed that both L1-L1 and L2-L2 dialogues exhibited structural alignment, adding to existing evidence of structural alignment in unscripted L2 communication. TI Enhancing Analytical Skills through Quantized-Text Activities in
   Chemical and Environmental Education
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Problem-Based Learning; Analytical Skills; Educational Technologies;
   Pedagogical Innovations; Academic Competence
AB This study presents a methodology for designing quantified text-based tasks for chemical and environmental disciplines aimed at enhancing analytical skills, improving academic performance, and facilitating the comprehension of educational material. The proposed methodology involved structuring tasks into quantized units, each representing a logically complete stage: familiarizing oneself with theoretical material, performing calculations, analyzing environmental consequences, and devising solutions. The methodology was tested on a sample of 140 students from Abai Kazakh National Pedagogical University (KazNPU) and Ualikhanov University, divided into experimental and control groups, as well as 7 lecturers who implemented the developed method. Feedback from lecturers and students also indicated a positive impact of the methodology on motivation and material perception. The results confirmed the effectiveness of the proposed approach in enhancing the educational process and developing professional competencies in the fields of chemistry and ecology.

TI Understanding beginning teacher turnover: The role of perceived
   preparedness
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Perceived preparedness; Alternative certification; Teacher turnover;
   Turnover intentions; Beginning teachers
ID ALTERNATIVELY CERTIFIED TEACHERS; JOB-SATISFACTION; RETENTION;
   INDUCTION; NOVICE; IMPACT; BARON
AB Alternative certification (AC) programs have emerged as a critical policy lever to address global teacher shortages. However, these pathways are associated with elevated early-career turnover. Drawing on three nationally representative datasets from the United States, this study examined the psychological mechanisms underlying this paradox. Results consistently indicated that AC teachers reported significantly lower perceived preparedness than traditionally prepared teachers, while the association between certification route and turnover intentions was non-significant. Mediation analysis revealed that certification route was indirectly associated with turnover intentions through initial perceived preparedness. TI From Simulation to Bedside: A Hybrid Rapid Cycle Deliberate
   Practice-Mastery Learning Curriculum for Serratus Anterior Plane Block
   Training
SO AEM EDUCATION AND TRAINING
LA English
DT Article
DE emergency medicine; regional anesthesia; serratus anterior plane block;
   simulation; ultrasound-guided procedures
AB Objectives The serratus anterior plane block (SAPB) is an effective ultrasound-guided regional anesthesia technique for anterolateral rib fracture pain. Formal SAPB training in emergency medicine remains limited, contributing to inconsistent adoption and procedural confidence. This study evaluated whether a simulation-based curriculum improves emergency physicians' confidence, knowledge, retention, and simulated procedural competency. Methods A prospective educational intervention was conducted at an urban academic center. Participants completed pre-and post-curriculum surveys assessing SAPB knowledge, procedural confidence, and barriers. Survey content was developed using a three-round Delphi process by emergency medicine ultrasound and simulation experts. The curriculum included didactic teaching and four simulation stations addressing consent, ultrasound-guided in-plane technique, anatomy, and SAPB performance using task trainers. Procedural competency was assessed using an ACEP-guidelines-based checklist. Pre-and post-curriculum outcomes were analyzed using paired t-tests (p < 0.05). Results Thirty-six physicians participated, including attendings (19.4%), fellows (8.3%), and residents (72.2%) distributed evenly across PGY1 to PGY4 levels. Two participants (5.6%) had prior ultrasound fellowship training and 5 (13.9%) had previously performed a SAPB. Self-reported confidence increased significantly following the curriculum (1.81 +/- 1.09 vs. 4.00 +/- 0.72; p < 0.001), as did willingness to perform the block (3.31 +/- 1.60 vs. 4.53 +/- 0.70; p < 0.001). All participants achieved simulated procedural competency and demonstrated improved knowledge scores following the curriculum (p < 0.001). Five clinical bedside SAPBs were performed during the first 6 months following training. Among 32 participants (88.9%) completing the 4-6-week follow-up, mean cumulative knowledge scores were 92.9% +/- 11.7 immediately after training and 90.9% +/- 10.3 at follow-up. Reported barriers to SAPB performance included time constraints, patient refusal, and limited availability of appropriate patients. Conclusions A simulation-based curriculum improved emergency physicians' self-reported confidence and knowledge regarding the SAPB, while supporting short-term stability of knowledge performance. These findings highlight the value of simulation as a scalable pathway to standardize ultrasound-guided regional anesthesia training and facilitate future evaluation of SAPB adoption in emergency medicine.

TI Incorporating instructor presence in a multimedia language learning
   context
SO INSTRUCTIONAL SCIENCE
LA English
DT Article
DE Multimedia learning; Instructor video; Video lectures; Instructional
   video; Computer-based learning; Eye-tracking
ID COGNITIVE LOAD; 2ND-LANGUAGE SPEECH; DESIGN; ATTENTION; VIDEO; TONES;
   PITCH
AB The present study investigated the effects of instructor presence in a multimedia learning situation where seeing the instructor was deemed relevant to the learning content and requirements, in this case a language learning setting. Fifty Japanese university students were asked to learn from two videos on the four Mandarin tones, one with the instructor video present and one without. While viewing the videos, participants' eye movements and skin conductance level were recorded, and measurements of learning performance and perceptions about learning were taken afterwards. Results showed no significant difference in overall learning performance when comparing the conditions with and without instructor presence, but learners indicated that they were more satisfied and perceived more learning when the instructor video was included. This suggests that instructor presence can influence learners' attention and perceived learning. However, in the present study, videos of instructors modeling tone production without providing other cues to tone production did not lead to measurable improvements in learning outcomes, even though learners attended to the instructor videos and perceived them as helpful. These findings indicate that instructor presence is unlikely to improve learning outcomes unless the instructor's visible behavior provides information learners can directly use for the task at hand. More broadly, the benefits of instructor presence may depend not only on the alignment between the information conveyed and the requirements of the learning task, but also on learners' ability to recognize and use that information effectively.

TI Between Force and Curvature: A Multimodal Analysis of Competing
   Conceptual Zones for Gravity in High School Students
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF SCIENCE AND MATHEMATICS EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Conceptual Profile; Gravity Conceptions; Gesture Analysis; Multimodal
   Analysis; Physics Education
ID SCIENTIFICALLY ACCEPTABLE CONCEPTIONS; SIMULATIONS
AB This study investigates how high school students simultaneously employ two modes of conceptualising gravity, force/attraction and curvature/geometry, when reasoning about gravitational phenomena. Drawing on the conceptual profile perspective, we examined how these modes coexist and distribute across different cognitive contexts and expressive modalities. Through multimodal analysis combining depictive gesture analysis, speech, drawings, and written responses, we investigated eight Brazilian Year-12 students who participated in a Special and General Relativity course. Data were collected from classroom discussions, written exercises, and individual interviews, enabling triangulation across spontaneous collaborative reasoning, deliberate written formulation, and retrospective individual explanation. Results reveal that (1) the two modes coexist actively within the same students rather than replacing one another; (2) their activation depends systematically on the type of cognitive demand, the geometric mode predominates in descriptive contexts while the force mode emerges in causal explanations; (3) pictorial modalities preferentially access the geometric mode even when speech accesses the force mode, producing multimodal discordances. These findings suggest that the conceptual transition from Newtonian to Einsteinian gravity involves a prolonged coexistence of conceptual zones rather than a substitution, and that multimodal analysis reveals aspects of students' conceptual repertoire that remain hidden in purely verbal analysis. Connections with the gesture-speech mismatch literature are discussed.

AB This paper presents a theoretical perspective of generative artificial intelligence (AI) as dialogic partner by extending Jonassen's notion of technology as partner through Bakhtin's dialogism and insights from science classroom discourse. TI Literacy Identity Construction, Negotiation, and Resistance Among Middle
   School Students of Color in Online Learning
SO JOURNAL OF ADOLESCENT & ADULT LITERACY

DT Article
DE adolescent development; literacy identity; middle school Students of
   Color; online learning; participation; recognition
ID QUALITATIVE RESEARCH
AB This qualitative multiple case study examines how middle school Students of Color construct, negotiate, and respond to literacy identities within classroom-based online learning contexts. Guided by racialized identity development in learning contexts, the study examines how access, participation, and recognition shaped students' experiences of competence and belonging during digital literacy instruction. Data were collected over 9 months at an urban middle school and included more than 300 h of classroom observations, semi-structured interviews with students, teachers, and parents, and digital artifacts from Google Docs, used for collaborative writing and peer feedback; Epic, a digital reading platform supporting teacher-assigned and student-selected texts; and Raz-Kids, a guided reading platform that supported oral reading, self-monitoring, and rereading. AB The question of how students navigate the transition from high school to college writing is of perennial concern to teachers and researchers of adolescent and adult literacy. This study contributes to this conversation through an in-depth analysis of the composing experiences that a group of eight, first-generation-to-college Latina students found most meaningful during their four years of high school and their first semesters of college. TI Teaching and Learning about Artificial Intelligence(AI) in Secondary
   Education Chemistry Classes
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Chemical Education Research; Secondary Education; Professional
   Development; Transfer; ArtificialIntelligence (AI)
ID MOTIVATION; RELEVANCE
AB Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming chemical research and practice, yet chemistry education has largely focused on students' use of generative AI tools rather than on understanding AI as a driver of modern chemistry. This mixed-methods study examined the feasibility of teaching "AI in chemistry" in secondary chemistry education (grades 10-13) and developed a practice-oriented model for future implementation and research. To this end, a 3-h professional development (PD) program for chemistry teachers and two 90-min lessons addressing AI applications in chemistry research, as well as associated benefits and risks, were designed and evaluated. Qualitative teacher surveys explored relevance, feasibility, and implementation. Student questionnaires assessed perceived importance of the topic, expectations that teachers address it, interest, attitudes toward AI in chemistry, and science-related AI competencies. Across both samples, prior knowledge of AI applications in chemistry was low but increased following the interventions. Teachers considered "AI in chemistry" highly relevant to the curriculum and emphasized the importance of classroom-ready examples for successful implementation. Students reported higher perceived importance of the topic, stronger expectations that teachers address it, and increased interest after instruction. Attitudes toward AI use in chemistry showed minor changes. In addition, students demonstrated improved ability to identify specific application areas of AI in chemistry. Overall, the findings indicate that instruction on "AI in chemistry" is feasible and educationally valuable. Effective implementation appears to benefit from focusing on tangible, real-world applications of AI in chemistry and from structured discussion of ethical risks, limitations, and trade-offs associated with its use.

TI A Solvothermal Approach for Synthesizing Pyrite (FeS2) in
   Undergraduate Inorganic Laboratories
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Upper-Division Undergraduate; Inorganic Chemistry; Laboratory
   Instruction; Collaborative; Cooperative Learning; X-ray Crystallography;
   Crystals; Crystallography
ID SULFUR
AB A new upper-level undergraduate laboratory experiment has been developed to synthesize pyrite using a solvothermal method in a pressure autoclave reactor, providing students with a safe and practical introduction to high-pressure synthesis techniques. Pyrite (FeS2) is an important mineral with applications in materials science and energy research, making it an ideal inorganic compound for students to explore structural relationships. Depending on instructional goals, this laboratory module can be adapted for inorganic or physical chemistry courses, but it is particularly well-suited for advanced laboratory curricula emphasizing interdisciplinary approaches and modern characterization techniques.

TI Intra-actions that decolonize postcolonial erasure in Safalibaland,
   Ghana
SO LINGUISTICS AND EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Safaliba; Ghana; Decoloniality; Intra-action; New materialism;
   Translanguaging
AB In Ghana, postcolonial early-childhood language-in-education policies supported by international donor funding exclude Safaliba-an understudied Indigenous language spoken in the rural Savannah region- and subordinate its speakers to Gonja, the officially funded regional language. This critical ethnography examines Safaliba teacher-activism as decolonial resistance to linguistic marginalization and erasure within public schooling, focusing on the material-discursive strategies through which activists intervene in policy, classroom instruction, and classroom materials development. It also investigates how everyday classroom literacy practices, understood through Barad's framework of intra-action, reconfigure what counts as language, literacy, and legitimate knowledge in school.
