Findings show that Safaliba resistance is adaptive, iterative, and serpentine- working within schooling through translanguaging, bilingual Safaliba-English book production, innovative orthographic practices, and proposed integration of song and local Safaliba cosmological knowledge into Safaliba language instruction. These practices function as agential cuts that redraw boundaries of school legitimacy by reshaping who can be authorized as knowers (including children, elders, and ancestors), which semiotic modes carry curricular authority, and what constitutes legitimate literacy for Safaliba activists. Rather than simply opposing the postcolonial regime, activists "Safalibanize" classroom life from within, demonstrating decolonial practice as ongoing intra-actions that continually remake the conditions under which linguistic erasure is produced.    transition success
SO RESEARCH IN AUTISM
LA English
DT Article
DE Kindergarten transition; Transition planning; Social-emotional
   adjustment; Caregiver/teacher perception
ID SPECTRUM DISORDER; INTERNALIZING PROBLEMS; SCHOOL; CHILDREN; ENGAGEMENT;
   CHILDHOOD; HETEROGENEITY; DISCREPANCIES; DISAFFECTION; PARENTS
AB Successful transitions to kindergarten improve children's short-and long-term outcomes. Autistic children are more likely than their typically developing peers to face challenges during these transitions. There are no standard transition planning practices for autistic students; therefore, decisions about classroom placement and supports rely primarily on caregiver and teacher perceptions. No published studies examine the predictive validity of caregiver and teacher perspectives or how to incorporate them into decision-making. We examined whether caregivers and preschool teachers could predict children's adjustment to kindergarten, and whether caregiver-teacher communication and teachers' autism experience moderated prediction accuracy. The sample included 93 caregiver-child dyads, 68 preschool teachers, and 54 kindergarten teachers. All children had either a medical diagnosis or educational classification of autism. Caregivers and preschool teachers completed a survey, predicting the success of their student/child in kindergarten. Preschool teachers' prediction of children's successful adjustment was positively associated with children's positive affect, like contentedness or excitement, in kindergarten. Caregivers' prediction of children's successful adjustment was negatively associated with children's interfering behavior. Neither caregiver-teacher communication nor teacher autism experience moderated the association between predictions and child outcomes. Findings suggest that teachers and caregivers offer complementary insights that should be included in transition planning to better support autistic children's transitions to kindergarten.

TI Cheating and the fascistic public pedagogy of gamed capitalism: Pyramid
   schemes, sexist advice, misogynist scams and the perfect perfect bastard
SO REVIEW OF EDUCATION PEDAGOGY AND CULTURAL STUDIES
LA English
DT Article
DE Cheating; gamification; capitalism; fascism; cultural critique
ID CRITIQUE
AB Cheating has become a pivotal political category in a moment of ascendant fascistic politics in the United States and elsewhere. This essay explores a number of examples from US popular culture where a reactionary politics around cheating take shape, constituting part of the public pedagogy of what I term gamed capitalism. That is a form of capitalism where our agency is elicited (rather than repressed) and where we are each conscripted to cultivate ourselves as a "player" of often exploitative games. Here, a contradictory reactionary politics circulate around the figure of the cheat: on the one hand, they would appear to undermine a capitalist meritocracy that is presumed fair; on the other, we all know that only cheaters win, and that we must all strive to win at all costs. By examining the public pedagogy of pyramid schemes, sexist romantic advice, misogynist influencers and professional wrestling, we can gain a more capacious understanding of how the dispositions, subjectivities, affects and forms of relationality of gamed capitalism tend toward fascistic politics.

TI Children's social and emotional development in the shadow of a pandemic:
   A prospective, quasi-experimental study
SO CHILD DEVELOPMENT
LA English
DT Article
DE child psychopathology; COVID-19 pandemic; parenting
ID SECURE BASE SUPPORT; DIFFERENTIAL SUSCEPTIBILITY; TEMPERAMENT;
   ATTACHMENT; CHILDHOOD; FAMILIES; BEHAVIOR; TRAJECTORIES; PERFORMANCE;
   CONFLICTS
AB This multi-method, multi-informant, quasi-experimental study examines trajectories of child psychopathology over an 8-year period pre-and post-COVID-19 pandemic. We examined parenting as a moderator of the COVID-19 impact. Participants were 310 low-to-middle-income families from the United States with a target child followed over 6 waves (Wave 1, Mage = 2.97, SD = 0.38; 55.3% girls; 55.2% White, 21.3% African American, 16.2% mixed race; Wave 6: Mage = 9.32, SD = 0.76). Pre-COVID parenting moderated this effect, such that low paternal structure and consistency and low parental secure-base provision strengthened the association between COVID impact and the growth of internalizing problems, yielding greater increases under high impact and lower increases under low impact.
   This prospective study tracked children's mental health over 8 years. To rigorously assess the pandemic effects, we designed and implemented three targeted waves of data collection following early lockdowns. We found that pandemic disruptions generally increased children's emotional struggles, such as sadness and anxiety. Importantly, parenting shaped these reactions. Children receiving fewer consistent rules and less emotional reassurance were highly sensitive to their environment. Under severe pandemic stress, these children developed the most emotional problems; under low stress, however, they showed fewer problems.

TI Guided completion at scale: completion worksheets and embedded review
   videos for microbiology
SO JOURNAL OF MICROBIOLOGY & BIOLOGY EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE guided completion; microbiology education; retrieval practice; worked
   examples; process diagrams
ID COGNITIVE-LOAD
AB Large-enrollment microbiology courses often leave little time for the guided practice students need to reconstruct complex biological processes. This Tips and Tools article describes a scalable guided completion workflow developed in a 285-student General Microbiology course. Instructors convert process diagrams into partially completed worksheets, provide answer keys for immediate self-check, and embed short document-camera walkthroughs into unit review videos. The workflow uses familiar instructional tools but organizes them into a reusable bridge between lecture, independent study, and assessment. This article describes implementation only and does not report student outcome data.

TI Pay disparities between male and female university graduates in
   Australia: Rethinking the role of fields of study
SO REVIEW OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Australia; fields of study; gender pay gap; university graduates
ID GENDER WAGE GAP; HIGHER-EDUCATION; HORIZONTAL STRATIFICATION;
   SEX-SEGREGATION; COLLEGE MAJORS; EARNINGS; EMPLOYMENT; EQUITY; WOMEN
AB Despite recent progress, gender pay gaps between men and women remain a persistent feature of modern labour markets, being observed even amongst highly skilled population groups-such as university graduates. These gaps are the product of multiple interrelated factors-including discrimination, imbalanced family responsibilities and educational and labour-market segmentation, yet some of these factors have been examined more than others. This study offers a comprehensive examination of gender pay gaps amongst university graduates in Australia, focusing on one under-researched contributor: fields of study and their feminisation rates. Leveraging rich and robust population-level administrative data from the Person Level Integrated Data Asset (PLIDA) (n = 549,893 graduates) and multilevel regression models, we first revisit key mechanisms underpinning the graduate gender pay gap within the Australian context. We then deploy this unique dataset to offer novel empirical contributions to the international literature-including the mediating and moderating effect of field of study in the relationship between gender and earnings, and their interaction with occupational gender segregation. Our results offer evidence of a substantial graduate gender pay gap in Australia, amounting to similar to 17% of annual average salaries among men. While standard socio-demographic factors fail to explain this gap, gendered differences in fields of study account for similar to 14% of it. Importantly, the magnitude of the graduate gender pay gap differs markedly by field of study (from similar to 2% to similar to 24% of average pay), being largest amongst graduates from gender-balanced fields. These findings bear important implications for equity policy and practice pertaining to both higher education and the labour market.Context and implications Rationale for this study: Despite women's growing educational attainment, gender pay gaps amongst university graduates persist. Existing research has paid limited attention to the contributing role of field of study. Why the new findings matter: This study uncovers substantial variation in gender pay gaps across fields of study, providing novel evidence that disparities are largest in gender-balanced fields. Implications for researchers, policymakers and practitioners: For researchers, our findings underscore the importance of considering detailed field-of-study measures and feminisation indicators in analyses of gender pay inequality. For practitioners and policymakers, the findings suggest that interventions aimed solely at altering gendered educational choices may have limited effects unless they are accompanied by efforts to address pay-setting mechanisms and within-field inequalities.

TI Quality is in the Eye of the Beholder: A Quality Model rethinking VET
   through the Eyes of Gen Z Learners - Individualization, Digitalization,
   and Meaningful Work
SO VOCATIONS AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Gen Z; Training Quality Model; Vocational Education and Training;
   Apprentice; Digitalization; Individualization
ID GENERATION Z; VALUES; PERSPECTIVES; PERIOD
AB As Generation Z (Gen Z) enters vocational education, their distinct expectations and digital fluency present new challenges for dual vocational education and training (VET). While these issues are frequently discussed in public discourse, empirical evidence remains scarce. This study examines how Gen Z apprentices define the quality of training in school- and company-based learning environments. Drawing on 15 semi-structured interviews with commercial apprentices in Germany, a qualitative content analysis was conducted. Six core dimensions were identified: (1) digitalization, including access to infrastructure, tools, and artificial intelligence (AI); (2) flexibility and work-life balance, with a focus on remote work and individualized schedules; (3) meaningful work, reflected in autonomy, relevance, and opportunities for impact; (4) job security and career opportunities, including transparent pathways and structured development; (5) individualization, such as customized feedback and learner-driven content; and (6) interpersonal relationships, emphasizing respectful communication, team cohesion, and emotional support. These findings extend existing models by foregrounding learner agency and socio-technological change, suggesting that VET quality models must become more learner-centered and digitally integrated to align with Gen Z apprentices' expectations.

TI From Mandatory Exposure to Guided Engagement: Investigating the
   Structured Integration of Generative AI in Higher Education
SO TRENDS IN HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE generative AI; higher education; perceived learning usefulness; DigComp
   2.2; mandatory AI integration; pedagogical scaffolding
ID INFORMATION-TECHNOLOGY; USER ACCEPTANCE
AB The rapid institutionalization of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in higher education has created an urgent need for empirical evidence on how structured course-level integration relates to student engagement and perceptions of learning. This study examines a usefulness-centered conceptual framework combining elements of the Technology Acceptance Model and the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (TAM/UTAUT) with the digital competence perspective of DigComp 2.2. A structured pedagogical pilot intervention requiring all students to use generative AI tools was implemented in an undergraduate Public Service Management course (n = 76). Students completed AI-supported group assignments and an immediate post-intervention questionnaire comprising 19 Likert-scale items, four demographic questions, and four optional open-ended questions that are not analyzed in the present paper. Ethical attitudes were also positive, but more weakly associated with frequency of use. Demographic group differences were observed mainly in specific usage patterns rather than in general attitudes towards AI-supported learning. These exploratory findings suggest that perceived learning usefulness remains relevant in mandatory AI-integration contexts. Pedagogical scaffolding-including prompt literacy, verification practices, and reflective documentation-provides a structured framework for guided and responsible use of generative AI tools in higher education.

TI AI literacy and ethical attitudes toward AI in medical students:
   evidence from a structural model
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial Intelligence; Literacy; Medical Ethics; Structural Equation
   Modeling; Regression; Medical Education; Medical Student
ID PLS-SEM
AB Background The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into healthcare has raised ethical concerns regarding autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, justice, accountability, and human oversight. While AI literacy is increasingly being adopted as a fundamental competency area in medical education, there is limited empirical evidence regarding its relationship with ethical attitudes toward AI. This study was conducted to examine the relationship between AI literacy and ethical attitudes toward AI among medical students and to explore how AI literacy is associated with ethical preparedness. Methods This cross-sectional correlation study was conducted with 461 medical students at a state university. Data was collected using a Demographic Information Form, AI-Literacy Scale, and AI-Ethics Scale. Descriptive statistics, independent samples t-tests, one-way ANOVA, Pearson correlation analysis, simple linear regression, and Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) were used to analyze relationships and associations between variables. Results A significant positive correlation was found between AI literacy and ethical attitudes toward AI (r = 0.648, p < 0.001). Regression analysis showed that AI literacy was significantly associated with ethical attitudes and explained 42% of the variance (R & sup2; = 0.420). Structural model analysis confirmed a strong positive path effect (beta = 0.655, p < 0.001; R & sup2; = 0.430; f & sup2; = 0.753). Students who received formal AI training achieved significantly higher scores in AI literacy and ethical attitudes, while no significant differences were observed between AI usage frequency and academic year. Although AI literacy did not differ by gender, female students reported higher ethical attitude scores. Conclusions AI literacy was significantly associated with medical students' ethical attitudes toward AI. No significant association was observed between frequency of AI use and ethical preparedness in the current study. These findings suggest that AI literacy should be conceptualized not only as a technical skill but as an important component associated with ethical preparedness in AI-enabled healthcare systems.

ID WORK; SCIENCE; INCIVILITY; CULTURE; ENTREPRENEURS; MASCULINITIES;
   PERSPECTIVES; HIERARCHIES; TECHNOLOGY; INEQUITY
AB This study explores the experiences of Iranian women engineers in industrial workplaces and investigates the mechanisms contributing to their exclusion from such environments. Data were collected through interviews with 26 women engineers employed in various industrial sectors using purposive sampling to ensure maximum diversity. The findings reveal that Iranian women engineers encounter a "male-dominated engineering culture" and adopt two primary strategies to navigate this context: adopting typically masculine traits and intensifying traditionally feminine characteristics that align with industrial expectations. A distinctive factor shaping the experience of women engineers in Iran is the pervasive patriarchal culture within state-owned industries, which comprise a significant portion of the country's large-scale enterprises. Additionally, as Iran remains in a transitional phase of industrialization, its industries continue to emphasize manual labor and prioritize "wrench-in-hand" workers over highly skilled professionals.

TI MENTORING FOR INCLUSION IN STEM: RECOMMENDATIONS FROM WESTERN AUSTRALIAN
   SURVEY FINDINGS
SO JOURNAL OF WOMEN AND MINORITIES IN SCIENCE AND ENGINEERING
LA English
DT Article
DE STEM; women in STEM; STEM education; gender equity; mentorship;
   barriers; enablers
ID EDUCATION SCHOLARSHIP; MENTORSHIP; SCIENCE; NEEDS; WOMEN
AB This paper reports the challenges, enablers, and mentoring experiences of women in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) fields, based on a mixed-methods survey conducted in Western Australia (WA) with female participants (n = 116) working or studying in STEM. Guided by elements of critical theory and feminist research methodology, the study prioritized the voices of women and aimed to highlight the power dynamics within STEM. The underrepresentation of women and girls in many STEM careers and courses of study is a persistent issue in Australia, and despite Western Australia's identity being inextricably linked to the resources industry, there is little research into WA women's experiences in STEM. From a critical theory perspective, diverse participation and female empowerment in STEM education and careers is a crucial social outcome. The survey findings showed the most significant barriers to pursuing STEM studies and careers for Western Australian women included sexism, a lack of female role models, and low confidence in STEM skills. Conversely, a sense of aptitude, enjoyment of STEM activities, and the alignment of careers or study with personal values were the key enablers. Findings also illustrate the key traits of successful mentors for women in STEM and indicate ways in which positive perceptions of STEM could be fostered among adolescent girls. These insights contribute to the discourse on gender equity in STEM and provide recommendations for stakeholders striving to create more inclusive environments for women in STEM.

   Foundation Phase education as a social justice imperative

LA English
DT Article
DE additive language teaching approach; conceptual fluency; Foundation
   Phase; mother tongue-based bilingual education; social justice in
   education
AB Background: Language remains a central determinant of epistemic access in South African Foundation Phase classrooms, where many learners begin schooling in a language other than their home language. The 2025 shift in language-in-education approaches renewed attention to mother tongue-based bilingual education (MTBBE) as a pathway to equity and meaningful curriculum access, particularly within Science, Technology, Robotics, Engineering, Arts and Mathematics (STREAM) education. TI Who attends PhD supervision training? A multi-year snapshot of gendered
   participation in a Nordic graduate school
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE academic development; gender differences; higher education; PhD
   supervision; professional development
ID IMPACT
AB PhD supervision training has become an increasingly important component of academic development in higher education, yet little attention has been paid to who actually participates in such initiatives. Because participation is typically voluntary, attendance may reflect patterns of self-selection rather than the composition of the broader academic workforce. In this Perspectives paper, we provide a descriptive snapshot of participation in PhD supervision seminars offered through a large Nordic graduate school in educational research, involving participants from approximately 15 universities and university colleges. The analysis draws on attendance records from six annual seminars conducted between 2019 and 2024. After excluding a small number of administrative staff and researchers, the final sample comprised 145 associate professors and professors. Women constituted a majority of attendees, and logistic regression analyses indicated that the estimated probability of an attendee being male was approximately 22% (OR=0.28). This gender imbalance did not vary meaningfully by academic rank and remained stable across the six-year observation period. A non-parametric bootstrap analysis with 1,000 resamples confirmed the robustness of the overall pattern. Results suggest that participation in voluntary academic development activities may diverge from the demographic composition of the underlying academic workforce, even in contexts where women already constitute a slight majority of academic staff. Although the present study does not address the causes of this pattern, it highlights participation itself as an underexamined aspect of academic development and raises questions about how such initiatives are communicated and structured within higher education.

TI Co-Constructing Literacy with AI: A Mixed-Methods Study of
   Comprehension, Motivation, and Multimodal Storytelling in Grade 4
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE artificial intelligence in education; AI-supported literacy; multimodal
   storytelling; reading comprehension; primary education; digital
   authorship
AB This exploratory, classroom-based mixed-methods study examined a five-phase, AI-supported multimodal literacy sequence implemented with 25 Grade 4 students over four weeks. The intervention combined interactive digital reading, collaborative narrative writing, AI-supported comic imagery, multimedia editing, and peer reflection. Quantitative analyses compared students' baseline and post-intervention comprehension scores and summarized responses to a 12-item post-intervention questionnaire. Qualitative data from open-ended responses, classroom observations, and student artifacts were analyzed thematically. Students' mean comprehension scores increased from 63.81 (SD = 9.70) at baseline to 75.37 (SD = 7.63) after the intervention, representing a significant within-group change, t(24) = 5.49, p < 0.001, dz = 1.10. Questionnaire responses were generally positive, particularly for original story writing, digital comic creation, and the addition of movement and sound. Three qualitative themes were identified: AI-supported representations as scaffolds for narrative comprehension, as catalysts for authorial identity and creative agency, and as mediators of collaborative meaning-making. Because the study used a single-group design and the comparability of the parallel assessment forms was supported through expert content review rather than large-scale psychometric equating, the findings should be interpreted as exploratory evidence of association rather than as causal effects of AI. The study nevertheless illustrates how developmentally appropriate, teacher-mediated AI activities may support multimodal literacy participation in primary education.

TI A Competency-Based Educational Methodology for Smart Maintenance:
   Integrating Condition Monitoring, IoT, and Generative Artificial
   Intelligence
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE smart maintenance; engineering education; Industry 4.0; competency-based
   education; Internet of Things; generative artificial intelligence;
   condition monitoring
ID ALPHA
AB The digital transformation associated with Industry 4.0 has increased the demand for engineers with competencies in condition monitoring, the Internet of Things (IoT), and artificial intelligence (AI). However, evidence on educational methodologies integrating these technologies within a competency-based assessment framework remains limited. This study developed and preliminarily evaluated a competency-based educational methodology and characterized the technical, digital, and analytical competency profiles of Mechanical Engineering students following participation in smart maintenance learning activities. A descriptive-exploratory case study was conducted with 31 students enrolled in an Industrial Maintenance course. The methodology integrated vibration analysis, infrared thermography, acoustic monitoring, IoT-based remote monitoring, and ChatGPT-assisted fault diagnosis. Competencies were assessed using an analytic rubric applied by six faculty evaluators, while students' perceptions were examined through a 22-item questionnaire. The Global Competency Index for Smart Maintenance (GCIIM) was 72.86%, indicating a moderate overall competency level. Critical evaluation of artificial intelligence achieved the highest score, whereas fault diagnosis, technical communication, and technological adaptability showed the lowest performance. Students reported a favorable overall perception score (75.04%) across the questionnaire dimensions. These findings provide preliminary evidence of the feasibility of an integrated competency-based framework for smart maintenance education and its potential to support the responsible incorporation of digital technologies and artificial intelligence into engineering curricula.

TI Science in School-Age Educare: Teachers' Experiences in the Mangling of
   a Didactic Model
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE didactic model; didactic modelling; extended education; mangling;
   school-age educare; science; teaching
ID ATTITUDES
AB The present study examines teachers' experiences of using a didactic model for teaching science content in the Extended Education setting of Swedish school-age educare (SAEC). The model was developed based on previous studies of what science education can entail in this context. Eight teachers from two SAECs participated in a mangling process. In this study, mangling refers to the iterative testing, accommodation, and refinement of a didactic model in practice. The process was carried out through workshops, focus group discussions, and teaching activities during the 2023/2024 academic year. The empirical material consisted of audio recordings from focus group discussions with the teachers, which were analysed thematically in relation to Pickering's theory, the mangle of practice, and the concepts of what works, resistance, and accommodation. The results show themes related to what teachers experienced as supportive, what forms of resistance they encountered, and the accommodations they suggested to further develop the model. The findings contribute to knowledge about how the model functions and how it can be further developed. They also contribute to an understanding of how teachers' contributions can play a central role in the mangling of didactic models.

TI Peer Mentoring, Perceived Affiliation, Sense of Belonging and Social
   Inclusion: Evidence from a Portuguese University
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE student's craft; student diversity; higher education; mixed methods
ID BENEFITS
AB This study analyzes peer mentoring as an institutional mechanism that may support students' transition to higher education, addressing a gap in the literature regarding how mentoring might influence academic affiliation, sense of belonging and social inclusion, simultaneously. Based on an integrated analytical framework that combines the concepts of the "student's craft," belonging and mentoring for social inclusion, the research adopts a mixed-methods approach grounded in methodological triangulation, including quantitative data from questionnaires applied to mentors and mentees, as well as qualitative evidence from sharing sessions and observation. In the context studied, results suggest that peer mentoring functions as a form of institutional mediation through which students access and interpret the norms and practices of university life, with relational support appearing central to translating that knowledge into meaningful engagement. Within the mentoring program in question, participation was also associated with students' reported sense of belonging and academic affiliation, as interrelated processes whose perceived impact varied across students' diverse trajectories, particularly among international students. Furthermore, the study highlights the reciprocal nature of mentoring, promoting development and participation among both mentees and mentors. Peer mentoring is not an isolated intervention, but rather part of a broader institutional ecosystem that can impact student inclusion, participation and success.

TI Conversation skills as a predictor of communication competence among
   university students
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE academic performance; communication competence; conversation skills;
   higher education; mediation; path analysis
AB Introduction: Conversational and communicative competence is increasingly recognized as a core transferable skill in higher education, yet the mechanisms linking academic variables to communicative outcomes remain underexplored. This study examined the relationships between year of study, academic performance, conversation skills, and communication competence among university students, and tested whether conversation skills statistically account for the link between academic performance and communication competence. Methods: A cross-sectional survey was conducted with 720 students from Babes-Bolyai University, Romania, enrolled in the exact sciences, social sciences and humanities, and arts. Conversation skills were measured with the Conversational Skills Rating Scale (CSRS; alpha = .945) and communication competence with the Communicative Competence Scale (CCS; alpha = .936). Data were analyzed using comparative tests, multiple regression, exploratory profiling analyses (K-means clustering and principal component analysis), and path analysis with bootstrapped indirect effects Results: Conversation skills showed a strong concurrent association with communication competence (beta = .52, p < .001), and academic performance had a small positive association with conversation skills (beta = .13, p < .001), which was statistically mediated to communication competence through conversation skills [indirect effect beta = .066, 95% bootstrap CI (.029, .104)]; given the small effect (R & sup2; = .018), this association should be interpreted cautiously. Male students reported slightly higher conversation skills (d = 0.21, p = .034), with no gender difference in communication competence, and no significant differences or interactions emerged across academic fields. The model showed an excellent fit, chi & sup2;(2) = 0.84, p = .656; CFI = 1.00; RMSEA = .000; SRMR = .010. Discussion: Findings position conversational ability as a proximal correlate of communication competence and support embedding structured conversational practice in university curricula.

TI Faculty perspectives on teacher leadership development in Chinese higher
   education: challenges and support needs
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE educational leadership; faculty development; higher education;
   leadership development; teacher leadership
AB This study reports the needs-analysis phase of a broader project on teacher leadership development in Chinese higher education, with particular attention to the challenges and support needs associated with faculty leadership development in under-resourced institutional contexts. Using semi-structured interviews with six faculty members from diverse higher education institutions in Guizhou Province, China, the study explored how teacher leadership is understood and experienced in this setting. The interview data were analysed thematically with the support of Atlas.ti 9. The analysis yielded six major themes: (i) leadership as professional influence rather than positional authority, (ii) teaching innovation as a core expression of teacher leadership, (iii) professional growth through mentoring, collaboration, and academic exchange, (iv) participation in governance as an important dimension of teacher leadership, (v) structural barriers to teacher leadership development, and (vi) support needs for strengthening teacher leadership. The findings suggest that teacher leadership in Chinese higher education is understood less as an administratively defined role than as a form of professional influence grounded in competence, relationships, and contribution to institutional improvement. At the same time, the study highlights the constraining effects of misaligned evaluation systems, workload fragmentation, and limited institutional support. These findings provide contextually grounded empirical input for the subsequent development of a culturally tailored teacher leadership development model and have implications for policy, faculty development, and future research.

TI The role of organizational and psychological effect on teachers'
   occupational stress
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE job satisfaction; occupational stress; organizational justice;
   psychological ownership; scientific research pressure; work-family
   conflict
AB Introduction Occupational stress among college teachers is a growing concern, particularly in emerging economies with rapidly expanding academic institutions. This study explores how job satisfaction, psychological ownership, work-family conflict, scientific research pressure, organizational justice, and organizational support affect teachers' occupational stress.Method A total of 633 valid responses the questionnaires and Structural Equation Modelling (SEM) were used to test research constructs and hypotheses.Result Job satisfaction has a positive and significant effect on organizational justice and teachers' occupational stress. Furthermore, psychological ownership and work-family conflict play an important role in influencing teachers' occupational stress. Additionally, this study also found that scientific research pressure has a positive and significant effect on organizational support. Organizational justice was identified as a mediator in the relationship between job satisfaction and teachers' occupational stress. Organizational support also plays an important role in addressing the relationship between scientific research pressure and teachers' occupational stress. The findings align with the social exchange theory which emphasizes the importance of supportive institutional environments and fair organizational practices in mitigating stress among academic staff.Conclusion It suggests that enhancing job satisfaction and organizational support, alongside addressing work-family balance and research pressures, are essential strategies for reducing occupational stress in higher education.

TI Curricular governance and teacher professional learning in specialized
   arts education: a multiple-case study of classical guitar teaching in
   Portuguese public conservatories (with a comparative lens on Spain)
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE assessment moderation; curriculum governance; digital competence; music
   education; professional learning; specialized artistic education;
   teacher education; territorial equity
ID MUSIC-EDUCATION
AB This original research examines how curricular governance arrangements shape teacher professional learning in Specialized Artistic Education by analysing Classical Guitar teaching in seven Portuguese public conservatories through a qualitative multiple-case study. Drawing on semi-structured interviews with guitar teachers conducted in focus groups (P1-P12), interviews with pedagogical leaders (D1-D7) and policy stakeholders (S1-S3), student questionnaires (n = 19), and documentary analysis of curricular and regulatory instruments, the study compares within- and across-case patterns of curriculum design, assessment, and professional learning routines. The analysis is framed by Young's argument on the specialisation of knowledge and Apple's account of curriculum as official knowledge. Findings indicate that one-to-one instrumental pedagogy supports strong personalisation and a hybrid performer-teacher identity, yet curricular autonomy without instrument-specific national reference points contributes to uneven coherence, fragile assessment comparability, and constrained student mobility, especially in peripheral and insular contexts. Assessment architecture emerges as a central governance lever: where evidence is distributed across shared rubrics, intermediate performance moments, and low-burden process records, participants report clearer expectations and more robust moderation; where high-stakes public examinations dominate, teaching priorities narrow and opportunities for collaborative learning weaken. Technology is valued when it serves concrete artistic functions and is constrained when introduced as an administrative layer without pedagogical purpose or data-protection safeguards. A comparative lens on Spain is used for policy learning by contrast, suggesting that national descriptors and moderation mechanisms can coexist with regional and institutional autonomy. The article advances the concept of a "light curricular contract" - cycle-based learning outcomes, core assessment rubrics, peer moderation, and minimal organisational conditions - as a feasible leadership framework for aligning artistic rigour with curricular justice.

TI A tri-theoretical framework for enhancing disaster preparedness in
   elementary schools: exploring collaboration, vulnerability, and
   constructivist education
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE collaboration; constructivist education; DepEd Region VIII; disaster
   preparedness; educational research; elementary school environment;
   exploratory research design; PLS-SEM
AB This research examined the key factors influencing disaster preparedness outcomes among elementary school teachers in the Department of Education (DepEd) Region VIII, anchored in an integrated framework combining Community of Practice Theory, Vulnerability Theory, and Constructivist Learning Theory. Rather than treating these theories as separate construct labels, the study positions them as complementary explanatory perspectives shaping collaboration, contextual risk conditions, and learning processes that collectively influence preparedness outcomes. A confirmatory quantitative design was employed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) via WarpPLS 8.0, with data collected from 141 validated responses of teachers, principals, and school heads across disaster-prone areas in Region VIII. The measurement model demonstrated satisfactory reliability and validity. Results indicate that vulnerability and constructivist education significantly influence disaster preparedness outcomes, while collaboration exerts an indirect effect through constructivist education based on the product-of-paths estimation approach. The findings further suggest that vulnerability may operate as a contextual condition that interacts with collaborative and learning mechanisms to shape preparedness. The study contributes to theory and practice by advancing a tri-theoretical model that explains how educational, social, and structural factors jointly influence disaster education outcomes, underscoring the role of education in strengthening sustainable disaster readiness.

TI Digital reading didactics in primary education: insights into
   differentiated digital reading instruction
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE digital reading; digital reading didactics; evidence-based reading; ICT;
   mixed-methods
ID KNOWLEDGE; LITERACY; 1ST
AB Reading texts on a screen has become a routine part of everyday life. While teaching reading in primary school, this calls for practical didactic approaches combining differentiation, digitalization and cross-curricular content. This study examines how digital differentiated cross-curricular reading materials (EFADIL) are implemented in Grade 3 classrooms in Austria. A mixed- methods design integrates teacher interviews (N = 34), classroom observations (N = 33), and student questionnaires (N = 605). The findings reveal tensions between perceived advantages, disadvantages, and enacted classroom practices. The materials provided a motivating learning environment and enabled differentiation and independent work. Simultaneously, they might lead to superficial and rapid task processing, along with variations in the use of the interactive digital features (e.g., glossary word function). Tasks requiring language production were often perceived to be more cognitively demanding. The study reveals instructional guidance, the teachers' role, and dimensions of instructional quality to be key factors in ensuring that digital differentiated materials support effective and inclusive reading instruction.

TI From avoidance to adoption: strategies for integrating AI in higher
   education contexts
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE academic integrity; AI literacy; AI skepticism; artificial intelligence;
   higher education; Northern Ireland
AB Introduction This paper aims to identify effective strategies for integrating Artificial Intelligence (AI) in higher education (HE), specifically addressing the challenges related to AI literacy, ethical concerns, and institutional variations. It provides a framework for incorporating an "embracing" approach to AI adoption, characterised by strategic incorporation of AI tools and underpinned by AI literacy and constructive AI skepticism.Methods The paper employs three main approaches. First, we explore current challenges faced by instructors in taking an embracing approach, particularly in relation to AI literacy. Second, we introduce instructor AI skepticism from a multi-layered perspective. Third, we present a series of case studies from universities in Northern Ireland reflecting on challenges of the embracing approach across STEM, Humanities, and Social Sciences, and how these challenges have been addressed.Results An exploration of AI adoption across different subject areas in four case studies demonstrates substantial variability in AI literacy, AI skepticism and acceptance across disciplines. Nonetheless, broader common themes emerge across the case studies. These themes generally involve critical thinking and application of subject area-specific theories to new contexts. Crucially, structured instructional approaches significantly reduce misconceptions and enhance ethical AI usage.Discussion This study uniquely integrates discipline-specific case studies and institutional context analyses. It contributes to understanding AI literacy as a multidimensional skillset. It further positions AI literacy as a critical means of addressing the underrepresented instructors' multilayered AI skepticism, with an emphasis on ethical considerations and critical student engagement. Our recommendations highlight the necessity for targeted faculty training, clear institutional policies, and structured curriculum integration strategies to foster AI literacy, address instructor skepticism, and enhance ethical awareness effectively.

TI Voices from the field: exploring academics' perceptions of scholarly
   publishing at a University of Technology
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE academic writing; collaborative networks; ecosystem; research
   productivity; scholarly publishing; University of Technology
ID CHALLENGES
AB Introduction This qualitative study examined academics' perceptions of scholarly publishing at a South African University of Technology (UoT). Guided by Bourdieu's theory of practice, the research explored how individual dispositions, collaborative networks and institutional structures shape publishing engagement.Method Using a purposive sample, data was gathered through semi-structured interviews and were analysed thematically.Results Findings revealed a layered scholarly writing ecosystem comprising three interdependent ecologies: an individual ecology (motivation, identity, and writing self-efficacy), a collaborative ecology (co-authorship, mentorship, and interdisciplinary ties), and a structural ecology (workload, key performance indicators (KPIs), funding, and technical support). Across these ecologies, participants described a tidal system of writing characterised by alternating periods of productivity and stagnation. Enablers included mentorship, distributed co-authoring, protected writing time, and accessible support. Constraints centred on heavy teaching and administrative loads, opaque resource allocation, negative peer-review experiences, and unequal network access. Interpreted through Bourdieu, the results underscore how uneven distributions of cultural, social and economic capital produce differential publishing trajectories.Recommendations The study recommends multi-level, equity-focused interventions, transparent funding, workload adjustments, structured mentoring and cohort writing practices, aimed at aligning UoT missions with realistic research support.Conclusion The findings have implications for UoTs and the broader higher-education sector, which seek to foster sustainable and just scholarly publishing.

TI Knowing intervention needs through the intersection of dropout factors
   and the CASEL framework: a case study of a tribal village in India
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE collaborative academic social emotional learning (CASEL) framework;
   dropout factors; mapping; participatory research approach (PRA); social
   emotional learning (SEL); tribal village
ID PARENTAL AWARENESS; PUBLIC-HEALTH; SCHOOL; STUDENTS; ADOLESCENTS;
   INTEGRATION; UNIVERSAL; EDUCATION; LIFE
AB Introduction One major obstacle to the realisation of a sustainable dropout reduction programme is the lack of an appropriate intervention design. This study employed a participatory research process to develop a sustainable dropout reduction design/solution by mapping community insights from a dropout factor study against the Collaborative, Academic, Social and Emotional Learning (CASEL) five SEL competencies framework as a guide.Methodology The study drew participants from seven stakeholder groups, namely, a village leadership group comprising key informants, panchayat officials, and Asha workers; a self-help group; a parent leadership group consisting of parents with a child in school; a youth leadership group involving young men and women; a student leadership group including current students, dropouts, and graduates; a school leadership group comprising teachers, administrators, and security officials; and a policy leadership group involving education officers, tribal affairs officers, and block development officers. In total, 36 unique participants participated in focus group discussions (FGDs; six per group, i.e., three males and three females); 24 of these participants (four per group, i.e., two males and two females) also underwent semi-structured interviews. This population was selected using purposive sampling. Using the interview and FGD codes, the study uncovered seven dropout factorial themes, namely, lack of interest, low parental awareness, insufficient income, unsuitable learning infrastructure, uncertainty of employment, negative beliefs about learning, and dislike for school boarding. The factors identified led to low performance, an increase in child labourers and child marriage, substance abuse, high absenteeism, low attendance, and an increase in withdrawal rate. The dropout factors identified from the interview and focus group discussions were coded into different themes using Atlas.ti, and themes from the FGDs and interviews were triangulated by matching common themes. These themes were then mapped to the five SEL dimensions of the CASEL framework using pattern matching.Results The overall findings of this study suggest that the dropout factors identified clearly associate with the five dimensions of the CASEL framework, with self-awareness, emotional, and social awareness factors considered most influential.Discussion It also indicates that dropout rates can be reduced by developing students' valuing skills (SA); emotional control and goal-setting skills (SM); empathetic and diversity appreciation skills (SA); communication and collaboration skills (relationship building skills); and resistance to challenges and good choice-making skills (problem-solving and relationship). These uncovered associations generate hypotheses for SEL-focused dropout prevention, which necessitates experimental research to test whether building SEL-specific competences will reduce dropout-risk behaviour among students.

TI The role of pedagogical knowledge base, creativity, and resilience in
   shaping EFL teachers' self-efficacy
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE creativity; EFL teachers; pedagogical knowledge base; resilience;
   self-efficacy
ID FRAMEWORK
AB Teacher self-efficacy is essential for effective English as a Foreign Language (EFL) teaching, particularly in Kazakhstan's multilingual educational environment. This study examined the relationships between pedagogical knowledge base, teacher resilience, creativity-fostering teaching behavior, and teacher self-efficacy using an explanatory sequential mixed-methods design. Quantitative data were collected from 86 Kazakhstani EFL teachers through standardized questionnaires, and Pearson correlation and multiple regression analyses were performed. Qualitative interviews with 10 teachers were subsequently conducted to explain the quantitative findings. The results revealed significant positive relationships between teacher self-efficacy and pedagogical knowledge base, resilience, and creativity-fostering teaching behavior. Classroom management, subject matter knowledge, equity and diversity awareness, professional commitment, response to contextual challenges, self-belief, integration, and frustration management were identified as significant predictors, whereas assessment literacy showed a negative predictive effect. The qualitative findings demonstrated that highly self-efficacious teachers employed differentiated instruction, peer collaboration, flexible lesson adaptation, scaffolding, and reflective practice to address classroom challenges. These findings indicate that pedagogical knowledge, resilience, and creativity-fostering instructional practices jointly contribute to strengthening teacher self-efficacy and provide practical guidance for designing professional development programs for EFL teachers in multilingual educational settings.

TI Developing the professional competence of future teacher-psychologists
   through Neuro-Linguistic Programming
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE communication and rapport; future teacher-psychologists;
   Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP); professional competence; school
   psychology; self-regulation
AB This study aimed to explore how future teacher-psychologists in Kazakhstan conceptualize professional competence and how they evaluate the usefulness, feasibility, and ethical boundaries of Neuro-Linguistic Programming (NLP) in educational settings. The study was designed within a qualitative phenomenological framework. The participants consisted of 56 undergraduate students enrolled in Pedagogy-Psychology programs at two universities in Kazakhstan. Data were collected during February-March 2026 through a semi-structured interview questionnaire including four main questions and four probe questions, and were analysed using thematic analysis. The findings were organized under four themes: understanding professional competence, communication and rapport, self-regulation and professional identity, and NLP use, feasibility, and ethics in educational settings. Participants defined professional competence as a multidimensional and practice-oriented construct involving the application of theoretical knowledge, child-centred support, collaboration, and ethical responsibility. Communication and rapport were viewed as foundational to effective school psychology practice, while self-regulation was associated with professionalism under stress. NLP was generally perceived as a potentially useful supplementary tool for rapport-building, motivation, and emotional support; however, participants emphasized that it should be used cautiously, ethically, and together with evidence-based methods. The study highlights the importance of integrating applied competence, relational communication, reflective self-regulation, and critical methodological awareness in the preparation of future teacher-psychologists.

TI Facebook as a learning node: a theoretical proposal of a private
   connectivist group for the collective construction of knowledge in
   higher education
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE collective construction of knowledge; connectivism; elementary
   education; facebook; higher education; instructional design; social
   networks; teaching role
AB Social networks have transformed the way young people relate to knowledge. The intended pedagogical use in higher education is still barely theorized. Our article proposes a theoretical design of a private Facebook group as a connectivist learning space for university students in the first levels of the Education career. The objective is to theoretically argue how a private Facebook group, structured under connectivist principles, can constitute an intentional learning node that favors the collective construction of knowledge about the role of the teacher in the digital age. Methodologically, we adopt a non-empirical approach, inscribed in the conceptual and theoretical tradition, which articulates the principles of connectivism of Siemens and Downes with the pedagogical possibilities of existing social networks. We include conceptual instructional design without reaching its empirical implementation. Our paper posits a closed, moderated space on a well-known social platform where students can reduce technological friction, activate authentic cognitive and relational connections. We conclude that the instructional design of the group is the determining condition for the emergence of connectivist learning and not the platform itself.

TI Classroom observation-informed course redesign in
   design-thinking-oriented art higher education: a teacher action research
   study
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE classroom observation; course redesign; design thinking; higher
   education; innovation pedagogy; pedagogical diagnosis; reflective
   practice; teacher action research
AB Introduction Course redesign in higher education is often guided by informal impressions rather than traceable classroom evidence. This study examined how routine classroom observation records can support teacher-led diagnosis and course redesign in design-thinking-oriented innovation courses in Chinese higher education.Methods Using a teacher action research design, we drew on a broader corpus of 111 observation records from 42 class groups. We analyzed a comparable baseline subset of 98 pre-redesign records together with 13 post-redesign follow-up observations from the same class groups and comparable module types. Descriptive analysis summarized attendance, comprehensive engagement, classroom atmosphere, and interaction quality. Thematic analysis of open-text observation fields identified recurring instructional issues and informed redesign decisions.Results The baseline data showed consistently higher attendance than active engagement and only moderate interaction quality. Four recurring issues were identified: insufficient contextual relevance, limited interaction diversity, inadequate discussion scaffolding, and misaligned task pacing. These findings were translated into redesign strategies that strengthened engineering-related case use, peer interaction, questioning opportunities, prompts, and task sequencing. The follow-up observations suggested descriptive upward trends in comprehensive engagement and interaction quality, while attendance remained broadly stable.Discussion These trends are interpreted as bounded indicators of observable classroom change rather than as causal evidence of redesign effectiveness. The study contributes a traceable observation-to-redesign framework for practitioner inquiry and shows how routine observation records can function as inspectable evidence for locally grounded pedagogical change and course refinement.

TI Measuring the impact of a sports-based STEM workshop using a developed
   questionnaire
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE 21st-century skills; competencies; impact measurement; science in
   sports; STEM interest
ID DELPHI METHOD; STUDENTS
AB Introduction The Science in Sports workshop was implemented to examine the impact of integrating sports-based activities with STEM concepts on high school students' engagement and learning. To evaluate these learning outcomes, this study presents a newly developed questionnaire designed for sports-integrated STEM interventions. Methods A total of 150 students from five schools participated in two workshop implementations (n = 98 in the first workshop set and n = 52 in the second workshop set). The questionnaire was developed and examined through a two-stage process. In the first phase, the instrument was refined through expert review using the Delphi method and examined using Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA) based on data collected during the first workshop implementation. In the second phase, the refined instrument was applied during the second workshop implementation to collect pre-and post-workshop data. Internal consistency was assessed using Cronbach's alpha, while Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Tests and correlation analyses were conducted to evaluate learning outcomes and relationships among the measured constructs. Results The EFA supported a clear and interpretable factor structure, while Cronbach's alpha coefficients demonstrated acceptable to excellent internal consistency across all dimensions. Results from the Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test indicated statistically significant differences between pre-and post-workshop scores across the measured dimensions (p < .05). Correlation analysis revealed moderate to strong positive relationships among the measured constructs. In addition, exit ticket analysis indicated high levels of student satisfaction, with 66.3% of participants selecting "Strongly Agree" on key items. Discussion The findings provide initial evidence supporting the use of the instrument for evaluating sports-integrated STEM interventions and comparable real-world learning programs. This study contributes a context-sensitive questionnaire for assessing STEM learning outcomes within sports-integrated secondary education contexts.

TI Designing challenge for discovery in skill learning: toward
   self-regulated and representative adaptation
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE learning; ecological dynamics; representative learning design;
   self-regulated learning; transfer of learning
ID MOTOR SKILL; PERFORMANCE; KNOWLEDGE; PERCEPTION; INSTRUCTION;
   AFFORDANCES; FREQUENCY; MEMORY
AB Skill learning is often discussed in terms of closely related but insufficiently integrated concepts: challenge, instructional methods, discovery, self-regulation, specificity, retention, and transfer. As a result, practice design is frequently reduced to either adjusting task difficulty or prescribing movement solutions more explicitly. Compounding this, learning is routinely inferred from immediate performance quality, even though performance and learning unfold on different timescales and across qualitatively distinct contexts. This Perspective article advances a different view: skill learning is best understood as the progressive differentiation and calibration of affordance relations under functionally representative constraints. On this view, challenge is not a fixed property of tasks but a learner-relative, information-generating relation among the learner, the task, and the performance context. Discovery is the exploratory process through which learners search, differentiate, tune, and stabilize affordance relations. Self-regulation is the recursive process through which learners define tasks, monitor consequences, sustain motivation, and adapt their actions over time. Specificity is reframed through representative learning design, where the critical requirement is not superficial resemblance or high-fidelity mimicry but functional equivalence between practice and performance: the preservation of the affordances, timing demands, and constraints that regulate skilled activity. Improvement, in turn, is judged not by immediate performance gains alone but by retention, transfer, adaptability, and the development of self-regulatory capacity. Together, these claims reposition challenge, discovery, self-regulation, and representative learning design as interdependent elements of a single learning-design problem. The reframing carries direct implications for how improvement should be defined and evaluated, and for how practitioners across physical education, sport, coaching, and therapy might design conditions for durable, transferable, and adaptive skill.

TI The regulation paradox: agentic AI, bounded autonomy, and self-regulated
   learning in higher education
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE agentic AI; bounded autonomy; regulation paradox; higher education;
   learner agency; metacognition; self-regulated learning
AB Agentic AI is moving educational technology beyond reactive assistance toward systems that can plan, remember, adapt, and initiate actions across time. In higher education, this development raises a basic pedagogical question: does greater AI autonomy help students become more capable self-regulated learners, or does it perform the regulatory work that students need to practice themselves? This Perspective uses self-regulated learning (SRL) to examine this question. It argues that agentic AI becomes educationally meaningful when its autonomy supports learning processes rather than only producing academic outputs. It also separates four risks within the regulation paradox: regulatory displacement, metacognitive laziness, reduced productive struggle, and epistemic over-trust. To address these risks, the paper proposes bounded autonomy as a pedagogical governance principle that limits the scope, timing, transparency, contestability, and duration of AI intervention. Bounded autonomy extends scaffolding and hybrid human-AI regulation by making decision authority explicit and by requiring regulatory responsibility to be returned gradually to learners. The paper further argues that responsible implementation depends on learner capability, teacher agency, institutional readiness, and evidence that regulatory skills transfer to tasks completed without AI. Agentic AI earns its educational value not by becoming more autonomous from learners, but by helping learners become more capable of learning without it.

TI Nursing intervention program for caregivers regarding care of
   intellectual disabled children: quasi-experimental study
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE caregivers; children; Egypt; intellectual disability; nursing
   intervention program
ID DISABILITIES; HEALTH
AB Introduction Caregivers of children with intellectual disability face significant challenges in meeting their care needs due to limited knowledge and inadequate training. Structured nursing interventions may enhance caregivers' competencies and improve health outcomes for children with intellectual disability. This study aimed to evaluate the effect of the nursing intervention program for caregivers regarding the care of children with intellectual disability in an institutional setting in Cairo, Egypt.Methods A quasi-experimental one-group pretest-posttest design was conducted with 62 caregivers of children with intellectual disabilities in an institutional setting in the Ain Shams district, Cairo, Egypt. Participants were recruited using a convenience sampling technique. Data were collected from caregivers using a questionnaire covering socio-demographic characteristics as well as caregivers' knowledge and practices related to dealing with intellectual disabled children. Statistical analysis was carried out using SPSS version 27.Result The mean age of caregivers of intellectual disabled children was 34.14 +/- 3.09 years, 77.4% of them were female, and 90.3% were diploma educational level. Regarding the total satisfactory level of knowledge, 8.1% of them had a satisfactory level of knowledge in preprogram and that increased to 90.3% in post program, also, the total good reported practice in pre-program was 9.7% and that increased to 96.7% in post program. These improvements were statistically significant (knowledge: X2 = 56.89, p = 0.000; practices: X2 = 14.401, p = 0.000).Conclusion The structured nursing intervention program significantly improved caregivers' knowledge and reported care practices for children with intellectual disabilities. These findings demonstrate that even caregivers with limited formal education can achieve substantial competency gains through targeted, institution-based educational programs. Integrating such training into routine institutional care frameworks is recommended to enhance the quality of care and health outcomes for children with intellectual disabilities in similar resource-limited settings.

TI Caregivers' understandings of resilience among young children in
   conflict-affected Myanmar
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE caregivers; early years; education in conflict-zone; resilience;
   wellbeing
ID YOUTH
AB Resilience in the early years lays the foundation for healthy emotional regulation, adaptability, and lifelong learning. It is especially vital for marginalized children, helping them overcome systemic barriers, build self-efficacy, and access equitable opportunities for learning and well-being. Caregivers' involvement significantly contributes to the development of resilience in children. This study adopts qualitative interviews with eight caregivers (four teachers and four parents) in Myanmar to explore how they define resilience, the risk factors affecting children's well-being from their perspectives, and the coping strategies they used to foster children's resilience. Caregivers largely define resilience as the ability to stay strong, persevere, and maintain hope despite immense hardship, often linking it to continued engagement in education and the capacity to adapt. Key risk factors include fear of airstrikes and gunfire, food insecurity, limited access to healthcare, and disrupted education. In response, caregivers described a range of everyday practices, providing emotional reassurance, maintaining predictable routines, prioritizing education where possible, drawing on community and faith networks, and using storytelling and play-based activities to help children cope and continue to learn. The findings highlight how these interwoven practices collectively support children's resilience in protracted crisis, and point to low-cost, caregiver-led strategies that can inform educational policy, humanitarian programming and future research in conflict-affected settings.

TI Student perceptions of flexible learning in Philippine higher education
   during COVID-19 and implications for crisis-responsive monitoring
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE COVID-19; crisis-responsive education; digital literacy; flexible
   learning; higher education; learning management system; Philippines;
   student perceptions
ID EXPERIENCES
AB Flexible learning system (FLS) became a centerpiece continuity strategy among Philippine higher education institutions during COVID-19. However, its structure and variations across groups of students were unknown. Data were collected from a sample of 12,525 students across higher education institutions in Luzon, Visayas, and Mindanao to study psychometric properties of an FLS questionnaire and relationship of retained domain scores to student profile and teaching-learning technology variables. Sample largely consisted of female respondents (67.5%), individuals who utilized a learning management system during the pandemic (57.9%), and individuals with slow internet connectivity (57.8%) while only 11.8% had fast internet connectivity. Results from our exploratory study provided support for the four-domain structure (Support, Resources and Digital Proficiency, Readiness for Self-Regulated Learning, Barriers and Challenges) which showed good factorability [KMO = 0.944; Bartlett's chi & sup2;(325) = 178,200, p < 0.001]. Confirmatory factor analysis indicated model fit was better than a one-factor model, however fit indices were not ideal (CFI = 0.850, TLI = 0.834, RMSEA = 0.098, SRMR = 0.071). Internal consistency was strong for Support (alpha = 0.862), Resources and Digital Proficiency (alpha = 0.824), and Readiness (alpha = 0.832), but weaker for Barriers (alpha = 0.658). In FDR-adjusted HC3-robust multivariable models, poor vs. fast internet was associated with lower Resources (B = -0.542, p < 0.001) and lower Readiness (B = -0.172, p < 0.001). In contrast, higher digital literacy and prior LMS experience were associated with more favorable scores across several domains (all p < 0.05, FDR-adjusted). Qualitative themes identified connectivity as the dominant challenge (69.6%), while better understanding or learning effectiveness (32.0%) and accessibility or convenience (14.6%) shaped preferred modes of instruction. Overall, FLS during the COVID-19 period was workable but uneven, with support and learner persistence rated more favorably than resource sufficiency and barrier relief. The instrument may serve as a low-stakes institutional monitoring tool during COVID-analogous disruptions, although the Barriers domain still requires refinement and revalidation.

TI Health science teachers' perceptions of the use of qualitative research:
   a phenomenological study
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE qualitative research; higher education; perception; interviews; content
   analysis
AB Introduction In Latin America, Peruvian university faculty are strengthening their scientific output, and qualitative research is gaining relevance due to its capacity to illuminate the human dimension of health processes and the socio-emotional determinants that cannot be captured through quantitative measurements. The innovative contribution of this study lies in incorporating this approach into ethical and contextualized training aimed at developing interpretive and reflective sensitivity across disciplines, particularly in the health sciences. TI Cross-cultural perspectives on career planning: a comparative study of
   self-perception among higher vocational students in China and Thailand
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE career planning; cross-cultural comparison; self-perception; social
   cognitive career theory (SCCT); vocational education
ID TRANSLATION
AB Introduction Career planning among vocational students is shaped by psychological, cultural, and institutional factors. This study examined how selfefficacy, career awareness, and cultural values relate to career planning behavior among vocational students in China and Thailand.Methods A concurrent mixed-methods design was used. Questionnaire data were collected from 400 students in each country and complemented by semistructured interviews with 18 participants. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, independent samples tests, thematic analysis, and covariance based structural equation modeling.Results Chinese students reported higher career awareness and cultural-value orientation, whereas Thai students reported higher self-efficacy. Cultural values were the dominant direct correlate of career planning behavior in China. In Thailand, career awareness was the dominant correlate. Self-efficacy was not significantly associated with career planning behavior in China but showed a weak negative association in Thailand.Discussion The findings demonstrate that SCCT mechanisms vary across cultural contexts. Career guidance should therefore be aligned with the cultural, informational, and institutional conditions of each vocational education system.

TI A Challenge-Based Learning Experience for Teaching Industry 5.0 in
   Management Engineering Education
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE Industry 5.0; challenge-based learning; engineering education;
   generative Artificial Intelligence; collaborative robotics; order
   sequencing; logistics education
AB Industry 5.0 demands that engineering graduates develop competencies that integrate technical knowledge with human-centricity, sustainability and resilience. However, engineering education has not always advanced at the same pace, and effective educational designs that operationalise these principles within applied learning contexts remain scarce. This paper presents Innovation Day, a four-hour challenge-based learning experience that operationalises Industry 5.0 principles through an artificial intelligence (AI)-supported cyber-physical logistics challenge in management engineering master's programmemes. The activity engaged 47 students organised into 14 teams across two master's degrees at the Universitat Polit & egrave;cnica de Val & egrave;ncia. Students progressively developed and integrated data structuring, QR-based identification, sequencing and storage assignment logic, computer vision and collaborative robotics within a single supervised automation workflow. All 14 teams completed the first three phases, while completion rates reached 71% in Phase 4 and 64% in Phase 5, reflecting the increasing demands of system integration. Results also show that generative AI acted as a pedagogical tool, enabling students with limited programming experience to develop functional Python applications while maintaining human validation and accountability. The experience demonstrates that complex Industry 5.0 scenarios can be translated into manageable, transferable educational activities through phased challenge design, functional validation gates and structured AI-supported learning.

TI Tangible Mathematics: 3D-Printing Manipulatives as a Tool in Mathematics
   Teacher Education
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE 3D-printing; teacher education; manipulatives; OpenSCAD programming;
   constructionism; TPACK (technological pedagogical content knowledge)
AB While manipulatives, physical learning materials reifying mathematical concepts, have been discussed for a long time, 3D-printing revitalized the discussion and allows teachers to have new manipulatives at their disposal, as well as to design their own using a fraction of the effort. How this can be achieved, i.e., how teachers need to be prepared to utilize 3D-printing, is being tested and implemented in current research. In this study, we report findings and the three-year-long design evolution of an elective seminar where student teachers, beginning in the third semester, are trained to use OpenSCAD programming to 3D-model and then print their own manipulatives, guided by scaffolding elements such as cookie stamps in the second session or a design profile. Each student conceives, models, prints, and didactically embeds their manipulatives over three phases during the semester: the input phase, resembling a "normal" seminar; the hands-on phase, akin to a makerspace; and a presentation phase, tying the project work together. This concept combines technical elements, mathematics didactics, constructionism, and modern teaching technologies innovatively, inviting other educators to adapt it based on the provided structure.

TI ESD conceptualization and enactment in Austrian teacher education
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE education for a sustainable future; education for sustainable
   development (ESD); professional identity; sustainability in higher
   education; teacher education
ID PROFESSIONAL AGENCY; KEY COMPETENCES; SUSTAINABILITY; IDENTITY
AB Education for sustainable development (ESD) has become a central framework for educational transformation in response to complex socio-ecological challenges. As higher education institutions are increasingly called upon to contribute to sustainability transitions, teacher education plays a pivotal role. Teacher educators act as key intermediaries between policy aims and pedagogical practice, shaping how future teachers implement ESD. Despite their central role, empirical research has paid little attention to how teacher educators conceptualize their professionalism in relation to sustainability and how institutional contexts shape their engagement with ESD. This study investigates how teacher educators in Austrian higher education understand and negotiate their professional role within the framework of ESD. Guided by a qualitative research design and informed by qualitative content analysis, seven semi-structured interviews were conducted with teacher educators across disciplines. Data were analyzed through open coding supported by MAXQDA. The findings indicate that the integration of ESD is shaped by institutional structures and professional identity. At the institutional level, fragmented responsibilities, weak structural anchoring and curriculum overload hinder systematic implementation. At the professional level, participants express strong normative commitment to sustainability but also reveal conceptual ambiguities, informally acquired knowledge and didactic uncertainty regarding ESD integration. These tensions indicate that ESD is often sustained through individual engagement rather than embedded in coherent institutional strategies. By analyzing the relationship between institutional conditions and professional identity and agency of teacher educators, the study deepens understanding of how sustainability can be meaningfully integrated-referred to here as ESD Star Enactment Model-into teacher education. It underscores the need to strengthen professional identity and agency development, supported by clear institutional structures.

TI What makes a highly productive PhD student?
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE China; computer science; doctoral research productivity; study duration;
