ID FINANCIAL-SUPPORT; COMPLETION
AB Understanding the factors associated with the doctoral research productivity is increasingly important in the context of performance-based evaluation systems and growing competition in academic labor markets. In this study, we examine the determinants of doctoral research productivity using a dataset of 192 PhD graduates from the College of Computer Science at Jilin University between 2020 and 2025. TI Experimental skills for undergraduate career preparation in quantum
   information science and engineering
SO PHYSICAL REVIEW PHYSICS EDUCATION RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
ID STUDENTS; GOALS
AB The growth of the quantum information science and engineering (QISE) industry has increased interest in how undergraduate programs prepare students for careers in this field. Prior research emphasizes the value of experiential learning as preparation for the quantum industry but lacks specificity regarding the experimental skills needed for positions available to bachelor's degree graduates. In this study, we investigate the experimental skills associated with bachelor's-level quantum industry positions through 44 semistructured interviews with quantum industry professionals. Guided by the American Association of Physics Teachers recommendations for the undergraduate physics laboratory curriculum, we characterize the experimental skills associated with positions described as requiring bachelor's-level preparation and thematically synthesize them into four categories: instrumentation, computation and data analysis, experimental and project design, and communication and collaboration. We further examine how these skills cluster across role types and articulate them as learning goals to provide guidance for educators interested in aligning undergraduate instruction with the needs of students wanting to pursue a career in the quantum industry. Our findings suggest the need to emphasize the discussion of hardware in QISE theory courses, expand experimental training through instructional laboratories, and intentionally integrate professional skills in undergraduate QISE education.

TI Framing intuitive ideas in physics: A proposal grounded in frame
   semantics
SO PHYSICAL REVIEW PHYSICS EDUCATION RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
ID RESOURCES; SCIENCE
AB The theoretical framework knowledge in pieces (KiP), proposed by Andrea diSessa, holds that intuitive knowledge in physics is organized through small cognitive structures called p-prims (phenomenological primitives). One of the heuristic principles on which the KiP framework is built-the principle of redescription-suggests that the descriptive framework of p-prims can be fine-tuned. However, the theoretical development of p-prim descriptions has remained largely limited to informal linguistic expressions drawn from students' explanations, without a clearly defined syntactic or semantic structure. This lack of systematicity has led to variations in the naming and conceptualization of p-prims, making their consistent identification and analytical use difficult. In response to this limitation, this paper proposes a formal schematization of p-prims based on Fillmore's Frame Semantics, supported by tools such as FrameNet. Our proposal aims to make explicit the core and peripheral components of each p-prim and to clarify the conditions under which they are evoked. By providing p-prims with a well-defined linguistic structure, the KiP framework is strengthened, opening new possibilities for the automated analysis of students' reasoning using artificial intelligence (AI), as well as for the design of visual representations to support the development of instructional materials. Theoretical, methodological, and technological implications of this proposal for future research in physics education research (PER) are also discussed.

TI Educational reconstruction of nuclear astrophysics in a design-based
   research project
SO PHYSICAL REVIEW PHYSICS EDUCATION RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
ID SCIENCE; ELEMENTS; ORIGIN
AB This paper presents the first iteration of development and classroom testing of Stars and Elements, a web-based learning resource for Norwegian upper secondary physics students focused on how heavy elements are produced in stars and neutron star mergers. Combining the model of educational reconstruction (MER) with the pedagogical link-making framework and design-based research (DBR), we identified core ideas to be communicated, reviewed the physics curriculum and research on student understanding and motivation, and formulated design hypotheses that guided development of a 90-min learning resource with animations, videos, interactive tasks, peer discussion, and teacher consolidation. Six classes (N = 120) participated; data comprised students' written responses to three open tasks, brief evaluations, and classroom observations. Most students could describe central concepts and processes concerning red giant stars and neutron star mergers as sites for heavy element production, notably the slow and rapid neutron capture processes, and many benefited from animations and varied task formats. Some displayed uncertain grasp of concepts such as fusion and beta decay. Nature of science (NoS) aspects concerning how physics knowledge is developed were found to be insufficiently represented. From these findings, we propose design principles for research-based learning resources on similar topics, including emphasizing explicit link-making across scales and prior knowledge, scaffolding for challenging nuclear concepts, multimodal visualizations, and explicit NoS focus. We argue that combining MER, link-making, and DBR is a promising approach for developing learning resources that reflect the frontiers of science while having a solid grounding in the classroom.

TI Undergraduate students' application of special relativity to paradoxes
SO PHYSICAL REVIEW PHYSICS EDUCATION RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
ID CONCEPTIONS; FRAMES; IDEAS; TIME
AB In this paper, the focus has been on students' application of special relativity theory after learning it. In order to determine students' understanding and conceptualization of the theory of special relativity, paradoxes, which are contradictory problems, have been used in the study. How students solved paradoxes related to the relativity of simultaneity, length contraction, and time dilation has been investigated, and an answer has been sought to the question "What is the state of undergraduate students who have learnt special relativity theory in applying the theory to paradoxes?" The students who participated in the study had previously attended Physics I, General Physics 2, and General Physics 3 courses in which classical physics topics (force and motion, electricity and magnetism, and optics and waves) were taught. The data were analyzed using a phenomenographic approach to identify the categories emerging from students' responses. Most students experience difficulty in understanding the nature of special relativity and applying the theory to other situations. For this reason, they did not use the concept of the reference frame in solving the paradoxes. From the students' responses, it is understood that they mostly think within a single reference frame and experience difficulty in understanding the contradictions that arise when viewed from different reference frames.

LA English
DT Article

ID RESPONSIBLE BEHAVIOR
AB Tourism development in natural tourism destinations often creates environmental pressures, particularly in sensitive ecosystems such as the Mekong Delta of Vietnam. This study examines pro-environmental Tourist Behavior in ecotourism and river destinations in the Mekong Delta, Vietnam. Drawing on an integrated theoretical framework combining the Stimulus-Organism-Response model and Norm Activation Theory, the research explores how environmental stimuli at destinations influence tourists' psychological processes and behavioral responses. A qualitative approach was employed using semi-structured interviews with 28 tourism employees-including tour guides, attraction staff, and boat operators-and field observations at key tourism sites in Can Tho City. While many tourists demonstrate pro-environmental behavior practices-such as proper waste disposal, reducing plastic use, and respecting natural landscapes-environmentally harmful behaviors still occur. By integrating Stimulus-Organism-Response model and Norm Activation Theory with qualitative evidence from frontline tourism staff, the study provides new insights into behavioral mechanisms and offers practical implications for promoting sustainable tourism in river-based ecotourism destinations.

TI When high scores no longer feel earned: A vignette study of students'
   psychological responses to AI-assisted design creation
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
DE GenAI; Design education; Psychological ownership; Attribution
ID OWNERSHIP; SUCCESS
AB Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is becoming deeply integrated into the creative processes of design students, yet little is known about how evaluative feedback influences students' psychological responses in AI-assisted creative contexts. This study employed a 3 (creation mode: conventional, AI-assisted without disclosure, AI-assisted with disclosure) & times; 2 (evaluation outcome: high score vs. low score) between-subjects vignette experiment to examine how AI use and disclosure shape students' immediate psychological responses to evaluative feedback. The results showed that, compared with conventional creation, AI-assisted creation was associated with lower perceived effort, psychological ownership, work attachment, and internal attribution. Under positive feedback, students found it more difficult to internalize success as evidence of their own competence and reported stronger feelings of impostorism. AI disclosure further influenced how students interpreted work ownership and the sources of success. These findings suggest that GenAI may reshape the psychological meaning of evaluative feedback, making positive evaluations less likely to translate into competence affirmation and a sense of ownership over creative outcomes. Because this study was based on vignette scenarios rather than authentic creative tasks, the findings should be interpreted as students' immediate psychological responses to AI-assisted design evaluation rather than the long-term effects of AI use.

TI Exploring Polar Organometallic Chemistry with Deep Eutectic Solvents in
   the Undergraduate Laboratory
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Second-Year Undergraduate; Laboratory Instruction; Organic Chemistry;
   Hands-On Learning/Manipulatives; Organometallics
ID ORGANOLITHIUM
AB Polar organolithium reagents are central to modern synthetic chemistry but are rarely used in undergraduate laboratories because of the need for inert atmospheric techniques and cryogenic conditions. This study introduces a deep eutectic solvent (DES) composed of choline chloride and glycerol as an accessible reaction medium that enables the nucleophilic addition of n-butyllithium to an imine under ambient conditions and in air. Students prepare the DES, carry out the organolithium addition, and analyze the reaction outcome using FT-IR spectroscopy to confirm imine to amine conversion. Across seven cohorts, the experiment consistently afforded average student yields of approximately 70% and produced reproducible FT-IR spectra that clearly differentiate starting material and product. These results demonstrate that DES-mediated organolithium chemistry can be safely and effectively incorporated into undergraduate teaching laboratories, broadening student exposure to reactive organometallic reagents while reducing logistical and safety barriers.

TI AI feedback effects on argumentative writing: The role of secondary
   students' feedback receptivity and writing skills
SO LEARNING AND INDIVIDUAL DIFFERENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence; Feedback; Receptivity to feedback;
   Argumentative writing
ID PEER FEEDBACK; LEARNING PROGRESSION; FORMATIVE ASSESSMENT;
   SELF-EFFICACY; SCIENCE; MODEL; METAANALYSIS; PERCEPTIONS
AB Background: Developing argumentative writing skills is key in secondary school. While AI feedback supports students, varying effects risk a Matthew effect. Ensuring equity requires determining which student characteristics explain differences in feedback effects. Objective: We investigated whether AI feedback promotes equity by examining how effects on argumentative writing varied by students' feedback receptivity and argumentative writing skills, as assumed in the student-feedback interaction model. ID SPECTRUM DISORDER; LANGUAGE; PROSODY; SPEECH
AB Autism is a neurodevelopmental condition for which timely and accurate identification remains an important clinical priority. Early and reliable identification can facilitate access to assessment, diagnosis, and appropriate support; however, current diagnostic pathways still rely largely on behavioural evaluation and clinical judgement. In this context, machine learning (ML) approaches have attracted growing interest because they can identify subtle and complex patterns in speech data that may not be readily captured through conventional methods. The current study investigated the potential of ML models to distinguish vowel productions from autistic and neurotypical adults based on acoustic speech features. Acoustic measures included fundamental frequency (F0), the first three formants (F1, F2, F3), duration, jitter, shimmer, harmonics-to-noise ratio (HNR), and intensity, elicited through a controlled production task. Four supervised ML models were evaluated: LightGBM, Random Forest, Support Vector Machine, and XGBoost. Under random token-level splitting, all models demonstrated good classification performance, with the best-performing model achieving an area under the curve (AUC) of approximately 0.89. However, performance decreased substantially under speaker-independent cross-validation, with AUCs approximately 0.60 and wider confidence intervals, indicating more limited generalization to vowel productions from unseen speakers. SHAP analyses nevertheless showed a broadly consistent feature-importance pattern across validation schemes, with F0 emerging as the strongest predictor, followed by intensity, while F3 and other acoustic measures made smaller contributions. These findings indicate that vowel acoustics contain information relevant to distinguishing autistic and neurotypical speech within a controlled dataset, while also demonstrating that classification performance is substantially attenuated under speaker-independent validation. The results highlight both the potential of interpretable speech-based ML for investigating acoustic markers of autism and the importance of rigorous speaker-independent evaluation.

TI Trait-based dimensional measures and WAIS-IV index scores for
   differentiating autism spectrum disorder with and without ADHD in adults
SO RESEARCH IN AUTISM
LA English
DT Article
DE Adult autism; ADHD co-occurrence; Empathy; Emotional dysregulation;
   WAIS-IV; Working Memory Index
ID COMORBIDITY; DIAGNOSIS
AB Background: Autism in adulthood is characterized by marked heterogeneity in cognitive, socioemotional, and affective functioning. Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) frequently co-occurs with autism, contributing to diagnostic complexity and variability in clinical presentation. Methods: Trait-based dimensions derived from self-report screening instruments (AQ, EQ, ALS-18, BAARS-IV) and WAIS-IV cognitive indices were examined in 164 adults diagnosed with autism, ADHD, or co-occurring autism + ADHD. Stepwise discriminant function analysis was used to identify multivariate profiles differentiating these clinical presentations. Results: Two significant discriminant functions emerged. The first (87.6% variance) was primarily defined by self-reported empathy (EQ) and autistic trait severity (AQ),distinguishing autistic from ADHD presentations. The second (12.4% of variance) was characterized mainly by workingmemory performance (WMI), current ADHD symptoms (BAARS-6), and affective lability (ALS18), contributing to the differentiation of adults with co-occurring autism + ADHD. The discriminant model correctly classified 65.2% of the original cases and 61.6% of cases following leave-one-out cross-validation. Conclusions: The findings support the value of combining cognitive indices with dimensional trait measures to characterize heterogeneity across adults with ADHD, autism, and co-occurring autism + ADHD. Although the discriminant model identified clinically meaningful multivariate profiles, its moderate cross-validated classification accuracy indicates that it should be regarded as exploratory and requires replication and external validation before clinical application.

TI Influences of modes and intensities of handgrip exercise on
   neuromuscular fatigue in young adults with cerebral palsy
SO RESEARCH IN DEVELOPMENTAL DISABILITIES
LA English
DT Article
DE Affordable rehabilitation devices; Fatigue; Electromyography; Handgrip
   exercise; Exercise prescription; Physical activity
ID CHILDREN; STRENGTH; MOVEMENT
AB Purpose: Exercise is an essential component for musculoskeletal care. However, there is no clear guideline for upper limb exercise for wheelchair users with cerebral palsy (CP). This study explored the influences of different modes and intensities of handgrip exercise on neuromuscular fatigue in adults with CP. Methods: A total of 14 adults diagnosed with CP completed four handgrip exercise protocols: isometric and dynamic handgrip exercises at 15% and 30% of maximal voluntary contraction. The isometric handgrip exercises lasted 30 s, while the dynamic handgrip exercises were performed at a frequency of 1 Hz for 60 s to ensure an equivalent exercise load. Muscle fatigue was quantified using the median frequency and spectral moment ratio (SMR) from electromyography (EMG) of four forearm muscles (flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS), extensor carpi radialis (ECR), flexor carpi ulnaris (FCU), and extensor carpi ulnaris (ECU)). Two-way analysis of variance with repeated measures (ANOVA) was used to examine the interaction and main effects of the handgrip protocols. Results: All four protocols were well tolerated in this sample, and no adverse events were reported. The results demonstrated a significant interaction effect for the median frequency of the ECR muscle (F=8.861, P = 0.013*, effect size: 0.446). All SMR conditions demonstrated a significant main effect handgrip intensity (P of FDS 0.049*, ECR 0.026*, FCU 0.016*, and ECU 0.031*). Two median frequency conditions also indicated a significant main effect of the intensity (P of FDS 0.071, ECR 0.068, FCU 0.006*, and ECU 0.012*). Conclusions: The results demonstrated a significant main effect of the intensity factor of handgrip exercise on neuromuscular fatigue in adults with CP. The findings support the use of low-cost handgrip exercise of both isometric and dynamic modes for exercise training in adults with CP.

TI Navigating identity tensions of languages other than English teachers
   amid precarity in marketized higher education
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE LOTE teachers; Identity tensions; Professional development;
   Marketization and performativity; Higher education
AB Despite growing research on languages other than English (LOTE) education, limited attention has been paid to LOTE teachers' identity tensions and professional development under marketized higher education. This study explores how LOTE teachers experience and navigate identity tensions amid marketization and performativity in Chinese universities. Guided by an integrated teacher identity framework, the study adopts a qualitative multiple case study design. Drawing on data from semi-structured interviews, document analysis, field observations, and informal communications, the findings reveal that LOTE teachers' identity tensions were shaped by marketoriented logics, performative evaluation regimes, and their marginal institutional positioning. In response, they engaged in pragmatic adaptation and strategic compliance to sustain program viability, while mobilizing moral professionalism and resilient agency to preserve their professional integrity. The study highlights the constrained yet agentive nature of LOTE teachers' identity negotiation and offers implications for supporting teacher development in marketized higher education.

   children's creativity and science motivation?
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Scientific creativity; Young children; Preschool; Motivation;
   Creativity; TTCT
ID LEARNING SCIENCE; SCHOOL; LITERACY; TEACHERS; VIEWS
AB This study aimed to explain the effect of the Early Childhood Scientific Creativity Program on children's creativity and motivation towards science. The study group consisted of children aged 60-72 months. An intervention design, a mixed methods design, was used in the study. The researcher developed and implemented the program for the experimental group four days a week over five weeks, while the control group received no intervention. To collect quantitative data, the Torrance Test of Creative Thinking Figural Forms and Preschool Children's Science Motivation Scale (PCSMS) were used. To collect qualitative data, child interview forms, a teacher interview form, and a researcher diary were used. In the present study, the quantitative data obtained were analyzed with the JASP program. The results indicated that there was a statistically significant difference in the creative thinking scores of the experimental and control groups. While the study revealed no statistically significant difference in motivation toward science between the two groups, the experimental group demonstrated a significant increase from pretest to posttest. The Scientific Creativity Program was found to be enjoyable for the children and had a positive effect on their knowledge of science and creativity. In addition, the teacher stated that the program contributed positively to the children's development and that the program was an applicable and functional program.

TI Developing Systems Thinking through Abstraction-Level Navigation:
   Evidence from Simulation-Based Project Learning in Microelectronic
   Circuit Design
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Project-based learning (PBL); systems thinking; abstraction; abstraction
   levels; simulation-based learning
ID DYNAMICS; SKILLS
AB Developing systems thinking through coordinated reasoning across multiple abstraction levels remains a persistent challenge in microelectronic circuit design education. Students often struggle to connect high-level system specifications with subsystem interactions and low-level transistor implementations, particularly when addressing complex integration and debugging tasks. While simulation tools are commonly used to support circuit analysis, their role in bridging abstraction levels within project-based learning contexts remains underexplored. This study examines how simulation-based project learning, implemented through LTspice, supports students' ability to navigate abstraction levels and develop systems thinking in a third-year microelectronic circuit design course. Over a 12-week semester, 49 undergraduate electrical engineering students engaged in a sequence of scaffolded design projects culminating in the construction and integration of an analog-to-digital converter. The projects required iterative movement between system-level architecture, functional block design, and transistor-level implementation, supported by continuous simulation-based testing and refinement. A qualitative-performance research design was employed, drawing on students' project artifacts, design reports, final practical examinations, and instructor observations. The analysis reveals a shift from isolated component-focused reasoning toward system-level debugging and cross-level explanations of circuit behavior across successive project phases. Later design reports frequently articulated how lower-level design decisions influenced overall system performance, particularly during integration and optimization phases. Performance outcomes further suggest improved effectiveness in diagnosing system-level errors and coordinating design tradeoffs across abstraction layers. The findings suggest that simulation-based project learning can function as a mediating mechanism that supports coordination between abstraction levels during system integration tasks. This study contributes to engineering education research by framing simulation as a mediator for systems thinking development in microelectronic circuit design and by offering instructional design principles for structuring project-based learning environments that explicitly target abstraction-level transitions.

TI Effectiveness of XR in vocabulary learning: A meta-analysis
SO COMPUTERS & EDUCATION: X REALITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Extended reality; Virtual reality; Augmented reality; Vocabulary
   learning; Meta-analysis; Language learning technology
ID VIRTUAL-REALITY; BIAS
AB Extended reality (XR), including virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR), has increasingly been applied in vocabulary acquisition. This meta-analysis synthesized empirical evidence on the effectiveness of XR technologies for second and foreign language vocabulary learning. Following PRISMA guidelines, searches were conducted in Web of Science, Scopus, and ERIC for studies published up to 2026. From 2,160 initially identified records, 29 experimental or quasi-experimental studies met the inclusion criteria. Effect sizes were calculated as Hedges' g and analyzed using random-effects and three-level meta-analytic models. The primary random-effects model showed a significant moderate-to-large positive effect of XR-based instruction on vocabulary learning, g = 0.775, 95% CI [0.545, 1.005], p < .001. A three-level model produced a comparable estimate, g = 0.773, confirming the robustness of the findings. Publication bias diagnostics indicated funnel asymmetry, but trim-and-fill analysis showed that the adjusted effect remained significant. Moderator analyses revealed that exposure frequency significantly influenced learning outcomes, with sustained or repeated XR exposure producing stronger effects than short exposure. Technology modality and assessment timepoint were not significant moderators. These findings suggest that XR can support vocabulary acquisition and may facilitate vocabulary retention over time, particularly when integrated through repeated instructional engagement.

TI Context and contest: how research university environments shape student
   success work
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF QUALITATIVE STUDIES IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Student success; critical discourse analysis; practitioner;
   administrator; context
ID CRITICAL DISCOURSE ANALYSIS; INSTITUTIONAL AGENTS; ENGAGEMENT;
   COMMUNITY; EDUCATION; FACULTY; CAMPUS
AB We explored how institutional actors' student success work gets done, in their contexts, from their perspectives. We used Sociocognitive Discourse Analysis, informed by van Dijk's theory of context, to answer the question: How do institutional actors' context(s) shape their student success work? TI A hypothetical learning trajectory for systems of equations: Building on
   students' units coordinations
SO JOURNAL OF MATHEMATICAL BEHAVIOR
LA English
DT Article
DE Constructivist Teaching Experiment; Hypothetical Learning Trajectory;
   Middle-grades Mathematics; Systems of Equations; Units Coordination
ID FRACTIONAL KNOWLEDGE; AGREEMENT
AB This study focuses on the development of a hypothetical learning trajectory (HLT) for learning to solve systems of equations involving letter-symbolic unknowns. A longitudinal constructivist teaching experiment was conducted, which followed a student, Kaelyn, from the spring semester of her sixth-grade year through the fall semester of her seventh-grade year. Kaelyn could perform mental operations on a unit of units. The HLT that was developed documents instructional methods that bridged the gap between her initial operations on a unit of units and the learning goal to solve systems of equations involving letter-symbolic substitution. The phases of the HLT included tacit reasoning about unknowns, explicit reasoning about multiple, related non-lettersymbolic unknowns, explicit reasoning about non-letter-symbolic substitution, and explicit reasoning about letter-symbolic substitution. This study contributes an HLT for middle-grades students' learning to solve systems of equations, including their critical transition from nonletter-symbolic to letter-symbolic reasoning about unknowns.

TI Social Equity in Public Budgeting and Finance Curricula: A Survey of
   NASPAA Accredited Master's Programs in Public Administration in the US
SO JOURNAL OF PUBLIC AFFAIRS EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE social equity; public administration; public budgeting and finance;
   NASPAA accreditation; public budgeting and finance curricula;
   Frederickson's compound theory of social equity
ID ES
AB Academic programs in public administration are increasingly expected to ensure that students are exposed to and competent in topics related to diversity, equity, and inclusion. Despite the growing prevalence of social equity in public administration, public budgeting and finance remains under-examined in the context of social equity. Through a survey of Network of Schools of Public Policy, Affairs, and Administration accredited graduate programs in public affairs in the United States and a content analysis of their course syllabi and assignments, this research finds that while social equity is rarely made explicit in public budgeting and finance curricula, the coverage of social equity topics falls in line with the literature review where many aspects of public budgeting and finance education touched on social equity issues. This research helps fill the void of literature and contribute to the pedagogical research on social equity in public budgeting and finance.

TI Motivational Profiles of Teaching Self-Efficacy, Task Value, Perceived
   Cost, and Transformative Experience in Kuwaiti Preservice Teachers: A
   Longitudinal Latent Transition Analysis of Intentions to Quit
SO JOURNAL OF TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE intentions to quit; motivational profiles; transformative experience;
   self-efficacy; task value; perceived cost
ID EXPECTANCY; CONSTRUCT; STUDENTS; DROPOUT
AB Student withdrawal in higher education is increasingly framed as a process in which intentions to quit may provide an early, context-sensitive risk signal, particularly in teacher education. Guided by situated expectancy-value-cost and self-efficacy perspectives, we followed 380 Kuwaiti female preservice teachers across three waves (920 person-wave observations; Full Information Maximum Likelihood [FIML]) to model longitudinal motivational profiles of teaching self-efficacy, task value, perceived cost, and transformative experience and to test links with intentions to quit teaching. Latent transition analysis supported four profiles: Thriving (41.1%), High-Cost (28.4%), At-Risk (15.8%), and Disengaged (14.7%). Profile stability increased within the later interval of the term, with earlier movement more often towards Thriving. Intentions to quit differed by profile (Wald chi(2)(3) = 35.67, p < .001) and were highest in At-Risk (M = 2.94), whereas High-Cost did not differ from Thriving despite the highest perceived cost. Mixed-effects models showed profile effects without wave or interaction effects, indicating stable between-profile risk.

TI Nurse educators' perspectives of trauma-informed educational practices
   in undergraduate nursing education: An interpretive descriptive study
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Nursing education; Trauma-informed pedagogy; Health equity;
   Trauma-informed care; Undergraduate nursing students; Curriculum
   development; Learning environment
ID CARE; STUDENTS; RESILIENCE; PROVIDERS; VIOLENCE; GROWTH; VIEWS; STATE;
   PTSD
AB Background: Trauma-informed care (TIC) is an essential framework for nursing practice, yet its integration into undergraduate nursing education remains limited. Trauma-informed educational practices extend TIC principles to teaching and learning contexts and have the potential to transform nursing education by addressing student well-being and reducing secondary traumatic stress. However, little is known about how nurse educators understand and implement TIC in undergraduate nursing programs. Aim: This study explored Ontario nurse educators' knowledge about TIC and its potential to transform undergraduate nursing education through trauma-informed educational practices. Design: This interpretive descriptive qualitative study was guided by Transformational Learning Theory. Setting: Undergraduate baccalaureate nursing programs in Ontario, Canada. Participants: A purposive sample of nurse educators (n = 28) with at least two years of teaching experience in undergraduate nursing education. Methods: Phase one survey data supported recruitment and theoretical sampling. Semi-structured interviews were conducted and analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. Data collection and analysis occurred iteratively, with coding supported by NVivo 14 (R). Reflexive thematic analysis generated key themes related to traumainformed educational practices. Results: This manuscript presents the third theme, Innovative Pedagogical Strategies, and its three subthemes: 1) Using Creative Learning Strategies to Grow Self-Awareness, highlighting experiential, arts-based, Indigenous pedagogies, and simulation to scaffold trauma-informed perspectives; (2) Creating Brave Spaces, emphasizing psychological safety, relational teaching, and proactive preparation for emotionally challenging content; and (3) Role Modelling Trauma-Informed Approaches to Enhance Application. A conceptual model is presented to illustrate how these intersecting trauma-informed teaching strategies promote transformational learning and support students' capacity to apply TIC principles in practice. Conclusions: Trauma-informed pedagogy offers a transformative lens for nursing education, prioritizing student well-being and advancing equity. Faculty development and structural supports are essential to prepare educators for this shift. Trauma-informed educational practices can catalyze cultural change in nursing, benefiting learners and the profession.

TI The dual burden of visibility: A qualitative exploration of the
   experiences of male faculty in nursing education programs
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Men in nursing; Nursing faculty; Nursing education; Gender;
   Intersectionality; Tokenism; Qualitative research
ID GLASS ESCALATOR; MEN
AB Background: Men are persistently underrepresented in nursing academia, holding fewer than 8% of full-time faculty positions, yet their experiences remain under-studied and are often treated as uniform. Existing work relies largely on small single-institution samples and rarely examines how sexual orientation, race, gender modality, and age shape these experiences. Objectives: To explore the lived experiences of male faculty teaching in accredited nursing programs, and to examine how intersecting identities shape their sense of belonging, professional treatment, and intent to remain in academia. Design: A qualitative descriptive study using an anonymous online survey with open-ended prompts. Setting and participants: Fifty male nursing faculty members in the United States, spanning the ranks of instructor through full professor, recruited through professional listservs, social media, a professional association for men in nursing, and snowball sampling. Methods: Twelve open-ended prompts elicited narrative responses, which were analyzed using Braun and Clarke's six-phase reflexive thematic analysis. A reflexive journal and an explicit positionality stance supported analytic rigor. Results: Six interrelated themes were generated: (1) a "welcome imposter" experience of simultaneous inclusion and exclusion; (2) a paradox of privilege and penalty, in which gendered advantage coexisted with resentment and attribution bias; (3) behavioral vigilance and communication adaptation, including self-censorship and heightened caution around physical boundaries; (4) role modeling experienced as both purpose and burden; (5) intersecting identities that compounded or buffered experience, including a notable pattern among gay faculty; and (6) structural barriers to retention, chiefly inadequate compensation and absent mentorship. Conclusions: Male nursing faculty occupy a paradoxical insider/outsider position in which privilege and penalty coexist and vary sharply across intersecting identities. Improving recruitment and retention requires more than increasing headcount; it requires structured mentorship, competitive compensation, recognition of invisible service, and intersectionally informed, inclusive department cultures.

TI Implementation and Evaluation of a Biochemistry Research Skills CURE for
   First-Year R1 University Students
SO BIOCHEMISTRY AND MOLECULAR BIOLOGY EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE course-based undergraduate research experiences; entering research
   learning assessment; first-year experience; instruction strategies
ID EXPERIENCES
AB Course-based undergraduate research experiences (CUREs) broaden access to authentic research opportunities by reducing structural and logistical barriers to student participation. Participation in CUREs during the first year of undergraduate study is associated with improved retention in STEM majors, academic success, and measurable gains in skills like scientific reasoning and data analysis. These gains are increasingly recognized as essential career-ready skills that align with national workforce development goals in the life sciences. Despite these benefits, few CUREs focus on and have been evaluated for first-year biochemistry students. Few curricula provide modular, adaptable frameworks designed for integration into existing courses without disrupting course structure or student workload. Using established and nationally utilized assessments and student reflections, we developed a CURE for first-year biochemistry undergraduates called "Introduction to Biochemical Research Skills". Students in the course evaluate protein structure-function relationships using computational biochemistry experiments, which allows scalable implementation for instructors and supports iterative hypothesis generation and testing by students. Student perspectives on practices learned while participating in the course suggest they gained practical research skills and scientific communication skills. Students also reported exposure to a variety of problem-solving techniques and indicated that engaging in protein structure-function focused research as part of the course enhanced their excitement about biochemistry. Here, we provide instructors with the resources to adopt and adapt this course and offer strategies for effective implementation. Future work will evaluate the longitudinal impact of the course on students' academic performance, conceptual understanding of protein biochemistry, and progression into independent undergraduate research experiences.

TI Chat as learning: Student-AI conversations as discipline-associated
   cognitive engagement patterns
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
LA English
DT Article
DE AI teaching assistant; Cognitive engagement; Bloom's taxonomy;
   Discipline-associated patterns; Within-person design; Learning
   analytics; ICAP framework; Generative AI in education; Higher education
ID LITERACY
AB Generative AI teaching assistants are increasingly adopted in higher education, yet debates persist over whether student-AI conversations engage students in genuine cognitive processes or function primarily as information retrieval. We propose "Chat as Learning," a measurement paradigm that treats student prompts as observable externalisations of in-progress learning cognition, complementing outcome-based assessment with a process-level signal aggregable at population, course, and student scales. We adopt the term learning to denote the paradigm's theoretical positioning; the present study measures cognitive demand reflected in students' prompts, classified via Bloom's Taxonomy, rather than learning outcomes per se. Building on prior work establishing that approximately 62% of student-AI messages on this platform reflect higher-order cognitive demand at the aggregate level (Chang & Li, 2026), we ask whether such engagement is stable across contexts or varies with disciplinary demands within the same individual. Drawing on data from the Uedu AI teaching assistant platform (https://uedu.tw), a multi-institutional deployment spanning four universities, we analysed over 60,000 student messages from 116 courses across two academic semesters using an automated Bloom's Taxonomy classification pipeline. The classifier was validated against two trained human raters on a 300-message stratified sample, giving binary higher-order vs. lower-order LLM-human Cohen's kappa = .426-.606 at the individual level and kappa = .753 under bestpair consensus (full 6 & times; 6 confusion matrix in Table 1). Our within-person, cross-discipline design-in which the same students were tracked across courses in different disciplines-revealed discipline-associated Bloom-level prompt profiles: STEM courses elicited Apply-prevalent prompts (20.8%), Language courses showed Understandprevalent patterns (31.7%), and Social Science courses were Create-prevalent (33.8%); patterns in Humanities courses are reported descriptively but should be interpreted with caution given the small course base (3 courses across two semesters). Paired within-person comparisons indicated that the same students produced significantly higher proportions of higher-order prompts in Social Science courses than in STEM courses (pooled n = 16, p < .001), with the same direction of effect observed in two semester-specific samples. A mixed-effects logistic regression with crossed random intercepts confirmed these contrasts and showed that course-level variation in higher-order engagement substantially exceeds student-level variation. These results are consistent with the view that student-AI conversations reflect discipline-associated cognitive engagement rather than fixed individual interaction styles, and they suggest that AI teaching assistants may benefit from being designed and evaluated with disciplinary context in min

TI Learning paths and patterns in learning design: Insights from 500+
   courses
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION OPEN
LA English
DT Article
DE Learning design; Learning analytics; Learning paths; Learning patterns;
   Markov chain; Pattern mining
AB Learning design (LD) has a prominent role in ensuring the quality of teaching and learning. It should be based on student-centered approaches and intended learning outcomes, which are constructively aligned with teaching and learning activities (TLAs) and assessment. To support overarching change management and mutual learning related to the pedagogically sound and feasible design of courses, we investigated practices in LD. We used the data on the LDs of 554 courses developed in an innovative and free-to-use LD tool, which has already been used in more than 3,000 courses in total. We used probabilistic models and machine learning (Markov chain, pattern mining) to examine around 29,000 TLAs belonging to the selected courses, to establish some basic patterns related to LD. First, we examined how LD elements correlate and how learning outcome levels (according to Bloom's taxonomy) relate to other features of LD. Second, we recognized patterns in the design of units of teaching and learning (which consist of TLAs), including the common composition in terms of learning types (Acquisition, Discussion, Investigation, Practice, Production, Assessment).

TI The incidence of quality assurance processes on dropout and degree
   completion. The case of economics programmes in Colombia
SO QUALITY IN HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Higher education, before-after comparison; accreditation; retention;
   graduation
ID HIGHER-EDUCATION; IMPACT
AB Education is both an opportunity and a challenge in developing countries to mitigate inequality and improve societal welfare. Quality assurance systems are essential in enhancing the opportunities for the most socially vulnerable populations to receive a quality education. This article uses a before-after comparison to evaluate the impact of external accreditation on Colombian programmes' student permanence. The results show that programme quality accreditation reduced the likelihood of dropout but did not affect graduation during students' educational trajectories. The study also demonstrates that quality assurance impacted the retention of students with more recognised risk factors for attrition, such as women and students from lower socioeconomic and academic backgrounds. The quality assurance policies underscore the importance of levelling the educational field for society. Still, these quality systems must seek ways to enhance student retention and degree attainment.

TI Using the Identify, Instruct, Incorporate (3-I) Framework to Teach
   Graphical Literacy Skills
SO READING TEACHER
LA English
DT Article
DE children's magazines; graphical literacy; graphics; informational text;
   visual literacy
ID VISUAL LITERACY; TEXT; COMPREHENSION
AB Graphical literacy, the ability to read, interpret, and create graphics, is essential for whole-text comprehension, especially when reading informational texts, including children's magazines. Our research examined the graphics (n = 416) in a popular children's magazine, Scholastic News (N = 30), for graphic category, type, function, and connection to text. Our findings showed that most graphics are representational photographs and general images that connect easily to the main text. Some graphics were more complex and may require explicit instruction. We also found an increase in infographics, both those associated with an article and those as the main article. Based on our findings, we propose the 3-I framework (Identify, Instruct, Incorporate) to guide teachers' graphical literacy instruction.

   from two Australian primary teachers participating in a 10-week Bush
   School program
SO AUSTRALIAN EDUCATIONAL RESEARCHER
LA English
DT Article
DE Teacher wellbeing; Nature play; Professional development; Outdoor
   learning; Case study
ID CLASSROOM; OUTDOOR
AB This study originated as an investigation into the impact of a 10-week nature play intervention on Year One students' wellbeing, school engagement, sense of belonging, and academic performance. While positive student outcomes were anticipated, the findings also revealed unexpected effects on the two participating teachers. Using a qualitative case study approach, teachers' lived experiences were explored through interviews, teacher journals, and researcher observations. Data were interpreted using reflexive thematic analysis to capture contextually grounded insights. Findings revealed strengthened teacher-student relationships, reduced behavioural management challenges, and a shift in teachers' understanding of engagement. Teachers also reported emotional renewal and professional reflection; outcomes conceptually linked to teacher wellbeing, job satisfaction and retention. As a small case study at a single site, these findings provide preliminary insights into the professional experiences of teachers implementing nature play and suggest that such approaches may have important implications for teacher wellbeing, job satisfaction, and professional engagement.

TI The Impact of a Multi-Source "3+1" Feedback Model on Formative
   Assessment and Student Development in Higher Education: A Case Study in
   Undergraduate Biochemistry
SO BIOCHEMISTRY AND MOLECULAR BIOLOGY EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE biochemistry; effective feedback; formative assessment; student-centered
   learning
AB Formative assessment and feedback are widely acknowledged as crucial for effective learning, yet their systematic application in discipline-specific contexts remains insufficient. This study introduces a structured "3 + 1" feedback model-combining teacher, teaching assistant (TA), peer, and exemplar-based feedback-to address recurring challenges in undergraduate biochemistry group assignments, such as weak rigor, limited teamwork, and ineffective presentation skills. Implemented across three modules (preparation, revision, and reflection), the model aims to enhance disciplinary knowledge, scientific communication, and collaborative competence. The model was implemented in the undergraduate biochemistry course in 2023 and 2024. Data sources included structured questionnaires and reflective essays collected in 2023 and 2024, together with longitudinal academic performance records from 2020 to 2024. Student surveys indicated high recognition of the model's effectiveness, with over 90% reporting improvements in PowerPoint content, design, and script writing. Thematic analysis of reflections revealed stronger task division, accountability, and group satisfaction. Performance data showed reduced failure rates (from 4.3% to 2.7%) and paired-sample tests confirmed significant draft-to-revision gains. Overall, the "3 + 1" model provides an effective, multi-source framework that improves assignment quality and fosters transferable academic and collaborative skills, offering practical insights for feedback-rich pedagogy in higher education.

TI Advancing Wetland Protection in a Province Prioritizing Growth
SO CASE STUDIES IN THE ENVIRONMENT
LA English
DT Article
DE wetland conservation; natural infrastructure; land-use planning;
   municipal finance; environmental governance
AB Wetlands provide critical hydrological functions that reduce flood risk, yet their protection remains uneven in jurisdictions undergoing rapid urban expansion. This case examines the strategic dilemma facing Ontario Nature, an environmental non-governmental organization, as it seeks to secure measurable wetland protection outcomes within a policy environment that prioritizes housing supply. Drawing on the institutional, fiscal, and regulatory context of land-use planning in Ontario, the case demonstrates how cumulative wetland loss can arise through individually compliant decisions shaped by fragmented governance, administrative discretion, and misaligned municipal incentives. The analysis focuses on four strategic pathways: provincial policy reform, targeted municipal intervention, strategic litigation, and fiscal reframing through natural infrastructure valuation. The case requires a defensible recommendation that balances ecological effectiveness, political feasibility, and organizational capacity, and enables readers to evaluate environmental governance strategies and determine where intervention is most likely to influence cumulative flood risk in urbanizing regions, while offering insights applicable to other jurisdictions facing similar tensions between environmental protection and growth-oriented policy frameworks.

TI Sustainability Challenges and Opportunities in a University Police
   Fleet: A Case Study of Idling, Emissions, and Electrification Potential
SO CASE STUDIES IN THE ENVIRONMENT
LA English
DT Article
DE fleet sustainability; vehicle idling; electric vehicles; public safety
   fleets; campus sustainability; telematics; environmental governance
AB This case study examines fleet sustainability challenges within the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley Police Department, a multicampus public safety agency operating aging gasoline vehicles central to daily patrol and administrative functions. Rising maintenance costs, increased vehicle downtime, and extensive idling created both operational strain and avoidable environmental impacts. Aging internal-combustion vehicles contributed to elevated emissions and fuel consumption, particularly under high-heat conditions and equipment demands typical of campus policing. Telematics monitoring indicated that approximately 48% of total engine-on time consisted of idling, highlighting a substantial source of avoidable fuel use and emissions. The study employed a qualitative case study design that triangulated multiyear maintenance records (FY2019-FY2024), telematics data from a 56-day observation period across eight vehicles, and semi-structured interviews with sworn, administrative, and technical personnel. Findings revealed that aging vehicles exhibited disproportionate repair frequency, increased emissions potential, and extended downtime, while idling emerged as a major driver of inefficiency. Electrification was feasible for administrative roles but remains constrained for patrol operations due to range limitations, charging infrastructure requirements, and duty-cycle demands. Governance gaps further limited evidence-based sustainability planning. The case demonstrates that sustainable fleet management in public safety contexts requires alignment between operational practices, technological capabilities, and governance structures. Role-based electrification, idle-reduction initiatives, lifecycle-based replacement, and structured fleet oversight offer practical pathways for reducing emissions while maintaining operational readiness.

TI Linguistic insights into professional identify development: analyzing
   reflective writing in instructional design education
SO ETR&D-EDUCATIONAL TECHNOLOGY RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT
LA English
DT Article
DE Reflective writing; Instructional design education; Professional
   identity development; LIWC
ID SELF; LANGUAGE; INCREASE; STUDENTS
AB This study analyzes linguistic patterns in reflective writing among graduate students in an instructional design course, using the Best Possible Self (BPS) method. The BPS exercise encourages students to envision their ideal professional selves, supporting early-stage professional identity development. We used Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC) to examine psychological processes, emotional tone, social orientation, and temporal focus in students' narratives. The analysis identified three reflective profiles-Causal Reflection-focused Individualists, Goal-Driven Pragmatists, and Social Collaborators-representing different approaches to identity development within a single course context. These profiles reflect emergent reflective patterns, not generalizable learner types. To assess whether professional identity development differed by cluster, we compared pre- and post-course survey responses. Results showed that Social Collaborators demonstrated significantly greater gains in professional identity scores compared to the other groups. While these findings are based on a short-term, context-specific study and do not imply causality, they suggest that socially oriented reflection may support identity growth. By integrating linguistic and narrative analysis, the study highlights diverse student approaches to constructing a professional identity. The results emphasize the value of adapting instructional strategies to support varied reflective orientations.

TI Perceived Algorithmic Bias, Perceived AI Surveillance, Linguistic
   Identity and Willingness to Communicate in AI-Mediated Education
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE AI surveillance; AI-mediated education; algorithmic bias; linguistic
   identity; WTC
ID MODEL
AB The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into language learning environments has raised important questions about equity, identity and learner psychology in digital contexts. This study examined the relationships among perceived algorithmic bias, linguistic identity, perceived AI surveillance and willingness to communicate (WTC) among 679 Chinese EFL learners in AI-mediated language learning environments. The data were collected through a self-report questionnaire and analyzed using structural equation modelling (SEM) with SPSS version 27 and AMOS version 24. The findings revealed significant correlations among all four constructs. Perceived algorithmic bias was negatively associated with WTC confidence (beta = -0.48, p < 0.001) and positively associated with WTC avoidance (beta = 0.55, p < 0.001). Linguistic identity pressure emerged as the strongest predictor of both WTC dimensions (confidence: beta = -0.31, p < 0.001; avoidance: beta = 0.35, p < 0.001), while linguistic identity pride showed the opposite pattern. Perceived AI surveillance, including both monitoring and stress components, also significantly predicted WTC. The predictor variables collectively explained 48% of the variance in WTC confidence and 52% of the variance in WTC avoidance. The results highlight the important roles that algorithmic bias, linguistic identity and surveillance play in shaping learners' communicative behaviour in AI-mediated environments. The findings suggest that educators and technology developers should work to reduce algorithmic bias, support learners' linguistic identities, and create learning environments that minimize surveillance-related stress to enhance WTC.

TI Integrating LLM with consortium blockchain for personalized and
   verifiable online education in higher education
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL TECHNOLOGY IN HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Consortium blockchain; AI; LLM; Online education; Higher education
ID CHALLENGES
AB Online Education in Higher Education is rapidly evolving through the integration of Large Language Model (LLM)-powered intelligent systems, which enable personalized tutoring, dynamic content generation, and automated assessment. However, the widespread adoption of LLMs in education is hampered due to their inherent limitations, including susceptibility to hallucinations, insufficient domain-specific knowledge validation, and output inconsistency. These deficiencies can lead to misleading or erroneous content, potentially causing significant negative learning outcomes. A core challenge lies in ensuring that such errors are immutably logged and traceable, thereby establishing a mechanism for accountability among the entities deploying these LLM services. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a novel framework that Integrates LLM with consortium blockchain for personalized and verifiable online education. Our design features a synergistic architecture in which LLM based services provide the intelligent educational interface, while a permissioned consortium blockchain serves as a secure and tamper proof ledger. This blockchain infrastructure records critical educational transactions ranging from learning process data and academic credentials to the outputs generated by the LLMs. This integration not only secures academic credentials but also establishes a fully auditable trail, making it possible to trace responsibility for educational deficiencies caused by AI errors. Collectively, this work demonstrates a robust and accountable framework for leveraging LLMs in education, effectively mitigating the risks of AI inaccuracies through the verifiable and immutable nature of consortium blockchain.

AB This scoping literature review characterizes research on mathematical modelling in pre-service teacher education. TI Inclusion matters: Learning in collaboration with students with profound
   intellectual and multiple disabilities
SO JOURNAL OF RESEARCH IN SPECIAL EDUCATIONAL NEEDS
LA English
DT Article
DE belonging; co-occupation; inclusive education; inclusive research;
   occupational science; profound intellectual and multiple disabilities;
   vignette
ID YOUNG-PEOPLE; OCCUPATION; CHILDREN; EXPERIENCE; EDUCATION; WORDS;
   EXCLUSION; ADULTS; LIVES; VIDEO
AB Children with profound intellectual and multiple disabilities are rarely included in discussions of inclusion/inclusive education. This paper begins from the premise that their inclusion matters and that it is helpful to begin at the level of the classroom where children and teachers have some agency. The aim is to make students with profound intellectual and multiple disabilities the focus of discussion of inclusion and belonging, and to show how, by seeking to research their lived experience with them, we can shed light on matters that are important. AB This qualitative study directly engaged 46 young people (YP) with Special Educational Needs and Disabilities (SEND), aged 14-25, who were in education, to discover their experiences during the COVID-19 pandemic (2020-2022). Moving beyond the steering at a distance framework (Kickert, ), we analyse EMI development through the lens of post-socialist state-building and marketisation. Employing social process tracing (Kaas et al., ), we analysed higher education policy documents and regulations, complemented by interviews with key decision-makers to map the trajectory of English-taught programmes. Contrary to the assumption that EMI growth is driven by explicit language planning, our findings reveal a consistent pattern of policy spillover. We demonstrate that while no national policy explicitly mandated EMI, successive reforms-aimed variously at multilingual inclusion, privatisation, marketisation, Bologna harmonisation, and institutional liberalisation-inadvertently created the conditions for EMI to thrive. This study contributes to the literature by reframing EMI institutionalisation not merely as a pedagogical or linguistic goal, but as an institutionalised by-product of broader governance transformations. These findings offer significant implications for policymakers and researchers, suggesting that effective language planning requires analysing the unintended consequences of macro-level governance reforms.

TI Differential affordances in gamified learning environments: how
   interactive features mediate calculus understanding in higher education
SO LEARNING ENVIRONMENTS RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
DE Environmental affordances; Calculus learning; Gamification; Higher
   education; Interactive learning; Learning environments
ID GAMIFICATION; OUTCOMES
AB Traditional calculus instruction often limits students to passive engagement with symbolic procedures, restricting opportunities for exploration, immediate feedback, and coordination of multiple representations. Despite its foundational role in science and engineering, calculus continues to pose significant challenges for conceptual understanding and engagement among undergraduate students. Gamified digital learning environments offer potential for redesigning learner-content interactions, yet empirical evidence on their impact within short-session, curriculum-integrated higher education contexts remains limited. This study examined how the gamified learning environment CALCULUS WHIZZ was associated with first-year engineering students' conceptual understanding of and engagement with core calculus concepts (limits, continuity, and derivatives). It specifically investigated patterns of engagement with three designed environmental affordances, immediate visual feedback, dynamic representational manipulation, and social comparison mechanisms. A mixed-methods convergent design was employed with 50 first-year engineering students across an 8-week implementation involving fifteen sessions of progressively increasing duration (15-45 min). Quantitative data included pre- and post-assessments of conceptual and procedural understanding, supplemented by platform analytics capturing 112,500 individual interactions. Qualitative data were gathered through semi-structured interviews (n = 20) and focus groups (3 groups, 4 participants per group; total N = 12) analysed via thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke, ). Conceptual understanding improved from pretest (M = 52.3%) to post-test (M = 74.1%), with a large effect size (d = 1.34) that exceeded gains in procedural fluency (d = 0.89). These gains were measured using author-developed assessments. Empirical discriminant validity between the conceptual and procedural instruments was not established. The magnitude of this difference should, therefore, be interpreted cautiously. Platform analytics revealed differential patterns of affordance utilisation: students who engaged reflectively with immediate feedback showed larger gains, while high-performing students more frequently coordinated graphical and symbolic representations. Three leader-board engagement profiles emerged (Strategic Observers, Competitive Validators, Minimally Engaged), with strategic social observation most strongly associated with positive learning outcomes. Qualitative themes highlighted reduced anxiety through iterative exploration, the value of dynamic visual metaphors for abstract concepts, and the effectiveness of short, focused sessions. The findings suggest that gamified learning environments may be associated with improvements in conceptual mathematics learning in higher education when designed around specific pedagogical affordances rather than relying primarily on motivational game mechanics. CALCULUS WHIZZ illustrates the potential for meaningful gains within short, curriculum-integrated sessions. Results provide exploratory empirical insights into how environmental affordances relate to student learning and offer tentative design principles for interactive mathematics environments.

TI Evaluating online learning environments through risk prioritisation: an
   FMEA-informed ADDIE framework
SO LEARNING ENVIRONMENTS RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
DE Failure mode and effects analysis; Instructional design; Learning
   environment evaluation; Online learning environments; Risk
   prioritisation
AB Evaluation plays a critical role in improving the quality of online learning environments. Within learning environments research, evaluation has drawn on a diverse methodological repertoire, including perception surveys, experimental interventions, multilevel modelling, and design-based research, to identify influential environmental factors. However, systematic risk prioritisation logic appears underdeveloped in the literature reviewed, even among studies employing experimental or design-based approaches. To address this limitation, this study reconceptualises evaluation as a risk-prioritised diagnostic process and proposes an integrated framework. Drawing on critical incident technique data from learners, potential failure modes affecting the online learning environment were identified and analysed using an enhanced failure mode and effects analysis approach. Risk priority numbers were calculated to rank risks according to their severity, occurrence, and detectability, thereby translating learner experience into prioritised design actions. The framework was implemented iteratively within the ADDIE instructional design model to support continuous refinement. The findings indicate that the most consequential risks are not primarily technical failures but disruptions to learners' perceptions of content relevance, learning effectiveness, and overall educational value. Post-intervention analyses show notable reductions in prioritised risks, particularly those related to outcome quality and resource alignment. This study's primary contribution is methodological and practical: It provides a structured risk prioritisation protocol that links learner perception data to learning environment and instructional redesign. While it advances conceptual thinking by reframing evaluation as diagnostic prioritisation, it does not propose a new theory of learning environments. Rather, it operationalises existing constructs through an engineering-derived analytical lens.

TI Covariate Selection and School Effectiveness Measures in Value-Added
   Models: A Systematic Review
SO APPLIED MEASUREMENT IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
ID STUDENT-ACHIEVEMENT; ADMINISTRATIVE DATA; PERFORMANCE; SENSITIVITY;
   STABILITY; ACCOUNTABILITY; MATHEMATICS; ENGLAND; SES
AB The appropriate selection of covariates in value-added models (VAMs) remains a subject of considerable debate, particularly regarding its implications for the accuracy of school-effectiveness measures. This systematic review synthesizes evidence from 25 empirical studies conducted across multiple national contexts and published between 1996 and 2023. The findings suggest that incorporating relevant covariates can improve the accuracy of school-effectiveness measurement in VAMs. Specifically, students' prior achievement, particularly prior achievement in the same subject, was consistently identified as a salient covariate. At the student level, demographic characteristics and socioeconomic status were also frequently identified as relevant covariates. In contrast, evidence concerning the relevance of school-level covariates was mixed. Moreover, the contribution of covariates to school-effectiveness measurement varied across subject areas, educational stages, measurement intervals, and student population characteristics. These findings provide methodological guidance for covariate specification in VAMs and offer practical implications for educational policy and school management.

TI Analyzing circulation of texts and reciprocal profiting across
   international platforms TikTok and Webtoon
SO EDUCATIONAL MEDIA INTERNATIONAL
LA English
DT Article
DE Platform ecologies; social media; digital texts; romance; participatory
   culture
AB Drawing from frameworks of participatory cultures and platform ecologies, this project explores two communities on digital platforms for media consumption, examining ways profit is connected to the promotion of the popular and lucrative genre of romance for readers. Each platform selected, TikTok and Webtoon, markets to international audiences and was familiar to one of the authors, while unfamiliar to the other. Applying the walkthrough method over the course of 7 weeks, each author created a research account to study the digital platform new to them, conducting recording think-alouds and maintaining field notes. We used concepts of reciprocal profiting and enshittification to examine types of profit (ranging from direct monetary profit to attention, affective, and social capital profit), tracing shifts in hierarchical influence of the platforms and alignment with larger corporate goals. We found users profiting from their engagement with these platforms, benefitting from text recommendations that helped them to select series appealing to very specific interests or to access international communities of content creators/readers. However, platforms also monetized user desires for affective and social capital, leading to tensions such as profit-forward recommendations, the spread of controversial information lacking credible sourcing, and addictive payment structures.

TI The Role of Perceived Teacher Fairness in EFL Students' Academic
   Outcome: Mediating Effects of Achievement Emotions on Engagement and
   Resilience

DT Article
DE achievement emotions; control-value theory; EFL students; engagement;
   resilience; self-determination theory; teacher fairness
ID CONNOR-DAVIDSON RESILIENCE; JUSTICE; CHINESE; SCHOOL; SCALE
AB As two significant elements in education, resilience and engagement have been at the center of attention in the English as a Foreign Language (EFL) research, as they both influence learners' academic achievement and their psychological growth. Among different factors, teacher fairness has progressively been known as a vital interpersonal element forming students' motivational and emotional performance; however, its effect in foreign language teaching is overlooked. By integrating CVT and SDT, the study provides a more comprehensive justification of how teacher fairness shapes learners' emotional experiences and their academic outcomes in EFL learning.

   hip arthroplasty (THA); training curriculum
ID SURGICAL SKILLS; SEGMENTATION; CURRICULUM
AB Introduction: The demand for structured training in orthopaedic surgery, particularly in total hip arthroplasty (THA), is increasing. Cadaver labs provide valuable experience for surgical access and anatomical exposure; however, the availability of specimens with predefined pathological features, such as dysplastic hip anatomy, is limited and difficult to standardize. This study presents a preliminary assessment of an integrated curriculum combining cadaver-based practice and patient-specific phantom simulation for task-oriented THA training. TI Developing a student-perceived satisfaction scale for design studio
   teaching in Chinese universities
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE analytic hierarchy process (AHP); Delphi method; design education;
   grounded theory (GT); studio teaching
ID EDUCATION; VALIDATION; CRIT
AB The studio teaching model, originating from the Bauhaus in Germany, has played a central role in design education; however, a systematic framework for evaluating its effectiveness remains underdeveloped. This study aimed to develop and validate a student-perceived satisfaction scale for university design studio teaching. A mixed-methods approach was adopted. First, a bibliometric visualization analysis of 4,719 publications identified five major research directions in design studio pedagogy through keyword clustering and co-occurrence analysis, providing the basis for a semi-structured expert interview questionnaire. Subsequently, semi-structured interviews with five experts generated 68,870 words of verbatim transcripts, which were analyzed using Grounded Theory (GT), resulting in 245 concepts, 82 open codes, 22 axial codes, and six selective codes. Based on these findings, an initial 110-item questionnaire was developed and refined through three rounds of Delphi consultation with 11 experts, establishing a three-level evaluation framework comprising six dimensions: Operational vision, Service management, Teaching model, Environment and atmosphere, Assessment system, and School-enterprise cooperation mechanism. The second-level indicators were then transformed into a student-perceived satisfaction scale and validated using reliability analysis and Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA). Finally, the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) was employed with 10 experts to determine the weights of the evaluation indicators. A total of 253 valid questionnaires were collected from studio students. The developed scale demonstrated excellent psychometric properties, with a Cronbach's alpha of 0.962, a KMO value of 0.953, and a significant Bartlett's test of sphericity (p < 0.001). The AHP results further established a hierarchically weighted evaluation framework for assessing design studio teaching. The proposed scale provides a theoretically grounded and empirically validated framework for evaluating university design studio teaching. It offers practical guidance for improving teaching quality, supporting evidence-based educational management, and facilitating the sustainable development of design studio education.

DE Belbin's team role model; IT education; IT students' professional
   training; project-based learning (PjBL); teamwork skills
ID VALIDATION
AB Despite the widespread use of Project-Based Learning (PjBL) in higher education, its role in developing teamwork skills among IT students remains insufficiently explored. This study evaluates the effectiveness of PjBL in a Web Technologies course and identifies the pedagogical conditions that promote teamwork competence. The study involved 93 students of the Information Systems educational program, who were divided into experimental (EG) and control groups (CG). For EG, the training was conducted within the framework of PjBL, a team project was carried out, while CG was trained using traditional methods. The project assignments were developed in collaboration with IT industry professionals and were designed to simulate authentic real-world professional tasks. Project teams were formed based on Belbin's team role model. Teamwork skills were assessed using Stephenson's Q-sort methodology, while academic performance was evaluated based on test results. Statistical analysis included Pearson's chi & sup2; test, Student's t-test, Cramer's V, and Cohen's d. The experimental group demonstrated improvements across all assessed dimensions of teamwork and a statistically significant increase in academic performance compared with the control group (p < 0.05): the mean score increased from 67.0% to 83.4% (Delta = 16.4%; p < 0.0001). The study shows that the effective implementation of PjBL in IT education depends not only on project tasks but also on balanced team and the objective assessment of teamwork skills. The findings advance the understanding of the mechanisms involved in developing teamwork competence and provide a methodological foundation for designing competency-based educational programs in IT education.

TI Unveiling the individual predictors of prestigious award-winning among
   gifted students: academic achievement, gender, and cognitive ability
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE academic achievement; cognitive ability; competitive success; gender;
   gifted students; prestigious awards; Saudi Arabia; talent development
ID INTELLIGENCE
AB Winning prestigious awards for gifted students is a highly valued goal sought by many educational institutions, as it reflects the excellence of their gifted students and the quality of their educational outcomes. Despite the importance of the issue, few studies have examined the factors that contribute to this success; this study examines the extent to which individual factors, namely academic achievement, gender, and cognitive ability, predict gifted students' likelihood of winning prestigious awards. A total of 304 officially identified gifted students ranging in the age group of 12 to 17 years attended intermediate and secondary schools in Saudi Arabia. The students reported winning prestigious local and international awards across various fields (academic, scientific, and artistic). The results suggest that academic achievement played an important role in winning local awards, while cognitive ability played a more prominent role in securing international awards. The results also show some gender-based differences. The implications of these results for the promotion of gifted students are discussed.
