TI Adaptive technology-change confidence among Saudi university faculty
   under Vision 2030: a three-wave longitudinal mixed-methods study
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE academic performance; digital transformation; faculty development;
   higher education; latent class growth analysis (LCGA); random intercept
   cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM); Saudi Arabia; self-efficacy
ID SELF-EFFICACY; USER ACCEPTANCE; METHOD VARIANCE; FIT INDEXES;
   PERFORMANCE; JOB; CONSERVATION; VALIDATION; RESOURCES; AGREEMENT
AB Purpose Saudi higher education under Vision 2030 imposes cycles of technical change shorter than typical academic tenures. This paper estimates within-person dynamics of adaptive technology-change confidence (ATCC)-a newly developed, exploratory personal resource construct (Conservation of Resources; Job Demands-Resources) requiring further validation-over 27 months, and tests whether decline is patterned by directly measured university-level substrate turnover. Design A three-wave panel of Saudi university faculty (T1 n = 431, 11 universities; T3 retention 77.7%) combined faculty self-reports, department chair ratings of academic performance (AP), and learning and development (L&D) lead reports of substrate turnover [the institutionally reported pace of major digital infrastructure change-learning management system updates, artificial intelligence tool adoptions, and platform deprecations], with 29 nested longitudinal interviews (longitudinal core n = 7). Analyses included latent growth modelling, the random-intercept cross-lagged panel model, and latent class growth analysis. Findings ATCC declined within person across the observation window (p < 0.001). Three trajectory classes emerged (stable, gradual decline, and steep decline). Within-person change in ATCC was associated with subsequent change in chair-rated AP more strongly than the reverse (directional asymmetry, p = 0.009; because the design is observational, this is interpreted as directional rather than causal evidence). Higher university-level substrate turnover was associated with steeper decline (p = 0.005), consistent with a preliminary timescale-dependency conjecture. Findings were robust across five quantitative sensitivity specifications, with qualitative-quantitative concordance support. Originality and practical implications The paper integrates longitudinal qualitative interviews and direct substrate-turnover measurement within a multi-source mixed-methods panel, providing within-person evidence on adaptive confidence in a non-Western higher education context. Faculty development centres operating under Vision 2030 may benefit from periodic (e.g., quarterly) ATCC monitoring as an early-warning indicator, with targeted L&D outreach to the steep-decliner trajectory class. Principal limitations include reliance on an author-developed ATCC scale requiring independent psychometric replication and a level-2 sample of only 11 universities, which constrains the substrate-turnover moderation. Findings should therefore be read as preliminary and specific to the Saudi single-sector context.

TI Cognitive adaptation in the intelligence era (CAIE): a dynamical systems
   framework for education reform in the age of artificial intelligence
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE AI in education; CAIE model; cognitive theory; digital learning;
   dynamical systems; education reform; reward prediction error
ID CAPACITY
AB This paper introduces the Cognitive Adaptation in the Intelligence Era (CAIE) model, a dynamical systems framework that formalises how major technological revolutions impose cognitive adaptation pressure on human populations, and what this implies for the structural reform of education. We hypothesise that technology-driven cognitive pressure can be represented as a time-varying forcing function in an ordinary differential equation (ODE) system, and that education design-when informed by motivational neuroscience-can sustain positive cognitive adaptation even under accelerating AI pressure. The theoretical model defines a seven-dimensional cognitive-affective ability vector S(t)is an element of R7 encompassing working memory, task-switching efficiency, indexical memory, multi-agent management, metacognition, emotional intelligence, and identity stability. The evolution of S(t) is governed by an ODE integrating four forces: (1) an effective education function modulated by dopamine reward prediction error (RPE), (2) Sigmoid-shaped technology pressure calibrated against three historical revolutions (steam engine, internet, AI), (3) a three-component cognitive resistance term grounded in neuroplasticity, information-theoretic bandwidth constraints, and habitual inertia, and (4) cumulative cognitive burden from prior technological epochs. Theoretical simulation using Runge-Kutta methods yields four hypotheses: (a) traditional curricula become insufficient after the AI inflection point (similar to 2023); (b) CAIE-designed education with RPE-driven motivation maintains positive adaptation across all seven dimensions; (c) the optimal number of concurrently managed AI agents peaks at n & lowast;approximate to 3 for untrained individuals (a prediction consistent with BCG 2026 empirical data, n=1,488) and extends to 5-8 with deliberate training; (d) a critical education delay threshold tau & lowast;approximate to 1.25 years exists, beyond which remedial intervention becomes significantly less effective. We emphasise that these numerical values (n & lowast;approximate to 3, tau & lowast;approximate to 1.25 years) are illustrative outputs of a theoretically parameterised model rather than empirically established constants; they are presented as quantitative hypotheses to be tested, not as calibrated measurements. These hypotheses are theoretically aligned with evidence from 20+ peer-reviewed studies spanning ADHD epidemiology, cognitive load theory, dopamine-driven learning, and working memory research. Four prospective experiments are proposed to empirically test the model's predictions. CAIE addresses a gap in the digital education literature by providing the first mathematically formalised, computationally solvable framework that simultaneously models technology-driven cognitive pressure, curriculum design, and motivational dynamics.

TI Neither Luddite nor enthusiast: interpreting teachers' AI use in
   teaching
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE artificial intelligence; interpreting teaching; Master in Translation
   and Interpreting; survey; perceived AI threat
AB This study investigates how Chinese English interpreting teachers in China position themselves in relation to the growing presence of artificial intelligence (AI) in interpreter training. While existing research has largely focused on student attitudes, tools, and curriculum-level discussions, the perspectives of interpreting educators remain less visible, despite their role in shaping pedagogical practice and professional norms. Drawing on a survey of 156 interpreting teachers in Master of Translation and Interpreting (MTI) programs, the study examines multiple dimensions of AI orientation, including readiness (enabling conditions and AI evaluative literacy), reported use of AI-enabled tools, critical evaluation practice, perceived usefulness and future intention, profession-related concerns (threat to professional autonomy and perceived labor devaluation), and restrictive responses (restriction behavior frequency, human judgment/skill protection, and restrictive orientation toward AI integration). Descriptive results indicate above-midpoint levels of readiness and perceived usefulness/future intention, alongside moderate reported use with substantial variability. Correlational analyses show that enabling conditions are positively associated with tool use and with perceived usefulness/future intention, whereas AI evaluative literacy shows a small negative association with tool use and perceived usefulness, and no association with future intention. Reported use is strongly associated with perceived usefulness and positively associated with future intention. Profession-related concerns are also evident: restrictive orientation is strongly associated with autonomy threat and positively associated with perceived labor devaluation, and autonomy threat and labor devaluation are positively related. In a regression model including role and teaching experience, autonomy threat and labor devaluation do not show unique effects on restrictive orientation, while teaching experience is strongly associated with restrictiveness. The findings suggest that interpreting teachers' engagement with AI is not captured by adoption-related constructs alone. Alongside perceived pedagogical value, profession-related concerns and experience-linked boundary-setting shape how AI is positioned in interpreter training. The study extends technology acceptance approaches by incorporating constructs related to autonomy and labor value, and it highlights the need for AI integration strategies that address pedagogical use as well as professional implications.

AB Children and adolescents benefit in various ways when their parents are supportive of their education at home and work in healthy collaboration with schools and teachers. Yet, schools still often struggle to optimize parent engagement. In part, this may be because there is still little consensus on what it means for a parent to be engaged. Mostly, researchers and practitioners have defined parent engagement in terms of parent actions and practices. To this end, the first aim of this study was to use qualitative methods to understand how parents, teachers, and students conceptualize parent engagement and parent disaffection in child education. A thematic analysis of qualitative data yielded themes that mapped onto a proposed integrative multidimensional framework, although participants found it easiest to describe engagement and disaffection in behavioral terms. The second aim was to describe how qualitative information from focus groups informed the generation of preliminary item pools for two proposed parent-report scales: the Multidimensional Measure of Parent Engagement (MMPE) and partner Multidimensional Measure of Parent Disaffection (MMPD).

TI Pedagogical prompting rather than technical mastery: Generative AI use
   by English and English-medium instruction teachers
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE AI literacy; EMI; generative AI; pedagogical prompting; prompt
   engineering; teacher agency; quality education
AB This perspective article is grounded in professional experience and classroom observation, and its aim is to raise an issue and open it for discussion rather than to settle it. AI is often presented to teachers as a way to make educational work easier, faster, and more flexible, yet they are simultaneously confronted with a growing array of AI platforms, agents, automation systems, and technical courses. This creates a practical tension: if AI is meant to reduce teachers' workload, it is not obvious why using it well should require them to keep learning new technical systems. One source of this tension, we argue, is the weak distinction between AI literacy and prompt engineering. We take AI literacy in language education to be a broad competence concerned with how teachers, students, and institutions learn to live, work, study, and teach responsibly in a world shaped by AI, whereas prompt engineering concerns more specifically how users design, refine, evaluate, and revise prompts to guide AI tools toward useful and responsible outputs. For English and English medium instruction (EMI) teachers, we propose that this difference matters because these teachers do not need to master AI technically; they need to learn how to make it serve teaching, learning, language support, content understanding, and student participation. We refer to this teacher-facing capacity pedagogical prompting and distinguish it from both broad AI literacy and technical prompt engineering. To make the idea concrete, we offer the Pedagogical Prompting Feedback Cycle as a teacher-oriented way of translating existing instructional expertise into AI-supported practice. We present it as a tentative conceptual model rather than a validated framework: it is meant to provoke inquiry and design, and it requires empirical validation across diverse languages, disciplines, and educational settings.

TI Psychometric properties of a short version of the questionnaire on
   factors influencing degree completion among Peruvian graduate students
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE academic achievement; educational evaluation; higher education;
   psychometrics; questionnaires
ID FIT INDEXES; VALIDITY; PACKAGE; NUMBER
AB Graduate degree completion remains a major concern for higher education institutions due to its implications for academic quality, student retention, and institutional efficiency. There is a growing interest in understanding the factors associated with delayed graduation; however, evidence regarding the psychometric robustness of instruments assessing these factors in Latin American contexts is still limited. This study aimed to evaluate the internal structure and reliability of the short version of a questionnaire designed to assess factors influencing degree completion among Peruvian graduate students. A sample of 363 graduate students from a private university in Lima participated in the study. Item analysis, exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses, as well as reliability estimation, and measurement invariance procedures were conducted. The findings revealed substantial psychometric limitations, including non-normal item distributions, weak item discrimination in several indicators, and inadequate global fit for the proposed four-factor correlated model estimated via WLSMV [chi & sup2;(2,768) = 12,046, CFI = .725, TLI = .716, RMSEA = .096, SRMR = .187]. While overall reliability based on Cronbach's alpha was satisfactory, the hierarchical omega values (ranging from .41 to .68) and low AVE estimates indicated that the multidimensionality and error variance compromised the internal structural validity of the 80-item version. These findings highlight the challenges of adapting instruments related to graduate degree completion across sociocultural contexts and underscore the need for further theoretical and psychometric refinement.

AB Purpose Drawing on Social Cognitive Career Theory, this study positions blended learning not merely as a technological enhancement but as a strategic pedagogical mechanism for operationalizing sustainable development. TI AI-enhanced communicative-situational technologies for developing
   linguocultural competence in pre-service language teachers
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE artificial intelligence; communicative-situational learning;
   intercultural communication; linguocultural competence; pre-service
   language teachers
AB The increasing internationalization of higher education and the growing cultural diversity of educational environments have highlighted the need to develop linguocultural competence among future language teachers. This study aimed to design, implement, and evaluate an AI-enhanced communicative-situational model for developing linguocultural competence among pre-service language teachers. A quasi-experimental pre-test/post-test design was employed with 280 undergraduate students enrolled in a Foreign Language Teacher Education programme. Participants were assigned to an experimental group (n = 140) and a control group (n = 140). The experimental group participated in a 12-week intervention integrating communicative-situational technologies and ChatGPT-5. The control group received traditional foreign language instruction based on reading comprehension, vocabulary and grammar practice, textbook-based discussions, and teacher-centered learning activities. Linguocultural competence was assessed through a rubric-based instrument measuring Cognitive-Conceptual, Pragmatic-Communicative, and Professional Cross-Cultural Competence. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, t-tests, mixed-design ANOVA, and Pearson correlation analysis. The findings revealed significant improvements across all dimensions of linguocultural competence, with the experimental group demonstrating substantially greater gains than the control group. Significant Time & times; Group interaction effects were found for Cognitive-Conceptual Competence, F(1,278) = 40.72, p < .001, eta(2)p = .128, Pragmatic-Communicative Competence, F(1,278) = 24.86, p < .001, eta(2)p = .082, and Professional Cross-Cultural Competence, F(1,278) = 19.41, p < .001, eta(2)p = .065. Strong positive correlations were identified among all competence dimensions (r = .630-.786, p < .001). The results suggest that AI-enhanced communicative-situational technologies effectively support the development of linguocultural competence by fostering authentic intercultural communication, reflection, and professional decision-making. The proposed model offers practical implications for teacher education in multilingual and multicultural contexts.

TI Contextual Factors Influencing Teachers' Familiarity with and
   Perceptions of 4IR Technologies in Nigerian Secondary Schools
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE technology enhanced education; public-private divide; technology
   acceptance model; mixed methods; Industry 4.0
ID EDUCATION
AB Nigerian secondary schools face significant challenges integrating fourth industrial revolution (4IR) technologies. Little is known about how contextual factors influence teachers' familiarity with these technologies and their perceptions of student engagement, learning outcomes, and instructional efficiency. Using a convergent parallel mixed-methods design, this study examined those factors in public and private secondary schools across one Local Government Area within each of four Nigerian states (Imo, Rivers, Osun, and Kogi). The quantitative component surveyed 189 teachers (92 public, 97 private). The qualitative component interviewed nine teachers and conducted two focus groups with 12 teachers (six in each group). Quantitative findings showed that teachers reported moderate familiarity with most 4IR technologies (grand mean = 3.11) and positive perceptions of their influence on student engagement (grand mean = 3.64) and learning outcomes (grand mean = 3.80). Private school teachers reported significantly higher familiarity with six of seven technologies and more positive perceptions of engagement (p < 0.001) and learning outcomes (p < 0.001) than public school teachers, except for WhatsApp (p = 0.332). Qualitative thematic analysis revealed four themes explaining these differences: (1) structural and infrastructural inequities (electricity, internet, devices) shape technology engagement; (2) teachers sustain integration through personal financial sacrifice and informal peer support; (3) professional development is perceived as contextually disconnected; and (4) technological engagement reflects interactions between generational confidence, pedagogical identity, and school culture. The joint display of quantitative and qualitative findings shows convergence on the conclusion that infrastructure, not teacher attitude, is the main barrier to 4IR adoption. Policymakers should prioritise investment in electricity, internet, and devices over blaming teachers.

TI How consistent is the algorithm? Examining the intra- and inter-rater
   reliability of LLM-based writing assessment
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE AI assessment; analytic rubrics; human assessment; inter-rater
   reliability; intra-rater reliability; LLM
ID WEIGHTED KAPPA; AGREEMENT; COEFFICIENT
AB Unlike constrained constructed-response assessments, the reliability of essay-based assessments has long been debated in language education research. Recently, AI-particularly large language models-has been proposed as a tool to enhance scoring reliability. This study examines the reliability of LLM-based scoring in writing assessment. OpenAI's ChatGPT assessed 192 essays written by EFL learners using a criterion-based analytic rubric covering task achievement, grammatical range and accuracy, lexical resources, organization, and mechanics. Scoring was replicated after three weeks under similar conditions. The two rounds were compared to assess intra-rater reliability and then contrasted with human ratings to assess inter-rater reliability. Results indicated high intra-rater reliability, particularly for task achievement and organization. Lower consistency was observed for mechanics and grammatical accuracy, suggesting a need for clearer criteria or further model training. Human-AI comparisons showed slight to fair exact agreement (Cohen's kappa) and moderate agreement when accounting for the degree of disagreement.

TI Exploring Pre-Service Teachers' Professional Learning Process in Iran
   Through a CBAM-Based Approach
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE Concerns-Based Adoption Model (CBAM); teacher identity; change; teacher
   professional development; pre-service stage
AB This study examined pre-service elementary school teachers' perceptions of a semester-long professional learning programme in Iran, focusing on perceived shifts in their concerns, drawing on the Concerns-Based Adoption Model (CBAM) as the theoretical framework. Adopting a CBAM-informed, directed (deductive-inductive) qualitative content analysis of the written reflections of 30 pre-service teachers across two provinces, the study traced perceived shifts in participants' concerns throughout their professional learning journey. Consistent with CBAM's developmental stages, the analysis of participants' reflections suggested a perceived transition from self-focused concerns to concerns about teaching effectiveness. This shift-from self-oriented concerns toward task- and effectiveness-oriented concerns-aligns with the model's prediction that individuals move through self, task, and effectiveness concerns as they adopt new practices. The findings also suggest that this progression is associated with the development of professional identity, personal beliefs, and the capacity for lifelong learning. Although the training process placed many participants in unfamiliar contexts, it provided valuable experiences that encouraged active engagement in curriculum design. Despite facing uncertainty and challenges, participants developed the psychological readiness to continue their professional journey. Because the study is based on self-reported written reflections rather than classroom observation, teaching performance, or pupil outcomes, the findings are presented as perceived shifts in pre-service teachers' reflections, concerns, and professional readiness, rather than as demonstrated impact on attitudes, practices, or teaching outcomes. Overall, these findings underscore the relevance of CBAM for understanding and informing the design of professional development for pre-service teachers.

TI Exploring Professional Playfulness: ECEC Principals' Perspectives on
   Teacher Competence in Early Childhood Education
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE ECEC principals' experiences; ECEC teacher education; professional
   playfulness; Swedish early childhood education and care (ECEC)
ID GUIDED PLAY; PEDAGOGY
AB Drawing on interviews with ten preschool principals who recruit, mentor, and evaluate preschool teachers, this study examines how playfulness is conceptualized as a professional competence within early childhood education and care (ECEC) practice. In Swedish ECEC, play and teaching are conceptualized as intertwined processes, and co-play is positioned as a central pedagogical approach that requires both personal dispositions and ongoing professional development. The study highlights the importance of integrating playfulness into ECEC teacher education in order to strengthen future teachers' capacity to co-play with children and engage in play-based teaching practices on children's terms. The findings also suggest that professional playfulness emerges as a multifaceted and context-dependent competence, shaped by institutional conditions as well as individual orientations towards play and teaching. By foregrounding leadership perspectives, the study contributes to ongoing discussions on the role of play in ECEC and emphasizes the need for deliberate efforts to support the development of professional playfulness in both practice and teacher education.

TI From Gradual Release of Responsibility to Gradual Release of Technology:
   A Case for the Staged Use of AI in Formal Education
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE gradual release of AI technology; generative artificial intelligence;
   cognitive offloading; learning versus performance; metacognition;
   expertise development; instructional scaffolding
ID INSTRUCTION; COMPETENCE
AB Debate over the role of generative artificial intelligence in formal education is marked by sharply divergent claims about its effects on student learning. Much of this disagreement reflects a failure to distinguish AI-supported performance from durable learning. This conceptual article aims to address a central gap in the literature by focusing on when and how students should be guided to rely on AI. It introduces the Gradual Release of AI Technology (GRAIT) model, extending Pearson and Gallagher's gradual release of responsibility to the staged use of generative AI technologies in K-12 education. The model distinguishes gradual release of responsibility, which concerns who performs the cognitive work, from gradual release of AI technology, which concerns when and how that work may be scaffolded, augmented, or offloaded to AI. Three phases are proposed: independent cognition, where foundational knowledge and skills are developed without AI; shared cognition, where AI is introduced through teacher-guided interaction; and offloaded and reallocated cognition, where learners strategically delegate and reallocate aspects of thinking while retaining evaluative judgement. Progression depends on demonstrated knowledge, skill proficiency, epistemic understanding, and AI literacy. The central question thus addresses when and how AI use should be staged according to learner readiness.

TI Interrogating Learner Progression Policy in South African Schools
   Through Teachers' Perspectives
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE learner progression; inclusive education; policy enactment; teacher
   agency; differentiated instruction; South Africa
AB Learner progression policy in South Africa is intended to promote inclusive education by reducing grade repetition and preventing learner dropout, yet its implementation remains contested, particularly in under-resourced schooling contexts. Drawing on teacher agency and socio-ecological theories, this study explored teachers' perceptions and experiences of learner progression policy in five underperforming secondary schools in Limpopo Province. A qualitative interpretivist design was employed, with data generated through open-ended questionnaires from eleven purposively selected teachers and analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. The findings reveal that, while teachers support progression as a mechanism for promoting access and reducing exclusion, they express significant concern about learners advancing without foundational knowledge, contributing to cumulative learning deficits. Teachers employ strategies such as differentiated instruction and extra lessons, yet these efforts are constrained by large class sizes, limited time, and inadequate resources. The study highlights the central role of teacher experience and professional judgment in mediating policy implementation, alongside the influence of socio-economic factors on learner outcomes. The study concludes that learner progression requires substantially stronger support structures, including structured academic support, robust monitoring systems, and improved alignment between policy intentions and classroom realities, to be effective. By foregrounding teachers' perspectives from under-resourced contexts, the study contributes to ongoing debates about the persistent tension between inclusion and academic quality, offering implications for strengthening inclusive education in South Africa and similar contexts.
